His blast has already removed Compound V abilities from other Supes and nearly did the same to Homelander. Releasing him creates another superhuman crisis, so the military would never treat him like an ordinary weapon. He would be one dangerous asset aimed at another, surrounded by plans for what happens if he refuses to cooperate.

The depowering evidence offers another direction because it shows that Compound V abilities can be removed or suppressed. Recreating that effect would be a difficult long-term research route, not an inevitable military breakthrough. A stronger possibility would be gaining access to an existing depowering asset, or to research from the Boys if they independently develop it in this altered timeline. Either route would let planners focus on weakening Homelander instead of trying to overpower his skin directly.

That possibility also gives commanders a reason to delay the most destructive option. If they ever obtain a method that can weaken Homelander for several seconds, they would no longer need a weapon that kills him through full durability. The operation could instead become a sequence in which one system attacks his powers and another attacks the human body underneath. The completed series proves how vulnerable he becomes after full depowering, but it does not guarantee the military can reproduce that result here.

The people running that operation would only get one clean surprise. If the effect reaches Homelander and fails to hold him, he learns exactly what the government has built and begins hunting everyone connected to it. That pressure would force commanders to wait for the strongest opportunity instead of testing the plan early.

If the military ever gains access to a power-removing effect, the first blast may only weaken him for a short time or fail to reproduce the complete depowering seen later in the series. Homelander could recover, escape, or kill everyone nearby before the next attack arrives. Normal weapons would need to be ready the moment his durability actually disappears. Every part of the plan would have to work during whatever window the effect creates.

If the question only asks whether he can remain alive, his best answer may be flight beyond the campaign's immediate reach. He could cross borders, hide among states unwilling to cooperate, or choose remote terrain where surveillance coverage is thinner. International movement creates diplomatic complications, and another country might shelter him as leverage. It also expands the intelligence partnership hunting him once governments recognize that he can overthrow their leadership too.

Permanent concealment clashes with his personality and his practical needs. He can survive without a salary, but he wants an audience and reacts badly when ignored. Any government protecting him would fear that his moods could turn their capital into a hostage. Over years, defectors, intercepted communications, and visible incidents would expose whatever sanctuary he builds.

His age gives him another problem because this hunt could last for years. The military can train new pilots, replace commanders, improve its sensors, and keep studying Compound V after the people who started the mission retire. Homelander would still have one body and the same emotional weaknesses. Even if he wins every early fight, time gives the government more chances to learn from each failure.

Some people may argue that Homelander could escape into space, but the show never proves he can survive there for long. Flight does not give him air or teach him how to travel beyond Earth. Giving him those extra powers would ignore the same evidence rules used for the military. We should treat him as an extremely fast flyer who still needs to remain near the planet.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: The United States military has weapons that could plausibly kill Homelander, but the completed series never gives us a direct test at the top end. A close nuclear blast is far beyond anything he has survived on screen, while intense radiation has been able to weaken him and specialized power-removing attacks can shut down Compound V. The largest normal bombs may also hurt or kill him, but canon never shows the exact amount of force his body can take. Creating the circumstances for a kill would be much harder than owning the weapon. Homelander's size, speed, low altitude mobility, senses, and willingness to use cities as cover make continuous tracking and clean targeting difficult. Early engagements would favor him, and any force that bunches up for a traditional battle would be punished. He could destroy bases, aircraft, units, and political figures while remaining unable to eliminate the national system behind them.

Over the long term, repeated public attacks would give the government more opportunities to adapt. Every engagement supplies data, the response can disperse, Vought's research becomes a military asset, and Homelander's emotional needs create predictable targets. That does not guarantee scientists eventually recreate a depowering weapon or that any single trap succeeds. It means Homelander keeps giving a much larger system chances to find a method that works.

Homelander could potentially survive indefinitely if he abandoned the country, stopped chasing attention, moved unpredictably, and treated every sighting as a threat. If he keeps trying to rule, punish enemies, or fight publicly, he repeatedly exposes himself to increasingly dangerous tracking, traps, heavy weapons, and possible anti-V research. The problem for Homelander is that the version we see has never shown the patience or emotional control required to live quietly forever.

So do you think Homelander would disappear before the military found a reliable way to depower him, or would his ego pull him into the trap that finally kills him? Let me know what you think, and tell me which fictional character should face the full US military next.

scripts.title: Could Humanity Stop A Viltrumite Invasion

sections.name: INTRO
paras: If the Viltrumite Empire came to our Earth, humanity wouldn’t have superheroes or alien weapons to fall back on. We'd have modern militaries, nuclear weapons, satellites, scientists, and billions of people facing enemies strong enough to tear through conventional forces almost effortlessly.

The first battles would go badly, but every failed attack would still teach us something. Survival would depend on whether humanity could identify a real weakness, build a usable countermeasure, and deploy it before the Viltrumites started destroying the governments, communications, and military systems organizing the resistance.
So this war wouldn’t be about matching them physically. It would be about whether humanity could learn fast enough to stay alive.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: The invasion would begin with only 3 Viltrumites because Earth isn’t important enough to justify throwing their entire surviving population at one planet. After the Scourge Virus, the Empire had fewer than 50 Viltrumites left, which forced them to conquer worlds with very small numbers of soldiers. One Viltrumite taking responsibility for an entire planet was already part of how the Empire operated.

Earth would be valuable for a different reason. Its biggest prize would be billions of humans biologically close enough to Viltrumites to make the population unusually valuable to an Empire devastated by the Scourge Virus. Our advanced industry, nuclear power, and global communications would make the planet even more useful instead of something to simply destroy. Their goal would be surrender. The 3 invaders would divide the planet into regions, force the largest governments to submit, and leave most infrastructure intact so they could rule what remained.

The first one could descend outside Washington while the other 2 appear near Beijing and Moscow within minutes of each other. That immediately tells every major government that this isn’t a single unknown being. Each Viltrumite delivers roughly the same message. Earth is being absorbed into the Viltrum Empire, national governments can continue handling local affairs if they cooperate, and organized military resistance will be answered with force.

Nobody would know what they are yet. Satellites might record objects entering the atmosphere without any visible spacecraft, and military radar could pick up strange tracks once they slow down enough to remain within sensor coverage, but the people reviewing those tracks wouldn't have a category for a human sized object flying under its own power. The first assumption would probably involve unknown aircraft, drones, or some kind of technology being hidden on the body.

The Viltrumites could use that hesitation. Their opening demand gives humanity a deadline of several hours instead of starting the invasion immediately, which sounds generous until governments realize what they are doing. The Viltrumites are giving every country time to identify its military leadership, move aircraft, activate command posts, and reveal which facilities become important during a crisis.

When the deadline passes, the Viltrumite outside Washington could disappear from the ground, reach a nearby military airfield before anyone there understands where he went, and destroy aircraft sitting on the runway while leaving most civilian infrastructure around it untouched. Another could do the same to a Chinese air base. The 3rd could attack a Russian strategic facility without touching the weapons stored there, making the point that he reached them before they could be used.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: The first serious military engagement would probably happen because one government decides it needs to know whether the Viltrumites can be hurt before agreeing to surrender. That test wouldn't begin with a nuclear weapon. It would begin with weapons that can be launched quickly, controlled more easily, and used without destroying a major city.

A Viltrumite moving away from a populated area gives that opportunity. Fighters could attack from multiple directions while surface based missiles are launched from farther away, forcing the target to deal with several threats instead of one. The first missiles may hit simply because the Viltrumite has no reason to avoid them. An experienced Viltrumite has survived far worse than ordinary human weapons, and allowing a missile to explode against his body would teach humanity exactly the lesson he wants it to learn.

The blast disappears and he’s still flying. After that, the engagement becomes horrifyingly short. A fighter can’t dogfight an opponent who can change direction without wings, survive forces that would destroy an aircraft, and physically tear through the airframe once he gets close. The Viltrumite wouldn’t need energy weapons or missiles of his own. He could break an aircraft by striking it, change direction, and reach the next one before pilots can reorganize around what just happened.

The first useful result might come from what the Viltrumite doesn’t do. Missiles produce pressure, fragmentation, heat, and acceleration at the same time. If none of them visibly damage him, researchers can start eliminating entire families of conventional weapons instead of spending days repeating tests that soldiers already died performing.

Naval weapons would create another source of information if the Viltrumites begin removing forces that could threaten their future control of the planet. A carrier group is too large to hide and too valuable to ignore. A Viltrumite could descend onto the flight deck, smash through key sections of the ship, destroy aircraft and command systems, then leave before escorts can bring enough weapons onto him.

That would be when nuclear weapons enter the discussion. Every nuclear power capable of participating would face the same problem. A warhead powerful enough to justify the attempt also creates a blast area too dangerous to use casually, while the target can simply leave if he sees the delivery system coming.

A ballistic missile would be especially poor against one moving person. The weapon is designed to strike a predicted location, and a Viltrumite does not need to remain there. Even a nuclear armed aircraft or cruise missile has to get close enough before the target decides to move. Humanity may possess destructive energy capable of testing their upper durability, yet delivering it becomes the harder problem.

That changes the military question. Governments stop asking which existing weapon has the biggest explosion and start asking how they can force a Viltrumite to remain in one place long enough for any serious weapon to matter.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: The Viltrumites would understand that Earth hasn’t surrendered even after losing the first engagements, so their next move would be aimed at organization rather than armies. They've conquered planets before. They wouldn’t need to destroy every soldier if they can make those soldiers stop receiving orders.

The 3 invaders could begin hitting military command centers, satellite ground stations, major intelligence facilities, and communication infrastructure across different countries. They don’t need to know where every bunker is on the first day. Public maps, visible bases, captured personnel, government broadcasts, and simple observation give them enough targets to start breaking the obvious parts of the system.

That creates a problem for the Viltrumites too. Earth’s command structure is much harder to erase than a single capital. The United States alone has layers of military command, state governments, continuity plans, independent communications, submarines, overseas forces, and thousands of officials who can keep parts of the country functioning. China, Russia, India, European states, and dozens of other countries have their own systems. Killing a president or destroying one headquarters would cause chaos, but it wouldn't switch the planet off.

The invasion would probably create global cooperation faster than almost any event in human history, though that cooperation would be messy. Governments would still hide information from one another at first. Nobody wants to hand over nuclear command procedures, intelligence sources, or classified weapons data simply because everyone now shares an enemy.

The most important discovery could come from hearing rather than damage. Viltrumites rely on a highly sensitive inner ear and equilibrium system for flight, and certain specific frequencies can disrupt that balance, causing intense pain and interfering with their ability to fly. It isn’t a general weakness to loud noises, which means humanity couldn't simply point stadium speakers at one and expect him to collapse.

The first clue could emerge from recordings of one Viltrumite attacking a hardened industrial complex. During the fight, several machines, alarms, turbines, and damaged electrical systems are operating at once. Analysts going through the footage notice that the Viltrumite briefly loses control in one room despite ignoring explosions that were far more powerful.

That would be easy to dismiss as random movement until another team reconstructs the audio from surviving equipment. They isolate several frequencies present during the exact second his flight changes and realize one source produced a narrow tone outside the range most people nearby would have noticed clearly.

Nobody would call it a weakness yet. Scientists would only have a correlation from a few seconds of chaotic footage. What makes it worth testing is a second independent recording from another attack, where a different Viltrumite briefly loses control while the same narrow frequency is present. That still wouldn't prove causation, but repeating the same reaction around the same signal would be enough to justify turning the accident into a controlled test without letting the Viltrumites realize what humanity suspects.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Humanity’s best chance to test the frequency would be a location the invaders are already likely to attack. Building a giant new sonic weapon would advertise the plan and take too long. Existing underground military facilities give humans a better option because they can hide equipment inside narrow spaces where sound can be concentrated at short range.

One command site could deliberately remain active after neighboring facilities have gone dark. Radio traffic, vehicle movement, and visible personnel make it look like a surviving regional headquarters that governments failed to evacuate. Most of the important staff would already be gone. What remains inside would be remote sensors, automated doors, conventional explosives, and acoustic equipment modified to sweep through the frequency range scientists want to test.

The trap only works if a Viltrumite decides the site is worth entering instead of punching through the entire mountain. That means humanity would need to give him a reason. False intelligence traffic could suggest that senior military officials are coordinating nuclear forces from inside. If the invader believes killing the people there saves him from hunting several separate targets later, walking inside becomes the efficient choice.

The first frequencies do nothing. Cameras record him moving through the tunnel while equipment cycles upward and downward through the planned range. He tears through a security door, keeps walking, and reaches the section where the supposed command room should be.

He grabs the wall, loses his balance, and drops instead of hovering. The reaction lasts only seconds because the equipment around him isn’t powerful enough to keep an experienced Viltrumite incapacitated once he understands he is being attacked. He destroys the emitters, tears through the facility, and escapes before the humans watching remotely can try anything else.

Humanity still gets what it needed. The response occurred inside a narrow frequency range and stopped when the equipment was destroyed. Researchers can compare every sensor in the tunnel and identify which signal was active when his balance failed.
The Viltrumite also gets info. Humans just found a way to hurt him.

That prevents the discovery from becoming an easy victory. The other 2 Viltrumites would hear about the trap almost immediately, and none of them would willingly enter another enclosed military site afterward. They would attack from outside, destroy buildings before approaching, and treat unfamiliar electronic or acoustic equipment as a possible weapon.

The frequency itself also has practical limits. Producing the right sound in a bunker from a few meters away is completely different from hitting a target flying across a city. High frequency sound loses energy through air, buildings interfere with it, and any emitter powerful enough to matter still needs to point that energy at a Viltrumite who can cross the distance and destroy it. Humanity has discovered a real weakness and gained almost no ability to use it.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: By this point the war would change because both sides finally understand what the other one is dangerous at. Humanity knows direct combat is nearly useless. The Viltrumites know humans can discover weaknesses quickly enough that leaving our scientific network intact is becoming a risk.

The invaders would start hunting the people behind the acoustic test. Facilities connected to the experiment could be destroyed within hours, which means governments can’t keep the project concentrated in one secret laboratory. The safest response would be the opposite. Every recording, sensor log, frequency measurement, engineering note, and partial design gets copied to research teams across multiple countries before the Viltrumites can erase it.

That makes the knowledge much harder to kill than the scientists who found it. A Viltrumite can destroy a laboratory in seconds, but the same data could already exist on military networks in Europe, isolated servers in North America, research centers in Asia, and offline drives being physically moved between facilities. Humanity’s numbers finally begin helping in a way that tanks and aircraft never could.

The next problem is delivery. A large speaker array sitting on the ground gives a Viltrumite an obvious target. Aircraft can move the equipment, but no pilot can count on surviving long enough to keep the beam aimed. Missiles can carry smaller acoustic systems, though a Viltrumite could destroy them before they get close if he recognizes the design.

Engineers would probably settle on disposable emitters rather than one giant weapon. Several smaller units can be hidden around the same area and activated at once. The goal is to create overlapping coverage so destroying the first source doesn’t immediately stop the effect. Humanity would still need to lure a Viltrumite into that area, and now the invaders are aware traps exist. The bait would have to be valuable enough that they can’t comfortably ignore it. Nuclear command becomes useful here for a reason beyond simply launching warheads. The Viltrumites know Earth has thousands of nuclear weapons spread across several countries, submarines, aircraft, and missile fields. Destroying every warhead individually would waste time, so they would have an incentive to target the systems and people capable of coordinating them. Humanity could exploit that by making one surviving command network look far more important than it is. The site broadcasts enough genuine military traffic to convince the invaders it controls part of a retaliatory strike, while the actual command function is moved elsewhere. Around the false headquarters, engineers hide multiple acoustic emitters, conventional explosives, sensors, and a nuclear weapon positioned for a ground detonation if the trap succeeds.

Using a nuclear weapon on your own territory would be an extreme decision, and governments wouldn't make it lightly. The surrounding area would need to be evacuated as far as possible, the target would have to be far from a major population center, and leaders would still have no guarantee the explosion can kill a Viltrumite. What the earlier battles have shown is that weaker weapons aren't giving them another realistic option.

The first attempt could become humanity’s most important battle even if it fails to kill him. The Viltrumite enters the kill zone expecting another command facility. Several emitters activate from different directions, and his flight immediately breaks down. He hits the ground hard enough to crater it, destroys one emitter, tries to rise, and gets hit by the same frequency from another side.

Then the nuclear device goes off. Humanity wouldn't know the result immediately because most equipment close enough to observe the blast would disappear with it. Satellites, distant aircraft, seismic sensors, and radiation monitoring would have to reconstruct what happened afterward. If the Viltrumite eventually leaves the blast area alive, the condition he leaves in becomes the most valuable piece of information humanity has collected yet.

Either result forces the next stage of the invasion. The Viltrumites can no longer treat Earth as a planet they can slowly frighten into surrender, and humanity can no longer assume discovering the right weakness automatically gives us a way to win.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: The nuclear trap would force the Viltrumites to change their plan even if the target survives. Up to this point they have treated Earth like a normal conquest, where a few demonstrations of overwhelming force should convince governments that resistance is pointless. The moment humans deliberately sacrifice their own facility and detonate a nuclear weapon just to injure one invader, that assumption falls apart.

If the Viltrumite comes out of the blast alive but visibly affected, stunned, or temporarily unable to fly properly, the other 2 would immediately pull him away instead of letting humanity continue observing him.
That retreat alone would tell every surviving government that Viltrumites can be hurt. They may be far beyond anything a human body can survive, but they are not indestructible.

The blast site would become more valuable than the destroyed command center. Military recovery teams would move in as soon as radiation levels and the risk of another attack allow it, looking for blood, tissue, fragments of clothing, or anything else the Viltrumite left behind. Even a few drops of blood would give scientists something they had never had before: actual biological material from the enemy.

Humanity would have to resist the temptation to pretend that a blood sample suddenly lets us invent a superweapon. Sequencing an alien genome does not produce a Scourge Virus ina week, and no real laboratory could reverse engineer Viltrumite biology fast enough to manufacture a species specific plague during an active invasion. What scientists could do is much smaller and still useful. They could examine cell structure, tissue density, oxygen use, healing, and any unusual anatomy present in the sample.

That work could confirm why the acoustic attack affected him. If researchers find structures connected to balance and spatial orientation that are unusually complex or sensitive, the earlier frequency stops looking like a lucky accident. Now humanity has battlefield evidence and biological evidence pointing toward the same vulnerability.

The Viltrumites would know there is probably material left behind too. Instead of simply attacking another military base, they could return to the blast zone and erase everything around it, forcing recovery teams to leave before they finish. That creates a race where the valuable object is not a weapon or a city. It is a freezer full of blood samples being moved between laboratories while one of the strongest beings on Earth tries to find it.

This would be the first point in the war where ordinary civilians become useful in a way the invaders cannot easily predict. University laboratories, private biotech companies, data centers, amateur radio networks, couriers, and technicians can all carry pieces of the same project without knowing the entire plan. The Empire can destroy the Pentagon. It cannot inspect every university basement, private server, storage unit, and laboratory spread across the planet.
That would force the Viltrumites to confront a problem strength cannot solve quickly. There are only 3 of them, and Earth has billions of places where information can hide.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: The invasion would start looking less like a war and more like an occupation before humanity officially surrendered. The Viltrumites could destroy almost any military force placed directly in front of them, but controlling 8 billion people is a different problem.

Human governments would begin exploiting that immediately. Large headquarters become liabilities, so command structures shrink. Military orders stop depending on one national center. Important people move constantly, while lower level commanders receive broader authority to act without waiting for permission from leaders who may already be dead.

Some of the most important communications would move backward technologically. A sophisticated network can be tracked, jammed, or destroyed by attacking major nodes. A message passed through short radio bursts, physical drives, printed instructions, or couriers is slower, but a Viltrumite cannot punch a single building and erase all of it.

The Viltrumites could answer by creating examples. Instead of hitting military targets, they might destroy a small city after an attack and announce that every future act of resistance will produce another civilian punishment. That would immediately divide humanity.

Some governments would surrender and some would pretend to. A country could publicly accept Viltrumite authority while secretly moving scientists, weapons, and communications underground. Military forces could stop wearing uniforms and disperse into smaller groups. Aircraft might remain hidden instead of trying to challenge the invaders in open air. Nuclear submarines become especially important because the Viltrumites have no easy way to know exactly where every one of them is beneath thousands of miles of ocean.

The political battle inside humanity would become almost as dangerous as the invasion itself. One side would argue that resistance is getting civilians killed for almost no chance of victory. Another would argue that surrender gives the Empire time to identify every remaining weapon and dismantle resistance permanently.

The Viltrumites would encourage that split. They would offer cooperating governments protection, food shipments, restored electricity, and the ability to keep local authority. Any country that continues fighting gets cut off from those benefits.

The resistance would need a result soon because every week without one makes collaboration more attractive. A dead Viltrumite could prove the invaders can be beaten. Another failed attack would prove the opposite.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: Humanity’s next attempt should not look anything like the first nuclear trap.

The Viltrumites already know about acoustic emitters hidden around fixed locations, so trying the same setup again would be suicide. Instead, military planners could use the one environment where humans already operate enormous sound systems over long distances. Modern navies use powerful active sonar to send acoustic energy through water, and water carries sound far more effectively than air. The exact equipment would still need modification because the Viltrumite weakness depends on a narrow frequency. Before building a strategy around it, engineers would test that frequency through water and verify that a usable band around the disruptive tone can still be transmitted effectively underwater. If those tests work, existing sonar and underwater transducers could be modified around that band, and humanity would no longer be trying to blast the frequency across open atmosphere.

The bait could be one of the ballistic missile submarines the Viltrumites have been trying to locate. Humans deliberately let evidence leak that a submarine carrying nuclear weapons has surfaced briefly in a remote section of the Pacific and is preparing to launch.

A Viltrumite would have every reason to go after it himself. The submarine would dive before he arrives, forcing him underwater if he wants to destroy it before the missiles can be used. The moment he enters the search area, several ships and underwater acoustic systems positioned far apart begin transmitting the frequency that disrupted the first Viltrumite.

The effect underwater could be far harder for him to escape. He already relies on balance and orientation while moving through a medium with no visual horizon, and the sound can reach him from several directions. If his equilibrium fails while he is moving quickly underwater, maintaining controlled movement and immediately navigating back toward the surface could become much harder.
The submarine itself would not try to fight him. Its only job is to keep moving and make him follow.

Surface ships would launch torpedoes and conventional weapons once the acoustic attack begins, not because those weapons are expected to kill him, but because every impact gives him another problem while he is struggling to orient himself. Aircraft above the area could drop additional sonobuoys and tracking devices, constantly updating where he is moving.

The Viltrumite would eventually figure out what is happening. He could destroy a ship, move beyond one acoustic source, or simply force himself upward until he reaches the surface. Humanity would plan around that. The real strike would happen when he breaks through the water. Instead of trying to hit a target freely flying through the atmosphere, missile crews would already know roughly where he has to emerge because the underwater tracking network has been following him the entire time. Several weapons could arrive within seconds of each other while the frequency continues from below.

This still would not guarantee a kill. The important difference is that humanity is finally combining systems that already exist instead of expecting one weapon to solve everything. Sonar disrupts him. Submarines control his movement. Sensors predict where he will emerge. Missiles arrive while his flight is compromised.

Even if the earlier nuclear test failed to leave serious lasting injuries, this attack could keep the Viltrumite disoriented long enough for concentrated conventional explosives to repeatedly hit him while he cannot maneuver normally.

For the first time, humans might see one of them bleeding heavily and once he slows down enough that aircraft can keep him inside a predictable area, another nuclear strike becomes possible without needing him to walk willingly into a bunker.
This time, he doesn’t come back out. Humanity has killed 1 Viltrumite.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: That victory would probably make the war worse. The remaining 2 Viltrumites would immediately understand that Earth is no longer a routine assignment. Humans discovered a biological weakness, adapted it across different environments, and killed one of their own within days or weeks of first contact.

They would stop trying to preserve every part of human civilization. The first target would be the nuclear arsenal. 1 Viltrumite could move between missile fields, air bases, and known storage facilities while the other attacks naval infrastructure and communications. They would not need to destroy every warhead. They only need to reduce the number of places from which humanity can coordinate another trap.

Then they would go after the acoustic network itself. Naval bases with sonar equipment would be destroyed. Research ships would disappear. Facilities known to work on the frequency would be hit without warning. Any aircraft carrying modified acoustic equipment becomes a priority target.

This is where the small number of Viltrumites becomes both their strength and their weakness. They are almost impossible to stop when attacking, but every hour spent hunting one category of weapon gives humans somewhere else to work.

The surviving governments could exploit that by flooding the planet with false targets. Hundreds of facilities begin broadcasting signals that resemble the sonic project. Trucks move fake equipment between bases. Civilian cargo ships carry containers designed to look important from satellite imagery. Governments deliberately leak contradictory information about where the remaining nuclear weapons and research teams are located.

That opens the possibility of turning ordinary vehicles into disposable traps. Trucks, helicopters, drones, boats, and even buildings can hide an emitter without looking like a military installation. The goal changes from trapping a Viltrumite for minutes to ruining one movement at exactly the wrong time.

A Viltrumite diving toward a target at extreme speed depends on perfect control. If a hidden emitter activates during the final seconds of the dive, even a brief loss of balance could send him into the ground instead of through the target he intended to hit.
The impact alone probably would not kill him. Humanity wouldnt expect it to but the point is to make him stop moving.

Once one of the remaining Viltrumites crashes near a prepared site, buried explosives and multiple conventional weapons could hit the same location immediately. The attack would be automated because human crews would not survive close enough to operate it manually.

The Viltrumite could still tear his way out. If he does, the entire site has kept him in the same place for several seconds which would be enough for humanity’s final remaining nuclear weapons to matter.
The problem is that the Empire now understands exactly what Earth is trying to do.

The last 2 Viltrumites would stop approaching obvious targets themselves. They could throw objects from distance, destroy facilities from above, or simply start killing population centers until the governments behind the resistance reveal themselves.
At that point, humanity would no longer have time to build another perfect trap.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: The final stage would come down to whether the Viltrumites still want Earth badly enough to avoid destroying the thing they came to conquer.

Humanity has probably killed 1 invader and injured another, but military infrastructure across the world is collapsing. Large air forces are mostly grounded or destroyed, naval forces are being hunted, satellites are disappearing, and many governments have either surrendered or lost contact with their own forces.
The remaining resistance would understand that defeating the last 2 Viltrumites in direct combat is becoming less realistic every day.
So the strategy would change again. Instead of threatening the Viltrumites, humanity would threaten the value of Earth.

The Empire’s biggest reason to preserve Earth would be its billions of biologically compatible humans, with our industry and infrastructure making that population even more useful. Humanity could use that against them by creating a distributed denial plan. Nuclear forces that are still hidden receive orders that if the Viltrumites begin mass extermination or eliminate the last recognized governments, weapons will be used against major industrial zones, ports, energy infrastructure, and other parts of civilization the Empire wants intact.

It would be an awful strategy because humans would be threatening their own planet. That is exactly why the Viltrumites might believe it. The Empire has already watched humans detonate a nuclear weapon on their own territory to kill one soldier. They have seen submarines used as bait and governments sacrifice military facilities just to collect data. The threat that humanity would destroy much of its own infrastructure rather than hand over a clean, productive world would no longer sound empty.

The remaining Viltrumites could still call the bluff and win physically. Even a global nuclear exchange would not necessarily make Earth useless forever, and Viltrumites can wait far longer than humans can. What it would do is kill a large part of the biologically compatible population that made Earth such an attractive conquest in the first place, while also destroying much of the industry and infrastructure that made ruling that population useful.

That gives humanity leverage, but not victory. The most realistic outcome is a compromise that looks a lot like losing. Several governments publicly accept Viltrumite authority. The remaining invaders stop destroying infrastructure and allow human institutions to continue operating because they need those institutions to keep the planet productive.

The sonic frequency is copied onto thousands of disconnected systems. Biological samples remain hidden. Nuclear submarines stay underwater. Scientists continue studying Viltrumite tissue. Military units that never formally surrender disappear into civilian populations.
The Viltrumites would rule the planet, but they would have to rule a species that has already killed one of them.

That matters because 3 Viltrumites can conquer governments far more easily than they can erase knowledge from 8 billion people. Every year the occupation continues gives humanity more time to improve the frequency weapon, study the recovered biology, and build traps that do not depend on surviving militaries.

If the Empire responds by sending a larger force, Earth probably loses completely. A few dozen Viltrumites could attack enough places at once that humanity’s advantage in dispersion stops mattering. No realistic modern military could survive that level of speed and destruction long enough to keep coordinating resistance.

Against only the original 3, though, humanity has a narrow path to survival. We probably could not repel them cleanly. We might kill 1, possibly kill or cripple another, and force the survivors to leave enough of our civilization intact to remain useful.

So humanity would not win the invasion in the normal sense. The Viltrumite flag could still end up over Earth but the Empire would discover that conquering humans and controlling humans are 2 very different problems.

scripts.title: Could Invincible Survive Final Destination

sections.name: INTRO
paras: Mark Grayson can survive things that would kill almost anyone in Final Destination. Car crashes, explosions, falling debris, getting thrown through buildings, even getting crushed under something huge usually aren't enough to put a Viltrumite down for good. So if Death wants Mark dead, it’s going to need a lot more than the usual chain of bad luck.

It would start with Mark having a premonition of a major disaster and realizing exactly what is about to happen a few minutes before everyone around him dies. He gets himself out, saves several other people with him, and probably thinks that’s the end of it. From Mark's point of view, he saw something horrible coming and stopped it.

Then the survivors start dying anyway, one after another, in the same order they were supposed to die during the disaster. Mark would catch onto the pattern much faster than most people. The problem is that saving someone doesn’t make death go away. Every time Mark interrupts one of these accidents, the pattern keeps moving and eventually comes back around.

At first, that barely matters because ordinary Final Destination deaths can’t do much to him. But once Mark’s turn arrives, the accidents would have to start using things strong enough to actually hurt a Viltrumite.
And Mark can’t punch his way out of this one, because there’s nobody standing in front of him to fight.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: Mark would get the premonition during a GDA weapons test, one of the few places where an accident could realistically contain enough force to kill him along with everyone else. Cecil could have him there while the agency tests a sonic weapon meant to disorient enhanced targets, capable of reaching the specific frequency range that disrupts Viltrumite equilibrium, with several other heavy energy systems running nearby. Mark has already dealt with enough experimental GDA technology to know the safest place during a test is usually somewhere else, but Cecil wants him close in case one of the systems fails and they need someone strong enough to shut it down manually.

The test begins normally until Mark suddenly sees everything around him change. The frequency jumps outside the intended range and hits the part of his inner ear that controls his balance, making it almost impossible to fly straight. He drops several feet before catching himself, then watches one of the engineers get thrown into a railing when a pressure line bursts beside the test floor. The observation glass above them cracks, alarms start going off, and people rush toward exits while Mark tries reaching the controls.

He can still move through the pain, but every pulse from the weapon throws off his sense of direction again. Mark crashes through part of the facility while trying to reach the emitter, which damages another system running nearby and starts a second failure. A materials testing chamber loses containment and begins dumping extreme heat into the same area while the people trapped inside are already trying to get away from the sonic weapon.

Mark would spend most of the vision trying to save everyone else. He catches a falling section of the observation level, carries several people through a damaged wall, then turns back because more voices are still coming from the test floor. The frequency catches him again while he is flying toward them, leaving him disoriented long enough for the overheated chamber to rupture beside him.

The explosion itself would not kill Mark. He has survived far worse physical impacts than anything the room can produce, but the heat keeps building while the sonic weapon prevents him from getting his balance back. He forces himself out once, badly burned, tries going back for the people still inside, and gets caught in another pulse before the damaged containment system floods the chamber again.
That is where he dies in the vision. Then Mark is standing outside the test floor again, a few minutes before the first warning appears.

He would not spend long wondering whether what he saw was real because the same engineer from the vision is standing in the same place, the same systems are running, and the control panel flashes the exact warning Mark remembers seeing moments before everything went wrong. Mark flies straight into the test area, tells Cecil to kill the power, then tears open part of the reactor housing himself when the normal shutdown does not happen fast enough.

The full disaster never gets the chance to happen, but the machinery has already started failing. One section of the test floor collapses, the observation level fills with smoke, and several people end up trapped behind damaged doors while emergency crews are still trying to figure out what went wrong. Mark moves through the facility faster than they can organize the evacuation, carrying people out 2 or 3 at a time and going back until he cannot hear anyone else inside. Several people survive only because Mark knew exactly where they were going to be. An engineer who died near the test floor gets carried out before the pressure line ruptures, a civilian observer Mark remembers losing beneath the observation level gets pulled away first, anda GDA security officer escapes a section of the building that should have collapsed on him.
A few days later, one of those engineers dies.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: The engineer could be working alone at a smaller GDA lab when a hydraulic platform carrying heavy equipment starts leaning. He notices the load moving and steps toward the emergency control, expecting to stop the platform before anything falls. The damaged hydraulic line gives out before he reaches it, dropping several tons of equipment across the section of floor where he is standing.

Mark would hear about it because Cecil knows the engineer was one of the people he saved during the test. The death would bother him, especially since he can still remember seeing the same man die during the premonition, but 1 accident would not immediately convince Mark that some invisible force is following the survivors. People survive disasters and die later all the time, and Mark has seen enough terrible coincidences to know that connecting everything too quickly can lead nowhere.

The next survivor would make that explanation much harder. One of the civilian observers could be leaving a parking garage after meeting with GDA investigators when the automatic gate begins acting strangely. A worn support cable above the exit starts slipping while she is walking underneath it, then the counterweight breaks loose and drops directly toward her.

Mark happens to be nearby because Cecil asked him to check on the survivors after the engineer’s death. He catches the weight before it reaches her, pulls her away from the gate, then hears the rest of the mechanism shifting above them. Instead of waiting to see what falls next, Mark rips the damaged assembly out of the ceiling and throws it into an empty section of the garage.

The woman survives without a scratch. Mark would remember where she was during the premonition because he had tried reaching her after the engineer died. The sequence is not perfectly clear in his head, but he knows she was supposed to die shortly after him.

The civilian from the garage was supposed to die after the engineer. The next person Mark remembers clearly is one of the GDA security officers who had been near the observation level. The officer would think Mark is taking the coincidence too seriously until a loaded equipment rack starts tipping inside a vehicle depot where he works. Mark catches it before it lands and moves the officer away from the area, then waits for another accident to start.

Mark could stay with him for hours while checking everything nearby. He would hear loose machinery long before it breaks, see vehicles approaching from blocks away, and have more than enough time to stop any normal accident that starts around them.

Eventually the officer leaves without another incident. Later that same day, another survivor from the test dies during a pressure test at a separate GDA facility. A vessel ruptures while technicians are preparing the room, and the blast kills him before Mark even knows there is a problem.

That would make the order harder to dismiss. The officer should have died first, Mark interrupted whatever was about to happen to him, and the next person Mark remembers from the original disaster died instead. Mark still couldn't know whether saving the officer truly moved Death forward or only disrupted that attempt long enough for the pattern to appear somewhere else.
He still would not understand the rule completely, but he would know the accidents are connected.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Mark would stop following the list 1 person at a time once he realizes protecting the next survivor can leave everyone else exposed. If he spends 6 hours watching the security officer, somebody farther down the order can still die if interrupting one attempt only redirects the pattern temporarily. Mark is fast enough to cross a city in seconds, but he still cannot be in 4 places at the same time.
His solution would be simple enough at first. Bring everyone together.

Cecil could give him access to a stripped down GDA training room that has almost nothing inside capable of killing a normal person. Heavy equipment gets removed, weapons are locked away, power is cut to anything unnecessary, and the remaining survivors are brought inside while GDA personnel watch the building from outside.

Mark would stay in the room with them because he is the best safety system Cecil has. He can hear someone fall before anyone else reacts, catch almost anything before it lands, and move a person out of danger long before a normal rescue team could even reach the door.

For a while, nothing happens. The survivors would probably start thinking Mark scared himself over a few coincidences. One of them could even joke that if Death is supposedly coming for them, it picked a pretty boring place to do it.
Then Mark hears a cargo aircraft losing control outside.

The plane is approaching a nearby GDA runway too low, and its damaged steering system is pulling it toward the same building where Mark put everyone. Mark leaves the room, flies outside, catches the aircraft before it can hit the complex, and carries it far enough away to put it down safely.
He’s gone for only a few seconds. When Mark returns, one of the survivors is choking.

The man had been drinking while Mark was outside and swallowed wrong when everyone started reacting to the plane. Nobody else in the room can clear the blockage fast enough, and the guy is already beginning to panic when Mark gets back.
Mark uses the Heimlich carefully enough that he does not crush the man’s ribs and gets the obstruction out.

That would bother him more than the aircraft. He had just put everyone inside one of the safest rooms Cecil could build, removed almost every obvious hazard, and watched Death nearly get someone with a mouthful of food while Mark was distracted by a plane falling out of the sky. Mark would realize that trying to create a perfectly safe room is impossible. Humans can choke, fall, bleed, have allergic reactions, or die from thousands of things that do not require a giant mechanical setup. Death does not need an elaborate machine every time if the person it wants is still human.

The survivor Mark just saved would remain alive, but another person on the list dies later after leaving the facility. Mark reaches the scene too late again and sees the same pattern repeat. The person he directly saved survives that attempt while someone who came later in the original disaster dies instead, reinforcing Mark's suspicion that intervention can disrupt the order without proving exactly how Death responds.
That would push Mark to start looking into older cases rather than treating what happened at the GDA test as unique.

Cecil's records could turn up reports of previous disasters where several people survived together and then died one after another in strange accidents. The details would not give Mark a perfect rulebook because the survivors themselves never understood everything that was happening. Some believed saving another person could change the order, others thought new life could break the pattern, and several cases ended before anyone figured out what had worked. One name keeps appearing around those older cases: William Bludworth, a mortician who seems to know far more about Death's design than the survivors ever did. Mark tracks him down, but Bludworth offers warnings and theories rather than a clean rulebook.

Mark would trust what he has already seen more than theories written by people who still ended up dead. He knows saving someone can disrupt an immediate attempt and that Death may appear to move farther down the order afterward, but he also knows the person he saved is not necessarily safe forever.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: The woman from the parking garage would eventually come up again, and this time Mark would already be watching for it. She could be crossing between 2 GDA buildings with Mark beside her when an underground transformer blows beneath the walkway and tears open part of the pavement.

Both of them drop into a maintenance shaft filled with damaged electrical equipment. Mark catches her before she falls far enough to get hurt, then notices coolant pouring across the floor while exposed systems begin arcing around them.

He does not wait for the rest of the chain to develop. Mark flies straight through the side of the shaft with the woman in his arms and gets her outside before the electricity reaches the flooded section below them.
She survives again and Mark barely gets time to think about it before another emergency starts somewhere else.

The security officer could be standing near an elevated roadway when a tanker crashes several hundred feet ahead and takes out part of the support structure. Mark hears the collision, reaches the officer before the road begins collapsing, and carries him away without bothering to hold the structure up.

That would be one of the advantages Mark has over everyone who dealt with Death before him. He does not have to solve the accident. If the entire road wants to collapse, he can simply remove the person from it and let the wreck happen behind them.

The man from the training room gets another turn afterward during an apartment fire. Mark reaches him before the gas line catches, tears through the outside wall, and carries him into the street while the rest of the building is evacuated.
By now Mark has interrupted enough deaths that all 3 survivors he knows were skipped are still alive after coming up again.

Mark would know it before anything happens because he remembers himself dying after the people he has just saved. He could tell Cecil that if his guess is right, whatever has been causing these accidents should come for him next.

Cecil would take that far more seriously than the survivors do. An invisible force targeting ordinary people is strange enough, but something trying to kill Mark means the GDA has to consider what kind of accident could even work.
For several hours, there’s nothing then Mark hears a frequency coming from inside the GDA complex.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: A sonic system in another section of the facility could activate after a power fault sends a command through equipment that was supposed to be offline. The weapon was designed to test how certain frequencies affect enhanced subjects, which means it can reach the same range that disrupts Viltrumite equilibrium.

Mark feels it before anyone else notices anything is wrong. His balance disappears almost immediately. He catches himself against the wall, tries flying toward the source, and ends up hitting the floor because his body can no longer tell which direction he is moving.

Cecil orders the entire system shut down, but the emitter keeps running while another failure begins somewhere else in the building. A high energy materials chamber loses containment and starts dumping extreme heat into the surrounding section.

Mark would recognize both parts of the setup from the original premonition. The first disaster killed him because the sonic frequency kept him inside an environment hot enough to damage a Viltrumite. Now the same 2 weaknesses are appearing together again even though the original test equipment was supposedly shut down and the systems involved are in different parts of the complex.

Mark tries reaching the sonic emitter first because he knows the heat becomes much easier to escape once he can fly properly again. Every time he changes direction, another pulse ruins his balance and sends him into a wall or the floor.

Mark points himself toward the emitter and starts breaking through whatever is between them. He goes through walls, support beams, and part of the equipment bay because flying straight is easier than trying to correct himself every few seconds.

When Mark finally reaches the sonic array, he cannot even stay upright long enough to shut it down normally. He grabs the entire assembly, tears it away from the wall, and crushes the equipment until the frequency stops.

His balance begins coming back, but the heat has already spread far enough to seriously burn him. Parts of his skin are damaged, his breathing is harder, and he realizes he stayed inside the chamber much longer than he should have because the sonic weapon kept slowing him down. Mark flies through the roof and reaches open air before the rest of the containment system fails. He would survive, but this would be the first accident after the original disaster that leaves him with injuries worth noticing. Mark has been hit through buildings and torn apart by Viltrumites before, so he is not going to panic because he got burned. What would bother him is how specific the accident was.

If it does, Mark has evidence that even Death cannot simply kill him whenever it wants. Surviving his turn appears to disrupt the design the same way his rescues have, but he still can't know whether Death has truly moved forward or is only postponing another attempt on him.

That would give him a plan. He doesn’t need to make everyone permanently safe right away. If Mark can keep reaching the survivors before their accidents finish, he may be able to keep disrupting the pattern long enough to look for a way to break it.
The problem is that Mark’s own turn will keep coming back too.

The first real attempt already put 2 things that can hurt a Viltrumite together, though Mark has no way to know whether Death is deliberately adapting to his weaknesses or whether the design is simply producing impossibly convenient accidents. Mark escaped because he understood what was happening quickly enough to destroy the sonic weapon before the heat finished the job.
If the next attempt uses a different weakness, Mark might not realize what Death is building until he is already inside it.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Mark would find out pretty quickly that surviving his own turn didn’t end anything. A few days after the GDA accident, the woman from the parking garage nearly dies again when a city bus loses control at an intersection and jumps the curb toward her. Mark hears the tires before she even reacts, gets her off the sidewalk, and watches the bus tear through the exact spot where she had been standing. The security officer comes up after her, then the man Mark saved from choking, which confirms the sequence has gone back through the same survivors again. Keeping all of them alive would start getting much harder because Mark can’t know which accident is meant for which person until it’s already happening. The security officer could be tiding with GDA agents when a truck crashes ahead of them and throws several cars across the highway. Mark reaches him almost immediately, catches the vehicle before it rolls over the barrier, and pulls everyone out before the wreck can get worse.
While he’s doing that, Mark hears screaming several miles away.

The man from the training room is inside a construction elevator that has suddenly dropped down its shaft. Mark leaves the officer with the other agents, reaches the elevator before it hits the bottom, and catches the car hard enough to stop the fall. A snapped cable tears through the roof while he’s holding it, so Mark grabs the survivor and gets him out before the rest of the mechanism comes apart.

By the time he flies back to the highway, the security officer is already dead. One of the wrecked cars had been leaking fuel underneath the overpass, and the fire spread after Mark left. The GDA agents tried getting him clear, but part of the damaged roadway came down before they could.

That death would hit Mark differently because he had already saved the officer twice. He didn’t miss the accident because he was too slow or too weak. He got pulled away by another person who was about to die at the exact same time.

From that point on, Mark couldn't rely on simply staying close and reacting faster than everyone else. Death can create 2 emergencies at once, and it only needs him to choose the wrong one for a few seconds.

Mark could go back to Bludworth and ask whether anyone ever found a way off the list for good. Bludworth wouldn't give him a clean answer, but he could bring up the idea that taking another person’s life may transfer whatever time that person had left.
Mark wouldn't even consider it. He isn’t going to murder somebody to test a rule he doesn't fully understand, especially when there’s no guarantee the trade works the way survivors thought it did.
That leaves him with fewer people to protect and no permanent way out.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: The remaining normal survivors would be the woman from the garage and the man Mark saved from choking, with Mark still coming after both of them in the order. By now they've watched enough people die that waiting for another accident would start getting to them in ways Mark can't fix.

The man could become obsessed with what Bludworth said about taking another life. Mark would notice him asking Cecil about old cases, then disappearing from GDA protection before his next turn comes around. Mark tracks him down because he assumes the guy panicked and ran, only to find him following someone he thinks has decades left to live.

Mark would stop him before he hurts anyone. The survivor could argue that Mark gets to reject the rule because most accidents barely touch him, while everyone else is waiting for a loose wire or broken machine to end their life. Mark would understand why he’s terrified, but he still takes the weapon away and brings him back instead of letting him kill a stranger.

Death would come for him on the way. A truck ahead of them blows a tire and sends part of its load across the road. Mark grabs the survivor and clears the debris, then a tanker comes through the wreckage behind them and forces him to move again. He lands on the roof of a nearby building with the man still in his arms and waits until the crashes below finally stop.
For a few seconds, it looks like he got him through another turn then the man collapses.

A small piece of metal from the first crash had gone through his side while Mark was carrying him away. With everything happening around them, neither of them noticed the wound right away. Mark gets him to a hospital almost instantly, but the internal bleeding is already too severe by the time doctors start working on him.

That death would teach Mark another ugly lesson about how hard these accidents are to read. He can save someone from the biggest danger in front of him and still miss the one piece that actually mattered.

The woman from the garage would now be next again. Mark could move her into the GDA medical wing instead of another empty room, with doctors checking her constantly so even a small injury gets caught immediately. Cecil would cut power to anything unnecessary, keep food and drinks supervised after the choking incident, and have Mark stay within a few feet instead of flying off every time something goes wrong elsewhere.

Death would still find a way into the room through ordinary equipment. A defect in an oxygen regulator could slowly raise the oxygen concentration while the monitor continues reading normally. A spark from another machine starts a flash fire, and Mark gets the woman out before the flames spread farther than the bed.

The heat damages part of the sprinkler system overhead, sending a metal fitting down toward her while Mark is carrying her through the hallway. He catches it, keeps moving, and gets her outside before anything else can start.
She survives again, which means Mark’s turn comes back around.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: Then the building loses power. Backup generators kick on automatically, and one of them develops a mechanical vibration that travels through the structure at a frequency close enough to Mark’s weakness to make him dizzy. It isn’t as strong as the weapon from the earlier attempt, but it doesn’t need to be. Mark only has to lose his balance long enough for the rest of the accident to build around him.

A fire suppression line ruptures in another section and floods several corridors. Mark tries leaving before the vibration gets worse, but a damaged elevator counterweight punches through the floor and sends him into a lower level where the GDA stores captured alien technology.

The fall barely hurts him. What matters is what he lands on. One of the damaged devices contains an alien power cell that starts overheating after its casing cracks. Cecil orders the entire section evacuated once he realizes what Mark landed beside, while Mark tries getting back toward the generator that’s messing with his balance.

He stops trying to fly cleanly and goes straight through the structure instead. Mark tears through walls and support beams until he reaches the generator, destroys it, then turns back toward the alien device once his balance starts coming back.

The power cell is already close to failing. Mark rips it out of the floor, carries it above the facility, and throws it high into the atmosphere before the stored energy releases. The explosion would be huge, but Mark is already moving away when it goes off and comes back with burns that are nowhere near as serious as the ones from the earlier attempt.

That would show Mark he can learn from what Death already tried. Once he recognizes the frequency, he knows what needs to go first, and once his balance comes back, most environments stop being traps because he can leave faster than they can finish collapsing.
He would still have no idea how many different ways Death can reach the same result.

Mark could start thinking about leaving Earth entirely. Most of the accidents so far have depended on machines, buildings, traffic, other people, or some piece of equipment failing at the right moment. If he gets far enough away from all of that, there may simply be less for Death to use.

Space would give Mark the longest quiet stretch he’s had since the original disaster. There are no roads, elevators, power lines, gas systems, or random civilians around him, and he can stay far enough from anything that even a freak mechanical failure has almost nothing to work with. He still couldn't stay there forever. Viltrumites can hold their breath for an extremely long time, but Mark eventually needs air, food, and somewhere to recover properly. He can stretch the time between attempts much longer than a normal person ever could, but that only delays the moment he has to come back.

When Mark finally heads back toward Earth, he gets a GDA distress signal from an inner-system research station already operating substantially closer to the Sun. The station has lost attitude control and its damaged propulsion is pushing it onto an increasingly dangerous solar trajectory. Cecil tells him several
people are still trapped inside, and Mark changes course immediately because he isn’t going to ignore them just to protect himself.

He reaches the station and starts moving the crew toward an escape vehicle while physically stabilizing part of the structure himself. The first problem is easy enough until one of the communication arrays develops a feedback loop that shifts into the same resonant frequency range that disrupts Viltrumite equilibrium and runs through the station’s frame.

The station is already rotating, so losing his equilibrium hits much harder than it did on Earth. Every time Mark tries correcting his flight, he ends up moving in the wrong direction while the structure keeps turning around him.

A damaged propulsion system fires while he’s trying to reach the antenna and changes the station’s trajectory. Mark eventually tears the communication array loose, gets his balance back, and starts carrying the crew out again.
Cecil realizes the damaged propulsion is pushing the already sunward station deeper into a dangerous solar approach.

Mark could move the whole structure, but doing that while keeping the remaining crew alive would take more time than he has. He tears the occupied section free, carries everyone toward the escape craft, and abandons the rest of the station instead of trying to save the entire thing. One crew member is still trapped inside a damaged compartment, so Mark goes back for him. Those extra seconds take Mark much closer to the Sun than he wanted to be. The heat starts hurting while he’s still inside the wreck. Mark gets the last person out, throws the escape craft toward a safer course, then turns back toward Earth and starts flying away.

Part of the station explodes behind him and knocks him farther along the station's already dangerous sunward trajectory while another damaged transmitter begins producing the same resonant frequency through the remaining structure. Mark would be stuck between the 2 things that nearly killed him during the original vision, except this time there’s no nearby building he can escape into and no cooler environment a few hundred feet away. He can destroy the transmitter, but every second he spends fighting the disorientation carries him deeper into heat that keeps getting worse.
Mark forces himself through it, tears apart what remains of the station, and finally gets his balance back.

His skin is already burning by the time he starts flying away. He’d still have a chance because once the frequency is gone, Mark can accelerate much faster than the wreck around him. The real danger is whether he got control back early enough for his body to recover from the heat.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: Mark could survive that attempt if he gets far enough away before the damage becomes fatal. He has survived extreme heat before, and there’s no reason a short exposure should instantly kill him, so he could reach a safer distance badly burned and spend a long time healing afterward.
While Mark is recovering, the last normal survivor would eventually die.

Once he learns what happened, Mark would realize the list has finally collapsed down to him. There isn’t another survivor for Death to move toward after a failed attempt anymore, which means every future accident can keep coming back to the same person.

That still wouldn’t make him permanently safe. Death only needs 1 attempt where Mark doesn’t recognize the setup fast enough. Enough heat for long enough can kill a Viltrumite, and the sonic weakness gives Death a way to keep Mark somewhere he would normally escape from in seconds. Another accident could use something completely different that Mark doesn’t understand until he’s already hurt.

He still wouldn’t murder somebody for Bludworth’s loophole, and even if he did, there’s no guarantee it would remove him permanently. Every solution Mark has found so far either disrupts an immediate attempt, delays the next one, or gives him more time to get out.

So Invincible could survive Final Destination for a very long time. He’d probably survive more attempts than anyone else because ordinary accidents are not enough, and the pattern would need circumstances capable of exploiting actual Viltrumite weaknesses to threaten him.

Eventually, though, one of those attempts would probably work. Mark could keep escaping for years or potentially even longer, and nothing here proves Death is guaranteed to succeed, but he only has to be trapped in the wrong place once for an attempt to finally kill him.

scripts.title: Could Iron Man Survive Resident Evil

sections.name: INTRO
paras: The first zombie Tony sees in Raccoon City probably dies in seconds. The Mark 85 can tear through normal infected without much trouble, and at first Tony could easily think the whole outbreak is beneath him.

Then he starts seeing what Umbrella actually made. Lickers can attack from ceilings and tight hallways, Hunters can pressure him in confined spaces, Tyrants keep getting back up, and repeated fights expose Tony to contaminated blood, collapsing structures, and more chances for already damaged sections of the suit to get worse. The creatures don’t need to cut through intact Mark 85 armor for the environment around them to become an attrition problem.
So the real question isn’t whether Iron Man can kill zombies. It’s whether Tony can figure out Umbrella, keep the suit functional, and get out of Raccoon City before Resident Evil wears him down.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: This would be Tony near the end of the MCU, using the Mark 85. The easiest way to get him into Resident Evil without dragging the setup out would be through one of his quantum tests before the final fight with Thanos. Tony already knows how to navigate the Quantum Realm by this point, but this particular malfunction would destabilize the jump’s dimensional coordinates as well as its temporal destination, throwing him into a reality his system doesn’t recognize. Instead of coming back to 2023, he drops into Raccoon City on September 28, 1998, right as the outbreak is tearing through the city.

Cars are abandoned in intersections, stores have been broken into, and fires are already spreading between buildings. Tony would come down expecting a riot, chemical attack, or some kind of military disaster. He’d hear emergency broadcasts telling civilians to stay indoors, but the police channels would be a mess. Officers are calling for backup that never comes, people are reporting attacks all over the city, and nobody seems to understand why wounded civilians keep getting back up.

The first infected Tony sees wouldn't scare him at all. A man covered in blood comes toward him near an overturned car, and Tony would probably try talking to him before realizing he isn’t responding normally. When the man lunges, Tony catches him by the chest without moving more than a step.

Tony wouldn’t know he’s dealing with a zombie yet. His suit could scan body temperature, heart rate, blood chemistry, and whatever else it can pick up from the surface, and the results wouldn't make sense. The man is badly injured, barely functioning, and still trying to bite through metal armor.

Tony would shove him away rather than kill him because he still thinks there might be a medical explanation. Then several more come out of the street behind him. He could knock them down easily, and the Mark 85 would make normal infected almost harmless as long as the armor stays sealed. Bites can’t get through the plates, fingernails aren’t scratching nanotech, and Tony can throw an infected person across the street without trying very hard. He'd still avoid using repulsors at full power because he has no idea whether these people can be treated.

He’d move deeper into the city and start looking for somewhere with information. The Raccoon Police Department would be an obvious choice because police broadcasts keep mentioning it, and it’s one of the few places still trying to coordinate survivors.

Flying there sounds easy, but Tony wouldn’t want to spend the entire night above the city without knowing what happened. He’d stay lower, moving between streets and rooftops so he can scan infected people, check emergency calls, and get a better picture of how widespread the outbreak is.

That’s when he’d start noticing things that don’t fit a normal disease. Some infected are badly mutated. Dogs are attacking people with exposed tissue and abnormal muscle growth. Several bodies show similar changes even though they were injured in different ways. Tony would also pick up traces of contamination around blood, water, and medical waste.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: The Raccoon Police Dept would give Tony his first real look at how badly the city has fallen apart. The building is full of blocked hallways, dead officers, survivors hiding in rooms, and infected people who got inside before anyone understood what they were dealing with.

Tony would immediately become useful because most of the problems that slow down Leon or Claire aren't problems for him. Locked doors can be opened through the building’s electrical system, barricades can be moved, and zombies in narrow hallways can be restrained with pieces of the suit instead of wasting ammunition.

He still wouldn’t start blasting everything. Tony would want samples. He’d use the suit to take blood and tissue readings from several infected people and compare them. Once he sees the same abnormal biological anomaly showing up again and again, FRIDAY could flag it as a consistent infectious agent without identifying exactly what it is yet. The speed of the mutations would bother Tony because ordinary infectious diseases don’t rebuild bodies this quickly or keep damaged tissue functioning after so much trauma.

The bigger problem would be transmission. Tony's armor protects him while it’s fully sealed, but he’d know that blood is getting everywhere. Every close range fight covers walls, floors, and sometimes the suit itself. If the infection can spread through bites or contaminated fluids, one damaged section of armor could turn into a serious problem later.
That would be the first sign that Resident Evil can wear him down even when nothing around him is strong enough to beat him directly.

The Mark 85 can form weapons, shields, and repairs by moving nanites around Tony’s body, but it isn’t creating unlimited material. If Tony leaves part of the armor attached to a door or abandons a restraint somewhere, that material is gone until he physically gets it back. He can afford that occasionally. He can’t do it hundreds of times across an entire city.

Tony would start using the building itself instead. He could weld doors shut, move shelves into entrances, and restore enough power to open safe routes for survivors. That costs him much less than turning the suit into disposable equipment.
While going through police records, he’d start seeing the same company name repeatedly, Umbrella.

The company has ties to Raccoon City’s medical industry, local research, and several incidents the police had been looking into before everything collapsed. Tony would also find references to the mansion incident from earlier that year, even if most of the details were buried or dismissed. Reports from surviving S.T.A.R.S. members would mention monsters, laboratories, and a virus connected to Umbrella.
