L would have a strong chance of identifying Dexter as the Bay Harbor Butcher because Dexter’s biggest advantage also creates a pattern. His access to police information, forensic knowledge, victim selection, and ability to stay ahead of Miami Metro all become suspicious once L starts looking inside the department instead of outside it.

The harder part is building a case. Dexter is extremely good at destroying evidence, controlling crime scenes, and giving investigators explanations that are technically possible even when they aren’t true. That means L could become almost certain Dexter is guilty while still lacking enough physical evidence to arrest him.

But Dexter’s normal escape through Doakes becomes much less reliable once L is involved. L wouldn’t automatically accept a suddenly perfect suspect, especially when that suspect had already been investigating Dexter. He would examine how the evidence reached Doakes, preserve him as a potential witness, and keep pressure on Dexter instead of allowing the case to close cleanly.

That is where Dexter eventually loses. Dexter could delay him, mislead him, and come close to escaping but under these conditions, L is more likely than not to identify Dexter, break the Doakes frame, and eventually gather enough evidence to expose the Bay Harbor Butcher.

scripts.title: Could L Catch The Joker

sections.name: INTRO
paras: L wouldn't get very far by trying to understand why Joker commits each crime, because the motive can change whenever Joker feels like changing it. What L could study is everything that has to happen before the crime starts. Joker still needs people, weapons, vehicles, chemicals, safe locations, and enough time to put each plan together.

Once Joker realizes someone is getting close through those details, he’d start feeding the investigation bad information on purpose. From there, L would have to figure out which clues were left by accident and which ones Joker planted specifically for him.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: L would begin by rebuilding the Joker case from the ground up instead of trusting the way Gotham police already organized it. He’d want every known attack placed on one timeline with the location, time, weapons used, vehicles involved, casualties, escape route, materials recovered, and any message Joker deliberately left behind. The jokes and theatrics would still be documented, but L would keep them separate from the practical parts of the crime because those details are much harder to fake consistently. A truck still has to be stolen from somewhere, chemicals still have to be obtained, explosives still need to be assembled, and a group of armed men still has to move through Gotham without being noticed before an attack starts.

That would quickly show him that Joker’s unpredictability has limits. The target can change, the motive can change, and the way Joker presents the crime can change, but preparation creates repetition whether he wants it to or not. L could compare where stolen vehicles were last seen before disappearing, which industrial areas give access to the chemicals used in multiple attacks, and which parts of Gotham make it easier to move large amounts of equipment without attracting attention. He wouldn’t assume Joker personally handles every part of that process either, because someone this active probably relies on other people for transport, storage, theft, and setup.

The people around Joker would become one of L’s first useful angles. Henchmen may not know the full plan, but they still have to be recruited, paid, threatened, or convinced to participate. L would have Gotham police recheck everyone arrested after earlier Joker incidents, focusing less on what they claim Joker told them and more on how they were contacted in the first place. If several people were approached through the same bar, criminal intermediary, abandoned building, or underground contact, that gives L a route toward the organization around Joker even if Joker himself never appears there twice.

He’d also look at how long each attack must have taken to prepare. A simple shooting can be planned quickly, but taking over a hospital, rigging multiple buildings, poisoning a large supply, or setting up a citywide threat requires time. Once L estimates the minimum preparation window for each major incident, he can compare that against when Joker was last seen somewhere else. The goal isn’t proving where Joker lives because Gotham criminals can move constantly. L wants to know how far in advance Joker commits resources to an idea, because that tells him when the next attack becomes detectable.

Batman would notice what L is doing almost immediately. Bruce already understands that Joker builds plans around psychology, but L would be coming at the same problem from a different direction by treating the setup itself like evidence. That could create tension between them because Batman knows Gotham, its criminals, and Joker personally, while L would be willing to question assumptions Bruce has carried for years. At the same time, Batman would be one of the few people in the city with access to enough information to make L’s reconstruction much faster.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Once the full timeline is built, L would start looking for connections between attacks that Joker probably never intended anyone to compare. One robbery might involve a stolen ambulance, another could use a delivery truck with altered plates, and a 3rd might involve vehicles taken from completely different parts of Gotham, but the way they disappear before the attack could still look similar. If each one vanishes into areas with poor camera coverage and easy access to old industrial roads, L can narrow down which parts of the city are useful for staging operations. He’d do the same thing with weapons and explosives. Joker can steal from different suppliers to avoid repetition, but every choice has consequences. Military explosives require one kind of access, industrial chemicals require another, and modified weapons leave marks that can be compared even if the gun itself is never recovered. L would have specialists examine how devices were wired, which components were reused, and whether the people building them show the same level of skill from one attack to another.

A pattern there could tell him whether Joker has one reliable bomb maker, several different crews, or does more of the technical work himself. That matters because every additional specialist becomes another person Gotham police can investigate without needing to find Joker directly. L would probably avoid mass arrests at first because grabbing everyone connected to one supply chain could tell Joker exactly what the investigation has discovered. Instead, he’d have people watched and compare their movements against the preparation windows he already built.

The next useful clue could come from timing. Joker might choose attack times that look random because the public event changes from one plan to another, but the movement before those attacks might repeatedly happen late at night or during certain shifts when fewer workers are present. L would compare traffic cameras, toll records, warehouse security, police patrol gaps, and anything else that shows when large objects can move through Gotham unnoticed. He’d be looking for the hours Joker’s operation is most comfortable using rather than the hour the actual crime begins.

That could lead him toward a small number of staging areas. An abandoned amusement building, warehouse district, old chemical facility, or underground route could become more likely because several attacks can be supplied from there without requiring long travel through heavily monitored parts of the city. L wouldn’t assume Joker stores everything in one headquarters, but he could identify places that make sense as temporary assembly points.

Joker would eventually notice some of those routes becoming less safe. A driver might report seeing police near a warehouse that was never connected publicly to a case, or one of his suppliers could stop answering after being questioned. He wouldn't know exactly how the investigation got there, but he’d understand that someone is finding pieces of his operation that the usual detectives ignored.

Instead of immediately abandoning every method, Joker would probably test how much L actually knows. He could use the same supply route again but send a useless shipment through it, then watch whether police follow. If they do, he knows the route is compromised. If nothing happens, he learns that L may be working from a narrower clue.

L would expect some kind of response once pressure reaches the right areas. The important part would be not reacting to every suspicious movement as though it’s the real attack. He’d let some activity continue under surveillance because seeing where a fake shipment goes could reveal who Joker uses to move it.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Joker would become interested in L once he understands that the investigation is changing his preparation rather than simply reacting after each attack. Gotham police tightening security around obvious targets wouldn’t impress him because that happens every time he makes a threat. What would stand out is losing access to a warehouse nobody was supposed to know mattered, seeing one of his couriers followed after a route that had worked before, or discovering that a supply chain has been watched without anyone publicly connecting it to him. He’d want to know who changed the investigation. Finding L would be difficult at first because L doesn’t work like a normal Gotham detective. There’s no public office to attack, no obvious daily routine, and very little reason for him to stand in front of cameras. Joker could still learn that someone outside the usual department structure is directing parts of the case by watching which officers suddenly receive unusual instructions and which evidence stops circulating through normal channels.

Rather than searching for L’s real name immediately, Joker would probably try getting his attention. The next crime could include a clue built around something only the new investigator is likely to notice, such as a deliberately repeated component from an older bomb or a route that mirrors one of the patterns L has been studying. The clue would be obvious enough to L that he understands it was placed there intentionally, while most of the police might miss why it matters. L wouldn’t treat that as proof that Joker knows who he is. It only proves Joker knows someone is looking at the preparation more carefully. That difference matters because L would avoid changing security around himself until there’s evidence that Joker has information about his location or identity.

L tries to narrow things down by feeding different groups different versions of a fake supply route to see which one leaks, with each version containing a unique fabricated identifier that L can recognize later. The version that reaches Joker would contain a detail that doesn't match the real criminal supply chain, telling him the information originated inside the investigation rather than from his own operation. He could suspect a canary trap and deliberately create activity around several possible routes, muddying the operational response, but if that unique identifier appears again in a message, instruction, or planted clue connected to Joker's network, L can still narrow the compromised channel to the group that received that specific version without assuming he has identified the individual mole.

Joker would probably notice the trap after one or two reactions and decide to make the game messier. He could create several fake routes at once, each with enough real criminal activity around it that police can’t dismiss them immediately. One might lead to stolen weapons, another to a kidnapped worker, and another to a building full of explosives that turns out to be disconnected from the real target. The point would be forcing L to decide which pieces matter while knowing Joker built some of them specifically to waste his time.

That would make the case harder, but it would also increase the amount of work Joker has to do. Every fake operation needs people, materials, transport, and coordination, which means trying to overwhelm L with false patterns creates more activity for L to examine. He could start comparing which operations received the most resources and which ones were designed mainly to look important. A fake warehouse filled with theatrical evidence might tell him less than the small delivery route Joker barely bothered disguising.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: The first real prediction would come from combining several practical limits instead of guessing what Joker finds funny. If Joker has recently stolen a large quantity of chemicals, recruited several known criminals, and moved vehicles through one part of Gotham, L could estimate which kinds of attacks those resources support and which locations they can realistically reach without crossing areas already under surveillance.

He’d narrow possible targets by access rather than symbolism. A hospital might fit one kind of threat because the stolen chemicals can be moved through service entrances, while a major public event might be less likely if the equipment involved is too large to reach it unnoticed. L could also compare how much time Joker has had since the last major attack, because a complex setup needs enough preparation to exist at all.

Batman would be extremely useful here because Bruce knows Gotham’s physical layout better than almost anyone. He can tell L which tunnels are usable, which abandoned buildings connect to active structures, and which parts of the city Joker has exploited before. L would use that knowledge without assuming Joker will repeat an old target, because the value is in understanding what routes and spaces are available.
Together, they could narrow the next operation to a small area before knowing exactly what Joker intends to do there.

That changes how Gotham responds. Instead of evacuating the entire city after another vague threat, police could place plainclothes teams around several likely access points and monitor movement without making the operation obvious. Batman could watch routes the police can’t cover easily, while L stays far enough away that Joker has no simple way to turn the predicted attack into a direct attempt on him.

Joker would notice something is wrong when his people start running into resistance before the crime has even begun. A vehicle might be followed before it reaches the staging area, one entrance could already have police nearby, or Batman might intercept a courier carrying something that had no public connection to the planned target.

He could still change the plan. Joker is capable of abandoning preparation if the new version of the crime amuses him more, and L would have to account for that without pretending every prediction stays valid. If Joker suddenly switches targets, the resources already moved into place still limit what he can do. A truck full of explosives can be redirected, but it can’t instantly become a completely different weapon. People stationed across one side of Gotham still have travel time if he sends them somewhere else.

L would follow those constraints instead of chasing the new public threat immediately. Suppose Joker announces an attack across town after realizing the original area is compromised. Most of the police would want to move everything toward the new target, while L would keep enough surveillance on the first staging routes to see what actually changes. If several vehicles suddenly leave and head east, then the new threat may be real. If nothing moves, Joker may only be trying to pull the police away.

Eventually, one prediction would work well enough that part of the attack is stopped before Joker wants it to start. Several henchmen could be arrested, a major explosive device might be found early, and one of the escape routes could be blocked before Joker reaches it.
Joker would respond by creating several credible leads that all look useful, then build different outcomes around whichever one the investigation acts on first.

L would expect that shift, so he wouldn’t let the task force move as one group every time a clue appears. One lead could be checked by a small team, another could stay under surveillance without being touched, and a third might be ignored publicly while Batman investigates it separately. That gives Joker fewer clean reactions to study because he can’t tell whether L believed a clue just from seeing police activity around it.

Joker would probably start targeting investigators once those games stop producing enough. He wouldn’t need to know where L sleeps to make the case personal because detectives, evidence technicians, and anyone carrying instructions from L become easier targets. A kidnapped officer could be placed into a situation where saving them requires the police to abandon surveillance somewhere else, forcing L to choose how much of his investigation he is willing to sacrifice for one person.

L wouldn’t treat the hostage as expendable, but he also wouldn’t give Joker the exact reaction he wants. He could send Batman toward the hostage while keeping the main surveillance operation running, then use the kidnapping itself to study how Joker moved someone through the city without being seen. If the officer disappeared from one district and appears hours later across town, cameras and traffic records between those points become another route to examine.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: By now, L would have enough examples to compare the crimes Joker built for himself with the ones he built specifically for the investigation. The difference would probably show up in how much work goes into each part. When Joker genuinely cares about the main attack, the preparation is usually deeper, with better escape routes, more backup options, and more time spent controlling the area. False leads can still be elaborate, but they often exist mainly to provoke a response.

Batman would help confirm those differences on the ground. He could check whether a location has hidden exits, whether explosives are actually wired for use, or whether Joker’s people are behaving like they expect a real operation to happen there. That combination of L’s wider analysis and Batman’s local observation would make false trails much less effective over time. Joker would start changing his approach again once he realizes the fake patterns are being separated from the real ones. He could make a decoy as expensive and carefully prepared as the actual crime, forcing L to consider two serious threats at once. That costs Joker more resources, but it also gives him the kind of uncertainty he wants.

L would answer by looking at what can’t be duplicated easily within the preparation window of the specific operation Joker is building. Joker can burn henchmen, abandon suppliers, and change methods between crimes, but once a large plan is already underway he may temporarily depend on 1 available driver, 1 chemical shipment, or 1 usable escape route that can't be replaced instantly without delaying the attack. The closer L gets to those short-term logistical bottlenecks, the more useful the investigation becomes.

One arrested henchman could give L another break without needing to know Joker’s plan. Maybe the man only knows where he picked up equipment and where he was told to wait. L could compare that location against the recent movement of other crews involved in the current operation and identify a temporary staging area several of them are converging on.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Once Joker understands that L is becoming harder to manipulate from a distance, he’d start trying to force him into the open. A direct threat against L wouldn't work well because Joker doesn’t know enough about where he is, and announcing that he wants the detective would only make L more careful. A better approach would be creating a crime that needs L’s presence to make sense.

Joker could leave a message containing information that was never public, something taken from one of L’s private deductions or from a meeting only a few people attended. That would tell L the investigation has been compromised somewhere, while also making it clear that Joker wants him to notice.

The message could point toward a location with a deadline attached, but L wouldn't simply go there because Joker asked. He’d first work out how the private information escaped. If only five people knew a specific theory and the message references it directly, those five connections become more important than the location itself.

That investigation might reveal a bug, a compromised officer, or someone who unknowingly passed information through another person. L could remove that leak before Joker realizes it has been found, then continue feeding limited information through the same channel to see what Joker does with it.

Suppose the compromised channel receives a false claim that L plans to personally inspect 1 of 3 locations. Joker could prepare an attack there because he thinks he finally knows where L will be, while L watches the area remotely and tracks everyone who arrives before the supposed meeting.

Joker would probably expect some chance of deception, so he may send people ahead rather than appear immediately. L would let that happen. Every vehicle, courier, and piece of equipment moving toward the location helps identify where the operation came from.

Batman could follow 1 of those routes backward instead of waiting at the decoy site. That might lead to a secondary building where Joker is actually coordinating the attack, giving L something he hasn't had before: a location connected to Joker while the crime is still being prepared. Joker could still escape if he realizes what happened in time, but the distance between him and the investigation would be much smaller now. L would also know that Joker reacted to false information placed through a channel the real task force no longer trusts, confirming that the channel is leaking information into Joker's network without yet proving exactly which person or mechanism carries it to him. That gives L a controlled channel he can keep exploiting while Batman traces the physical chain backward.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: After the failed attempt to draw L out, Joker’s network would be under much heavier pressure. Several staging areas are compromised, at least one information source has been identified, and the police now know more about how his crews move equipment before attacks. Joker can still disappear into Gotham, but building another large operation without touching any of those systems becomes harder.

L would use that pressure instead of rushing toward an arrest. He could keep watching the remaining suppliers and routes while making it look like the task force is focused on something else. Joker would have to choose between delaying his next crime or using resources he knows may already be watched, and either choice gives L something useful.

Joker would probably keep moving because disappearing for too long gives L control over the pace of the case, which is exactly what Joker hates. He’d start assembling another attack with fewer trusted people and more direct involvement, which increases the chance that someone catches him on camera, tracks his vehicle, or sees him near a staging location.

By watching the remaining network, L could first establish what Joker has already committed to the current operation: explosive components moving through one route, a large vehicle being stolen or acquired through another, and several people disappearing in circumstances that suggest they are being held as hostages. L would compare those observed resources against the locations still available to Joker. Any site that can’t hide the explosives, vehicle, and hostages can be eliminated, while access roads, building size, distance from likely targets, and available exits keep shrinking the map.

Batman could inspect the final few areas without making the police presence obvious. If one contains fresh tire marks, recently disturbed locks, stolen power equipment, or signs that people have been living there temporarily, the search becomes much narrower.

L would instead watch for the moment Joker has the least flexibility. If vehicles arrive carrying the final equipment, several known henchmen enter, and communication around the site suddenly increases, then the operation is close enough to starting that Joker probably can’t abandon everything without losing the plan.

The arrest still wouldn’t be simple because Joker would have prepared for someone eventually finding him, but L would finally be attacking a real operation before Joker controls the entire scene. The difference now is that the investigation has reached him during preparation, where all the supposedly random parts of his crimes are still sitting together in one place.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: By the time L moves on the final location, he’d already know that simply surrounding the building won’t be enough. Joker has had too many opportunities to prepare exits, traps, hostages, and some kind of distraction designed to split the response. L would keep the outer perimeter quiet at first and have Batman confirm which entrances are actually being used before police close anything off. The goal would be to avoid giving Joker enough warning to abandon the entire setup before anyone gets close.

Inside the building, Joker would probably have everything arranged so that entering too quickly creates another problem somewhere else. One room could contain hostages, another could hold explosives connected to a timer, and one of the exits might be wired specifically to punish anyone trying to block it. L would expect that kind of structure because Joker has spent the entire investigation trying to force people into choices where every option looks bad. Instead of committing everyone to the same problem, he’d divide the response around what they already know. Batman could handle the part of the building that requires direct entry while bomb technicians work from whatever access point gives them the safest route to the devices.

Joker would realize the trap is closing once his outside contacts stop responding or one of the routes suddenly goes silent. That gives him a limited amount of time to decide whether he can still finish the attack, escape, or turn the raid into the real crime. He’d probably choose the third option because it lets him keep control of the story even after L finds him. If he can force Batman or the police into causing the casualties themselves, then getting located doesn’t feel like losing.

L would already be watching for that. He’d have every instruction from Joker checked against the physical evidence inside the building before anyone acts on it, especially if Joker starts claiming that one door, one hostage, or one device has to be handled immediately. By this point, L has seen too many false deadlines and planted choices to accept any of them at face value. The pressure would still be enormous because some of Joker’s threats would be real. L can’t assume every bomb is fake just because Joker likes deception, and he can’t leave hostages in danger while searching for the perfect answer. He’d have to make decisions with incomplete information, which is exactly where Joker is strongest.

If Joker can create enough simultaneous problems, L’s advantage in analysis starts shrinking because the case becomes less about deduction and more about how fast people on the ground can act. Batman would be essential there because he can physically reach threats L can only identify from a distance. L could tell him which route is most likely to be real, which device matches the bomb-maker they’ve been tracking, and which supposed escape route doesn’t fit the preparation they observed, but Bruce still has to execute those decisions under pressure. That cooperation would probably keep the situation from collapsing. One of Joker’s decoys could be ignored, a real device could be disabled before the timer runs out, and police could secure enough exits that his movement becomes much more limited. Joker would still try slipping through a maintenance route or service tunnel he kept hidden for exactly this situation. L would have prepared for that possibility by looking at the building itself before the raid. Any exit that connects to an alley, utility corridor, sewer access point, or neighboring structure would already be marked as a possible escape. L would have every physically viable route quietly monitored without visibly sealing them too early, while Batman stays mobile enough to intercept once Joker commits to one. Officers could remain far enough back that Joker doesn't see the trap until his movement reveals which exit he is actually using.

Joker could fight, trigger another distraction, or try using a hostage as cover, but he’d be operating with fewer options than he normally has because L spent the entire case cutting those options down before the arrest attempt began. His suppliers are compromised, his staging areas are known, his information leak is gone, and several of his escape routes are already being watched.

The capture itself probably wouldn’t feel clean. Joker could still manage to injure people, damage part of the building, or turn one of the final traps into a last-minute problem before Batman gets him under control. L would accept that because the standard for winning against Joker can’t be preventing every possible consequence once the operation is already active. What matters is whether the investigation reached him early enough to stop the larger plan and put him in custody.

He wouldn’t catch Joker by figuring out some perfect psychological formula that makes every future crime predictable. He’d catch him by reducing the number of places, people, and resources Joker can use until one of his plans becomes visible before it starts. Joker can keep changing the performance, but every large operation still creates a physical trail somewhere. OUTRO L could catch Joker, but he’d have a much harder time than he did with criminals whose behavior follows a cleaner pattern. Joker’s ability to change plans, plant clues, and deliberately react to the investigation would ruin any method that depends too heavily on predicting motive. L’s best chance would come from ignoring most of that and focusing on preparation. Vehicles have to move, explosives have to come from somewhere, henchmen have to be recruited, and locations have to be prepared before Joker can turn any of it into a spectacle. Once L starts connecting those pieces across multiple attacks, Joker’s options gradually shrink.

Joker would still make the investigation dangerous because he’d realize what L is doing and start designing crimes around him. That means L could absolutely be manipulated, injured, or even killed if Joker gets enough information about where he is. With Batman and Gotham police handling the physical side of the case, though, L has enough distance and enough evidence to keep narrowing the search without exposing himself too early.

So the answer is yes. L could locate and catch the Joker during an active investigation, although he probably wouldn't ever make him fully predictable. That doesn't mean L permanently solves Gotham's separate problem of keeping Joker contained afterward or guarantees that Joker could never escape custody again.

scripts.title: Could L Catch Walter White

sections.name: INTRO
paras: L wouldn’t know Walter White was Heisenberg when he entered the case. He’d start with the same thing everyone else had: an unusually pure blue meth showing up through an operation that kept changing hands without the product disappearing.

The chemistry would narrow the field first. Whoever was making it understood far more than a normal street cook, but the people moving it didn’t fit that profile. Jesse Pinkman would stand out almost immediately because he was close to the product, close to several people who died around it, and clearly involved in the business, while still not looking like the person capable of producing meth at that level.

That would push L toward the people around Jesse rather than Jesse himself. Once he starts looking at who had the chemistry background, who had access to lab equipment, and who suddenly had strange gaps in their routine around the same time Heisenberg appeared, Walter would eventually end up on the list.

The problem for Walter is that L wouldn't need to prove everything at once. He’d be willing to suspect Walt long before the police had enough to arrest him, then start testing that suspicion directly.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: L wouldn't be brought in because the DEA suddenly decides a meth cook deserves the world’s greatest detective. He'd become interested once the blue product keeps appearing after the people distributing it change. Tuco Salamanca can disappear, smaller dealers can get arrested, and different crews can move the meth, yet the same unusually pure product keeps coming back. To L, that suggests the chemist is more stable than the network around him, which makes finding the person who actually knows the chemistry more useful than chasing whoever happens to be selling it that month.

Once L shows federal investigators why the stable chemist may matter more than the changing distribution network, he agrees to consult through a tightly controlled federal liaison arrangement. The DEA still handles subpoenas, records requests, surveillance, and anything requiring official authority; L supplies the investigative strategy and decides which patterns are worth testing.He’d start with the lab work. The purity immediately tells him the manufacturer has real chemical knowledge, while the consistency tells him the process isn’t being improvised by somebody learning from a recipe. Jesse Pinkman would still become one of the first obvious names because he has a history of cooking meth and keeps appearing close to people connected with the product. L would look at him seriously, but Jesse’s background wouldn't fit the level of work coming out of the lab. Jesse can cook, especially after working with Walt, but nothing in his education or earlier product explains why he would suddenly start producing meth at a level that surprises professional chemists.

The stronger lead would already be sitting in the DEA's evidence. Equipment from the J. P. Wynne High School chemistry lab was found connected to the meth investigation early in the case, and the inventory issue had already brought Hank to the school, where Walter White was the chemistry teacher responsible for the lab. Once L compares that theft with Jesse's background, he can learn that Jesse attended the same school and that Walt had taught him chemistry years earlier. That puts a technically qualified person with access to the missing equipment directly into Jesse's past without L having to search blindly for every chemist Jesse might have known.

L still wouldn't decide Walt is Heisenberg from that. A school chemistry department has students, faculty, custodians, substitute teachers, and plenty of people who could have entered the room. Walter also looks terrible as the center of a serious drug operation. He’s an underpaid teacher with a pregnant wife, a teenage son, and no known criminal history, while Jesse is already inside the meth world. L would keep Walt on the list because dismissing him for looking ordinary would be exactly the kind of assumption he doesn't like making.

He’d also notice that the chemistry theft and the appearance of the new product happen in the same general period. If the manufacturer needed basic equipment during the first stages of the operation, somebody with easy access to a chemistry lab becomes more interesting. Walt had that access, understood exactly what was missing, and would’ve known which pieces could be taken without immediately making the entire lab unusable.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Jesse would give L far more to work with because almost every road around Heisenberg seems to pass through him. Krazy 8 and Emilio were connected to Jesse before both disappeared, Tuco later becomes Jesse’s distributor, and the blue meth follows Jesse into each new stage of the business. A normal investigation could easily decide Jesse is either Heisenberg or the person directly underneath him, especially because Jesse has every reason to lie about where the product comes from.

L would be more interested in the gap between Jesse’s role and Jesse’s ability. If Jesse were secretly the chemist, L would expect some sign that he could work at that level before the blue meth appeared. Instead, Jesse's earlier operation with Emilio was much rougher. The quality jumps after Jesse reconnects with someone from outside his normal criminal circle, which gives L a narrower question to answer: who enters Jesse’s life shortly before the product changes? That search could bring Walter back into the investigation without L forcing it. Walt taught Jesse chemistry years earlier, and the 2 would have a reason to recognize each other without appearing in gang records together. L could also learn that Walt had recently been diagnosed with cancer and that his behavior changed around the same period. The diagnosis by itself means nothing criminally, but it gives Walt a new financial pressure and a reason his routine might suddenly become less predictable.

L wouldn’t treat cancer as a motive strong enough to explain Heisenberg. Plenty of people face medical bills without starting meth empires, and Walt’s family would still appear financially strained rather than suddenly wealthy. What would keep L interested is how several weak details keep landing around the same person. Walt has the chemistry background, access to the
stolen equipment, an old connection to Jesse, and a major personal change around the same time Jesse’s product improves.

He could begin checking Walt’s schedule against the earliest known appearances of the meth. That wouldn't produce a perfect match because the DEA doesn’t have an exact timestamp for every cook, but Walt already has unexplained absences from home and work that Skyler notices long before law enforcement does. L wouldn’t automatically have access to private arguments inside the White household, though he could compare school attendance, medical appointments, phone records available through the investigation, and times when Walt simply wasn’t where his normal routine says he should have been.

He’d want surveillance on Jesse before he ever lets Jesse know how much attention he’s getting. The goal wouldn't be catching him with a bag of meth. L would want to see who Jesse meets when he needs product, money, equipment, or advice.
Walter would have no idea yet that his former student is being watched by someone who isn’t satisfied with arresting the dealer.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: L’s first serious jump toward Walt could come from Tuco. By this point, Jesse’s connection to the Salamanca operation is impossible to ignore, and Tuco gives investigators a much clearer picture of how the blue meth is moving. When Hank finds Jesse’s car at Tuco’s location and kills Tuco during the confrontation, the DEA has every reason to focus even harder on Jesse.

L would look at the same event from the other direction. Jesse’s car is sitting at the home of a violent distributor, Jesse is missing, and Tuco has clearly been dealing with whoever controls the product. If Jesse is only one half of the manufacturing operation, then whoever cooks with him may have been pulled into the same crisis.
Walter disappears during that exact period.

His family eventually finds him after the fugue state story, with Walt claiming he wandered off and has no memory of where he had been. L would immediately compare the dates because Walt is already on his list. The coincidence is much stronger than the earlier school evidence. Jesse vanishes during a crisis involving Tuco, Walt disappears at the same time, and both return without giving investigators a truthful account of what happened.

That still doesn’t tell L what actually happened in the desert. He wouldn't know Tuco kidnapped Walt and Jesse unless he finds evidence supporting it, and he couldn't simply announce that the simultaneous disappearances prove they were together. It would make him start treating Walt as
someone worth testing directly rather than another name connected to Jesse through old school records.

L could ask the DEA to reexamine Walt’s fugue state without telling Walt why. Medical records and the circumstances of his return wouldn't necessarily disprove it, but L would want to know whether there was any independent evidence that Walt had actually spent those missing days wandering around Albuquerque. The lack of a clear trail would leave the story dependent heavily on Walt’s own account.

He'd also look more carefully at Walt’s car, phone activity, and movements around the disappearance if any records are still available. Even partial gaps could matter because L isn’t trying to prove the entire case yet. He’s trying to decide whether Walt belongs close enough to Jesse that the 2 disappearances should be treated as connected.

Walter would probably handle a normal follow up interview well enough. He can appear embarrassed, sick, overwhelmed, and confused, and all of those things fit what people around him already believe. L wouldn’t expect a confession or some obvious slip. He'd care more about whether Walt gives details that can be independently checked.

The interview could also show L how comfortable Walt becomes when chemistry enters the conversation. Rather than asking him directly whether he can make meth, L could approach the missing school equipment again and ask which pieces would be useful to someone trying to build an improvised lab. Walt could answer accurately because that’s his job, so the knowledge itself wouldn't incriminate him. L would simply be comparing the man in front of him with the manufacturer he’s been building in his head.

By the end of the conversation, L still wouldn’t have evidence strong enough to accuse Walt of anything. He would have a teacher who fits the technical profile, knew Jesse before the investigation, had access to equipment connected to the first cook, and disappeared during the same window Jesse became entangled with Tuco.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Walter would become harder to follow once Gus Fring enters the operation because Gus gives him exactly the kind of separation L has been looking for. The meth no longer has to move through Jesse’s obvious street connections, and the distribution becomes cleaner, larger, and much less dependent on the person actually cooking it. If L follows the product from the street upward, Gus can easily look like the center of everything.

L would take Gus seriously. Los Pollos Hermanos gives him legitimate infrastructure, Gus has connections that can hide movement and money, and his public life is carefully built to survive normal scrutiny. Once the DEA begins circling Gus, L wouldn’t ignore the possibility that Heisenberg is simply a chemist working inside Gus’s organization rather than the man running the entire operation.

Gale’s death would make the case more complicated instead of solving it. The notebook and laboratory evidence can connect him to advanced chemistry, while Jesse’s involvement around his murder pulls the investigation back toward the same group L has already been watching. L could reasonably consider the possibility that Gale was Heisenberg, or that he worked with the real Heisenberg, until the product continues after Gale is gone.

That continuation would be one of the strongest clues L gets. If the same blue meth keeps appearing at the same standard after Gale’s death, then Gale wasn’t the only person capable of making it. Jesse is still around, but L already has reasons to doubt Jesse developed that skill on his own. Walter is still alive, still connected to Jesse, and still sitting outside the criminal network on paper.

L could begin building a timeline of who survives every collapse around the product. Krazy 8 disappears, Tuco dies, Gale dies, Gus eventually becomes a target, and the meth operation keeps rebuilding itself around different people. Walter’s name barely appears in the criminal files, yet his connection to Jesse continues through the entire period.

Walter also begins making mistakes that are harder to explain away as ordinary family problems. His money situation changes, his behavior becomes more erratic, and people close to him start seeing a version of him that doesn’t match the mild teacher L first interviewed. L wouldn't have Skyler explaining everything to him, but financial investigators could still become useful once there’s enough cause to start looking at whether Walt’s household is spending beyond his salary.

The car wash would draw attention eventually because it gives the White family a legitimate business capable of absorbing cash. Buying a business isn’t evidence of meth trafficking, especially when the Whites can claim gambling winnings as the source of their money, but L would want the gambling story checked rather than accepted. If the timeline of the supposed winnings can’t be independently supported, it becomes another part of Walt’s life that only makes sense because the family says it does.
By this point L probably wouldn’t call Walter Heisenberg publicly. He’d be much closer to believing it privately, while still lacking the kind of evidence that survives a courtroom.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: L would start testing Walt more aggressively once Gus becomes the main target of the DEA. Gus gives Walter an unusual advantage because law enforcement has a much more convincing criminal mastermind standing directly in front of them, and almost every major piece of evidence points toward Gus’s organization rather than Walt’s house.

L could use that assumption against Walter. Instead of telling the DEA that Walt is his leading candidate, he could allow the investigation to keep treating Gus as the center while quietly watching what Walt does whenever pressure increases around the superlab. If Walt really is the cook, major changes around Gus should affect his behavior even when he has no legitimate reason to know anything is happening.

One test could involve information that L controls. He could arrange for a small piece of false investigative information to reach a limited group, such as a claim that the DEA has identified a surviving witness who can connect Jesse to the superlab. The goal wouldn't be tricking Walt into confessing or identifying the cook immediately. L would watch whether Jesse suddenly changes plans, whether Saul’s people begin moving, or whether somebody inside Gus’s operation reacts to information that should have remained confined to law enforcement. If the criminal network reacts at all, that gives L proof that controlled information can reach whoever is making decisions inside it.

Walter’s response might not point back to him cleanly because Saul and Mike give him layers L has to work through. Walter could tell Saul, Saul could contact somebody else, and by the time anything visible happens, L may only know that his false information leaked into the criminal network. That would still tell him the network has a way of reacting to pressure unusually fast.

That first reaction would not tell L which person inside the network received the information, so he would save the more specific test for later, once he has a better map of the people around Walt, Jesse, Saul, and Gus.

Walter would eventually notice that the investigation feels different. Hank tends to chase physical evidence and people he can connect directly to the drug trade, while L would keep asking questions that seem unrelated until Walt realizes they're all touching parts of his life. His school, Jesse, the missing equipment, the fugue state, his finances, and the timing around Tuco would stop feeling like separate coincidences once the same investigator keeps returning to them.

That realization would make Walter dangerous earlier than L might expect. Walt has already killed when he believed his survival depended on it, and he wouldn't assume L can be handled by giving him another convincing lie. He’d want to know who L is, how much he knows, where he’s staying, and whether Saul or Mike can get close enough to learn anything useful.

Saul could start digging through contacts, but L’s anonymity makes that difficult. L doesn’t have a normal public identity, and he wouldn’t need to operate from a local DEA office where Walter can simply follow him home. Mike would have a better chance because he understands surveillance and counter surveillance, although even he would need L to expose a routine before he has something to follow.
L would expect some response once he starts applying pressure. He wouldn't know exactly what Walter is capable of yet, but Jesse’s network has already touched people who disappear
or die when they become dangerous. That would make L careful about revealing how strongly he suspects Walt until he has a way to turn that suspicion into evidence.
He would need Walter to make another mistake while L is watching.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: L would get the mistake he needs from Walter’s need to stay ahead of everyone around him. Once the DEA’s attention on Gus gets serious, Walt can’t just sit back and hope the investigation never touches the lab. He starts making decisions faster, pushing Jesse harder, and trying to predict what Gus, Mike, Hank, and the DEA are going to do before they do it. That makes him more dangerous, but it also gives L more chances to watch him react to information he shouldn't have.

L could arrange a controlled leak about the superlab, something narrow enough that only the real cook would care about it. He might have the DEA circulate an internal claim that investigators recovered chemical residue from an old piece of equipment and believe the manufacturing process has a very specific weakness that could identify whoever designed it. The claim would be false, but L wouldn’t need Walt to believe the science forever. He’d only need him to believe the DEA is close enough that leaving certain equipment or records in place becomes dangerous.

Walter's reaction would probably travel through Saul instead of going directly back to him. Saul could suddenly start asking Mike about old equipment, Jesse could get told to stay away from certain locations, or somebody connected to the operation could move materials that had been sitting untouched for months. L wouldn’t pretend that one reaction proves Walt heard the leak, but if the movement begins shortly after the false information is planted, he’d know somebody close to the cook is changing behavior because of it.

That would push him toward Saul Goodman. Saul is publicly connected to Jesse, known for representing criminals, and keeps appearing around people tied to the meth business. L would see him as a bridge rather than the mastermind, because Saul doesn’t have the chemistry background and his role makes far more sense as someone cleaning up problems after they happen. He could have Saul watched carefully, then compare who enters his office or contacts him during the exact periods when the meth operation is under pressure.

Walter would be harder to catch because he has legitimate reasons to know Saul. The car wash, family finances, and Jesse could all provide excuses for contact if investigators ever ask. L wouldn't waste time treating a visit to Saul’s office like a smoking gun. He’d look for the moments when Walter contacts Saul immediately after events that only someone inside the meth operation should care about.

The strongest opportunity would come after Hank gets close to Gus. Walt knows enough about Hank’s investigation through family conversations to understand what the DEA is seeing, while also knowing what Gus is planning from the other side. L would notice that Walter sits in an unusually useful position between both worlds even though nobody around him thinks of him that way. He can hear what Hank is working on at dinner, then pass information into the criminal network through Jesse or Saul without ever appearing in the DEA case file.

L could start monitoring the timing of those conversations. If Hank discusses a new lead with the family and Saul or Jesse changes behavior shortly afterward, Walter becomes much more interesting because he’s one of the few people who could connect those 2 groups without looking suspicious. That still wouldn’t prove he’s the cook, but it would give L a reason to stop treating Walt as somebody who merely knows Jesse and start treating him as a possible source of intelligence for the operation.

Walter would notice the pressure building around Saul before he realizes L is watching him personally. Saul might complain that somebody keeps asking questions about clients, Mike might spot surveillance that doesn’t behave like normal DEA work, and Walt would understand that the investigation is beginning to move through the people he uses to stay hidden.

He'd start changing how he communicates. He could stop calling Saul directly, send Jesse with messages instead, or avoid discussing anything important in places he thinks might be watched. L would expect that once the network starts tightening up, which is why he’d care more about what changes than whether he catches Walter saying something incriminating.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Gus’s death would completely reshape the investigation because it removes the most convincing alternative explanation for everything L has been following. The superlab is destroyed, Gus is dead, and the DEA finally gets proof that Los Pollos Hermanos was tied to a large meth operation. For most investigators, that could look like the case reaching its answer. Gus ran the network, Gale worked in the lab, and the organization collapsed with them.

If blue meth starts appearing again, then the cook survived the destruction of Gus’s operation. Gale is dead, Gus is dead, and the superlab is gone, yet somebody is still able to produce the same product. Jesse remains an obvious possibility, but L has spent enough time looking at Jesse’s history to know that the chemistry improved before Jesse ever had the skill to design the process himself.

Walter becomes much harder to keep in the background once the new operation starts. The timing works against him because his biggest cover has just disappeared, while the product continues anyway. L could compare known periods when Walt was unavailable, Jesse’s movements, and the appearance of new batches. He wouldn’t expect a perfect match, but
repeated overlap would make it harder to explain the relationship as an old teacher occasionally helping a troubled former student.

The new pest control setup would give L a completely different kind of evidence. Instead of one hidden superlab, Walt and Jesse begin cooking in houses being tented for fumigation, which creates a moving pattern of locations. L could recognize that the houses aren’t random once enough product appears around the same time certain pest control jobs happen. The DEA might initially treat the company as a possible distributor or storage front, while L would care about who has the technical skill to turn those temporary spaces into workable labs.

That investigation could bring Vamonos Pest into focus before Walt realizes it. L wouldn't need to raid every house. He could place passive surveillance around a small number of future jobs and wait to see who arrives outside normal working hours. If Walt shows up at even 1 location with Jesse or people connected to Saul, his ability to explain the contact becomes much weaker than another meeting at a lawyer’s office.

Walter would probably sense the danger before he gets photographed carrying lab equipment through somebody's backyard. Mike understands surveillance too well to let the new operation run carelessly if he knows L is still active, and Jesse would already be nervous about being followed. They could vary cars, arrive separately, and use the pest control crew to move equipment so the cook never looks like the person bringing it in.

L would respond by attacking the logistics instead of the people. A meth operation using temporary houses still needs methylamine, glassware, protective equipment, transportation, storage, and a way to move the finished product afterward. None of those pieces has to point directly at Walter, but their movement can reveal when a cook is happening. L could build a calendar from supply thefts, pest jobs, Jesse’s disappearances, Saul’s contacts, and the arrival of blue meth in distribution.
Walter's schedule would begin lining up far too often.

That still wouldn’t be enough to arrest him. A prosecutor would need physical evidence tying Walt to manufacturing, and L would know that a clever suspect can survive a mountain of suspicious coincidences if the government never catches him with the drug, the lab, the money, or a witness willing to talk.
So L would stop trying to make the timeline do all the work and start looking for a way into Walt’s house.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: Walter's home would be difficult to search legally because L still wouldn't have the clean probable cause a judge wants for a warrant. The school equipment, Jesse connection, simultaneous disappearance, strange finances, Saul contact, and cook timing make Walt look worse every month, but most of those facts can still be explained separately. L would know that forcing a bad warrant risks exposing how close he is without giving him anything usable in court.

He could instead test Walter through Hank. By this point, Hank is emotionally invested in finding Heisenberg and has already shown that he can become obsessive when the case gets personal. L wouldn't tell him everything at once because Hank is close to Walt and that relationship creates a leak risk whether Hank realizes it or not. He could give Hank a smaller question, asking him to revisit the missing school equipment and compare Walt’s access with Jesse’s timeline.

Hank would probably resist the idea at first. Walter is his brother in law, has been sick for years, and has spent most of the investigation looking like the last person capable of running a drug empire. L wouldn't try to convince Hank with personality. He’d give him the coincidences in order and ask him to explain why Jesse’s product changes after reconnecting with a chemistry teacher whose lab equipment goes missing, why both men disappear during the Tuco crisis, and why the meth survives every criminal organization built around it.

Hank wouldn't accept it immediately, but he would start noticing things he had previously laughed off. Walt’s sudden money, the gambling story, his strange behavior around the Gus investigation, and the way Jesse keeps returning to the edges of Walt’s life would look different once somebody tells Hank to stop assuming Walt is harmless.

By then, the earlier controlled leaks and surveillance around Saul and Jesse have given L a better map of how sensitive information moves through the network. He could use Hank’s family access for a more targeted test of Walt specifically. He wouldn't ask Hank to search Walt’s house illegally. He could ask him to casually mention a detail that only the investigation knows, then watch the already-mapped contacts around Walt for a reaction.

The detail could involve methylamine. Hank might tell Walt over dinner that the DEA thinks a specific batch can be traced to a storage facility and that agents plan to move on the location within 48 hours. The information would be false, and Walt would have no reason to do anything with it if he isn’t involved.

Walter would recognize the danger almost instantly. He’d know that if the DEA thinks it can trace the methylamine, whatever supply he still has could become evidence. He might call Jesse, Saul, or somebody connected to the operation and tell them to move it.

If the methylamine changes location shortly after Hank tells Walt, L finally gets a piece of behavior that’s much harder to explain away. It still wouldn't prove Walt ordered the movement, but Hank can establish that Walt personally received the false information, while surveillance can test whether the same people L has already linked to Walt and the operation react to that exact fake lead before anyone outside the controlled group should know about it.

Walter would realize there’s a leak test only after the movement happens. Once he understands that Hank gave him information designed to trigger a reaction, he’d know somebody has moved past general suspicion.
That would change Walter's priorities immediately. Finding L would become more important than protecting the next cook.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: Walter couldn't kill L the way Light could. There’s no supernatural shortcut, and L’s identity isn’t sitting in some public database Saul can pull up. Walter would need to locate him physically, which means using the same criminal network that has already become part of L’s investigation. Mike would be the obvious person to try. He understands surveillance, can follow people without being obvious, and has enough experience to recognize when someone else is running countersurveillance. Walter could tell him that an outside investigator is threatening the entire operation and needs to be identified before the DEA builds a case.

Mike might agree to find out who L is without agreeing to murder him. By this point in the story, Mike has his own reasons to dislike Walt and wouldn’t automatically follow every order. He could still investigate because knowing who is watching them protects everyone involved.

L would assume somebody will try to follow him once the methylamine test works. Instead of hiding completely, he could use that response to expose who Walter turns to when he feels threatened. A car that repeatedly appears around L’s meetings, a burner phone activated shortly after Walt realizes the trap, or Saul suddenly asking questions about an investigator nobody publicly named could connect Walt’s reaction to the same network L has been mapping for months.

Once Walter realizes L is building the case around the identity of the indispensable chemist, he has another defensive option: push Jesse as the alternative. Jesse can eventually reproduce extremely high-quality meth, so Walt could try to make the investigation believe the former student was the real cook all along or had become capable of replacing whoever started the process.L wouldn't dismiss it. He’d compare when Jesse actually reached that level with when the blue meth first appeared. If Jesse can reproduce Walt’s formula later, that doesn’t explain who gave him the method at the beginning. Gale can explain part of Gus’s period, but he enters after the product is already established and dies before it disappears.

Walter could then try pushing blame toward Mike or the remnants of Gus’s network, which would work even worse as an explanation for the chemistry. Mike can organize people, move money, and protect a distribution system, but nothing about him explains the product itself.

The more Walter tries to give L a different Heisenberg, the more he risks showing that he understands exactly which parts of the case need alternative explanations. L would be careful with that because smart suspects can guess what investigators are thinking, but Walt’s responses could still reveal which evidence scares him most.

L’s best chance to finish the case would come through Jesse. Jesse has been the human connection running through almost every stage of the operation, and unlike Walt, he eventually reaches points where guilt matters more to him than protecting the business. L wouldn't approach him like a normal DEA interrogation and demand that he confess to everything. He
could show Jesse how many people around the operation are already dead and make it clear that Walt is increasingly willing to let other people take the risk for him.

L could keep pressure on Jesse and make clear how many deaths now surround Walt, but that still may not be enough to make Jesse fully cooperate. One possible trigger is the same realization that breaks Jesse from Walt in the original chain of events: if the altered timeline still reaches the point where Walt uses Saul to make Jesse disappear, Huell taking Jesse's marijuana can make Jesse realize Huell could have lifted the missing ricin cigarette the same way, letting him reconstruct Walt's manipulation around Brock. But L cannot count on that exact sequence surviving. His strategy is to keep pressure on the increasingly fractured relationship and be ready if Walt's lies, another betrayal, or evidence Jesse encounters finally gives Jesse a reason to turn. If that break comes, Jesse knows where they cooked, how Walt made the product, how they worked with Gus, how the new operation runs, and where physical evidence might still exist. His testimony alone would need corroboration because he’s a criminal accomplice with every reason to bargain, but he can tell L exactly where to look.
Walter would understand immediately how dangerous Jesse becomes once he stops answering calls.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: Once Jesse starts cooperating, L’s problem changes from identifying Heisenberg to building a case that can survive Walter’s lawyers. Jesse could give investigators details nobody outside the operation should know, including the original RV, the early cooks, the superlab, the pest control houses, and Walt’s role in designing the process. L would use those details to find evidence rather than asking a jury to trust Jesse on faith.

L wouldn’t need every murder around the meth business to convict Walt as Heisenberg. Proving conspiracy to manufacture and distribute methamphetamine, possession with intent to distribute, money laundering, and related offenses could already put Walt away for decades. The killings would matter where investigators can tie him directly to them, but L wouldn't weaken the case by treating every death around Gus, Mike, or the cartel as something Walter automatically ordered.
Walter would still have one final option before the arrest...and that is to kill L.

By now, though, arranging that becomes extremely difficult. L knows Walter is capable of using other people, Jesse is cooperating, and Mike may no longer be willing to protect Walt. Saul is good at making problems disappear legally or financially, but hiring somebody to murder the investigator leading a federal case creates another trail Walter has to trust somebody else to hide.
If Walter becomes desperate enough to target L personally, L could potentially exploit that too. He might

deliberately present a small apparent opening, such as making it look like he'll be alone at a specific location with important evidence, while treating the entire situation as a monitored trap. But L wouldn't need Walter to take that bait to finish the case.

Walter has fallen for this kind of pressure before when pride gets involved, so it remains possible that he takes the opening if he believes removing L gives him one last chance to discredit Jesse and survive the investigation.

L wouldn’t actually be alone. The location could be under surveillance with federal agents nearby, while Walter’s arrival becomes the final piece the prosecution never had. If he brings a weapon, attempts to destroy evidence, or openly discusses why L needs to die, the case gets stronger in a way that has nothing to do with interpreting old coincidences.

Whether Walter takes the bait or ignores it entirely, L could still have enough once Jesse’s information is corroborated. Physical evidence from the cook locations, financial records, communications through Saul, surveillance from the later operation, and the controlled leak tests could build a case that finally connects Walter to the chemistry and the organization around it.

So L probably would catch Walter White. It wouldn’t happen because L looks at him once and somehow knows he’s Heisenberg. Walter’s ordinary public life would protect him for a long time, Gus would give him an excellent layer of cover, and Jesse would initially look far more connected to the meth than Walt does. L would need months of watching the product survive different organizations before Walt becomes the only chemist who keeps fitting every version of the operation.

Walter would also realize he’s being hunted before L has enough to arrest him, which gives him chances to lie, move evidence, redirect suspicion, and eventually consider murder. Against most investigators, that might be enough.

L’s advantage is that he’d be willing to sit on a suspicion while he keeps testing it. Walter tends to survive because people either underestimate him or move too early without understanding the whole operation. L would do neither, and once Jesse finally turns against Walt, the evidence he needs would start coming together very quickly.

scripts.title: Could L Outsmart Jigsaw

sections.name: INTRO
paras: L wouldn't know who Jigsaw is when he enters the case, but he’d notice pretty quickly that the murders are more organized than they look.

The victims are being chosen for specific reasons, the traps are built around details from their lives, and whoever is behind them has enough time, money, and IQ to prepare everything without getting caught. L would start by working backward from those choices, looking at what Jigsaw would need to know about each victim and where that information could’ve come from.

John would eventually realize L is getting closer than the police ever did, and from that point, he’d start planning around L specifically. If Jonn captures L before L can identify him and prove it, then L has to survive one of Jigsaw’s traps himself.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: L wouldn’t begin by trying to guess who Jigsaw is. He’d begin with the cases that already exist and look for the parts investigators have been treating separately.

The first thing he’d notice is how personal the games are. Jigsaw isn’t choosing random victims and placing them into whatever trap happens to be available. The device, the rules, and the reason the victim was chosen usually connect back to something specific about that person. Amanda Young was struggling with addiction when she was placed in the Reverse Bear Trap, while Dr. Lawrence Gordon’s game was built around his family and the life he had been neglecting. Whoever is designing these games knows far more about the victims than someone picking names from the news.

L would have the police rebuild every known victim’s life from the months before they disappeared. He’d want medical records, employment, arrests, treatment history, financial problems, family connections, and anywhere they regularly spent time. He wouldn’t expect 1 obvious connection between everyone because Jigsaw’s reasons for choosing them are too personal for that. Instead, L would look at how a stranger could have learned enough to judge them in the first place.

That would quickly separate Jigsaw from most killers L has investigated. Someone has to watch these people, understand what they've done, decide what lesson they supposedly need, build a device around that lesson, find somewhere to run the game, then move the victim there without being seen. Every new test creates another chance to leave something behind.

L would be especially interested in the traps themselves. They aren’t improvised devices built from whatever happens to be nearby. Even the simpler ones require someone who understands mechanisms, timing, restraints, load, and how much punishment a human body can survive before the game becomes impossible. L wouldn’t immediately conclude that Jigsaw is an engineer, but engineering, construction, industrial maintenance, and similar work would become useful areas to examine.

The medical side would matter too. Some traps require detailed knowledge of anatomy, and the killer clearly understands pain, blood loss, and how much time a victim can be given before an injury becomes fatal. That doesn’t prove Jigsaw is a doctor because someone could learn those things elsewhere, but L would keep medical knowledge somewhere in the profile rather than forcing himself into one profession too early.

He’d also notice something about the killer’s behavior that the police already understand but may not be using effectively. Jigsaw wants the victims to hear him explain the game. The tapes are part of the ritual, and the instructions usually tell the person what they did, what will happen, and what they need to do to survive. John genuinely sees these tests as opportunities for people to change, even though the methods are horrific.

L would take that seriously because it means Jigsaw needs the victim to understand why they were chosen. He isn’t simply trying to hide a murder behind an elaborate machine. The explanation matters to him.

L would have every tape transcribed and compared. He’d look at repeated words, the way Jigsaw talks about survival, whether certain ideas become more common over time, and how much personal knowledge appears in each recording. He’d also compare when the recordings were likely made with when each victim disappeared. If several tapes were prepared well before the kidnapping, then surveillance on the victims probably started much earlier than police assumed.

He wouldn't share every conclusion with the full department either. L has never needed investigators to know everything he knows, and the Jigsaw case gives him a good reason to hold information back. If the killer has any connection to law enforcement, leaking the wrong conclusion could destroy the investigation before L knows who he’s looking for.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Once L has the victim files together, he’d start looking for places where their lives overlap with the kind of person Jigsaw would need to be.

Lawrence Gordon would stand out immediately because he had already been investigated as a Jigsaw suspect. His penlight was found at a crime scene, and detectives Tapp and Sing questioned him before eventually learning that he wasn't the killer. L wouldn't accept the planted evidence at face value, especially after seeing how deliberately every other part of the games is arranged.

The penlight would tell him something useful anyway. Whoever planted it either knew Gordon personally or had access to somewhere Gordon used it. That means L would go through Gordon’s professional life in far more detail than the original investigation did.

He’d want the hospital staff, patients, former patients, anyone with access to Gordon’s office, and anyone who could have learned enough about his family to build the bathroom game around him. Gordon would have too many patients for L to treat every name equally, so he’d filter them against the profile he had already built. Patients with mechanical, engineering, construction, or industrial experience would receive more attention, especially if they had also experienced a severe medical crisis or personal trauma and had access to properties where a game could be prepared. This is where John Kramer could first appear in L’s files without immediately becoming the main suspect.

John was Gordon’s patient and had terminal cancer, which already puts him near one of the people Jigsaw targeted. That alone wouldn’t be enough for L. A doctor has hundreds of patients, and being sick doesn’t make someone a serial killer.

L would keep going. John’s professional background would become much more interesting once L checks it. Kramer was a civil engineer and property developer, which fits the mechanical side of the traps far better than most people connected to Gordon. His work also involved large properties and redevelopment projects, giving him familiarity with industrial spaces that could potentially be used without attracting attention.
He’d want a 2nd connection that has nothing to do with Gordon.

That could come from Amanda. Amanda survived one of Jigsaw’s games, which makes her extremely valuable to L because she’s one of the few people who has experienced the process and lived. He’d study everything surrounding her kidnapping rather than only asking what she remembers from inside the trap. Where was she spending time beforehand? Who knew about her addiction? Who might have seen her at her worst? Was she attending treatment anywhere?

That path would eventually lead toward Jill Tuck’s clinic. Treatment and intake records would give L a documented connection between Amanda and the recovery facility, while a deeper look at the clinic’s history would expose the incident involving Cecil that destroyed John and Jill’s family. Jill ran the facility for people struggling with addiction, and John had a direct personal connection to it through his marriage to her.

L still wouldn’t know the full story immediately, but now John Kramer is connected to two important areas of the case through completely different routes. He was Gordon’s cancer patient, and his former wife’s clinic connects him to the world Amanda came from.

That would move him much higher on L’s list. L would then look into John himself instead of assuming his background ends with engineering and cancer. He’d find the death of John and Jill's unborn child, the collapse of their marriage, the cancer diagnosis, and John’s suicide attempt. In the Saw timeline, those events are central to the philosophy he later builds around people failing to appreciate their lives.
For L, the suicide attempt would be particularly important because Jigsaw's tapes repeatedly focus on survival and whether someone has the will to keep living.

Once John’s engineering background, connection to Gordon, link to Jill’s clinic, cancer diagnosis, and suicide attempt are all sitting in the same file, L would have enough to take him seriously as a suspect, but not enough to accuse him. He’d keep John under surveillance and start looking for something physical that connects him directly to one of the games.

That distinction matters for L because he’d rather watch a strong suspect behave naturally than confront him with a theory that isn’t finished. John may also be terminally ill, which means L can’t assume he has years to slowly build the case. If Kramer is Jigsaw, every day spent waiting could mean another game.

L would have Watari help run the surveillance through people John doesn’t know. He’d track where John goes, what buildings he has access to, what materials he purchases, and how often his movements line up with disappearances connected to new Jigsaw cases.
The police would also receive one instruction that seems strange at first and that is don’t approach Kramer.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: John has spent enough time studying police behavior to know what a normal Jigsaw investigation looks like. Detectives visit crime scenes, follow physical evidence, question people connected to the victim, then react when another game begins. L wouldn't work that way for long.

Victims from older cases would suddenly be investigated again. People who were never considered important would be questioned about where the victims spent time months before their disappearances.
