Police would quietly request property records, construction history, medical access, and information that doesn’t seem directly connected to the latest body.

John could begin testing the investigation without exposing himself. The next game might include a clue that points toward one type of background, perhaps something suggesting medical knowledge more strongly than engineering, and he could watch where police attention goes afterward.

He already knows Jigsaw carefully controls what investigators find, so any evidence that suddenly narrows the suspect pool too neatly would become suspicious by itself. Instead of moving resources toward the obvious lead, L might deliberately allow the police to appear interested while privately continuing surveillance on Kramer.

That gives L another piece of information. If the next Jigsaw game suddenly reacts to a line of investigation that was never made public, then someone around the case is leaking information or Jigsaw has another way to watch the police. L would reduce the number of people receiving his real conclusions and begin giving different pieces of information to different investigators.

He has used similar information control tactics before because it lets him identify where a leak is coming from. Here, the goal wouldn’t necessarily be catching a police accomplice right away. L would be watching which piece of false information Jigsaw responds to.

Suppose 1 group is told that investigators recovered a distinctive fabricated material signature from a trap, another is told about a fake victim connection that never existed, and a 3rd is given a false property lead. None of those details would appear anywhere else in the investigation. If the next Jigsaw game specifically reacts to one of those invented details, L now knows that information could only have reached John through the group that received it.

John would eventually realize he’s being tested too. That’s when the case becomes much more personal for him. He’d want to know who is controlling the investigation, and L’s secrecy would make that difficult. L doesn’t normally appear publicly, uses Watari as an intermediary, and can work with law enforcement without giving the outside world his real name. John could learn that an outside detective has joined the case without having a face or address to attach to him.

So John would investigate the police instead. He has already shown that he can gather detailed information on the people he chooses, and he'd start watching who receives unusual orders, which officers suddenly change routines, and where information seems to be coming from. If one detective leaves a meeting and immediately contacts Watari through a protected channel, John doesn’t need to break the encryption to understand that the contact matters.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: The surveillance on John would eventually start producing stronger evidence.

L wouldn't expect to catch him dragging a victim into a van or carrying a trap through the front door of a warehouse. John is far too careful for that. Instead, L would look for small things that don’t make sense when they’re placed together.

John may visit industrial properties that appear abandoned or unused. He may purchase mechanical components that seem harmless individually but match pieces recovered from traps. He may disappear for periods that line up with preparation before known games.

1 suspicious purchase proves almost nothing. Several purchases followed by a victim disappearing becomes more useful, especially if the materials resemble mechanisms recovered later. The same applies to locations. John having access to one empty building isn’t evidence of murder, but repeated links between his property history and areas used by Jigsaw would be difficult to ignore.

L would also reconsider John’s cancer. A terminal diagnosis creates urgency. Jigsaw is building complicated games that take enormous time to plan, yet the person behind them behaves as though his work needs to continue quickly. L could reasonably consider whether the killer knows he has limited time left.

That would explain part of the intensity behind the games without proving Kramer is responsible. L would want direct observation before moving. He could arrange for John to be followed after one of his medical appointments, using multiple teams that rotate so no single car stays behind him for too long. If John changes his route repeatedly, stops in unusual places, or begins testing whether he’s being followed, L gets information even if John never goes near a trap location.
John would eventually catch one of the teams.

He doesn’t need L’s level of deduction to notice surveillance when he already suspects someone is watching him. Once he does, he wouldn’t confront the person following him. He’d use them to learn how the surveillance works.
John could drive somewhere ordinary, remain long enough to see who arrives, then leave by a route that forces the teams to switch. Over several days, he could start identifying the pattern.

Instead of following him continuously, L could move toward fixed observation around specific locations already connected to the profile. That gives John fewer opportunities to spot a tail because nobody has to stay directly behind him.

At the same time, L would investigate Jill Tuck. He wouldn't assume she’s involved. Her value is that she may explain John’s personal history, and L could learn far more by speaking with her carefully than by accusing her former husband. Jill could tell investigators about John before the cancer, the loss of Gideon, his emotional decline, and the way his view of life changed afterward.

That would be enough for L to privately treat John Kramer as his leading Jigsaw suspect. He still wouldn’t arrest him. A defense attorney could explain away engineering experience, cancer, property access, and indirect victim connections as coincidence unless police find something physical tying Kramer to a game. L also has to consider the possibility that John isn’t working alone. Some traps require too much preparation for a severely ill man to handle comfortably by himself, and Amanda’s survival gives her a relationship with Jigsaw that deserves another look.

Arresting John too early could leave an accomplice outside destroying evidence or continuing the games. So L would try to force movement without letting John know how much he has. He could increase visible police activity around a property John has used before while leaving another suspected location untouched. If John believes one site is about to be discovered, he may move evidence from it.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: John’s next priority would become finding L himself. He’d already know someone unusually careful is controlling the case because every time he tries to steer the police, the investigation responds differently than expected. The obvious leads attract attention without changing the deeper surveillance, false information stops producing useful reactions, and officers who used to know everything about the case suddenly know only small pieces.

John would work outward from Watari. Watari is one of the few consistent links between L and law enforcement, so anyone watching the investigation closely enough could eventually notice that certain instructions arrive through the same intermediary. John wouldn’t know who Watari really represents at first, but he could follow the relationship rather than the man himself.

He’d study when Watari appears, which officers meet him, and what changes afterward. L would know that Watari is a vulnerability and could deliberately let John learn a little. This is where L could take a risk that most investigators wouldn’t. He might allow a meeting location to become discoverable while preparing surveillance around it, hoping John sends someone to watch. L wouldn’t need John himself to appear. A vehicle, a camera, or a person checking the building could give him another path back toward Jigsaw.

John would expect the meeting to be protected, so he’d avoid personally walking into the trap. If Amanda is already working with him at this point, she could handle part of the observation while appearing unrelated to Kramer. Her history as a known Jigsaw survivor gives her an unusual advantage because police already think of her as someone Jigsaw victimized rather than someone helping him. John’s recruitment of Amanda is part of the established Saw timeline.

L would eventually notice Amanda behaving strangely. He wouldn't immediately decide she’s an accomplice because survivors of extreme trauma can behave unpredictably, but her movements would deserve another look once they start overlapping with parts of the investigation she shouldn't care about.

That creates a second line leading back toward John. L could now be close enough to understand that Kramer may have help without knowing exactly how much Amanda has done. That would make him even less willing to arrest John on suspicion alone.

He may not get L’s real name, but Amanda or another observer could begin building a physical trail around the investigation. They could identify a supposedly secure location where Watari meets an investigator, watch which task-force members leave immediately afterward, then follow those movements to another surveillance point without ever approaching Watari directly. Repeating that process across several meetings could reveal that the same heavily protected location repeatedly correlates with Watari’s appearances and sudden changes in the investigation. John still wouldn’t know L’s real identity, but he could eventually learn his habits, his appearance, and where the hidden investigator is operating.

That’s enough for John to start thinking about a game. He wouldn't want to simply kill L because that goes against how John sees himself. L has to be tested for something, and John would need a reason that fits the philosophy he uses with everyone else.

L gives him 1 very easily. L treats cases like puzzles. He takes enormous risks when he believes those risks improve his chance of proving a theory, and he can become so focused on winning an intellectual battle that he puts himself directly beside people he already suspects of murder. He did exactly that with Light Yagami, keeping his main suspect close because observing him was more valuable than staying safely removed from him.

John wouldn’t build a trap where L has thirty seconds to break a lock with brute force because that tests almost nothing about him. He’d build one where the rules appear simple but the room contains information that changes how those rules should be understood.

Before John can do that, though, he still needs to get L into the room. That would be much harder than abducting an ordinary victim because L already knows Jigsaw may be looking for him. He’d have security around his location, Watari would know where he is, and L would probably have instructions in place for what happens if he disappears.

John would need to make L move willingly. The easiest way would be another victim. If John creates a game that contains information only L would understand, L would recognize immediately that Jigsaw is communicating directly with him. A clue could point toward a location connected to one of L’s private investigative theories, something John shouldn't know unless he has been watching the investigation closely.

L would know it could be a trap. He’d go anyway, but he wouldn't go blindly. Before entering, he’d give Watari the location, have the exterior watched remotely, and arrange an initial sweep of the accessible section while police teams maintain a perimeter outside. He’d also set a deadline: if L doesn’t make contact by a certain time, they move in regardless of what he tells them afterward.

John could predict that much. So the trap wouldn't begin at the door. The accessible section would appear safe enough to survive the initial sweep, and John would leave evidence suggesting that a newly exposed section deeper inside contains the real game. L would keep moving because each piece of evidence makes Kramer seem closer, but the threshold into that section would be part of the mechanism. Once L crosses it, the route behind him seals and redirects access through the building, separating him from the outside team before they realize the game has actually begun. Multiple reinforced barriers would then lock into place behind the sealed route while false corridors and redirected access points turn the obvious paths inside into dead ends. The police perimeter could still breach the building when L misses his deadline, but reaching the actual game room would require breaking through the barriers and correcting those false routes in stages, giving John the uninterrupted window his one-hour game requires. By the time L understands that the apparently safe approach was itself part of John’s design, John already has the opportunity he was waiting for.
For the first time in the investigation, L would wake up on the other side of a Jigsaw tape.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: When L wakes up, he’d know almost immediately that John has been watching him for longer than he expected. The room would be built around the way L investigates rather than around physical strength. His wrists could be secured to a chair in the center, with several locked boxes around him, a clock on the wall, and a tape recorder within reach. The 1st recording would explain that he has 1 hour to get out before the room seals permanently, and every box contains part of what he needs.

L wouldn't start opening things at random. He’d first check the restraints, the chair, the floor, the walls, and anything else he can reach because John usually gives his victims rules, but those rules don’t always explain everything in the room. L would want to know what John expects him to notice before he makes the first move.

One box might require a 4 digit code, another could be connected to a mechanism above him, and a 3rd might already be unlocked. The obvious move would be opening the unlocked box first, which is exactly why L would hesitate. John knows L expects deception, so making 1 choice look suspicious could be enough to waste time even if there’s nothing wrong with it.

He’d eventually test the room instead of committing to a full solution. If the chair can move even slightly, he could use it to reach objects John probably expected him to ignore. If one box is connected to a wire, L would trace where that wire actually goes before touching the lock. He’d also inspect the clock because anything John places prominently in a room could be part of the mechanism rather than a simple timer.

The biggest clue would probably come from something John assumes L will recognize. Maybe the numbers on the locks match dates from earlier Jigsaw cases, or the order of the boxes follows the sequence L used when presenting his suspect profile. John would be showing L how much of the investigation he has seen, and L could use that against him because it also reveals which parts of his work John had access to.
That information matters outside the room too. If John knows details that were only shared through one specific channel, L can narrow down where the leak came from once he survives.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: John would design the game assuming L tries to solve everything logically, so L’s best chance comes from recognizing when the puzzle itself is wasting his time.

John would build the game around L’s compulsion to solve the intellectual problem in front of him. Several boxes would contain components that appear to form the only sequence capable of releasing his restraint, forcing L to spend time assembling and interpreting them in the order John intended. But one of those components has to mechanically interact with the restraint as part of the intended solution. L would trace that interaction instead of continuing the puzzle and realize that the release mechanism doesn’t verify whether he solved the sequence correctly; it only registers whether a particular latch inside the restraint has been moved. Using another supplied component, L could reach and trigger that latch early. John’s intended solution is still functional, but his assumption that L would be compelled to complete the puzzle creates the single engineering vulnerability L needs.

If the chain is attached to the chair with a weaker bolt than the lock itself, he’d go after the bolt. If the mechanism holding his wrist can be jammed with part of the box, he’d use that instead. John’s games usually have intended solutions, but the room still has to obey normal mechanics, and L wouldn't care whether he solves it the way John planned as long as he gets free.

John is extremely good at predicting fear, panic, guilt, and desperation because most of his games are built around those reactions. L is harder to push in the same way. He’d still understand that he could die, but he wouldn't waste much time arguing with the morality of the test while he’s inside it. He’d treat the room like evidence.

Once his hands are free, L no longer needs to beat every puzzle John placed in the room. He can use the freedom created by that one flaw to reach the exit mechanism and survive the game. He gets out because he separates what John wants him to solve from what the machine actually requires, exploiting the specific assumption John built into the test rather than relying on the room being full of accidental weaknesses.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: John would expect L to survive longer than most people, but he may not expect him to bypass parts of the game entirely. Once L reaches the exit, he’d have something more valuable than just proving he can escape.

He’d know the trap was built specifically for him, which means John needed information that very few people had. The references inside the room would tell L exactly which pieces of his investigation reached Jigsaw and which ones didn’t.

If John knew about a theory L only discussed with Watari and 2 investigators, the suspect pool becomes extremely small. If one of those people recently interacted with Amanda, or if surveillance catches Amanda near somewhere connected to the game, L can finally start proving the relationship rather than simply suspecting it.

The location itself would matter too. L would have police search the building after he escapes, and John would have had to leave something behind even if he cleared most of it. Tool marks, mechanical parts, fingerprints from an accomplice, fibers, transportation records, or ownership history could all help. 1 clue probably wouldn't be enough, but L no longer needs to solve the entire case from scratch because John has just given him a fresh crime scene built specifically around his investigation.

John would realize that mistake pretty quick. By trying to test L personally, he created the first game where the victim is also the person most capable of studying the trap afterward. L would remember where every object was placed, which mechanisms activated in what order, and which details seemed newer than the rest of the room.
The police could then compare those materials against purchases linked to John, while surveillance on Amanda becomes much tighter.

At this point, L would be ready to move. John was already L’s leading Jigsaw suspect before the kidnapping, but now he has evidence that the person watching his investigation had access to the same world John and Amanda move through.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: L wouldn’t approach John alone after escaping. He’s already seen what happens when he lets the case pull him into a situation John controls, so the next move would be built around making sure John can’t choose the location.

Police would watch John, Amanda, and any properties connected to either of them while L waits for movement. John would know staying still is dangerous because the trap location can now be traced back toward him, and moving equipment or preparing another game gives the surveillance teams something to follow.
That’s where L finally gets the physical connection he was missing.

If Amanda moves materials from one property to another, police can follow without immediately intervening. If John visits a workshop or warehouse tied to earlier trap construction, L can get a warrant once the evidence is strong enough. The goal would be catching them with something that can’t be explained away as engineering work or coincidence.

Once police enter, they could find partially built mechanisms, recordings, victim files, or equipment matching pieces recovered from earlier games. At that point, John’s background and connections stop being a theory because there’s direct evidence tying him to the murders.

The investigation only became dangerous once L stopped chasing the messages inside the traps and started studying everything John needed to do before a trap could exist. John tried to turn that intelligence against him by building a game specifically for L, but the game gave L 1 more crime scene and much more information about how John had been watching him. L would survive the trap and come out closer to the answer than he was when John captured him.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: L could identify John Kramer, but he’d need time because John does a good job of keeping the evidence around each game separated from himself. The connections through Gordon, Jill’s clinic, John’s engineering background, his properties, and his personal history would eventually put him under serious suspicion, and surveillance would give L a way to turn that suspicion into something police can actually use.

If John captures him first, L still has a good chance of surviving as long as the game has a real solution. He’d read the rules carefully, test the mechanisms, and look for ways around the intended choice instead of assuming John’s instructions describe every option available.

John could absolutely make L’s investigation dangerous, and capturing him would come close to ending it, but putting L inside one of his games would also give L direct access to the thing he’s been studying the entire time.
Once L gets out, John probably doesn’t stay free for much longer.

scripts.title: Could Spider-Man Build A Lightsaber

sections.name: INTRO
paras: The first time Peter Parker turns on the lightsaber, he immediately realizes he’s made a mistake.

The blade cuts through the steel table in front of him before he can even move his hand. Peter jumps backward, drops the hilt, and watches the glowing blade disappear as it hits the floor. For a few seconds, he just stands there staring at it. He’s spent weeks trying to make this thing work, and now he has a much bigger problem.
He actually succeeded.

Peter Parker has the scientific ability to build some ridiculous things, but a lightsaber should be outside his reach. The technology comes from another universe, its most important component doesn’t exist in the MCU, and the energy involved would be enough to make a homemade version really dangerous. Peter would have to find substitutes for almost every part of the weapon while working with technology he doesn’t fully understand.

So what happens if he actually tries? Could Peter use Stark technology and alien materials to create a functioning lightsaber, or would the first prototype turn into a very expensive way to burn down his apartment? And if he does get it working, would Spider-Man become more dangerous with a weapon capable of cutting through almost anything?

To answer that, we have to go back to the period after Peter meets Tony Stark in Civil War, but before the events of Spider-Man: Homecoming, when Peter decides that building a lightsaber is actually a good idea.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: Peter’s first instinct would probably be to figure out how much of a lightsaber he could actually reproduce. He wouldn't start by trying to copy the weapon piece by piece because he has no reason to believe the technology works the same way as anything he’s already built. Instead, he’d break the idea down into its basic functions. The weapon needs to produce an extremely concentrated blade of energy, keep that energy under control, and fit the entire system inside a handle small enough to hold. Peter has experience with all three problems in different forms, but he hasn't solved anything quite like this before.

The power source would be the first major obstacle. Peter’s normal equipment isn’t designed to produce anything close to the amount of energy a weapon like this would require. His web shooters use compact cartridges, his suits have relied on Stark technology, and his homemade equipment has generally been built around whatever he can afford or salvage. A normal battery wouldn’t suddenly become powerful enough just because Peter modified it. If he wants to build something remotely comparable to a lightsaber, he needs access to technology that is already far beyond modern human equipment.

The MCU gives Peter a few possible places to look. Alien technology has been left behind after several major battles, and Stark’s inventions have demonstrated energy systems far beyond anything available to an ordinary engineer. Peter has already spent time working with Stark technology, so he would have a better starting point than most people. He doesn't need access to Tony's workshop to start. Between small pieces of Chitauri technology still circulating in New York and the Stark suit already in his possession, Peter has enough advanced hardware to study how a compact power system could actually work. That doesn’t mean he could simply copy an arc reactor or turn an alien weapon into a lightsaber overnight. Modifying high level alien tech without fully understanding each component could still lead directly to dangerous failure.

There is another problem that Peter can’t solve by simply finding a stronger battery. A lightsaber isn’t just a glowing energy source attached to a handle. Star Wars technology uses a kyber crystal as a central part of the weapon, and that creates a problem Peter can’t ignore. The MCU has no established equivalent that he can simply pick up and install. Vibranium is one possibility worth investigating because it’s an unusually advanced material with properties that have already allowed Wakandan technology to do things normal materials can’t, but there is no canon evidence that vibranium can perform the same function as kyber.

Eventually, Peter could reach a point where he has an energy source and a material capable of helping control it, but he still wouldn’t have a lightsaber. He’d have an incredibly dangerous energy system with nowhere safe for that energy to go. The blade has to remain contained, and this is where Peter would need to borrow ideas from technology the MCU has already shown us. Stark’s weapons are capable of controlling enormous amounts of energy in a remarkably small space, giving Peter something he can study and adapt. He wouldn't be copying a repulsor and turning it into a lightsaber. He’d be trying to solve the same basic engineering problem from a different direction.

The first working prototype would probably look nothing like the elegant weapons used by the Jedi. Peter would have a bulky metal hilt with cooling components, power controls, and whatever containment system he manages to build. It would also be much less reliable than the finished weapon. The blade might only stay active for a few seconds before the system overheats, or the energy could become unstable if Peter pushes it too hard. Before Peter ever thinks about using it against a supervillain, he’d have to make sure the thing doesn’t destroy the person holding it.

That leaves Peter with a very different problem from the one he started with. Building something that produces a bright, incredibly hot energy blade is one challenge. Building a weapon that can safely contain that energy inside a handheld device is another. And until Peter solves that problem, he doesn’t have a lightsaber. He has a machine that could hurt him just as easily as it could hurt anyone else.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Even if Peter manages to make the blade stable, he still has to learn how to use it. A lightsaber isn’t something he could pick up and immediately handle like a normal sword. Peter has never been trained as a swordsman, and his fighting style is built around movement, webbing, punches, kicks, and using his surroundings. Adding a weapon with an extremely dangerous cutting edge would force him to change the way he fights.

His Spider-Sense would help, but it wouldn’t magically give him the skills of a Jedi. Peter’s danger sense warns him when something is about to hurt him, allowing him to react far faster than a normal person. That could be extremely useful with a lightsaber because the weapon itself would be dangerous at close range. Peter could use his reflexes to avoid his own blade and react to attacks while keeping track of where the weapon is. He’d still need practice, though. Knowing that something is dangerous doesn’t automatically tell him how to swing a sword properly.

The more Peter practices, the more he’d realize that the lightsaber doesn’t need to replace everything he already does. His webs would still be useful for controlling enemies, pulling himself around buildings, and disarming people. His strength would let him move the hilt quickly without needing the same physical effort as an ordinary person. His agility would also let him attack from angles that a conventional swordsman couldn’t easily reach. Instead of suddenly becoming a Jedi, Peter would develop a fighting style that combines the weapon with the abilities he’s already spent years mastering.

There would also be a serious limitation. Peter’s Spider-Sense doesn’t make him invincible, and the lightsaber doesn’t become harmless just because he’s good at using it. A mistake could still have permanent consequences. If Peter swings too close to himself, catches the blade against part of his suit, or loses control of the hilt, his own weapon could become a liability. That's why he’d need to build safety features into the weapon itself. If the containment system becomes unstable or the hilt detects a major failure, Peter would want the blade to shut down rather than stay active until something goes wrong.

Eventually, Peter would become comfortable enough to take the weapon outside the workshop. At that point, he has something that could genuinely change the way he approaches a fight. His webs can restrain someone, his strength can knock them down, and the lightsaber gives him an option for cutting through objects that would normally take much longer to get past. A locked metal door, reinforced machinery, or part of a vehicle could become much easier to deal with.

The problem is that Peter doesn’t usually need a weapon capable of cutting through everything. Most of the criminals he fights aren’t armored aliens. They’re ordinary people with guns, knives, or stolen technology. Bringing a weapon like this into those situations would create a completely different level of risk, especially because Peter’s entire approach to being Spider-Man is built around stopping people without killing them.

His first real test would therefore need to involve someone who could actually survive the encounter. Someone like Adrian Toomes is a much better candidate than a random criminal because the Vulture’s suit gives Peter a clear reason to consider using the weapon. In the original timeline, Peter has to fight around the suit’s weapons and durability. With his new prototype hanging from his belt, Peter would finally have something capable of cutting through the technology he’s been struggling against.
And that’s where the lightsaber stops being an experiment and starts changing Peter’s story.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: If Peter finishes his first usable lightsaber before the events of Spider-Man: Homecoming, Adrian Toomes is probably the first major villain where the weapon would make an obvious difference. Peter already knows that the Vulture’s suit is dangerous, and he has trouble damaging it with his normal attacks. A lightsaber would give him an entirely different option, but Peter still wouldn’t know exactly how the blade would interact with Toomes’ alien-derived equipment until he tried it.

During their fight, Peter would initially use the weapon carefully. He wouldn't start swinging it at Toomes because one mistake could turn the fight into a killing. Instead, he’d look for a way to use it against the suit itself. The Vulture’s wings are his biggest advantage because they give him speed, mobility, and several ways to attack from a distance. If Peter could damage the equipment without seriously injuring Toomes, he’d have a much easier time stopping him.

The lightsaber could make that possible. If its blade is capable of cutting through materials at the level seen in Star Wars, the metal components of the Vulture suit would be much less difficult to damage. Peter could cut through part of a wing or sever a mechanical connection, forcing Toomes back onto the ground. But this is where the What If needs to stay honest. We don’t know that a hypothetical MCU lightsaber would automatically slice through every material in the MCU. The weapon’s effectiveness would depend on how successful Peter’s containment system actually is and how durable the material he’s cutting happens to be.

Peter would also have to be careful around the environment. In the original fight, the Vulture uses his strength and flight to throw Peter around the building. With a weapon that can cut through metal and concrete, Peter could create new dangers for himself if he uses it carelessly. Cutting through a support structure might stop Toomes, but it could also bring the entire building down. His Spider-Sense could warn him that something is about to happen, but Peter would still have to make the right decision.

Eventually, Peter would find an opening and use the blade for something his webs couldn't do which is slicing through one of the suit's mechanical wing connections away from the volatile Chitauri power core, damaging the flight system without cutting into the core itself.

A damaged wing would leave Toomes without the same control he had at the start of the fight. Peter could then use his webs to pull him down and restrain him. That would be much more in character than simply cutting through the suit and leaving Toomes seriously injured.

The encounter would also teach Peter something important about the weapon. He’d built it because he wanted a tool that could handle problems his webs couldn’t, but he now has to think about what happens when that tool is used against a person. Even if Peter is careful, a weapon this dangerous makes every fight more serious.

Tony Stark would eventually find out about it. Peter has been using Stark technology as part of his equipment, and Tony already has a complicated relationship with Peter’s decision-making. If Tony learned that Peter had built a handheld energy weapon capable of cutting through armored equipment, he wouldn’t treat it like another web-shooter upgrade.

That could lead to Tony taking the prototype away from Peter, at least temporarily. Peter would be frustrated because he knows the weapon works, but Tony would have a point. Peter isn’t an assassin, and giving him a weapon designed around cutting through almost anything creates a responsibility that his normal equipment doesn’t.

Peter eventually gets it back, but the experience changes how he uses it. He stops thinking about the lightsaber as something that makes him stronger and starts treating it as a last resort. That distinction becomes important later, because the MCU is about to put Peter against enemies far more dangerous than the Vulture.

Against a criminal with a mechanical flight suit, the lightsaber could be enough to change the outcome of a fight. Against someone like Cull Obsidian, it would finally get a chance to prove whether Peter’s invention can actually stand up against the kind of threats the Avengers face.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: The lightsaber would be far more useful against ordinary armor than Peter’s normal equipment, but that doesn’t mean it suddenly makes him capable of fighting anyone in the MCU. That becomes clear when he faces Thanos on Titan. Peter could use the blade to attack from close range, but Thanos has the strength, durability, and experience to deal with him without needing to meet the weapon head on. With the Infinity Stones, Thanos could manipulate space around Peter, redirect his attacks, or simply overpower him before Peter gets a clean strike. The lightsaber gives Peter another weapon, but it doesn’t erase the enormous difference between them.

The more important test comes later in Peter’s own life. After losing Aunt May, he finds himself fighting the Green Goblin with an entirely different mindset. The blue glowing blade gives him a way to end the fight permanently, and for a moment, Peter is willing to consider it. He has the strength to overpower Norman, and the weapon gives him the means to do something his fists can’t. But before he can cross that line, the other Peter Parker stops him. He reminds him that killing Norman won't bring May back, and Peter finally lowers the weapon.

That decision gives the lightsaber a purpose beyond being another upgrade. Peter has spent the entire story trying to make the weapon work, and he succeeds. He proves that his intelligence and engineering ability are enough to create something remarkably close to a lightsaber using technology from his own universe. But when he finally has the perfect opportunity to use it, he realizes that it doesn’t belong in Spider-Man’s hands.

After the spell erases everyone’s memory of Peter, he starts over with almost nothing. His new suit is simple, his equipment is limited, and his life is much harder than it was when Stark technology was available to him. The lightsaber could still make that life easier, but Peter chooses not to keep it. He takes the weapon apart, saves whatever components can be reused, and leaves the most dangerous parts behind. He doesn’t destroy the idea because it failed. He destroys it because it worked.

So could Spider-Man build a lightsaber? A true Star Wars lightsaber is probably beyond what Peter can reproduce with MCU technology, especially without a kyber crystal. But a Marvel equivalent is much more believable. With enough time, advanced materials, alien technology, and Peter’s engineering ability, he could potentially create a handheld energy weapon that performs many of the same functions. The bigger question is whether Spider-Man would actually want one. By the end, Peter has his answer. He’d rather be the hero who saves someone with his webs than the one carrying a weapon designed to harm them.

scripts.title: Could Spider-Man Escape The Death Note

sections.name: INTRO
paras: Light Yagami writes a name. A few seconds later, someone dies. That’s what makes Spider-Man such a strange target.
Light doesn’t need to find him. He doesn’t need to chase him through New York. He doesn’t even need to know where Spider-Man lives.
He just needs to identify the person underneath the mask. Normally, that wouldn’t be difficult for someone like Light. Except Peter Parker has already been erased.

At the end of Spider-Man: No Way Home, Doctor Strange’s spell made everyone forget Peter Parker. His friends forgot him. His former allies forgot him. The people who knew him best no longer knew that he existed.
So Light begins with a name he can’t reliably recover.
And Peter has no idea that somewhere across the world, a killer is trying to discover it. Because this isn’t a fight between Spider-Man and Kira.
It’s a race to see who can uncover the other’s secret first.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: Light wouldn't start by hunting Spider-Man. He’d start by finding out what the public already knows about him.

Spider-Man has been active in New York for years. He’s appeared in countless recordings, stopped crimes in public, fought other superhumans, and become recognizable enough that people know exactly who they’re looking at when he swings past them.
That gives Light plenty of information. It just doesn’t give him the one thing he needs. A name.

The Death Note can’t kill someone simply because they’re known by a nickname. Light has to identify the person he’s targeting, and Spider-Man’s mask keeps his face hidden from almost everyone who encounters him.
So Light begins with the footage.

He studies Spider-Man's appearances and looks for patterns. Where does he operate? How quickly does he respond to emergencies? Does he favor certain parts of New York? Does he arrive from a consistent direction? Does he interact with the same people?
Spider-Man creates a different problem.

Light can’t simply identify the person behind the mask from a public record because the MCU’s current continuity has Peter Parker living in a world where people no longer remember him. That means Light is dealing with 2 separate questions.
First, who is Spider-Man? Second, how does Spider-Man fit into the life of Peter Parker? The first question is easy.
The second is where the investigation becomes difficult. Light can collect footage. He can examine reports. He can compare witness statements. He can study Spider-Man’s behavior.
None of that gives him Peter Parker.
The difference here is that Spider-Man isn’t part of a police investigation. He’s the person Light is trying to identify.
So Light has to create a connection between a masked superhero and an ordinary human being.
And Peter’s current life gives him very little help.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Light's first breakthrough would come from realizing that Peter Parker is the name he’s looking for.

That distinction matters. Spider-Man's identity has already been exposed to the public before. Mysterio revealed Peter’s identity to the world, and by the beginning of No Way Home, his life had been turned upside down because everyone knew he was Spider-Man. Doctor Strange’s spell eventually reversed that situation by making the world forget Peter Parker.

So Light can’t simply start with an old news report and work backward. Whatever Strange’s spell did to the records surrounding Peter Parker, it left no usable public connection that simply hands Light Spider-Man’s identity. He can find footage of Spider-Man. He can find reports about his fights. He can find people discussing him online. What he can’t immediately find is a living person whose life connects all of those events to Peter Parker.
That leaves Light with a conventional investigation. He watches Spider-Man’s behavior.
He studies where he appears and when he appears. He looks for people who interact with him repeatedly. He pays attention to the way Spider-Man speaks and the decisions he makes during emergencies.
Most importantly, Light looks for mistakes.

Spider-Man has spent years protecting his identity, but Peter still has to live in the same city as everyone else. He needs food. He needs somewhere to sleep. He needs equipment. He has to move through New York without constantly wearing his mask.

Those ordinary parts of Peter’s life are more useful to Light than Spider-Man’s powers. If Light can identify one place where Spider-Man’s private life overlaps with his public activities, he can start narrowing the possibilities. The Death Note makes that investigation even more valuable because Light doesn’t need to build a case against Peter. He doesn’t need proof that Peter committed a crime.
He only needs the information required by the notebook. That changes how Light approaches the problem. He’s not trying to expose Spider-Man to the public.
He’s trying to identify him once. And if he succeeds, the investigation is over.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Spider-Man’s movements aren’t random. He responds to crimes, appears in particular parts of New York, and repeatedly puts himself in situations where an ordinary person would have no reason to go. Light starts cataloguing those appearances. A robbery happens in Queens. Spider-Man arrives. A fight breaks out in Manhattan. Spider-Man arrives.
Light can use that. Instead of asking, “Who is Spider-Man?” He asks, “Who could consistently be in the right place to become Spider-Man?” That produces a much smaller list.

Students. Delivery workers. Police officers. First responders. Anyone whose schedule gives them unusual freedom to disappear when something happens. Then Light starts comparing those people with Spider-Man’s behavior. He’s looking for coincidences. A person who disappears shortly before Spider-Man appears.

Someone who seems to know where a crime is happening before the police do. Someone who has access to technology or equipment that could explain Spider-Man’s web shooters. Someone young enough to fit the physical profile witnesses have described.

None of those clues proves anything. Light knows that. He also knows he doesn’t need proof. He only needs one person who gives him enough reason to investigate further. And that’s where Peter’s current situation makes things harder.

Peter isn’t living the same life he had before the spell. He doesn’t have the people around him that once connected him to his civilian identity. He isn’t maintaining the same relationships, and the people who once knew Peter Parker aren’t walking around New York looking for him. That doesn’t make Peter impossible to find. It makes him difficult to connect to Spider-Man.

Light can find people who resemble Spider-Man. Finding the right person is another problem entirely. And Light has a second option. He can stop looking for Peter Parker altogether. He can make Spider-Man reveal himself.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Light doesn’t need Peter to confess. He needs Peter to make a mistake. That’s why his first move wouldn't be an elaborate kidnapping or an attempt to physically capture Spider-Man. It would be much simpler. He’d create a situation where Spider-Man has a reason to show up, then watch what happens.
Peter has spent years doing exactly what Light would expect from a superhero. When someone is in danger, he helps.

That makes Spider-Man predictable in one important way. Light can create problems and wait for him to respond. The first attempt wouldn't be designed to kill Peter. It would be designed to collect information. Light could manipulate a criminal into creating a situation in which Spider-Man has to intervene. While the police and the public focus on the crime itself, Light watches Spider-Man's behavior. How does he arrive? How quickly does he react? Does he come alone? Does he communicate with anyone? Does he remove his mask when he thinks nobody is watching?

Peter wouldn’t know any of this is happening. He’d simply see another emergency and respond. That’s what makes the investigation difficult for Peter. There isn’t anything obviously suspicious about the situation. Spider-Man has spent years dealing with criminals who set traps for him, so a trap isn’t enough to make him walk away from someone who needs help.

That gives Light something he can work with. He doesn’t need to find Peter’s friends. He needs to find Peter’s habits. And Peter has habits. He responds to emergencies. He moves around the city. He maintains equipment. He has to eat, sleep, and live somewhere. Even with his identity erased from the people around him, Spider-Man still has a physical life that leaves patterns behind.
Light starts looking for those patterns. Peter, meanwhile, doesn’t know there’s a pattern being built around him. He only knows that New York has become strangely busy.
A few crimes feel too perfectly timed. A few situations seem to draw Spider-Man into exactly the places where someone would want him.
At first, Peter doesn’t have enough information to connect them. Then it happens again. And this time, his Spider-Sense reacts before he even reaches the scene.
Peter stops.
He looks at the building ahead of him. There’s nothing obviously wrong. No gunfire. No explosion. No person running for help. Just an ordinary street.

But something about it feels dangerous. Peter doesn’t know who set the trap. He doesn’t know what they’re trying to learn. And he has no idea that the person watching him doesn’t care about Spider-Man’s strength at all.
Light is looking for the moment Peter Parker appears.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: Peter doesn’t immediately conclude that someone is hunting him. That would require information he doesn’t have.

What he does notice is that several recent emergencies have felt different from the usual calls he responds to. The situations themselves aren't impossible. People commit crimes, police respond, and Spider-Man gets involved. That’s normal.
The problem is the timing.
He doesn’t have a name for the pattern yet. He just knows something is off.
Another incident happens. Then another.
This time, Peter changes his approach. Instead of immediately entering the situation, he watches from a distance. He studies the people involved before he gets close enough for them to notice him.
Nothing stands out. That makes the situation more concerning.
If someone is deliberately setting these incidents up, they’re being careful enough that Peter can’t identify the connection from the surface.
Peter starts doing what he does best when he doesn’t understand a problem. He investigates.
What doesn’t make sense is why the incidents seem designed to get him into specific places rather than simply attack him.
Then Peter notices something else. People aren’t trying to fight him. They’re watching him. That changes the problem.
Someone isn’t testing whether Spider-Man can be beaten. Someone is trying to learn something about him. Peter doesn’t know who. He doesn’t know what they’re looking for.
But he starts taking fewer chances.

That becomes difficult because Peter’s current life is built around being Spider-Man. He can’t simply disappear from New York without abandoning the role he’s chosen for himself. Light only needs Peter to keep being Spider-Man. And Peter is going to keep doing that.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Light eventually reaches the same conclusion Peter has reached from the opposite direction. Spider-Man isn’t giving him enough information.
So Light stops trying to identify Spider-Man through his normal life. He starts looking at the mask.
The mask tells him something important. Spider-Man goes to considerable lengths to prevent people from seeing his face. That means his identity has value.
He only needs to know that Spider-Man is protecting something. That gives him a new objective.
Make Spider-Man believe that revealing himself is the safest option.

This is where Light’s greatest strength becomes more useful than the Death Note itself. The notebook can kill someone once Light knows who they are. Before that happens, Light still has to solve a human problem.
He has to manipulate Spider-Man. The most obvious approach is to put other people in danger.
Light knows Spider-Man's behavior is based on his willingness to help people. If a situation is serious enough, Peter is likely to intervene even when doing so creates a personal risk.

But Light can’t simply write an impossible command into the Death Note and expect reality to follow it. The notebook has rules governing how victims can be controlled, and Light has spent years learning how to work within those limits rather than treating the Death Note as an unlimited mind-control device.
So he starts with people who can realistically influence Spider-Man.
A police officer. A criminal. A witness. Someone who can deliver a message.
Someone who can create a situation that makes Spider-Man believe another person needs him. None of them needs to know they’re helping Kira.
And this is where Peter’s situation becomes difficult.

Peter doesn’t have the support network he once had. The world still doesn’t remember Peter Parker. He’s living alone and has committed himself to Spider-Man, which means Light can’t simply follow the old connections that once surrounded Peter.
But Peter still has one weakness Light can predict.

He cares about people he doesn’t know. Light can use that. He doesn’t need Peter’s friends. He needs strangers. A hostage situation could work. A staged emergency could work. A criminal threatening innocent people could work.
The more convincing the situation, the more likely Peter is to respond exactly as Light expects. And Light doesn’t need Spider-Man to remove his mask permanently.
He only needs him to remove it once.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: This is where the investigation changes completely.

Light already knows that the Death Note requires a person’s name and face. If he can obtain both, Spider-Man’s physical abilities become almost irrelevant. The notebook doesn’t require Light to overpower his target.
The problem is obtaining the information. The Shinigami Eyes provide a solution.

A human who makes the eye deal with a Shinigami can see the names and lifespans of people by looking at their faces. That ability exists specifically because the Death Note’s normal requirement of knowing a person’s name can otherwise make certain targets difficult to identify.

There is one problem. Using them costs half of the user’s remaining lifespan. Light has always treated his own life as something worth protecting because his plans depend on him remaining alive. Giving up half of his remaining lifespan is therefore a serious decision.

But Light doesn’t necessarily need to make the deal himself. At his peak, Light already had someone willing to act as his eyes. Misa Amane possessed the Shinigami Eyes, and if she could identify Spider-Man for him, Light wouldn’t have to sacrifice his own lifespan.
Misa still needs to see the person's face.

So Light’s investigation narrows down to one specific objective. He needs Peter’s face. Not Peter’s social security number. Not a government record. Not an old school file. His face. If Misa gets a sufficiently clear view of Peter’s uncovered face, the identity problem changes immediately. The Eyes aren’t dependent on whether Peter’s name appears in a database. They provide the information needed for the Death Note directly.
That means Peter’s greatest defense isn’t that the world forgot him. It’s keeping Misa from ever seeing him.
And Peter doesn’t know that yet.
Light, meanwhile, has finally reduced the entire investigation to one problem. Get Peter Parker to show his face. Once that happens, the rest could take seconds.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: Light's first serious attempt to expose Spider-Man’s identity would need to accomplish two things at once. It would have to put Peter in a situation where he couldn't simply walk away, while also giving Light a way to observe what Peter does when he believes nobody is watching. A direct attack wouldn't tell him enough. If armed criminals surrounded Spider-Man, Peter would fight them. If someone tried to ambush him, his Spider-Sense could warn him. Light needs something that forces Peter to make a decision.

A staged emergency gives him that opportunity. Light doesn’t need to personally operate in New York to arrange it. He can work through intermediaries, recruit people remotely, and keep the real purpose of the operation hidden from everyone involved. A group of criminals can create a situation that looks serious enough to attract Spider-Man’s attention, while another group observes what happens from a distance. The people involved don’t necessarily need to understand why they’re there. Light has used people as pieces before, but he doesn’t need every person involved to be controlled by the Death Note. Most of them can be recruited, paid, threatened, or manipulated without ever knowing why Spider-Man is being watched. Once Light narrows down where Peter is likely to expose his face, Misa only needs to be in New York for that final stage.
Peter arrives because that’s what Spider-Man does.

He doesn’t immediately rush into the building. The earlier incidents have already made him cautious, and his Spider-Sense gives him another reason to slow down. He watches the entrances, checks the surrounding buildings, and looks for anything that doesn’t fit the situation. He doesn’t know that someone is studying him, but he has enough experience to recognize when a crime scene doesn’t look normal.
That's the first problem with Light’s plan.
Peter isn’t just physically difficult to surprise. He’s experienced at dealing with traps.
Light therefore can’t rely on a single staged incident. He needs repeated observations.
That’s where the mask becomes important.

Light knows Spider-Man is careful about it. If Spider-Man never removes it in public, then Light needs to create a situation where Peter believes removing it is necessary. The trap doesn’t have to involve an obvious threat to Spider-Man himself. In fact, threatening Spider-Man directly may make him more cautious. A threat against someone else is more likely to force a predictable response.

Light could arrange for a hostage to be used as part of the deception. The hostage doesn’t have to be someone Peter knows. That’s the point. Peter’s willingness to help strangers means Light doesn’t need access to his personal relationships.
But there is a limit to how much control Light has.

The Death Note isn’t a general-purpose mind-control system. When Light specifies actions for a victim, those actions still have to be possible under the circumstances. He can manipulate a person’s behavior within the rules of the notebook, but he can’t simply use a victim as an all powerful puppet and make them accomplish anything he wants. The more complicated the plan becomes, the more opportunities there are for it to fail because the victim can’t carry out some part of the instructions.
Light understands those limitations better than almost anyone. So he keeps the plan simple.
The victim creates the situation. Spider-Man responds. Someone records the encounter. The person controlling the operation watches for an opportunity to see his face.
Peter reaches the scene and realizes something is wrong.

The hostage isn’t where the criminals claim they are. The exits are positioned too conveniently. The people holding the weapons don’t behave like ordinary criminals, and the entire situation seems designed to keep Spider-Man in one specific location.
Peter doesn’t know why.
He also doesn’t know that one of the people observing the scene has a very specific objective.
They aren't trying to identify Spider-Man through his voice.
They aren't trying to determine his height. They aren’t trying to figure out what kind of technology he uses.
They're waiting for his mask to come off. Peter gets the hostage out anyway.
He disables the criminals without killing them, gets the civilians away from the danger, and leaves before anyone gets the clear image Light wanted.
The attempt fails. But Light learns something.
Spider-Man is cautious enough that an ordinary threat won’t make him remove his mask.
That means the next attempt has to be different.
He also has evidence that Spider-Man will risk himself to save strangers.
Those two facts give Light a strategy.
He needs to put them against each other.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: Peter eventually realizes that the strange incidents aren't separate.
The timing is too consistent.

Someone is creating situations specifically because they expect Spider-Man to respond, and the people involved aren't behaving like criminals who simply want money or control. Their actions are serving another purpose.
Peter starts treating the incidents as an investigation instead of a series of crimes.
That changes how he operates.

Rather than arriving immediately, he watches first. Rather than approaching from the most obvious direction, he takes another route. He uses his webs to observe from a distance and avoids giving anyone a predictable view of his face. If someone is expecting Spider-Man to enter through a particular doorway, Peter doesn’t give them that opportunity.
This doesn’t tell him who is behind the operation. It does tell him that someone is collecting information.
He has to work it out from evidence. The first useful clue comes from one of the people being manipulated.

Most of the people connected to the traps lead nowhere. Then one of them behaves strangely and suddenly dies under circumstances similar to Kira’s known victims. That’s worth noticing. One death doesn’t prove anything, but it gives Peter a reason to start looking at Kira.
Peter has heard of Kira.

He can start with the simplest question. Why would Kira care about Spider-Man? At first, the answer isn’t obvious. Spider-Man stops criminals and saves people. That alone doesn’t make him an obvious enemy of Kira.
But Peter is no longer just stopping crimes. He’s investigating the person behind them.

That changes the situation. The closer Peter gets to understanding how the traps connect to Kira, the more dangerous he becomes to Light. Light has killed investigators before when they threatened to expose him. Spider-Man is becoming another person who could work backward toward his identity.
Light doesn’t need to hate Spider-Man personally. He needs to stop Peter before Peter identifies him.

He doesn’t confront Kira directly. Doing that would give Light information he doesn’t need to have. Instead, Peter changes the way he responds to suspicious situations. If a crime appears designed to attract him, he approaches differently. If someone is clearly trying to force him into a particular location, he finds another way to reach the civilians.
This creates a problem for Light. His plans are becoming harder to predict because Peter is adapting.

That leaves him with the same fundamental obstacle. The face. If Light can obtain Peter’s uncovered face and has Misa available to use the Shinigami Eyes, the investigation can end almost immediately. If he can’t, he has to keep working through conventional methods.
Peter eventually realizes that this is probably what the traps are about. Someone isn’t trying to kill Spider-Man.
Someone is trying to identify him.
Once Peter reaches that conclusion, his behavior changes completely. He starts protecting his face with the same priority he gives to his life.

That makes photographs a problem. Surveillance cameras become a problem. Reflections become a problem. Any situation where another person could get a clear view of his uncovered face becomes a potential vulnerability.
So he becomes more careful about when and where he unmasks. That makes Light's job harder.
It doesn’t make it impossible. Light now has to find a way to separate Peter Parker from Spider-Man without ever being able to ask Peter directly.
And that’s where the two characters’ strengths become clear. Peter has the physical ability to escape almost any ordinary trap. Light doesn’t need an ordinary trap. He needs information.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: There isn’t one answer until we establish what information each character has. That’s the most important part of this matchup.

If Light begins with no knowledge of Spider-Man’s identity and no access to the Shinigami Eyes, Peter has a realistic chance of avoiding him for a very long time. Light would have to identify Spider-Man through conventional investigation, and Peter is unusually difficult to connect to a civilian identity because of the events of No Way Home and the life he’s living afterward.

Peter isn’t invisible. Spider-Man is a public figure. His appearances have been recorded, his behavior has been observed, and people have interacted with him. Light could analyze those appearances and try to identify people whose lives overlap with Spider-Man’s activities.

Before the spell, Peter’s identity was exposed because Mysterio revealed it. After the spell, the people who knew Peter Parker forgot him. That means Light can’t simply follow an existing chain of relationships from Spider-Man to Peter. He has to rebuild that connection himself.
If Light never obtains a clear view of Peter’s face, the Death Note becomes much less useful against him.

It means Light has been forced into an investigation where Peter’s abilities are unusually valuable. Peter can move through New York quickly, his Spider-Sense can warn him of immediate danger, and his intelligence allows him to adapt when he recognizes a pattern. He can also choose when to engage with suspicious situations instead of automatically following the path someone has prepared for him.

Now change the conditions. Give Light access to Misa and the Shinigami Eyes. The entire matchup changes. The Eyes solve the most difficult part of the investigation. Light no longer needs to discover Peter’s name through government records, old acquaintances, school records, or financial information. If Misa gets a sufficiently clear view of Peter’s face, she can see the name required for the Death Note.
Peter’s erased identity doesn’t prevent that. That’s why the spell isn’t an automatic victory over Kira.
So the decisive question becomes whether Light can obtain Peter’s face. This is where Spider-Man has a real advantage.

Peter’s mask is extremely effective at preventing identification. His Spider-Sense also makes direct attempts to surprise him dangerous. If Light sends ordinary people after Peter, they aren’t likely to overpower him. If Light uses a staged situation to expose him, Peter can potentially recognize that something is wrong and change his approach.
Light therefore has to be patient.
The longer this continues, the more dangerous it becomes for Peter.
Peter has to be right every time. Light only needs one successful opportunity. That imbalance matters.

Suppose Light creates a hostage situation and demands that Spider-Man remove his mask on camera. Peter doesn’t have to comply. His first priority would be getting the hostages to safety, and he has enough abilities to approach the situation from another direction. He could disable the criminals, rescue the civilians, and destroy the equipment being used to broadcast his face.

Now suppose Light arranges a situation where Peter believes someone he has rescued is about to die unless he removes his mask. Peter still has options. He can intervene without complying with the demand, use his webs, move the victim, or find another solution.
But now imagine Light doesn’t make the demand at all. Instead, he arranges for Misa to observe a location where Peter is likely to unmask naturally.
That is much harder to defend against.

Peter doesn’t know what Misa is looking for. He can’t react to a supernatural ability he doesn’t know exists. His Spider-Sense can warn him about danger, but it doesn’t give him a detailed explanation of an invisible supernatural investigation taking place somewhere else.
This is the scenario where Light has the strongest advantage.

If Misa gets a clear view of Peter’s face and gives Light the name required by the Death Note, Peter’s physical abilities don’t save him from the notebook itself. Spider-Sense can’t dodge a name being written into a notebook. Superhuman strength can’t stop a supernatural cause of death that doesn’t require physical contact.

Peter would need to prevent the information from ever reaching Light. That could still happen. If Peter discovers what Kira is doing before Misa sees him, he can change his behavior. He could avoid unmasking in public, stop allowing himself to be photographed, and deliberately make himself harder to observe. He could also investigate the people connected to the Kira operation and potentially work backward toward Light.
But Peter faces another problem. He doesn’t have the same information about Light that Light has about him.

If Peter somehow learns Light's identity and can establish where he is, the matchup changes again. Peter is physically capable of confronting Light, and Light has no comparable physical abilities. The Death Note gives Light an enormous advantage, but only if he can use it before Peter reaches him.

That makes the first successful identification extremely important. If Peter identifies Light first, Peter has a realistic path to stopping him. If Light identifies Peter first, Peter has very few options.
Now consider both characters operating at their absolute peak.

Light knows everything the Death Note can do. He understands the limitations of the notebook, understands how the Shinigami Eyes work, and has no reason to reveal his identity unnecessarily. Peter has his full MCU abilities, his Spider-Sense, his intelligence, his experience with superhuman enemies, and the lessons he’s learned from losing the people closest to him.
In a long investigation, Light probably has the strategic advantage. Not because Peter is unintelligent. Because Light’s win condition is much smaller.

Peter needs to keep his identity hidden indefinitely. Light needs one successful identification. That's the difference. Peter can avoid traps. He can destroy cameras. He can change his routes. He can refuse demands. He can investigate suspicious people. He can even defeat the people Light sends after him.
None of that permanently solves the problem if Light keeps learning. Eventually, Light could find a situation Peter doesn’t recognize as a trap.
And if Misa gets a clear view of Peter’s face during that situation, Peter’s advantage disappears.
The most realistic conclusion is therefore conditional.

Against Light without the Shinigami Eyes, Peter has a strong chance of escaping the investigation for a very long time. His anonymity, intelligence, Spider-Sense and physical abilities make him an unusually difficult target, and the post-No Way Home situation makes the connection between Spider-Man and Peter Parker much harder to establish.

Against Light at his peak, with Misa and her Shinigami Eyes available, the situation becomes much worse for Peter. The Eyes bypass the conventional identity problem. Once Peter’s face is exposed to Misa, the name required by the Death Note can be obtained without relying on the records or memories affected by Strange’s spell.
And if Light gets both pieces of information, Peter can’t fight his way out of it.
That's why Spider-Man doesn’t permanently escape the Death Note. He can escape Light’s traps. He can evade his investigators. He can even prevent Light from identifying him for years.
But if Light is given enough time, understands Peter’s behavior, has access to the Shinigami Eyes, and eventually obtains a clear view of Peter Parker's face, Light has the winning move.
The fight therefore comes down to one moment.
Peter has to keep his face hidden.
Light has to see it.
Whoever wins that part of the investigation controls everything that comes afterward.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: Spider-Man has a way out of almost every situation we’ve seen him face.
Against Kira, that way out is simple.
Don't let him identify you.

Peter’s strength, Spider-Sense, intelligence, and mobility give him plenty of ways to survive Light's attempts to expose him. His life after No Way Home also makes the investigation harder because the people who once connected Peter Parker to Spider-Man no longer remember him. But Light doesn’t need Peter’s entire history.
He needs his face and his name.
If he never gets them, Peter can keep operating as Spider-Man. If Misa gets a clear look at Peter’s face and gives Light the name he needs, the fight is effectively over.
So could Spider-Man escape the Death Note? Yes. Could he stay hidden from Light forever?
That's much harder to believe. At his absolute peak, Light’s greatest advantage isn’t the Death Note itself. It's his patience.
And against a target who only has to make one mistake, patience might eventually be enough.

scripts.title: Could Spider-Man Survive World War Z

sections.name: INTRO
paras: INTRO Peter arrives in a city that’s already starting to fall apart.
At first, he has no idea what he’s looking at. People are running, traffic is blocked, and fights are breaking out everywhere. Then he sees someone get bitten and turn almost immediately.

Peter is now trapped in the world of World War Z, where the infection spreads so quickly that entire cities can collapse before anyone fully understands what’s happening. The easy part is that he could probably keep himself alive.
The harder part, is that Peter isn’t going to stop and watch everyone else die. PART 1

Peter lands in Philadelphia less than an hour before everything starts to collapse. He doesn’t know where he’s at first. The city looks normal enough, but nothing around him matches the New York he left behind. His phone has no useful connection, there’s no sign of anyone he knows, and whatever brought him here is already gone. Before he can spend much time figuring that out, the streets around him start filling with sirens.

The first few incidents don’t look like anything unusual. People are running from something several blocks away, cars are trying to force their way through traffic, and police are struggling to keep intersections open. Peter moves toward it because that’s what he always does when something goes wrong.
Then he sees the infection happen.

Someone is dragged down near the side of the road and bitten. Peter gets there quickly enough to pull the attacker away, but the person he’s trying to help starts convulsing almost immediately. Within seconds, they're back on their feet and attacking the nearest person.

Peter doesn’t understand what he’s looking at yet, but he understands one thing very quickly. This spreads through direct contact, and it spreads fast enough that saving someone a few seconds too late can make the situation worse.

Peter stays above the main crowds whenever he can, using buildings and web lines to move past blocked roads, but he keeps dropping back down whenever people get trapped. He pulls passengers from crashed cars, webs infected people to walls, and clears routes through intersections long enough for civilians to escape.

At this stage, individual infected aren’t a serious physical threat to him. Peter can throw them aside without much effort, and his Spider-Sense gives him warning whenever one gets close enough to attack. The problem is how quickly each rescue grows into something larger.

A car crash traps 3 people. Peter stops to help them. That delay gives the infected behind him time to reach the intersection. More civilians panic and run in the wrong direction. Peter has to double back because leaving immediately means abandoning people he can still reach.

He begins using his webs differently. Instead of trying to restrain every infected person he sees, he starts sealing doors, blocking stairwells, and pulling obstacles into narrow streets to slow the flow of the crowd. He can’t stop the outbreak, but he can redirect it for a few seconds at a time.

So he becomes more selective. He uses his strength when the numbers are small and saves the webs for situations where distance matters. Peter reaches the top of a building and finally gets a clear view across several blocks. What looked like isolated violence from street level is spreading through entire sections of the city. People are pouring out of buildings. Traffic has stopped moving. Infected are chasing anyone they can reach, and every person caught creates another attacker within seconds.
Peter can move faster than almost anyone below him, but he can’t be everywhere at once. That's when he sees a family trapped inside a vehicle several blocks away and he goes back down.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Peter reaches the car before the infected surrounding it can break through the windows. He pulls the family out through the roof and gets them onto the top of a nearby building, then immediately returns for another group trapped further down the street. By now, he’s stopped thinking of the city as something he can clear. He’s on salvage mode.

Peter starts creating temporary evacuation routes above ground. He webs ladders and fire escapes into place, helps civilians reach rooftops, and moves people between buildings where the streets below are already too dangerous. It works well for small groups because the infected remain focused on the people they can reach at ground level.

But Peter's presence also creates a new problem. People begin following him. Anyone who sees Spider-Man moving through the area assumes he knows where it’s safe. Groups start gathering near the buildings he’s using, and the larger those groups become, the more infected they attract.
That creates obvious bottlenecks. He doesn’t know enough about the city to guide anyone toward a guaranteed safe zone, so his goal becomes simpler, get them off the street and buy them time.

That works until the infected begin climbing. Not straight up the buildings, but over one another. Peter watches a group pile against the side of a bus while trying to reach people standing on top of it. More infected hit the same point from behind, pushing the ones in front higher. Within moments, hands are reaching the roof.

Peter pulls the civilians away before the swarm can get to them, but he’s just learned something important. Height isn’t automatically safe. The infected don’t slow down because there’s an obstacle in front of them. Enough bodies will eventually turn that obstacle into part of the path.

Peter changes tactics again. He stops leaving civilians on low rooftops unless there’s another escape route available. He prioritizes buildings with locked upper floors, narrow access points, or enough vertical distance that a pile of infected can’t reach the top easily. Whenever possible, he destroys or webs shut the route he used to get people inside.

There’s no long delay after a bite. Someone can be standing beside you one moment and become part of the horde seconds later. Peter sees it happen more than once, and it forces him to make decisions he normally wouldn’t have to make.

That's the first real change World War Z forces on him. Peter is used to rescuing someone first and figuring out the rest afterward. Here, the rescue itself can become dangerous if he doesn’t understand what happened to the person he’s saving.

But below, roads are gone beneath moving crowds of infected. Police lines have broken apart. Cars are abandoned everywhere, and every route Peter opens eventually closes again as more infected arrive. Peter finally understands what kind of situation he’s trapped in.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: As Philadelphia collapses, Peter starts picking up reports that organized evacuations are still moving people farther northeast. He follows that route while helping whoever he can along the way. By the time Peter reaches Newark, , the outbreak has spread far beyond anything he saw in Philadelphia. The roads between the cities are packed with abandoned cars, and the military is
already pulling back from areas it can’t hold. Peter spends most of the trip moving along rooftops and elevated sections of highway, stopping whenever he finds people trapped below.

He eventually notices helicopters moving toward the coast. Unlike the civilian traffic, they're flying with a purpose, so Peter follows them until he reaches one of the evacuation areas still being used by the military. That's where his situation finally changes. Soldiers have already heard reports about someone in a red and blue suit pulling people out of infected streets. Peter doesn’t have identification that means anything in this world, but nobody needs much convincing after watching him carry two injured people to safety and cross a building without using the stairs.
