He’s taken to the same naval fleet where Gerry Lane and his family have been brought after their escape from Newark.

Peter doesn’t immediately become part of Gerry’s mission. From the military’s perspective, Peter is useful, but he’s also an unknown person who appeared in the middle of a global emergency wearing a mask. Peter can’t explain where he came from without sounding impossible, and there’s no record of Peter Parker or Spider-Man anywhere they can check.

He’s spent hours close to the infected and has already noticed how consistent the transformation is after a bite. He’s also seen how quickly a small group can become a swarm once the infection gets into a crowded area. Gerry has been collecting similar information from every source available to him, and Peter becomes another eyewitness with an unusual advantage. He’s been able to stay close enough to watch the infected without being forced to run immediately.

The United Nations team is preparing to send Gerry to Camp Humphreys in South Korea, where one of the earliest reports mentioning zombies came from. A young virologist, Andrew Fassbach, is being sent with him because they still don’t know what the infection actually is or where it started.
Peter volunteers to go.
Camp Humphreys proves almost immediately that his presence can change more than casualty numbers.

The team arrives in darkness and is attacked while leaving the aircraft. In the original chain of events, Fassbach panics while trying to get back onto the plane, slips on the wet ramp and accidentally fires his own weapon into his head.

Fassbach panics while trying to get back onto the plane and loses his footing on the wet ramp. Peter sees the gun coming up as Fassbach falls and reacts before it can accidentally fire into him, catching Fassbach and knocking the weapon away. Fassbach survives. It's a small moment compared to everything happening around them, but it changes Gerry's investigation immediately. Instead of losing the scientist who was supposed to help him understand the pathogen within minutes of arriving, Gerry now has Fassbach with him when they reach the soldiers inside the base.

They still don’t find the origin they were hoping for. The soldiers explain that the infection appeared at the base after a doctor came into contact with an infected soldier, and the information available is too limited to tell them where the wider outbreak began.

The more useful lead comes from the imprisoned CIA operative at the base. Israel had reacted before most of the world understood what was happening, building its defenses around Jerusalem while other governments were still trying to decide what they were dealing with.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Jerusalem is the first place Peter has seen since arriving in this world that appears capable of surviving.

The walls have kept the infected outside, soldiers control the entrances, and refugees are still being allowed into the city. After watching Philadelphia and Newark disappear into chaos, Peter can finally see what organized preparation looks like when it happens early enough.

Gerry meets Jurgen Warmbrunn, the Mossad official responsible for acting on intercepted reports about the outbreak. Warmbrunn explains how Israel heard references to Indian troops fighting what appeared to be zombies and treated the warning seriously enough to prepare before the infection reached them.

Fassbach is interested in the biology of the infection. Peter is more interested in its behavior. He’s already learned that fighting the infected individually doesn’t tell him much, so he watches how they move when they're outside the wall. They don’t wander without purpose. When something draws their attention, entire sections of the crowd react and move toward it.

That becomes important when the refugees inside Jerusalem begin celebrating loudly. Peter notices the infected changing direction before most people inside understand what's happening. Thousands begin pressing toward the same section of the barrier. The first bodies hit the wall and disappear beneath the ones behind them. Then the pile starts rising.

Peter gets there before the infected reach the top, but there’s nothing he can do that solves the larger problem. He can pull infected away from the highest point and web sections of the pile together, but more bodies keep arriving from behind. Every layer he removes is replaced almost immediately.

The wall was built to stop a crowd pushing against it. It wasn’t built for a crowd that could turn itself into a ramp. Peter warns the soldiers around the breach and starts getting civilians away from that section before the infected begin pouring over. That warning saves people who would've still been standing nearby when the wall fails, but it doesn’t save Jerusalem.

Once the infected reach the other side, Peter stops trying to hold the wall. He moves through the streets ahead of the swarm, pulling people from alleys and carrying injured civilians toward routes that haven't been cut off yet. Gerry, Fassbach and the Israeli soldiers assigned to them are trying to reach an aircraft before the city becomes impossible to leave.
Peter rejoins them when their route starts collapsing. This is also where Gerry notices something Peter hasn’t been looking for.

In the middle of thousands of people running from the infected, certain people aren't being attacked at all. Gerry sees an elderly man left alone as the infected rush past him. Later, he notices them ignore a sick looking boy as well.

They don’t have time to investigate it in Jerusalem. One of the Israeli soldiers escorting Gerry is bitten on the hand during the escape. Gerry reacts immediately and amputates her hand before the infection can spread far enough to turn her. Peter helps get her away from the swarm while the others continue toward the aircraft.
He gets Gerry, Fassbach and the wounded soldier to the aircraft. Jerusalem still falls behind them, but the group leaving it is no longer the same one that escaped in the original timeline.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: The plane gives Peter the first quiet stretch he’s had since arriving in this world. Segen is alive, but she’s weak from blood loss. Fassbach helps treat her while Gerry goes over what he saw in Jerusalem. The infected had moved straight past people who should've been easy targets. Gerry had noticed something similar before, but Jerusalem gave him enough examples to believe it wasn’t random.

Fassbach starts working through possible explanations with him. Age alone doesn't fit. Neither does physical weakness. Some injured people are attacked while others are ignored, which suggests the infected are responding to something more specific.

Fassbach has experience working through biological problems under pressure. He starts separating what they actually know from what they’re assuming. The infected attack healthy people almost immediately. They don’t appear interested in feeding. Their behavior is focused on spreading the infection, and the people Gerry saw being ignored all appeared physically unwell in some way.

That gives them a theory, but not proof. Gerry contacts the pilots and changes their destination to Cardiff, where a World Health Organization research facility may have the equipment and medical staff needed to test it. They never get the chance to finish the discussion. A zombie has gotten onto the aircraft. The first infection happens away from Peter, deep enough inside the cabin that his Spider-Sense doesn’t give him a useful warning until the danger starts moving toward them. By then, passengers are already screaming and the infection is spreading from row to row.

Peter moves before Gerry can reach for a weapon. The small cabin works against him. He can’t swing, there’s almost no room to maneuver, and every passenger between him and the infected becomes someone he has to avoid hurting. Peter webs the first infected to the ceiling and forces his way farther down the aisle, but another passenger turns behind him.

Then another. The same speed that destroyed the streets of Philadelphia becomes much worse inside an aircraft. There’s nowhere for the passengers to run, and every person who gets caught adds another infected body inside the same enclosed space.

Peter starts pulling uninfected passengers over seats and toward the rear of the plane while using webbing to clog the aisle behind them. For several seconds, it works. Then one of the infected comes over the seats instead. Peter catches it by the throat before its teeth reach a passenger, but another grabs his arm from the side. His Spider-Sense fires again as a third lunges toward the exposed part of his neck.

Peter twists away just before the bite lands. It’s the closest he’s come since the outbreak began. The infected can’t overpower him individually, but the cabin has taken away most of the space that normally lets him use his speed. Peter throws the attackers backward and tears one of the overhead panels loose, using it to block part of the aisle while Gerry gets Segen farther away.

More infected are already coming through. Peter can hold the passage for a while. He can’t guarantee that none of them will get around him, and there are still passengers turning on both sides of the barrier.

Gerry sees that before Peter does and finds a grenade. Peter understands what Gerry is planning and uses his webs to secure himself, Gerry, Fassbach, Segen and as many nearby passengers as he can to fixed parts of the aircraft.

Gerry detonates the grenade. The blast tears open the side of the plane. Air, debris and bodies are ripped toward the opening as the cabin depressurizes. Peter’s webbing keeps their section from being emptied with it, but the aircraft is badly damaged and starts going down.

Peter can survive impacts that would kill an ordinary person but the people around him can’t. He webs Gerry, Fassbach and Segen tightly into their seats, braces himself against the aircraft and adds web lines anywhere he thinks they might help keep the cabin from breaking apart around them.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Peter wakes inside the wreckage. His suit is torn in several places, his body hurts but he can move. The same can’t be said for most of the passengers. Gerry is badly injured but alive. Segen survived as well. Fassbach is unconscious several rows away, still held in place by the webbing Peter used before the crash.

Peter gets to him first. Fassbach is breathing. He pulls the 3 of them out of the aircraft and finds that they've come down close enough to Cardiff to continue toward the WHO facility. Gerry can barely walk, so Peter carries him for most of the distance while Segen and Fassbach follow as best they can.
By the time they reach the facility, Gerry's injuries have caught up with him.

The WHO staff take all 4 of them inside. Gerry requires treatment and remains unconscious for days, just as he did after the crash in the original timeline. Peter doesn’t need the same recovery time, which means the investigation doesn’t stop while Gerry is unconscious. Fassbach is able to explain what they were working on before the plane went down.

So Peter doesn’t argue that they've solved anything. He asks what would have to be true for the theory to work. If the pathogen depends on living humans to spread, then attacking a host who's already seriously ill could be a poor use of that host. That would mean the infected aren’t simply responding to movement, sound or proximity. They're detecting some sign of whether the person in front of them is suitable.

The WHO facility gives them records, samples and people who can compare Gerry's observations against cases from other outbreaks. They start looking for reports of infected behaving strangely around hospitals, elderly patients and people with serious illnesses. The pattern isn’t perfect, but it’s strong enough to keep testing.
their working theory is that the infected avoid people whose bodies are already carrying serious diseases because those people make poor hosts for spreading the infection.
Now they need to prove it. The problem is that the pathogens they could use for a test are stored in another section of the facility, and part of that building has infected wandering through it.

In the original timeline, Gerry has to enter that section himself with Segen and one of the WHO doctors. Peter changes that immediately. There’s no reason to send Gerry. Peter can move through the building faster, he can climb across walls and ceilings, and his Spider-Sense gives him a much better chance of reaching the storage room without being bitten. The damaged web shooter limits how much webbing he has left, but he doesn’t need much if he can avoid contact.
Get the samples back so they can find out whether Gerry is right. PART 7

Peter enters the infected section of the WHO facility alone. This is one of the few places where his usual advantages don’t help as much as they did outside. There’s no room to swing, the hallways are narrow, and he can't afford to make enough noise to draw every infected person in the building toward him. With one web shooter damaged, wasting web fluid on fights would also leave him with fewer options if something goes wrong.

So Peter avoids fighting whenever he can. He moves across ceilings and upper walls, staying above doorways and out of the infected’s normal line of sight. His Spider-Sense gives him warning whenever one wanders too close, but the goal isn’t to test how many he can get past. He only needs to reach the storage area, retrieve what the WHO team needs and get back.

That works until he reaches the lab. Several infected are moving through the room between Peter and the storage cabinets. He can get around them, but opening the cabinets and searching through the samples will take time. Peter waits until they spread apart, drops behind one of the counters and starts checking the labels.

He finds them and loads several options into a medical case. Getting back out is harder. One of the infected enters the lab while Peter is still packing the samples. His Spider-Sense warns him before it reaches the counter, and Peter moves onto the ceiling without letting it touch him. Another infected follows the sound, then another.
Peter could knock all of them across the room, but doing that would bring more. Instead, he webs a door shut behind the first group and slips into the corridor before the rest can surround the room.

For most of the return trip, that’s enough. Then an infected comes through a doorway directly below him as another approaches from the opposite side of the hall. Peter moves between them, but the med case catches against the doorframe and slips from his hand.

He catches it before it reaches the floor. The movement puts him close enough for one of the infected to lunge. Peter’s Spider-Sense gives him the warning, but he can’t simply jump away without dropping the samples. He blocks the infected with his forearm, turns its head away from him and throws it into the wall. Peter retrieves the case and gets back to the secure section.

Now Gerry's theory can actually be tested. Fassbach helps the WHO doctors identify a pathogen they know they can treat if the theory works. There is no time for a normal trial, and Gerry refuses to ask someone else to take the risk for a theory he helped build. He volunteers himself. Peter initially offers to do it instead, but there’s no reason to assume his altered physiology would respond to the disease the same way an ordinary human would. Using Peter could ruin the test before it starts.
Once the infection has had enough time to produce symptoms, the volunteer is brought close enough to the contained infected for their reaction to be observed.

Gerry is brought near the contained infected. They rush toward the healthy people around him, then pass him by. The camouflage works. With the hypothesis finally proven, the WHO can begin turning that single desperate test into a controlled protocol using treatable pathogens.

The infection has a weakness, but it isn’t a cure. The zombies are still infected, the cities they've taken are still lost, and billions of people remain in danger. What humanity now has is a way to stop looking like a target.

What Peter changed was the speed at which it could be proven. Fassbach survived South Korea, the group reached Cardiff with another scientist who already understood the theory, and Peter could retrieve the samples without forcing Gerry to gamble his own life inside the infected section of the facility.
The WHO begins preparing the information for distribution. For the first time since Peter arrived, humanity has something it can use.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: Until now, almost every rescue has forced him to work around the same problem. Civilians attract the infected, which means moving people through an occupied area usually creates another swarm. The new treatment changes that. If survivors can be temporarily infected with a curable disease, they can pass through groups of zombies without immediately being attacked.

Peter still can’t fix what's happened to the people who've already turned, but he can start reaching places that were effectively cut off before. The first priority is getting the discovery out of Cardiff. The WHO sends the findings to governments and military forces that are still functioning, along with instructions for using treatable illnesses as camouflage. Gerry stays involved in that effort while Fassbach works with the doctors on making the process safer and easier to repeat.

He can cross infected areas without needing roads, and now the people he’s escorting don’t immediately draw a horde toward them. That means he can reach hospitals, shelters and isolated groups that would’ve been almost impossible to evacuate earlier. The difference is obvious the first time he moves a group through an infected street.

Peter helps wherever his abilities matter most. He reaches trapped med teams before normal rescue units can get to them. He carries medicine across collapsed routes. He retrieves equipment from buildings surrounded by infected and helps evacuate people from upper floors without forcing them back through the streets.
Fassbach is alive because Peter was at Camp Humphreys. Gerry reaches Cardiff with more
help than he had in the original timeline. The theory behind the camouflage is tested sooner,
and the people distributing it have Spider-Man available for jobs that would’ve required entire military teams.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: So could Spider-Man survive World War Z?
Probably, but not because the infected stop being dangerous.

Peter has too many ways to avoid getting trapped under normal circumstances, and Spider-Sense makes a successful bite much harder to land. If he only cared about keeping himself alive, he could stay away from population centers and avoid most of the outbreak entirely.

Most of the danger comes from the people he refuses to leave behind. Every rescue puts him back near the infected, and World War Z spreads quickly enough that one mistake could still end with Peter getting bitten.

What changes the outcome is that Peter doesn’t spend the entire outbreak fighting zombies. His presence keeps Fassbach alive, gives Gerry another person capable of studying what the infected are doing, and makes the Cardiff test much less dangerous.
Spider-Man would survive it, and because he was there, a lot more people probably would too.

scripts.title: Could Spider Man Survive The Last Of Us

sections.name: INTRO
paras: Peter Parker would have a huge advantage in The Last of Us. His Spider-Sense could warn him before infected get close, he can climb above most danger, and even a Clicker would struggle to overpower him in a straight fight.

The problem is that Peter can still get infected. His powers make a bite much harder to land, but there’s nothing about his body that guarantees Cordyceps can’t take hold if it gets inside him. He also has no Stark support, a small amount of web fluid, and no way to replace everything he uses once it’s gone.
So surviving this world would come down to more than beating infected. Peter would have to overcome so many obstacles where saving 1 person could mean giving up humanity’s best chance at a cure.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: This would use Peter after the events of No Way Home. By this point, he’s already been through enough that he doesn’t rush into every situation assuming he can fix it alone. That would matter almost immediately, because the first thing Peter would understand about this world is that nobody is coming to help him. For this scenario, I’m using the continuity of The Last of Us games.

He’d be pulled out of his universe during patrol and dropped onto the roof of an abandoned building in Boston years after the Cordyceps outbreak. At first, he’d think he landed somewhere in his own world after some kind of attack. Cars would be rusted into the streets, plants would be growing through buildings, and old military signs would still be hanging around checkpoints. His phone wouldn’t have a signal, and there’d be no way to reach anyone he knows.

Peter’s Spider-Sense would warn him before he sees the first infected. He’d hear movement deeper inside the building, climb down carefully, and find a Runner wandering through one of the rooms. When it charges him, Peter could dodge easily and web it against a wall before it gets close enough to bite. He’d probably stare at it for a few seconds because the fungal growth would make it obvious that this isn’t a normal person.

More Runners would hear the noise and start moving toward him. Peter could handle them without much trouble. He’d climb onto the ceiling, web 2 of them together, then kick another one far enough away to clear a path. He wouldn't need to hit them anywhere close to full strength. He’d start understanding the real danger once he finds an old fedra checkpoint and reads the infection warnings. Bites are enough to spread the infection, and areas filled with spores are treated like death traps without a mask. Peter would have no reason to assume his powers protect him from any of that. His healing is better than a normal person’s, but nothing he’s experienced proves that his body can stop Cordyceps once it gets inside him.
From that point on, he’d treat every bite like it could kill him.

By the end of that first day, Peter could already move through infected areas much more safely than a normal survivor. He’d also be down several web shots, carrying food he doesn’t know how long he can stretch, and looking for a respirator because there are parts of this world his Spider-Sense can’t help him breathe through.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Runners would be the easiest infected for Peter to deal with. A single one has almost no chance of catching him, and even a group would struggle in open space because Peter can climb out of reach whenever he needs to.

He’d still avoid killing them when possible. Peter would see enough human features underneath the infection to keep trying to restrain them instead. He could web someone to the floor, stick their hands to a wall, or block them behind a door and keep moving.

Peter could enter an abandoned hotel looking for supplies and hear voices deeper inside. His Spider-Sense would already be active because Stalkers are moving through the building, hiding behind furniture and staying out of sight. Peter could deal with them by placing thin web strands across doorways and halls. If something brushes one of the strands, he’d feel the movement and know where the infected are coming from.

A Stalker could rush him from a side room while another comes from behind. Peter would duck under the first, stick it to the floor, and turn before the second reaches him. The fight itself would be manageable.
Then he’d find 4 survivors trapped upstairs.

One of them could barely walk after hurting a leg while escaping the infected. Peter could climb out through a broken window and leave the whole building in less than a minute, but the people inside can’t follow him that way.

Peter could carry the injured survivor while using his free hand to web doors shut behind them. He’d move furniture to block hallways and pull people across gaps they couldn’t jump themselves. Every person he helps makes him spend more web fluid and move more slowly, but he’d keep doing it because leaving them behind wouldn't even feel like an option to him.

The group could explain more about what happened to the country while they travel. FEDRA zones, Fireflies, hunters, quarantine checkpoints, and infected cities would all be new to Peter. He’d learn that people have spent years making decisions he still isn’t comfortable with, especially when someone gets bitten.

Peter might notice that the person is getting slower and breathing differently several hours later. When he asks what’s wrong, the truth would finally come out. Peter would immediately start looking through whatever medicine the group has, asking whether anyone has ever slowed the infection or survived longer than expected.
The others would already know how this ends. Peter wouldn’t have anything to offer them except time.

He could sit with the person while the others move ahead, then watch the symptoms get worse. When the infected survivor starts losing control, Peter would have to restrain them before they hurt anyone else.
That would stay with him because there was never a fight he could win there. He could keep the person from hurting someone, but he couldn’t bring them back.

Peter would keep helping the remaining survivors until they reach somewhere safer, then move on with fewer webs than he started with and a much clearer idea of how expensive it is to protect people in this world.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Peter would hear a Clicker before he sees one. The sound alone would tell him this infected has been around much longer than the Runners and Stalkers he’s already fought. Once he sees the fungal growth covering its face and head, he’d understand that getting close is a bad idea even if he’s stronger.
Physically, Peter still has the advantage. If a Clicker grabs him, Peter can break the hold and throw it away. The problem is letting one get close enough to test that in the first place.

He’d start using ceilings and walls much more often once he realizes Clickers react to sound. Instead of walking over broken glass or loose debris, Peter could move above them and keep most of his weight off the floor.

Spores would be worse. Peter could enter a lower level of an old building and see fungal growth covering the walls. The air would be thick enough that any normal survivor would put on a mask immediately. Peter wouldn’t gamble on his Spider-Man mask filtering something it was never designed for, so he’d back out and look for a working respirator before going any farther.

That would change how he searches buildings. Peter could crawl through upper windows, ventilation openings, and damaged walls to avoid heavily contaminated sections instead of walking through every hallway.
A damaged gas mask would become more frightening than a broken flashlight.

If Peter has to cross a spore-filled room, he’d check the seal more than once and keep his time inside as short as possible. His powers don’t remove the need to breathe. Clickers would become much more dangerous whenever Peter has somebody with him.

He could be helping 2 survivors through an underground station when several Clickers start moving toward them. Peter could escape onto the ceiling immediately, but the survivors would be stuck on the ground.

He’d have to stay close. Peter could web 1 Clicker against a support beam, kick another away from the group, then grab the third before it reaches anyone. He’d use just enough strength to create space instead of throwing infected around the room and making more noise.

During the fight, one Clicker could tear part of Peter’s sleeve while he pulls a survivor away. Peter would get everyone behind a door and web it shut before checking the damage. There’d be no bite underneath, but he’d patch the tear before moving again because he knows the next infected could reach the same spot.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Peter would probably approach survivors more openly than most people in this world would, especially if someone looks injured or stranded.
That would eventually get used against him.

A group of hunters could stage an accident along a road, leaving one person lying near a damaged vehicle while the others hide in nearby buildings. Peter would notice something feels wrong before he gets close, but he wouldn’t know exactly what the setup is until someone fires. His Spider-Sense would hit just before the shot.

Peter could move out of the way, web the rifle out of the shooter’s hands, then cross the road before another hunter gets a clean angle. He’d pin 2 people to a wall and pull another off a rooftop before anyone can reload.

He wouldn't kill them. Peter would question them about nearby settlements and supply routes instead, but the hunters wouldn’t suddenly start telling the truth because he spared them. Peter would have to decide what information is useful and what sounds like someone trying to send him into another trap.
After that, he’d stop showing everyone exactly what he can do.

Peter could cover the Spider-Man suit with normal clothes whenever he approaches a settlement and avoid using his full strength unless he needs it. People who see someone climbing walls and throwing infected across rooms could easily decide he’s valuable enough to capture.
He’d also get much more careful about who he tells about his web shooters.
The shortage would already be getting worse.

Peter knows the formula, so he could search places that might still have the chemicals he needs. Some university labs would be stripped. Pharmacies might have useful materials but nothing close to a full batch. Industrial buildings could have more options, although getting there might mean crossing infected areas.

When Peter finally finds enough to make more web fluid, the batch might still be worse than what he made at home because some chemicals have been sitting around for decades or stored badly. He’d test every cartridge before trusting it.
A weak batch could snap too early. A thick one could jam a shooter.
Peter would also start taking jobs from settlements because he still needs food and supplies.

He’d clear infected out of a storage building, recover medicine from somewhere dangerous, or move debris blocking access to a safe area. The work would keep him supplied, but it would also keep giving him new people to worry about.
Every settlement would have someone missing, sick, trapped, or running out of something important.
Eventually Peter would realize he hasn't slept properly in days and is using his last good web cartridges on people he met that morning.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: Peter’s first Bloater would happen while he’s helping a small group recover medicine from an old school.
The group would reach the medical supplies before they hear something much heavier moving through another part of the building.
Peter would see the Bloater come through a doorway and immediately notice how much fungal armor covers its body.
He’d tell everyone else to start moving toward the exit.

The Bloater could charge, and Peter would jump onto the wall before it reaches him. He'd fire webbing across its legs to slow it down, but weaker cartridges could start tearing once the Bloater puts enough force against them.
Peter could hit it hard enough to throw it across the room.

That would create another problem. The impact could smash through old walls, knock debris into the hallway, and send enough noise through the school to wake up infected they had avoided earlier. Peter would hear Runners and Clickers starting to move deeper inside the building while the survivors are still trying to get out.
Now Peter has to control where the Bloater goes.

He could keep himself between it and the exit, use webbing around its arms to pull its attacks away from the survivors, and hit it toward empty rooms instead of sending it through whatever happens to be behind it.

The Bloater would still be able to take a lot of punishment because of the fungal plates, but Peter wouldn’t need to stand there trading hits with it. His goal would be keeping it away from everyone until they’re clear.

Fire would help finish the fight faster. If the survivors have Molotovs, Peter could web one out of somebody’s hand and place it directly onto the Bloater without making anyone get close. Once the fungal armor catches, Peter could keep it inside a room and web the doorway enough to slow it down while it burns.
Peter could grab the medicine, carry the slowest survivor, and lead the group out through an upper window instead of trying to clear every infected in the school.

They’d get away with the supplies. Peter would be left with damaged web shooters, several empty cartridges, and another reminder that his strength doesn’t make crowded infected buildings safe for the people around him.
Later, while trading some of the recovered medicine, Peter could hear a story that sounds different from the usual rumors.

A man has been traveling west with a girl, and Peter starts piecing together fragmented stories from people who crossed their path. One person remembers an old bite on the girl, another heard her claim she couldn’t turn, and the descriptions of the same man and girl traveling west stay unusually consistent.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Peter would eventually catch up with Joel and Ellie after following enough rumors about a man traveling west with a girl who had somehow survived a bite. He’d find them before they reach the University of Eastern Colorado, and Joel would immediately be suspicious because Peter doesn’t move like anyone he’s ever seen before. Peter could approach with his hands visible and keep his distance, but Joel would still have a weapon ready while Ellie tries to figure out why this dude is wearing patched clothes over something that looks like a costume.

Peter wouldn’t explain everything about where he came from right away. He’d tell them that he’s been following stories about Ellie because he heard she was bitten and never turned, which would make Joel even more guarded. Ellie might try to brush it off at first, but Peter has already seen enough infected people to know how quickly bites normally become fatal. Once Ellie shows him the old mark, he’d realize the rumor was real.

Peter would start asking how long she has been immune, whether anyone has tested her, and what the Fireflies believe they can do with that information. Joel would keep the answers short because his only goal is getting Ellie where she needs to go, while Ellie would be more willing to explain why the trip matters. Peter would understand why the Fireflies want to study her, especially after seeing entire cities destroyed by Cordyceps, but he’d also notice how quickly people talk about Ellie’s immunity before talking about Ellie herself.

Ellie would probably understand both sides better than either of them expects. She knows Joel’s caution is what kept them alive, but she’d also see Peter use his powers to save people without turning every rescue into a disaster. Over time, Joel would stop treating Peter like a stranger who could become a threat at any moment and start treating him like someone useful enough to include in the plan.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: The university would still be one of their major stops because Joel expects to find Fireflies there. Peter could search the upper floors and rooftops much faster than either of them, but he’d eventually find the same problem. The medical team has already moved, and the remaining evidence points toward Salt Lake City.

The human attack around the university would play differently because Peter’s Spider-Sense would warn him before the group is fully surrounded. Joel could still get pulled into a fight, but Peter would be able to reach him before he suffers the same serious injury he originally gets during this part of the journey. Peter could web weapons away, pull attackers off Joel, and use enough force to end the fight without leaving bodies everywhere.

That would remove the long stretch where Ellie originally has to keep Joel alive almost by herself. Joel would still get hurt sometimes because Peter can’t cover every angle every second, but he wouldn’t spend weeks near death while Ellie searches for medicine and food. The group could keep moving toward Salt Lake with fewer delays. Because Joel never spends weeks incapacitated, Ellie never has to hunt alone for them, so the chain of events that originally led her to David would most likely never happen.

Peter would get closer to Ellie during the quieter parts of the trip. She’d ask about his world, and Peter could tell her about schools, crowded cities, movies, restaurants, and other normal things she has mostly experienced through old stories and abandoned buildings. Peter would eventually realize that describing his old life too casually can sound strange to someone who grew up after civilization collapsed, so he’d spend more time listening when Ellie explains what normal life looks like to her. As they get closer, Ellie could eventually tell Peter about Riley, Tess, Sam, and some of the other people she lost to the infection.

Joel would also start noticing that Peter isn’t treating Ellie like a medical answer. Peter is interested in her immunity, but he talks to her directly and includes her whenever the subject comes up. That would matter later because Joel has become protective enough that any conversation about a cure starts sounding to him like someone is deciding what Ellie is worth. As they get closer to Salt Lake, Peter would keep thinking about the Fireflies more seriously. He has enough science knowledge to understand that Ellie being immune could be incredibly important, but he also knows that 1 unusual patient doesn’t guarantee anyone can turn that into a cure. He’d want to hear what the doctors have actually learned before assuming they can save the world.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: The group would eventually reach Salt Lake City and start moving toward the Firefly hospital. Peter could help them through flooded buildings and infected areas by creating web lines across gaps, carrying Ellie through places where the water becomes dangerous, and checking upper routes before Joel has to risk entering them. His powers would make several parts easier, but Peter would still be watching his remaining web fluid because he has been using and remaking it for months without the equipment he normally has.

The Fireflies would find them before they reach the hospital properly. Peter’s Spider-Sense would warn him that armed people are closing in, but once he realizes who they are, he wouldn’t attack. Ellie came all this way to reach them, so Peter would let the Fireflies take the group inside while keeping a close eye on what they do.

The situation would change once Peter learns what the Fireflies intend to do. Their doctors believe the Cordyceps growing in Ellie’s brain behaves differently from normal infections, and they think studying it directly could help them understand why she never turned. The problem is that removing it requires brain surgery Ellie won't survive.

Peter would immediately ask what they already tested and whether they can learn more without killing her. He’d want to know what samples they took, what evidence supports their theory, and how certain they are that the operation could lead to anything useful. The doctors could explain their reasoning, but they still wouldn’t be able to promise that Ellie’s death produces a cure.

Peter would also learn that Ellie hasn’t been told she’s going to die. She’s unconscious while the surgery is being prepared, and the Fireflies have already decided the possible benefit is worth the risk without waking her first. Joel would react almost immediately because by this point Ellie has become family to him, but Peter would spend a little longer asking questions because he wants to know whether there’s any medical reason the operation has to happen right now. Once it becomes clear that the Fireflies are going ahead without asking Ellie, Peter would tell them to stop preparing the surgery and wake her up. He’d make it clear that Ellie can decide what she wants to do after she understands the risks, but nobody gets to make that decision while she’s unconscious.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: The hospital confrontation would begin with Peter trying to avoid a fight. He’d tell the Fireflies to wake Ellie and explain the surgery to her, while Joel makes it obvious that he wants her out of the building immediately. Some Fireflies might understand why Peter is asking, but the people running the operation would believe they can’t risk losing their only known immune patient after waiting this long. They would refuse to delay the operation long enough to wake Ellie and let her decide, leaving Peter no safe way to stop the surgery except getting her out of the hospital first.

Once armed guards try moving Joel away and keeping Peter from the operating room, Peter would act. He could web rifles to walls, trap people’s arms against doors, and pull weapons away before anyone gets a clean shot. His Spider-Sense would make fighting through hospital corridors much safer for him than it was for Joel originally, and his strength means he can stop someone without needing to shoot them.

Joel would still be much more willing to kill anyone standing between him and Ellie. Peter would have to keep moving toward the operating room while also stopping Joel from shooting people who are already disarmed or unable to follow them. Joel would hate being slowed down, but he’d know Peter is still helping him reach Ellie faster than he ever could alone.

When they reach the operating room, Peter wouldn't need to kill the surgeon. He could web the surgical tools away, pull the doctor back from the table, and pin his arms somewhere he can’t interfere. Peter would check that Ellie is stable before lifting her because he doesn’t want to move someone under anesthesia without knowing whether anything has already started.

Peter could carry Ellie out while Joel covers the route behind them. Instead of taking every hallway the Fireflies expect, Peter could use stairwells, upper windows, and exterior walls to move around blocked sections while keeping Ellie secured against him. The escape would still be tense because Peter has to protect an unconscious person while armed Fireflies are trying to stop him, but Spider-Sense and wall-crawling give him routes nobody in the hospital is prepared to defend.

Marlene would still confront them before they leave. She could argue that Ellie would probably choose to die if it gave everyone else a chance, and Peter would take that seriously because Ellie has already told him how much her immunity means to her. He still wouldn't accept Marlene making that choice for Ellie without asking her.

Peter would leave Marlene alive if he can disarm her safely. Keeping her alive also leaves someone who knows what research the Fireflies completed before the surgery and gives Ellie the option of speaking to them again later if she chooses. Joel would want as much distance from the hospital as possible, so Peter would get Ellie into the vehicle and make sure they’re gone before more Fireflies arrive.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: Peter wouldn’t be comfortable letting Ellie wake up believing the Fireflies simply gave up. Joel might want to tell her that there were other immune people or that the doctors couldn’t do anything, because keeping Ellie away from the truth feels safer to him. Peter would understand why Joel wants that, especially after seeing how desperate he became at the hospital, but he wouldn’t help him hide something this important from her.

Once Ellie is awake, stable, and able to understand what happened, Peter would explain it carefully. The Fireflies believed they could learn something from the Cordyceps in her brain, but removing it would have killed her. Joel and Peter stopped the surgery because Ellie had never been told that was the plan and never got the chance to say whether she was willing to die for it. Ellie would probably be furious with both of them. She could tell Peter that she would have agreed because Riley, Tess, Sam, and everyone else who died from infection still matters to her. Peter wouldn’t try to talk her out of feeling that way or claim the Fireflies had nothing worth studying. He’d tell her that if she still wants to help after hearing everything, then she deserves to decide what happens next while she’s awake and knows what the doctors are asking.

Joel would have a much harder time accepting that. He’d want Ellie away from the Fireflies permanently, while Peter would know that protecting someone can’t mean controlling every decision they make afterward. Peter could offer to help Ellie search for other surviving doctors or researchers, recover whatever medical records the Fireflies already created, or even return to the Fireflies later under conditions Ellie actually agrees to. He’d also be honest that there may not be another team with the people or equipment to study her immunity properly.

There wouldn’t be an easy answer waiting for them. The Fireflies might still be the best researchers they can find, Ellie could still decide someday that she wants to take a serious risk for a cure, and Joel would still be terrified of losing her. Peter’s presence gives Ellie more information and more time to decide what she wants to do with her immunity instead of waking up after everyone else has already decided for her.

Peter would survive the infected world much more easily than most people because Runners, Stalkers, Clickers, and even Bloaters have a hard time catching someone with his strength, speed, wall-crawling, and Spider-Sense. The harder part would always be staying beside people who can’t move the way he does. Every rescue costs food, web fluid, sleep, and sometimes the chance to escape before an area becomes worse.

He still couldn’t rebuild civilization by himself. Peter could clear infected buildings, recover medicine, protect settlements, and help Ellie search for doctors, but factories, hospitals, farms, governments, and supply networks don’t come back because Spider-Man can lift a truck. He’d keep doing what he can wherever he happens to be, which is probably the closest this world could get to having Spider-Man without suddenly turning the last of us into a completely different story.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: Spider-Man could survive the last of us, and most infected would have a very hard time killing him once he understands how Cordyceps spreads. His Spider-Sense makes ambushes much less effective, his mobility lets him avoid fights other survivors are forced into, and his strength gives him ways to protect people who would normally have no chance.

The harder part would come from everything his powers can’t solve. Peter would still run out of supplies, watch infected people he can’t cure, and eventually have to decide what happens when the Fireflies are willing to kill Ellie for a possible cure. He’d stop the surgery long enough for Ellie to make that decision herself, then keep helping her search for an answer without pretending he can fix the entire world alone.

scripts.title: Could Spider Man Survive The US Military

sections.name: INTRO
paras: If Spider-Man became the most wanted man in America, Peter could probably escape the first few attempts to catch him pretty easily. MCU Peter after No Way Home is fast, insanely mobile, strong enough to tear through most physical restraints, and Spider Sense gives him warning before danger even reaches him.

I'd start him in New York with his homemade suit, limited web fluid, no Stark support, and no one helping him. The government wants him captured alive, and at the beginning they only know Spider Man’s abilities, his usual operating area, and the places he’s been seen before. For the first phase, Peter would be a nightmare to chase. He can cut through alleys, cross rooftops, climb straight up buildings, swing over traffic, and change direction faster than ground teams can follow. Every escape also gives the government more information though. Camera footage, witness reports, traffic systems, drones, and old Spider-Man sightings would slowly build a clearer picture of where Peter goes and how he moves.

That's where surviving starts getting much harder. The hunt would keep spreading until Peter isn’t just avoiding the people behind him anymore. He’d have to start thinking about every camera above him, every place he sleeps, every time he buys food, and every decision that could narrow down where he goes next.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: Peter's first problem would start in New York, where the government already has years of public footage showing what Spider-Man can do. For this scenario, I'd say he’s wanted after being blamed for interfering with a federal operation involving enhanced weapons, and the order is to capture him alive. The military response is supported by federal and local law-enforcement agencies, so the hunt can draw on investigative work and surveillance information those agencies already have access to instead of treating the military as if it independently controls every camera and record in the country. Nobody knows who's under the mask yet. They've got footage of Spider-Man fighting, moving through the city, and appearing around major incidents, while Peter only knows that federal authorities are looking for him and that the response is getting bigger.

This is Peter after no way home, so he’s working with a homemade suit and the web shooters he built himself. He doesn’t have access to Stark satellites, drones, instant suit repairs, or anyone who can refill his equipment for him. Whatever web fluid he has on him has to last until he can get somewhere safe enough to make more, and every damaged piece of gear becomes his problem to fix.

The first attempt to grab him probably goes badly for the people trying it. Peter spots tactical vehicles moving into the area around one of his usual patrol routes, then Spider Sense kicks in before the actual trap closes. Teams start sealing streets while officers move onto rooftops and helicopters circle above, but Peter can leave the street almost immediately. He swings across the block, runs along the side of a building, cuts through a construction site, and changes direction before anyone on the ground has time to follow.
A helicopter can keep him in sight for longer than a police car, so Peter starts moving underneath bridges, through narrow streets, and between buildings where the aircraft can’t

maintain a clean angle. Cameras keep catching pieces of the chase, which means he’s leaving a trail even while the teams behind him are falling farther away. Peter doesn’t know how much of that footage is being collected yet, so he’s still thinking about the people physically chasing him rather than the people watching from somewhere else.

When a team finally corners him inside a parking structure, Peter doesn’t have to fight them for long. Spider Sense tells him where the first shots are coming from before anyone fires, webbing takes weapons and shields out of hands, and his strength lets him rip open a metal barrier that was supposed to close the exit. He’s gone before the team can reorganize.

That first escape would probably give Peter confidence because every person he actually sees is manageable. The bigger problem is that the government now has footage of how he escaped, which streets he chose, how fast he moved, and which parts of the city he used to break line of sight.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: The next response would be built around making Peter’s movement easier to follow. Teams on the ground would still matter, but cameras, drones, helicopters, and analysts would start working together so every escape doesn't reset the search. New York already has an enormous amount of surveillance infrastructure, and the government can add temporary systems around places Spider-Man has used before.

Peter starts noticing small drones above intersections where he normally swings. Some are far enough away that Spider Sense doesn’t react because they aren't attacking him, which makes them more useful than anything carrying a weapon. They're just watching. Peter can web one out of the sky if he spots it, but doing that tells whoever’s monitoring the feed exactly where Spider-Man is.

His civilian needs also start becoming part of the problem. Peter still needs food, water, sleep, clothes, web fluid, and somewhere to repair the suit. Going back to his apartment would be easy, but he has no way of knowing whether anyone connected Spider-Man's movements to that neighborhood yet. He stays away and spends the night in an unfinished building where he can sleep above street level without checking into anywhere.

The next morning, he has to make web fluid with whatever he can access. That becomes much harder once he can’t freely buy chemicals or walk into a normal workspace carrying Spider-Man equipment. Peter can improvise because he’s extremely intelligent, but improvising still takes materials and time. Every hour spent making more web fluid is an hour where he has to stay in one place.

By the time Peter realizes how much surveillance is following him, simply crossing the city has become harder. He can still escape individual teams, but each appearance creates another cluster of footage that gets added to the same map.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Peter eventually decides New York is becoming too predictable. Every street he knows well is also a street where years of Spider-Man footage already exist, and staying close to the same neighborhoods keeps giving the search more material. He waits until late at night, changes into normal clothes, hides the suit under them, and leaves the city without using webs.

Getting out quietly is harder than it sounds. Airports require identification, buses and trains create records, toll roads are covered by cameras, and carrying Spider-Man equipment through any security checkpoint could end the run immediately. Peter avoids the obvious options and starts moving through less direct routes, using cash whenever he can and walking long stretches when transportation feels too exposed.

For a while, that works. The search is still concentrated around New York, and a teenager in ordinary clothes doesn’t automatically look like the person everyone is chasing. Peter keeps his head down, sleeps in places where nobody asks for identification, and only uses his powers when he absolutely has to. Even wall crawling becomes something he has to think about because a single person recording him climbing somewhere could bring the search right back.

His biggest advantage here is that Spider Sense protects him from the moment a stop turns dangerous. If federal teams set up a checkpoint ahead, Spider Sense could hit as Peter gets close enough that continuing would put him in danger of being intercepted, giving him a chance to turn around while he still has room. That doesn’t tell him exactly what's waiting or that a checkpoint specifically exists, but it gives him a warning ordinary fugitives would never have.

Nobody immediately gets a file that says Peter Parker is Spider-Man. The spell after No Way Home leaves Peter’s situation complicated enough that | wouldn't invent a clean database answer the movies never established. Investigators would have to work from physical evidence and patterns that still exist in the world.
Peter doesn’t know they've started doing that. He only notices that moving as a civilian is becoming more dangerous even when he hasn’t worn the suit for hours.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: The identity hunt would probably become the biggest turning point in the entire scenario. Once analysts suspect Spider-Man is a young man who spent years operating around Queens, they can start comparing his activity with people who consistently disappear from normal records or appear near the same incidents.

Peter has another problem because he can’t completely stop being Spider-Man just because he’s running. If he sees a car crash, a fire, or someone about to die, he’s still Peter. The first few times he helps, he does it quickly and leaves before anyone gets a clear look, but every rescue risks giving away another location.

One of those rescues finally costs him. Peter is passing through a smaller city when he sees part of a building collapse after an accident. He tries to stay out of sight, but there are people trapped underneath debris and no way he’s walking away from that. He pulls several people free, holds part of the structure long enough for firefighters to move underneath it, then leaves before emergency crews can question him.
Several phones caught pieces of it anyway.

The footage reaches the search teams quickly because Spider-Man’s abilities are too distinctive to ignore. Peter never puts the full suit on, but one shaky video shows someone in a hood lifting weight far beyond anything normal and another catches him sticking to the side of the damaged structure for a second. Analysts now have a city and a rough time, but the videos never catch a clear look at his face.

Peter realizes he made a mistake once he notices drones several hours later. He changes direction again and gets away before teams arrive, but he’s exhausted and has barely slept. Spider Sense can warn him about danger, and it can’t replace sleep when his body starts slowing down.

The government now starts checking everything around the rescue. Traffic cameras, store cameras, transit footage, and people who passed through the area all become useful. Peter never used a phone or credit card there, but cameras can still follow the same person backward until the trail becomes messy.
That pushes Peter into a much harsher style of hiding. He starts avoiding towns whenever possible, sleeping outdoors, stealing short periods of rest in abandoned buildings, and carrying
whatever food he can get without creating another record. The suit stays packed away because every Spider-Man sighting now brings the search down on him faster.
The manhunt still hasn’t physically caught up with him, but Peter’s life has already changed from escaping teams to constantly thinking about whether any ordinary action could expose him.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: Once the search expands nationwide, Peter’s mobility starts working differently. In New York, he could disappear vertically into a city built around rooftops and narrow streets. Outside dense urban areas, there are fewer buildings to swing from, fewer crowds to disappear into, and longer stretches where anyone moving unusually fast stands out immediately.

He starts choosing cities based on how easily he can move through them rather than how far they are from the last search area. Dense downtowns still give him options, while open highways, suburbs, and rural roads can leave him exposed to aircraft and cameras for much longer. Peter’s capable of covering distance quickly on foot, but doing that repeatedly burns energy he can’t easily replace when he’s already avoiding stores and restaurants.

Those tricks buy him time, and the search keeps learning from them. Analysts start studying how long Spider-Man usually stays hidden after a sighting and how far someone with his speed could travel during that gap. Teams begin positioning ahead of him instead of always reacting to where he was last seen.

Peter notices the shift during an attempted crossing between 2 cities. He changes direction when Spider Sense warns him as he gets close enough to one checkpoint for interception to become a threat, then finds another team already positioned farther down the route. He doubles back and sees aircraft moving toward the area he originally came from, which tells him they're starting to anticipate several possible exits at once. He still escapes. Peter climbs underneath a bridge, waits while the first search passes overhead, then drops into the water and follows the structure far enough to reach the other side without appearing on the road. It's exactly the kind of solution Peter is good at finding when everyone thinks the obvious routes are closed.

He comes out exhausted, soaked, and nearly out of web fluid. His suit has damage he hasn't had time to repair, he’s sleeping in short stretches, and every new escape requires more effort than the one before it. The military still hasn’t found a soldier who can physically keep up with Spider-Man, and that isn’t what's making Peter’s situation worse. His safe options are disappearing faster than he can replace them.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: By now, Peter's running into a problem he can’t dodge with Spider Sense. His equipment is starting to wear down, and replacing it without exposing himself is getting harder. The suit has tears he’s patched more than once, some of the web shooters are starting to need parts, and every cartridge he uses matters because he can’t just walk into a lab and make more whenever he wants.

Peter starts rationing the webs instead of using them for every movement. He'll still swing when he needs speed, but long stretches of travel get replaced with climbing, walking, and moving through places where he can stay off cameras. That saves fluid, but it slows him down and keeps him in one area longer, which gives the search more time to build around him.

He eventually reaches the point where making more web fluid is worth the risk. Peter knows exactly what he needs, so he waits until late at night and slips into a research building after checking the area from several blocks away. He avoids the main entrances, goes in through an upper maintenance section, and gets to work without touching anything he doesn’t need.

That part goes well. The problem starts because Peter has to stay still long enough to finish making the fluid. A security system logs movement in a restricted section, and Spider Sense hits before the response team ever reaches the building. Peter packs what he has, leaves the rest, and gets onto the roof just as drones start moving toward the block.

He escapes, but the government gets something useful out of it. Spider-Man just risked entering a chemistry lab and stayed long enough to collect specific materials. Analysts start comparing that with everything already known about his webbing and realize he’s making his web fluid on the run, which means his supply has to come from somewhere they can watch.

From that point on, they don’t watch every lab in the country. They narrow it down to places in whatever region Peter is believed to be moving through, then prioritize buildings that carry the kind of chemicals or hardware he might actually use. Peter can still avoid them, but now even resupplying has become part of the manhunt.

He adapts by taking smaller amounts from different places instead of getting everything from one building. That lowers the chance of one trip exposing him, but it means more trips, more time outside, and more chances for somebody to notice the same young man moving through areas where Spider-Man later appears.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: That gives them a starting pool instead of a name. They compare old Spider-Man appearances with school events, emergencies, transit patterns, and places where he showed up unusually fast. Midtown and Queens start coming up often enough to matter, especially when older incidents involving students and Spider-Man are placed on the same timeline, but the spell leaves them reconstructing an unknown civilian candidate rather than pulling a complete pre-spell identity from a database.

The No Way Home spell keeps this from turning into a clean database search. Even the old Mysterio broadcast that named Spider-Man as Peter Parker doesn’t solve it, because after the spell that name doesn’t connect to anyone people actually remember, and the movies never show what happened to that footage. Nobody remembers Peter Parker as Spider-Man, and the movies never give us a perfect answer for what every surviving record looks like afterward, so the government can’t just pull up an old file and solve the whole thing. They have to work from whatever physical records and public footage still make sense in the world.

Peter eventually becomes one name among several possible candidates only after investigators find at least one surviving physical or digital record that attaches the name Peter Parker to the same unknown young man they have been reconstructing from footage and physical evidence. The script doesn't need to assume his complete pre-spell school history survived intact; it only needs one coherent surviving record to give investigators a name they can test against the age range and repeated activity around Queens and Midtown. None of that proves anything yet, so they keep watching instead of moving on him.

Peter makes the next clue possible because he still cares about people from his old life. Investigators don’t remember MJ or Ned as being connected to Peter, but Midtown and other locations repeatedly adjacent to historical Spider-Man activity are already receiving light surveillance. Peter doesn’t walk up to either of them or do anything as obvious as standing outside their homes in costume. After being on the run for weeks, he spends a few minutes watching one of them near one of those Spider-Man-associated locations from far enough away that he thinks he’s invisible in the crowd.

A long range camera catches only part of his face and clothing, but the sighting matters because the same person is later seen leaving an area where Spider-Man appears that night. Investigators still don’t have a clean confirmation, but Peter Parker moves much higher on the list.

They keep testing the theory through observation. Locations that independently keep appearing around historical Spider-Man activity get watched lightly enough that Peter won't immediately notice, and the search teams compare any unusual movement around those places with later Spider-Man activity. One pattern lines up, then another.

Peter realizes something has changed when he sees the same kind of surveillance around a place nobody should care about if they're only looking for Spider-Man. That's when he understands they're starting to look for Peter too, which takes away one of the few advantages he still had.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: The military also stops treating every possible sighting like an emergency. Rushing straight at Peter has already failed too many times, so teams begin building wider containment zones around places where they think he’s operating. One group watches the route he’s most likely to take, another covers the direction he usually changes toward when he notices danger, and aircraft stay farther back where Peter can’t simply web them out of the sky.

Peter runs into one of those setups in an industrial district late at night. Spider Sense warns him away from the first road before he reaches the checkpoint, so he cuts through a loading yard and climbs onto a warehouse roof. From there, he spots movement farther out and realizes they aren't chasing the building. They’re covering the whole area around it.

He drops inside before the aircraft can keep a clean line on him. The warehouse is still operating, which gives Peter workers, machinery, service halls, and several exits to work with. He moves through overhead maintenance spaces until he reaches the opposite side, then waits instead of leaving immediately.

That escape works because the search was built around Peter’s usual movement, and he finally stopped moving like Spider-Man. The next time the military sets up a containment zone, workers leaving buildings are checked more carefully and exits stay covered longer.

Peter notices the difference almost immediately. The same kind of escape that worked once now takes twice as long because people are waiting for it. He still gets away, but the search is getting better at keeping old mistakes from happening twice.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: Peter can change routes, clothing, sleeping spots, and the way he moves through a city. The one thing he keeps doing the same is stopping when somebody needs help.

The government catches onto that after comparing several Spider-Man sightings that don’t fit the rest of his travel pattern. A fire in one city, a crash in another, and a collapsing structure farther west all get Spider-Man appearances even when Peter had clearly been trying to stay hidden before each one. Those incidents give analysts a better way to narrow him down because emergencies can pull him out of hiding without anyone knowing where he was sleeping.

They don’t create disasters or start hurting people to lure him. They start watching real emergencies inside whatever region Peter is already suspected to be in. When something serious happens, nearby surveillance gets more attention because there’s a chance Spider-Man will show up before normal responders can handle it.

Peter exposes himself during a major highway pileup. Several cars are trapped under part of an overturned truck, and a fire is spreading toward people who can't get out. Peter is already nearby when he sees the smoke, so he puts the mask on and gets involved even though he knows exactly what that might cost him.

He tears open one vehicle, webs another away from the fire, and lifts part of the truck long enough for people underneath to crawl out. By the time the last person is clear, multiple cameras have already caught him and the location has been passed up the chain.
He keeps moving because stopping near the accident would only bring the search back on top of him.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: The endgame starts after another few days of movement with Peter still carrying the injury from the highway. The government has narrowed him to a broad industrial region because of sightings, supply activity, and the routes he used after the rescue. They still don’t know which building he’s sleeping in, so they keep surveillance spread out and wait for a confirmed reason to tighten it.

That reason comes from a real industrial accident. An explosion inside a processing facility starts a fire and traps workers before local crews can reach all of them. Peter is close enough to see the smoke and hears the emergency response moving toward it.
He knows the search will be watching something this big. He goes anyway.

Peter reaches the site from the back and starts helping before most of the perimeter is even established. He pulls workers through a damaged wall, webs loose machinery away from one exit, and holds part of a collapsed section long enough for several people to get clear. By the time he’s finished, everybody looking for Spider-Man knows exactly where he is.

The military doesn’t rush the building. Teams spread outward around the industrial area and start controlling the routes Peter has used during earlier escapes. Aircraft stay back and watch the larger perimeter, while drones cover gaps between structures without getting close enough to become obvious targets.

Peter feels danger when he heads for the first exit and changes direction before the nearest team closes. He goes through a service tunnel instead, comes out several blocks away, and finds that route watched too. He climbs onto a roof, sees aircraft covering the open side of the district, then drops back down before anybody gets a clean angle.

The setup keeps forcing him to move through the same shrinking area. Peter still finds ways through individual layers. He webs a gate open, crawls underneath a loading platform, crosses between rooftops, and uses a moving freight vehicle to break one line of sight. Every time he gets farther out, another part of the perimeter has already shifted because the teams aren't waiting in fixed positions.

His injured leg gets worse as the chase goes on. The web cartridges are almost empty, and Peter has already been awake long enough that the quick decisions he normally makes start taking more effort. Spider Sense keeps warning him when a route is dangerous, but several directions begin feeling bad at once because different teams are covering different exits.

Peter finally reaches a section of open ground between industrial buildings where he can see a way toward the edge of the perimeter. He starts across and Spider Sense fires hard enough to make him change direction before a containment team moves into the route ahead. Peter swings toward another building, gets halfway there, and the last usable web cartridge runs dry. He catches the wall with his hands instead and keeps climbing, but his injured leg slips when he tries to pull himself over the edge. That delay gives the teams below time to close the distance while another group is already moving toward the far side of the building.

Peter still makes them work for it. He drops back down, webs one weapon away with the little fluid left in the other shooter, and gets through the first group before they can restrain him. The next escape route sends him toward the same interior yard he crossed earlier, where more teams are waiting after seeing that pattern during the chase.

At that point, Peter is exhausted, hurt, and almost completely out of web fluid. He dodges the first attempt to grab him, breaks one restraint, and gets several meters farther before another group closes from the side he was already moving toward.

Peter’s Spider Sense is still working. It can warn him where the restraints and people closing around him are coming from, but it can’t make his exhausted, injured body move fast enough to avoid several threats at once. The teams have already learned that a normal restraint won’t hold Spider-Man, so the capture procedure is layered around denying him leverage rather than trusting one stronger pair of cuffs. They pin him long enough to secure his wrists and arms, add restraints across his torso while multiple people keep pressure on him, and continue immobilizing him faster than his exhausted body can break each layer before the next one is applied.
So | don’t think the U.S. military catches MCU Spider-Man quickly. Peter could stay free for weeks if he keeps moving carefully, and most direct attempts to grab him would go badly
because Spider Sense, his speed, and his mobility are far beyond what normal personnel are built to handle.

He eventually runs out of room through a much slower process. His equipment wears down, his supplies expose patterns, his identity gives investigators more places to watch, and rescuing people keeps pulling him back into view. Once enough of those pieces line up at the same time, the military can keep the pressure on long enough for Peter’s body and equipment to fail before the search does.

scripts.title: Could The Death Note Kill Deadpool

sections.name: INTRO
paras: If you wrote Wade Wilson's name in the Death Note while picturing his real face, the notebook should be able to target him. Wade is still human, Wade Wilson is his real name, and for this we're using Earth-616 Deadpool with his normal healing factor active instead of stacking every temporary immortality effect he’s had across different points in the comics.

That makes the first test simple. If no cause is written, the Death Note gives Wade a heart attack, but Wade has survived damage that destroys organs and would kill almost anyone else immediately. The important question is whether the notebook only causes the heart attack itself, or whether its supernatural rules guarantee that Wade stays dead once his name has been written.

And that still leaves the harder part. Deadpool has come back after deaths that genuinely killed him at the time, so even if the Death Note can stop his body, we still have to figure out whether it can prevent him from returning afterward. The answer depends on how the notebook handles regeneration, how far a written cause of death can go, and whether killing Wade once is enough to keep him gone.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: The Death Note has a few rules we have to lock in before Deadpool even enters the equation. The notebook kills a human when the correct name is written while the writer has that person’s face in mind, and if no cause is added, the default is a heart attack. A cause can be written within 40 seconds, with additional details added during the next 6 minutes and 40 seconds, but whatever the writer asks for still has to be physically possible for that person.

That last part matters because the Death Note does not work like unlimited reality warping. The writer can control actions leading into the death, but the victim cannot suddenly do something physically impossible just because it was written down. The notebook also has rules preventing a written death from directly causing the deaths of people whose names were never entered, which immediately removes a lot of ridiculous solutions like telling Wade to crash a passenger plane into a city just to make sure nothing is left of him.

For Deadpool, we're using Earth-616 Wade with his standard healing factor active and leaving the old Thanos immortality curse out of the test. That curse existed during a specific period of Wade's history and was later removed, so using it here would answer a different question before we even test the notebook. Marvel still describes Wade as possessing an accelerated healing factor capable of making him extraordinarily difficult to kill, which gives us plenty to work with without adding a separate magical effect that literally kept him alive.

The notebook still gets one advantage before any of those powers matter. Its first rule does not say the target has to be healthy, easy to kill, or biologically normal; it says the target has to be human. The first real test is therefore whether Wade still qualifies as one.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Wade should qualify as human under the way Earth-616 normally treats him. He began as an ordinary human, developed cancer, and later received the healing factor through experimentation connected to Weapon X. The procedure radically changed what his body can survive, but Marvel still presents Wade Wilson as a human whose body was altered rather than a completely separate species.

The cancer does not change that either. Wade’s healing factor constantly rebuilds damaged tissue while his cancerous cells are also part of the body it keeps regenerating, which is why his appearance remains scarred instead of simply healing back to normal. That physiology is extremely abnormal, but nothing in the Death Note rules gives us a reason to say a medically altered human stops being eligible once his cells regenerate too quickly.

The name is more annoying than it first appears because Deadpool comics have deliberately played games with Wade's identity. T-Ray once claimed that the man calling himself Deadpool had stolen the Wade Wilson identity, and different stories have left pieces of Wade's early history unreliable enough that simply seeing “Wade Wilson” on a file is not the safest possible proof. The Death Note has an answer for that kind of ambiguity because Shinigami Eyes reveal the specific name required to kill a human even if that name is not officially registered anywhere.
