So if Light only knows Deadpool as a masked mercenary called Wade Wilson from secondhand information, there is a small uncertainty worth acknowledging. If he has the Shinigami Eyes, that issue disappears because the notebook’s own system gives him whatever name is actually required. If we want to test the Death Note itself instead of letting an old identity mystery decide the entire matchup, the clean assumption is that the writer has the correct killing name for Earth-616 Wade.

The face requirement is easier once the mask comes off. The notebook needs the writer to picture the target’s face so people with the same name are not affected, and Deadpool’s damaged skin does not stop his face from being his face. A clear photograph of Wade unmasked would be enough for somebody who already knows the correct name. Shinigami Eyes solve the remaining name ambiguity if the eye user can actually see Wade's face directly, rather than relying on the eyes to identify him from a photograph.

With the name and face handled, there is no obvious rule preventing the notebook from activating on Wade. His healing factor only becomes relevant after the Death Note has already accepted him as a valid target. That brings us to the simplest possible entry Light could make, Wade Wilson, with no cause written at all.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: If no cause is specified, Wade gets a heart attack. The Death Note treats that as its default death, and ordinary victims die without the writer needing to describe anything else. Wade’s body would therefore have to deal with whatever supernatural event the notebook uses to produce that heart attack.

This is where the crossover stops giving us a clean canon answer. Death Note never tests its default heart attack against somebody with Deadpool’s level of regeneration, because humans in that series do not have healing factors that can rebuild destroyed organs. Marvel also has no story where Wade is targeted by a Death Note, so either side claiming an explicit answer here would be inventing a rule neither franchise has shown.

There are 2 reasonable ways to read the notebook, and the wording slightly favors one of them. The first rule says that the human whose name is written shall die, while the heart attack is presented as the method used when the writer leaves the cause blank. Under that reading, the supernatural effect is aimed at Wade’s death and the heart attack is simply how the notebook gets there, which would mean his healing factor cannot turn the result into a harmless medical episode because the rule has already determined that he dies.

The other interpretation treats the heart attack as the complete physical effect. Wade's heart fails, his body technically reaches a fatal state, and then his healing factor starts repairing the damage the same way it reacts to other destroyed tissue. Marvel consistently treats Wade's regeneration as strong enough to repair severe internal injuries and replace damaged tissue, so a heart failing is nowhere near the most extreme physical destruction his body has dealt with.

I would lean toward the Death Note getting the initial kill because of how its own rule is written. The notebook is not described as “causing an injury that would usually be lethal”; it explicitly says the named human dies, then tells us which cause happens when none is supplied. Under that interpretation, Wade's heart attack continues far enough for his body to cross into actual death instead of his healing factor stopping the event first. But because neither series tests this rule against regeneration like Wade's, that remains the stronger Death Note reading rather than a confirmed crossover mechanic.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Writing a more detailed cause sounds like the obvious solution because Light could try to choose damage Wade cannot easily repair. The notebook does allow a cause and circumstances to be specified, but those conditions still have to remain physically possible, and the target’s behavior cannot become supernatural just because the writer wants a more

dramatic death. If the written scenario cannot happen under the rules, the Death Note falls back on the default heart attack rather than inventing a new power to make the description work. Something simple such as “Wade Wilson dies after shooting himself in the head” should be physically possible for Wade. He knows how to use firearms, he could physically perform the action, and the scenario does not require the notebook to create an object or ability that is unavailable to him. The problem is that a gunshot to the head is still the kind of localized trauma his healing factor is built to repair, so specifying the injury gives the notebook a worse route than simply relying on its supernatural default.

The writer could escalate by sending Wade somewhere dangerous before the time of death. Wade could be made to enter an industrial site, stand somewhere exposed, or put himself into circumstances where a physically available hazard destroys much more of his body. The notebook gives considerable control over a victim’s actions before death, but those actions still have to be believable enough for Wade to perform and achievable with whatever exists around him.

A careful writer could still isolate Wade first. Telling him to travel alone to a remote location is far more plausible than demanding he teleport somewhere, and once he is there, the written death could involve an existing hazard that does not put unnamed people at risk. The Death Note is strongest here when the writer uses normal cause and effect instead of trying to make the notebook directly perform feats it has never demonstrated.

Even then, the notebook cannot casually write “Wade Wilson is completely erased from existence” and expect reality to obey. Death Note lets the writer control a death within physical possibility; it has never shown the ability to disintegrate matter through pure description or grant a victim whatever impossible method is needed to satisfy a sentence. Permanently beating Deadpool therefore depends on arranging enough real physical destruction before the notebook’s control ends.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: That brings the test back to Wade’s healing factor, because localized fatal damage is exactly where he is hardest to keep down. Marvel describes the healing factor as capable of restoring destroyed tissue at a rate far beyond an ordinary human, and Wade has survived injuries involving lost body parts and severe internal destruction throughout his publication history. The exact speed varies between writers, which is another reason we are using the general Earth-616 ability rather than cherry-picking the single wildest regeneration panel ever printed.

A Death Note heart attack can still count as a successful kill under the stronger Death Note interpretation we established earlier. But if Wade genuinely crosses into death rather than merely suffering fatal cardiac damage, whether his standard biological healing factor can restart him afterward is not established. If the notebook only produces damage his regeneration can reverse, he may recover; if it supernaturally enforces genuine death first, what happens next remains uncertain.

There is nothing in the Death Note rules saying a corpse can never be revived by an outside process after the notebook kills it. The series has no resurrection system comparable to Marvel's and never needs to answer what happens if magic, regeneration, cloning, or another cosmic force restores someone afterward. Saying that the Death Note permanently blocks resurrection would therefore add a rule that does not exist in its canon.

The writer can make that harder by choosing a death that leaves less body behind. Severe burning, crushing, dismemberment, or another physically achievable form of destruction gives Wade much more work to regenerate than a failed heart. Marvel has published versions of Wade's healing factor capable of surviving extraordinarily severe damage, so the amount of destruction needed becomes the next meaningful threshold instead of repeating the heart attack test with different organs.

This is also where leaving Thanos’s old curse out starts mattering. During the period where Thanos supernaturally prevented Wade from dying, destroying Wade’s body and making Wade stay dead were even farther apart because an external cosmic effect was keeping death from holding him. We are testing Wade after removing that extra protection, so a sufficiently complete destruction of his body still has a real chance of ending him if there is no viable tissue left to regenerate and no separate resurrection mechanism steps in.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: The next test is complete destruction, because that is where Wade's healing factor stops being a simple answer. Cutting off his head, destroying his heart, or blowing apart most of his body still leaves surviving tissue that can potentially regenerate, and Earth-616 Deadpool has recovered from injuries far beyond anything a normal person could survive. The Death Note would need a cause that removes enough of Wade's body that regeneration has nothing useful left to work with.

The notebook cannot simply write that Wade disappears from existence. Its control over a death still has to operate through actions and circumstances that are physically possible, so the writer needs a real method of destroying the body rather than a sentence that gives the Death Note a new power. That pushes the problem away from the notebook itself and toward whatever environment Wade can realistically be forced into before the written time of death.

An isolated industrial furnace is one possible route if Wade can realistically reach and enter it within the Death Note's control window, has whatever access the sequence requires, and the written circumstances remain physically possible under the notebook's rules. The writer could similarly try an environment involving extreme pressure, corrosive material, or another existing hazard that continues damaging the body after Wade loses consciousness. None of those routes are guaranteed to be valid just because the hazard exists. The important part is that the Death Note would be arranging feasible circumstances rather than directly vaporizing Wade through supernatural force.

Even those options are harder than they sound because Wade's regeneration has survived extremely destructive injuries across different Earth-616 stories. Burning most of his body or tearing him apart does not automatically guarantee that no viable tissue remains, and Deadpool’s healing factor has never operated with one perfectly consistent numerical limit from writer to writer. We therefore cannot point to one temperature or percentage of body loss and pretend Marvel has established it as the exact point where Wade permanently stops regenerating.

A much cleaner attempt would involve destruction that continues until essentially nothing biological remains. If Wade could be forced through a physically valid written sequence into a process that completely incinerated the body and kept destroying material until no meaningful tissue remained, that would create the strongest case for overwhelming his standard healing factor. Earth-616 does not give Wade one perfectly consistent regeneration cutoff, so we cannot say with certainty that zero surviving tissue universally switches his healing off. What we can say is that normal Wade has no consistent rule guaranteeing automatic regeneration from literally nothing. The Death Note can plausibly attempt that situation only if the sequence fits its normal limits and does not require unnamed people to die along with him.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: This is where the distinction between regeneration and resurrection matters. If Wade’s heart stops and his healing factor repairs it afterward, the body itself is doing the work. If his entire body is destroyed and some outside cosmic or supernatural mechanism restores Wade later, the Death Note has already succeeded at killing him and something else has reversed the result.

The Death Note never establishes a rule saying that a person it kills is permanently barred from resurrection. That question simply does not come up in its own world, where the notebook is being used on ordinary humans and there is no Marvel-style system of gods, cosmic beings, magical realms, cloning, or reality alteration routinely bringing dead people back. Extending its rules far enough to say Wade’s soul can never return would give the notebook an ability it has never demonstrated.

For the matchup itself, we should separate those outside interventions from Wade’s normal powers. If Light writes Wade's name, successfully arranges total destruction, and Wade remains dead unless somebody else deliberately brings him back, then the Death Note has beaten the version of Deadpool we agreed to test. Saying it failed because Doctor Strange or some cosmic entity could resurrect Wade later would turn the question into whether death can ever be permanent anywhere in Marvel.

Wade’s own history still creates one complication because he has crossed the line between life and death more than once. Some stories have treated his consciousness, soul, or relationship with Death as separate from whatever physical condition his body is in, while other stories simply rely on his healing factor and move on. Those stories cannot be compressed into one universal rule that says Wade always resurrects automatically whenever every cell is destroyed. So the fair standard is narrower. We ask whether Wade’s normal Earth-616 healing factor can bring him back from the specific death the notebook causes, then acknowledge separately that Marvel has outside resurrection mechanisms the Death Note has never been shown to prevent. Under that standard, destroying the body completely is the first scenario where the notebook has a serious path to making the death stick.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: There's still a practical problem for whoever is writing the cause because the Death Note only controls Wade for a limited period leading to the written death. The writer needs a sequence Wade can actually complete, using resources that exist and actions his body is capable of performing, while avoiding circumstances that directly kill unnamed people. A complicated plan with 15 separate steps becomes less reliable every time one of those steps depends on information or access Wade does not have.

Wade himself makes that harder because his normal life is unpredictable. He carries weapons, moves constantly, works around other people, and has enough combat experience to survive situations that would make a normal Death Note victim easy to steer. The notebook can control his behavior within its rules, but it cannot give him secret passwords, teleport him into a secure facility, or create a perfectly isolated destruction chamber because the writer described one.

A simple cause therefore works better than an elaborate one. The writer could try to direct Wade to an isolated location he can realistically reach, have him enter an existing destructive environment, and specify that he dies there once the process begins. If the notebook accepts those circumstances, the surrounding hazard could plausibly keep destroying the body after death through ordinary physics. Death Note never demonstrates this exact postmortem workaround, though, so it should be treated as a proposed loophole rather than a guaranteed extension of the notebook’s control.

That difference is important. The notebook does not need to personally overpower Wade’s healing factor forever if it can put him somewhere that keeps damaging the body faster than the healing factor can recover. Wade could technically die early in the process from organ failure or brain destruction, while the surrounding hazard continues until the corpse is reduced beyond any plausible regenerative starting point.

The weakness is that Death Note canon never demonstrates the notebook deliberately engineering a death against a target with regeneration this extreme. We know it can specify plausible circumstances and we know impossible conditions fail, but we do not have an example proving how it handles a victim whose body can repair normally fatal injuries during the sequence. Any claim that the notebook automatically increases the destruction until Wade stays dead would therefore be interpretation rather than explicit canon.

That is why the normal heart attack and the complete-destruction scenario should receive different conclusions. The heart attack almost certainly lets the notebook satisfy its own requirement that Wade dies, but his healing factor has a strong argument for bringing the body back afterward. A carefully arranged destruction that removes the body entirely gives the notebook a much better chance of producing a death Wade's normal regeneration cannot reverse.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: There is another way people might try to solve the matchup by arguing that the Death Note’s statement that the named human “shall die” overrides everything Wade can do. Under the strongest version of that interpretation, regeneration is irrelevant because the notebook’s supernatural command determines the end result first and the physical cause only explains how the death happens. Wade could heal as much as he wants during the process, but the notebook would continue forcing the outcome until the required death occurred.

I think that interpretation works for the initial death and becomes much weaker once we ask what happens afterward. The Death Note rules tell us that the victim dies, but they never say the notebook continues controlling the corpse forever or prevents later restoration. If Wade reaches a genuine state of death, the notebook has already completed the instruction written into it.

That means the strongest Death Note reading and the strongest Deadpool reading can both remain plausible at different points. Under the notebook-first interpretation, Wade cannot simply shrug off the effect before dying because the supernatural rule is aimed at his death. Under the regeneration-first interpretation, the notebook may only be producing the specified physical mechanism, leaving open whether Wade can repair through it before death is completed. If Wade does reach a genuine state of death, nothing clearly states that the notebook remains attached to him as a permanent anti-resurrection effect.

This also keeps us from making Wade's healing factor stronger than it is. Regeneration does not mean Wade has never died, and Earth-616 has repeatedly treated severe enough damage as capable of putting him into a genuinely dead state even when he later returns. The Death Note does not need to erase his healing factor to score a technical kill; it only has to push his body across that line once.

The permanent-death question therefore depends on how much body remains afterward. A heart attack leaves almost everything intact, so Wade has the best argument for regeneration. Massive physical destruction gives him less to work with, while total destruction removes the ordinary biological route back entirely.

If Wade later returns because another Marvel mechanism recreates him, that says more about Marvel's resurrection systems than it does about the Death Note failing to kill him. The notebook would have done exactly what its rules promised, while another force subsequently undid the result. That distinction is the only way to answer the matchup without quietly turning either franchise’s mechanics into something they never claimed to be.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: So if Light has Wade Wilson’s correct name and can clearly picture his real face, the Death Note should recognize him as a valid target. Wade is still human despite the experiments that gave him his healing factor, and nothing in the notebook’s rules says an altered human becomes immune simply because his body can regenerate. The old Thanos curse would change the matchup, but we deliberately left that temporary period of Wade's history out.

A basic heart attack gives the Death Note a strong argument for an initial kill, but the crossover does not establish that result with certainty. The notebook explicitly states that the named human dies, which supports the interpretation that Wade reaches actual death rather than his healing factor interrupting the process first. The competing reading is that the notebook produces its specified physical mechanism and Wade's regeneration may repair through it. If the first reading wins, his body is still largely intact afterward, giving his healing factor a strong chance of repairing the damage and bringing him back once the Death Note has finished doing what it was supposed to do.

Writing a more violent cause can improve the notebook’s chances, although the writer remains trapped by the notebook’s own restrictions. Wade cannot be ordered to perform impossible actions, the written sequence cannot casually kill unnamed people, and the notebook cannot invent a supernatural form of disintegration simply because the writer wants a cleaner result. The cause has to lead Wade into a physically real situation capable of destroying enough of his body.

If the writer manages to arrange complete physical destruction, Wade’s standard healing factor faces its strongest possible problem. There is no clear Earth-616 rule guaranteeing that normal Wade recreates himself automatically from literally nothing every time his body is erased, especially once the separate Thanos immortality curse is removed from the version we are testing. Deadpool's regeneration has also varied too much to declare a universal biological cutoff, so total destruction is best treated as the Death Note's strongest plausible route to keeping him biologically dead rather than a guaranteed switch that turns his healing off.

Marvel can still complicate the result afterward because resurrection exists through mechanisms outside Wade's healing factor. The Death Note has never shown that it can permanently block magic, cosmic intervention, reality alteration, or any other outside process from restoring somebody after death. Calling those possibilities proof that Wade is immune would go much farther than either franchise supports.

The final answer is that the Death Note has a credible claim to killing Deadpool, but the basic heart-attack interaction is not explicitly resolved by either franchise. The notebook's “shall die” wording supports Wade genuinely dying at least once, while his regeneration gives a reasonable competing argument if the effect is limited to the physical heart attack itself. Making him stay dead is much harder either way because localized damage leaves a body his healing factor can repair. A carefully written, physically possible sequence that achieves essentially total destruction gives the Death Note a much stronger path to a lasting death, without making that outcome canonically guaranteed.

With standard Earth-616 Wade and no outside immortality curse, that gives the Death Note a plausible permanent win if the cause is written carefully enough to achieve total destruction. If the notebook only gives him the default heart attack or another ordinary fatal injury, Wade dying for a while is much easier to defend than Wade staying dead.

scripts.title: Could Wolverine Survive The Last of Us

sections.name: INTRO
paras: If Wolverine was dropped into The Last of Us, the infected would be terrifying for about 5 minutes.

I'd use prime Fox Wolverine, so Logan has his adamantium skeleton, claws, enhanced senses, and one of the strongest healing factors we’ve seen from that version. A Runner or Clicker could still bite him, and that's where this actually gets interesting because Cordyceps isn’t just a wound his body can close. It’s a living infection trying to spread through his tissue and eventually reach his brain.

Logan would probably survive the first few infected encounters easily, but he’d have no idea whether the fungus is still growing inside him after the bite disappears. And if his healing factor can keep rebuilding whatever Cordyceps damages, then the real question becomes whether his body can actually kill the infection or if the fungus just keeps fighting its way back.

If Logan can clear it, then The Last of Us becomes a very different world for him. Clickers stop being the main threat. Hordes, starvation, getting trapped, and other survivors become much more dangerous, especially once he ends up crossing paths with Joel and Ellie.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: I'd use prime Fox Wolverine and drop him into the game version of The Last of Us, since that continuity gives us spores as a major environmental threat. Logan has the adamantium skeleton, claws, enhanced senses, decades of combat experience, and the healing factor we see before the decline in Logan. He can recover from gunshots, stab wounds, burns, and injuries that would kill a normal person, but Cordyceps creates a different problem because it can keep spreading after the bite itself closes.

His first encounter would happen before Logan understands any of that. He hears several people moving inside an abandoned building and assumes they’re survivors until the smell gives him pause. The infected don’t smell right to him. There’s sweat, blood, rot, and another biological scent underneath it that Logan can’t place yet, which lets him know there’s a problem before the first Runner comes through the doorway.

A normal survivor would be panicking the second several infected rush them. Logan lets the first one get close enough that it bites into his forearm before he understands what the creature is trying to do. The teeth break skin, Logan drives his claws through its chest, and the wound starts closing almost immediately while the rest of the infected pile toward him.

The fight itself doesn’t last long. Logan’s skeleton can’t be broken by the infected, his claws cut through them easily, and the injuries they cause disappear faster than they can build up. He gets scratched across the face, bitten again near the shoulder, and knocked through part of a wall before killing the last Runner and realizing he’s covered in blood from creatures that were still technically human.

The bites disappearing would usually be the end of the problem for Logan. This time, though, he can tell something may still be wrong even after the skin closes. If Cordyceps manages to establish itself temporarily before his regeneration overtakes the damage, Logan could start running a fever or feeling other signs that his body is under unusual stress. He doesn’t know the word Cordyceps yet, and he has no way to tell whether the fungus is actually gone or whether his healing factor is simply keeping it from progressing.

That still wouldn’t make him magically untouchable. A huge exposure could put far more fungal material into his body at once, and inhaling spores would spread the problem across a much larger surface inside his lungs. Logan doesn’t know any of that yet, so he leaves the building thinking the bite was strange and keeps moving while his body spends the next several hours regenerating whatever tissue the infection damages. Whether that actually eliminates every trace of Cordyceps or simply keeps it from establishing control is something he has no way to know yet.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: The group assumes he got lucky until one of them notices the torn fabric around his shoulder. Logan tells them the bite happened days ago, which sounds impossible to anyone who's lived through this outbreak. That earns him a gun pointed at his chest before he can explain anything, and Logan decides pretty quickly that telling strangers his body can heal from almost anything probably isn’t going to make them calmer.

Clickers would still be unsettling the first time he meets one. Logan hears the clicking inside a dark building and can smell the fungal growth covering the creature before he sees it. Once it attacks, though, the difference between fighting Logan and fighting a normal survivor becomes

obvious. A Clicker can tear into human flesh incredibly quickly, but Logan can let it commit to the attack, take the damage, and drive his claws through it before the injury becomes meaningful. His senses also reduce one of the biggest advantages clickers normally have. Darkness doesn’t blind Logan in the same way, and he doesn’t need to rely entirely on seeing them when he can hear and smell where they're moving. He’d still avoid making noise because attracting more infected gains him nothing, but a single Clicker in a hallway is far more dangerous to an ordinary survivor than it is to him.

Spores would worry him more once somebody explains them. Logan can smell that the air is wrong before walking into a heavily contaminated building, which would help him avoid large spore zones before he ever sees the fungal growth. The problem comes from situations where he has to enter anyway.

| wouldn't give Logan perfect immunity to inhalation. If he walks through a dense cloud without a mask, thousands or millions of spores could reach his nose, throat, and lungs, giving Cordyceps far more opportunities to establish itself than one bite. His healing factor would start replacing damaged tissue immediately, but the first exposure could still make him extremely sick while his body tries to keep the infection from gaining ground.

If Cordyceps manages to establish itself temporarily, he could spend hours coughing, running a fever, and dealing with respiratory irritation while his body continually repairs the damage. Prime Fox Logan's best chance is that his constant regeneration replaces compromised tissue faster than Cordyceps can establish irreversible control, but the movies give us no direct test of his healing factor against this fungus. Repeated exposure could still be miserable. Every trip through a spore-filled basement could mean another biological fight inside his body, and there’s no reason Logan would willingly keep inhaling them once he understands what they are. He’d start using masks when he can find them because surviving an infection doesn’t mean he has to enjoy getting sick every time he walks through a contaminated building.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Once Logan understands the infected, moving through the country becomes easier for him than it is for almost anyone else. His senses let him check a building before entering, his claws mean ammunition isn’t necessary for every fight, and injuries that would end somebody else’s journey can disappear while he keeps moving. He can also travel through areas most survivors avoid because one bad encounter doesn’t automatically mean death.

Food becomes one of the first problems his powers don’t solve. Logan’s body still needs energy, and constantly regenerating from wounds would probably make that need worse. He can hunt because his senses make tracking animals easy, but game is scarce around heavily populated or infected areas, and carrying enough food while moving long distances is still difficult.

Large hordes are where his physical advantage finally runs into a problem that claws don’t automatically fix. Logan can kill Runners and Clickers one after another, but hundreds of infected can surround him faster than he can clear space. They can pile on top of him, drag him down, keep biting while he’s trying to stand, and bury him under enough bodies that movement becomes difficult even if they can’t kill him permanently.

That creates situations where Logan has to think like a survivor instead of treating every infected encounter as a fight. If his senses pick up a large group moving through a building, he changes route. He can climb, break through weak walls, or cut through a smaller group before the rest arrive, and that keeps him from wasting hours getting torn apart by creatures he could’ve simply avoided.

Humans would become more dangerous than most infected once people understand what Logan is. Hunters trying to rob him could still hurt him with rifles, traps, explosives, or fire, and getting shot from a distance is much harder to prevent than hearing a Runner coming through a doorway. Logan can survive the wounds, but the attack can destroy supplies, separate him from shelter, or leave him pinned somewhere while more people arrive.

If hunters do catch him, the fight ends badly for them once they get close. Logan can take a bullet, keep moving, and reach someone before they understand why he’s still standing. He also has decades of experience fighting trained people, so ordinary survivors with homemade weapons aren't giving him the same trouble they'd give Joel.

The part Logan would struggle with is what comes after. Killing infected is simple because there’s very little of the person left by the time they're trying to tear him apart. Human groups still have frightened people, families, and members who may be doing terrible things because the world around them collapsed. Logan has lived long enough to know that killing everyone in front of him usually creates another problem somewhere else.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Logan would eventually cross paths with Joel and Ellie during their journey west. I’d bring him in after they've already spent enough time together for Joel to be protective of her, because Logan walking into their story should change what happens without replacing the relationship at the center of it.

He finds them before they find him. Logan smells 2 people moving through an abandoned area and picks up infected nearby at the same time. Joel is already trying to get Ellie through without drawing attention, but a Clicker moves into their route and forces them toward another room where several Runners are waiting.

Logan comes in because he can tell exactly how bad the situation is getting. Joel sees a stranger run straight at a Clicker with metal claws coming out of his hands, which would probably be one of the stranger things he’s seen even after 20 years of Cordyceps. Logan kills the Clicker, clears enough Runners for them to move, and takes a bite during the fight without reacting much beyond getting annoye d but Joel notices.

Once they're safe, Joel immediately wants to know why Logan isn’t panicking about the bite. Logan tells him it won't be a problem, which sounds ridiculous until the wound closes in front of them. Ellie is much more interested than scared because she’s spent months knowing her own bite didn’t turn her, and now she’s looking at another person whose body reacts to Cordyceps differently.

The difference between them becomes clear pretty quickly. Ellie can carry the infection without turning, while Logan’s body appears to keep regenerating compromised tissue fast enough to prevent the infection from progressing normally. That makes both of them medically unusual for completely different reasons, and Logan would understand enough from his own history to know how dangerous that becomes once other people hear about it.

Joel doesn’t trust him immediately, and Logan wouldn't expect him to. Their routes are heading the same direction for now, and after watching Logan survive a bite and clear the infected around them, Joel reluctantly agrees to let him travel with them through the area instead of splitting up immediately. What starts as a temporary arrangement lasts longer as Logan keeps proving useful. They're both experienced, suspicious, and used to making decisions without asking permission, so they'd probably clash constantly over routes and risk. Joel knows this world better than Logan does, though, and Logan learns quickly that knowing how to kill infected isn’t the same as knowing which roads are controlled, where food might still exist, or which settlements are safe enough to approach.

Ellie gets along with him faster. She’d ask about the claws, the healing, how old he is, and whether he can survive being shot in the head until Joel tells her to stop asking questions. Logan would complain about it, but her curiosity wouldn’t bother him nearly as much as he pretends.

That doesn’t make Ellie somebody they can stop worrying about. Logan can survive getting dragged into a room full of infected, and Ellie still has a body that can be broken by claws, bullets, falls, or explosions even if Cordyceps doesn't turn her. Protecting her gives Logan a reason to avoid some fights he’d happily take alone because getting buried under a horde for 20 minutes doesn't help if Ellie is standing behind him.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: The journey starts changing more once Logan understands exactly why Joel is taking Ellie across the country. Hearing that she may be the key to a cure immediately gets his attention, but he doesn’t react with the same excitement the Fireflies would. Logan has spent too much of his life around people who saw unusual biology and immediately started thinking about what they could extract from it.

He doesn't tell Ellie to abandon the trip. She wants her immunity to mean something, and Logan understands why after seeing what this world looks like. What he does is start asking questions Joel hasn’t been able to answer. He wants to know what the Fireflies have actually tested, what they know about Ellie’s infection, and what they're planning to do once she reaches their doctors.

Those questions become more uncomfortable when Logan realizes nobody has given Ellie a clear answer. The Fireflies know she’s immune and believe that matters, but Joel and Ellie are traveling toward a medical procedure without knowing what that procedure is going to require. Logan recognizes that situation immediately because Weapon X started with people deciding his body could be useful to them too.

He'd become especially protective when they run into human groups trying to take Ellie. Logan doesn't have Joel's hesitation about putting himself between her and armed people because bullets aren’t going to stop him for long. At the same time, his presence gives Joel more room to focus on Ellie instead of constantly having to be the person who handles every threat alone.

A hunter ambush that might normally force Joel and Ellie into a long escape could end much faster once Logan gets close. He smells the attackers before the first shot, pushes Joel and Ellie toward cover, then goes around the position from a direction the hunters aren't watching. Gunfire still tears into him, but watching the same man keep moving after several hits would break the nerve of most people before the fight reaches the claws.

That changes Joel too. He starts trusting Logan with Ellie because he’s seen him take risks that would kill anyone else, and Logan sees how far Joel will go the second Ellie is threatened. They don't suddenly become close friends, but there’s a growing understanding between 2 men who've both spent a long time surviving by keeping other people at a distance.

Ellie also starts asking Logan more about his past once she realizes his healing factor made him valuable to people who wanted to experiment on him. Logan doesn't give her every detail, but he tells her enough to explain why somebody promising to use your body for a greater purpose doesn’t automatically mean they get to decide what happens to it.

That idea stays with him as they keep moving west. By the time they're getting close to the Fireflies, Logan isn’t worried about whether their doctors can hurt him. He’s paying attention to how they talk about Ellie, whether they treat her like a person, and what they think her immunity gives them the right to do.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Logan still can’t carry the whole journey by himself. He doesn’t know every quarantine zone, smuggling route, abandoned checkpoint, or settlement the way Joel does, and he doesn’t have Joel's experience reading how this version of America changed after the outbreak. Joel knows when a road is too obvious, which buildings are likely to have been stripped years ago, and which kinds of people are more dangerous to approach than avoid.

Food becomes harder once the 3 of them are moving together because Logan’s healing factor likely burns through energy faster whenever he’s recovering from major damage. If he spends a day fighting infected and healing from multiple injuries, he’s going to need more calories afterward than somebody who stayed out of the fight. That doesn’t make him weak, but it means his body still has a cost attached to everything it repairs.

They take a longer route through a maintenance tunnel instead. Logan goes first, moving slowly enough to check every side passage before the others follow. A Clicker is hiding deeper inside and never gets close enough to surprise them because Logan hears it moving against the concrete long before they reach the turn.

That kind of moment starts changing how Joel uses him. Logan stops being the guy Joel expects to charge into danger and becomes the person who can tell him where the danger is before they're committed to a route. Joel still makes the final call on where they go, but he starts trusting Logan's senses enough to change plans before things go wrong.

Ellie notices that trust building before either man says anything about it. Joel starts asking Logan what he smells ahead instead of telling him to stay back, and Logan starts listening when Joel says a road or building isn’t worth the risk. They still argue constantly, but the arguments are becoming more useful because each of them knows things the other doesn’t.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Human enemies become a bigger problem as the journey goes on because they're much better at using distance than infected are. A Clicker has to get close enough to bite Logan. A group with rifles can stay hundreds of feet away, spread out, and keep firing while forcing Joel and Ellie to stay behind cover.

Logan’s senses still give him an edge, especially when people are waiting in buildings or tree lines. He can smell cigarette smoke, gun oil, fresh sweat, blood, and food long before a normal person would notice anyone is nearby. That doesn’t tell him exactly where every shooter is, but it gives him enough warning to slow down and look instead of walking into the center of an ambush.

A group of hunters eventually gets close enough to prove the difference. They're positioned along a narrow road with a disabled truck blocking one side and shooters covering the other. Logan smells them before the first shot, pulls Ellie behind cover, and tells Joel where the closest 2 are hiding before either one exposes themselves.

Joel starts returning fire while Logan moves around the flank. He takes several rounds getting there because the shooters adjust once they realize somebody is coming toward them, but the wounds keep closing while he keeps moving. The people watching him realize pretty quickly that putting bullets into the same man over and over isn’t solving anything.

Logan still doesn’t just run through the whole group with his claws out. There are people hiding deeper inside the building who aren’t armed, and he can hear them. That keeps him from turning the place into a massacre while Joel and Ellie are still trying to get through.

He incapacitates the people blocking their route and leaves the rest once they stop shooting. Joel doesn’t love leaving armed people behind, but Logan points out that chasing everyone through the building is only going to waste time and ammunition while making it easier for more people to find them.

That choice matters later because it's one of the first times Ellie sees Logan pull himself back when killing would've been easier. She's used to adults saying survival means doing whatever works. Logan has survived longer than almost anyone she’s met, and he’s still choosing not to treat every person in his way like they're disposable.

The bigger danger from human groups comes from explosives and fire. Logan can heal from gunshots, but being trapped under rubble or set on fire can slow him down badly enough that somebody can separate him from Joel and Ellie. The adamantium skeleton keeps him from being crushed normally, yet all that metal also means he’s carrying enormous weight if he ever gets pinned somewhere he can’t move.
That's why he starts paying more attention to terrain during human encounters. Narrow rooms, burning buildings, collapsing floors, and places where exits can be blocked become much more
dangerous than open fights. Logan can survive almost anything people throw at him, but surviving while trapped doesn’t help if Joel and Ellie are taken somewhere else.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: As they get closer to the Fireflies, Logan starts asking more questions about Ellie’s immunity. He's already seen that she can be bitten without turning, and he knows his own healing factor handles Cordyceps differently, but neither of those facts tells them what the Fireflies actually intend to do once they reach their doctors.

Joel doesn’t have many answers. Ellie was told her immunity could help make a cure, and that was enough to keep them moving. Logan understands why she wants to believe it, especially after seeing so many people die from the infection, but he doesn’t like how vague everything still is this close to the destination.

He starts asking Ellie what she was told directly. She knows the Fireflies need to study her, but she doesn’t know what kind of procedure they're planning or how dangerous it might be. Logan doesn't turn that into a speech about Weapon X. He just tells her that if somebody wants to do something to her body, she should know exactly what it is before they start.

That gets Joel’s attention because it’s something he’s clearly been avoiding thinking about. He wants Ellie to reach the Fireflies because that's what Tess wanted and because Ellie still believes the trip has a purpose. Logan starts making him consider what happens if the doctors decide Ellie’s life is an acceptable price for that purpose.

Ellie pushes back because she wants her immunity to matter. Logan understands that too. He doesn't tell her she’s wrong for wanting to help people, and he doesn't try to decide for her before they even reach the hospital. He only keeps coming back to whether anyone has actually asked what Ellie is willing to risk.

That becomes important when they finally reach the Fireflies and are separated almost immediately. Once they notice healed bite marks and learn Logan has survived repeated infected encounters without turning, the doctors immediately want to know why his body reacts differently to Cordyceps. Logan refuses to let them run tests beyond anything he agrees to. The reaction he gets from the doctors tells him they're already thinking about him as another biological opportunity.

He starts asking about Ellie as soon as he realizes she’s been moved somewhere else. The answers stay vague until he hears enough to understand that the doctors believe the Cordyceps growth in her brain is the source of her immunity and that removing it will kill her.

Logan’s entire attitude changes at that point. He wants to know whether Ellie is awake, whether she understands the procedure, and whether she agreed to it. The Fireflies talk about how many lives a cure could save, but none of that answers the question he’s actually asking.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: Joel learns the same thing and reacts exactly the way Logan expects. The Fireflies aren't planning to wait for Ellie to wake up and make a decision, and they're already preparing for surgery. Joel wants to get to her immediately, while Logan starts looking at how many armed people are between them and the operating room.

This is where Logan’s presence changes the hospital completely. Joel is still dangerous, but he has to move carefully because one bad shot could end the whole rescue. Logan can take that risk for him. He goes first through the areas where the Fireflies have concentrated guards, drawing most of the attention while Joel uses the openings behind him.

The Fireflies realize very quickly that normal gunfire isn’t stopping Logan. He gets hit repeatedly in the corridors, but the bullets slow him for seconds instead of ending the fight. Logan uses his claws mostly to destroy weapons, cut through doors, and get around barricades while keeping the fight moving toward Ellie.

Joel follows with far less pressure on him than he had in the original story. Instead of clearing every hallway himself, he can focus on getting closer to the surgery floor while Logan keeps larger groups occupied. That makes the rescue faster and gives the Fireflies less time to move Ellie somewhere else.

A grenade eventually knocks Logan through part of a load-bearing wall and brings a large section of the ceiling down with it, pinning him beneath heavy concrete, twisted metal, and tangled reinforcement. He survives, but cutting and forcing his way out takes long enough for the Fireflies to block another section of the hospital. That’s the kind of threat that still matters against him because they don’t need to kill Logan if they can keep him stuck long enough for the surgery to start.

Logan forces his way out and catches up while Joel is already closing in on the operating room. By then, both of them know there isn’t enough time for another conversation with the Fireflies. Ellie is unconscious, nobody asked her, and the doctors are already preparing to remove the infected tissue from her brain.

Logan gets there before Joel has to fight everyone alone. He sees Ellie on the table and immediately understands why Joel isn’t leaving without her. Logan doesn’t care how many projections the doctors have about a cure if Ellie never got to hear the risk herself.

He doesn’t kill the medical staff once they back away. He makes it clear the surgery is over, while Joel gets Ellie disconnected from the equipment and carries her out. The remaining guards still try to stop them, but Logan stays behind long enough to keep the route open until Joel is clear.

That changes the hospital from Joel barely escaping with Ellie into something much harder for the Fireflies to recover from. Logan can physically hold the pursuit back, survive the injuries, and leave after Joel already has enough distance that catching up becomes almost impossible.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: Ellie wakes up later without knowing exactly how close she came to dying. Joel still has to decide how much of the truth he’s going to tell her, and Logan can tell immediately that he’s planning to simplify what happened. That creates one of the few situations where Logan and Joel stop agreeing after working together for so long.

Logan understands why Joel took her out of the hospital. He would've done the same thing once he learned the Fireflies were going ahead without Ellie’s consent. He’s much less comfortable with deciding that Ellie never gets to know what they planned or why Joel stopped it.

He doesn’t force Joel to tell her everything immediately because Ellie has just survived a cross-country journey and woken up after nearly being killed for a procedure she didn’t understand. Logan also knows that telling someone a truth and dumping it on them at the worst possible moment aren't always the same thing.

What he does make clear is that Ellie deserves to know eventually. Her immunity belongs to her, and if another group ever comes looking for her because of it, she should understand what happened the first time. Joel doesn't like hearing that, but Logan has spent enough time being lied to about his own body that he isn’t going to pretend the hospital was only Joel's decision to carry forever.

As for whether Wolverine survives this world, | think prime Fox Logan has an enormous advantage over almost everyone living in it. A bite probably wouldn’t turn him under the assumptions we've used here because his healing factor would likely keep replacing compromised tissue faster than Cordyceps could establish stable neurological control. Dense spore exposure would be much rougher, but his regeneration should still give him a very good chance of surviving it. Whether his body ever completely eliminates the fungus, rather than simply preventing it from taking control, is something neither universe gives us enough evidence to know for certain.

The infected themselves wouldn't kill him easily either. Runners, Stalkers, and Clickers can tear him apart, but the damage they cause is exactly the kind of thing his body is built to recover from. Large hordes are much more dangerous because they can pin or bury him, and stronger infected can slow him down long enough for the environment around him to become the bigger problem.

The threats that matter most are the ones that don’t care how quickly his skin closes. Fire can keep damaging him, explosions can bury him, starvation can drain him, and human groups can trap or separate him from whoever he’s protecting. Logan could survive those things too, but he’d have to make smart choices instead of assuming healing means every fight is worth taking. His presence would change Joel and Ellie’s journey far more than it changes the Cordyceps outbreak itself. He can make individual routes safer, protect them from infected, and give Joel another person capable of handling the worst encounters, but he can’t cure the world by walking through it.
The biggest change happens at the hospital. Logan has spent too much of his life watching people decide that unusual biology gives them ownership over the person carrying it. Once the
Fireflies make that same decision with Ellie, they're dealing with 2 people determined to get her out instead of 1.

So Wolverine could survive the last of us, and he'd probably do it for a very long time. Cordyceps could hurt him, hordes could trap him, and people could still find ways to slow him down, but this world doesn’t have many reliable ways to permanently kill someone with Logan's skeleton and healing factor. The part he’d have a much harder time surviving unchanged is everything that comes with protecting people who can still die.

scripts.title: Gojo VS Superman

sections.name: INTRO
paras: Gojo has spent his entire life fighting people who can’t touch him. Infinity keeps attacks from ever reaching his body, the 6 Eyes let him process a ridiculous amount of information in combat, and Unlimited Void can overwhelm someone the moment they’re caught inside his domain. Put that against Superman, and the matchup gets kinda strange because having better physical stats doesn’t automatically explain how Clark gets his hands on Gojo.

We're using Gojo at his peak during the Sukuna fight, with his full Limitless arsenal and Reverse Cursed Technique available. Superman will be his modern mainline Earth 0 version with his standard abilities, leaving temporary amps and alternate versions out so we’re comparing 2 characters with abilities they've consistently had access to.

Superman brings an enormous physical advantage into this fight, while Gojo has abilities that don’t work like conventional punches or energy blasts. Infinity has to deal with Superman’s speed, Unlimited Void has to catch someone who can move vastly faster than Gojo, and attacks like Hollow Purple still have to damage a character who regularly survives punishment far beyond anything in Jujutsu Kaisen. Once we work through those interactions, we'll see just how much Infinity can protect Gojo and whether he can turn that protection into an actual win.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: Before getting into Infinity, Superman owns almost every normal physical category here. Modern Earth-0 Clark has super strength, flight, invulnerability, super speed, heat vision, freeze breath, enhanced senses, and a healing factor powered by yellow sun energy. Gojo is extremely strong inside Jujutsu Kaisen, especially during the Sukuna fight, but his physical showings operate on a much smaller scale than someone who regularly deals with threats built for the Justice League.

Gojo’s durability needs a little more explanation because a lot of what looks like durability is really Infinity preventing contact. When attacks do reach him, he can reinforce himself with cursed energy and repair enormous amounts of damage through Reverse Cursed Technique. His fight with Sukuna shows how difficult he is to put down once he starts healing continuously, even after Malevolent Shrine gets through Infinity and repeatedly cuts him.

Superman can take far more punishment before healing even becomes relevant. His Kryptonian body under a yellow sun gives him extreme durability alongside a healing factor, and sunlight replenishes the energy his body uses for those powers. If Clark lands a completely unprotected
hit with serious force behind it, Gojo’s Reverse Cursed Technique isn’t a convincing answer because Gojo still needs enough of himself left to perform it.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: By the time we’re using Gojo, keeping Infinity active isn’t the exhausting manual process it was when he was younger. After his fight with Toji, he learned to maintain it automatically while using Reverse Cursed Technique to keep his brain refreshed, and the Six Eyes make his cursed energy usage extraordinarily efficient. Superman isn’t waiting for Gojo to notice a punch and consciously activate Infinity every single time.

That’s why Clark’s speed advantage needs to be handled carefully. Moving much faster than Gojo doesn’t demonstrate an ability to cross manipulated space, and Superman's normal super speed isn’t the Speed Force. The Speed Force is the mechanism behind Flash’s stranger speed abilities, while Superman’s super speed is part of his Kryptonian abilities.

So Clark flies forward and throws a punch. He covers the ordinary distance almost instantly, reaches the space affected by Infinity, and the punch stops short of Gojo. Trying again with more speed produces the same basic problem because nothing about increasing velocity removes the spatial effect separating his fist from the target.

Superman can also switch to ranged options like heat vision or freeze breath when his punches fail to connect. Infinity should plausibly interfere with effects that still have to travel toward Gojo through the space around him, though the exact crossover interaction is not directly established. Blasting material or cold toward his body would face the same uncertainty, and destroying the battlefield could become useful tactically without giving Superman a clean hit by itself.

Superman’s enhanced senses help him realize what's happening quickly. After the first punch stops without touching anything visible, Clark can observe Gojo from range, listen to what his body is doing, and test the barrier with less dangerous attacks. He doesn’t need many attempts to understand that Gojo has some kind of spatial defense, even if he has no reason to know the mechanics of Limitless immediately.

Gojo gets information from those exchanges too. The Six Eyes won't identify Kryptonian biology or hand him a list of Superman's powers, but watching Clark cross the battlefield and hit Infinity tells Gojo enough about the physical difference between them. Standing there trading reinforced punches would be pointless when Clark can generate vastly more force.

Infinity buys Gojo something more useful than physical parity. It gives him time against an opponent who should otherwise be capable of ending the fight before Gojo could match his movement, and that time lets him reach the parts of his arsenal where Superman's strength matters much less.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Blue is the first technique that gives Gojo control over where the fight happens. By creating an attraction through Limitless, Gojo can pull targets, objects, and parts of the environment toward a selected point. He also uses Blue on himself to improve his movement, which helped him keep up during the Sukuna fight even though it still doesn’t close the enormous raw speed gap against Superman.

Clark can resist a huge amount of physical force, so simply dragging him around with Blue isn’t going to finish the fight. Gojo can still use that attraction to interfere with positioning for brief moments, especially before Superman understands exactly what the technique is doing. Those moments matter when Gojo’s stronger options depend on creating an opening rather than overpowering Clark physically.

Red reverses the effect and produces violent repulsion. Sukuna survives Red, and Gojo can use its trajectory creatively enough to have it circle back into another attack, but Superman has survived forces well beyond the destructive output Gojo has demonstrated with it. A clean Red could move Clark or catch him off guard without giving us much reason to believe it would seriously injure him.

Hollow Purple gets exaggerated in these matchups because it’s sometimes described like Gojo fires an automatic eraser that deletes anything from existence. The manga doesn’t establish Purple as unconditional existence erasure. Sukuna survives Gojo’s enhanced opening Purple and later survives the large unrestricted Purple during their fight, taking severe damage without being erased from reality.

That creates a huge problem if Gojo tries to win through Purple alone. Clark’s standard powers include invulnerability and a solar-powered healing factor, and his overall durability operates beyond the physical punishment demonstrated by Jujutsu Kaisen characters. Purple can absolutely be treated as Gojo’s strongest direct destructive attack, but its canon performance doesn’t justify skipping Superman’s durability and declaring a one-shot.

Gojo would figure that out quickly if he manages to land one. Superman’s speed makes hitting him difficult in the first place, and a Purple that Clark sees coming gives him plenty of opportunity to move. If it connects and Clark remains functional, Gojo has learned that throwing larger destructive attacks isn’t where his best chance sits.

Superman faces the opposite frustration. He can circle Gojo, attack from different directions, switch between physical strikes and heat vision, and destroy the surrounding terrain, yet none of those standard options has demonstrated the spatial interaction needed to remove Infinity. Clark’s overwhelming physical advantage keeps failing at the final fraction of distance.

Magic deserves mention because Superman has a complicated history with it, but Gojo’s cursed techniques can’t simply inherit every property of DC magic for the sake of the matchup. Cursed energy and DC’s magical systems come from different settings, so treating Limitless as automatic Kryptonite because Gojo is a sorcerer would give him an advantage the source material doesn’t establish.

Gojo has already learned enough by this stage of the fight. Blue and Red can affect the battle without providing reliable finishing damage, Purple asks too much against Clark’s durability, and Infinity is keeping Superman’s standard offense away. The technique Gojo needs next attacks a completely different part of Superman.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Superman’s durability doesn’t directly answer that effect. His skin surviving enormous impacts and his body handling extreme energy aren't evidence that his mind can simply ignore Unlimited Void’s sure hit. Clark has encountered telepathy and mental attacks throughout his career, but Unlimited Void has its own mechanics, so giving him immunity because he has resisted unrelated psychic abilities would require another assumption.

His speed gives him a much better defense: avoid being caught when the Domain forms. If Clark knows what Unlimited Void does and decides to disengage the instant Gojo begins using Domain Expansion, his movement advantage gives him an excellent chance of creating distance before the barrier finishes enclosing him. Even without that knowledge, though, his vastly superior perception and reactions make the first activation a contested interaction. Clark might stay close because he doesn’t recognize the threat and get caught, or he might react to the sudden barrier formation quickly enough to leave before it closes. Neither series establishes that exact crossover timing.

Clark doesn’t begin this fight with knowledge of jujutsu. So far, he’s watched physical attacks fail against Infinity and seen Gojo manipulate attraction, repulsion, and destructive energy. Gojo bringing his hands together for another technique doesn’t automatically tell Superman that remaining within the surrounding area could incapacitate him.

If Unlimited Void closes with Superman inside, the sure-hit doesn’t require Gojo to physically catch Clark after the barrier is established. Information begins flooding the target, and even a brief loss of movement would give Gojo an opportunity he could never create by trying to match Superman’s speed. The uncertainty is whether Clark is actually enclosed before his reactions let him create distance in the first place.

There’s still a fair question about how Superman responds if he is caught. His brain can process information at extraordinary speeds, and his mental capabilities operate beyond those of an ordinary human. That could reasonably affect how he experiences the information, but Unlimited Void isn’t presented as giving someone a fixed amount of data that a faster brain can simply finish processing. The technique keeps forcing information into the target while they’re exposed. Gojo also has direct experience controlling Domain duration. He used the 0.2 second activation in Shibuya specifically because ordinary humans were nearby, and against Superman there is no reason for him to deliberately keep the exposure that short if the fight is isolated. That makes sustained exposure Gojo’s strongest plausible route to incapacitation, but neither universe establishes how long Superman could remain functional inside it or whether his abnormal cognition could leave him enough control to attempt an escape. Once Clark has experienced Unlimited Void and recovered enough to understand it, assuming he can do so, his speed makes landing a second Domain much harder because he now knows what Gojo is attempting. The first activation carries so much weight precisely because neither fighter starts with knowledge of the other’s abilities.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: One possibility is exhausting Gojo. Superman can operate for extremely long periods while sufficiently charged by yellow-sun energy, and Gojo’s techniques consume cursed energy even with the extraordinary efficiency provided by the Six Eyes. If the fight turns into hours of Gojo repeatedly using expensive techniques while Superman avoids them, Clark has a route that
doesn’t require immediately crossing Infinity. Superman's solar-powered biology and healing are established parts of his standard powerset.

Gojo’s efficiency makes reaching that point difficult. The Six Eyes reduce the cursed energy lost when he activates techniques to an extremely small amount, and he can keep Infinity operating continuously while maintaining his brain through Reverse Cursed Technique. Sukuna forced him into far more expensive behavior because Gojo repeatedly opened Domains, healed enormous injuries, restored his burnt-out cursed technique, and continued using high-output attacks.

Clark would have to understand that attrition is useful before Unlimited Void catches him. His personality matters here because we’re using Superman as he normally behaves, rather than imagining him with perfect matchup knowledge and orders to kill immediately. Clark commonly evaluates unfamiliar opponents, tries to understand what they're doing, and controls his force when he doesn’t know how durable they are.

Gojo has a similar information problem. The first time Clark survives Blue, Red, or even Purple, Gojo has to accept that normal damage is giving him very little return. That pushes him toward Unlimited Void because incapacitation gives him a result Superman’s physical durability can’t answer as cleanly.

There is another Superman ability people sometimes bring up here: the Phantom Zone. Mainline Superman has access to Kryptonian technology in his wider resources, but carrying a Phantom Zone projector as standard equipment during an ordinary encounter isn’t part of the powerset we've locked for this fight. Giving Clark any piece of Fortress technology that could solve the matchup would change the rules from Superman’s standard abilities to Superman with preparation.

The same rule applies to Gojo. He doesn’t get outside cursed tools, allies, or some invented extension of Limitless that he never demonstrated. He has the techniques available to peak Gojo during the Sukuna fight, and his path has to come from those abilities.

Gojo has a more dangerous next step because Unlimited Void doesn’t ask him to overcome Superman’s durability through raw damage. Once Clark has spent the opening exchanges testing Infinity and learning that ordinary contact isn’t working, Gojo has every reason to bring out the technique that attacks his ability to process and act instead.

If Clark is caught during that first Domain, Gojo finally gets a stationary Superman in front of him. What Gojo can do with that opening, how long Unlimited Void can realistically hold Clark, and whether Superman has any less obvious method of dealing with Infinity are what decide the second half of the fight.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Unlimited Void gives Gojo the opening his other techniques couldn't create if the barrier catches Clark. Once enclosed, Clark is exposed to the Domain’s sure hit and flooded with information continuously. Superman’s brain works far faster than a human brain, but Unlimited Void keeps feeding information into the target for as long as the exposure continues, so this isn’t simply a fixed amount of data he can finish processing. Exactly how his Kryptonian cognition responds to sustained exposure is still an unresolved crossover interaction.

His history against telepathy and mind control doesn’t map cleanly onto this either. Those feats show that Clark has exceptional mental resistance, but Gojo isn’t trying to control his thoughts or force him to obey. Unlimited Void overwhelms the target's ability to act by forcing information into their mind. That gives Gojo a serious incapacitation route, but Superman’s unusual cognition also means we can’t establish exactly how quickly the effect would disable him or whether he could retain enough function to attempt an escape.

Gojo would watch Clark’s response immediately. If the person who had been moving faster than he could physically follow suddenly stalls or loses coordination, that tells him far more than another Red or Purple ever could. He can keep Unlimited Void active and continue the exposure while Infinity remains around him, trying to turn that disruption into a full incapacitation before Clark can recover enough control to escape.

Gojo also has no reason to end the Domain after 0.2 seconds. That duration in Shibuya was chosen because ordinary humans were caught nearby, while this fight gives him a single target whose mental capabilities are vastly greater. If Clark requires more exposure than a human, Gojo can keep supplying it without changing what the technique is doing. What canon cannot settle is how much exposure Superman would actually need or whether he could remain functional enough to act while it is happening.

Killing Superman isn’t required from there. If sustained Unlimited Void leaves Clark unable to coordinate himself and continue fighting, incapacitation gives Gojo a win without requiring him to somehow punch through Superman or pretend Hollow Purple ignores durability. That is Gojo’s strongest path because it attacks a category Clark’s physical durability doesn’t directly answer, even though the exact effect on a Kryptonian mind remains uncertain.

Superman’s speed could protect him even without perfect knowledge if his reactions let him clear the forming barrier in time. Lack of jujutsu knowledge still helps Gojo because Clark has no reason to recognize the hand movement as a uniquely dangerous mental attack, but it doesn’t erase the enormous reaction gap. The first Domain therefore becomes a genuine contested moment rather than a guaranteed trap.

That timing is why Superman’s enormous speed advantage isn’t an automatic answer, but it also can’t be ignored. Clark can react to Gojo far faster than Gojo can react to him; the unresolved question is whether he reacts by leaving the Domain’s forming area before understanding what the threat actually is. If he doesn’t, Gojo gets his best chance to incapacitate him. If he does, landing another Domain becomes much harder.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Superman’s remaining abilities don’t provide an established clean answer to Infinity. Heat vision propagates toward Gojo through intervening space, so Infinity should plausibly interfere with it rather than letting it simply appear on his body, although the exact cross-universe interaction has never been tested. Freeze breath is similar: it spreads toward Gojo through the surrounding space, making Infinity the most defensible obstacle, but not one we can prove from a direct canon comparison.

Destroying the ground doesn’t strand Gojo either. Limitless allows him to maintain himself in the air and control his movement without needing a surface beneath him, so Clark can’t simply remove the street and let gravity solve the problem. Carrying Gojo into space would require grabbing him first, bringing the fight straight back to Infinity.

Clark could cause destruction on a scale Gojo couldn't reproduce, but blowing apart a city or destroying the planet isn’t a reasonable standard tactic for Superman. It also wouldn't demonstrate that he personally crossed Infinity. Turning Clark into someone willing to annihilate everything around Gojo would abandon the version and behavior we established simply to manufacture another win condition.

His enhanced senses are much more useful because they let him study what Gojo is doing. Clark can follow tiny movements, hear changes in Gojo’s body, and recognize patterns far faster than an ordinary opponent could. That helps him understand Blue, Red, and eventually the hand sign for Unlimited Void, but learning those patterns takes exchanges that Infinity allows Gojo to survive.

That's the recurring problem for Superman. His toolkit contains plenty of abilities capable of killing Gojo if they connect, while the selected version doesn’t bring a repeatable spatial counter that makes those attacks connect. Making the punch stronger or the heat vision hotter keeps improving an attack that’s already powerful enough to kill Gojo without addressing why it stops before touching him.

Gojo’s position is much simpler once he understands Clark’s durability. He can stop spending cursed energy trying to damage Superman conventionally and move toward the ability that already demonstrated an effect unrelated to whether the target can survive enormous physical force. Infinity gives him the safety to make that adjustment.

By the time Clark has gathered enough information to understand both Infinity and Unlimited Void, Gojo has already had the opportunity to use the Domain. Clark’s intelligence makes him much harder to catch a second time, but Gojo may not need a 2nd attempt if the first one produces sustained incapacitation.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: Their actual fight makes the mismatch between useful stats and useful abilities obvious almost immediately. Superman closes the distance before Gojo could hope to match his movement and throws a controlled opening punch, expecting to learn how durable his opponent is. The punch slows before touching Gojo and leaves Clark staring at a man he reached almost instantly but still can’t physically contact.

Clark backs away and changes the test. Heat vision appears to run into the same spatial problem rather than reaching Gojo directly, and another physical approach from a different angle confirms that the defense surrounds him. The exact heat-vision interaction is a crossover assumption, but Clark understands within seconds that he’s dealing with a spatial effect, while Gojo understands that allowing this man to touch him directly would be a terrible idea.

Gojo uses Blue during Clark’s next movement and catches him with an attraction he hasn't experienced yet. Superman powers through the displacement quickly, and Red catches him once before his speed makes repeating the trick much harder. Clark takes the attack without suffering the kind of damage Gojo would expect from almost anyone else.

Purple confirms the physical problem. Even if Gojo manages to catch Clark with part of it through surprise or positioning, Superman’s durability gives Gojo no reason to expect a clean finish, and Clark’s speed makes another attempt increasingly difficult. Gojo now knows exactly which part of his arsenal is wasting his time.

Superman has learned less that helps him finish the fight. He knows Infinity is responsible for stopping his attacks and can tell Gojo is manipulating space, but identifying a defense doesn’t automatically provide the missing counter. Every normal attack he tries still has to deal with the same distance around Gojo.

Gojo brings his hands together while Clark remains close. Superman sees it immediately, but the previous techniques have given him no reason to interpret that specific movement as the beginning of an attack that will overwhelm his mind. This is the fight’s biggest timing question: Clark might remain close long enough for Unlimited Void to close because he doesn’t recognize the threat, or his vastly superior reactions might carry him outside the forming barrier anyway. If he stays, the Domain closes around them.

If Clark is caught, the entire rhythm of the fight changes. He had been controlling when every physical exchange happened because Gojo couldn't match his speed, but Unlimited Void begins flooding him with information once the sure-hit applies. Any hesitation or loss of coordination gives Gojo something he could never create through speed alone.

Gojo keeps the Domain open while watching for that effect. If Clark stops advancing, firing heat vision, or escaping, there’s no reason to trade a working win condition for another attempt at damaging Kryptonian skin. Sustained Unlimited Void can continue pressing that advantage, although how long Superman remains impaired and whether he can regain enough control to escape are not established by either series.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: Superman’s mental feats could materially affect how long he remains impaired. His brain processes information at superhuman speed, and he’s resisted powerful forms of mental interference throughout his career. Giving Clark more resistance than an ordinary human is reasonable, while Unlimited Void continues supplying information for as long as he remains exposed. That makes the interaction dangerous without giving either side a guaranteed result: faster processing doesn’t establish immunity, but Jujutsu Kaisen also never demonstrates how sustained Unlimited Void interacts with a mind operating on Superman’s level. Clark may be incapacitated before he can act, or he may retain enough function to attempt an escape.
This is also where the matchup stops needing increasingly complicated theories about how Gojo could kill him afterward. If sustained exposure leaves Clark unable to coordinate himself
