I'm staying home. If people around me start turning to dust and | don't, I’d know immediately that we failed.

That would also mean | know what comes next. Thanos has gone to the Garden. Thor, Rocket and the remaining Avengers eventually find him, only to learn that he has already used the Stones again to destroy the Stones. Thor kills him, and for the next 5 years everyone assumes the Snap can’t be undone.
I'd know they’re wrong. The problem is proving it without breaking the one chain of events that eventually brings everyone back.

Scott Lang needs to return from the Quantum Realm. Tony needs to solve time travel. The surviving Avengers need to retrieve the Stones from the past. If | interfere too much during those 5 years, | could accidentally destroy the exact circumstances that lead to Endgame. That means if | survive the Snap, my strategy changes again. Before Infinity War, knowing the future makes me interfere as much as | safely can because stopping the Snap is better than allowing it.

After the Snap, the first future event I'd protect is Scott Lang's Quantum Realm situation. I'd make sure his van and equipment aren't thrown away or destroyed during the chaos, because that's one small butterfly effect | absolutely don’t want.

Then I'd stop trying to control every event. If Scott comes out earlier because someone checks the van, the timeline changes again, but that may actually be worth it. Five years of suffering only happens because nobody knows he’s trapped there.

If they can recover him quickly, Tony could start working on the Quantum Realm years earlier. And suddenly surviving Thanos isn’t just about whether I’m lucky enough to make it through the Snap. It becomes whether the warning | gave before the invasion can stop the Snap completely, or whether the information | still have afterward can bring everyone back much sooner.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: If the Snap still happens and | survive it, the first thing I’d have to accept is that my original plan failed. At that point I’m not trying to chase Thanos or convince myself there’s some second shot hidden on Earth. | already know he leaves for the Garden, uses the Stones again, and destroys them before the Avengers can take them back. The surviving Avengers are going to find him either way, and me trying to insert myself into that mission would accomplish nothing except putting a normal human next to Thor, Carol, Rocket, Nebula, Steve and Bruce while they go after the most dangerous person in the universe.

What | would do is get one message to the Avengers before they leave. I’d tell them that Thanos has already destroyed the Stones by the time they reach him, and that Thor is going to kill him once he realizes there’s no way to undo the Snap there. | wouldn't expect that warning to stop them from going, because they'd still need to confirm it themselves, but it gives them a reason to start thinking about another answer earlier instead of spending years believing there isn’t one. Then I'd bring up Scott Lang. Scott is trapped in the Quantum Realm when the Snap happens because Hank, Janet and Hope disappear before they can pull him back out. | know where the van came from, and | know his experience there eventually becomes the clue that points the Avengers toward time travel. I wouldn't deliberately leave him trapped for 5 years just to preserve the movie's exact sequence. I'd tell the Avengers he's alive, protect the van and tunnel, and let people who actually understand the technology work out how to retrieve and study him safely.

If Scott comes back much earlier, his experience may be different from the one | remember, and Tony may not solve time travel immediately. But the mismatch between time inside the Quantum Realm and time outside it, combined with my warning that the Realm eventually matters, gives the Avengers a reason to investigate the idea years earlier instead of waiting for a random accident.

My own life during the first few months would be much less exciting. Half the world is gone, so there are going to be empty jobs, empty apartments, broken families, shortages in weird places and entire systems trying to function with half their staff. I'd want to stay somewhere with stable

utilities and away from anything that suddenly becomes strategically important. I’m not moving to Avengers Compound because Tony knows my name. If anything, being known by them makes me more careful because | don’t want the surviving world deciding | somehow caused the disaster | predicted.

I'd keep everything | know written down in multiple places. The names of the people needed for the time heist, the dates | remember, Vormir, the 2012 Battle of New York, the Tesseract at Camp Lehigh in 1970, Pym Particles, Nebula’s connection to her 2014 self and the fact that Thanos eventually follows the Avengers back to their own time. My memory is now the only thing connecting this world to a version of Endgame that hasn’t happened yet, so forgetting one stupid detail 4 years later could matter more than anything | do physically.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: From that point on, I’d have to fight the urge to treat Endgame like a schedule. If Scott is recovered early and the Avengers start investigating the Quantum Realm years sooner, Tony, Bruce and everyone else could develop very differently from the future | remember. My remaining knowledge is still useful, but now it's reference material for dangers and possibilities rather than a checklist of events I should preserve.

Tony is the biggest example. I know that in the original timeline Scott eventually brings him the time travel idea and Tony initially refuses because undoing the Snap could threaten the life he built with Pepper and Morgan. In this timeline, that conversation could happen much earlier or under completely different circumstances, so | wouldn't spend years trying to force Tony toward the exact decision I remember.

What | can do is give Tony and Bruce the concepts I remember: the Quantum Realm becomes a route to navigating time, changing the past doesn't simply erase the present they came from, and a successful plan can bring Infinity Stones forward and return them afterward. | can give them the destination. | can’t give them the equations because I’m still an ordinary person who watched a movie, not someone who secretly understands Stark’s physics.

If their solution eventually resembles the original time heist, I'd also warn Bruce that removing an Infinity Stone from the past can create a dangerous branch unless it is returned. If their solution works differently, that memory becomes a warning to investigate the consequences rather than a rule | pretend automatically applies to every new plan.

So instead of waiting for a specific 5 year mark, I'd keep the Avengers updated on the pieces | remember and let their scientists decide when they actually have a workable Quantum Realm solution. The earlier changes may erase the exact Endgame setup completely, and that would be fine if they produce a safer way to restore everyone.
If events still converge on something close to the time heist | remember, that's when my detailed warnings become useful again.
At that point I can tell them where the original plan failed and let them adapt those warnings to whatever mission they actually design.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: If the Avengers eventually decide to use the Quantum Realm for a mission resembling the original time heist, | would not ask to go with them. That might be the dumbest possible thing | could do. Everyone on that mission would be far more qualified than me, and I'd be an extra person consuming resources while trying not to get killed by events that may no longer unfold like the movie.

One of my most important warnings would still be Nebula. In the original Endgame plan, Rhodey and Nebula go to Morag in 2014 for the Power Stone, and 2023 Nebula’s cybernetics connect to the network used by her 2014 self. Thanos starts seeing future Nebula’s memories through the younger Nebula, learns that people from the future are collecting the Stones and eventually sends 2014 Nebula back in her place. If their new plan sends Nebula anywhere near that point in 2014, they need to know that risk before she goes.

The same logic applies to the other failures I remember. If a team goes to 2012 New York, I'd warn them that Loki escaped with the Tesseract in the original attempt after Hulk knocked Tony down. If anyone is sent to Vormir, they need to know the Soul Stone demanded the loss of someone the seeker loved. These are hazards from one version of the mission, not guarantees that our altered plan will recreate every scene.

The exact method is up to the people actually designing the mission. My job is to tell them which failure points existed in the timeline I remember so they can avoid repeating them if those situations come up again.

Vormir is the warning I'd hate giving the most. In the timeline I remember, Natasha and Clint go there thinking the Soul Stone is another object they can collect. Red Skull tells them that one person has to lose someone they love, and Natasha eventually sacrifices herself before Clint can stop her. If the Avengers still need to retrieve the Soul Stone from that point in history, | already know that price exists.

If they want the Soul Stone, someone still has to die. The difference is that they don’t arrive on another planet and discover the cost after they're already trapped in the decision. Steve, Natasha, Clint and the others can decide beforehand whether they're willing to pay it and who should even make that trip.

There may not be a clean answer. | can’t invent some loophole because the script needs one. The Soul Stone demands a sacrifice, and if they still choose to complete the time heist, one of them probably isn’t coming home.

If the eventual mission resembles Endgame closely enough for those warnings to apply, avoiding the Nebula connection and the New York Tesseract failure could make it dramatically cleaner. But by then I'd expect the Avengers to redesign the mission around everything that has already changed rather than trying to reproduce the movie perfectly.
That changes my chances of surviving Endgame more than anything | could do with a gun. PART 9
If a Quantum Realm plan eventually succeeds in recovering the Stones, the most dangerous place on Earth could become wherever the Avengers bring them back, which means | want to be nowhere near it.

Bruce is still probably the best person to perform the reverse Snap because his body can survive gamma radiation far better than a normal human. I’d already know the Gauntlet is going to badly injure him, but that’s different from knowing someone else can safely do it. Thor wants to use the Stones in Endgame and the others stop him because he isn’t in the right condition, while Tony is physically human underneath the armor and eventually dies from using them himself.
So I’m not changing that just to feel useful.

I'd make sure the Avengers know exactly what Bruce is trying to do. Bring back everyone Thanos erased 5 years ago without undoing the last 5 years for the people who survived. That distinction matters because Tony is terrified that fixing the Snap means losing Morgan. Bruce can restore the vanished population while leaving the current timeline intact.

If the mission still involves 2014 and my Nebula warning prevents Thanos from discovering the time heist through his connection to Nebula, then the specific chain that brought the 2014 version of him into the future may never happen.

If that specific chain is prevented and no new complication replaces it, Avengers Compound may avoid being bombarded by his army, the giant final battlefield may never happen, and Tony may never need to take the Stones from Thanos and use them himself.

Tony could actually survive the restoration. That would be one of the biggest possible changes my future knowledge produces, and it comes from warning the team about a failure point rather than trying to reproduce every event around it.
But that outcome is conditional on the new plan ever creating the same danger in the first place.

My job after everyone is restored would be getting out of the Avengers’ way again. If they borrowed Stones from earlier points in time, they would still need a plan to return them so those branches aren't left without them. Who handles that and exactly where each Stone goes depends on the mission they actually carried out. There’s also no reason for me to hang around hoping somebody gives me an Avengers membership after all this. | still can’t fight. Knowing the future made me useful because the future hadn’t happened yet. Once we get past the point | remember, that advantage disappears. And honestly, that’s probably the safest moment of the entire scenario.
| can finally become irrelevant again.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: So could | actually survive Thanos?
If everything goes perfectly, I think | could give myself a much better chance than a normal person in the MCU, but most of that comes from staying away from the fights.

I'd avoid New York when Maw and Cull arrive. I’d never go to Wakanda. I’d never step onto Titan. I'd keep as much distance as possible between myself and every Infinity Stone while getting information to people who can actually use it.

The harder part is stopping the Snap. My best shot is warning Strange before Bruce lands in the Sanctum, getting Vision to Wakanda early enough for Shuri to remove the Mind Stone, and destroying that Stone before Thanos reaches Earth. If that works, Thanos never completes the Gauntlet and my 50 percent survival problem disappears entirely.

If that plan fails and I survive the Snap anyway, then | have another path. Protect Scott and the Quantum Tunnel, tell the Avengers that the Quantum Realm is connected to the solution I remember, and let them investigate it as early as they realistically can. If their eventual plan resembles the original time heist, I can warn them about the specific failures I remember without assuming every one of those events still has to happen.

The Nebula warning could still matter enormously if their plan involves 2014. Stop that connection from giving past Thanos access to the future and the final Endgame battle may never happen. But after changing this much history, the goal isn't to force the movie's ending. It's to use whatever parts of that ending are still relevant to help the Avengers build a safer one.
There are still plenty of ways I could screw this up. Strange could dismiss me before the first prediction comes true. Tony might make a different decision once he learns too much.

Destroying the Mind Stone early could make Thanos attack Earth sooner. Saving Scott’s van could change how the Quantum Realm gets discovered. Every successful warning makes the next thing | remember less reliable.
That's the real danger of knowing the future.

| only get to use the original timeline as a map until | start changing it. So | wouldn’t try to control everything. I’d target the moments where one warning gives the biggest advantage, then stay out of the way. Strange before New York. Vision before Scotland. Scott after the Snap. Nebula before the time heist.
I'm never beating Thanos myself but if | know exactly where the MCU went wrong, | might not have to.

scripts.title: If Homelander Was Charged For His Crimes

sections.name: INTRO
paras: If Homelander were prosecuted like a real person, the case against him would go far beyond a few obvious murders.

You’d have intentional killings, assaults, threats, unlawful confinement, possible conspiracies, obstruction, destroyed evidence, and crimes spread across different jurisdictions. Some incidents would support multiple charges, while others that look criminal at first would fall apart once you apply the actual legal elements.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: The first charge prosecutors would have to deal with actually happens years before the main story begins, Becca Butcher’s rape. Becca later explicitly states that Homelander raped her. She tells Billy directly what happened, and that she went to Vought after discovering she was pregnant because she was afraid Billy would go after him. Earlier in the series, Billy had already described the same event as rape, but Becca’s own statement is the much stronger piece of evidence because she is the victim describing what happened to her.

If the assault occurred in New York, which is the most likely jurisdiction given Becca’s work around Vought, prosecutors would look at New York’s rape statutes. First-degree rape under Penal Law § 130.35 includes vaginal sexual contact accomplished by forcible compulsion, and New York’s jury instructions define forcible compulsion around physical force or threats that compel the victim. First degree rape is a class B felony.

The problem here is proof. Becca’s statement establishes non consent from her perspective, but a prosecutor would still need evidence of the exact sexual act and the force or threat used. We never see the assault itself, so the case would rely heavily on Becca’s testimony, her behavior immediately afterward, the pregnancy, any contemporaneous statements she made to Vought, and whatever records Stillwell or Vogelbaum kept. The fact that she sat alone for hours afterward and then went directly to Vought would support her account, but it wouldn't replace proof of the statutory elements.

Homelander’s powers would matter to the forcible compulsion analysis too. If Becca testified that she submitted because physical resistance against someone who could kill her instantly was impossible, a jury could consider whether that amounted to compulsion through force or an implied threat. Prosecutors wouldn’t need to prove that Homelander physically injured her during the assault if they could prove she was compelled by force or fear of immediate harm. There is also no statute of limitations problem for first degree rape under current New York law. A prosecution for that offense may be commenced at any time. If convicted as a first time felony sex offender, a class B felony sex offense can carry up to 25 years in prison, with post-release supervision added afterward.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: The next major case is much cleaner. In Season 1, Homelander learns that the Mayor of Baltimore knows about Compound V after listening in on the mayor’s conversation with Stillwell. The mayor then leaves on a private jet with his son. Homelander flies alongside it and uses his heat vision to cut the aircraft apart, killing the mayor, his child, and everyone else aboard.

This is deliberate homicide. Homelander identifies a person who possesses information dangerous to Vought, follows his aircraft, and destroys it while knowing everyone inside will die. There is no self-defense argument because the mayor poses no physical threat to him, and nothing about the scene suggests an accidental use of his powers.

The exact federal theory depends on aircraft jurisdiction. Because Homelander is outside the mayor’s jet when he attacks it, 49 U.S.C. § 46506 is not the clean route: that provision applies the listed federal offenses to conduct by an individual on a qualifying aircraft. The more direct federal count is 18 U.S.C. § 32, which makes it a crime to willfully damage or destroy covered aircraft used in interstate, overseas, or foreign air commerce.

That distinction matters because prosecutors should not casually treat the jet like a New York crime scene or use an onboard-aircraft statute against someone flying beside it. If the government establishes that the mayor’s aircraft falls within § 32, Homelander’s deliberate destruction of it is the cleaner federal charge. Because that violation results in deaths, 18 U.S.C. § 34 can raise the punishment to life imprisonment or potentially death, but any death sentence would still require the government to satisfy 18 U.S.C. § 3591 and the federal capital procedures.

Premeditation would still be obvious from the sequence of events even if prosecutors do not have an independent federal murder jurisdiction under § 1111. Homelander learns the mayor knows about Compound V, follows the jet instead of confronting him openly, and destroys it once it is in the air. Any separate murder charge would therefore depend on establishing an additional jurisdictional basis, while the § 32 aircraft-destruction count and § 34 death-resulting penalty provide the cleaner federal path on the facts we actually have.

This incident could also support an obstruction theory if prosecutors prove Homelander killed the mayor specifically to prevent disclosure of Compound V to investigators or government officials. Federal witness tampering law covers killing someone with intent to prevent that person from communicating information about a federal offense to federal law enforcement. The evidence would have to establish that Homelander’s purpose lines up with the statute, though, so the murder charge should stay separate unless investigators can prove exactly what disclosure he was trying to stop.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Flight 37 is legally more difficult because Homelander does not intentionally board the plane planning to kill the passengers. He and Maeve are sent to rescue a hijacked flight traveling from Paris to Chicago. After they kill several hijackers, a final terrorist shoots the remaining pilot in the cockpit. Homelander kills that terrorist with heat vision, but the beams pass through him and destroy the aircraft's control panel. Maeve then asks Homelander to save the passengers individually, including at least a mother and child, and Homelander refuses because survivors could expose what happened. The aircraft eventually crashes into the ocean.

Simply failing to rescue somebody is usually not enough for homicide. Criminal law generally does not turn every person who could have saved someone into a murderer. Homelander’s situation is different because his own careless use of heat vision destroys the controls and contributes to the danger that ultimately kills everyone onboard.

The first question would be whether his destruction of the controls was criminally reckless. He uses a weapon capable of cutting through aircraft material inside a cockpit where critical systems are directly behind his target. He may have needed to stop an armed hijacker, but prosecutors could argue that the way he used that force created an obvious and enormous risk to everyone on the plane.

Federal aviation jurisdiction would again matter because the flight is over international waters on a Paris to Chicago route, but this incident is materially different from the mayor’s jet. Homelander is physically aboard Flight 37 when he destroys the cockpit controls. If the flight falls within the special aircraft jurisdiction of the United States, 49 U.S.C. § 46506 can apply the listed federal offenses, including federal murder and manslaughter law, to qualifying conduct committed by an individual on that aircraft.

Charging Homelander with intentional murder for every passenger would be difficult because the evidence does not show that he destroyed the controls intending to kill them. A manslaughter or 2nd degree murder theory based on extreme recklessness is much more realistic, depending on exactly what federal statute prosecutors use and how they prove causation.

That initial recklessness question is separate from what happens after the controls are damaged. His decision at that later stage strengthens the case. Maeve specifically proposes saving some of the passengers, and Homelander refuses because he does not want witnesses telling the public that they abandoned everyone else. At that point, his choice is tied directly to protecting himself rather than an inability to save anybody at all. The prosecution could argue that once he contributed to the peril, his deliberate refusal to take even available rescue steps becomes part of the causal story.

There is still a defense here that would need to be taken seriously. Homelander says he cannot physically lift the aircraft because there is nothing solid to push against and that trying to support it would tear through the fuselage. He also argues there is not enough time to fly everyone to safety individually. Those statements could defeat any theory that assumes he could have saved the entire flight.

What they do not explain is why he refuses to save even the passengers Maeve identifies as realistically reachable. His stated reason is the possibility that survivors would expose him. That is extremely damaging evidence of his state of mind, even if prosecutors ultimately choose manslaughter rather than intentional murder.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Madelyn Stillwell’s death is much simpler. In the Season 1 finale, Billy Butcher has already kidnapped Stillwell and strapped explosives to her when Homelander arrives. Homelander learns that Stillwell lied to him about Becca and Ryan, listens to her admit that she is afraid of him, then places his hands around her face and burns through her eyes with heat vision, killing her.

Assuming this occurs in New York, the straightforward charge is 2nd degree murder under Penal Law § 125.25. New York requires intent to cause death and the actual death of the victim. Homelander’s conduct satisfies both without needing a complicated theory. He deliberately aims a lethal power at Stillwell’s head at extremely close range and keeps using it until she dies. Second degree murder is a class A-I felony.

The fact that Butcher has kidnapped Stillwell does not give Homelander a self defense or defense of others justification for killing her. Stillwell is the hostage. Extreme emotional disturbance could theoretically be raised because New York recognizes it as an affirmative defense that can reduce an intentional murder case under certain circumstances. The standard still requires a reasonable explanation or excuse when viewed from the defendant's situation. Homelander discovering that Stillwell lied to him about Ryan could explain why he is furious, but prosecutors would have an extremely strong argument that deliberately burning her face off is far outside anything reasonably excused by that discovery.

New York’s sentencing range for a class A-I felony generally requires life as the maximum, with a minimum term somewhere between 15 and 25 years depending on the sentence imposed. For ordinary second degree murder, that commonly means a sentence such as 25 years to life rather than automatic life without parole.

There is an additional evidentiary issue because Butcher detonates the explosives moments later, destroying much of the scene. That does not erase the murder. Butcher witnesses Homelander kill Stillwell, and forensic evidence consistent with heat damage could potentially survive enough to support his testimony. If Homelander participated in a later Vought cover up, separate evidence tampering or obstruction charges could arise, but we should not automatically attribute every corporate cleanup decision to him without proof that he personally joined it.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: Season 2 adds 2 crimes that are much easier to prosecute because Homelander attacks fellow Supes inside Vought with no legitimate justification. The first is Blindspot. Ashley introduces Blindspot as a possible new member of The Seven, and after briefly pretending to approve, Homelander slams both hands against Blindspot’s ears. The attack destroys his hearing, which was the ability Blindspot relied on to compensate for being blind.

Under New York law, that conduct fits assault in the first degree much better than a minor battery charge. Penal Law § 120.10 covers intentionally causing serious and permanent disfigurement or intentionally destroying or permanently disabling a bodily organ. Homelander targets Blindspot’s ears specifically and causes exactly the kind of disabling injury that provision describes. First-degree assault is a class B felony.

If prosecutors cannot establish that the damage was permanent, second degree assault becomes the safer fallback because New York also criminalizes intentionally causing serious physical injury. The strongest prosecution would charge the highest supported degree and allow the jury to consider the lesser offense if medical evidence shows Blindspot eventually recovered.

Doppelganger is even more straightforward. After spending time impersonating Stillwell for Homelander, Doppelganger transforms into Homelander himself during one of their private encounters. Homelander responds by grabbing Doppelganger and snapping their neck with one hand, killing them instantly. There is no fight and no indication Doppelganger is threatening him physically when it happens.

That supports another New York 2nd degree murder count if the killing occurred in New York. Snapping someone’s neck with enough force to kill them allows a jury to infer intent to cause death, particularly when the defendant has Homelander’s strength and knows exactly what his own body can do. This would be another class A-I felony carrying a potential sentence up to life with a minimum term generally set between 15 and 25 years.

There is no serious self defense argument in the scene. Doppelganger is attempting to please Homelander rather than attack him, and Homelander’s own reaction shows that the killing comes from his decision that he no longer needs the relationship.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Season 3 gives prosecutors a very different set of offenses because Homelander starts using explicit threats and intimidation to control people around him. The clearest example is Starlight. After she threatens to release the Flight 37 video, Homelander tells her that if the public turns against him, he will destroy major infrastructure, attack New York, and kill Hughie and everyone else she cares about. Starlight backs down because she believes he can carry those threats out.

For New York prosecutors, coercion in the 1st degree is much cleaner than trying to force a terrorism charge. New York Penal Law § 135.65 applies when someone uses fear of physical injury to compel another person to act or refrain from acting. Homelander is telling Starlight that people will die if she refuses to cooperate, and her compliance follows directly from that threat. Coercion in the 1st degree is a class D felony.

I would reject terroristic threat as the primary charge here. Homelander describes mass violence, but the New York terrorism statute requires a particular intent involving intimidation of a civilian population or influence over government conduct. His immediate purpose in this conversation is controlling Starlight personally. The prosecution already has a stronger charge without stretching those elements.

Supersonic gives prosecutors another straightforward homicide. After A Train tells Homelander that Supersonic is helping Starlight organize against him, Homelander kills Supersonic and later shows Starlight the body. The corpse itself becomes part of the threat because Homelander uses it to prove what happens to people who join her.

Assuming the killing happens in New York, the appropriate charge is murder in the 2nd degree under Penal Law § 125.25. The statute covers intentionally causing another person’s death, and the surrounding conduct gives prosecutors strong evidence of intent. Supersonic is killed after Homelander learns about the plan against him, and Homelander then uses the result to intimidate Starlight. There is no self defense theory because Supersonic is not attacking him when he is killed. Murder in the 2nd degree is a class A-I felony.

Queen Maeve requires more care. Vought publicly claims she entered rehabilitation while she is actually being held in secret custody. Homelander visits her while she is confined and speaks as though her continued captivity is something he accepts and intends to use for his own purposes. If prosecutors can prove Homelander ordered or knowingly participated in keeping her there, kidnapping in the 2nd degree is a realistic charge. New York defines abduction as restraining someone while intending to prevent liberation by secretly holding the victim somewhere they are unlikely to be found, or by using or threatening deadly physical force. Kidnapping in the 2nd degree applies when a defendant abducts another person and is a class B felony.

The secret nature of Maeve’s confinement is important. She is hidden from the public while Vought gives everyone a false explanation for her disappearance. The remaining evidentiary issue is proving Homelander’s role in the original seizure. If the evidence only shows that Vought employees captured her and Homelander later knew she was being held, unlawful imprisonment may be easier to prove than kidnapping. If witnesses, orders, or records show that he directed the confinement, the kidnapping case becomes much stronger.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Black Noir’s death is one of the easiest murders in the entire prosecution. Homelander learns that Noir knew Soldier Boy was his biological father and kept that information from him. He confronts Noir about it, confirms that Noir knew, then punches directly through his abdomen and leaves him dying.

If this occurs at Vought Tower in New York, prosecutors would charge murder in the 2nd degree under § 125.25. Homelander’s intent can be inferred from the force he uses, the location of the blow, and the fact that someone with his strength would understand the likely result. Noir is not posing an imminent threat when Homelander attacks him, which eliminates any serious self defense claim.

The Season 3 rally killing is equally direct. A protester throws an object that hits Ryan, and Homelander immediately uses heat vision to kill the man in front of the crowd. The fact that Ryan was struck does not justify deadly force once the immediate threat is over. A thrown drink or similar object does not create a reasonable need to kill someone with heat vision.

The original charge would again be murder in the 2nd degree if New York has jurisdiction. The evidence is unusually strong because the killing occurs publicly and is witnessed by a large crowd. In the show, Homelander is later tried and acquitted for that death. If we are treating the fictional proceedings as legally valid, double jeopardy would prevent a second prosecution for the same homicide after a final acquittal. For this video, however, the point is what he could properly have been charged with when the prosecution was first brought.

Season 4 then produces a major accomplice liability case. Homelander and Sister Sage use Todd and 2 other Homelander supporters as part of a plan to manufacture political violence. Homelander directs members of The Seven to kill the 3 men, after which the bodies are used to create the appearance that Starlight supporters murdered them.

New York does not require the person physically holding the weapon to be the only person guilty of murder. Penal Law § 20.00 makes someone criminally liable for another person’s conduct when, with the required mental state, that person solicits, requests, commands, or intentionally aids the other person in committing the offense. Homelander ordering the killings while intending the victims to die would make him liable for the murders themselves if New York law applies. That means prosecutors would not need to settle for solicitation merely because Homelander did not swing the weapon. Each completed killing can support a murder in the 2nd degree charge through accessorial liability. Prosecutors could also charge conspiracy in the 2nd degree if they prove Homelander agreed with others that conduct constituting a class A felony would be carried out. Murder in the 2nd degree is a class A-I felony, and conspiracy in the 2nd degree specifically covers agreements intended to cause a class A felony.

The conspiracy count would remain separate from the murders because the criminal agreement is a distinct offense, although sentencing and merger questions would still need to be handled carefully. The prosecution should also avoid automatically charging Homelander with every falsified Vought record created afterward. His participation in the staged killings is clear. Separate obstruction or falsification counts require proof that he knowingly participated in those specific cover up acts.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: Anika’s death gives prosecutors another clean intentional murder. Homelander, Sage, and Ashley question her because she has communicated with Starlight’s organization. Before she can finish explaining herself, Homelander kills her with heat vision. There is no physical threat from Anika and no emergency that would justify the use of deadly force. Assuming the killing occurs at Vought Tower in New York, prosecutors would charge murder in the 2nd degree under Penal Law § 125.25, because Homelander intentionally causes her death without justification.

Attempted murder in the 2nd degree requires proof that Homelander intended to kill Hughie and came dangerously close enough to completing the offense under New York attempt law. Repeatedly firing heat vision directly at a fleeing Hughie would make that intent easy to establish. The fact that another person is struck during the chase would need a separate analysis based on whether that victim dies and what Homelander’s mental state was toward them.

The laboratory massacre is more complicated because jurisdiction depends on the actual location of the facility. I would not assign New York statutes until that location is verified. The conduct itself still gives prosecutors several extremely strong homicide and assault cases. Homelander returns to the laboratory where he was raised and deliberately takes revenge on the staff. He places Frank in the same heated chamber once used on him and kills him. He humiliates Marty by forcing him to perform a sexual act in front of coworkers, then uses heat vision on Marty’s genitals and later kills him. Homelander then kills the remaining staff while leaving Barbara alive and trapped inside the room with the bodies.

Frank’s killing is intentional and planned long enough for Homelander to place him inside the chamber and operate it. Marty’s death is also an intentional homicide, while the genital injury would support a serious assault charge before the murder. If the applicable state has an offense equivalent to New York assault in the 1st degree, prosecutors would look for provisions covering intentional permanent disfigurement or destruction of a bodily organ. New York’s version expressly includes that type of conduct and classifies assault in the 1st degree as a class B felony.

Barbara’s treatment supports unlawful confinement and could support kidnapping depending on the jurisdiction. Homelander knowingly seals her inside after killing the others, leaving her unable to leave. If the evidence shows an intent to prevent her liberation by secreting her in a place where she is unlikely to be found, the conduct would resemble kidnapping under New York’s definition of abduction.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: The Season 4 political plot creates some of the most serious federal charges because Homelander moves from personal violence into an agreement to manipulate control of the United States government.

Homelander, Sage, and their allies work toward removing President elect Robert Singer and replacing him with a government that will give Supes vastly more power. By the finale, the plan includes an attempt to assassinate Singer, the use of political violence, a Vought purge, and eventually martial law under President Calhoun with Homelander exercising enormous practical control.

The Singer plot falls directly within 18 U.S.C. § 1751 because the statute specifically protects the President elect as well as the sitting President. The assassination fails, but § 1751 does not require prosecutors to fall back on a generic conspiracy theory. Subsection (d) expressly criminalizes conspiring to kill the President or President elect when one or more conspirators commits an act to effect the object of the conspiracy, and it permits any term of years or life.

Prosecutors would therefore focus first on whether Homelander knowingly agreed that Singer would be assassinated and whether a conspirator acted to carry that plan out. The events provide substantial evidence because the assassination is part of the larger scheme to change who controls the government, and Homelander ultimately directs that Singer be killed. Once the assassin takes a substantial step toward killing Singer, prosecutors could also examine liability for the attempted assassination itself, including 18 U.S.C. § 2 if Homelander intentionally commanded, induced, or aided the attempt. Seditious conspiracy under 18 U.S.C. § 2384 is also realistic, but it is a separate and more element-dependent theory. The statute requires an agreement involving force to overthrow or destroy the government, oppose its authority, prevent execution of federal law, or seize federal property against lawful authority. It carries a maximum of 20 years.

Homelander’s case is stronger than a simple political conspiracy because the plan uses assassination, violent Supes, fabricated unrest, and eventually a national enforcement force to change how the government operates. Prosecutors would argue that the agreement involves using force to oppose federal authority and prevent the lawful execution of government power. The defense would likely argue that Homelander is manipulating succession rather than literally attempting to overthrow the constitutional structure, so the exact communications between him, Sage, Neuman, and Calhoun would matter enormously.

The Vought purge adds another set of charges. Homelander orders that employees who could incriminate The Seven be eliminated. Under New York accessorial liability, anyone killed pursuant to an order Homelander gives with intent that they die can become another murder in the 2nd degree count against him if the offense occurs within New York jurisdiction.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: Once Calhoun becomes President and gives Homelander control over a national Supe force, the civil rights case becomes much stronger. The Season 4 finale shows the new administration declaring martial law while Homelander directs Supes against people identified as enemies, and members of The Boys are captured as the new system begins.

Federal prosecutors would look closely at 18 U.S.C. § 241, conspiracy against rights. The statute makes it a crime for 2 or more people to agree to injure, oppress, threaten, or intimidate someone in the exercise of rights protected by federal law or the Constitution. The basic maximum is 10 years, but the penalty can rise to any term of years or life when the conspiracy involves kidnapping, attempted killing, aggravated sexual abuse, or when death results.

That could apply to an agreement between Homelander and others to use a government backed Supe force to seize and imprison political opponents because of their protected activity. Prosecutors would still have to identify the actual constitutional or federal right being targeted. They could not simply say that the victims dislike Homelander politically and stop there.

Once Homelander is exercising authority through the government, 18 U.S.C. § 242 could also become relevant. That statute applies when someone acting under color of law willfully deprives another person of federally protected rights. A person does not need to hold a traditional police title, but prosecutors would still have to prove that Calhoun’s government actually vested or delegated governmental authority to Homelander, or that he acted jointly with government officials, rather than relying on his political influence or control over Vought alone. The maximum can rise to life imprisonment, and potentially death, when the offense results in death or includes kidnapping, attempted kidnapping, aggravated sexual abuse, or attempted killing. Season 5 gives prosecutors stronger factual support because the regime is no longer theoretical. Political detainees are being held in Vought Freedom Camps, armed Supes guard them, and Homelander operates through the system created under Calhoun. That allows prosecutors to connect the earlier agreement to actual detentions rather than relying only on statements about what Homelander planned to do.

Homelander also commits fresh murders. During the Freedom Camp escape, he kills Ivy with heat vision and then goes after Hughie. A Train intervenes, saves Hughie, and flees. Homelander pursues him until A Train crashes while avoiding a civilian, then catches him and intentionally snaps his neck.

Ivy would support an intentional murder charge under the law of the jurisdiction where the camp is located. Hughie supports attempted murder because Homelander is about to use lethal force on him before A Train intervenes. A Train’s death is another completed intentional homicide because Homelander catches him after the chase and deliberately kills him while A Train is no longer attacking anyone.

sections.name: PART 11
paras: Firecracker is killed after Homelander becomes convinced she betrayed him. He deliberately uses physical force against her head and kills her. Unless the jurisdiction has unusual homicide classifications, prosecutors would treat that as an intentional murder because the act is purposeful, directed at a vulnerable part of the body, and carried out after a personal confrontation rather than during self defense.

President Calhoun is legally far more significant. Once Calhoun is the sitting President, 18 U.S.C. § 1751 applies directly to anyone who kills him. The statute specifically covers the President and sends the punishment question to federal murder law.

If prosecutors prove Homelander intentionally killed Calhoun after deciding the President was no longer useful or loyal, federal 1st degree murder becomes the likely theory because the killing would be willful and deliberate. Premeditation does not require days of planning. It can form over a much shorter period if the evidence shows Homelander reflected on the decision before acting.

Under federal law, 1st degree murder can carry life imprisonment or the death penalty where the government satisfies the federal capital requirements. That means Calhoun’s murder alone could expose Homelander to the most severe punishment available under federal law. Frenchie’s death should be treated more cautiously, but the basic sequence is known. Frenchie deliberately lures Homelander into the uranium chamber and activates it as a sacrifice to protect Kimiko and Sage. Homelander fatally injures Frenchie during that encounter, and Frenchie emerges mortally wounded before dying shortly afterward.

That makes self defense a serious issue rather than an excuse to treat the entire event as factually unknown. Prosecutors would need to determine whether Frenchie’s uranium attack created an imminent threat that justified Homelander’s use of deadly force at the exact moment he inflicted the fatal injury, and whether the force remained necessary and proportionate. If Homelander kills or fatally injures Frenchie after the threat has been neutralized, the murder case becomes much stronger. If the fatal force is used while Frenchie is actively subjecting him to an unlawful deadly attack, this is one of the incidents I would leave out of the indictment unless prosecutors can defeat self defense.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: Homelander’s strongest prosecution would include numerous counts of murder in the 2nd degree for victims like Stillwell, Doppelganger, Supersonic, Black Noir, Anika, Todd and the other supporters he ordered killed, plus the other intentional killings prosecutors can tie to him directly or through accomplice liability.

He would also face attempted murder, coercion in the 1st degree, serious assault, kidnapping or unlawful imprisonment where the facts support it, conspiracy to kill President elect Robert Singer under 18 U.S.C. § 1751(d), potential liability for the attempted assassination itself, conspiracy against rights, and possible seditious conspiracy. The Singer charge is especially serious because § 1751(d) can carry any term of years or life, while the seditious conspiracy theory remains more dependent on proving its specific elements. President Calhoun’s death would create a separate federal murder in the 1st degree case under 18 U.S.C. § 1751.

Some charges should stay out. Flight 37 should not automatically become 123 counts of murder in the 1st degree, every Vought cover up should not be blamed on Homelander without proof, and unclear deaths like Frenchie’s should only be charged if prosecutors can defeat self defense.

Even after removing those weaker counts, Homelander could potentially face multiple life sentences, leaving him with little realistic possibility of release if prosecutors secure convictions on the strongest counts. The Calhoun murder could also expose Homelander to the federal death penalty if prosecutors seek it and satisfy the capital requirements.

scripts.title: What If Aang Was In The Boys

sections.name: INTRO
paras: Aang would probably believe The Seven were heroes at first.

That’s what makes this world dangerous for him. Vought has spent years making people like Homelander look like exactly the kind of protectors Aang wants to believe in, and nothing about arriving in a new world would immediately tell him how much of that image is fake.

The first time Aang sees what Supes are like when the cameras aren’t around, Vought stops looking like a group of heroes and starts looking like something he’s dealt with before: powerful people using fear and control while convincing everyone it’s necessary.

He still believes people can change, he still refuses to kill, and he’s going to keep trying to solve this without becoming like the people he’s fighting. But in a world where even the heroes are used to getting whatever they want, that approach is going to be tested harder than anything he faced during the war.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: Aang arriving in this world wouldn’t immediately understand that anything was wrong.

The cities are different, the technology is far beyond anything he knows, and there are people flying through the sky or appearing on giant screens as superheroes. None of that would make him suspicious by itself. He’s spent his entire life around bending, spirits, giant animals, and people capable of destroying buildings with their bare hands. A world with superheroes would seem strange, but not impossible.
What would stand out first is how differently people treat them.

Back home, powerful benders could become soldiers, rulers, or heroes, but nobody had companies building entire brands around them. Here, Homelander’s face is everywhere. The Seven appear in adverts, interviews, movies, and public events, and everyone seems to know exactly who they are.

If an entire country sees these people as protectors, he has no reason to assume they’re lying. He’d be curious more than anything, especially once he learns that some of them can fly, move at extreme speed, or survive injuries that would kill normal people.
His own powers would get attention just as quickly.

Aang wouldn’t be able to stay hidden for long because he isn’t the kind of person who watches someone get hurt just to protect his identity. The first serious accident or attack he comes across would give him away. Airbending makes rescuing civilians almost effortless compared to most Supes. He can slow people falling from buildings, redirect debris, and cross a city without needing roads or vehicles.

That would be enough for people to start filming him. Aang doesn’t look like any Supe in their system. There’s no record of him receiving Compound V, no childhood contract, and no family history they can trace. Yet he can clearly manipulate air, and before long they’d probably see him use earth or water too.

Their entire business depends on controlling the story around superheroes. If someone appears with powers they didn’t create and starts helping people without a contract, they can’t simply pretend he doesn’t exist.
So instead of treating Aang like an enemy, their first move would be much friendlier.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Aang’s first meeting with Vought would probably go better than anyone expects. He isn’t interested in money, fame, or becoming a celebrity, but he’s also not going to walk into the building assuming everyone there is evil. If they tell him The Seven protect people and that Vought helps organize them, he’ll listen. That gives Vought plenty of room to control what he sees. They’d show him the public facing version first. Training facilities, charity events, rescue footage, merchandise, and carefully selected stories about how The Seven have saved people. Homelander would be presented as the greatest hero in the world, while the rest of the team would be framed as different kinds of protectors serving the same mission.

Aang would actually like parts of it. The idea of people using extraordinary abilities to protect others is something he understands completely. He’d probably be especially interested in Starlight because she still genuinely wants to help people at this point, and she’d feel much more sincere than some of the others.

Homelander would also seem friendly at first. There’s no reason for him to threaten Aang immediately. From his perspective, Aang is a strange kid with impressive powers who doesn’t appear interested in fame or challenging him. If anything, Homelander might find him amusing.

That changes once Aang starts asking questions. He’d want to know why superheroes need a corporation deciding where they go. He’d ask who helps people when there aren’t cameras around. He might question why so much of the conversation is about ratings, public appearances, and branding instead of actual emergencies.
Still, nothing he sees on the tour would be enough to convince him that the entire system is corrupt. Vought is too good at controlling appearances for that.

Aang would notice how some of them behave once they think nobody important is watching. The Deep’s arrogance, A-Train’s complete lack of concern for normal people, or Homelander’s need to dominate every room would all feel wrong to him.
The difference is that everyone here keeps calling them heroes anyway. That’s when Aang would start looking beyond what Vought wants him to see.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: The first incident that truly changes Aang’s opinion wouldn’t need to involve Homelander.

A-Train alone could do it. Once Aang starts looking beyond Vought’s public image, he begins by investigating A-Train’s recent public incidents. That leads him to news coverage of Robin’s death and the settlement Vought offered Hughie afterward. The official story is unusually sanitized, and Vought’s effort to make the incident disappear makes Aang suspicious enough to track down Hughie himself. Learning that A-Train ran through Robin and then kept living his public life like nothing happened would be almost impossible for him to accept. Accidents can happen even to powerful people, but the way Vought handles the aftermath would bother him more than the accident itself.
There’s no real accountability. Everything is managed through lawyers, money, and PR while Hughie is expected to live with what happened.

Aang grew up in a world where powerful people hurting weaker ones was exactly the kind of thing he was supposed to stop. The fact that A-Train can do it while still being praised as a hero would make him question everything Vought showed him.

Starlight would probably be one of the first people inside The Seven he could speak to honestly. She already knows the reality doesn’t match what she believed before joining the team. Aang wouldn’t need her to give him every secret at once, just hearing that Vought controls where heroes go, what they say, and what gets covered up would confirm that his instincts were right.

From there, he’d start watching more carefully. He’d notice that Homelander doesn’t act like someone trying to help people. He acts like someone who expects obedience. Aang has seen that kind of authority before, especially from the Fire Nation, and it would become harder to ignore once he understands how afraid everyone around Homelander actually is.
That comparison wouldn’t make Aang decide Homelander is beyond saving. If anything, it would make him more determined to understand him.

Most people who discover what Homelander really is either become afraid of him or start looking for a way to kill him. Aang’s first instinct would be to find out why he became this way and whether there’s anything left in him that can change.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Butcher wouldn’t trust Aang for a second. From his perspective, a new superpowered kid appearing out of nowhere is still a Supe until proven otherwise. The fact that Vought has already shown interest in him only makes that worse.

Hughie would be less hostile. Once he learns Aang has been asking questions about A-Train and Vought, Hughie would see that he’s clearly not working for them. That gives The Boys enough reason to make contact instead of treating him like another target.

The meeting would be uncomfortable almost immediately. Butcher’s entire strategy is built around the belief that Supes can’t be trusted with that much power. He’s seen too many people lie while Vought protects the ones responsible. Aang is basically the worst possible argument for his worldview because he has enormous power and genuinely doesn’t want to use it selfishly.

Butcher wouldn’t see that as proof he’s wrong. He’d see Aang as the exception. Aang, meanwhile, would understand why Butcher hates Vought without agreeing with what he does about it. He can accept exposing corruption, rescuing people, and stopping dangerous Supes. What he won’t accept is Butcher treating killing them as the default answer.

That disagreement would start with Homelander. Butcher would make it clear that Homelander isn’t someone Aang can talk into becoming better. He’d explain enough of what Homelander has done for Aang to understand how serious the situation is, especially once Becca becomes part of the story.

Aang still wouldn’t agree to kill him. That would probably infuriate Butcher more than anything else. Aang has already faced someone who spent years conquering other nations and still refused to take his life. From Aang’s perspective, deciding that someone is too evil to leave alive is a line he’s already chosen not to cross.

Butcher would argue that this world doesn’t give people the luxury of making that choice. That becomes the heart of their relationship. Aang thinks Butcher has let pain convince him that violence is the only thing people like Homelander understand. Butcher thinks Aang’s beliefs only work because he hasn’t lived in this world long enough to see what happens when someone like Homelander is allowed to keep breathing.

Neither of them would change their mind after one conversation. They would still work together, Aang needs information about Vought, and The Boys have more of it than almost anyone outside the company. The Boys need someone powerful enough to stand in front of a Supe without immediately dying, and Aang can do that without Compound V.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: That cooperation would give them access to things they’ve never had before. Aang can reach rooftops, ledges, and other positions The Boys can’t access easily, letting him get physically close enough to overhear conversations without approaching through guarded entrances. He can also escape without needing a car or a safe route through the streets. Earthbending lets him create entrances without explosives, while airbending gives the group a way out when an operation collapses.

More importantly, he refuses to let their missions turn into executions. That means every operation starts changing. The Boys now have someone with enough power to stop Supes without automatically killing them, and Aang has people showing him exactly how deep Vought’s corruption goes.

Eventually, that combination would lead him to Compound V. And once Aang learns that these “heroes” weren’t born as some natural part of this world, but were deliberately created and controlled by Vought, he’d stop treating the company as something that could be fixed from the inside.

Up to this point, he could still tell himself that the problem was mostly about corrupt people abusing powers they already had. Compound V changes that. Vought has been creating Supes on purpose, giving children abilities before they could understand what that meant, and then building an entire industry around controlling what those people became.

Aang would see that as more than corruption. To him, power is supposed to come with responsibility because of what someone chooses to do with it. Vought has turned that process into a business model. They create the power first, shape the person around it, and then protect the result as long as it remains useful.

That would make him much less patient with the idea that the company can simply be exposed through one scandal. The Boys would want to use the Compound V evidence aggressively. Butcher would push for anything that tears Vought down quickly, even if that means threatening people inside the company or using information without worrying about who gets caught in the fallout.

Aang would still support exposing them, but he’d want the focus on the people being exploited by the system. That would naturally pull him toward Starlight. By this point, she’d already be questioning Vought herself, and Aang would see that as proof of something Butcher keeps refusing to accept. Being a Supe doesn’t automatically make someone part of the problem. Some of them were manipulated too.

Butcher would argue that this distinction stops mattering when those same people keep working for Vought but Aang wouldn’t agree. That disagreement would become more important once they start looking at the other members of The Seven individually. A-Train has done terrible things, but he’s also trapped by his addiction and fear of losing his position. The Deep is selfish and cruel, but he’s still someone Vought knows how to exploit. Starlight is actively trying to resist the system from inside it.

Homelander is different. The more Aang learns about how he was raised, the more he’d understand why Homelander became the person he is. Being raised in a lab, treated as a product, and denied any normal emotional development explains a lot. Aang would still believe Homelander can make choices.
And every time Homelander chooses fear and control anyway, Aang would become less willing to simply wait for him to change on his own.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Once Aang knows what Vought is doing, he stops being someone the company can manage with invitations and good publicity.
At first, his interference would be difficult for them to frame as an attack.

He’d show up where Supes were being reckless and stop civilians from getting hurt. He’d help people leave areas Vought wanted locked down. If security tried to block him from reaching someone being held against their will, earthbending could open another route without Aang having to injure anyone.

Vought would eventually try a different approach. They’d start presenting him as dangerous. The easiest angle would be that nobody knows where he came from, his powers don’t come from Compound V, and he refuses to submit to any recognized authority. Vought could push the idea that Aang is an uncontrolled enhanced threat who happens to look harmless.

That changes the first time Homelander tries to intimidate him directly. Aang isn’t fearless, but fear doesn’t work on him the way Homelander expects. He spent most of his childhood being hunted by the Fire Nation, faced Azula, fought Ozai during Sozin’s Comet, and carried the responsibility of ending a hundred-year war before he was old enough to drive in this world.

Homelander standing too close and making threats would still register as dangerous. It just wouldn’t make Aang submit. That would get under Homelander’s skin quickly. Aang also wouldn’t challenge him in the way Butcher would. He wouldn’t insult him just to provoke a reaction or try to prove he’s stronger. He’d speak to him like someone making choices he’s responsible for.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Homelander’s first real attack on Aang probably wouldn’t be an attempt to kill him. If Aang keeps interfering with Vought and refuses to show fear, Homelander would eventually decide to remind him who the strongest person in this world is. He might start with a sudden rush, a shove hard enough to launch Aang across a room, or heat vision aimed close enough to force a reaction.

That gives Aang his first proper understanding of how dangerous Homelander is. Airbending would be his best defense against the initial physical pressure. Aang is extremely mobile and can change direction quickly, but Homelander’s flight means he isn’t limited to attacking from the ground. Aang would need to keep moving rather than treating the fight like one of his usual bending duels.

Earthbending also becomes useful almost immediately. Aang can raise barriers between them, break Homelander’s line of sight, or reshape the ground to create distance. Those defenses probably won’t hold forever against someone with Homelander’s strength, but they force him to keep changing his approach instead of simply flying straight through Aang.

Heat vision is the bigger problem. Aang can redirect fire because he understands firebending, but Homelander’s beams aren’t fire in the normal sense. He wouldn’t be able to casually catch them and send them back. He’d need to evade, use earth for cover, or move the attack away from civilians by changing his own position.

Water gives him another defensive option if enough is available, but even then, Aang’s goal wouldn’t be overpowering Homelander. It would be controlling the fight without letting it turn into something lethal and Homelander would realize that quickly.

Aang keeps escaping attacks that should’ve ended the encounter, but he also keeps refusing to hit back with anything that looks designed to kill him. That makes Homelander even more aggressive. He’d interpret restraint as weakness right up until Aang starts using stronger combinations. Air can knock him off course. Earth can pin or trap him for short periods. Water can restrain limbs or freeze around him if Aang has enough of it nearby. Firebending gives Aang another way to create space without relying on the same defensive pattern.

None of these techniques guarantees a win. Homelander is too strong and durable for Aang to assume one good hit settles anything. But the fight proves something Vought can’t easily hide anymore. Homelander can’t casually put Aang down. Once footage of that starts spreading, Aang becomes a threat to him in a different way. People have spent years believing Homelander is untouchable. Now there’s someone who can stand in front of him, refuse to be afraid, and walk away.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: So they’d try to control the next confrontation. The Seven wouldn’t all approach Aang the same way. Starlight would resist going after him if she has any choice, while someone like The Deep would follow orders without having a serious plan for what happens once the fight starts. Black Noir would be much more dangerous because he wouldn’t waste time arguing or showing off.

Aang’s advantage against a group is that bending already trains him to manage multiple directions at once. Airbending keeps him mobile enough that surrounding him becomes difficult. Earth gives him control over the battlefield, letting him split opponents apart with walls or force them onto different levels. If water is nearby, he can restrain one person while dealing with someone else.

Black Noir would require more attention. He’s fast, quiet, and willing to attack from angles Aang can’t always see. Aang would have to stay in constant motion and use wide defensive bursts of air to disrupt attacks across the space around him rather than trying to detect exactly where Noir is coming from. Noir’s experience would still make him difficult to track in a crowded environment.

A-Train creates a different problem because he can cross distance much faster than Aang normally moves on foot. The safest answer is not trying to chase him. Aang could stay airborne, remove clean running paths with earthbending, and use wide air currents instead of trying to hit one exact point. A-Train’s speed is terrifying when he has room to build it, but a battlefield that keeps changing underneath him becomes much harder to navigate.

If Homelander joins the fight, everything shifts. Aang can handle several members of The Seven because most of them have weaknesses he can exploit without seriously injuring them. Homelander is the one person who can keep breaking through whatever Aang creates and force him to spend more energy just staying ahead.

The moment Aang’s eyes and tattoos begin to glow, the balance of the fight changes immediately. And Homelander would finally realize that everything he’d seen from Aang so far had been the restrained version.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: The Avatar State changes the fight because Aang stops having to deal with Homelander using one element at a time. Air, earth, water, and fire can all be used together, and Aang gains access to the experience of the Avatars who came before him. That gives him much better control over the battlefield than Homelander has ever had to deal with.

Homelander would still have the physical advantage. If he gets through Aang’s defenses and lands a clean hit, Aang can be seriously hurt. The Avatar State doesn’t make his body as durable as a Supe’s. It makes him much harder to reach. Aang can keep himself airborne while moving enormous amounts of earth, create layers of stone between himself and Homelander, and use water to attack or restrain from directions Homelander isn’t watching. He can also keep changing the ground underneath everyone which makes it much harder for The Seven to support Homelander while the fight is happening.

Aang would also start using the environment against him rather than trying to hurt him directly. He could bury Homelander under enormous amounts of earth, compress stone around his limbs, or repeatedly knock him off course with powerful air currents. None of those attacks needs to kill him. They only need to keep him from reaching civilians. Homelander would become more frustrated every time Aang refuses to turn the fight into a straight brawl.

Aang has spent years dealing with opponents whose anger made them easier to read. Eventually, Homelander would make the mistake of committing too heavily. Aang could trap him in earth from several directions at once, use water to reinforce the restraint if enough is available, and keep constant air pressure on him so he can’t simply build momentum and fly out immediately.

That brings him back to the solution he used against Ozai. Energybending. If Aang can physically restrain Homelander long enough to make the necessary contact, he could attempt to remove his ability to use his powers rather than kill him. But this would be an experiment, not a solution Aang knows will work. Homelander’s abilities come from Compound V instead of bending, and Aang has never used energybending to remove chemically created superpowers. He used it to take away Ozai’s bending by directly manipulating the energy within him, so whether the same technique can affect Homelander at all would remain completely uncertain.

If it works, it gives Aang an outcome almost nobody in this universe has considered: Homelander survives but loses access to the powers that made him untouchable. If it fails, Aang’s real option is still containment, keeping Homelander restrained long enough to stop the immediate threat and expose what he is in front of everyone.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: Homelander losing publicly would make the Compound V evidence much harder for Vought to contain. The Boys can expose how Vought created and controlled its heroes, while footage of the most powerful Supe in the world losing control against a teenager who refuses to kill him tears apart the heroic image Vought built around its most valuable asset. Together, those revelations make the entire system much harder to defend.

The public would also have proof that someone with extraordinary power can exist outside Vought without becoming what Vought created. That might be Aang’s biggest effect on the world. He becomes living evidence against both sides of the argument controlling the story. Vought says powerful people need Vought to guide them. Butcher says powerful people eventually become monsters.

Butcher would see the situation as a chance to finish the job, and Aang would see a group of people who were often given powers before they were old enough to understand them and then raised inside a system that rewarded the worst parts of their behavior. Some of them still deserve to be stopped but that doesn’t mean they all deserve to die.

Hughie would probably understand Aang’s position much more easily than Butcher does, and Starlight would become the clearest example of why it matters. She has powers, but she also chose to stand against Vought when she understood what it was doing. Aang would want more Supes to have that chance. That doesn’t mean his philosophy survives untouched. This world would test it constantly. He would meet people who waste every opportunity to change, people who use kindness as something to exploit, and people like Butcher who can make violence sound reasonable because the people they’re fighting really are dangerous.

Aang wouldn’t leave those experiences exactly the same person who arrived. He’d become less trusting. He’d ask harder questions before believing someone’s public image and understand that saving someone from becoming worse doesn’t always mean they’ll become good.

What he wouldn’t lose is the line he refused to cross with Ozai. Power doesn’t give him the right to decide who deserves to live. That belief would probably frustrate almost everyone around him at some point, but it’s also the reason Aang can exist in this world without becoming another version of Homelander.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: Vought built heroes around fame and control. Butcher built his entire worldview around expecting Supes to eventually become monsters. Aang would force both of them to deal with someone who has more than enough power to dominate people and still refuses to use it that way, Homelander would probably be the hardest test of that belief.
But if Aang can stop him without becoming like him, then this world proves how difficult it actually is to keep that philosophy.

scripts.title: What If Anakin Skywalker Was A Viltrumite

sections.name: INTRO
paras: What if the Jedi found Anakin Skywalker on Tatooine and eventually realized the Chosen One wasn’t even human? His connection to the Force would still be extraordinary, but as he grows older, the Jedi would discover that his body is developing abilities no training can explain.

That means Anakin’s abilities would grow alongside everything Obi-Wan is already trying to teach him. The more powerful he becomes, the harder it would be for the Council to treat him like any other Jedi, especially once the Clone Wars begin and Anakin starts doing things almost nobody else can survive.

By the time Palpatine makes his move, he’d be trying to turn someone far more dangerous than the Anakin we know. And if that version of Anakin still falls, Mustafar may never create Darth Vader at all.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: Anakin’s life would still start on Tatooine with Shmi, and she would still tell Qui-Gon that there was no father. In this scenario, the Viltrumite biology originates directly in Anakin as part of the crossover premise rather than coming from Shmi. His fatherless conception still happens through the Force, but the body it produces has Viltrumite biology alongside the same extraordinary Force potential. Shmi remains biologically human, so her own life on Tatooine does not have to change before Anakin is born.

Qui-Gon would still meet Anakin during The Phantom Menace in 32 BBY and become interested because of the Force. His reactions, instincts, and midi-chlorian count would still point toward something the Jedi have never seen before. Anakin also looks completely human, so Qui-Gon would have no reason to start thinking about another species at first.

The questions would start once Anakin reaches Coruscant and the Jedi actually examine him. His blood and tissue wouldn't match a normal human body as closely as they should. His muscles would be denser, his body would repair damage unusually fast, and some of his cells would behave in ways the healers can’t explain. The midi-chlorian count is already strange enough, but now the Council would know there is something unusual about his body too.

The Jedi Archives probably wouldn't give them a perfect answer. The healers could document that Anakin is physiologically different from a normal human, but without any established record of Viltrumites in the galaxy, they would have no reliable species name to attach to what they are seeing. For years, the Jedi would only know that Anakin's body has abilities and limits they do not fully understand.

After Qui-Gon dies, Obi-Wan would have to figure most of this out while training him. Anakin would still be very young, and some of the bigger Viltrumite abilities probably haven’t appeared yet. He might not be able to fly, but his strength and healing would already make normal training harder to manage. Falling during an exercise barely teaches him anything if he can get back up with no real injury, and sparring becomes dangerous once he starts hitting harder than another Padawan expects.

Obi-Wan would have to spend a lot of time teaching Anakin to hold back. That would be easy enough when Anakin is young, but it becomes harder once he starts realizing just how much stronger he is than the people training beside him.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: As Anakin gets older and spends years pushing himself through Jedi training, the Viltrumite side of him would become much more obvious. His strength and durability keep developing as his body is tested, injuries heal faster than a human's, and it takes more force to seriously hurt him. Flight could appear slowly. At first, Obi-Wan might notice that Anakin stays in the air longer than he should during jumps, and eventually Anakin realizes he can keep himself up without using the Force at all.

That would cause problems during training because most Jedi exercises are built around normal bodies. Anakin could eventually fly through sections where other Padawans have to climb or use Force jumps, and endurance training would stop wearing him down the same way. Obi-Wan would still make him do the exercises because the point is discipline, but Anakin would start wondering why he is being trained around limits he doesn’t have.

Lightsaber practice would be even more important. Anakin couldn’t simply swing as hard as he wants because another student could get hurt even if they block correctly. Obi-Wan would make him focus on control and accuracy instead, teaching him to know exactly how much strength he is using.
