Peter's life slowly settled into its new routine. He worked, paid his bills when he could, kept improving his equipment and continued learning what his evolving abilities could do. He didn’t tell everyone about the Enigma Force, and there were parts of the experience he wasn’t sure he could explain even if he tried. He had seen things that most people would never know existed, and he had learned that the universe was far larger and more complicated than he had imagined.
Peter was still Peter, though.

One night, he sat on a rooftop overlooking Manhattan and thought about the time he’d spent as Captain Universe. The memory no longer felt like something that had happened to another person. He remembered the power, the awareness and the responsibility that came with it, but he also remembered how quickly that power had started pulling him away from the life he actually wanted.

Peter stood up and pulled his mask over his face. His Spider-Sense picked up trouble somewhere below, and he moved toward the edge of the building. The city stretched out in front of him, full of people who had no idea what Peter had experienced beyond their world.
That was fine with him.
He jumped.
The web caught the next building, and Peter swung into the night.

Somewhere far beyond Earth, the Enigma Force continued moving through the universe, searching for its next host and the next crisis that required a champion. Peter didn’t know when their paths would cross again.
If they ever did, he would be ready.
For now, Peter Parker was exactly where he wanted to be.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: Peter Parker had briefly held enough power to protect worlds, but he chose not to let that power define him. The Uni-Power showed him what he was capable of, but it also reminded him why he became Spider-Man in the first place.
He didn’t need cosmic power to be a hero. He just needed to keep showing up for the people who needed him.
Cosmic Spider-Man could protect worlds.
Peter Parker chose to protect his city.
And no matter how powerful he became, he was Spider-Man first.

scripts.title: What If Darth Vader Had The Infinity Gauntlet

sections.name: INTRO
paras: Darth Vader getting the Infinity Gauntlet would give him access to the one thing he’s spent years believing he can never have again…Padmé. With the Time, Reality, and Soul Stones in his hand, he could finally try to reach back into the moment that destroyed Anakin Skywalker and change what happened.

The problem is that Vader has spent years turning grief into anger, and the Gauntlet gives that anger enough power to reshape almost anything around him. Palpatine would realize very quickly that his apprentice now has access to something far beyond the Force, while Vader would have to decide whether he still wants to serve the Empire once he can rewrite the life that led him there.

For this scenario, the Gauntlet follows the MCU Stones rather than the effectively unrestricted comic version. Vader can build outward from abilities those Stones have demonstrated, but anything beyond those demonstrated uses has to be treated as an experiment rather than an automatic function. His damaged body and life-support systems could already be strained by ordinary Stone use, while a massive reality-scale use of all six would expose him to the kind of catastrophic energy that permanently injured Hulk and badly damaged Thanos.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: Vader would first treat the Gauntlet like any other unknown weapon the Empire recovered from somewhere it shouldn’t exist. He’d want it isolated, scanned, and taken apart before Palpatine ever heard about it, especially once the technicians report that none of the six objects inside behave like normal energy sources. The readings would be inconsistent, the materials wouldn’t match anything in Imperial databases, and every attempt to remove one of the Stones with ordinary tools could produce effects nobody in the room understands.

Vader would feel something from it before he fully understands what he’s looking at. The Stones aren’t part of the Force, but the amount of power inside them would be impossible to ignore once he gets close. The Space Stone could distort the room around it, the Mind Stone might affect technicians standing nearby, and the Reality Stone could create brief changes that disappear as quickly as they form. Vader would probably assume the device came from some ancient civilization that learned to manipulate parts of existence in ways even the Jedi never understood.

He’d put the Gauntlet on only after exhausting the safer ways of studying it. The first contact would be violent because his body is already badly damaged and dependent on cybernetics, so having all 6 Stones connected to him at once would send energy through systems that were never built to handle anything like it. His suit could overload in places, internal components might burn out, and Vader would have to use the Force just to keep himself upright while the Gauntlet settles onto his arm.

Once he survives that first moment, he’d begin testing individual Stones instead of assuming he understands everything their domains might allow. The Power Stone would be the easiest to understand because its purpose becomes obvious as soon as he channels even a small amount of it into something nearby. Vader already knows what overwhelming destructive force feels like, so he’d immediately recognize that this is far beyond any weapon he normally carries. From there, any use that goes beyond what the MCU Stones have clearly demonstrated would have to be discovered experimentally.

The Space Stone would interest him more because it changes what movement means entirely. Vader could create a portal across a room first, then farther away, and eventually across huge distances once he understands the controls. That would make Imperial travel look primitive by comparison because entire fleets depend on hyperspace while Vader can now cross space directly from one point to another.

The Mind Stone would be where the situation starts becoming personal. Vader already uses the Force to sense emotions and influence weaker minds, so realizing that one of the Stones can reach directly into thought would make him wonder what else the Gauntlet can access. If thoughts can be altered, then memory might be reachable too, and once memory becomes part of the equation, Padmé would be impossible for him to ignore.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: The first real use of the Stones would revolve around Padmé, and he’d spend time testing exactly what the Time Stone can do before risking anything permanent.

He could begin by reversing small events in front of him, breaking an object and restoring it, damaging part of his armor and watching the damage disappear, or moving something across a room and rewinding it back into place. Once he sees that the Stone can genuinely reverse physical events instead of just creating illusions, the possibility of Mustafar becomes real.

Vader would probably try reaching back toward the moment before Padmé dies. He knows roughly when it happened, where she was, and what led to it, but the MCU Time Stone has not established that its user can simply select a decades-old event, enter it, and rewrite history. Vader would first test whether the Stone can reach that far into the past at all. If he manages to produce even a stable temporal view or reconstruction of Mustafar - Padmé alive again, Obi-Wan nearby, and his younger self standing in the middle of the choices that ruined everything - he would immediately start asking whether observation can become intervention.

The first attempt would likely be observational because Vader would need to understand what happens when he pushes the Stone that far. Seeing the past play out would be brutal because he’d have to watch himself accuse Padmé, attack her, fight Obi-Wan, and end up on the lava bank knowing exactly what comes next.

That experience would probably make him more aggressive with the Stone. He could attempt the much more extreme step of interfering with the event itself, trying to stop his younger self before he chokes Padmé or move her away from Mustafar before the confrontation happens. There is no guarantee the MCU Time Stone can alter a remote event from decades earlier this way, and Vader would be testing the limit rather than using an established function. If it does work, changing one moment creates consequences he can’t fully predict. If Padmé survives but Anakin still falls to the dark side, then the Empire may still rise. If he prevents the duel with Obi-Wan, then Anakin never receives the injuries that create Vader, which raises the question of what happens to the version of Vader using the Gauntlet in the first place.

The Reality Stone would give him another path. Instead of rewinding history, Vader could try creating a version of Padmé in the present. He could shape reality around his memories of her face, voice, and appearance, then use the Mind Stone to fill in everything he remembers about how she thought.

The person in front of him could look exactly like Padmé and say things he recognizes, but Vader would know he created her from memory. Every answer she gives would make him wonder whether it comes from Padmé or from whatever he expected her to say. That uncertainty would make the Soul Stone the next thing he focuses on, because if souls are real and one of the Stones can interact with them directly, then he finally has a way to ask whether Padmé still exists somewhere beyond memory.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: The Soul Stone would be the hardest for Vader to understand because it doesn’t behave like anything he has used through the Force. He already knows that people can remain connected to the living after death through Force spirits, but Padmé was never trained as a Jedi and there’s no reason for him to expect her to appear the same way Obi-Wan or Yoda eventually could. The MCU Soul Stone also has not demonstrated that it can simply locate and retrieve any dead person, so Vader would be probing an unknown limit rather than using a known resurrection ability.

He’d start by using the Stone around places connected to her. Naboo would probably be the first location because it still holds parts of her life that existed before Anakin destroyed everything between them. Vader could stand in the places where they lived together and use the Soul Stone while focusing on her presence, trying to separate his own memories from whatever the Stone is actually showing him.

It might be a brief image, a feeling that clearly isn’t coming from him, or a direct glimpse of Padmé as she was before her death. Vader would recognize enough to believe the Soul Stone is reaching something real, and that would make him push far harder than he did during the earlier tests.

If the Soul Stone gives Vader enough evidence to believe something of Padmé still exists, he could attempt something none of the MCU Stones have demonstrated as a reliable resurrection method. He could use Reality to reconstruct a physical body, Soul to try to reconnect whatever he has found to that body, and Time to restore or stabilize its physical condition. Vader would not know whether the result would genuinely be Padmé, a recreation built from his memories and the Stones, or nothing at all. For this scenario, the experiment succeeds: the woman who wakes up genuinely is Padmé. The attempt would still be one of the most complicated uses Vader makes of the Gauntlet, and his already damaged cybernetics and life-support systems could begin failing under the strain.

His cybernetics could start failing while he does it. The Gauntlet might burn through part of his arm, shut down sections of his life support system, and force Vader to keep himself alive with the Force while he finishes the process. He’d still continue because this is the one outcome he’s willing to destroy himself for.

If Padmé actually comes back, the moment would be very different from what Vader imagined during all those years without her. She’d wake up in a galaxy ruled by the Empire, see Anakin standing in front of her as Darth Vader, and quickly realize that everything she feared on Mustafar happened anyway.

Vader would want her to understand that he can fix it now. He has control over time, reality, and space, and he could remove Palpatine, end the Empire, or reshape the galaxy if that’s what it takes to keep her. Padmé would see the same problem she saw before her death, except now Anakin has access to power far beyond anything he had when he fell.

Vader could change her surroundings, heal injuries, and even alter memories if he chose to use the Mind Stone that way, but doing that would destroy the reason he brought her back. If he has to rewrite Padmé until she accepts him, then the person he saved is no longer the person he wanted.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Palpatine would notice the change before Vader ever tells him about the Gauntlet. Vader would disappear from Imperial operations without explanation, stop reporting certain discoveries, and begin moving around the galaxy in ways that don’t match normal hyperspace travel. The Emperor would also feel a shift in Vader himself because the old balance between them depended on Vader needing him.

Palpatine could summon him and immediately realize something is wrong when Vader arrives wearing an artifact he doesn’t recognize but can feel radiating power. He’d try to understand it through the Force first, then through whatever Imperial research he can gather afterward. The more he learns, the more obvious the danger becomes because a weapon that manipulates space, time, minds, souls, and reality makes the Sith hierarchy almost meaningless.

Palpatine would probably try manipulating Vader instead of attacking immediately. He could remind him that unlimited power always carries a cost, question whether the Gauntlet is truly under his control, and offer to help study it. Vader would know what that offer means because Palpatine has spent his entire life turning other people’s power into something he can control.

Palpatine’s usual advantage is that Vader is powerful enough to be useful but damaged enough to remain beneath him. The Gauntlet removes that calculation. Vader could use the Space Stone to control Palpatine’s position, attempt to overwhelm his ability to act through the Mind Stone, or simply change the room around him with Reality before Palpatine has time to turn the confrontation into a normal Sith duel. The Mind Stone would give Vader a powerful mental weapon, but Palpatine’s own Force abilities and discipline mean that kind of override would not be automatic.

The Force would still matter during that confrontation because Palpatine is one of the strongest Sith Lords in Star Wars, and he’d feel Vader’s intent before the attack begins. He could respond with lightning, telekinesis, or an attempt to rip the Gauntlet off his arm, but Vader has all six Stones and only needs one clean use to control the fight.

Vader would probably avoid killing him immediately because Palpatine knows things he still wants. He knows more about Sith history, the nature of death, and Anakin’s fall than almost anyone alive, and Vader could force answers out of him before deciding what comes next.

The Mind Stone could still make the interrogation far more dangerous for Palpatine. Vader could attempt to push through his mental defenses and force out information connected to Padmé, the prophecy, or the promises he made about defeating death. Palpatine might resist or obscure parts of what Vader is looking for, but a successful breach could expose how much of his manipulation was built around telling Anakin exactly what he needed to hear.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: With Palpatine no longer controlling him, Vader would have to decide what happens to the Empire. He could take the throne almost immediately because there’s nobody in the Imperial military capable of stopping someone with the completed Gauntlet. Any admiral who refuses him can have their fleet stranded somewhere else through the Space Stone, and entire rebellions inside the chain of command could be ended before they start.

Vader could start dismantling parts of the Empire because he thinks that will prove he has changed. He might order executions stopped, pull troops out of occupied worlds, and remove officials who built their power through Palpatine’s cruelty. With the Gauntlet, those decisions can happen immediately because nobody can threaten him militarily.

Padmé would still have serious problems with the way he does it. If Vader replaces Palpatine and keeps absolute control over the galaxy, then changing a few policies doesn’t bring back the Republic she fought for. She’d push him toward restoring institutions instead of ruling through fear, and Vader would struggle with that because control has become the way he handles almost every problem.

Luke would become another major reason for him to change course. Once Vader learns his son is alive, the Space Stone means reaching him is much easier once Vader knows where to go. He could use the Mind Stone on captured Rebels or other people with relevant knowledge to try to extract information about Luke’s movements even if the Rebellion tries to hide him, then use the Space Stone to cross the distance without needing fleets or trackers. Vader would probably go alone because he’d want the meeting to be personal.

Luke meeting a Vader who has already brought Padmé back and removed Palpatine would be completely different from the original story. He’d still know what his father did, and none of those crimes disappear just because Vader now has the power to undo some of their consequences. Luke would see someone trying to rebuild the family he lost while still holding enough power to dominate the entire galaxy.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Once Luke and Padmé are both back in his life, Vader would eventually stop thinking in terms of fixing individual consequences and start looking at the moment where everything went wrong. He knows Palpatine manipulated him for years, knows Mace Windu’s confrontation changed the course of his life, and knows what happened after he chose to intervene. If his earlier Time Stone experiments suggested that a remote past event can be reached at all, he would be tempted to push that uncertain ability much farther and try to reach the decision before Anakin becomes Darth Vader.

He’d probably begin by watching it again, the same way he did with Mustafar. Seeing himself enter Palpatine’s office and attack Mace would hit differently now because Vader has enough distance to understand how much fear controlled him in that moment. He could also watch Palpatine shift between weakness and aggression, which would make it easier to see how carefully the situation was designed to corner him.

The obvious solution would be stopping his younger self before he attacks Mace, but Vader would know by now that changing history at that scale can create consequences he can’t control. Padmé survives if Palpatine falls there, Order 66 is not given, Luke and Leia grow up under completely different circumstances, and the version of Vader holding the Gauntlet may never exist at all. He’d still be tempted because that timeline gives Anakin almost everything he wanted without decades of suffering.

That temptation would become one of the hardest choices he faces. Vader has spent most of his life believing he’d sacrifice anything to get Padmé back, and now he actually has the power to make a version of history where she never dies. The problem is that doing it could erase the lives Luke and Leia have already lived, along with every relationship and choice that came from the galaxy they know.

Luke would almost certainly oppose changing the entire timeline if he understands what Vader is considering. He’d see the danger in deciding that one person has the right to erase decades of history because he regrets his own decisions, even if the new timeline looks better from Vader’s perspective. Padmé would probably feel the same way because she spent her life fighting against people who believed they had the right to reshape everyone else’s future.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: The Rebellion would have no reason to trust Vader just because Palpatine is gone. From their perspective, the Emperor has disappeared and Darth Vader now controls the most powerful weapon anyone in the galaxy has ever seen. Even if Imperial occupations begin ending, nobody knows whether Vader is dismantling the Empire or simply rebuilding it around himself.

Leia would be especially difficult for him to deal with. Once Vader learns she is his daughter, he’d want the same connection he wants with Luke, but Leia’s entire life has been shaped by resisting the Empire. She watched Alderaan get destroyed, fought Imperial forces for years, and knows Vader as one of the people responsible for enforcing Palpatine’s rule. Learning that he is her father wouldn’t suddenly undo any of that.

The Gauntlet also makes every conversation with him uncomfortable because everyone knows he could force the outcome if he wanted. The Mind Stone could change memories or emotions, the Reality Stone could create whatever surroundings he wants, and the Time Stone could erase mistakes before anyone else remembers them. Padmé, Luke, and Leia would need to know that Vader is deliberately choosing not to use those powers on them before any real trust can begin.

The Rebellion could eventually agree to negotiations once Vader begins transferring real authority away from the Imperial military. He could release political prisoners, open systems that were held under military rule, and allow surviving senators to rebuild a civilian government. Those choices would show more change than any speech because they reduce his own power instead of expanding it.

There would still be Imperial loyalists who refuse to accept any of it. Some would see Vader as a traitor for removing Palpatine, while others would want the Gauntlet for themselves. That creates another test because Vader could erase every rebellion against him almost instantly, but doing that would make him exactly the kind of ruler Padmé is afraid he could become.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: The physical cost of the Gauntlet would become harder to ignore the more aggressively Vader pushes it. His body is already barely functional without the suit, so even ordinary Stone use can overload cybernetics or life-support systems that were never designed for this energy. The danger rises with the scale of the effect rather than following a simple Stone-count formula: combining Stones for a precise or enormous alteration could stress him much more severely, while a full six-Stone, reality-scale action risks the catastrophic feedback seen with Hulk and Thanos. The suit could compensate temporarily, but repeated major uses could leave Vader needing extensive repairs just to keep breathing normally.

The Force would help him survive longer because Vader is already extremely good at functioning through pain. He could use it to keep himself conscious, control his breathing when systems fail, and continue moving after injuries that would stop most people. That helps him endure the Gauntlet, but it doesn’t make the physical damage disappear.

Padmé would probably be the first person who tells him to stop using it. From her perspective, she has already watched Anakin destroy himself once trying to prevent her death, and now he is doing something similar again by using the Gauntlet every time he sees a problem he thinks only he can fix.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: The final turning point would come when Vader faces a crisis large enough that using all six Stones together looks like the easiest answer. Imperial loyalists could launch coordinated attacks across several systems, or remnants of the old regime could threaten Padmé, Luke, and Leia at the same time. Vader would know he could end the whole conflict in seconds if he uses the Gauntlet at full strength.

That would also be the point where he’s closest to becoming worse than Palpatine. Palpatine needed armies, fear, bureaucracy, and decades of manipulation to control the galaxy. Vader could achieve the same result with a thought if he decides that nobody else gets a say in what the galaxy becomes. The fact that he believes he’s doing it to protect his family would make the choice even more dangerous because that’s the same kind of justification that started his fall in the first place.

Luke and Padmé would both understand what’s happening before Vader fully admits it to himself. They wouldn’t need to defeat him physically because there is no realistic way to overpower a fully prepared Vader holding all 6 Stones. Their only chance would be getting him to recognize that using the Gauntlet to force peace means repeating the same mistake on a much larger scale.

This time, he could choose differently. Vader could use the Stones one final time to end the immediate threat without rewriting everyone involved. He might destroy the weapons being used against civilians, move fleets away from populated systems, or contain the people responsible long enough for the new government to arrest them. Because the action is broad and demanding, it could still badly overload his already compromised body and suit, but he would leave the political outcome to everyone else instead of deciding it himself.

Afterward, he’d remove the Gauntlet. Keeping the Stones anywhere accessible would always leave the temptation there, so before giving them up Vader could make one final combined command that scatters all six to separate destinations determined by the Gauntlet rather than consciously chosen or revealed to him. Once the Stones are gone, Vader would not know where they were sent, leaving the empty Gauntlet useless and preventing him from simply using remembered coordinates to retrieve them later. For Anakin, that would probably be the closest thing to actually fixing his greatest mistake. Padmé is alive, Luke and Leia know who he is, Palpatine is gone, and the Empire is being dismantled, but none of those outcomes came from forcing the people around him to become what he wanted.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: Darth Vader with the Infinity Gauntlet would have enough power to defeat Palpatine, reshape the Empire, and even bring Padmé back, but those things would only solve the easiest part of his problem. Vader’s real struggle has always been what he does when he’s terrified of losing someone, and the Gauntlet gives him a way to answer that fear with extraordinary control over reality around him.

He could use the Stones to rewrite Revenge of the Sith, change people’s memories, or build a reality where his family never leaves him. The harder choice would be letting Padmé, Luke, and Leia decide what they want even when those choices hurt him.

If he reaches that point, the Gauntlet could finally give Anakin a chance to repair some of the damage he caused without becoming another Emperor. If he doesn’t, Palpatine’s Empire would eventually look small compared to what Vader could build with all 6 Stones in his hand.

scripts.title: What If Deadpool Was In FNAF

sections.name: INTRO
paras: Deadpool taking the night shift at Freddy Fazbear’s Pizza would sound like an easy paycheck until the animatronics start moving after midnight. The first time Bonnie or Chica gets into the office, Wade would probably assume someone built the world’s most committed haunted mascot until one of them actually attacks him and leaves injuries that would kill a normal security guard. Regeneration means Wade can actually survive mistakes that would kill a normal guard. Once Wade starts digging into the restaurant’s history, the missing children give him an actual reason to stay. He’d want to know why they ended up connected to the animatronics, who killed them, and whether that person is still around. That investigation would eventually lead him toward William Afton, who now has to deal with a security guard he can’t get rid of the same way he dealt with everyone else.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: Wade taking the security job at Freddy Fazbear’s Pizza would probably happen for the dumbest possible reason. The pay is terrible, the building looks half dead, and the guy explaining the night shift is clearly leaving out half the story, but Wade has taken worse jobs for less money. Once he hears that all he really has to do is sit in an office, watch cameras, and make it until morning, he’d assume the biggest problem is going to be boredom.

The restaurant sounds different once everything shuts down. Wade would hear motors moving somewhere out in the dining area, footsteps where nobody should be walking, and the occasional scrape of something heavy against the floor. At first, he’d probably assume the animatronics are running some kind of automatic routine, especially after hearing the recorded instructions about them moving around at night.

Wade would check the camera again, notice one of the mascots is gone, then start flipping between rooms to find it. Seeing Bonnie standing much closer to the office than before would probably make him laugh at first because the whole situation looks ridiculous from behind a security monitor. That reaction changes once Bonnie actually reaches the doorway.

A normal guard would panic and slam the door immediately. Wade would probably wait too long because he still doesn’t believe a giant rabbit mascot is about to attack him. The second Bonnie gets inside, Wade would learn exactly how wrong that assumption was.

The animatronic could grab him, slam him into the office wall, and do enough damage that anyone else would be dead before the clock reaches one in the morning. Wade would be torn up badly enough that Bonnie eventually leaves him there, probably assuming the threat is gone.
A few minutes later, Wade starts healing.

That would be the first moment where the night shift stops feeling like a normal bad job and becomes something he wants to understand. Bonnie didn’t come straight for him, used enough force to kill him, then left once it believed he was dead.

Wade would spend the rest of the night testing what he can without making himself too easy a target. He’d keep track of which cameras lose movement first, how often Bonnie changes rooms, and whether Chica follows the same route. Freddy would stay more patient, which makes him harder to read, while Foxy’s behavior would stand out because he isn’t moving through the restaurant the same way as the others.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: The second night would look less like survival and more like Wade deliberately poking at the system to see what happens.

He already knows the animatronics can hurt him, so the fear that controls a normal guard isn’t going to work the same way. That doesn’t mean he can ignore them, because being crushed, bitten, or stuffed inside a suit is still painful, and regeneration doesn’t make any of that pleasant. It just gives him more room to make mistakes and learn from them.

Wade would start with Bonnie and Chica because their movement is easier to follow. He could leave one door open longer than he should and watch which one reaches the office first, then compare that with what the cameras showed before the attack. If Bonnie tends to approach from one side and Chica from the other, Wade would learn their routes much faster than a normal guard who spends every night terrified of letting either one inside.

Foxy would be more dangerous because his movement is faster and less forgiving. The first time Wade gets distracted and lets Pirate Cove go unchecked for too long, Foxy could sprint straight toward the office before Wade understands what’s happening. He might barely get the door closed or fail completely and take another brutal attack.

Instead of constantly appearing in obvious places, Freddy could stay just outside the limits of what Wade expects and move whenever attention shifts somewhere else. Wade would notice that Freddy seems more aware of being watched, which makes him feel less like a machine running a loop and more like something making choices.
That would make Wade start talking to them.

Not because he expects a conversation, but because Wade talks when he’s uncomfortable and because he wants to see whether they react differently to certain things. He might use their names, mention the restaurant, or joke about whoever designed their night behavior.

Most of the time, nothing obvious happens. Then one of them reacts. Maybe Chica stops moving when Wade mentions children, or Bonnie stays in front of a camera longer when he talks about the old restaurant. The response could be subtle enough that Wade isn’t sure whether he imagined it, which would make him test the same idea again later.
By the end of the second or third night, he’d stop treating the animatronics like defective robots. Something about them is reacting to people and places in a way their programming doesn’t explain.
That would give Wade a reason to start looking into what happened at Freddy’s before he ever took the job.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Wade wouldn’t need long to find out that Freddy Fazbear’s Pizza has a history people don't like talking about.

Old articles, employee records, and anything left around the office would start filling in pieces of what happened years earlier. Children went missing, the restaurant was connected to the case, and whoever was responsible never got properly exposed in a way that explains what Wade is seeing now.
The missing children would immediately stand out once he compares that history with the animatronics’ behavior.

Bonnie, Chica, Freddy, and Foxy don’t just patrol the restaurant and attack anything that moves. They seem focused on adults inside the building, especially after hours, and Wade would start wondering whether they're mistaking him for someone else.

Instead of only tracking routes, Wade could start bringing old photos or newspaper clippings into the office and watching how the animatronics react when those images appear on camera. A photo of the restaurant from the time of the disappearances might get a stronger response than anything else.

He could also start checking parts of the building that night guards are clearly not supposed to care about. Storage rooms, old maintenance areas, and anything tied to earlier versions of Freddy’s would become more interesting than sitting in the office until six.
The first time Wade leaves the office and walks through the restaurant at night, the whole balance changes.

He’d be much easier to attack, but regeneration gives him a chance to survive long enough to keep moving. If Bonnie corners him in a hallway, Wade could take the hit, recover, and follow the animatronic afterward instead of retreating straight back to the office.

That could lead him somewhere important. An animatronic might linger near a back room or refuse to enter a certain area, giving Wade the first physical clue that parts of the restaurant carry more meaning than others. He’d start checking old employee access points and maintenance spaces for anything connected to the disappearances.

This is where William Afton begins entering the story, but ordinary articles and employee records wouldn’t be enough to identify him as the killer. Wade wouldn't know the full connection yet. He’d need to find concealed company material in restricted maintenance spaces, private records that were never part of the public story, or something the restaurant kept buried that ties William to the back rooms and the period when the children disappeared. That would give Wade a specific name worth investigating without making the old public record solve the mystery for him.

The joke stops being the night shift at this point. Wade can handle murderous animatronics because they can’t permanently kill him, but murdered children are different. Once he realizes the machines may be carrying whatever is left of those kids, he wants the person responsible.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: The next few nights would be where Wade gets enough evidence to stop wondering whether the animatronics are simply acting strangely.

He’d start watching for behavior that can’t be explained by programming or damaged hardware. Freddy might react to a name from an old article, Chica could become aggressive around something connected to one of the missing children, and Foxy might move differently when Wade enters an area tied to the old incidents.

Wade would also notice the smell. The restaurant already has a reputation for the animatronics being disgusting up close, and once Wade starts inspecting them more carefully, he’d realize there are signs that something was hidden inside these suits a long time ago.

That would be enough for Wade to form a strong theory that the missing children are somehow attached to the machines. He wouldn’t suddenly understand every detail about spirits, remnant, or how possession works in this universe, and he couldn’t prove literal possession from what he has seen. If children disappeared, the animatronics are behaving like they remember things, and the suits themselves show signs of what happened, the supernatural connection would be strong enough for Wade to keep investigating on that theory.

That realization would also explain why the animatronics keep attacking him. They don’t know who Wade is. From their perspective, he’s an adult security guard walking around Freddy’s after closing, and whoever hurt them likely wore a similar role or moved through the same building without being stopped. Wade’s face doesn’t matter much if whatever is inside the suits is reacting to fear, memory, and suspicion instead of carefully identifying every person it sees.

He’d probably try approaching them differently after that. Instead of baiting Bonnie into the office to see what happens, Wade could leave the doors open and stay still while talking about the missing children. That’s incredibly risky, but risk works differently for him.

If Bonnie attacks again, Wade could keep talking even while getting torn apart, which would probably be the strangest thing the spirit inside the animatronic has dealt with since dying. Eventually, one of them might hesitate. That hesitation would be enough for Wade to know he’s getting somewhere.

He’d start treating the animatronics less like enemies and more like victims who have no idea how to communicate what happened to them. They can still kill him, and he’d still have to defend himself when they attack, but the goal would shift toward understanding what they’re trying to lead him toward.

If Wade notices Freddy or the others reacting differently around information connected to the murders, he could add those moments to the pattern he’s building, but the responses would be inconsistent enough that he couldn’t treat them like answers. He’d have to compare several nights of behavior with physical evidence instead of relying on the animatronics to tell him what happened.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: By the time Wade starts looking specifically at William Afton, the investigation would move much faster because he already knows what kind of connection he’s trying to prove.

He’d compare the concealed material that first pointed toward William with the disappearances, the restaurant’s old staff, and any location the animatronics seem to react strongly to. The private evidence still wouldn’t prove murder on its own, but it would give Wade enough of a connection to decide William deserves a much closer look.

Breaking into places connected to William would be easy compared to surviving Freddy’s. Wade could search old properties, storage areas, workshops, or anything tied to the company without worrying much about normal security. If somebody tries to stop him, he can get through them without killing anyone and keep moving.
What he finds would start filling in the pieces the restaurant couldn't.

Old suit parts, tools, maintenance equipment, or records connected to the springlock suits would tell Wade that William knew Freddy’s technology far better than an ordinary employee should. Any evidence tying him to the back rooms or the missing children would move him from interesting suspect to the person Wade is preparing to confront.

Afton is used to hiding what he does behind the restaurant, the suits, and people’s inability to prove anything. Wade creates a different problem because hurting him doesn’t make the investigation disappear.

If William sends someone after him, Wade survives. If he tries setting up an accident, Wade gets back up. Even killing him directly only buys time. That would force William to learn what Wade actually is before making another move.

Wade would be doing the same thing from the other side. He knows William is connected to the murders now, but he still needs to understand how much of the supernatural side William understands and whether there are other victims he hasn’t found yet. Going straight after him without learning that could leave important parts of the case buried.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Once William realizes Wade is searching through old Freddy’s records and checking places tied to the disappearances, he’d start treating him like a real threat. A normal security guard could be scared off, blamed for something, or killed if they got too close, while Wade has already survived enough attacks that none of those options give William a clean solution. That would push him toward watching Wade instead, learning how often he leaves the restaurant, which locations he visits, and what parts of the old case seem to matter most to him.

William would probably test Wade before confronting him directly. He could feed him false information through old records or leave something in an abandoned property that points toward the wrong location, then see whether Wade follows it. Wade would notice if too many clues suddenly start appearing in places that feel convenient, especially after spending several nights learning that Freddy’s only gives him useful information in fragments. If one lead sends him somewhere empty while another old record quietly points back toward the same group of buildings William has already been connected to, Wade would start assuming someone knows he’s looking.

William would eventually realize Wade is using the animatronics’ abnormal behavior as part of his investigation, which makes the restaurant more dangerous for him than it used to be. William knows what he did there and has enough experience with the machines to suspect the murders are connected to the way they behave, but he doesn’t need a complete understanding of exactly what each child became. Keeping Wade around Freddy’s still gives him more chances to piece the story together. That could push William into sabotaging the night shift itself by cutting power earlier, disabling cameras, or changing access to parts of the building so Wade has fewer ways to track what the animatronics are doing. Wade would probably notice the changes after one night goes wrong in a way that doesn’t match the others. A camera that always worked could suddenly die, a door could fail at exactly the worst moment, or a maintenance route that was open before could be locked from the other side. After enough nights studying the building, Wade would know which failures feel normal and which ones look deliberate, and that would tell him William is much closer to the restaurant than the old records suggested.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Wade's best lead would probably come from one of the areas William keeps trying to steer him away from. If the same storage room, maintenance hallway, or old section of the building keeps disappearing from records while security around it gets tighter, Wade would eventually stop treating that as coincidence and start checking it directly. Getting inside would be easier for him than it would be for almost anyone else because a locked door only slows him down, and if there’s a trap waiting on the other side, regeneration gives him a chance to survive it and keep going.

Inside, he could find evidence that finally ties the murders to William in a way the old articles never did. Alongside old suit parts, personal tools, photographs, and private employee records, Wade could uncover a concealed record placing William in the restricted safe-room area during the period of the disappearances together with an item or identifying material belonging to one of the missing children that should never have been in William’s possession. That still wouldn’t explain every piece of the timeline, but it would connect William directly to a victim and the hidden area involved instead of merely proving he had access to Freddy’s equipment.

The discovery would change how Wade approaches him. Up to this point, he’s been trying to understand what happened and whether William is really the person behind it, but now there’s enough connecting everything that Wade can stop treating him like a suspect and start planning around the possibility that he’s still dangerous. He’d assume William knows the restaurant better than he does, has access to places the cameras don’t cover, and understands the springlock suits well enough to use them against someone.

William would probably choose the restaurant for their first real confrontation because it gives him the biggest advantage. He knows the layout, knows where the animatronics move, and can use the building’s old sections to separate Wade from the office and cameras. Wade would realize fairly quickly that he’s being guided somewhere, but by then he’d have a reason to follow because William finally being close means the investigation can actually end.

Their first face to face meeting wouldn't need to turn into a long fight immediately. William would want to know what Wade has found and how much he understands, while Wade would be trying to work out whether there are more victims, more locations, or anything else William has hidden. The conversation would be tense because Wade can joke through almost anything, but the subject underneath it is children who were murdered and left trapped inside machines for years. If William tries attacking him once he realizes Wade knows too much, the result would be completely different from what he expects. A knife, blunt weapon, or even a springlock related trap could hurt Wade badly, and for a few minutes William might think the problem is solved. Once Wade starts healing and gets back up, William finally understands that killing this security guard isn’t going to end anything.

That would shift the balance between them. Wade still doesn’t know every secret William has, and William still knows more about Freddy’s than Wade does, but the simplest way William usually removes a threat has stopped working. From there, the conflict would become less about whether Wade can survive another attack and more about whether he can corner William before Afton finds a way to disappear, destroy evidence, or use the animatronics to cover his escape.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: After surviving the first direct attack, Wade would understand that William’s biggest advantage is still the restaurant itself. He knows which rooms are hidden, which doors still work, where the cameras fail, and how the animatronics behave when somebody enters certain parts of the building. Wade would start taking that advantage away by learning those same details and watching which places seem to matter most. More importantly, Wade staying active inside Freddy’s would interfere with William’s chance to isolate and dismantle the animatronics one by one. In this timeline, Wade prevents that part of William’s usual path from playing out, leaving the possessed animatronics intact and creating a different route toward the Spring Bonnie confrontation.

Freddy, Bonnie, Chica, and Foxy would react differently once William starts appearing around the building again. The aggression aimed at Wade would begin shifting whenever William gets close, especially if the spirits recognize him more clearly than they recognize a random night guard. Wade could treat those reactions as another clue to where William might be moving without relying entirely on the cameras. If Freddy suddenly leaves his normal route and heads toward a back hallway, Wade might suspect there’s a reason, but he’d still need markers, sounds, or other evidence before trusting the pattern. The animatronics could point his attention in useful directions without becoming a reliable tracking system.

Wade would also start preparing the building before each shift. He could leave doors open in places where William expects them shut, move equipment around to block certain exits, and place simple markers near hidden routes so he knows when someone has passed through. His regeneration gives him room to take risks, but he’d still want the confrontation to happen somewhere William can’t disappear the second things go wrong.

One of those attempts could involve luring the animatronics toward Wade rather than controlling them directly. William could use noise, movement, or something familiar from the restaurant to draw attention toward a specific part of the building, hoping several of them converge on Wade at once. He wouldn’t control how the possessed animatronics respond, which makes the trap dangerous for William too. The attack would be brutal because regeneration doesn’t stop him from getting overwhelmed. Bonnie could pin him while Chica tears into him, Foxy could hit before he has time to recover, and Freddy joining the attack would leave Wade with no clean way to fight back without damaging the bodies holding the children.

That restriction would matter because by now Wade doesn’t want to destroy the animatronics unless he has no other option. He knows they're victims, so his goal would be getting away from them rather than cutting them apart. He could use his swords to block or wedge doors, his guns only against objects around the room, and his own body to absorb attacks long enough to reach somewhere safer.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: Wade would spend the next night forcing William into fewer and fewer options. He could shut down routes he already knows about, keep the animatronics moving through areas William usually uses, and stay out of the office long enough to make it impossible for Afton to predict where he'll be. Freddy’s would become much harder for William to control once both Wade and the animatronics are moving through it with their own goals.

The confrontation would probably end near one of the old safe rooms because that’s where William’s history with the restaurant becomes most important. Wade could follow signs of movement into an area missing from the normal cameras and find evidence that William has been using it for years. Old suit parts, tools, and anything connected to the murders would give Wade enough to understand why William keeps returning to places like this even after the restaurant is falling apart around him.

William would still try to use the springlock suit once he realizes he’s cornered. Wade is blocking the cleanest human escape while the animatronics are closing off the remaining routes, leaving Spring Bonnie as William’s last plausible way to exploit whatever recognition or confusion the old costume can still trigger and get past them. He knows the suit is dangerous, but with Wade and the animatronics closing in, taking that risk becomes more rational than staying exposed. Wade would know what the suit means by then, even if he doesn’t understand every mechanical detail inside it.

Because Wade prevented William from dismantling them earlier, the animatronics themselves could now reach the confrontation instead of the sequence playing out exactly as it originally did. Their arrival would turn the room into something William can’t manage anymore. Freddy, Bonnie, Chica, and Foxy could react violently to Spring Bonnie and the man inside it, while Wade would finally have the person responsible standing in front of the victims he’s spent nights trying to understand.
William could try backing deeper into the room while Wade keeps him from reaching another exit.

The springlocks would eventually become the real danger. Small clicks and changes in tension could make it obvious that something inside the old suit is becoming unstable, but Wade wouldn’t understand the mechanism better than William does. William knows exactly what a springlock failure means, and his reaction would tell Wade that the noises are serious. Wade wouldn't need to touch the suit or create the failure himself because William’s movement, moisture, and panic could already be enough to push the mechanisms toward failure.

When the locks finally snap, Wade would understand what happened from William’s warning reaction and the violent mechanical failure in front of him. William would collapse inside the suit while Wade stays nearby long enough to make sure he isn’t getting back up. The animatronics could remain around the room, and for the first time since Wade started working there, they wouldn't be focused on attacking him.

William becoming trapped inside Spring Bonnie can still happen, but now Wade is there when it happens and knows who is inside the suit. The disappearance doesn’t become another mystery buried under Freddy’s history because there’s someone alive who can explain what happened and where the body is.
Wade would also know that killing William doesn’t automatically free the children.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: Once William is gone, Wade would turn his attention back to the animatronics because the reason he stayed at Freddy’s was never just to find a killer. He knows the children are still attached to these machines somehow, and leaving them there after dealing with William would feel unfinished.

He’d start searching through everything William left behind for information about possession, the suits, and anything that explains why the spirits stayed. Most of it would be difficult to understand because William’s knowledge of the supernatural side of Freddy’s developed over years, while Wade is trying to piece it together from scraps.

The animatronics could help by reacting to things connected to their old lives. Names, photographs, belongings, or rooms tied to the murders might produce stronger responses, giving Wade enough information to identify who some of the children were. He could start matching those reactions with old missing person records and return pieces of their identities that had been buried under the restaurant’s mascots.

If there are ways to dismantle the animatronics without destroying what remains of the children, Wade would want to find them. The problem is that FNAF’s supernatural rules are far more complicated than taking apart a robot and assuming the spirit leaves. Wade could damage the wrong thing, spread whatever is binding them somewhere else, or create another problem he doesn’t understand.

For once, regeneration wouldn’t help much. He can survive anything Freddy’s throws at him, but he can’t heal someone else’s soul by taking more damage himself. That would force Wade to slow down and stop treating the problem like something he can solve through persistence alone.

He’d probably keep returning to the restaurant even after the security job no longer matters. The animatronics might become less aggressive around him over time after everything that happened with William, but Wade couldn’t count on that or assume helping them earned their trust. There would still be nights where whatever drives their old aggression takes over and one of them attacks. Wade would survive those too. Only this time, he’d have a better idea of why it might be happening.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: Deadpool would survive Freddy Fazbear’s Pizza much more easily than a normal night guard because the attacks that end the game for everyone else only slow him down. Bonnie, Chica, Foxy, and Freddy could crush him, stab him, or tear him apart, and Wade would still have another chance to learn what went wrong and come back the next night.

That extra time would eventually expose the part of Freddy’s that matters more than the night shift itself. Wade would connect the animatronics to the missing children, follow the evidence toward William Afton, and keep investigating through every attempt William makes to remove him.

William’s biggest problem would be that killing Wade never solves anything. Every failed attempt gives Wade more information, and once the animatronics begin reacting to William directly, the restaurant stops being a place where Afton controls all the important pieces.

The timeline would change once William ends up trapped in the Spring Bonnie suit with Wade there to witness it. His identity wouldn’t stay buried as another unanswered part of Freddy’s history, and Wade could start working on the harder problem of helping the children afterward. Freddy’s would still be dangerous, and Wade would probably complain about never getting paid enough for any of it, but William Afton choosing the 1 night guard who can’t stay dead would turn out to be one of the worst mistakes he could make.

scripts.title: What If Deadpool Was In The Boys

sections.name: INTRO
paras: Deadpool landing in The Boys might be one of the few crossovers where everyone around him looks almost normal by comparison.

Vought would see a regenerating mercenary they could turn into their next edgy superstar, while Butcher would see someone impossible to control and Homelander would eventually see a problem on his hands.

At first, Wade would probably enjoy all of it. The money, the cameras, the ridiculous celebrity culture. Then he'd start seeing what Vought does when the cameras are off, and that’s when being impossible to kill becomes a much bigger problem for them.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: Wade would land in The Boys universe during the mess after Translucent’s death, when Vought is already trying to convince the public that everything inside The Seven is under control. He’d be finishing a mercenary job in his own world when stolen tech from the target overloads and tears open a portal across the room. Wade gets pulled through with most of his weapons, hits pavement somewhere in New York, and watches the opening close before he can crawl back through it. By the time he gets his bearings, every superhero name around him is wrong, nobody has heard of the Avengers or X-Men, and a giant Vought billboard is advertising people he’s never seen before.

He wouldn't spend days quietly researching the universe because Wade has never been built for that. He’d start asking strangers where all the superheroes came from, assume Vought is some kind of discount S.H.I.E.L.D., and eventually learn that Supes are celebrities with movies, sponsorships, theme parks, and entire marketing departments behind them. That part would make perfect sense to him faster than almost anything else, especially once he realizes several of them are getting paid to do things Wade has been doing for money for years.

Vought would discover him because Wade gets involved in something public before he understands how controlled superhero appearances are here. A low-level Supe could lose control during a promotional event and send debris into a crowd, leaving Wade to pull people out before security can clear the area. The Supe hits him hard enough to tear open his torso in front of dozens of phones, only for Wade to keep moving while the wound starts closing.

Wade would eventually walk into Vought Tower himself because he assumes the company with a database of superheroes has the best chance of telling him where he landed. He’d get through security mostly because everyone is more confused than threatened, then sit through a meeting where executives ask about his powers, his origin, and whether somebody else created him. Wade would tell them the truth badly enough that it sounds like a joke, including the part where his healing came from experiments that had nothing to do with Compound V.

That answer would matter more to Vought than anything else he says. Their entire business depends on controlling where superheroes come from, and now someone has walked into their building with a power they didn’t create. Wade would leave the meeting with a temporary contract, a ridiculous amount of money, and absolutely no guarantee that Vought intends to help him get home.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Vought’s first mistake would be assuming Wade needs to be cleaned up for television. After several unusable interviews, somebody in marketing would realize the opposite works better and start selling him as the Supe who says whatever everyone else is afraid to say. They'd give him late night appearances, violent promotional spots, and enough freedom to make the whole thing feel spontaneous while still trying to keep him inside a contract.

For a few weeks, it would work. Wade would become popular because audiences can tell he isn’t pretending to be wholesome, and Vought would happily take credit for the authenticity even though they had nothing to do with creating it. He’d make fun of their slogans on camera, insult other Supes during press events, and admit that he kills people for money without understanding why the producers keep cutting to commercial.

His first real problem with Vought would come from doing exactly what they hired him to do. During an interview, Wade could casually mention that one of the heroes being advertised as sober was using drugs backstage, then make another joke about how many assistants he’s seen cleaning blood out of places that supposedly never had a fight. Those comments wouldn't expose Vought by themselves, but people would start clipping them together with old rumors and asking questions the company doesn’t want answered.

His meetings with The Seven would make the place even stranger. Maeve would barely react to him because she has already seen too much inside Vought to care about one more unstable celebrity, while A-Train would hate how quickly Wade gets attention without playing the same image game everyone else has to follow. Homelander would tolerate him at first because Vought is treating Wade like another temporary product, and nothing about his strength makes him a serious physical threat.

The part Vought wouldn't know is that Wade is still taking mercenary work between appearances. He’d start accepting small jobs around New York partly because he’s bored and partly because he wants cash nobody at Vought can track, and one of those jobs would eventually put him in the middle of something Butcher has already spent days planning.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: The Boys would meet Wade while trying to intercept a Vought middleman who sells information on the side. Frenchie has already worked out the route, Hughie is waiting near the handoff point, and Butcher wants whatever is inside the courier’s case before Vought realizes it’s missing. Wade arrives for an entirely separate reason because somebody paid him to steal the same case, and neither side knows the other exists until he walks through the operation wearing his full suit.

The first few minutes would be a disaster. Wade grabs the case, Kimiko slams him through a wall, and the courier uses the confusion to run while Vought security closes in from the street. Hughie would be trying to figure out why the man Kimiko just folded in half is getting back up, while Butcher realizes Wade is the new Vought mascot he has been seeing all over television. They'd escape the security team separately and end up chasing the same courier through the building. Wade would catch him first, then find Butcher pointing a gun at both of them and demanding the case. Wade could hand it over simply because the person who hired him never explained what was inside, which would annoy Butcher even more because he has no idea whether Wade is stupid, unpredictable, or setting something up.

The case wouldn't contain a convenient file explaining Wade's biology. Instead, it would hold payment records showing Vought has been using outside contractors to bury several incidents involving smaller Supes, including settlements, fake witness statements, and money routed through shell companies. Wade recognizes one of the incidents because he joked about it during an interview after seeing damage backstage that Vought claimed never happened.

That would be the first time he realizes one of his jokes was closer to the truth than he knew. Butcher would tell him Vought has been doing this for years, while Wade would point out that Butcher seems like exactly the kind of person who would say that whether it was true or not. They would leave the meeting disliking each other enough that neither side suggests working together.

Wade would keep the name of 1 contractor from the payment records before handing the case back. He’d track the man down himself and learn that Vought doesn’t only bury embarrassing stories. The contractor has helped move witnesses, pressure families, and clean up deaths caused by Supes whose public versions of events were completely different.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Wade wouldn't quit Vought immediately because leaving would cut off the easiest access he has to the company. Instead, he’d keep taking their money while paying much closer attention to what people tell him not to look at. That gives him a weird advantage nobody at Vought expects because they already decided he’s too unserious to notice patterns.

One assignment would make the situation personal without involving his healing factor yet. Vought could send Wade after a supposedly dangerous blackmailer who stole internal material, expecting him to solve the problem with the same violence he jokes about on television. Wade finds the target and discovers a terrified former employee carrying video of a Supe killing civilians during an operation that Vought later presented as a successful rescue.

The employee would expect Wade to kill him because that is exactly what Vought hired him to do. Wade could sit there watching the footage, make a joke to buy himself time, then realize Vought chose him specifically because they assumed a mercenary wouldn't care what the target had done. He'd take the evidence, tell the employee to disappear, and return to Vought claiming the problem has been handled.

That lie would put Wade in a much more dangerous position than simply resigning. Vought now believes he destroyed evidence that is still out there, while Wade has proof that could hurt them if released properly. He wouldn't immediately dump it online because the company has enough influence to bury one random video and turn the former employee into the villain before anyone checks the details.

Wade would go back to Butcher because he now has something more useful than suspicion. Butcher would enjoy being right far too much, which would immediately make Wade regret showing up, but Frenchie and Hughie could verify enough of the footage to know it’s real. They'd start discussing how to release it alongside other evidence rather than letting Vought isolate the incident.

The arrangement would work until Wade unknowingly walks into one of Vought’s traps. Someone inside the company has noticed that one of the blackmail targets is still alive, and Wade's access logs show he has been visiting places unrelated to his official assignments. Instead of accusing him directly, Vought would quietly change what information he can see and wait to see where the false details end up.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: The trap would use Wade’s own confidence against him. Vought could plant information about a shipment containing Compound V research and make sure Wade hears about it through a conversation he thinks he wasn’t supposed to overhear. He passes the location to Hughie because it sounds like something The Boys would want, and Butcher decides it's worth checking without knowing Vought deliberately created the lead.

The warehouse would be empty except for a security team waiting inside. Wade would realize what happened the moment the doors close, and the attack would tell him something new about his position inside Vought because the guards aren't trying to kill him. They use restraints, sedatives, electrical weapons, and enough force to incapacitate him while avoiding anything that could permanently destroy the body.

The Boys would escape before the full team closes in because Wade stays behind and turns himself into the obvious target. Kimiko could help clear a path for Hughie and Frenchie while Butcher refuses to leave until Wade throws him through the exit and seals the door behind him. Wade would keep fighting until enough tranquilizer overwhelms his ability to stay coordinated and conscious, even while his regeneration keeps repairing the physical damage, and Vought gets him unconscious.

He'd wake up inside a medical facility he has never seen before, which is where the healing factor storyline would finally become something bigger than curiosity. Vought has already spent weeks studying the blood taken during his original medical checks, and once they decide Wade has betrayed them, there’s no longer any reason to ask permission for more.

The doctors wouldn't be trying to copy his entire healing factor overnight. They'd be trying to understand why tissue from someone with no Compound V continues repairing damage that should be irreversible, and the easiest way to study that is having the source restrained in front of them. Wade could lose tissue, regenerate it, and then lose it again while the same samples are compared against Vought’s existing Supes.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Wade's escape would start with Vought making the mistake of assuming pain is enough to control someone who has spent years learning how to function through it. He’d let the sedatives keep him limp during another round of tests, wait until one restraint is loosened, then use a surgical tool to cut himself free before the staff realizes he’s awake. He’d still be half-drugged and without his weapons, so getting out would depend more on improvising than fighting cleanly.

The deeper he gets into the facility, the more obvious it becomes that his room is only one part of what Vought has been doing there. He’d pass cells containing adults from Vought’s still-secret Sage Grove program whose Compound V treatments went wrong, people with unstable powers, and subjects being kept alive because somebody still thinks they might become useful. Wade could leave alone and probably make it out faster, but after spending days strapped to the same kind of table, he’d start opening doors as he goes.

That decision would turn a quiet escape into chaos. Some subjects would run, others would attack security, and Wade would end up helping people who can barely move while alarms spread through the building. The guards would still try to recover him alive because Vought wants the regenerative tissue back, which gives Wade room to use their own restraint weapons and gas systems against them instead of just trying to shoot his way through every corridor. The Boys would be looking for the facility at the same time. Hughie would push the search because he knows Wade was taken alive, while Frenchie tracks the security convoy from the warehouse through contractors Vought uses for medical transport. Butcher would still complain that rescuing Wade sounds like a punishment designed specifically for him, but a hidden Vought lab full of enhanced test subjects is too valuable to ignore.

They'd reach the perimeter while Wade is already breaking the place apart from inside. The reunion would be messy, with Wade dragging one injured subject toward the exit while Butcher is trying to figure out why there are alarms, smoke, and several terrified people following him. There wouldn't be time to argue because Vought response teams are already moving in. Getting everyone out would leave Vought with a public problem they can’t explain. They can’t admit Wade was imprisoned for medical testing, so the company would immediately rewrite the story. By morning, Vought would be claiming that Deadpool attacked a research facility, freed dangerous enhanced subjects, and assaulted employees who were trying to contain him. Wade would watch the same media machine that made him famous turn every clip of his escape into proof that he was unstable from the beginning. That would give him a new reason to stop treating the situation like a private fight with Vought because now they're using his own public image to hide what happened to everyone else inside that building.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: The escaped subjects would give The Boys more than testimony. One of them could remember enough about their treatment to identify the facility as part of Vought’s Sage Grove program for adult Compound V trials, and Frenchie would start matching that against medical records copied from the facility before they left. Instead of finding one neat document explaining everything, they’d have to build the picture from dosage charts, failed treatments, tissue reports, and names that disappear halfway through the files. Frenchie would also pull network credentials and internal access information from the facility's systems, giving them a possible foothold into Vought's infrastructure if they could get inside the Tower.

Wade’s samples would show up repeatedly in the research beside subjects who survived longer than expected. Vought hadn’t cracked his healing factor or turned his tissue into a treatment, but studying how his cells responded to catastrophic damage had given researchers ideas for modifying their own Compound V protocols and supportive treatment. The results were inconsistent and several subjects still died, yet even a small improvement in survival would matter to a company trying to control what V does outside childhood dosing.

The records would show that Vought moved the remaining Wade samples and related research after the escape. Most of it went into secure storage inside Vought Tower because Ashley no longer trusts outside facilities to hold anything connected to Wade. The same transfer includes backup copies of the adult trial data, which gives The Boys 2 reasons to get inside.

Butcher would want to steal everything and expose it through people Vought can’t easily silence. Wade would have another idea because the company is already using television to convince the world he attacked innocent researchers. If they simply dump files online, Vought gets time to call them fake, bury them under lawyers, and turn the whole story into another argument over leaked documents.

That means the next operation wouldn't be a normal break in. They’d need the research, but they’d also need access to Vought’s own broadcast infrastructure before the company realizes what they’re doing.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: Wade would use the smear campaign to get himself invited back into the one building Vought definitely doesn’t want him inside. He could release a short video saying he'll surrender publicly if Vought lets him do it live, knowing the company now has to choose between refusing and looking afraid or accepting and trying to control the event.

Ashley would take the second option because Vought believes television is where it has the advantage. They'd build a scripted press appearance in the lobby, surround Wade with security, and plan to cut the feed the second he says anything they don’t approve. Wade would agree to all of it while The Boys prepare to enter through service access during the media chaos.

The plan would depend on Wade keeping everyone focused downstairs long enough for Hughie and Frenchie to reach the internal broadcast systems. Kimiko would move with them because once the alarm goes up, they'll need somebody who can get through security without waiting for Wade to create another distraction.

Wade would walk into the lobby unarmed, surrounded by cameras and reporters who have spent the last day calling him dangerous. He'd start with the apology Vought wrote for him, read just enough of it to make Ashley relax, then go off-script and ask why the company has a medical program built around prisoners nobody is allowed to know exist.

Security would move immediately, but cutting the public feed wouldn't work the way Vought expects. Using the access information Frenchie pulled from the facility, Hughie and Frenchie would already have control of enough of the internal system to replace Wade’s camera with files from the facility, treatment footage, and records showing where the subjects came from. Instead of one leaked document, people watching would see Vought’s own medical records appear inside a Vought broadcast.

He’d understand instantly that Wade is the reason the building is losing control of its own cameras, and Wade would understand just as quickly that the plan has reached the point where talking is about to become physically expensive. Homelander could cross the lobby before Wade gets another full sentence out and hit him hard enough to put him through one of Vought’s display walls.

Wade wouldn't try fighting him straight. His job would be keeping the broadcast alive long enough for the evidence to finish moving outside Vought’s servers. Every time Homelander goes after him on camera, Wade would keep crawling back toward whichever camera is still running and make sure the audience sees exactly how Vought treats someone the company was calling one of its own a few weeks earlier.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: Homelander would eventually stop playing along with the cameras and tear the broadcast equipment apart, but by then Hughie and Frenchie would have pushed the files through several outside channels. The live feed itself would only need to stay up long enough for journalists, independent streamers, and people recording at home to start copying what Vought can no longer erase.

The Boys would still need to get out of the tower, and this time Wade's role wouldn't be standing in a hallway waiting to get beaten again. He’d use what he learned during his time as a Vought celebrity and start triggering the building’s own systems against them. He knows where certain studios are, which elevators executives use, where security routes guests during emergencies, and which areas Vought tries hardest to keep cameras away from.

Wade could set off different alarms on separate floors, force security teams toward the wrong exits, and dump archived internal footage onto screens throughout the building. Some of it would be harmless promotional garbage, while other clips could show enough behind-the-scenes behavior to make every employee stop wondering whether the breach is contained.

That confusion would give The Boys a route out without Wade needing to physically hold Homelander back. Wade could send Hughie, Frenchie, and Kimiko toward an employee evacuation path he learned during his media days while he heads somewhere else entirely. The remaining biological samples are the one part of the operation that can’t be fixed by releasing information. As long as Vought still has them, the company can keep studying Wade's actual biology even if copies of what it already learned survive somewhere else. Wade would reach the secure medical storage using credentials stolen from the lab staff and destroy the remaining biological samples and research stored at that location before the company can move them again. He couldn't know whether every copied dataset or analysis Vought had already created was gone.
