Yuji and Maki would still fight Sukuna shortly after the takeover, and the same issue with Megumi fighting from inside would still matter. Megumi’s soul interferes with Sukuna’s cursed energy output whenever he attacks his friends, which gives Yuji and Maki a chance to stay in the fight longer than they normally could.

They still wouldn’t be able to finish him there. Uraume arrives, Sukuna escapes, and the Bath is used to sink Megumi’s soul deeper. Sukuna would then kill Yorozu while she’s using Tsumiki’s body, which pushes Megumi even further down. Before the final confrontation, Sukuna would also make sure Mahoraga is properly subjugated so he can use it freely. Yorozu would still use Construction to leave Kamutoke behind as her final gift.

That would leave the rest of the group with a problem much worse than anything they'd prepared for. Sukuna now has Megumi’s Ten Shadows Technique and access to Mahoraga. Megumi had interested Sukuna for a long time because of his technique and his potential as a vessel, but Sukuna also waited for a moment when Megumi’s soul was vulnerable enough that he was less likely to suppress him the way Yuji could. He also isn’t sitting inside Yuji anymore, so killing Sukuna now means risking Megumi's life too.
Yuji would still want to save Megumi because that’s who he is, but the group wouldn’t have Gojo there to take the first shot at Sukuna.

Kashimo would want to fight him immediately. That was the entire reason he agreed to work with Hakari in the first place, and he wouldn't care much about waiting for everyone else to build the perfect plan.
Yuta would probably be the one pushing against that. Sending Kashimo in alone against Sukuna before they understand the Ten Shadows setup could waste one of their strongest fighters for nothing.
Maki would be more willing to look at the fight practically. She knows what Megumi means to Yuji and the others, but she also knows Sukuna can’t be allowed to keep getting stronger while they argue.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: The group’s first decision would probably be to stop thinking about Sukuna as someone they can beat through normal damage.

Yuta, Maki, Hakari, Kashimo, Yuji, Higuruma, Choso, Kusakabe, and everyone else together still give them a lot of power, but Sukuna has too many ways to punish a bad attack. Malevolent Shrine can hit a huge area without using a closed barrier, Cleave can adjust to the target, and now Sukuna also has the Ten Shadows Technique.

The problem is that Higuruma doesn’t control exactly what gets taken. If Sukuna has Kamutoke, there’s a good chance the cursed tool gets confiscated first, just like it did in canon. That would still help, but it doesn’t remove Shrine. Yuta would probably build his part of the plan around Jacob’s Ladder. Angel’s technique is especially useful because Sukuna is an incarnated sorcerer inside Megumi’s body. A strong enough hit could damage the connection between Sukuna and the vessel, and Yuta can copy the technique.

Yuji would be the other person the plan starts depending on. His punches can reach the boundary between Sukuna and Megumi’s souls. He doesn’t need to overpower Sukuna in 1 hit. He needs enough openings to keep hitting that boundary and weaken Sukuna’s hold on Megumi.

That would give Maki a very clear job too. She can use the Split Soul Katana to damage the soul directly, and Sukuna can’t read her cursed energy the way he reads normal sorcerers. If Yuta or Yuji can keep Sukuna busy long enough, Maki has a chance to land attacks from places he isn’t watching.

Hakari could handle keeping another threat busy or hold Sukuna’s attention during a section of the fight if he gets jackpot. Kashimo would still demand his turn, but the group would try to use that fight for information instead of letting it happen with no plan around it.

They'd also know Mahoraga has to be dealt with before it gets enough time to adapt. Its adaptation isn’t reset just because they switch attacks, so letting it stay active while they cycle through techniques would only give it more phenomena to begin adapting to.

The real goal would be to destroy Mahoraga quickly with something powerful enough to finish it before the relevant adaptation develops. Yuta’s copied techniques, Maki’s physical attacks, and Kashimo’s one time technique give the group different options for trying to land that decisive attack, but variety by itself doesn’t cancel Mahoraga’s progress. What they wouldn’t have is anyone who can stand in front of Sukuna for as long as Gojo did. That changes everything about the order of the fight. They can’t send people in one after another and hope Sukuna gets weaker each time. If the first group gets wiped out too quickly, everyone after them is fighting almost the same Sukuna.
They’d need to hit him with several parts of the plan close together, force him to defend against different abilities, and keep creating chances for Yuji to reach Megumi’s soul.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: At the same time, Kenjaku is still alive. That means they can’t put every strong fighter against Sukuna. Someone still has to deal with the Culling Game, Tengen, and the merger before Kenjaku finishes what he started.

Takaba would still be one of the best ways to reach him because his technique doesn’t work like normal jujutsu. Kenjaku can understand cursed techniques, barriers, and most normal combat choices, but Takaba drags him into something completely different. A Takaba and Yuta setup could still potentially work, but unlike canon, Yuta can only make the surprise attack if the Sukuna fight gives him a window to leave at the necessary moment.

Kenjaku’s death wouldn’t automatically end the Culling Game, though. His plans had already gone too far, and the merger setup would still be hanging over everyone. They’d need to deal with whatever control he left behind and make sure the merger can’t start while they're fighting Sukuna.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Here, none of that happens. For this version, Sukuna would stay in Megumi’s form while he’s exploiting Ten Shadows and Mahoraga, because canon never establishes whether he could still use Ten Shadows after fully incarnating into his original body. Either way, he has much more energy left because he hasn’t spent a long fight dealing with Limitless, and he hasn’t been pushed anywhere near the same point.

That makes Kashimo’s role much worse. Kashimo would still demand to fight Sukuna because that was his whole reason for joining the group. The others might try to convince him to wait, but Kashimo isn’t someone they can control forever. If he decides he wants his fight, he’s going. He’d use Mythical Beast Amber and push Sukuna much harder than most fighters could, but the gap would still be huge. Sukuna wouldn’t already be tired or damaged from Gojo, and he’d still have more options available. Kashimo could force him to move and show parts of his technique, but he probably dies faster here than he did in canon.

The others would have to use that time instead of just watching. Yuta, Yuji, Higuruma, Maki, and Kusakabe would already be getting into position because they can’t afford to let Sukuna reset after every fight. They need the pressure to stay on him.
Higuruma would probably go next because his domain gives them one of the few chances to remove something before the main fight really starts.

Uraume would later deliver Kamutoke to Sukuna, preserving the same cursed tool problem for Higuruma. If Kamutoke is still there, Confiscation would most likely take the cursed tool first, just like in canon. That would be frustrating, but it still removes one weapon from Sukuna and gives Higuruma a chance to get the Executioner’s Sword.
Sukuna at this point would still be far too strong for Higuruma to handle alone. Yuji would need to stay with him, and the others would have to help create openings.
If Higuruma dies without landing the sword, they lose one of their cleanest win conditions which means the group can’t waste time.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: Yuta’s domain would normally be one of the most important parts of the whole fight, but here there’s a major problem: Sukuna still has Malevolent Shrine. If Yuta closes Sukuna inside his barrier while Shrine is available, Sukuna can answer with his own open-barrier domain and attack Yuta’s barrier from the outside. That means the group can’t build the plan around Authentic Mutual Love staying up unless they first create a reason Sukuna can no longer use Domain Expansion.

Yuta would still build his part of the plan around Jacob’s Ladder because Sukuna is living inside Megumi’s body, but he may have to use his copied techniques without relying on the domain as a stable battlefield. If Sukuna’s Domain Expansion somehow becomes unavailable during the fight, then Authentic Mutual Love becomes a much safer option for forcing Jacob’s Ladder into the exchange.

Yuji would still need to fight alongside Yuta because his punches can hit the boundary between their souls. That gives the group a real plan even if Yuta can’t safely keep his domain active. Yuta keeps Sukuna busy with copied techniques and looks for chances to land Jacob’s Ladder. Yuji keeps landing hits on the soul boundary. Every clean punch weakens Sukuna’s hold and gives Megumi a better chance to respond from inside.

This would still be incredibly dangerous because Sukuna hasn’t taken Gojo’s damage, and Malevolent Shrine means Yuta can’t simply reproduce the domain sequence from canon. Mahoraga becomes another huge problem if Sukuna brings it out early. If it survives long enough to adapt to one of the group’s key attacks, that option becomes much less reliable, and switching to something else wouldn’t erase the adaptation it already gained.

Yuta would probably try to stop that by using his copied techniques to create an opening for a decisive attack before Mahoraga can adapt far enough to survive it. Maki would wait outside the main exchange. Her best chance is attacking when Sukuna’s attention is on Yuta and Yuji. Since she has no cursed energy, Sukuna can’t track her the same way he tracks everyone else.
The Split Soul Katana also gives her a way to damage him that doesn’t care as much about normal toughness.

If Yuta can keep Sukuna occupied for even a few seconds, Maki could land a serious hit. The problem is that Sukuna knows what she can do. From there, she’d have to rely on speed, physical strength, and timing. She can fight at a level most sorcerers can’t reach, but Sukuna is still much faster and stronger than almost everyone around him.
Yuji would keep becoming more important as the fight goes on because every hit he lands on the soul boundary can weaken Sukuna’s control over Megumi.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: Yuta would help create those openings. His copied techniques give Sukuna more things to deal with at once, and Jacob’s Ladder is especially useful because Sukuna is an incarnated sorcerer living inside someone else’s body. Every strong hit from it could put more pressure on that connection, which gives Yuji a better chance of reaching Megumi with his own attacks.

Megumi’s condition would make this difficult. Sukuna already used the Bath to sink his soul deeper and then killed Yorozu while she was using Tsumiki’s body. By the time Yuji reaches him, Megumi has already been pushed through everything Sukuna could use to break his will.

That’s when Maki becomes especially useful. She can move without giving off cursed energy, and the Split Soul Katana can damage the soul directly. If Sukuna is already dealing with Yuta and Yuji, Maki has a better chance of getting close from an angle he isn’t watching.

Todo could also help if he enters around this point. Boogie Woogie would make it much harder for Sukuna to keep track of where Yuji is coming from, especially when several fighters are already moving around him. Yuji only needs a few clean chances for the soul attacks to start adding up, and Todo is one of the best people in the series at creating those chances.

The fight would still cost them badly. Kashimo would probably be gone by now, Higuruma could already be dead, and Yuta could take serious damage once Sukuna starts focusing on him. Maki would only have so many chances before Sukuna starts tracking her movement more carefully.

Megumi responding from inside would only become useful if Yuji’s soul attacks and Jacob’s Ladder weaken Sukuna’s hold enough for Megumi to push back again. That resistance could then help the process, but the progressive drop in Sukuna’s control would come from the group forcing the two souls apart, not from Megumi simply recreating the suppression he managed immediately after possession.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: Their chances would be much worse than they were in canon because Sukuna reaches this fight in much better condition. He hasn’t already gone through a long battle with Gojo, and as long as he remains in Megumi’s form here, he still has Ten Shadows and Mahoraga available along with much more cursed energy when everyone else starts attacking.

Mahoraga would probably be one of the biggest problems in the entire fight. If Sukuna brings it out before the group has done enough damage, they can’t afford to let it stay active long enough to adapt to their best options. The group would likely focus everything they have on destroying it with a decisive attack before the relevant adaptation develops, rather than assuming that switching techniques can reset its progress.

That would cost them a lot. Yuta might have to use more cursed energy earlier than he wants, Maki could take serious damage, and Yuji would have to keep fighting while Sukuna is still far stronger than the version he faced later in canon.

If they manage to remove Mahoraga and keep weakening Sukuna’s hold over Megumi, the fight starts getting closer. Yuji’s soul attacks could keep lowering Sukuna’s control, while Jacob’s Ladder puts more pressure on the connection between Sukuna and the vessel. If that creates enough separation for Megumi to start resisting again, his response from inside could help the process further.

Even then, that only gives the group a theoretical path to separating Sukuna from Megumi. Against a Sukuna who never took Gojo’s enormous amount of damage and resource drain, they would have almost no margin for error. Their best soul-separation tools would need to land early and in sequence before Sukuna can wipe out the coordinated group, and far more of them could die before that happens.

Kenjaku could still potentially be beaten through the Takaba and Yuta plan, provided Yuta can actually be freed from the Sukuna battle at the necessary moment, so the bigger question comes down to whether Yuji can keep reaching Megumi before Sukuna kills too many of the people helping him.

I think an upset is still possible, but Sukuna would be the overwhelming favorite. Yuji would have to keep reaching the soul boundary, Yuta would have to keep Jacob’s Ladder in play, and they would need to weaken Sukuna’s hold enough for Megumi to respond before Sukuna dismantles the plan. If any major piece fails too early, there probably isn’t a second chance.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: Gojo staying trapped in the Prison Realm would change almost everything after Shibuya because the rest of the sorcerers would lose the person who could normally take on the strongest threats by himself.

Kenjaku could still be stopped, but Sukuna would reach the final battle in far better shape. The group would have to rely much more on Yuta, Yuji, Maki, Higuruma, Todo, and Angel’s technique while keeping the pressure on Sukuna from the start.

They’d still have a theoretical path to winning, but it would be an extremely narrow one. Yuji reaching Megumi’s soul and Yuta keeping Jacob’s Ladder in play would need to weaken Sukuna’s hold fast enough for Megumi to respond before a near-fresh Sukuna wipes out the group. Without Gojo’s attrition first, Sukuna would be the overwhelming favorite.

scripts.title: What If Guts Had The Venom Symbiote

sections.name: INTRO
paras: Guts would first see Venom as another creature that wants something from him. By the time they meet, he’s already carrying the Brand of Sacrifice, hunting Apostles, and dealing with monsters that follow him almost everywhere he goes, so a black creature trying to attach itself to his body isn’t exactly going to earn his trust.

Venom would keep coming back because Guts is the kind of host it rarely finds. He’s strong and willing to keep fighting long after most people would’ve collapsed. Once the symbiote finally bonds with him, those traits would get pushed even further as it starts helping him move faster, heal through damage, and control the Dragon Slayer with more force than before.

The more Venom helps him survive, the easier it becomes for Guts to rely on it, especially once he realizes how much stronger it makes him against Apostles. The real problem starts when that strength begins affecting the way he fights and how far he’s willing to go.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: Venom would first encounter Guts during the Black Swordsman period, after he had already spent years hunting Apostles and carrying the Brand of Sacrifice. By this point, Guts had the Dragon Slayer, the cannon built into his prosthetic arm, a repeating crossbow, throwing knives, and enough experience fighting monsters that seeing another strange creature wouldn’t surprise him much.
What would bother him is the way Venom approaches him.

The symbiote would sense almost immediately that Guts is different from the ordinary humans around him. His body has survived years of injuries, he can swing a sword that most men could barely lift, and he keeps fighting even when he’s exhausted or bleeding badly. More importantly, the Brand guarantees that supernatural creatures keep finding him, so Venom wouldn’t have to wait long before seeing exactly what Guts is capable of.

Guts would probably meet it during one of those nights when the Brand draws evil spirits toward him. Venom wouldn’t understand what the spirits are at first, but once they start attacking its potential host, it has every reason to fight back. Black tendrils could tear through weaker possessed bodies while Guts handles the rest with the Dragon Slayer, and Guts would notice that the creature seems far more interested in staying near him than chasing anything else.

Venom can survive that kind of rejection, and Guts wouldn't have an easy way to permanently remove something that can reshape itself and reconnect after being torn apart. Fire could hurt it badly if Guts discovered the weakness, although he wouldn't know that during their first encounter.

The symbiote would also begin experiencing Guts from the inside whenever it manages to make contact. His anger would be impossible to miss. There’s hatred toward Griffith, hatred toward Apostles, guilt over the Band of the Hawk, and a constant need to keep moving because stopping means being forced to think about everything he lost.

Venom has bonded with angry hosts before, but Guts would give it more aggression than it needs. That would make the connection intense almost immediately, even though Guts wants nothing to do with it. The anger wouldn’t literally make Venom stronger, but it would make Guts more willing to let the symbiote use its existing strength and abilities as aggressively as possible.

The bond would finally happen during a fight where Guts is badly injured. An Apostle could tear into his side or damage his remaining arm badly enough that continuing normally becomes difficult, and Venom would attach itself while Guts is still trying to stand. He’d feel the bleeding slow and the damaged area stabilize enough for him to move again, while Venom temporarily supports muscles that were already reaching their limit. The injury would still need time to heal afterward.

The Dragon Slayer would become much easier to control once the symbiote reinforces his arm, shoulder, back, and legs at the same time. Guts already knows how to use the sword’s weight better than almost anyone else could, so giving him more strength wouldn’t replace his technique. It would let him put even more of his body behind movements he has already spent years perfecting.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Guts wouldn’t let Venom cover his entire body every time they fight. He’d spend the first few days testing what the symbiote can actually do while keeping as much control as possible. The most obvious change would be his injuries.

Venom could seal smaller cuts, slow blood loss, support damaged muscles, and accelerate Guts’ recovery from wounds that normally require days of rest. Serious injuries wouldn’t simply disappear in the middle of a fight; Venom could stabilize them and temporarily compensate enough to keep Guts moving, but his body would still need recovery afterward. It also shouldn’t restore the missing eye and arm, which remain beyond what this healing support can replace. The prosthetic arm would remain, and Guts would still rely on the cannon hidden inside it.

He already has a habit of fighting through injuries because he doesn’t care what happens to his body as long as the enemy dies first. Venom makes it easier to keep doing that, which means Guts has even less reason to stop when he should.

Wrapping the sword becomes useful in specific situations. Venom could form extra grips along the flat of the blade, helping Guts pull it back after it gets buried inside a large Apostle. A tendril attached near the hilt could change the sword’s direction faster after a missed swing, or help Guts recover his balance when the weight carries him too far forward.

His cannon arm would remain useful too. Venom covering the prosthetic wouldn’t remove the mechanism inside it, so Guts could still fire the cannon at close range. The symbiote would learn very quickly that it needs to move away from the barrel before Guts shoots because the heat and explosion would hurt it.

That would probably be how Guts discovers one of Venom’s main weaknesses. The first time the cannon fires while Venom is spread too far over the arm, the symbiote would recoil immediately. Guts would notice. He might not know exactly how vulnerable Venom is to heat yet, but he now has something he can use if the creature ever tries taking more control than he allows.

Venom would understand the message as well. Their early bond would develop around that constant tension. Guts lets it help because it makes him stronger, while keeping a weapon available that can hurt it if the bond starts becoming something he can’t control.

Guts wouldn't appreciate that observation. Still, Puck would become useful because he can watch the changes from outside. If Venom begins spreading further over Guts whenever he gets angry, Puck would notice before Guts does. That would happen more often once they reach stronger Apostles.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: A fight against someone on the level of the Snake Baron would show how much Venom changes Guts without making Apostles harmless.

Guts already defeated the Snake Baron through his own weapons and willingness to fight brutally, but with Venom attached, the fight would become much shorter. The Baron’s physical strength and transformed body could still send Guts flying if he gets caught, although Venom could absorb part of the impact, stabilize a fracture, and temporarily support the damaged area enough to keep Guts moving. He would still be genuinely injured and need recovery afterward.

He likes creating openings rather than standing still and trading hits. Venom could grab a wall or beam while Guts is thrown backward and change his direction before he lands. If the Apostle reaches for him, a tendril could catch the arm for a second, giving Guts enough time to bring the Dragon Slayer around.
The combination would be ugly because neither Guts nor Venom has much interest in fighting cleanly.

Guts would still use explosives, knives, the cannon, and anything else available, while Venom adds another way to attack from angles Apostles aren’t expecting. A creature focusing on the Dragon Slayer could suddenly have its leg pulled out from under it by a tendril, and Guts would already be swinging before it gets back up.
Against weaker Apostles, that would make Guts terrifying. The Slug Count would show him that stronger Apostles are still a serious problem.

The Count can survive enormous damage after transforming, and his body is large enough that simply making Guts stronger doesn’t solve the fight. Guts would still need to understand how the Count moves and find openings rather than hacking at him until something works. Venom would struggle with the Count’s body too. Tendrils could tear through flesh, but the Apostle can keep fighting through damage that would kill anything human. If Venom tries holding him in place, the Count has enough strength to pull Guts across the room with him.

That fight would push the bond further than anything before it. Guts would take heavier injuries, and every time Venom stabilizes damaged tissue or compensates enough for him to continue, the symbiote would spread farther across his body. His speed would increase, the Dragon Slayer would start moving with less effort, and Guts would rely more on direct attacks because he can survive mistakes that used to punish him.

That’s where Venom begins changing his behavior. Guts normally survives because he understands how fragile he is compared to Apostles. He takes ridiculous risks, but there’s still a human body underneath the armor and weapons. Venom starts removing some of that limitation.

During the Count fight, Guts might take an attack he could have avoided because he knows Venom will keep him standing. The hit could smash him through stone, and he’d come back out with the symbiote already holding damaged parts of his body together.

Puck would see the problem immediately. Guts is winning faster, but he’s also giving the enemy more chances to hit him because each injury feels less permanent. The final attack against the Count could be far more direct. Venom reinforces Guts’ entire body while tendrils hold pieces of the Count away from the main target, giving Guts the opening to drive the Dragon Slayer through him with more force than he could normally produce.

That still wouldn’t change everything surrounding the Count. The God Hand’s involvement and the Count’s refusal to sacrifice Theresia come from choices Venom can’t simply overpower. Guts would still be reminded that the Apostles are connected to something much larger than the monsters he kills one at a time.
Venom would experience that moment beside him and for the first time, it would understand that the things Guts is hunting are much worse than the creatures it has fought since arriving.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: The Brand would probably create one of the strangest parts of the bond because Venom can't remove it.

The mark isn’t a normal wound sitting on Guts’ skin. It ties him to the Interstice and marks him as a sacrifice, which is why evil spirits and other supernatural beings are drawn toward him. Venom could cover the Brand or help with the bleeding when spirits are nearby, but healing the skin wouldn't break what the Brand actually does.

Guts would learn that quickly. If Venom covers the mark and it still begins bleeding when something dangerous approaches, Guts knows the symbiote hasn't fixed anything. The spirits would keep coming at night, and now they’d have two minds inside the same body to target. That could create problems neither of them expects. Possessing Guts is already difficult because of his willpower, but neither Guts nor Venom would know at first whether the spirits can interact with the symbiote through their bond at all. Venom is alien to the Berserk world and doesn’t necessarily follow the same rules as a human soul. If a spirit eventually tries to exploit that mental connection and Venom is actually able to resist it, they could learn that the symbiote provides another layer of opposition, but that interaction would have to be discovered rather than assumed.

Nights that were already exhausting for Guts would become easier physically, but they’d also give Venom constant exposure to the supernatural side of his mind. That includes Guts’ dreams. Venom would begin seeing pieces of the Eclipse through him, whether Guts wants to share them or not. It would understand why Apostles make him angry, why Griffith’s face produces a reaction stronger than almost anything else, and why Casca occupies a part of his mind he tries to bury while he’s hunting.

Guts would hate having something that close to those memories. He could tolerate Venom wrapping around his body during a fight, but feeling it inside his thoughts would remind him too much of losing control. He’d start forcing the symbiote back whenever it reaches too deeply into something personal, and the cannon becomes a real threat whenever Venom refuses.

Their arguments would get worse as the bond strengthens because Venom would also feel everything Guts refuses to say. The symbiote wants a host who survives. Guts regularly behaves like survival is optional. When Guts charges into a group of spirits without resting, Venom has to spend energy keeping him moving. When he refuses to treat a wound because there’s another Apostle nearby, Venom has to compensate. Eventually it would push back against choices that damage the body both of them now depend on.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: The biggest change would build across dozens of smaller fights as Guts realizes he doesn’t have to spend as long recovering between them.

Normally, his war against the Apostles destroys his body piece by piece. Even when he wins, cuts, broken bones, blood loss, and exhaustion follow him into the next fight. Venom could shorten that recovery enough that Guts starts hunting again much sooner.
It also means Guts spends even less time doing anything except fighting.

Puck would notice that first. Guts already pushes people away during the Black Swordsman period, and Venom makes isolation easier because he no longer needs as much help when he’s injured. A wound that might have forced Guts to stay somewhere for several days can now be managed while he keeps traveling.

Venom wouldn't mind that lifestyle. Every Apostle gives it another powerful enemy to fight, and Guts’ body responds to danger with exactly the kind of aggression the symbiote can amplify. Eventually, Guts would begin letting Venom cover more of him before the fight even starts.
Then the fights start lasting longer because Guts stops holding himself back.

Against an Apostle that mocks the Band of the Hawk or mentions the Eclipse, Venom would feel the shift in Guts immediately. His anger spikes, and the symbiote responds by using more of the strength and coverage it already has available because Guts stops restraining how aggressively they fight.

The Guts-and-Venom combination could start becoming dangerous after the enemy is already beaten. Guts has always been brutal toward Apostles, so killing one violently wouldn’t bother him, but Venom could keep pushing his body forward when there’s nothing left to fight.
Puck trying to get his attention might be the first thing that snaps him out of it.

When the symbiote pulls back, Guts would see how far the fight went and realize he barely remembers parts of it. Venom didn’t fully take control of him. Guts made the attacks himself, but the bond made it much easier to stay inside that anger once he was there. He knows what losing himself to rage looks like because he’s spent years feeling it happen without needing Venom. Now there’s another living thing inside him that becomes more aggressive and responsive when he lets that rage take over.

Guts would start setting limits after that. Venom can reinforce his body, heal injuries, and help with movement, but he’d try keeping the full transformation for enemies strong enough to require it. He’d also keep using the cannon partly because its heat gives him a way to force Venom off if those limits stop working.

Venom wouldn't necessarily agree with any of this, but staying bonded to Guts means learning that force won't work. If it tries controlling him outright, Guts will fight it as hard as he fights any Apostle. That tension would follow them through the rest of Guts’ solitary hunt. Venom could make encounters like Lost Children easier physically, but it wouldn’t remove the experiences that force Guts to confront what revenge is turning him into. The Conviction-era crisis and Casca’s danger would still give him the reason to abandon the purely solitary Apostle hunt and choose protecting her again. That means the broad path back to Casca can remain intact even though Venom changes how Guts survives the battles along the way.

She would be seeing a version of him that already looks harder and more distant than the man she knew before the Eclipse, and now there’s something else living beneath his skin that reacts whenever his anger rises.

During the Black Swordsman period, Guts can afford to throw himself into fights because most of the people around him are temporary companions. Casca changes that. She can’t protect herself the way she used to after the Eclipse, and Guts has to think about where she is every time something attacks them.

Venom would understand why Casca matters through Guts before it fully understands her as a person. Every time she’s threatened, Guts reacts faster and more violently than he does for almost anyone else. The symbiote would pick up on that and start treating her survival as part of keeping Guts stable.

That would help during the journey, especially when the Brand draws spirits toward both of them. Venom can defend Guts from several directions at once, which gives him more room to protect Casca instead of constantly choosing between attacking and shielding her. Tendrils could pull her away from danger while Guts keeps the Dragon Slayer between them and whatever is coming.

The problem comes when Guts gets angry around her. Casca is already frightened by him at different points after everything that happened, and seeing black material spread across his body when he loses control wouldn’t help. She wouldn’t understand Venom or know that Guts still has control underneath it. To her, it could look like another monster is taking him over. Guts would notice that reaction. He’d stop using the full symbiote form around her unless he absolutely needs it. Venom could still reinforce his arms, legs, and wounds under his clothes, but Guts would keep the more obvious parts restrained whenever Casca is close.

That creates one of the first real compromises in their bond. Venom wants to protect the host efficiently, which means using as much of itself as necessary when danger appears. Guts now has another reason to hold it back because winning the fight isn’t the only thing he cares about anymore.

Farnese, Serpico, and Isidro would all react differently once they join the group. Isidro would probably think the symbiote is incredible the first time he sees it helping Guts swing the Dragon Slayer, while Farnese would initially treat it like another demonic presence attached to him. Serpico would be more interested in whether Guts controls it or the other way around.

That matters because Guts is already moving toward another problem inside himself. The Beast of Darkness doesn’t come from Venom, and the symbiote wouldn’t replace it. The Beast represents the violent urges and hatred Guts already carries, which means Venom would end up sharing a mind with something that pushes Guts toward the same kinds of choices.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Venom would first become aware of the Beast of Darkness through Guts’ thoughts.

At the beginning, it might mistake the Beast for another supernatural creature connected to the Brand. Guts has spirits following him constantly, so the presence of something hostile inside his own mind wouldn't immediately make sense.

Over time, Venom would realize the Beast reacts differently. It appears when Guts is angry, exhausted, or tempted to give up on the people slowing down his revenge. It pushes him toward killing, abandoning Casca, and returning to the simpler life where all he had to do was hunt Apostles.

Venom wouldn't automatically oppose all of that. The symbiote already responds well to aggression, and Guts’ strongest emotions can make their connection more intense without generating extra power by themselves. If the Beast pushes Guts toward violence while Venom reinforces his body, the two influences can reinforce the same behavior without actually being the same thing.

Guts would feel it during fights first. An enemy hurts Casca or one of the others, the Beast pushes him toward rage, and Venom immediately responds by covering more of his body. Guts starts using more of the symbiote’s existing reinforcement and mobility at once, and the fight becomes much easier to finish because he stops caring how much damage he takes in return.

He could start relying on that state because it works. The Dragon Slayer becomes even more destructive when Venom reinforces both arms and stabilizes Guts through every swing. Tendrils can hold enemies in place or pull Guts toward them, and injuries that would normally slow him down can be held together long enough to keep fighting.

After one battle, Guts could keep attacking a dead Apostle or possessed enemy because the Beast is still pushing forward and Venom is still responding to the same anger. Someone from the group would have to get his attention before he finally pulls back.
Guts would begin separating the 2 influences more carefully after that.

Venom can speak to him directly, which means Guts can argue with it and set rules. The Beast can’t be managed the same way because it comes from Guts himself. He can blame Venom for making his body stronger, but he’d know the decision to keep attacking started inside him.

Instead of pretending every violent impulse comes from the symbiote, Guts would have to recognize when Venom is amplifying something he already wants to do. The bond becomes safer once he starts giving Venom clear limits before the fight begins rather than trying to regain control after his anger is already at its worst.

Venom would also start changing because of Guts. It would become more protective of the group after spending enough time around them, especially once it understands that losing Casca or the others would damage its host far more than losing a fight. That gives Venom reasons to resist the Beast when the Beast starts pushing Guts toward abandoning everyone. The symbiote could even become another voice telling Guts to stop when he starts going too far. That doesn’t make Venom harmless, and it wouldn’t suddenly become morally perfect. It still enjoys violence and has no problem killing things that threaten Guts. The bond simply becomes more complicated than Venom feeding his anger every time something goes wrong. Then Guts receives the Berserker Armor.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: The Berserker Armor would be both one of the best and worst things that could happen to this version of Guts. The armor already lets him ignore his body’s normal limits by suppressing pain and forcing damaged limbs back into working position. It can keep Guts fighting through broken bones and severe injuries, but the cost is that he can destroy himself without realizing how badly he’s hurt.

When Guts first wears the armor, the symbiote could reinforce his body underneath it. If a bone breaks, Venom can help hold it in place while the armor forces him to keep moving. If he starts bleeding heavily, the symbiote can slow the damage and keep more of his body functioning. That would let Guts stay effective for longer than he normally could. It would also make it easier for him to ignore injuries that should be telling him to stop.

The Berserker Armor already pushes Guts deeper into the Beast of Darkness, and Venom would be trapped inside that same state with him. Instead of Guts simply becoming faster and more savage, the symbiote could respond by covering any exposed parts of his body and extending tendrils through gaps in the armor.

His fighting style would change immediately. The Dragon Slayer could be pulled back toward him with a symbiote tendril if he loses his grip. Venom could anchor Guts to the ground when a larger Apostle tries throwing him, or help him change direction while the armor is driving his body beyond what normal muscles should manage.

That cooperation would probably take time because Venom’s instincts initially tell it to keep the host alive by making him stronger. Eventually, it would learn that making Guts stronger isn’t always the same as keeping him alive.

The Berserker Armor’s spikes and internal mechanisms would keep damaging Guts’ body, forcing Venom to spend more and more effort slowing blood loss, stabilizing tissue, and supporting injuries while the armor keeps him moving. The armor wouldn’t need to directly injure the symbiote itself for that constant stabilization to drain Venom and leave both of them weaker once the fight ends.

Guts would still need rest. He might recover faster than canon, but Venom can’t provide unlimited energy, and healing Guts after one of those battles would take a lot out of it. The group would start seeing both of them weakened at the same time instead of Venom functioning like an endless source of regeneration.

It also means Guts can’t simply use the combination every time something difficult appears. And when Griffith finally becomes the center of his attention again, Guts would have to decide whether he keeps those limits in place.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: Griffith would affect Venom more than any Apostle because of what he does to Guts emotionally. By the time Guts meets the reborn Griffith, Venom would already know who he is through memories of the Eclipse. It would know what happened to the Band of the Hawk, what happened to Casca, and why Guts spent years hunting Apostles afterward.

The first time they stand near Griffith together, Venom would feel Guts’ anger before he makes a move. Guts would probably struggle even more to stay still because Venom gives him the physical ability to act on that anger faster. He doesn’t need several seconds to build momentum behind the Dragon Slayer anymore. The symbiote can reinforce him almost instantly, and tendrils give him ways to attack from farther away.

That could change the Hill of Swords encounter. When Guts attacks Griffith in canon, Zodd intervenes and the fight becomes another reminder of how far Guts still is from reaching Griffith. With Venom, Guts would perform much better against Zodd. The extra strength and healing let him keep up longer, while tendrils make Zodd’s size easier to deal with because Guts can anchor himself or pull toward openings.

Zodd would still be extremely dangerous. He’s one of the strongest Apostles, and Venom doesn’t suddenly give Guts enough power to overpower him without effort. Zodd can take enormous punishment, transform, and continue fighting after injuries that would destroy weaker Apostles.

Guts could hurt him more consistently, though, and that would make the encounter last longer. Griffith would notice the symbiote through what it visibly does for Guts. He wouldn’t need to automatically sense that Venom comes from outside the normal rules of his world; seeing the living black material reinforce Guts, form tendrils, and change how he fights would be enough to recognize that Guts has gained another source of power. Whether Griffith understands exactly what Venom is would remain uncertain. Guts would want to keep pushing past Zodd and reach Griffith, but Casca being there would keep the situation from becoming a simple revenge fight. Once she’s endangered, Guts has to choose where his attention goes.

Venom would already know what that choice should be. After spending enough time with Guts, it would understand that losing Casca to reach Griffith would destroy the person it’s bonded to. It could urge Guts toward her, then reinforce his movements once he chooses to protect her rather than feeding the attempt to chase Griffith.

Griffith would still leave, and Guts would still hate that he couldn’t reach him. The difference is that Venom gives him a better chance when they finally fight again. Guts would have the Dragon Slayer, the Berserker Armor, Schierke helping him control it, and a symbiote that has spent years learning exactly how his body moves. Against Apostles and other physical enemies, that combination would make him far stronger than his canon version at the same point.

Griffith remains a much harder problem because his existence after becoming Femto isn’t something raw physical strength easily solves. Venom can help Guts reach enemies, survive attacks, and put more force behind the Dragon Slayer, but it can’t automatically remove the supernatural gap between Guts and a member of the God Hand.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: Venom would make Guts stronger almost everywhere that matters in a normal fight. He’d recover faster, survive worse injuries, move the Dragon Slayer with more control, and gain tendrils that work extremely well with the way he already fights.
Against most Apostles, the improvement would be huge.

The harder part would be keeping the bond from making Guts more willing to stay angry because anger keeps producing results. During the Black Swordsman period, that could easily make him worse. Once Casca, Puck, Schierke, and the others become part of his life again, Venom would also be exposed to the people keeping Guts connected to something beyond revenge.

By the time he gets the Berserker Armor, Venom could either make the Beast of Darkness much harder to control or become another thing helping Guts pull himself back, depending on how much the symbiote has changed with him.
That’s probably where the bond ends up. Venom becomes one of Guts’ strongest weapons, but Guts would still have to decide how much of himself he’s willing to give it every time he uses that power.

scripts.title: What If Henry Emily Became A Killer

sections.name: INTRO
paras: Henry Emily becoming the killer would change FNAF long before the missing children ever disappear. Fredbear’s would still begin with Henry and William building something together, but Henry’s role as the engineer gives him a very different path once things start going wrong.

Once Henry sees one of his machines moving in ways he never programmed, he’d know something is off. At that point, hiding the murder gets harder because the animatronics are starting to behave like the person he killed is still there.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: Fredbear’s Family Diner would still start with Henry Emily and William Afton building the business together, and Henry would still spend most of his time around the machines. He’d be the 1 fixing small mechanical problems, adjusting the springlock suits, and staying after closing because something about Fredbear or Spring Bonnie still wasn’t working the way he wanted. William would handle more of the business side while Henry kept pushing the technical side forward, and for a while that arrangement would work because they needed each other.

The problem starts when one of the employees gets badly hurt while using a springlock suit. Henry would know straight away how serious it is because he understands exactly how much can go wrong when the mechanism slips. The employee survives, but afterward he starts talking about going to the authorities and showing people that the suits were unsafe long before the accident happened. He has enough photos, maintenance notes, and firsthand experience to make Fredbear’s look reckless, and Henry knows an outside investigation could shut the place down.

At first Henry would try to contain it the way he usually handles problems. He’d offer to pay for medical bills, promise the suits are being redesigned, and insist that nobody else is going to be allowed near the same mechanism until he fixes it. The employee keeps pushing because he believes management already knew the suits were dangerous, and eventually the argument turns into something Henry can’t solve with another repair.
That’s where Henry crosses the line for the first time.

He could ask the employee to come back after hours, saying he wants to show him what failed and prove that the problem has already been corrected. Once they’re inside the maintenance area, Henry knows every blind spot, every door, and every machine loud enough to cover noise from the rest of the building. The confrontation gets physical, and Henry kills him by deliberately triggering an animatronic mechanism the employee is working against, leaving the victim trapped in direct contact with the same mechanism long enough for Henry to stage the scene afterward.

Henry would panic afterward, but he’d also understand the scene better than anyone who comes in later. He could damage part of the springlock mechanism and make the death look like another failure involving equipment the employee already complained about. The explanation would sound believable because Henry can describe exactly how that kind of accident happens, and nobody else around Fredbear’s understands the machinery well enough to challenge him immediately.

William would notice that Henry acts different after the death, especially because some maintenance records from that week are suddenly missing or rewritten. He’d probably assume Henry is covering up negligence before he assumes murder, which gives Henry room to get away with it. The restaurant stays open, the investigation goes nowhere serious, and Henry gets to see that the story he built around the machine worked.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: After the first murder, Henry would become much harder to work with. He’d start keeping more maintenance work to himself, locking rooms that used to stay open, and limiting which employees are allowed to inspect the springlock suits. Anyone asking why would hear that he’s trying to prevent another accident, which sounds reasonable enough after someone already died inside the building.

William would eventually get tired of it because the business is growing and Henry is making basic repairs slower by refusing to trust anyone else. More technicians are needed, especially if they want to expand beyond one small diner, while Henry keeps treating every new employee like another person who might notice something he missed during the cover-up. Their partnership would start getting tense because William sees Henry becoming controlling without understanding the full reason behind it.

The next real problem could come from a technician who notices something wrong with the original accident report. He doesn’t have to know Henry killed anyone. All he needs to notice is that the damaged mechanism doesn’t match the kind of failure Henry described. Maybe a piece was bent from the wrong direction, or a safety part was removed before the damage happened, and the technician mentions that he wants someone outside the company to look at it.

Henry would have more time to think this time, which makes the second murder much worse. He could arrange for the technician to work alone on one of the animatronics after closing, then disable a safety stop or alter the movement range before leaving the machine in a position where it can crush or trap someone. When the body is found, Henry can point to another mechanical failure and explain how old equipment caused it.

By then William would start keeping copies of anything Henry touches. He’d save maintenance logs before Henry changes them and pay more attention to which employees have problems with the equipment before something happens to them. He still wouldn’t have proof that Henry is killing people, but two serious incidents connected to people questioning the machinery would be hard to ignore.

Charlotte would also start seeing a different side of her father because Henry would become much more protective of where she goes inside Fredbear’s. He’d keep her away from the workshop and get angry if she wanders toward locked areas because he knows there are things inside the building she can never find. To her, it would feel like Henry has become obsessed with rules for no clear reason.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: The supernatural side of the story would begin after Henry notices the same animatronic involved in the employee’s death behaving strangely afterward. He might find an animatronic active after the power should be off or see it repeatedly turn toward a maintenance room it has no reason to recognize. His first instinct would be to treat it like a technical problem, so he’d pull the machine apart, replace components, and check the programming until he’s sure the behavior shouldn't still be happening.
When it keeps happening anyway, Henry would start testing it instead of reporting it.

He could move the animatronic into another room, switch parts between machines, and remove anything he thinks might be causing the behavior. If the same machine still reacts to places or people connected to the death, Henry would realize he’s dealing with something he can’t explain through normal engineering. That wouldn’t make him immediately understand possession, but it would be enough to make him curious.

That curiosity would become dangerous because Henry is already used to solving problems by taking things apart and testing them. He’d want to know whether the strange behavior only happened because of that specific death or whether it can happen again under similar conditions. The more he tests, the more he starts looking at the people around Fredbear’s as variables in something he thinks he can understand.

The first child he targets could be someone who regularly stays late and trusts him because he’s one of the owners. Henry wouldn’t need a costume or some elaborate act to get the child into a back room because the kid already knows him. He could say one of the characters needs help or that there’s something new in the workshop, and once the child follows him, Henry would have full control over the environment.

After the murder, he hides the body inside or in direct contact with one of the animatronics because he wants to see whether the same behavior happens again. When the machine starts moving differently afterward, Henry finally has the result he was looking for. He then removes and disposes of the physical remains before routine maintenance can expose them, while keeping contaminated components, altered internal parts, and detailed notes from the machine for later experiments. It still wouldn’t explain how the effect works, but now he knows the first incident wasn’t isolated.

That’s how the Missing Children Incident could begin in this version. Henry keeps targeting children because each disappearance gives him another chance to compare how different machines respond afterward. He’d document what changes, which characters become more aggressive, and whether certain movements repeat around places connected to the victims. His background as an engineer would shape the murders because he’d treat every supernatural reaction like data.

William would start seeing the pattern from the outside. Children are disappearing from places tied to the business, Henry keeps spending extra time around the animatronics afterward, and certain machines suddenly need private maintenance whenever another family reports someone missing. He’d begin checking staff schedules and security records on his own, especially once he realizes some of the disappearances happened while Henry was still inside the building.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: William would reach the point where he can’t keep treating the disappearances like something happening around the business by coincidence. He’d start checking Henry’s movements against the nights children vanished and comparing those dates with maintenance records. If Henry repeatedly logged work on the same animatronics shortly after a disappearance, William would have enough reason to keep digging even if he still couldn’t prove what happened.

He’d also start asking his own children whether they’ve noticed anything strange around the restaurant. The Crying Child could tell him that Henry repeatedly acts strange around restricted rooms, becomes angry when children get too close to employee-only areas, or appears in back hallways at times when nobody else is supposed to be there, while Michael might remember that certain areas always got locked after closing. Those details wouldn't solve the case, but they would line up with the records William is already collecting.

Charlotte would become important because she knows Henry’s habits better than almost anyone. William could ask whether her father has been staying late, taking work home, or getting angry whenever she goes near specific rooms. Charlotte might not understand why the questions matter, but she could remember enough to make William more certain that Henry is hiding something.

Henry would notice William getting closer. He’d find copies missing from a file cabinet, catch him checking a maintenance room without asking, or realize that William knows about a schedule he never shared with him. Henry wouldn’t know exactly what William has found, which would make him more nervous because he can’t tell whether the investigation is still private or whether someone outside the company is involved.

Charlotte would also feel her father changing around her. If William quietly spoke to her about the disappearances and Henry somehow found out, Henry would probably become much stricter about where she goes and who she talks to. He’d still try to explain it as concern for her safety, but Charlotte would know the rules appeared right after she answered questions about him.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: The Crying Child could still end up terrified of Fredbear’s, although the reason would be more connected to what he has seen around Henry and the back rooms. He wouldn't understand the murders, but he would know people disappear around the restaurant and that his father becomes tense whenever Henry is nearby. Michael could still tease him because from his perspective his younger brother is terrified of cartoon mascots and dark hallways.

If Michael and his friends carry the Crying Child toward Fredbear as a joke, Henry would be there when everything goes wrong. The moment Fredbear bites down, Henry would rush over and try to release the mechanism himself because he knows exactly how the jaw system works. William would be watching his son get pulled out of a machine Henry built while he’s already spent months connecting Henry to disappearances and suspicious accidents, so from that point on, anything Henry says about safety would mean very little to him.

The Crying Child could still die from the injuries. William would understand that the Bite itself came from Michael and his friends putting the child into an operating Fredbear rather than from another secret mechanical failure engineered by Henry, but watching his son die in one of Henry’s machines would still push him to go through every older incident connected to Fredbear’s with much more urgency. The first employee death would come back into focus because William now knows Henry has been involved in several suspicious incidents around the machinery, and some of the explanations from years earlier would look much less convincing once he compares them with newer maintenance documents.

Henry would have problems of his own because the Bite could shut Fredbear’s down or force major parts of the equipment into storage. Machines he kept in controlled rooms would suddenly be moved, inspected, and handled by technicians who have no idea why Henry is so protective of them. That makes it much harder to hide the bodies, strange behavior, and modifications he’s been studying.

The possessed animatronics could become more unstable once they’re moved. One might activate during transport, another could react violently when a technician tries to dismantle it, and Henry would know those incidents are connected to whatever supernatural effect the children's deaths left behind in the machines, even if he still couldn't prove that literal spirits were trapped inside them. William would only see another reason to believe something deeply wrong is happening around Henry’s machines.

Elizabeth’s future would change heavily from here because William wouldn’t be building the same child-capturing animatronics he creates in the original timeline. He has no reason to design Circus Baby as a machine made to lure and kill children, which gives Elizabeth a much better chance of surviving childhood. Michael’s life would also move in a different direction because instead of eventually being sent to clean up William’s crimes, he’d grow up watching his father try to prove that Henry is responsible for what happened to their family.

Charlotte would still be alive as well, which makes Henry’s situation worse because she’s old enough to see how much everyone around him is changing. She could start comparing what William says with what she remembers from Fredbear’s and realize that several of her father’s stories don’t line up. Henry would know his own daughter is getting closer to the truth at the same time William is pushing harder.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Once Fredbear’s starts shutting down and equipment gets moved around, William would finally get access to things Henry had controlled for years. Old maintenance rooms would be cleared out, storage would be inventoried, and records that used to sit under Henry’s supervision would pass through other hands. William would use that chance to compare early accident reports with newer technical notes and look for anything that shows Henry changed his story over time.

The first employee death would probably become the easiest place to start. William could find that parts Henry described as failed had damage that doesn’t match normal wear, especially once another technician looks at the same assembly without knowing the original explanation. From there, William could connect that accident to the later technician death and start seeing the same pattern in how Henry handled both scenes. In each case, Henry controlled the machinery, wrote the explanation, and had access to the area before anyone else understood what happened.

The missing children would be harder because there may be less physical evidence left, but William would know where to look by then. He could focus on the animatronics Henry repeatedly serviced after disappearances and start checking inside them with another technician present. That could lead to stains, clothing fibers, damaged internal parts, or something else that makes it clear the machines were used to hide more than mechanical problems.

Charlotte could end up confirming one of the last pieces without knowing how important it is. She might remember Henry behaving unusually around the workshop and restricted areas, or hearing him working late on a machine the same night someone vanished. William wouldn't need her to know what happened inside the room. He’d already have enough surrounding evidence to know that Henry’s access and the disappearances line up.

At that point, William would stop treating the situation as a private business problem. He’d begin preparing to take the evidence outside the company, knowing Henry has already killed people who got too close. He’d probably keep Michael and Elizabeth away from the restaurants completely and make sure Charlotte isn’t left alone with Henry either, even if that means openly breaking whatever trust is left between the two families.

Henry would see that as William taking his daughter away from him along with the company they built together. He’d be under pressure from every direction by then, and instead of admitting what he did, he’d start thinking about how to keep William from handing over the evidence.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Henry would know he can’t handle William the same way he handled employees. If William suddenly dies in another mechanical accident after months of openly questioning him, the timing would be impossible to ignore. Henry would need something that looks less connected to Fredbear’s, which would push him toward using the skills he has outside the restaurant.

He could build a small device into William’s car or workshop equipment, something designed to fail later without immediately pointing back to him. Henry’s engineering background gives him plenty of ways to make an accident look believable, but William is already suspicious enough to check anything unusual around him. If he finds tampering before the device works, then Henry loses the last bit of uncertainty William still had about whether he’s capable of deliberate murder. That discovery would probably push William into confronting him before the police investigation is fully ready. He’d want to know how far the killings go, whether the children are really inside the animatronics, and whether Henry has done anything else that hasn’t been found yet. Henry would know that answering any of those questions honestly ends his life as he knows it, so the argument would turn into the first time the 2 of them openly acknowledge what's been happening.

The confrontation could become physical once Henry realizes William intends to leave with evidence. William may not be the murderer in this version, but he still understands the springlock systems and knows enough about the buildings to defend himself. Henry would have the stronger technical advantage, while William would know him well enough to expect that he'll try to use the environment.

Charlotte could arrive during or shortly after that confrontation and finally see enough to understand what her father has become. She might find William injured, see evidence from the missing children laid out, or hear Henry admit enough during the argument that there’s no way to explain it away afterward. Henry would have to face the fact that Charlotte now knows the truth too.

He wouldn't be able to bring himself to kill her. That hesitation would matter because it gives William and Charlotte time to get away with the evidence Henry was trying to recover. For years, Henry had been able to control what other people saw because he controlled the machines and the rooms where the crimes happened. Once Charlotte leaves with William, that control is gone.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: Henry would disappear before police can properly arrest him, taking whatever notes and equipment he can carry while leaving behind most of the company. By now he knows the victims’ deaths have left some persistent supernatural influence attached to the animatronics and has spent years trying to understand what that influence actually is, so his next move would revolve around that instead of trying to rebuild Fredbear’s.

He could start recovering parts from the machines before authorities seize everything, especially components from the animatronics connected to the children. Henry would already know that moving parts between machines sometimes changes how they behave, and that would lead him toward experimenting with whatever supernatural effect is inside them.

This version of Henry could become obsessed with separating the children from the machines because that would solve 2 problems at once. It would remove some of the evidence against him and give him a better understanding of what he accidentally created. He might tell himself he’s trying to free them, but his experiments would still involve taking the animatronics apart and treating the spirits inside them like another system he can test.

Michael’s role would be very different from the original timeline. He wouldn't be trying to undo William’s crimes or follow instructions from a father who caused everything. He’d be helping William track Henry and recover the animatronics before Henry can dismantle them further. Michael would also have a personal reason to stay involved because the Crying Child died in one of Henry’s machines, even if that death itself was still an accident.

Charlotte would probably become the person most determined to understand what her father was doing. She’d have access to his habits, his old notes, and his way of thinking, which could make her more useful than anyone else when William tries to predict where Henry went. That also creates a painful dynamic because every new clue confirms that Henry had been lying to her for years while using the same machines she grew up around.

Eventually, they could track him to an abandoned Fazbear location where he has been working with the remaining animatronics. Henry would have fewer resources by then, but he’d know the building and the machines better than anyone coming after him.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: The final confrontation could happen when William, Michael, and Charlotte find Henry trying to dismantle one of the possessed animatronics. By this point, Henry would believe he’s close to understanding how the spirits are attached to the machines, and he’d be too far into the obsession to leave the work behind.

The animatronics themselves would make the situation harder because the children inside them would recognize Henry. They could become aggressive as soon as he’s cornered, especially if he’s already taken apart parts of the suits they’re attached to. William and the others would be trying to avoid getting caught between Henry and machines that have spent years reacting violently to adults inside Freddy’s.

Henry would still know how to use the building to his advantage. He could shut doors remotely, cut power to certain rooms, or trigger old mechanisms to slow William and Michael down. Charlotte would probably be the one person he keeps trying to avoid hurting directly, which gives her more freedom to move through the building and reach him.

When she finally confronts him, Henry would have nowhere left to hide behind technical explanations. Charlotte knows about the murders, William has the evidence, and the animatronics around them are proof that whatever Henry thought he was studying came from children he killed.

Henry could try retreating into one of the old springlock suits because his earlier experiments showed that the possessed animatronics sometimes hesitate or misidentify a person hidden inside a familiar character suit. That would mirror William’s original fate without simply copying it for the sake of familiarity. Henry knows exactly how dangerous the old springlocks are, but with the animatronics closing in, the suit looks like the only option that has previously made them hesitate. He chooses the immediate chance of surviving them over the mechanical risk because it is one of the few pieces of technology he still understands completely. The problem is that the suit is old, damaged, and being used under pressure.
The locks would fail around him, leaving Henry trapped inside the suit.

William would know better than to assume that ends everything, especially after years of seeing the animatronics continue moving after death. He’d have Henry’s body and the suit contained instead of sealing him inside a forgotten room, because by now everyone involved understands that death around these machines can make the situation worse.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: If Henry Emily became the killer, FNAF would end up looking very different because his crimes would grow out of control, secrecy, and his obsession with understanding the machines he built. The first murder could start as an attempt to protect Fredbear’s, but once Henry learns how easily his technical knowledge can hide what happened, he’d keep using that advantage until the disappearances become part of something much worse.

William would spend most of this timeline trying to figure out what his business partner is hiding, while Michael, Elizabeth, the Crying Child, and Charlotte all end up with different lives because William never becomes the person building machines to kill children. Elizabeth could survive, Charlotte would never become the Puppet through her original death, and Michael could grow up helping his father stop Henry instead of cleaning up after him.

Henry discovering possession would also make him more dangerous because he’d treat it like another engineering problem and keep experimenting until he understands enough to make things worse. By the time William and Charlotte finally expose him, the company and both families would already be damaged by years of murders and cover ups.

scripts.title: What If Invincible Had The Omnitrix

sections.name: INTRO
paras: If Invincible had the Omnitrix, Mark would become a superhero before his Viltrumite powers even showed up.

I'd have the Omnitrix reach Earth when Mark's still waiting for his powers and starting to wonder if he’ll ever be like his dad. It gives him another way in. One minute he’s a normal teenager, and the next he can turn into alien species strong enough to let him start saving people on his own. Then his Viltrumite powers finally kick in.

Now Mark can fly and hit hard without the watch, while the Omnitrix gives him completely different bodies whenever strength isn’t enough. And once Nolan sees Mark transform for the first time, he’d immediately want to know where that watch came from and what else it can turn his son into.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: The Omnitrix would reach Mark a few months before his Viltrumite powers finally develop. He's 17 and starting to wonder whether those powers are ever coming. Nolan keeps telling him Viltrumite abilities can develop late, but that doesn’t make it any easier watching his dad fly off to save the world while Mark goes to school and works at Burger Mart.

One night after work, Mark sees a green object tear across the sky and disappear beyond the city. He knows chasing unidentified objects from space is probably a terrible idea when your dad spends half his life fighting aliens, but he goes anyway. He eventually reaches a small crater and finds a damaged pod sitting in the middle of it. The pod opens as he gets closer, revealing what looks like a watch inside, and the second Mark reaches toward it, the device launches onto his wrist and locks itself around him.

Mark spends the next few minutes pulling at it, pressing buttons, and trying everything he can think of to get it off. Instead, he accidentally raises the dial and sees a strange silhouette appear across its face. He presses it down and green light fills the crater as his entire body starts changing. When Mark can see himself again, he’s several feet taller, bright red, and looking down at 4 enormous arms.

He has no idea he’s become a Tetramand or that the alien is called 4 Arms. Mark just knows he finally has strength. He grabs a fallen tree and lifts it easily, then tries something heavier and realizes he can move that too. He starts laughing because after years of waiting for his Viltrumite powers, an alien watch has somehow given him exactly what he wanted in less than 10 minutes.

The Omnitrix times out while Mark is still experimenting, changing him back before he can understand why. The symbol turns red and stops responding, so Mark hides the device under his sleeve and goes home. He considers telling Nolan immediately, but that would probably end
with the watch being taken away before Mark gets another chance to use it. He decides he'll figure out a little more first and tell his parents once he knows what he’s dealing with.

That plan survives until the following afternoon. Mark is walking home when a driver loses control at an intersection and a car jumps toward a crowded sidewalk. Mark reaches for the watch before he has time to think about getting caught. Four Arms appears again, and Mark plants himself in front of the car and catches it hard enough that his feet tear through the pavement. He puts it down, checks that everyone is okay, then notices half the intersection pointing phones at him.

Mark gets away before the Omnitrix changes him back, but the footage is everywhere by the time he reaches home. Debbie is watching a news report about a mysterious red alien that saved several people downtown, while Nolan is standing behind the couch studying the footage much more carefully. Mark tries to walk upstairs until Nolan asks him to show him what's underneath his sleeve.

Mark tells them about the pod and transforms in front of them. Debbie is mostly concerned that an alien device attached itself permanently to her son, while Nolan wants to know where the pod came from, whether anything else arrived with it, and how many species Mark can become. Mark doesn’t know. Nolan has spent centuries traveling between inhabited worlds and has seen technology far beyond anything humans can build, yet he can’t identify the device his son is wearing.

Nolan tells Mark to stop using it until they understand it better. Mark agrees because arguing with Omni Man while standing in his living room probably isn’t getting him anywhere, but finding the Omnitrix has already changed what he thinks he can do. For the first time, Mark doesn’t have to wait for his Viltrumite blood before he can start becoming a hero.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Mark starts experimenting whenever he can get away without Nolan noticing. He still can’t read the symbols properly, so most of his early transformations are guesses. Four Arms is the only one he recognizes immediately, and Mark naturally keeps going back to him because strength is the power he spent his entire childhood expecting to have.

The watch forces him out of that habit pretty quickly. Mark sees an armed robbery while he’s out one afternoon and tries selecting Four Arms before running inside. The transformation finishes and he looks down to find a much smaller body with wheels on his feet. He barely has time to complain before one of the robbers points a gun at him, and Mark moves instinctively.

Mark crosses the store before the robber can finish pulling the trigger, takes the gun, and keeps moving until he slams into a display because he has no idea how to stop. He gets back up and tries again, this time slowing before each turn. Within seconds, he’s taken the weapons from the other robbers and moved the customers outside. By the time the police arrive, XLR8 has become Mark's favorite transformation.

Another fight introduces him to Diamondhead when the Omnitrix gives him the wrong alien again. A bullet hits Mark before he can get behind cover and breaks apart against his chest. He looks at the fragments on the ground, realizes his body barely felt it, and starts experimenting during the fight. Crystal grows from his hands when he focuses on it, letting him block the next shots and trap the criminals behind a wall instead of trying to punch everyone.

Nolan catches him first. Mark comes home after another fight and finds Nolan waiting in his room. Nolan has already seen enough footage to know Mark ignored him, so instead of asking whether he used the watch, he tells Mark to transform and show him exactly what he’s learned. Mark picks Four Arms and Nolan tells him to attack.

Mark throws a cautious punch that Nolan catches with 1 hand. Nolan tells him to hit harder, so Mark plants his feet and throws another with everything the transformation can give him. Nolan catches that too, although this time Mark can tell he had to put slightly more effort into it.
