Preventing it could save them while giving him his first chance to strike at the organization decades before it openly reveals itself.

The problem is that Tony doesn’t have an Iron Man suit yet. Arc reactor technology hasn't been miniaturized, his later fabrication systems don’t exist, and most of the materials he eventually uses haven't been developed in the forms he remembers. He can picture Mark armor designs perfectly, but remembering a finished machine doesn’t give 1991 manufacturing the ability to produce it overnight.

So Tony would work with what already exists. He still has access to Stark resources, and more importantly, he knows which technologies are worth accelerating. Instead of trying to recreate the Mark 85 20 years early, he’d start with surveillance, encrypted communications, lightweight body armor, vehicle tracking, and compact electronics that are only a few steps beyond what his current labs can realistically build. The goal for now is keeping two people alive and figuring out who else is involved.

Howard would notice the change in him almost immediately. Tony is still physically his younger self, but he suddenly stops acting like the son Howard remembers. His technical work becomes more focused, his drinking drops, and he starts asking questions about S.H.I.E.L.D., Zola, old HYDRA assets, and security around Stark Industries that he shouldn’t have any reason to care about yet.

Tony would know how dangerous it is to tell Howard the whole truth. Explaining Thanos, time travel, the Avengers, and a daughter who hasn't been born would make him sound unstable even if Howard believed parts of it. He’d keep the story smaller and tell his father he found evidence that someone connected to Stark’s defense work is planning an attack against the family.

Howard wouldn't accept that without proof, so Tony would give him just enough. He knows the date, the rough circumstances, and that the attack is tied to the Super Soldier Serum Howard is transporting. He could also point toward security weaknesses around the route and explain details no ordinary threat assessment should predict.

Maria would be much easier for Tony to be around and much harder emotionally. He remembers losing her when he was young, then living the rest of his life with only memories and old recordings. Having her speak to him normally would make the second chance feel real in a way the date on a computer never could.

That’s also when Morgan would hit him hardest. Tony can save his parents because they already exist in this timeline. Morgan only exists if an enormous number of events happen in roughly the right way. Pepper has to become part of his life, their relationship has to survive years of chaos, the Snap has to happen or at least enough of Tony’s life has to follow a similar path for them to have the same child.
On December 16, Howard and Maria would never take the route HYDRA expects them to take. Tony would make sure somebody is waiting for the Winter Soldier instead.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Tony wouldn't try to fight Bucky himself. Even with decades of memories in his head, his younger body has none of the physical experience that later lets him survive battles in armor, and Bucky in 1991 is a brainwashed super soldier sent to complete a clean assassination. Walking into that encounter with a gun would get Tony killed.

He’d build the trap around information. Howard and Maria would be moved to a secure location before the original trip begins, while a decoy vehicle follows enough of the expected route to make HYDRA believe the plan is still intact. Tony would put cameras and trackers throughout the area because he wants more than survival. If he can record who attacks, where they go afterward, and what equipment they’re using, he has a path back toward the people controlling Bucky.

The Winter Soldier would still hit the vehicle with overwhelming force. The attack happens quickly because HYDRA expects two unprepared civilians, and Bucky would realize something is wrong as soon as he reaches the wreck and finds no one inside.

Tony’s trap would activate before he can leave. He wouldn't have repulsors yet, but Stark Industries already builds weapons and advanced electronics. Tony could use remotely triggered explosives to close roads without hitting Bucky directly, electrified restraint systems designed around the strength he remembers, and multiple armored barriers that force Bucky toward one route. None of those tools can hold a super soldier for long, but Tony only needs enough time to identify him and track his escape.

Bucky would tear through the first restraint and likely destroy several cameras once he notices them. Tony would expect that and bury redundancy into the setup. One camera gets destroyed while another records from farther away, and the trap is designed to attach a small tracker to Bucky, his vehicle, or equipment he takes with him, giving Tony a trail once Bucky retreats.

The most important moment comes when Tony sees his face. He already knew who was coming, but seeing Bucky in 1991 would bring back the Siberia fight in a way memory alone couldn't. Tony remembers trying to kill him, Steve standing between them, and the rage that made every explanation meaningless for those few minutes.

He has enough distance from that version of himself now to make another choice. Tony would follow the tracker instead of chasing Bucky personally. The signal could lead toward a HYDRA safe location or at least a transfer point connected to the Winter Soldier program. Tony would copy everything he can before the site realizes it has been compromised, then pull back before somebody inside recognizes the scale of the breach.

Howard would have no choice but to take Tony seriously after that. His son just predicted an assassination attempt down to the date and exposed a brainwashed enhanced assassin tied to an organization that supposedly died during World War II. Howard’s first instinct would probably be contacting S.H.I.E.L.D., which is where Tony would have to stop him. Tony knows HYDRA is already inside. He can’t identify every compromised agent in 1991 from memory, and handing the evidence to the wrong person could warn HYDRA before he understands how much of the organization has been infected. He’d tell Howard enough about Arnim Zola’s infiltration and the recruitment that followed to convince him that S.H.I.E.L.D. itself needs to be treated as compromised until they can verify individual people.

That creates a very different relationship between Tony and his father. Howard is still difficult, proud, and used to being the smartest person in the room, but now Tony is operating with knowledge that repeatedly puts him ahead. They would argue constantly over how much to reveal and who to trust, yet Tony would finally have something he never got in his first life: time to actually work with his father as an adult.

Saving Howard also changes Stark Industries immediately. Obadiah Stane no longer has the same path toward controlling the company after Howard’s death, and Tony doesn’t inherit the business while he’s still emotionally unprepared to run it. He has to work beside Howard instead of replacing him.

Tony would accept that because his priorities have already moved far beyond becoming CEO. There’s a hidden HYDRA network inside American intelligence, Bucky is still being controlled somewhere, Steve is frozen in the Arctic, and Tony knows all of those problems can be addressed years before anyone originally finds them.
He’d start with HYDRA because every other plan becomes safer once they stop listening from inside S.H.I.E.L.D.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Tony’s memories give him names, but they don’t give him a complete map of HYDRA in 1991. Alexander Pierce eventually becomes one of the organization’s most important leaders inside S.H.I.E.L.D., Arnim Zola’s mind survives digitally, and the Winter Soldier program operates for years without the agency admitting what’s happening. Tony knows enough to begin looking, but he can’t assume every person involved in 2014 holds the same position more than twenty years earlier.

Howard would quietly give Tony access to old S.H.I.E.L.D. records and Stark defense contracts, letting him search for patterns around Zola’s work after Operation Paperclip. Tony could compare personnel transfers, unusual black budget projects, missing research, and any programs that overlap with the Winter Soldier attack. His later experience with Ultron and artificial intelligence would also make him recognize the importance of Zola’s digital preservation much earlier than anyone else.

Tony could warn Howard that Zola’s work survived inside S.H.I.E.L.D. far longer than anyone realized, without pretending to know exactly how or where. Howard’s knowledge of Zola’s postwar projects could give them a starting point, but locating him would still take a sustained investigation. Tony and Howard could trace unusual computer requisitions made around Zola’s work, maintenance records that continue after his physical death, power demands from otherwise obsolete facilities, and transfers of hardware tied to his research. Following those overlapping records could gradually narrow the search to the specific legacy computer infrastructure where they discover that Zola preserved his consciousness digitally. Once they confirm what happened, HYDRA loses one of its biggest advantages. Zola’s information could identify compromised agents, early versions of the algorithm that eventually becomes Project Insight, and locations connected to HYDRA operations around the world. Tony would be careful about trusting any single file because Zola is intelligent enough to feed him bad information once he realizes he’s trapped, so every name would be checked against outside evidence before Tony acts.

Hydra originally had decades to grow inside S.H.I.E.L.D. Tony is attacking it before many later operations happen, which means people will move, projects will be abandoned, and new leadership could emerge once the organization realizes someone is hunting it. Every successful raid makes his memories of 2014 less useful because the enemy begins adapting to a future that no longer exists.

Natasha hasn’t joined S.H.I.E.L.D. yet. Clint hasn’t become the person Tony later knows. Fury is younger and may not hold the same authority. Steve is still missing. Tony knows who these people become, but approaching them now could change their lives before they reach the experiences that made them useful in the first place.

Bucky is the exception. Tony has no reason to leave him under HYDRA control for another 20 years. Using information recovered from Zola and the assassination site, Tony and Howard could begin narrowing down the facilities connected to the Winter Soldier program. They wouldn't storm one with Stark security and hope for the best. Tony would use surveillance and remote systems to identify when Bucky is being moved, then target the people controlling him rather than trying to overpower him directly.

If Tony and Howard can keep following the Winter Soldier network before HYDRA fully adapts and disappears underground, they could eventually get an opportunity to recover Bucky alive. Helping him afterward would take time. HYDRA has repeatedly wiped and conditioned his mind, and Tony has none of Wakanda’s later technology or expertise available. What he does have is knowledge of what Bucky becomes once that control is broken, so he’d treat him as a victim of the program even when Howard struggles with the idea of keeping the man sent to murder them anywhere nearby.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Finding Steve early would still be possible, but it wouldn’t be one of Tony’s easier changes. Tony can’t provide exact coordinates because he never personally recovered Steve, but he can tell Howard with certainty that the Valkyrie survived somewhere in the Arctic and that Steve is still alive inside it. That certainty changes the search completely. Instead of eventually accepting that Steve is lost, Howard can keep directing Stark resources toward improved radar, imaging, and ice-penetrating search technology over the following years until they narrow down the wreck. Howard would have personal reasons to keep supporting the effort. He spent years looking for Steve after the war and never found him, so learning from Tony that Steve is still alive somewhere under the ice would reopen something Howard had already accepted as impossible.

The Steve Rogers who wakes up in the 1990s isn’t the man Tony fought beside against Thanos. He hasn't met Sam, hasn’t watched S.H.I.E.L.D. collapse, hasn’t learned Bucky survived, and hasn't gone through any of the experiences that eventually led to Civil War. Tony remembers years of friendship and conflict with someone who sees him as Howard Stark’s young son.

He could explain that Bucky is alive much earlier, and once Steve sees him recovering from HYDRA conditioning, Tony gains someone who will never stop pushing to help him. That could dramatically improve Bucky’s recovery because Steve is one of the strongest connections to his original identity.

Tony would also know how easily Steve can become suspicious if people hide things from him, so he’d tell him most of the truth about HYDRA without revealing the entire future at once. Steve can help dismantle the organization because he already understands what HYDRA is and has experience fighting it, while his existence gives Howard and Tony someone they can trust outside the compromised intelligence structure.

Steve’s return would become public eventually, and that creates a huge change in American history. Captain America is alive in the 1990s instead of returning after 2011, while the government suddenly has to explain how he was recovered and what happens to him now. Tony would push against letting any agency simply take control of Steve's life, especially because he knows S.H.I.E.L.D. still needs to be cleaned out.

The Avengers as Tony remembers them may never form. Steve is active early, Bucky is free, Howard is alive, and HYDRA is being dismantled years before Project Insight. Tony hasn’t become Iron Man because Afghanistan is still far in the future, and Bruce hasn’t become Hulk yet. Thor is still on Asgard and has no reason to come to Earth.

Tony would see that as proof the second life is working. Then he’d remember that changing the team doesn’t remove the threats that forced them together. Loki is still out there. Thanos still wants the Infinity Stones. The Tesseract is already on Earth, and Tony knows exactly how dangerous that becomes once someone starts experimenting with it.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: By the late 1990s, Tony would already be years ahead of where he was during his original life, but he still wouldn't have recreated every piece of Endgame technology. Progress would come through infrastructure. Better processors allow better simulations, improved manufacturing gives him materials closer to what later suits need, and advances in energy storage move him toward the compact power systems he knows are possible.

He'd start working on arc reactor miniaturization long before Afghanistan forces him to solve it under pressure. Howard already understands the larger arc reactor concept, and Tony knows the small version can work because he built one in a cave from scraps. With proper laboratories and years of research, the development would happen much earlier and with far fewer dead ends.

Tony would also begin designing armor, although the first versions would look closer to experimental powered exoskeletons than the Iron Man suits he remembers. Flight is one of the hardest parts because stable repulsor control requires software, materials, and power density that all need to mature together. Tony can accelerate that process by skipping design mistakes he already remembers making, but he still has to physically build each step.

The first Iron Man suit originally comes from Tony realizing his weapons have been used to hurt innocent people and deciding he needs to take responsibility personally. This Tony already lived through that lesson. Stark Industries would begin leaving the weapons business much earlier, creating major political and financial consequences while Howard is still alive to argue with him about it.

Tony would have to explain why he suddenly wants to dismantle one of the company’s most profitable divisions. Howard may eventually understand after seeing HYDRA manipulate Stark technology, but governments and contractors depending on those weapons won't simply accept the decision. Other companies would rush to fill the gap, and some of the weapons Tony prevents Stark from selling could still be built by competitors with fewer restrictions.

Tony would start thinking more carefully about Thanos for the same reason. He knows the Infinity Stones are eventually spread across different worlds, but several of them aren't realistically accessible to him yet. He can secure the Tesseract more carefully and warn people about what it is, but he can’t travel to Vormir, take the Time Stone from the Ancient One, or simply collect the entire set before Thanos does.

That memory would keep him from repeating the exact project, but it wouldn't stop Tony from wanting a planetary defense system. He’d begin developing satellites, early autonomous response technology, and armor that can be operated remotely, while making sure no single artificial intelligence gets unrestricted control over the entire network. Steve would push him whenever the system starts becoming too centralized. Their disagreements would begin years before the original Avengers ever meet, but this time Tony already understands where their worst argument eventually ends. He’d listen more often, even when it frustrates him, because he remembers what happened when both of them became convinced the other person was refusing to see reason.
Tony would eventually need to think about the people who still haven't entered his life.

Bruce Banner will become Hulk if the gamma experiment happens as he remembers. Natasha will eventually become one of his closest friends after a life Tony knows only in pieces. Clint will build a family Tony eventually risks everything to bring back. Thor will arrive on Earth after being cast out by Odin.

Pepper would be the person Tony struggles with most. By the time their paths are supposed to cross, Tony has already spent years remembering a marriage she knows nothing about. He knows how she takes her coffee, what scares her, how she handles him when nobody else can, and the exact way she looks at him during the final moments of his first life.

Tony couldn't simply recreate that relationship by following the same steps. He’d have to meet her again as the person she is now and let her decide who he becomes to her. Morgan would stay in the back of his mind every time he does.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: By the time Tony reaches the early 2000s, his life has already moved too far away from the one he remembers. Howard and Maria are alive, HYDRA has been badly damaged, Steve returned years earlier, and Bucky has had time to recover instead of spending decades under HYDRA control. Stark Industries also looks very different because Tony pushed it away from weapons long before Afghanistan ever happened.

Pepper would still enter Tony’s life through Stark Industries, but Tony would have to be careful around her from the beginning. He remembers years of love, arguments, breakups, marriage, and raising Morgan together. Pepper remembers none of it. Tony could easily ruin the relationship by treating her like someone she hasn't become yet, so he’d have to let things develop on their own. That would be harder than any technical problem he has solved so far. Tony knows how important Pepper becomes to him, which means every normal interaction carries memories she can’t share. If she gets annoyed with him, he remembers a dozen older arguments. If she helps him through a problem, he remembers all the times she did the same thing in his first life. He'd have to stop himself from trying to force the relationship toward the future he wants.

Bruce Banner creates a similar problem for a very different reason. Tony knows the gamma experiment is going to change Bruce’s life forever. He also knows Hulk later saves people, fights alongside the Avengers, and becomes one of the most important members of the team.

He could approach the research before the accident, warn Bruce that the gamma exposure is unstable, and help redesign the experiment. That creates one of the biggest risks of the second timeline because preventing Hulk removes one of Earth’s strongest defenders. Tony knows that, but letting Bruce suffer just because Hulk becomes useful later would mean treating him like a tool.

The experiment could still go wrong even with Tony involved. Tony could reduce the damage, improve the safety systems, and make sure Bruce has help much earlier if the transformation still happens. Bruce would enter the story with people around him who already understand what he is dealing with, which could keep some of his worst years from ever happening.

Tony would also begin reaching out to Natasha and Clint as they move through the intelligence world. He knows who they become, but he’d let them reach those choices themselves. Natasha especially needs that freedom because her entire life has been shaped by other people deciding what she should be.

By this point, Tony has started building something close to the Avengers years before the original team ever formed. Steve is active, Bucky is recovering, Natasha and Clint are becoming trusted allies, Bruce is either spared the worst version of the Hulk accident or supported much earlier, and Tony has functional armor long before Afghanistan.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Tony remembers Thor’s arrival on Earth, so the activity around New Mexico gets his attention as soon as it appears. By now, Stark satellites and monitoring systems are far more advanced than anything he had in the original 2011 timeline, which lets him identify the event early and travel there before S.H.I.E.L.D. has fully taken control of the area.

Meeting Thor again would feel strange for Tony because this version of Thor has never fought beside him. He is still proud, reckless, and focused on getting Mjolnir back. Tony remembers the man who later fought Thanos beside him and survived losing almost everything. Tony would already know that pushing Thor too hard rarely helps, so he’d give him room while keeping an eye on what happens around him. Thor still has to go through the experience that changes him. If Tony solves every part of that lesson for him, he risks stopping Thor from becoming the person Earth eventually needs.

Loki’s part of the story would still create trouble because Tony’s changes on Earth don’t erase what is happening on Asgard. Thor’s exile, Loki learning the truth about his heritage, and the conflict around the throne can still happen close to the way Tony remembers.

The big break comes with the Tesseract. Tony has spent years warning trusted people that it can attract attention from outside Earth, so the cube would be far more secure when Loki eventually comes for it. The people guarding it would know that something like this can happen, and Tony would already have systems monitoring the Tesseract for unusual energy spikes or changes because he knows it can be used to open portals, even if he doesn’t know exactly what Loki’s arrival will look like to those sensors in this timeline.

Loki could still arrive, but his attack would meet an Earth that has been preparing for him. Steve already knows Tony well. Natasha and Clint have worked with him before. Thor already understands Loki’s methods. Tony has armor built with alien threats in mind, and the team has trained together long enough that they don’t spend the first half of the crisis arguing over who is in charge.

Loki would still be dangerous because Tony’s memories can’t account for every change his own actions created. Maybe HYDRA's collapse forces Loki to use different people on Earth. Maybe Clint is never placed close enough to the Tesseract for Loki to control him. Maybe the portal opens somewhere other than Stark Tower because Tony never builds the same tower in the first place.

The team is more prepared, Steve has years of modern combat experience, and Tony understands the Chitauri before the first one comes through. Thor can focus on Loki, while the others handle the invasion. If Bruce still became Hulk, he enters the fight with far more control and support than he had the first time.

The battle would likely end faster, and Tony would be far less likely to need to carry a nuclear missile through the portal because the people involved have been preparing for that exact kind of failure for years.
Once the portal closes, Tony would know the biggest threat is still coming and Thanos now has proof that Earth is stronger than expected.

PART 8 Preparing for Thanos would become much harder after the first alien invasion because Tony can no longer rely on the order of events he remembers. Loki’s attack already played out differently, the Avengers formed in another way, and several Infinity Stones may end up in different places because Tony changed who controls them.

He would push Earth toward stronger defenses, better space tracking, and earlier contact with Thor whenever Asgard learns something about the wider universe. Tony could also warn the people around him about the Infinity Stones without trying to gather all of them in one place. Keeping them together would make Earth an even easier target.

Ultron would never happen in the same form because Tony already knows exactly where that road leads. He could still build AI and automated defense systems, but he would keep them separated, limited, and under human control. Bruce and Steve would both be involved in those decisions, which gives Tony people willing to challenge him before a project gets too far.

Civil War would also lose most of the conditions that originally created it. HYDRA was exposed early, Bucky was freed decades sooner, and Tony already knows what happens when fear and guilt push the Avengers into opposite camps. Governments may still want control over enhanced people, especially after an alien invasion, but Tony would enter those debates with much more patience than he had the first time.

When that happens, Tony's old memories would only give him broad guidance. He knows how dangerous Thanos is, how the Stones work, and how quickly a fight can collapse once Thanos starts collecting them. He can’t know which allies will be standing beside him anymore because this world has had decades to grow in another direction.

Steve, Thor, Bruce, Natasha, Clint, Bucky, Pepper, and everyone else have lived their own lives in this new timeline. Tony has spent years trying to protect them from the future he remembers, but eventually he has to let them make decisions without treating his first life like a script they all need to follow.

Earth would probably be far better prepared for Thanos this time, although Tony couldn’t know whether that preparation translates into an easier war. The Avengers are more experienced together, their technology is years ahead, and the planet has been preparing for an alien attack long before Thanos arrives, but decades of changes could also alter when and how Thanos makes his move.

The exact sacrifice from Endgame may never become necessary because the Infinity Stones, the battlefield, and the people involved have all changed. Tony may never reach the moment where snapping his fingers is the only way to win. That leaves him with something he never expected when he woke up in 1991.

Morgan may still be part of it if Tony and Pepper eventually build the same family together, but Tony would have to accept that he can’t control every detail that leads there. If Morgan is born again, she grows up in a world where her father has already learned how dangerous it is to spend his life trying to solve every threat alone.
If events change enough that she isn’t, Tony would carry that loss with him for the rest of his second life. He would still know why he made the choices that changed everything.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: Tony’s second life would probably create a safer MCU, but it wouldn’t recreate the future he lost. He could save his parents, attack HYDRA early, free Bucky, bring Steve back sooner, improve Earth’s technology, and prepare the Avengers for threats years before they originally arrived. Each success would also push the timeline farther away from the memories he started with. Eventually, Tony would have to live without knowing what happens next.
For someone who spent most of his life trying to stay one step ahead of every problem, that may be the hardest part of starting over.
This time, he would have people around him long before the end of the world arrives, and he’d finally understand that building a better future doesn’t mean controlling every part of it.

scripts.title: What If Marvel Never Made The Avengers

sections.name: INTRO
paras: In 2012, Marvel was supposed to find out whether all those Nick Fury cameos and post-credit scenes could actually pay off. Iron Man had worked, Thor had worked, Captain America had worked, and Marvel had spent years telling audiences these characters were eventually going to meet.
Now imagine Marvel backs out before that happens.

The solo movies would still exist, but there’d be no Avengers team bringing them together, no $1.5 billion crossover proving the idea worked, and no clear reason for Marvel to keep building every movie toward the same larger story.

That one cancelled movie could change almost everything that came after it, from Civil War and Infinity War to the way DC and the rest of Hollywood spent the next decade trying to build their own connected universes.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: By 2010, Marvel had already committed to the idea that its solo movies could eventually connect. Iron Man had worked, Iron Man 2 was already bringing in Black Widow and more S.H.I.E.L.D., Thor was on the way, and Captain America was being built as another piece of the same world. The risky part was what came next. Marvel still had to put all of those characters, actors, contracts, effects, and storylines into 1 movie and somehow make the whole thing work. That’s where this timeline changes. Instead of casually abandoning a plan it had spent years building, Marvel hits an unusual business and production crisis as the crossover grows more expensive and complicated than expected. If Disney and Marvel decide the escalating cost and ensemble risk have pushed the project beyond what they’re willing to gamble on, the movie could be delayed first and then cancelled, with the studio retreating to the solo franchises it already knows can work.

The solo movies still come out. Thor still introduces Asgard and Loki. Captain America still ends with Steve waking up in the modern day. Iron Man 2 still expands S.H.I.E.L.D. and gives Black Widow a place in the world. Marvel could even keep some of the post credit scenes because the idea of a connected universe wouldn't disappear right away. The difference is that there’s no date where all of those promises finally come together.

That creates an awkward problem by 2012. Marvel has spent several movies teaching people that Nick Fury is building something, but the thing he’s building never shows up. Thor returns to Asgard. Steve starts adjusting to the modern world. Tony keeps doing his own thing. Black Widow and Hawkeye stay connected to S.H.I.E.L.D., but there’s no reason for all of them to meet.

The biggest loss comes from what Marvel never gets to prove. Before 2012, nobody knew if people would actually show up in huge numbers for a movie built around several heroes they’d already seen separately. Marvel had spent years setting that up, and without The Avengers, they never get the answer.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: If Marvel keeps making solo movies, Iron Man becomes the safest place to put money. The first movie was a huge success, Iron Man 2 also performed well, and Robert Downey Jr. had already become the face most people connected with Marvel Studios. If there’s no Avengers movie in 2012, Marvel would probably lean even harder on Tony because he’s the character they already know can carry a big release.

Iron Man 3 would still make a lot of sense. The movie could probably still happen around 2013, but the story would need major changes because the version we got was built around Tony’s experience in New York. His anxiety, the portal, and the feeling that he’d seen something much bigger than himself all come from the Avengers battle. Remove that, and Tony needs a different reason for being worn down.

The Mandarin and Extremis could still be used. Tony could be dealing with the fallout from his own weapons, the growth of people trying to copy Stark technology, and the fact that his enemies are getting more dangerous every year. That still gives the movie enough material without needing aliens or a team up.

Marvel might also give Iron Man more sequels than he got in the real timeline. In our timeline, Tony stopped having solo movies after Iron Man 3 because he could keep appearing in Avengers movies and other projects like Civil War and Homecoming. Without those team movies, Marvel has a much bigger reason to keep the Iron Man series going.

Marvel would probably push hard for Iron Man 4 and make it one of the studio’s preferred projects in the middle of the decade. Tony could deal with another armored villain, a larger version of A.I.M., or something involving S.H.I.E.L.D. and technology. But whether that movie actually happens would depend more than ever on keeping Robert Downey Jr. Marvel would need him because there’s no Avengers brand sitting above the solo franchises.

That also gives Downey more leverage. Marvel would know that losing him means losing its biggest movie character. His contracts were already becoming expensive in the real timeline, and without Avengers movies bringing in huge amounts of money, every negotiation around Tony could matter more.

If Downey decides he doesn’t want to keep making Iron Man movies forever, Marvel could end up facing a serious problem much earlier. They'd either have to pay him more, recast Tony Stark, or accept that their most successful franchise is ending while the rest of the universe still hasn’t produced anything on the same level.

Iron Man would probably remain Marvel’s biggest character through most of the 2010s. Captain America and Thor could still grow, but Tony already had the advantage of getting there first and having 2 successful movies before either of them had a sequel.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Captain America would still have plenty of room to continue because The First Avenger already gives Marvel a clean setup for another movie. Steve wakes up in the modern world, and that alone can carry his next story. Instead of joining Tony, Thor, and the others almost immediately, Steve would spend much more time dealing with S.H.I.E.L.D. and trying to understand the world he came back to.

A version of The Winter Soldier could still happen, and it might actually become even more important for Captain America because there’s no Avengers movie between his first and second solo films. Steve’s relationship with Nick Fury, Black Widow, and S.H.I.E.L.D. would have more time to grow inside his own franchise.

Hydra could still be hiding inside S.H.I.E.L.D., Bucky could still return, and Steve could still uncover what happened to the organization. That story doesn’t need the Avengers to exist. Some of the details would change because Steve wouldn’t have already spent a major battle fighting beside Tony and the others, but the core story still works.

Black Widow could become almost a Captain America supporting character during this period. She already fits naturally into the spy side of Marvel, and without Avengers movies giving her a place to appear regularly, Steve’s franchise becomes one of the easiest places to keep using her.

Thor would be even more separate. His first movie already takes place across Earth and Asgard, and most of his problems come from Loki, Odin, and the larger cosmic side of Marvel. Thor: The Dark World could still happen because Malekith, the Aether, and Asgard don’t depend on an Avengers team.

The bigger change would be Loki. In the real timeline, The Avengers turned him from Thor’s villain into someone connected to the whole MCU. Without that movie, he stays much more tied to Thor. Marvel could keep bringing him back in Thor sequels because Tom Hiddleston was popular, but he wouldn't have the same role across the larger universe.

Thor’s movies could also become more fantasy focused. There’d be less pressure to connect every story back to Earth or other heroes, so Marvel could spend more time on Asgard, the Nine Realms, and Thor’s own supporting characters.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Hulk would be one of the characters hit hardest by the cancellation because his place in the MCU was already strange. The Incredible Hulk came out in 2008, Edward Norton played Bruce Banner, and Marvel later replaced him with Mark Ruffalo for The Avengers. That team movie ended up becoming the place where the MCU version of Hulk really found his audience. Without The Avengers, Marvel has to decide whether it even wants another Hulk movie. The rights around Hulk were already more complicated because Universal still had distribution rights connected to solo films. Marvel could use the character, but making another standalone movie wasn’t as simple as doing another Iron Man or Thor. The Avengers gave Marvel a way to keep Hulk around without having to build his own franchise.

Take that away and Hulk could disappear for years. Marvel might eventually bring him into somebody else’s movie, especially if it wants to avoid the solo distribution problem. A Thor and Hulk movie could still happen much later, but there’s no reason to assume Marvel gets there quickly. The character could end up being one of the biggest missed opportunities of the early MCU.

Black Widow has a different problem. She’s introduced in Iron Man 2, but most of her importance comes later through The Avengers, The Winter Soldier, Age of Ultron, Civil War, Infinity War, and Endgame. Without those team movies, Marvel has to decide much earlier whether she deserves her own project.

An early Black Widow solo film would probably become less likely, not more likely. Without The Avengers giving Natasha a much bigger showcase, Marvel would have less evidence that audiences wanted her as a lead, and the studio's pre-2015 leadership was already resistant to prioritizing female-led superhero films. A grounded spy movie would still be cheaper than Avengers, but the safer choice would be to keep Natasha as a supporting player in Captain America, Iron Man, or S.H.I.E.L.D. stories rather than build a standalone franchise around her.

That makes Black Widow more likely to remain a supporting character through this period. Hawkeye would have an even smaller role. He appears briefly in Thor before getting a much bigger part in The Avengers. If that movie never happens, most audiences only know him as the guy with the bow who showed up for a few minutes. Marvel could use him in S.H.I.E.L.D. stories or put him beside Black Widow, but there’s no big reason for the studio to build around him.
He might end up becoming a tv character instead. Marvel was already moving into tv with Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D., and someone like Hawkeye could fit there much more easily than in a $150 million movie.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: Marvel could keep the movies connected for a while without making The Avengers. Nick Fury can still show up, S.H.I.E.L.D. can still connect different stories, and references can keep reminding audiences that these heroes all exist in the same world. But if a version of The Winter Soldier still exposes Hydra and brings S.H.I.E.L.D. down in 2014, Marvel loses that connective tissue too. Fury no longer has the same organization linking everyone together, while Black Widow and Hawkeye lose the institution that gave them a natural place between franchises.

The problem is that those connections have less value when they never lead anywhere. If Tony Stark mentions Captain America, that can be fun. If Thor’s hammer shows up in a post credit scene, people can speculate. After several years, audiences would start asking when these characters are actually going to meet. Marvel can only keep teasing a crossover for so long before people stop expecting it.

That would probably make the studio pull back on some of the connections even faster. Iron Man movies could focus almost entirely on Tony. Captain America could continue dealing with the fallout from S.H.I.E.L.D.'s collapse. Thor could stay with Asgard. Marvel might still throw in cameos from time to time, but the whole idea of every movie pushing toward the next big event would fade.

That changes how Marvel plans its slate too. In the real timeline, The Avengers made more than $1.5 billion worldwide and gave Disney proof that Marvel's entire strategy could work at a level much bigger than any of the Phase 1 solo films. That gave the studio a lot more confidence going into Phase 2.

Without that money, Marvel would be working from a much smaller record. Iron Man is successful, Thor is successful, Captain America is successful, and the studio has a useful brand. They still don’t have the movie that shows these separate franchises can combine into something bigger.

That would make stranger projects harder to approve. Marvel could still make sequels because those already have audiences. Spending a lot of money on unknown characters becomes a tougher argument when the studio hasn't proven that every corner of the universe can feed into a bigger franchise later.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Without the Avengers proving that Marvel could bring several franchises together and make more than $1 billion from it, the studio would probably get more careful with what it approves next. Guardians of the Galaxy becomes a much harder sell in that timeline. In the real MCU, Marvel could take a chance on characters most moviegoers had never heard of because the brand itself had become trusted. By 2014, audiences were willing to show up because Marvel Studios had already built a track record.

Without The Avengers, that trust would be much weaker. Marvel could still make Guardians, especially if James Gunn still comes in with a strong pitch, but the budget could be smaller and Disney might push harder for something safer. There’d also be less reason to believe a strange space movie will eventually connect back to everything else.

Civil War changes even more. The MCU version depends on Steve and Tony already knowing each other, fighting beside each other, and building years of tension. If they’ve spent most of the 2010s in separate franchises, Marvel loses the relationship that makes the conflict work.

You could still make a Captain America movie about government control over superheroes, and Tony could still appear if Marvel finally decides to cross them over. The emotional side would be much weaker because the audience never watched them become teammates first. Spider-Man’s MCU entrance would change with it. Civil War gave Marvel the perfect place to introduce Tom Holland’s Spider-Man, so that specific 2016 entrance almost certainly disappears. Sony and Marvel could still have reasons to work together if Marvel Studios remains successful, but the timing of any deal, the version of Peter they use, and the way he enters the MCU become much less predictable.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Infinity War and Endgame would be almost impossible to build in recognizable form, and even Thanos isn't guaranteed to enter this version of the MCU. His first MCU appearance came from the tag attached to The Avengers, so removing that movie also removes the moment that originally puts him on the board. Marvel's cosmic side could instead grow around Thor's Asgardian enemies, the Kree, or whatever direction a possible Guardians movie takes, without automatically building toward Thanos or an Infinity Stone hunt.

If Marvel eventually introduces Thanos somewhere else, he could become the villain of a smaller cosmic franchise, but that would be a new choice rather than a preserved roadmap. Infinity War only works because audiences already know Tony, Steve, Thor, Hulk, Black Widow, Doctor Strange, Spider-Man, Black Panther, the Guardians, and everyone around them. Marvel spent years moving those characters closer together before Thanos finally arrived. In this timeline, Tony could still be making Iron Man movies while Steve is dealing with the fallout from S.H.I.E.L.D. and Thor is off in Asgard. Guardians might not even exist. Hulk could barely be appearing at all. Marvel would have to build all those relationships inside one movie, and that would make a crossover on that scale much harder to sell.

Endgame disappears with it because there’s no earlier Avengers team to bring back together. Tony’s death, Steve going back in time, Thor fighting beside the Guardians, and the portals scene all depend on years of crossover history that never happened.

Marvel would probably still make big finales for its individual heroes. Tony could get a final lron Man movie. Steve could finish his story in a Captain America sequel. Thor could have his own ending around Asgard.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: The change outside Marvel could be just as big. The Avengers gave Hollywood a very clear example of what a shared universe could do. Separate movies introduced the characters, then the crossover made more than $1.5 billion. After that, studios started looking for ways to build their own connected franchises.

DC would still make superhero movies because Batman and Superman were already huge. Man of Steel could still happen in 2013. What changes is the rush to get from Superman to Batman v Superman and then Justice League.

Without The Avengers giving Hollywood such a clear proof of concept, Warner Bros. would have less competitive pressure and less proven evidence that rapidly connecting separate superhero properties is the winning strategy. DC could still pursue Batman v Superman and an eventual Justice League because those characters were valuable regardless of Marvel, but there’d be less reason to rush several heroes into the same plan right away. Superman could get another solo movie first. Batman could start separately. Wonder Woman could have more time before a Justice League crossover happens.

Sony would still look for ways to expand Spider-Man, and Fox would still have X-Men. Shared universes and crossover movies wouldn't disappear as ideas, but without The Avengers proving how profitable that specific model could be, Hollywood would probably pursue them with less urgency and confidence.

Marvel itself could keep going through the 2010s, but the MCU would look very different. Iron Man would probably stay the biggest series, Captain America and Thor would have their own stories, and smaller characters would get movies only when Marvel feels confident enough to take the risk. That confidence wouldn't return all at once. Every successful Iron Man, Captain America, or Thor sequel would give Disney and Marvel more evidence that the studio could survive bigger bets, gradually rebuilding the risk tolerance they lost when the 2012 crossover collapsed.

There could still be occasional crossovers. Tony might appear in a Captain America movie years later. Black Widow could move between different franchises. Nick Fury could keep showing up. The big yearly or every few years team events probably wouldn’t become the center of the studio. Marvel might eventually try the Avengers again once enough solo movies succeed, but by then the timing would be completely different. The team could arrive in the late 2010s instead of 2012, and the entire shape of the franchise would change around that delay.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: Marvel Studios could still survive without The Avengers because Iron Man, Thor, and Captain America had already proven there was an audience for its solo movies, but that survival would be much less secure than it was after 2012. Without the enormous financial validation of an Avengers crossover, Marvel would have less room to expand aggressively, take expensive risks, or assume its separate franchises could support one another.
What Marvel loses is the movie that showed all of those franchises could become something much bigger together.

Without that 2012 crossover, Guardians becomes a harder risk, Civil War loses its setup, Infinity War and Endgame never form the same way, and Hollywood has less proven reason to rush through the 2010s chasing shared universes.
The MCU could still exist, but it would probably look like several Marvel franchises sharing the same world instead of one giant story built around the Avengers.

scripts.title: What If Mega Knight Cost 1 Elixir

sections.name: INTRO
paras: Mega Knight costs 7 Elixir. If you waste him, you can lose the match off that one play.
Now imagine Supercell drops his cost to 1.
Nothing else changes. Same health, same spawn damage, same jump, same splash damage. He just costs less than a Fire Spirit.
At first, it would probably look like one of the funniest balance mistakes Supercell had ever made. Then people would actually start playing with it.
Within hours, Mega Knight would be everywhere. Not because he suddenly became unbeatable, but because getting that much value for 1 Elixir would be almost impossible to ignore.
And once players started building entire decks around cycling back to him as fast as possible, Clash Royale would stop playing anything like the game people were used to.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: The first few hours would be chaos because most players wouldn’t even know what the best version of the card looked like yet. They’d just know that Mega Knight now cost 1 Elixir, so almost every deck would add him immediately. Hog decks would use him. Bait decks would use him. Control decks would use him. Even decks that normally had no reason to touch Mega Knight would suddenly have a reason because there’s almost no downside to spending 1 Elixir on him.

The biggest change would happen on defense. Mega Knight already gets value by landing on groups of ground troops, but at 7 Elixir you have to be careful about when you use him. At 1 Elixir, that decision becomes much easier. If your opponent sends in something like a Bandit, Royal Ghost, or a group of support troops near the bridge, you can drop Mega Knight onto them and still have almost your entire Elixir bar left for whatever comes next.

That would ruin a lot of normal Elixir trades. Players are used to forcing out expensive defenses and then attacking while the opponent is low. Against a 1 Elixir Mega Knight, that plan stops working. You could force Mega Knight out and still be facing a player with enough Elixir to add a second defensive card, start a push in the other lane, or support the Mega Knight that just survived.

The card still wouldn’t solve everything. Air troops would still ignore him, buildings could still pull him, and strong single target units could still kill him if they were placed correctly. The problem is that beating the Mega Knight wouldn’t necessarily mean you won the trade anymore. Spending 4 or 5 Elixir to deal with a card that only cost your opponent 1 could leave you behind even if the Mega Knight never touched your tower.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: You still can’t play Mega Knight twice in a row. After using a card, you have to cycle through 4 other cards before it returns to your hand. That rule stays exactly the same. So the fastest way to abuse a 1 Elixir Mega Knight would be to fill the rest of the deck with cards that let you reach him again without spending much.

That’s where the game would start getting ridiculous. Players would test cheap cycle cards, Spirits, Skeletons, and other low cost options just to get back to Mega Knight faster. Instead of building around a traditional win condition first, some decks would start building around one question, how quickly can I get another Mega Knight?

The result wouldn’t be an endless stream of them from the opening second, but surviving Mega Knights would begin stacking. One Mega Knight defends and walks forward. The player cycles 4 cheap cards while that first one is still alive. Now another Mega Knight is available for 1 Elixir. If the opponent tries to stop the first counterpush with ground troops, the second Mega Knight can land directly on that defense.

That creates a completely different problem from fighting one Mega Knight. Normally, killing him ends the threat and gives you time to reset. Here, the player can be getting back to another one while you’re still dealing with the first.

The Evolution would make certain cycles even more annoying. As of recent balance changes, Evolved Mega Knight’s uppercut happens every other attack, while his heavier knockback was restored to 4 tiles. You still wouldn’t get Evolved Mega Knight every time he returned to your hand. You’d have to complete his Evolution cycle first. But when every Mega Knight deployment only costs 1 Elixir, cycling through those required deployments becomes dramatically cheaper and easier to sustain, even though the normal card-cycle requirement itself does not change.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Cards that can handle Mega Knight efficiently would shoot up in value. PEKKA would become an obvious answer because she can beat him cleanly in a direct fight, but even that trade starts looking strange when you’re spending 7 Elixir to remove something that cost 1. Mini PEKKA, Inferno Tower, Inferno Dragon, Mighty Miner, and other strong single target answers would all become more important for the same reason. Players wouldn’t just need cards that can kill Mega Knight. They’d need cards that can kill him without ruining the rest of their defense.

Kiting would matter even more too. If you can pull a Mega Knight toward the middle, make him walk farther, and let both Princess Towers help, you’re wasting more of the opponent’s time without throwing a huge amount of Elixir into him. Cheap cards would become much more valuable because nobody wants to spend half their bar every time another Mega Knight crosses the bridge.

Air decks would also become more attractive. Mega Knight can’t hit air, so cards like Balloon and Lava Hound don’t suddenly stop working because he costs 1. The problem is everything around him. A player who spends only 1 Elixir on Mega Knight still has enough left to defend the air push with other cards. So even archetypes that avoid fighting him directly wouldn’t escape the bigger problem with the update.

That’s what would start killing older deck structures. Some decks are built around getting a specific Elixir advantage, forcing out a certain defense, and then punishing the opponent while that card is out of cycle. Those ideas become much weaker when Mega Knight barely affects the opponent’s Elixir bar. You can’t treat forcing out Mega Knight as a major win anymore because they barely paid anything for him.

The meta wouldn’t become 8 Mega Knights because the game doesn’t work that way. It would become decks built around either abusing the 1 Elixir Mega Knight better than everyone else or surviving against the people who do.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Then players would start finding the really stupid interactions.

The first wave of decks would probably just throw Mega Knight into whatever people were already using. The second wave would be much more calculated. Players would start pairing him with cards that are normally difficult to support because Mega Knight no longer eats most of the Elixir needed for the push.

A normal Mega Knight counterpush can be expensive to build around. If you spend 7 on Mega Knight and then start adding support behind him, you can run yourself dry very quickly. At 1 Elixir, that disappears. You could defend with Mega Knight and still have enough Elixir to add a win condition, ranged support, or pressure the opposite lane almost immediately.

That would make split lane pressure much harder to read. A Mega Knight walking down one side normally tells you that your opponent has already spent a big chunk of Elixir there. With the new cost, it tells you almost nothing. They might support him. They might ignore him and attack the other lane. They might cycle back to another Mega Knight before the first one even dies.

Players would eventually start using Mega Knight almost like a cycle card that happens to have the body of a tank. That’s where the update stops being funny. A 1 Elixir Skeletons placement is cheap because the card is supposed to give limited value. A 1 Elixir Mega Knight can absorb damage, clear groups of ground troops, threaten a jump, and force an answer while also moving you one card deeper into your cycle.

That means even bad Mega Knight placements become less punishable. If somebody drops him too early, misses the best spawn damage, or uses him against a weak push, they’ve only spent 1 Elixir. Normally, poor Mega Knight usage can cost a player the match because recovering from 7 wasted Elixir is difficult. Here, the punishment is almost gone.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: Ranked would be where the problem becomes impossible to ignore. At lower levels, plenty of players would still use Mega Knight badly. They’d drop him into obvious counters, waste his spawn damage, or build terrible decks just because the card only costs 1. But once you reach stronger players, those mistakes disappear. Everyone already understands how much value the card gives, so matches start revolving around who can use that 1 Elixir better.

That would make deck variety collapse fast. You’d still see different win conditions, but Mega Knight would start taking one slot in almost everything. Hog Rider with Mega Knight. Balloon with Mega Knight. Graveyard with Mega Knight. Control decks with Mega Knight. Cheap cycle decks built specifically to get back to Mega Knight as quickly as possible. Even if another card technically fit the deck better, it becomes difficult to justify leaving out something this efficient.

And mirror matches would become much more common. If both players have Mega Knight, neither side gets the huge advantage of having access to the broken card while the other doesn’t. The match instead becomes about how each player handles the constant 1 Elixir bodies being dropped onto the arena.

That would also change how people track Elixir. Normally, seeing a Mega Knight gives you useful information. Your opponent just spent 7, so you can estimate what they can afford next. At 1 Elixir, that information almost disappears. They could place Mega Knight and immediately follow it with an expensive win condition or a full defense. You’d have to assume they still have most of their Elixir every time he appears.

Players who refused to use Mega Knight would basically be giving themselves a handicap. They could still win, especially with decks designed to punish the surrounding meta, but they’d be choosing to play without the most efficient defensive card in the game while almost everyone else gets it for 1.
That’s when people would stop treating the update as a funny mistake. Ranked would still function mechanically, but the actual choice behind deck building would start shrinking.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Professional players would spend hours testing the cheapest possible ways to cycle Mega Knight, which counters still produce acceptable trades, and which win conditions benefit most from having almost free defense behind them. Anything that looks ridiculous on ladder would get optimized much further once top players started testing it seriously.

The biggest advantage would be consistency. A professional doesn’t need Mega Knight to jump onto the tower every push. If a 1 Elixir Mega Knight absorbs several attacks, removes a few Elixir worth of troops, or forces the opponent to spend more than 1 defending him, he’s already done his job.

That would create ugly decisions during tournaments. Imagine spending 4 Elixir on a proper Mega Knight answer, watching it kill him, and knowing the opponent can already be cycling toward the next one. You won the interaction on the arena, but you may have lost the Elixir trade badly enough that the next push becomes harder to defend.

Deck preparation would start revolving around that reality. Players would either bring Mega Knight themselves or make sure nearly every deck had a reliable plan for him. Cards that struggle into repeated Mega Knights would become risky regardless of how strong they were before the update. Entire strategies could disappear simply because they give the opponent too many good 1 Elixir defensive placements.

The matches wouldn’t necessarily become mindless. At the highest level, players would still kite, count cards, track Elixir, protect counters, and punish positioning mistakes. In some ways, people might even develop a very technical new meta around dealing with Mega Knight.

A functioning meta can still be terrible if one card decides how almost every deck has to be built. And once tournament results started showing the same Mega Knight centered patterns over and over, Supercell would have a much bigger problem than angry ladder players.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Supercell would probably know very quickly that the update had gone too far. The problem is that if they decided to leave it live for even a few days, players would keep finding better ways to abuse it.

The community reaction would also change fast. The first few hours would be memes and people posting ridiculous replays. After that, it would turn into frustration. Players who normally hated Mega Knight would now see him in almost every match, while players who liked the card would be running into the exact same thing from the other side. The joke would wear off once ranked started feeling like everyone was being forced into the same card.

Supercell could try to solve the problem without immediately putting Mega Knight back at 7 Elixir. They could nerf his health, damage, jump, or spawn damage, but that creates a bigger design issue. If Mega Knight is still only 1 Elixir, the nerfs would have to be extreme before the card stopped being worth using. At that point, it might barely resemble Mega Knight anymore.
The cleanest fix would obviously be restoring the cost. Anything else would mean balancing the entire card around a price it was never designed to have.

And the longer Supercell waited, the worse the backlash would get. Players would spend resources, practice decks, and build around the new meta. Then any correction would wipe out everything they had just spent time learning.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: If Supercell somehow refused to change anything, Clash Royale would eventually settle into a new meta. It just wouldn’t be a healthy one. Players would get better at dealing with Mega Knight. They’d learn the best placements, the cheapest counters, the safest ways to kite him, and which pushes were still worth making into a player who could defend with him for 1 Elixir.

Over time, the strongest decks would probably stop looking like random Mega Knight spam and start becoming very refined. Some would use him mainly as cheap defense. Others would build around fast cycle. Some would take advantage of the fact that he barely affects the Elixir available for a second lane.
That means the game wouldn’t become literally unplayable. Good players would still beat bad players. Matchups would still matter. Positioning and timing would still matter.

That’s the real problem. A card doesn’t need a 100% win rate to break a game. If one card is so efficient that every serious deck either has to use it or specifically prepare for it, then the rest of the card pool starts losing importance.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: So could Clash Royale survive Mega Knight costing 1 Elixir?
Technically, yes.
Players would adapt. Counters would appear. New decks would be built, and eventually people would figure out the best ways to play around him.
But the game would be worse for it.

Mega Knight wouldn’t become unbeatable. He’d become too efficient to ignore, and that’s arguably even more damaging. Every deck would start revolving around one card, either by using him or trying to stop him.
Clash Royale could still function. It just wouldn’t really feel like Clash Royale anymore.

scripts.title: What If Modulo Yuji Was In The Boys

sections.name: INTRO
paras: Yuji would realize pretty quickly that the world of The Boys has no jujutsu society waiting for him. There are no sorcerers responding to curses, no schools training people like him, and no one around him who even understands what cursed energy is. Instead, the strongest people are Supes working under Vought, and most of the world treats them like celebrities.

At first, Yuji wouldn't know how bad that system actually is. He’d just see people with powers, assume they're supposed to protect civilians, and start noticing how often Vought cleans up the consequences when they don’t. That would bother him more the longer he stays because Yuji has spent most of his life watching powerful people decide who gets sacrificed for everyone else.

By the Modulo era, he’s experienced enough that he wouldn't charge straight at the first Supe who makes him angry. He'd watch, learn who controls what, and figure out why everyone seems terrified of the same handful of people.
That approach would eventually put him in the path of the Boys, Starlight, and Vought at the same time.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: By the Modulo era, Yuji wouldn’t be the same teenager who spent most of his life being thrown from one disaster into the next. Nearly 70 years have passed since Sukuna’s defeat, Yuji still hasn't physically aged, and he’s spent decades becoming comfortable with abilities he was only beginning to understand during the Shinjuku fight. He’s also lived long enough to watch most of the people from his generation grow old or die, which is part of why he keeps himself away from the jujutsu establishment unless there’s a reason he actually needs to step in.

That's where the crossover could begin. Yuji could be investigating a barrier failure outside Tokyo after several people disappear near an abandoned research site containing a damaged piece of experimental equipment nobody has been able to identify. By 2086, jujutsu and technology have started overlapping far more than they did in Yuji’s youth, but the readings around this device don't match anything Yuji recognizes, so he wouldn't assume it was normal jujutsu technology or just another curse. He’d go in alone because the disturbance looks small enough to handle without dragging younger sorcerers into it.

Inside, Yuji would find a barrier folding back into itself around the damaged equipment. He could destroy the cursed spirits gathering around it easily, but the barrier would keep changing shape instead of collapsing, almost like the space inside the building is being stretched in different directions. Yuji wouldn't know what the device is actually doing, only that the distortion is centered around it, so he uses Shrine to cut through the structure around the anomaly before the barrier can spread farther.

That fixes the immediate problem and creates a much worse one for him. Shrine cuts through the structure around the already unstable device, damaging part of the equipment in the process. The anomaly itself immediately malfunctions, the barrier tears open for a few seconds while Yuji is standing inside it, and instead of throwing him across Tokyo, it pulls him completely out of the space he recognizes. Yuji didn't create the dimensional opening with Shrine; he simply damaged something whose actual function he never understood. He’d try anchoring himself with cursed energy, but there’s nothing solid left to grab before the opening closes behind him.

Yuji would land hard in the middle of New York and immediately know he isn’t anywhere near home. The city looks older than the one he left, the technology is decades behind what he’s used to, and when he reaches out with his senses, almost none of the familiar jujutsu presence is there. He can still feel and use his own cursed energy, but there aren’t sorcerers moving through the city, barriers covering important locations, or anyone responding to the kinds of spiritual disturbances he’d expect around millions of people.

He'd spend the first few days figuring out where he landed before trying to find a way back. Yuji has lived through enough strange situations that he wouldn't walk into Vought Tower and announce that he came from another universe. He'd listen, learn how the country works, and notice that nobody has any idea what cursed energy is whenever he asks about unusual spiritual phenomena.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Yuji’s first problem with a Supe could happen before he ever meets anyone important. He'd be walking through Brooklyn when a Vought sponsored hero chases an armed robber through a crowded street and decides stopping him matters more than everyone standing nearby. The Supe throws the robber through the front of a store, sending glass and part of the wall toward people on the sidewalk while the hero keeps moving without even checking who got hit.

Yuji would react before anyone understands what happened. He catches a section of falling concrete, pushes a woman and her son clear with his other hand, then crosses the street fast enough to grab the robber before the Supe can throw him again. The entire thing takes a few seconds, but half the street has phones pointed at them by the time it’s over.

The Supe would assume Yuji is another enhanced person because nothing else makes sense. Yuji doesn’t recognize the costume or understand why the guy seems more concerned about being interrupted than the people he nearly killed, so he tells him to stop throwing someone around while civilians are standing behind him. That would be enough to turn an ordinary arrest into an argument Vought can’t control.

Yuji still wouldn’t start a fight. He’s spent decades learning what happens when powerful people throw the first punch without understanding the situation, and there's no reason to beat somebody into the pavement just because he acted recklessly. He'd hand the robber over once the police arrive, make sure the injured civilians are being treated, and leave while the Vought hero is still trying to explain the scene to his own camera crew.

The part Yuji would remember is what happens after. A Vought representative reaches the scene almost as quickly as emergency services, starts asking witnesses what they recorded, and tries getting ahead of the story before anyone has even finished checking the store. The hero who caused the damage gets moved away while employees begin talking about an unfortunate accident during a successful arrest.

Yuji has seen institutions protect powerful people before, so the behavior wouldn't be completely unfamiliar. He still wouldn’t know enough to decide Vought itself is rotten, especially because 1 careless hero doesn't tell him what thousands of other Supes are like. What catches his attention is how practiced the cleanup feels.

There’s no childhood publicity deal, no Vought hospital record, no known Compound V treatment, and no social media history before the day he appeared in New York. That would makee him more interesting than another unknown street level Supe because Vought can’t explain where his abilities came from.

Starlight would see the footage too. By early Season 3, Annie already knows exactly how much Vought hides from the public and how quickly the company turns anyone useful into a product. She wouldn’t assume Yuji is dangerous just because Vought doesn’t own him, especially after watching him spend most of the video protecting civilians instead of fighting the Supe who caused the problem.

She could find him before Vought does by going back to the people he helped rather than using corporate surveillance. Yuji would recognize her from the Seven almost immediately, which means his first real conversation with someone from Vought happens with the one member most likely to tell him the company isn’t what it looks like.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Annie wouldn't tell Yuji everything in their first conversation because she has no reason to trust him yet either. She could ask where he got his powers, whether Vought approached him before, and why there’s no record of him anywhere. Yuji would answer the important part honestly and
tell her he didn't get his abilities from Vought, although explaining cursed energy and another universe to someone he met 5 minutes ago probably wouldn't be his first choice.

What gets Yuji’s attention is Compound V. Annie could assume he already knows about it until she realizes he genuinely has no idea what she means, then explain the scandal that had already become public: Supes weren’t naturally chosen heroes the way Vought spent years claiming. Most of them were injected as children, usually because their parents agreed to it, and Vought built an entire industry around the results. She could also explain that the public revelation didn't expose everything about how Vought still operates behind the cleaned-up story. Yuji would have a lot of questions after that. In his world, being born with a cursed technique can decide a person’s entire life before they're old enough to understand what happened, so hearing that a company deliberately creates powerful children for profit would sit badly with him. He still wouldn't jump from that to believing every accusation Annie makes about Vought, but he’d start paying attention to the gap between the company’s public image and how it treats the people whose powers it created.

Annie could also tell him to stay away from Vought Tower if they contact him. An unknown Supe with no contract is useful enough already, and someone whose abilities don’t come from Compound V would be far more valuable once the company realizes what that means. Yuji wouldn't be interested in becoming famous anyway, so refusing the offer would be easy.
The Boys would be watching the same video for completely different reasons.

Butcher would see a guy with unexplained super strength standing in the middle of New York and assume Vought is hiding another experiment. Hughie might point out that Yuji saved civilians and stopped the fight from getting worse, while Butcher would care more about where a person that powerful came from without appearing in any of their files.

They wouldn't approach him politely. Frenchie and Kimiko could follow Yuji after Annie leaves and try figuring out whether he reports back to Vought. Yuji would notice long before they expect him to because decades of fighting sorcerers have made being followed by ordinary people fairly easy to recognize.

Instead of confronting them immediately, he could let them keep going until they lead themselves somewhere quiet, then turn around and ask what they want. Frenchie would probably try talking his way through it, while Kimiko stays ready in case the unknown Supe decides to attack.

Yuji would notice something strange about Kimiko almost immediately. She has the physical presence of someone much stronger than a normal human, but there’s no cursed technique behind it. Seeing her up close would give him his first chance to understand that Compound V actually changes the body itself rather than functioning like cursed energy.

Butcher would eventually step out once the attempt at quiet surveillance is already ruined. He’d tell Yuji enough about Vought to see how he reacts, including what happened with Compound V and how often Supes kill people without facing consequences. Yuji would listen until Butcher starts talking about Supes like all of them belong in the same category.

That's where they'd disagree. Yuji has spent too much of his life judging people by what they choose to do to accept that having powers makes someone guilty by default. Kimiko standing beside Butcher would make the argument even weaker because she’s living proof that someone can be given dangerous abilities and still decide what kind of person they want to be.

He wouldn't join the Boys after 1 conversation, but he also wouldn't walk away from what they tell him. Instead, Yuji would start checking pieces of the story himself, which would frustrate Butcher and probably make Annie trust him more than if he immediately agreed with either side.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Yuji wouldn't need long to confirm that Vought’s problems go much deeper than one reckless hero. Annie could point him toward cases where civilians were paid to stay quiet after Supe accidents, while the Boys have their own collection of footage, reports, and witnesses the company managed to bury. Yuji wouldn't need to believe every story to see that the same pattern keeps appearing around different heroes.

One case could involve a low level Supe Vought quietly stopped promoting after several violent incidents. The company never publicly fired him and still keeps his contract alive because admitting what happened would create another scandal, so he spends most of his time using his abilities wherever he thinks nobody important is watching. When the Boys learn he’s been threatening people connected to one of the old settlements, Butcher decides the easiest solution is to kill him before Vought moves him again.

Yuji would find out because Hughie tells Annie, and Annie knows exactly what Butcher means when he says he’s going to “handle” the guy. Yuji gets there before the Boys finish the job and sees enough of the Supe’s behavior to understand why they came. The man is dangerous, violent, and completely comfortable hurting people who can’t fight back.

The confrontation itself wouldn't need to become another major test of Yuji's power. The Supe could be strong enough to throw cars and survive gunfire, making him dangerous to everyone else there, but Yuji would realize almost immediately that the gap between them is enormous. A few controlled reinforced strikes would be enough to put him down without Shrine, Blood Manipulation, or anything Yuji considers a serious technique.

What would matter is what happens after the fight. The Boys would see how easily Yuji can stop a dangerous Supe without killing him, and Butcher would immediately expose the deeper disagreement between them by trying to finish the man anyway. Yuji's control matters here less as a new power benchmark and more because it proves he had every opportunity to kill the Supe and deliberately chose not to.

Butcher would still try finishing the Supe once he’s down. Yuji would stop him. He wouldn't defend what the man did or pretend Vought's legal system is going to handle everything properly. He’d simply refuse to stand there while Butcher kills someone who can't fight back, especially when they already have witnesses and enough evidence to expose what happened.
