He’d be trying to understand what kind of strength exists here and whether any of it is worth his attention.

That’s also why his first encounter with S.H.I.E.L.D. probably wouldn't turn into a massacre unless they force it. Agents sent to investigate him would immediately notice that normal intimidation doesn’t work. Sukuna wouldn't react to guns the way a human should, and attempts to surround him would only confirm that whoever these people are, they don’t understand what they’re dealing with.

The first real warning comes when one of them pushes too far. Sukuna doesn’t need a visible weapon to attack. A single Dismantle can cut through a firearm, a vehicle or the environment around an agent before anyone understands what happened. He doesn’t even need to kill the first team. Leaving them alive after demonstrating that he can take them apart whenever he wants would give him more information, because now he gets to see what Earth sends next. That report reaches Nick Fury quickly.

At roughly the same time, Fury is already dealing with the Tesseract, Loki’s arrival and the collapse of the S.H.I.E.L.D. facility holding it. He doesn’t have the luxury of ignoring a second unknown superhuman, especially one who seems completely unrelated to Loki.
The difference is that Fury can at least understand Loki. Loki wants the Tesseract and is building toward something larger. Sukuna doesn’t appear to want anything which makes him harder to predict.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: S.H.I.E.L.D.’s first instinct would be to classify Sukuna using categories they already understand.

He isn’t wearing powered armor, so he isn’t another Tony Stark. There’s no obvious mutation or radiation signature tying him to someone like Bruce Banner. His abilities don’t resemble Asgardian technology, and he doesn’t seem connected to the Tesseract.
The strangest part is that their equipment may not give them much useful information about cursed energy at all.

S.H.I.E.L.D. can detect heat, radiation, electromagnetic activity and plenty of other physical signals, but cursed energy isn’t part of the scientific framework they normally operate within. That doesn’t make Sukuna invisible to every sensor. It means the cause of what he’s doing remains unclear.

Natasha would probably be one of the first Avengers-connected people to get a closer look at him, especially because S.H.I.E.L.D. would want information before attempting another direct confrontation. Sukuna would recognize what she’s doing almost immediately. He has spent too much time reading opponents and manipulating people to mistake careful questioning for casual conversation.

That exchange gives him his first useful picture of Earth’s power structure. There’s a government agency coordinating enhanced individuals, an Asgardian who has already fought on Earth, a man in advanced armor, and another human capable of transforming into something strong enough that S.H.I.E.L.D. treats him like a disaster waiting to happen.
Bruce would stand out immediately.

Sukuna wouldn’t know the Hulk yet, but the idea of a human carrying something that dangerous inside his own body would be interesting for obvious reasons. He understands better than most what it means for one body to contain something far more powerful than the person living around it.
Fury, meanwhile, would be trying to decide whether Sukuna belongs anywhere near the Avengers Initiative. The answer would almost certainly be no.

Sukuna has shown no interest in following orders and no concern for collateral damage. Even if he hasn't started killing people at random, there’s nothing about him that suggests S.H.I.E.L.D. could control what happens if he gets bored or decides someone has insulted him.
For the moment, Fury would rather keep eyes on him than provoke him but Loki wouldn't be nearly as patient.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Loki would hear about Sukuna through S.H.I.E.L.D.’s response. Once he has Clint and Selvig under his control, he has access to enough information to know that another dangerous figure has appeared around the same time he did. From Loki’s perspective, that looks useful.

His plan already depends on turning Earth’s strongest people against one another. Sukuna appears to be powerful, unaffiliated and hostile to authority, which makes him seem like exactly the kind of person Loki could point at his enemies.

Loki’s entire approach to conquest is built around hierarchy. He believes humanity should submit because he sees himself as naturally above them. Sukuna understands hierarchy too, but his version of it is far more personal. Strength doesn’t give someone the right to rule because of a title, bloodline or throne. If Loki wants obedience, he has to prove he can take it. That makes their first interaction tense very quickly.

Sukuna would let Loki explain enough to understand the situation. There’s an army coming. Loki intends to use the Tesseract to open a portal, seize New York and force Earth into submission. Sukuna wouldn’t object because innocent people might die.
He’d object to the assumption that Loki can walk into this world and expect everyone in it to kneel simply because he arrived with an army.
Loki could still try the Mind Stone.

That becomes one of the most dangerous moments in the early story, because there’s no clean canon answer for how the scepter would interact with Sukuna. What is clear is that Sukuna’s mind isn’t normal, and attempting to control him would be an enormous gamble. He has overwhelming self awareness, a highly developed sense of his own soul, and experience existing within another person’s body without losing his identity.
Even if the scepter could influence him under the right conditions, Loki wouldn’t know how much resistance he was about to meet.

More importantly, he may never get the chance to test it. Sukuna is far too observant to casually let an unknown weapon touch his chest after watching Loki use it on other people. The moment Loki attempts it, Sukuna would likely respond with Dismantle before the weapon ever reaches him.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Sukuna crossing paths with the Avengers before New York would make their already unstable team dynamic even worse.

Steve would immediately distrust him. Sukuna doesn’t hide the fact that he values strength over rules, and nothing about his behavior suggests he feels any responsibility toward the people around him. Steve can work with difficult personalities, but Sukuna isn’t simply difficult. He’s someone who might kill a person because he finds them irritating.
Tony’s reaction would be different.

He’d be more interested in understanding how Sukuna’s abilities work, especially after hearing that S.H.I.E.L.D. can’t explain the cuts he produces. Stark technology can model trajectories and identify weapons, but Dismantle doesn’t give him a projectile to track in the usual sense. That would bother Tony almost as much as Sukuna’s personality does.
Thor would probably get Sukuna’s attention faster than anyone else.

Unlike the agents and most of the Avengers, Thor immediately feels like someone built for direct combat. His durability, strength and connection to a world beyond Earth make him the first person Sukuna has encountered here who clearly isn’t operating on a normal human level.
If they clash, it wouldn’t need to become a full fight.

Thor could survive an opening attack that would end most human opponents, while Sukuna would realize very quickly that Mjolnir and Asgardian durability make him a completely different problem from the S.H.I.E.L.D. agents he’s already seen.
Bruce is the other person Sukuna would watch closely.

S.H.I.E.L.D. may try to keep him calm, but Sukuna would immediately understand that everyone in the room is reacting to Bruce differently. They aren’t worried about the scientist. They’re worried about what happens if he stops being the scientist.
Once Sukuna eventually sees Hulk, that curiosity turns into genuine interest.

Hulk can take punishment that would erase almost anything Sukuna has encountered since arriving, and his physical strength is immediately obvious. Sukuna would enjoy testing that far more than dealing with soldiers or agents.

That leaves Fury with an uncomfortable choice. Keeping Sukuna near them risks provoking a fight. Sending him away means losing track of someone who could become even more dangerous once Loki’s invasion starts.
So Sukuna remains close enough to watch. Then Loki attacks the Helicarrier.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: The Helicarrier attack is where Sukuna stops being an outside problem and becomes part of the Avengers’ crisis. Loki’s original plan works because he doesn’t need to beat everyone himself. He uses Barton and the controlled agents to attack the carrier from within, damages the engines, releases Hulk and lets the Avengers’ own instability do the rest.

Sukuna makes that much harder. He still wouldn’t care about keeping the Helicarrier in the air for S.H.I.E.L.D.’s sake. What gets his attention is Barton’s assault, Hulk being unleashed, and the chance to see how the Avengers respond when everything starts collapsing at once. He steps in because the chaos is finally interesting, and keeping the carrier from going down simply keeps that fight from ending too soon.

The controlled agents are the easiest part. They’re still human. Sukuna could cut through weapons, doors and attackers so quickly that Barton’s team loses much of the advantage they originally had. He wouldn't bother fighting with the same restraint as Natasha or Steve either. Anyone actively trying to kill him becomes expendable immediately.
That changes how much damage the boarding team can cause before the Avengers respond. The bigger problem is Hulk. When Bruce transforms, Sukuna finally gets the fight he’s been waiting to see.

Hulk would immediately register as physically stronger than almost anything else around him. Sukuna’s normal slashing attacks could hurt him, but there’s no reason to assume a casual Dismantle would simply cut Hulk apart. The Hulk has survived enormous blunt force trauma, energy attacks and punishment from other enhanced beings, so Sukuna would have to start adjusting quickly.

If Sukuna gets his hands on Hulk, Cleave becomes more useful because it adapts its cutting strength based on the target, but even then, Hulk’s durability and healing make him difficult to put down cleanly.

The fight probably wouldn't last long enough for either of them to settle it. Thor is already trying to contain Hulk, and the Helicarrier is still failing around them. If Sukuna starts enjoying himself too much, Steve and Tony would realize they now have two separate disasters happening inside the same aircraft.

This is also where the Avengers learn that Sukuna doesn’t panic. The carrier is under attack, Hulk is loose, Loki has escaped, and everything around him is collapsing, but Sukuna treats the entire situation like a chance to gather more information. He’s learning how strong Hulk is, how Thor fights, how quickly Tony reacts in armor, and how well the team operates under pressure. By the time the Helicarrier stabilizes, Fury’s original concern has become much worse. Loki is still the immediate enemy, but Sukuna has now seen nearly every major Avenger fight. And instead of being intimidated by any of them, he looks more interested than before. That becomes especially dangerous once they realize where Loki is going next. Because when the portal opens over New York, Sukuna won’t need anyone to convince him to join the battle. PART 6
Once the portal opens over Stark Tower, Sukuna finally gets the kind of battlefield that keeps his attention.

The Chitauri aren’t human soldiers, and they aren’t arriving in small numbers. They’re pouring into Manhattan from another world with flying transports, heavy weapons and Leviathans large enough to tear through buildings. For the Avengers, that means protecting civilians while trying to contain an invasion. For Sukuna, it means there’s suddenly no shortage of opponents. He’d enter because the Chitauri have turned the city into something worth stepping into. That changes the Avengers’ first few minutes in New York. Steve still takes control on the ground, Tony handles the air, Thor targets the portal area, Natasha and Clint deal with the streets, and Hulk becomes the team’s answer to anything too large for everyone else.
Sukuna doesn't fit into that structure.

He can clear entire groups of Chitauri without needing backup, and because his slashes don’t require him to physically reach every target, he can cut through soldiers and vehicles before they get close to him. The Avengers would quickly realize that keeping him pointed toward the invasion is useful, even if nobody wants to pretend he’s part of the team. The problem is collateral damage. Sukuna isn’t going to prioritize keeping buildings intact if destroying one gives him a cleaner attack. Steve would notice that immediately and start directing civilians away from wherever Sukuna is fighting, because expecting Sukuna to change his methods for people he doesn’t care about would be a waste of time.

That tension gets worse when the first Leviathan reaches him. Instead of waiting for Hulk, Sukuna could test how much punishment one of them can take with Dismantle. If the first slash doesn’t cut deeply enough, Cleave gives him a better option once he gets close enough to make physical contact and use it properly. The Leviathans are heavily armored, but they’re still biological machines with physical bodies, and Sukuna can increase the force behind his cuts when a target requires it.
If he brings one down, Tony immediately starts reassessing him.

Until now, Stark has seen Sukuna as an unexplained human shaped threat with unusual attacks. Watching him tear apart something designed to survive military weapons makes it clear that whatever cursed energy is, the Avengers don’t have an easy counter for it. Hulk would probably be the only one enjoying the comparison. The 2 of them could tear through different sections of the invasion almost independently, which means the Avengers gain ground faster than they did originally.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: As the battle spreads, Sukuna would start experimenting.

The Chitauri soldiers themselves aren’t difficult enough to force him into anything serious. A few slashes can clear groups at a time, while anything that reaches him physically is dealing with someone strong enough to survive direct combat with Jujutsu sorcerers at the highest level. The interesting targets are the Leviathans and the larger concentrations of troops around them. This is where Sukuna might consider using Malevolent Shrine, but doing so in the middle of Manhattan would immediately create another problem. His domain doesn’t separate enemies from civilians. Everything inside its effective range can be caught in the cutting attacks, which means activating it carelessly could kill the same people the Avengers are trying to save. Sukuna would know that. He just wouldn’t care about it for the same reason they do. The Avengers only realize something worse is coming when Sukuna begins to deliberately set himself in the middle of a dense section of the battlefield and makes it clear he could wipe out everything around him much faster if he wanted to. Tony and Steve may not know what a Domain Expansion is, but that is enough warning to understand he is preparing a large-area attack that would put civilians at risk.
Steve would make it clear that if Sukuna uses an attack that starts killing civilians, the Avengers are going to treat him as another enemy.

That wouldn’t intimidate Sukuna, but it could still influence the decision. Not because he suddenly cares about Steve’s rules. He simply doesn’t need Malevolent Shrine yet. The Chitauri aren’t forcing him into it. That’s important because it keeps the battle from becoming a cheap instant win. Sukuna has no reason to burn through his most destructive options when normal techniques are already working. After already using Dismantle and Cleave throughout the battle, Sukuna has satisfied the prerequisite for Divine Flame, and he’d probably enjoy testing Furnace against one of the Leviathans more. The attack gives him a way to deal huge damage to a large target without filling an entire section of the city with indiscriminate slashes, although the blast itself would still be dangerous enough that the Avengers would want him away from civilians before he uses it. The result is that New York gets cleared faster. Hulk and Thor no longer have to deal with every major Chitauri target themselves, while Tony has more freedom to focus on the portal and the incoming missile. That changes the timing of the endgame. Loki gets isolated sooner. And Sukuna has already decided he wants to see what kind of god started all of this.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: Loki’s confrontation with the Avengers becomes much worse for him once Sukuna reaches Stark Tower.

By this point, Loki has already seen enough to know that Sukuna refused to join him and has spent most of the invasion destroying his army instead. What he didn’t expect was how quickly Sukuna would lose interest in the Chitauri once he understood their limits. Loki is more interesting. He’s stronger than a normal human, durable enough to survive attacks from the Avengers, and capable of using illusions and magic to make a direct fight less predictable. Sukuna would finally have a reason to test him properly.

Loki’s illusions could create problems for most fighters, but Sukuna is extremely good at reading opponents and has experience dealing with techniques that hide information or distort what someone perceives. That doesn’t mean he automatically sees through every illusion, but Loki wouldn't be able to rely on confusion for long.

Loki can survive being thrown around by Hulk without dying, so Sukuna would quickly realize he needs more than a casual slash to end the fight. If Sukuna closes the distance and makes physical contact, Cleave becomes much more dangerous once he adjusts to how tough Loki actually is.
Loki’s best chance would be keeping distance and using the scepter or his other magic before Sukuna gets close enough to start controlling the exchange.

Sukuna isn’t going to let it touch him. The fight would therefore end much faster than Loki expects. He may survive several attacks, but once Sukuna realizes Loki is the person responsible for bringing the Chitauri here, he has no reason to keep the fight going for long.

Hulk might not even get his famous chance to throw Loki around the tower. That creates another butterfly effect. With Loki incapacitated earlier, he can no longer interfere with the Avengers or personally affect the battle, but Natasha still has to reach Selvig, recover the scepter, and close the portal through essentially the same process as before.
The nuclear strike still becomes the biggest immediate threat. And Sukuna, for once, is standing in a situation where cutting the enemy isn’t enough to solve the problem.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: Tony would still be the one most likely to intercept the missile. Sukuna can destroy things from range, but a nuclear weapon detonating over Manhattan isn’t something he can safely treat like another Chitauri craft. Cutting it apart over the city could be even worse if the warhead still detonates. That means Tony’s original plan remains the safest option. He carries the missile through the portal. The difference is that the battle below is already under much better control. The Avengers aren’t being overwhelmed as badly, and Sukuna has destroyed enough of the Chitauri force that the city has more breathing room while Natasha works on the portal.

The army he had been fighting simply shuts down before he can finish testing everything he wanted to test. The Avengers would feel the opposite. New York survives, Loki is captured, and the portal closes. Then everyone remembers Sukuna is still standing there. That becomes the most uncomfortable moment of the entire battle.

During the invasion, it was easy to accept his help because there were thousands of alien soldiers trying to kill people. Now the Chitauri are gone, and nothing is keeping Sukuna pointed in the same direction as the Avengers.
Steve would be the first person to treat that seriously.

Thor would likely stand beside him because he has already seen enough of Sukuna to understand that he isn’t just another unpredictable enhanced human. Hulk is still nearby, Tony still has his armor, and Natasha and Clint know exactly how dangerous the situation has become.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: After New York, S.H.I.E.L.D.’s priority would change almost overnight. Loki is leaving with Thor. The Tesseract is gone. The immediate alien invasion is over but Sukuna is staying.

That difference matters because Loki was ultimately a problem with a destination. Thor could take him back to Asgard, the Tesseract could leave Earth with them, and S.H.I.E.L.D. could at least tell itself that the crisis had ended. There’s no equivalent solution for Sukuna. Fury would want every piece of information they collected during the battle analyzed immediately. Tony would start going through footage of Dismantle and Cleave frame by frame, trying to work out whether there’s any detectable pattern before the cuts appear. He’d probably get frustrated quickly because there’s no visible projectile, no muzzle flash, and no conventional energy signature his armor can simply lock onto.

Bruce would approach it differently. Instead of trying to build a counter immediately, he’d want to understand what cursed energy actually is. The problem is that Sukuna has no reason to cooperate with him, and even if Bruce somehow got a blood sample or readings from one of the fights, cursed energy doesn’t behave like gamma radiation or anything else he already understands.

But nobody on Earth understands Domain Expansion yet and nobody knows what Malevolent Shrine looks like. Obviously Sukuna wouldn’t volunteer that information. That means every contingency Tony or Fury builds is based on an incomplete version of him. Tony would still build them. He’d begin treating Sukuna more like a problem that needs layers of responses rather than one perfect counter. If direct armor can’t reliably stop the slashes, then distance matters. If distance doesn’t help, remote suits start becoming more valuable. If Sukuna can heal, then simply hurting him isn’t enough. Tony would also notice that Sukuna often studies people before showing more of what he can do, which means unpredictability becomes part of the plan.

Steve would hate the idea of preparing to kill someone who hasn't attacked them since New York, but he wouldn’t ignore the risk either. Helping during the invasion doesn’t erase what Sukuna is. Steve would probably be the person most focused on setting a clear line. As long as Sukuna isn’t hurting civilians, the Avengers don’t start a war they may not be able to finish. The moment he does, they respond together.

He’s seen enough warriors like Sukuna to recognize what arrogance backed by real power can turn into. Thor also knows that Sukuna isn’t impressed by titles, armies, or threats, so trying to intimidate him with Asgard wouldn’t accomplish much. If anything, telling Sukuna there are stronger beings beyond Earth might only give him another reason to keep looking.

Bruce would have his own concern. Sukuna now knows Hulk exists. During the Helicarrier fight, Sukuna didn’t react to Hulk with fear. He reacted with interest, and Bruce would understand exactly why that’s dangerous. Sukuna might eventually seek Hulk out simply because he wants to finish the fight they never got to complete.

That creates a strange pressure on Bruce. In the original timeline, he wants distance from the Avengers because he’s afraid of what Hulk can do around other people. With Sukuna around, staying connected to the team suddenly becomes safer than disappearing alone.

Natasha and Clint would also change how they work. Neither of them can survive a direct fight with Sukuna, so they’d focus on information. Where does he go? What gets his attention? What makes him lose interest? Does he avoid certain situations because they’re boring, or because they actually pose a threat?

His presence would also keep the Avengers closer together after New York. In the original timeline, the team separates after the battle because there’s no immediate reason for all 6 of them to remain in the same place. Here, Fury has a reason to maintain much tighter communication. Tony still returns to Stark Tower, Steve still works with S.H.I.E.L.D., Thor eventually leaves Earth, and Bruce still tries to find some peace, but there’s now a standing contingency that can bring everyone back quickly if Sukuna becomes active.

That changes later MCU events before they even begin. HYDRA operating inside S.H.I.E.L.D. becomes much more dangerous because any internal conflict could accidentally draw Sukuna’s attention. If he discovers that one organization has been pretending to be another for decades, he may not care about the political consequences, but he could absolutely interfere if someone involved interests him.

Ultron would create an even stranger situation. A self aware Al capable of controlling armies of machines is the kind of thing Sukuna has never encountered before. He wouldn't automatically side with Ultron, and Ultron would have no obvious way to understand cursed energy either. Their first meeting could become less about morality and more about two dangerous beings trying to determine whether the other is worth taking seriously.
Eventually, one of them would learn why that doesn’t work. The Avengers would know better by then. They wouldn’t trust Sukuna, but they’d understand him enough to know that keeping Earth
safe sometimes means making sure whatever new threat arrives is more interesting to him than the people living here.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: Sukuna being in The Avengers wouldn’t turn him into Earth’s 7th hero.
He’d help stop Loki because the invasion gives him something worth fighting, and his presence would make the Battle of New York much easier for the Avengers to survive.

Earth now has a threat that can’t be sent back to Asgard, locked in a normal prison, or trusted to stay on anyone’s side. The Avengers still form because of Loki, but Sukuna gives them a reason to stay ready long after Loki is gone.
And sooner or later, the same person who fought beside them in New York is going to decide he wants to find out whether Earth’s mightiest heroes have gotten any stronger.

scripts.title: What If Sukuna Was In The Boys

sections.name: INTRO
paras: Vought would notice Sukuna almost immediately because nothing about him fits the system they understand. He has no Compound V in his body, no history with the company, and no reason to cooperate with anyone trying to study him. The more footage they collect, the worse the situation looks, because he can tear through Supes without using anything Vought recognizes.

Sukuna wouldn’t care much about the company itself, but he would notice how everyone talks about The Seven. In this world, they’re treated like the strongest people alive, even though most of them would look weak compared to the sorcerers and curses he’s fought before.
That would eventually bring Homelander into it. At first, he’d probably expect another Supe who could be controlled, but Sukuna would quickly show him otherwise.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: For this scenario, Sukuna would be using his peak late-manga incarnation in his original Heian-form body, with the endgame abilities he has demonstrated, including Dismantle, Cleave, Reverse Cursed Technique, Malevolent Shrine, and Furnace. Sukuna’s first problem would be figuring out where he is, although it probably wouldn’t take long for him to understand the basics. This world has no cursed spirits, no sorcerers, and seemingly nobody who can sense cursed energy, yet superhuman people are everywhere in the news. Most of them work for one company, their fights are filmed, and civilians buy merchandise with their faces on it. Sukuna would find the whole thing strange, but he wouldn’t need a complete explanation before moving on.

His arrival would draw attention after the first Supe tried to stop him. It wouldn’t need to be anyone important either. Vought has heroes working across the country, and one of them responding to a violent incident involving Sukuna would be enough to create the first footage of him. The Supe would approach him expecting another powered criminal, while Sukuna would probably let the situation continue long enough to see what this person can actually do. Once he realizes there isn’t much there, a Dismantle could end the fight before anyone nearby understands what happened.

That footage would reach Vought quickly. A man they’ve never seen before just killed one of their Supes with an attack that the cameras barely picked up, and there’s no known weapon at the scene that explains the wounds. Vought could cover up one dead hero easily enough, but they'd still need to know who did it. Facial rec wouldn’t return anything useful, and there’d be no employment records, medical history, or past connection to another superhero organization because Sukuna simply doesn’t exist in their world.
He'd eventually come across another one, and this time Vought would make sure they were watching.

Instead of sending someone important, they’d use a lower level Supe and monitor the encounter from a distance. They'd want to see whether Sukuna’s first kill came from a weapon, some hidden technology, or an ability they haven't identified yet. The Supe might have enough durability to survive gunfire and enough strength to tear through a normal person, which would usually be plenty for Vought’s purposes, but Sukuna has spent his life fighting opponents who can survive far worse.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Vought’s first real approach would probably look friendly because that’s how they handle valuable people before force becomes necessary. Sukuna has no public identity yet, which gives them room to decide what story they want around him, and someone inside the company would immediately see the potential. A powerful unknown man with abilities that don’t come from Compound V could be sold as a new hero, studied as another source of powers, or quietly kept away from the public while Vought works out where he came from.

They'd arrange a meeting somewhere controlled and send people who know how to handle Supes without making the situation feel like an arrest. Sukuna might even go, mostly because Vought has become one of the few things in this world worth looking into. Their people keep following him, their heroes are treated like royalty, and they clearly know more about the Supes than the public does.

Sukuna doesn’t need any of those things. Vought would eventually move toward the part they actually care about and ask for testing. They’d want scans, tissue samples, and controlled demonstrations of whatever ability produced the cuts seen in the earlier footage. Sukuna might tolerate some of it if he’s curious enough to see what they discover, but the moment they start acting as though his cooperation is expected, the meeting would become much less comfortable.

The strangest result would come later, when Sukuna voluntarily allows Vought's scientists to take a blood sample during their controlled testing because he's curious enough to see what they think they'll discover. Compound V wouldn't be there. Every Supe Vought understands ultimately traces back to the same substance, even when the public is told a different story, so finding someone with abilities this dangerous and no V in his body would become more important than the dead hero itself.

The scientists wouldn't find anything they recognize. His body would look human in ways they understand, but cursed energy has no equivalent in their research, and their equipment wouldn't suddenly explain how Cleave or Dismantle works. They would notice the obvious physical abnormalities of Sukuna’s Heian-form body, although the bigger issue remains that none of their tests lead back to Compound V.
Sukuna would notice before they actually make their move.

He wouldn’t need special knowledge of modern security systems to recognize people preparing for a fight, and once Vought commits, he’d finally get a better look at what their forces can do. Bullets wouldn’t matter much against him, while stronger restraints designed for Supes would only become interesting if they could hold him long enough to be tested. He could cut through doors, weapons, and the people carrying them without needing to touch any of them, which would leave Vought trying to understand an attack they still can’t see.

The company would bring in a stronger Supe once normal security fails. The original Black Noir makes the most sense here because Vought can send their silent assassin off the books without creating a public scene. Long before he was replaced by a comedic actor later in the show, the original Noir was a ruthless black ops veteran with extreme durability, giving Sukuna an actual fight instead of an instant slaughter.

Sukuna would notice that immediately. Noir moves with purpose, doesn’t waste time talking, and can keep fighting through injuries that would stop most people. Their exchange could last longer because Sukuna would actually want to see what Noir can survive, especially once regular slashes fail to put him down right away.

Noir’s durability still has limits, though. At range, Sukuna could keep testing Noir with stronger Dismantles, while Cleave becomes relevant if Sukuna gets physical contact with him. Cleave adjusts its cutting power to the target when it is used rather than progressively evolving past durability. Noir could survive the beginning of the fight and maybe land a few attacks of his own, but eventually Sukuna's stronger slashes and close-range Cleave could cut deeply enough that regeneration and pain tolerance stop being enough.

He wouldn't necessarily kill Noir there. If Noir keeps getting back up, Sukuna may leave him alive simply because he was more interesting than the others, although Vought would come away from the encounter with a much worse problem. One of their most reliable fighters couldn't contain him, the facility is damaged, and Sukuna has now seen what happens when Vought stops asking nicely.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: The Seven wouldn't all react to Sukuna the same way because most of them have very different ideas about what being powerful actually means. Maeve would take the reports seriously once she sees what happened to Noir, while A-Train would probably be more interested in how someone with no V managed to appear out of nowhere. Starlight, still learning what Vought is really like during this point in the timeline, would immediately notice how quickly the company went from offering Sukuna a place to trying to lock him inside a facility.
Homelander would hear the same information and focus on the one part Vought can’t answer. They don’t know how strong Sukuna actually is.

Every fight so far has ended before Sukuna needed to show much. Vought has footage of invisible cuts, dead Supes, and a badly injured Noir, but nothing that tells them where Sukuna’s limit is. That uncertainty would bother Homelander more than the deaths themselves because Vought normally has files on everyone around him. He knows what Maeve can do, he knows how fast A-Train is, and he knows which members of The Seven would have no chance against him. Sukuna arrives without any of that history.

That wouldn't stop the rest of The Seven from crossing paths with Sukuna. A-Train could be the first one Sukuna meets outside the controlled environment. His speed works differently from the straightforward strength and durability Sukuna has seen from other Supes, and his first attack could genuinely catch Sukuna if Sukuna initially underestimates an unfamiliar speedster and gives him an opening before understanding what he's dealing with.

A-Train would realize quickly that another pass could get him killed and retreat rather than keep testing it, especially if this happens before his obsession with staying on top pushes him further into Compound V abuse. He’d return to Vought with something the cameras couldn't provide: Sukuna was able to adjust to his speed after seeing it.

Maeve would understand the danger more clearly from that. She has enough experience to know that durability and raw strength only go so far when the opponent can cut from a distance, and she wouldn't be eager to fight someone just because Vought wants more data. Starlight would have even less reason to help the company contain him once she understands that Vought provoked the facility incident themselves.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: The Boys would hear about Sukuna through the damage he leaves behind rather than anything Vought says publicly. A dead Supe can disappear from the news, but a damaged Vought facility and injured employees create records, and Butcher already spends enough time digging into the company to notice when something unusual happens.

At first, the obvious theory would be another secret Vought project. Compound V explains nearly every superhuman they've dealt with, so someone capable of cutting through Supes without a weapon sounds like another experiment the company doesn’t want anyone knowing about. Hughie would probably assume Sukuna is another victim of Vought before they find evidence showing the company is just as confused as everyone else.

A Supe that Vought can’t control is useful, and someone who can hurt members of The Seven becomes even more useful. Butcher has already built his entire fight around exploiting weaknesses in people who seem untouchable, so footage of Sukuna injuring Noir and forcing A-Train away would immediately give him ideas.

Mother’s Milk would be much more cautious because none of the evidence suggests Sukuna wants to help anyone. The deaths connected to him aren’t targeted attacks on Vought leadership or part of some larger cause. He kills because someone gets in his way, and there’s no reason to assume civilians would be safer around him than Supes are.
That would make their first attempt to approach Sukuna one of the more dangerous mistakes they could make.

Butcher would probably go in trying to give Sukuna something useful rather than asking for help directly. Information on Vought, Homelander, or where powerful Supes can be found might be enough to keep Sukuna interested for a few minutes, and Butcher would quickly realize that hatred of Vought isn’t something they share. Sukuna doesn’t care about Compound V being used on children, the people Vought has killed, or the damage Homelander has done. None of it means anything to him unless it leads somewhere interesting.

By this point Sukuna already knows Homelander, so hearing that even Vought has trouble controlling him would fill in some of the gaps. Butcher would happily explain enough about Homelander’s strength to make him sound worth finding because having those two focused on each other could solve a huge problem for The Boys.

Sukuna would understand what Butcher is doing. Manipulation itself wouldn't offend him, but Butcher acting like he can point Sukuna toward an enemy and then benefit from the result would make it clear how desperate The Boys are.

Still, he might let them leave. They’re weak compared to the people he’s fought since arriving, but they know things Vought won't tell him, and that makes them useful for the moment. Butcher would walk away believing he may have created an opening against Homelander, while MM would understand they've just given Sukuna another reason to look for him.
For the first time, Vought and The Boys would be researching the same person and reaching the same conclusion.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: Homelander wouldn’t stay away once he realizes how much attention Sukuna is getting inside Vought. Employees are talking about him, security teams are being redirected because of him, and people who usually rely on Homelander to solve their worst problems are suddenly trying to keep the 2 of them apart. That alone would be enough to make him want the meeting.

He’d find Sukuna himself rather than wait for Vought to arrange it, and Sukuna would probably recognize him before Homelander even says anything. His face is everywhere, and after hearing about him from both Vought and The Boys, Sukuna would finally be standing in front of the person this entire world treats as its strongest Supe.

Homelander would start by trying to understand what Sukuna wants. Someone this powerful appearing without a public identity creates a problem, but it also creates an opportunity if he can be brought under control. He could offer Sukuna a place near the top of Vought, especially if he believes giving him status is easier than forcing him into submission.

Sukuna wouldn’t care about the offer, but Homelander himself would hold his attention. He can see the confidence in the way Homelander moves, recognize the physical presence behind it, and combine that with everything he has already learned from Vought and The Boys to tell that this one is far stronger than the people Vought has already sent. Sukuna would probably enjoy that part because he has finally found someone in this world who might survive long enough to show him something.

Homelander would notice that Sukuna is studying him, and that’s where the conversation would start going wrong. He’s used to controlling the pace when he speaks to people, especially once they understand who he is, but Sukuna would have no reason to play along. If Homelander moves closer to intimidate him, Sukuna would stay where he is. If he lets his eyes glow to make the threat obvious, Sukuna would be more interested in seeing what the attack does than backing away from it.

Homelander could test him with a quick burst of heat vision. Sukuna has no reason to stand there and take it, so he’d move as soon as he sees the attack coming, then send a Dismantle back. Homelander’s durability would immediately separate him from the Supes Sukuna fought earlier. A slash strong enough to tear through a normal Supe might only cut into his skin, and seeing that would change Sukuna’s approach because he finally has a target worth testing properly.

Homelander would feel the cut and realize Sukuna can actually hurt him. That’s enough to make the encounter much more serious, but it still wouldn’t have to become their full fight yet. Neither of them knows enough about the other. Homelander has speed, flight, strength, heat vision, and durability Sukuna hasn't fully measured, while Homelander has only seen one part of a cursed technique that goes much further than invisible slashes.

Sukuna would likely let the exchange continue for a little longer, using stronger attacks to see how Homelander’s body responds while avoiding the heat vision rather than wasting cursed energy healing damage he can prevent. Homelander could use his flight to change angles and attack from above, which immediately gives Sukuna something different to deal with because most of his opponents don’t stay hundreds of feet in the air while attacking from range.

If Homelander rushes him physically, Sukuna gets an even better idea of what he can do. The impact could send Sukuna through a wall or across the street, and Homelander would probably assume that finally established the gap between them until Sukuna gets back up. Reverse Cursed Technique means injuries that would end a fight against most people can be repaired as long as Sukuna still has the cursed energy and control to heal them, so Homelander would have to do far more than land one clean hit.

Sukuna would be learning throughout the exchange. Homelander is faster than most opponents in this world, physically stronger than the other Supes he has encountered, and durable enough that basic slashes aren’t enough to end things quickly. At the same time, his fighting style would look crude compared to the sorcerers Sukuna is used to. Homelander relies heavily on having better physical abilities than whoever stands in front of him, and he rarely needs the kind of technical combat knowledge Sukuna developed across constant battles.

The first encounter could end when Vought intervenes from a distance and convinces Homelander that continuing in public is creating a disaster they can’t hide. He wouldn't like walking away after being cut, although Sukuna wouldn’t chase him either because he now knows the fight is actually worth having later.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: After the first clash between Sukuna and Homelander, Vought would have a problem they can’t solve with PR. Homelander was hurt in public, there’s footage of the damage, and Sukuna is still walking around with no deal, no handler, and no reason to listen to anyone inside the company. Vought would probably stop trying to recruit him and focus on keeping him away from anything important. That means tracking his movements, clearing locations before he reaches them, and feeding Homelander as little information as possible whenever Sukuna shows up again. The company would still want to study him, but every attempt to get close now carries the risk of another fight that could destroy half a building.

Homelander wouldn’t handle that well. He’d already know Sukuna can hurt him, and the fact that Vought is suddenly being careful around someone else would only make him more interested. He’d want another fight, especially once he realizes the first one ended before either of them had really shown what they could do.

Sukuna wouldn't rush it either. He knows Homelander is strong now, and that makes him one of the few people in this world worth keeping alive long enough to fight properly. Until then, he’d keep moving wherever he wants, and Vought would be forced to react every time he gets close to something they care about.
The Boys would be watching all of this from the outside, and Butcher would see exactly where it's heading.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Butcher would want the 2nd fight to happen as soon as possible because it gives him the best chance he’s had in years of seeing Homelander seriously hurt. He wouldn't care who wins as long as the fight leaves one of them dead or weak enough to finish afterward.
The problem is getting close enough to matter without Sukuna killing them first.

Hughie and MM would push against any plan that depends on treating Sukuna like an ally because by now they’ve seen enough to know he isn’t one. He has no interest in helping civilians, exposing Vought, or protecting anyone caught between him and Homelander. If a fight starts in a crowded area, Sukuna isn’t going to stop because innocent people are nearby.

That means The Boys have to play the long game. Trying to steer 2 god level killers away from the city is impossible, so they focus entirely on tracking the clash from the shadows. While the rest of the crew braces for the inevitable devastation, Butcher only cares about one thing: staying close enough to ambush and put down whichever monster survives the bloodbath. Sukuna would eventually notice them following him. He might leave them alone because they’re still occasionally useful for information, but that wouldn’t mean he trusts them. Butcher would have to be careful with how far he pushes, because Sukuna already understands what he’s trying to do.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: The 2nd fight would start much harder than the first because Homelander would already know basic slashes can hurt him. He’d stay in the air longer, use heat vision from different angles, and rely on speed to keep Sukuna from settling into the fight.

That would work for a while. Homelander is fast enough to force Sukuna to react, and a direct hit from his heat vision could burn through flesh before Reverse Cursed Technique repairs it. Sukuna would still keep learning every time Homelander attacks, especially once the pattern becomes clear. Homelander likes using overwhelming speed and force because it usually ends fights before technique matters.

Sukuna would start timing his slashes around those rushes. Instead of chasing Homelander through the air, he could cut across the path Homelander needs to take, forcing him to either change direction or take the hit. The stronger those slashes become, the harder it gets for Homelander to keep relying on the same approach.

Once Homelander closes into physical contact, Cleave becomes another serious threat. Outside the domain, Sukuna needs to touch the target to use it, and when used it adjusts its cutting power to the target rather than gradually evolving over the course of the fight. Homelander keeps giving Sukuna chances to attempt it every time he tries to overpower him physically. A slash deep enough to reach muscle or bone would be something Homelander has almost no experience dealing with.

Homelander could still hurt Sukuna badly. He’s strong enough to throw him through buildings, fast enough to catch him between attacks, and his heat vision gives him a ranged option Sukuna has to respect. The difference in fighting experience would become more important the longer they stay alive, because Sukuna is constantly changing what he does while Homelander keeps falling back on the same advantages.

If Homelander still refuses to back off, Sukuna would eventually use Malevolent Shrine. For this crossover, living beings from The Boys would count as valid living targets for the domain's Cleave targeting even though cursed energy does not naturally exist in their universe, preventing the absence of native cursed energy from creating an unintended targeting loophole.

That’s where the fight likely ends. Homelander has incredible durability, but Malevolent Shrine doesn’t depend on landing one clean attack. It fills the area with repeated slashes, and under the crossover rule already established, Homelander counts as a valid living target for Cleave despite lacking native cursed energy, while Dismantle continues cutting the surrounding environment inside the domain’s range. Homelander’s body could survive longer than most Supes, but surviving one slash doesn’t help much when another follows immediately.

Because Malevolent Shrine is an open-barrier domain with a finite effective range, Homelander's best response would be to accelerate out of it immediately. His flight and speed give him a legitimate chance to cross that distance, but he still has to survive the sure-hit slashes accumulating across his body while he escapes. The question becomes whether he can clear the domain's effective radius before the repeated cuts damage him badly enough to stop the attempt.
Homelander would eventually go down from damage, and Sukuna wouldn’t need Furnace unless he wanted to finish the fight in a more destructive way.
PART 9 Homelander dying would tear apart the balance Vought built around him.

The company loses its strongest Supe and the person everyone else was afraid to challenge, while the public has to process the fact that someone killed him in a fight Vought couldn't control. Any story they create afterward would have to compete with whatever footage escaped online.

The Seven would start breaking apart almost immediately. Maeve would have no reason to step into Homelander’s role, A-Train would be thinking about survival, and Vought would be trying to keep investors, politicians, and the public from realizing how exposed they really are.

The Boys would get what they wanted in the worst possible way. Homelander is gone, but Sukuna is still alive, and they helped move the situation toward a fight they had no way to control afterward. Butcher might still think about killing Sukuna, but there’s no realistic plan available with the tools they have.

Sukuna probably wouldn’t stay around Vought for long after that. Homelander was the strongest thing they had, and once he’s gone, most of the remaining Supes wouldn't offer much that interests him. He could leave the company collapsing behind him and move on until something else catches his attention.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: Sukuna wouldn't take over Vought or join The Boys because neither side offers him anything he actually wants. His presence would still change both of them just by removing the 1 person holding so much of their world together.

Homelander could make the fight competitive through speed, strength, heat vision, and durability, but Sukuna has more ways to adjust once the fight keeps going, and Malevolent Shrine gives Homelander very little room to survive once Sukuna decides to end it.
The Boys would finally live in a world without Homelander, although Sukuna would still be somewhere in it, which might be an even worse problem.

scripts.title: What If Superior Spider-Man Was In The Boys

sections.name: INTRO
paras: Otto Octavius would hate almost everything about Vought.

He’d see a company full of people with enormous power, unlimited resources, and barely any discipline, then immediately decide he could run the entire operation better himself. The Seven wouldn’t impress him either. Most of them rely on abilities they were handed, while Otto is used to fighting people stronger than him by studying them first and building around whatever advantage they have.

Vought would want to recruit Spider-Man, Butcher would assume he’s just another Supe with an ego, and Homelander probably wouldn't take him seriously until Otto started digging into things Vought wanted buried.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: Otto’s first reaction to this world wouldn't be fear. He’d be annoyed that he had no idea where he was, then immediately start gathering information. Being trapped in Peter Parker’s body has already forced him to adapt to circumstances he never wanted, so appearing in another universe would become another problem to solve. He still has Peter’s powers, his own intelligence, and the Superior Spider-Man technology he built specifically to make Spider-Man more efficient than Peter ever was.

That technology gives him a much easier start than most people dropped into The Boys universe would get. His suit already contains enhanced sensors, while the Spider-Bots Otto normally uses for surveillance can spread across an area and feed information back to him. In his own New York, he used them to monitor crimes and keep watch over huge sections of the city. Here, they would become his fastest way of learning who actually controls things. Before Otto trusts news broadcasts, police reports, or anything Vought says publicly, he can start building his own picture.

At first, what he finds would look almost impressive. Superheroes are openly recognized, supported by a major company, and organized into teams with enormous resources behind them. To Otto, that sounds closer to how superhero work should operate. He spent years thinking Peter wasted his abilities by reacting to crime instead of building systems that could prevent it, so seeing Vought coordinate Supes on a national scale would interest him.

The Spider-Bots would start recording things Vought never intended the public to see. Supes arriving after crimes instead of preventing them, security teams cleaning up mistakes, and incidents getting buried once cameras stop rolling would quickly make the entire system look less impressive. Otto would notice that a lot of these heroes rely almost entirely on raw powers because they've never needed anything else. There’s little planning, almost no technical discipline, and even less accountability when something goes wrong.

It needs someone competent in charge. A Spider-Man appearing without any Compound V record would already be strange, but Otto’s behavior would make him even more valuable. He isn’t simply stopping crimes. He’s deploying surveillance technology, identifying patterns, and responding before Vought’s own Supes can reach some incidents. The company would realize very quickly that they’re looking at someone who might actually improve the product.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Vought’s first approach would be friendly because Otto looks like the easiest kind of problem to turn into an asset. Spider-Man is recognizable, visually marketable, and already behaving like a hero. There’s no public scandal attached to him yet, no contract tying him to anyone else, and no obvious organization protecting him.
Otto would agree to meet them for reasons that have almost nothing to do with joining The Seven.

The moment he sees Vought Tower, the labs, security systems, databases, and access to Supe research, his interest would shift toward what the company can give him. Vought has spent decades studying Compound V and documenting people with abilities Otto has never encountered before. If he can get inside that system, he can learn far more than he could by watching public footage from rooftops.

He’d let Ashley and the executives explain how Vought works while quietly judging almost everything they say. They’d pitch sponsorships, public approval, access to resources, and eventually some form of official position. Otto wouldn't care about most of it, but he’d understand the usefulness of letting them think he does.

A-Train would immediately annoy him. Otto would look at someone capable of moving at extreme speed and see how much more effective that power could be with actual discipline behind it. The Deep probably wouldn’t earn enough respect for Otto to bother hiding his contempt, while Starlight would stand out because she still approaches hero work like it should mean something.

Black Noir would interest him more because Noir actually behaves like someone trained for the job. Otto would watch how he moves, how little information he gives away, and how quickly everyone else treats him differently. Even before Otto knows exactly what Noir can survive, he’d recognize that this is someone worth studying rather than dismissing.
Homelander would be harder to read at first.

Publicly, he looks like exactly what Vought claims he is. He can fly, has enormous strength, survives things that would kill almost anyone else, and has spent years presented as the greatest hero in the world. Otto wouldn’t instantly decide he’s evil just because he dislikes his personality.

Otto understands arrogance because he has more than enough of it himself. Homelander expects everyone around him to adjust the moment he enters a room, and the Vought employees do it automatically. Nobody treats him like an employee despite Vought technically being the company in charge. They treat him like something they're trying not to upset.

Homelander, meanwhile, would probably find Spider-Man irritating before he finds him threatening. Otto doesn’t react with the admiration most people give him, and he asks too many technical questions about Vought’s Supes. Homelander could tolerate that while he still believes Spider-Man is beneath him.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Otto wouldn’t hack Vought simply because he’s suspicious of them. He’d do it because he has already decided the company is withholding information he needs, and Otto rarely respects a boundary once he believes he has a better reason to cross it.

The Spider-Bots make that much easier. A few can remain inside Vought Tower after his visit, moving through places where normal surveillance would struggle to follow them. They can listen and transmit images, then map physical access points, watch employees enter credentials, and plant small interfaces on exposed terminals or network hardware. Otto would still have to exploit those openings himself, but the bots mean he doesn’t need to personally break into every restricted floor to start compromising specific Vought systems.

Compound V would be the first major discovery that would completely change how he views The Seven. Until then, Otto could assume these people developed powers through different accidents or biological conditions the same way superhumans often do in his own world. Discovering that Vought created many of them deliberately and has been controlling the process for years would make the company much more interesting and much more dangerous.

Otto wouldn't react to Compound V the way Butcher does. His first instinct would be to understand how it works, why different subjects develop different abilities, what failure rates Vought has buried, and whether the effects can be reproduced or countered. That curiosity would be one of the first signs that Otto isn’t as far removed from Vought as he thinks. Vought sees people as products whenever doing so benefits the company. Otto is already starting to look at their biology as another scientific problem he could solve.

Deaths connected to Supes disappear into settlements. Evidence gets altered. Witnesses get pressured. Some incidents never reach law enforcement at all because Vought handles them before anyone outside the company can investigate.

A-Train running through Robin would stand out because of how little consequence follows something so horrific. Otto wouldn't need to know Hughie personally to understand the problem. A Supe with that much speed made a reckless mistake that killed someone, and the system responded by protecting the asset instead of fixing the behavior.

Peter would’ve focused first on the person who died. Otto would focus on why nobody prevented it. That pushes him toward building his own solution. He’d expand the Spider-Bot network, start tracking individual members of The Seven, and create profiles for each of them. Their patrol patterns, public appearances, known abilities, injuries, behavioral habits, and any information he can steal from Vought would all go into the system.
Homelander’s file would quickly become the largest. Otto still wouldn’t be planning to fight him. He’d simply recognize that anyone with that much power and that little oversight needs a contingency.

Vought would eventually notice data going missing, but by then Otto’s planted interfaces and stolen credentials would have given him enough access to copy key files before the company can shut those specific routes down. And that’s roughly when Butcher would hear that Spider-Man has started digging around the same company he’s spent years trying to tear down.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Butcher would approach Otto expecting another Supe who thinks he’s different from the rest. That assumption wouldn't survive the first conversation.

Otto would have no interest in defending Vought once he understands what the company has been doing, but he’d dislike Butcher almost immediately too. Butcher’s methods are messy, emotional, and built around a hatred of Supes that Otto would see as intellectually lazy. Treating every enhanced person as the same kind of problem makes no sense to someone who has spent his life categorizing threats by what they can actually do.

Butcher wouldn’t be impressed by Otto’s confidence either. As far as he’s concerned, Spider-Man is another powerful man explaining why he should be trusted because he believes he’s smarter than everyone else. The fact that Otto genuinely is smarter than most people in the room wouldn’t make Butcher more comfortable.

Hughie would probably be the one keeping the meeting useful. Once Otto learns Hughie is the person connected to Robin’s death, he would already know most of what happened from Vought’s records. That gives The Boys proof that Spider-Man has access to information they don't, while Otto realizes they've been investigating Vought from the outside for much longer than he has.

Working together becomes useful even if neither side likes the arrangement. The Boys know people inside Vought, understand the company’s habits, and can point Otto toward things that aren't stored neatly in a database. Otto can give them surveillance coverage they could never build themselves and technical analysis far beyond anything Hughie or Butcher can do alone. Butcher would still push Otto on what happens once they have enough evidence. Otto’s answer would be much harsher than Peter’s. If a Supe is genuinely dangerous and refuses to stop, Otto isn’t going to pretend every situation needs another chance. He has already crossed lines Peter wouldn't, and The Boys universe would reinforce his belief that restraint can become negligence when the person being restrained keeps hurting people.

Butcher would agree with the conclusion and hate the person saying it. That creates an uneasy partnership where both men think the other is dangerous for almost opposite reasons. Butcher believes Otto will eventually become another Supe who decides rules don’t apply to him. Otto sees Butcher as someone whose hatred has replaced actual judgment. Homelander would bring that argument into focus. The more information Otto gathers, the clearer it becomes that Homelander isn’t simply Vought’s strongest asset. The company is afraid of him. He can hear far more than most people realize, move faster than Otto can comfortably deal with in a direct exchange, and survive almost every conventional attack Vought has data for.

Otto would also start seeing the behavioral pattern underneath all of that. Homelander wants control, reacts badly when people stop treating him as superior, and often relies on intimidation before using his full strength because he expects fear to solve the problem first.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: Otto wouldn't challenge Homelander the moment he decides he’s dangerous. He knows better than that, especially once the data starts showing how badly a direct fight would go. Peter’s body gives him superhuman strength, speed, durability, and Spider-Sense, but none of that puts him in Homelander’s physical class. If Otto gets caught in a clean exchange, the fight could end before any of his planning matters.

Otto would identify several things he could potentially exploit. The first is confidence. Homelander rarely expects someone weaker than him to have a real answer, which means he tends to approach threats as if intimidation will solve them before force is necessary. Otto would build around that habit. He’d want Homelander to think Spider-Man is still just an irritating outsider who got too curious, because the less threatened Homelander feels, the more likely he is to walk into a controlled situation without looking for traps.

Otto would also study how Homelander uses his senses. Enhanced hearing and vision make sneaking up on him extremely difficult, so the answer wouldn't be simple stealth. Otto could instead flood the environment with information. Multiple Spider-Bots transmitting on different frequencies, false movement, decoy heat signatures, and overlapping sound sources would make it harder for Homelander to identify what actually matters. None of that disables his senses, but it gives Otto room to control where his attention goes.

The heat vision needs a separate response. Otto knows he can’t trust his suit to absorb repeated hits, so he’d modify it around brief survival instead of trying to become immune. Reflective or ablative layers, deployable shields, and remote drones could buy him fractions of a second at a time. Spider-Sense helps him know when the attack is coming, but even that only matters if the suit and environment give him somewhere to move.

Then there’s the durability problem. Otto would quickly realize that beating Homelander through punches is a waste of time. He’d start looking for ways to restrict movement, interfere with breathing or balance, attack sensory weak points, and exploit the fact that Maeve was able to injure his ear with a metal object during their fight. That doesn’t mean Otto suddenly has a reproducible weak spot. Maeve is enormously strong herself, so Otto can’t assume precision alone would let him recreate what she did. It only gives him evidence that the ear may be a more promising place to test concentrated force than Homelander’s exterior.

The Boys would notice what he’s doing and understand where it’s heading. Butcher would love the idea of finally having someone capable of building a real contingency. Hughie would be less comfortable with how far Otto is willing to go, especially once the plans stop looking like self-defense and start looking like a premeditated takedown.

Otto wouldn't care much about the distinction. From his perspective, waiting until Homelander kills more people just to preserve the moral comfort of reacting later would be irresponsible. That argument would sound familiar to Butcher.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Vought would eventually realize Spider-Man is no longer behaving like a recruit. The missing data, Spider-Bot activity, and increasingly specific questions about Homelander would make it obvious that Otto has moved from curiosity into investigation. Ashley would first try to control the situation quietly, because turning Spider-Man into an enemy creates another public problem they don’t need.

They’d offer him more. Better lab access, private research agreements, a larger role in Vought’s technology division, and enough money to make most people stop asking questions would all get put on the table. Otto would listen because he never wastes an opportunity to learn what someone is willing to give away, but the offer itself would confirm that Vought knows he’s close to something important.

Homelander would take the entire situation more personally. Spider-Man’s lack of fear had already annoyed him. Finding out that Otto has been studying him would feel like disrespect. Homelander is used to people either admiring him or being too scared to challenge him openly, and Otto fits neither category. He treats Homelander like a technical problem.

That would push Homelander into confronting him before Vought wants him to. The first meeting wouldn’t have to become a full fight. Homelander would want to make Otto understand how quickly he could end things if he chose to, and Otto would deliberately keep his response calm. He knows there’s nothing useful about provoking someone he hasn't finished preparing for. Homelander would probably make some kind of demonstration anyway. A burst of heat vision close enough to damage the wall beside him, a sudden movement meant to trigger Spider-Sense, or simply grabbing Otto hard enough to make the physical difference clear would all accomplish the same thing.
Otto would leave with more data which would infuriate Homelander even more. He'd realize afterward that Spider-Man wasn’t frozen by fear.

Vought would understand the danger before Homelander does. If the 2 of them fight publicly and Spider-Man survives, Homelander’s image takes damage even if he still wins. If Otto somehow exposes classified information during the conflict, the company has an even bigger crisis.

Ashley would push for containment through other means. That’s where Black Noir becomes useful. Sending Noir after Otto gives Vought a way to remove the Spider-Bots, recover stolen equipment, or at least pressure him without putting Homelander in front of cameras. Noir is also disciplined enough to follow the objective instead of turning the encounter into a personal contest.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Black Noir is dangerous to Otto because he fights in a way Homelander usually doesn't.

He doesn’t announce himself, he doesn’t need to prove he’s stronger, and he’s willing to wait for the right opening. Spider-Sense protects Otto from being caught completely unaware, but that doesn’t mean the fight becomes easy. Noir is fast, experienced, durable, and comfortable using blades and the environment instead of relying on one obvious power.

That would make him more aggressive. Superior Spider-Man has always been more willing than Peter to use his strength without pulling punches as carefully, and Noir’s durability would encourage him to push even further. The first few hits might throw Noir through walls or across a room, only for him to get back up and keep coming.

The fight would become a test of control rather than raw strength. Otto could web his joints, use Spider-Bots to track him through blind spots, and force him into spaces where Noir can’t use stealth effectively. Noir would keep cutting through webbing and looking for close-range openings, while Otto would gradually remove those options with more restraints and environmental traps.

Eventually, Otto should have the advantage, but not because Peter’s body simply outscales Noir. Spider-Sense makes Noir’s ambushes much harder to capitalize on, while Otto’s mobility, webbing, Spider-Bots, and prepared restraints let him progressively remove the close-range openings Noir needs. He could pin Noir under reinforced webbing, use electric restraints, or trap him inside a controlled space rather than trying to beat him unconscious. What happens after the fight would matter more than the victory itself. Peter would stop once Noir is contained. Otto would be tempted to go further. By now, he knows Noir has been used to carry out Vought’s worst orders and that simply letting him return to the company could put more people at risk. The logic is easy for Otto to justify: if someone is dangerous enough and the system keeps protecting them, removing them permanently prevents future harm.
He’d stop himself, but not quickly enough to feel comfortable about why he wanted to keep going.

That moment would stay with him. He came into this world convinced that The Seven proved heroes became ineffective when they were too soft. Now he’s standing over someone he already defeated and realizing how easy it would be to start deciding who deserves another chance.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: Homelander wouldn't tolerate Noir losing to Spider-Man quietly. By this point, Otto has stolen Vought data, resisted recruitment, survived intimidation, and beaten one of the company’s most reliable operatives. Homelander would stop seeing him as an irritating outsider and start seeing him as someone openly challenging his position.

Otto still wouldn’t want the fight on Homelander’s terms. He’d choose the location himself, somewhere away from civilians and dense enough with infrastructure that his traps actually matter. An abandoned industrial site or decommissioned Vought facility would give him walls, power systems, enclosed spaces, and enough metal to build around without risking a city block.

A controlled leak through one of Vought’s systems, a message designed to look like Otto has found something damaging, or even a Spider-Bot deliberately allowing itself to be traced could bring Homelander exactly where Otto wants him.
Homelander would still think he’s walking into a confrontation he can end whenever he gets bored. The first few seconds would prove why Otto prepared so carefully.

Spider-Sense warns Otto that the attack is coming before Homelander fully commits, but Peter’s body still can’t simply react to Homelander at full speed. Otto has already positioned himself so Homelander has only a few clean approaches, and the warning lets him trigger the prepared sequence before the rush reaches him. The floor collapses along the expected path, automated web launchers fire from multiple angles, and drones flood the space with false targets and sound.

None of that is strong enough to hold him for long. Otto only needs every layer to cost Homelander a little time. Heat vision burns through the first restraints, so Otto redirects him into another section where reflective panels and sacrificial shields reduce how cleanly he can keep the beam on target. Homelander tears through those too, but now he’s moving exactly where Otto expected.

Homelander would eventually get a hand on him. One clean hit sends him through reinforced material hard enough to damage the suit and leave Peter’s body struggling to recover. Another like that could finish the fight.

Otto would respond by escalating. He’d target the ears with concentrated sonic attacks, combine them with webbing around the face and joints, and use everything he learned from Maeve’s fight to focus pressure on places where Homelander has shown some vulnerability. It wouldn’t suddenly make Homelander weak, but it would hurt enough to make him angry.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: Once Homelander starts fighting emotionally instead of carefully, Otto gets the chance to find out which parts of the plan actually work. Homelander would begin ignoring some of the drones and environmental traps because he’d want to reach Otto directly, making his movement easier to predict. Otto could use the Spider-Bots to track his approach, trigger restraints before Homelander reaches each position, and keep shifting the fight through prepared areas while testing the sonic emitters, restraint timing, and possible ear vulnerability. He would only commit harder to a tactic after Homelander’s reactions show that it is producing a real effect.

The sonic attacks would become one of Otto’s biggest experiments here. Homelander has shown sensitivity to high frequencies, but Otto has no proof that sound alone can seriously incapacitate him. High frequency emitters hidden throughout the site could hit him from several directions while Otto keeps changing position, letting Otto test whether sustained pressure can disrupt his hearing, concentration, or enhanced senses enough to matter. If it barely affects him, the rest of the plan still has to function without treating sound as a hard counter.

Homelander would eventually start destroying the emitters, which is exactly why Otto wouldn't build the plan around one device. Every time Homelander removes 1 source, another activates somewhere else, and Otto can use the distraction to add web restraints or redirect him into another section of the facility. The webbing itself won’t hold Homelander for long, but it can slow an arm cover his eyes for a second, or force him to waste time tearing through material instead of attacking.

Otto would still take damage. There’s no realistic version of this fight where he controls every exchange perfectly. Homelander is too fast and too strong, and sooner or later he’d get through part of the setup and land another hit. Peter’s body can survive an enormous amount of punishment, but Homelander could eventually overwhelm it if Otto lets the fight become close-range for too long.

That would force Otto to use the most dangerous part of the plan. He’d have prepared a concentrated sonic chamber built around everything he learned from Vought’s files and Maeve’s fight. Once Homelander follows him inside, the room could close around them and hit him with the strongest frequencies Otto’s earlier testing suggested were disruptive while automated restraints attack his joints and neck from several directions. Otto wouldn’t know whether that will genuinely overload Homelander’s hearing or merely irritate him. The chamber is a gamble meant to create whatever brief disorientation it can, not a proven way to incapacitate him.

That’s where Otto’s ruthlessness becomes the real advantage. Peter would probably use the opening to escape or try to restrain Homelander again. Otto would go straight for the injury point. A reinforced Spider-Arm, specialized projectile, or piece of equipment designed to deliver concentrated force could be driven into the ear while Homelander is struggling with the sound. Otto has already seen Maeve injure this area, so he’d treat it as his best experimental target rather than assume he can reproduce her result. The finishing move would be built around testing whether concentrated force there can do meaningful damage at all.
