His Infinity has been automated to identify approaching danger, and the Six Eyes gives him the precision and efficiency needed to keep the technique running continuously.

That change in formation would immediately tell Gojo what the Avengers are doing. He’d know Tony has realized the obvious attacks aren’t going anywhere, and the Six Eyes would let him read the energy and movements around the battlefield with far more precision than the Avengers expect. It wouldn’t automatically explain every piece of MCU magic to him, but he’d see that Strange and Wanda are doing something different from Tony’s armor or Thor’s physical attacks.

Gojo could start targeting the support members before they finish testing him, which would force the heavy hitters back into the fight. Blue could drag Strange away from the group, but the Cloak of Levitation gives Strange another way to correct his movement while he prepares a spell. Tony could use drones and armor pieces to keep Gojo’s attention divided, while Spider-Man and Black Panther focus on pulling injured teammates out of danger instead of trying to attack.

This is where the Avengers’ numbers finally start helping. They still can’t overwhelm Infinity, but they can create enough movement around Gojo that Strange and Wanda get time to work. Tony would also start considering whether Gojo has to consciously see an attack coming. A shot from behind gives him the answer when Infinity stops it anyway, and environmental attacks show that simply hiding the source doesn’t bypass the technique. Once that possibility is eliminated, Tony would have very few conventional options left.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Strange would approach the problem differently because he already works with space, dimensions, and effects that don’t always behave like physical attacks. Sling Ring portals can connect distant locations and open paths into other realms, while his magic also includes binding spells, shields, and astral projection.

The obvious first test would be a portal. Opening one beneath Gojo wouldn't require a projectile to travel toward him. Strange would be changing the space around his location, which creates a much more legitimate question about whether Infinity prevents the effect. There’s no clear canon answer across the two universes, so the safest way to treat it is as an uncertain interaction: the portal itself doesn’t obviously have to cross Infinity, but neither series establishes whether Strange can form one directly in space being controlled by Limitless.

If Strange can form a portal beneath Gojo, it could potentially drop him somewhere else on the battlefield or into the Mirror Dimension, but that still wouldn’t make it a confirmed Infinity bypass. Gojo would notice the spatial change almost immediately and could use Blue to move before falling through if he has room to react. Strange has at least identified a more promising experiment than Tony’s physical attacks, but whether it actually works has to remain uncertain.

Strange could try binding spells next, but anything that forms outside Gojo and then moves inward should still run into Infinity. The bands or magical constructs might be made from mystical energy instead of normal matter, yet they’re still approaching him from a distance. Unless the spell creates its effect directly at Gojo’s position, there’s no strong reason to assume magic gets a free pass.

Astral projection creates a stranger interaction. Strange has shown the ability to separate a person’s astral form from their physical body, which raises the possibility that he could affect Gojo without physically touching him in the normal sense. The problem is that Strange has usually done this through direct contact, and getting his hand onto Gojo is exactly what Infinity prevents.

The Mirror Dimension remains much more useful. Strange could shift the battlefield into another dimension and manipulate the environment there, which wouldn’t turn Infinity off but would give him more control over the space surrounding Gojo. Folding buildings, changing gravity, and altering the layout could keep Gojo occupied while the others look for a real opening.

Gojo would still be extremely dangerous inside it. Infinity remains around him, Blue and Red still function, and Strange has no reason to assume another dimension disables cursed techniques. The Six Eyes would also make it easier for Gojo to study the changes around him and recognize that Strange is the one controlling most of them.

Gojo could use Blue to close the distance rapidly, forcing Strange to defend instead of setting up more portals. Strange’s shields can block physical impacts and energy attacks, but Blue is manipulating the space around him rather than throwing a conventional blast. That could pull Strange out of position and make maintaining complex spells much harder.

The rest of the Avengers would need to protect him. Thor, Captain Marvel, and Hulk still couldn’t overwhelm automated Infinity by making Gojo process more incoming attacks, but they could pressure his positioning, damage the battlefield around him, intercept him when he moves offensively, and physically shield Strange while he prepares another portal. Tony could coordinate those movements based on Gojo’s position, while Steve keeps the team from clustering together where Blue or Red could hit several people at once.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: Wanda is much harder to judge against Infinity because her powers don’t always behave like normal projectiles. By Infinity War and Endgame, she can restrain people, move objects, tear apart machinery, and overpower Thanos directly with telekinesis. Her power manifests around targets in ways that aren't always shown traveling from her hands as a normal physical object, which makes her one of the few Avengers with a plausible way to affect Gojo without punching through the space in front of him.

That interaction is much less clear than Hulk trying to punch him. If Wanda’s telekinesis creates force directly around a target rather than sending something across the distance, Infinity may not have an approaching object to slow. On the other hand, if the MCU power still travels outward from Wanda as an energy effect before taking hold, Infinity should stop it like any other incoming threat.

She could first grab the ground around Gojo and lift the entire section upward. That would work because she isn’t touching him directly, and Gojo would simply move off it. Then she could try closing her power around his arms or torso while Tony watches whether the energy stops outside Infinity or forms directly on him.

If the force appears around Gojo without crossing the space, Wanda may be able to move him. That still wouldn't give her an easy win. Gojo can use Blue to reposition himself, Red to blast her away, and the Six Eyes would tell him very quickly that Wanda is one of the few people on the battlefield who can potentially affect him through a different route. She also lacks the durability of Thor, Hulk, or Captain Marvel, so once Gojo starts targeting her seriously, keeping her conscious becomes one of the Avengers’ biggest problems.

The whole team would have to reorganize around that possibility. Captain Marvel could stay close to Wanda and absorb attacks meant for her, Strange could use portals and shields to change Gojo’s angles, while Tony coordinates the physical fighters so Gojo doesn’t get a clean path toward her. Spider-Man could move Wanda out of danger if the ground starts collapsing, and Thor could use lightning to tear apart the surrounding battlefield, create debris and terrain hazards, and make the approach toward her less convenient even though the directed lightning itself is still assumed to be filtered by Infinity.

Gojo would respond by using Blue more aggressively. Pulling Wanda toward him would disrupt her concentration, while Red could send her across the battlefield before she gets another chance to restrain him. If Strange tries opening a portal between them, Gojo can use Limitless-enhanced movement to change direction and force the team to keep rebuilding the formation around her.

Gojo would start taking the matchup much more seriously once both of them are working together. He has no reason to keep relying only on Infinity and light uses of Blue when the Avengers are narrowing down the mechanics around him, which means the next stage would bring Red, Hollow Purple, and eventually Unlimited Void much closer to the center of the fight. PART 6

Once Strange and Wanda show they can create problems that the rest of the team can’t, Gojo would stop giving the Avengers time to test him one ability at a time. He’d focus on breaking their formation before they can build a clean setup around Wanda, because she’s the one person who might be able to affect him without relying on a normal attack crossing Infinity. Strange matters for the same reason, so those two would become his main targets while Thor, Captain Marvel, Hulk, and the others try to keep him away from them.

Blue would make that difficult because Gojo can control positioning without physically grabbing anyone. A strong enough pull could drag Strange away from the group before he finishes opening another portal, while Wanda could be forced to break concentration just to stop herself from being thrown into a wall or pulled toward Gojo. Tony would react by spreading the team out more, because keeping everyone close gives Gojo too many chances to disrupt several people with the same attack.

Red would start removing some of the weaker members from the fight entirely. War Machine, Falcon, Winter Soldier, Spider-Man, and the Guardians can survive plenty compared to normal people, but a direct Red would hit hard enough to launch most of them away from the battlefield or injure them badly. Gojo wouldn't need to kill everyone to reduce the Avengers’ numbers. Getting them out of position and making the stronger heroes protect them would already help. Captain Marvel would be one of the few people who could take a Red and keep coming. Thor could probably do the same, although repeated hits would still wear him down, and Hulk’s durability means Gojo would need to use more than 1 casual attack if he wants him gone. The problem for all three is that they still can’t make contact through Infinity, so every time they come back they’re mostly buying time for Strange and Wanda.

Tony would realize that and start using them to control the battlefield instead of treating them as the answer to Infinity. Carol could cut off Gojo’s movement from above, Thor could reshape dangerous areas with lightning, and Hulk could destroy the ground or structures around Gojo whenever he tries to close on Wanda or Strange. None of them needs to make Infinity actively defend against a punch for that pressure to matter; their job is to protect the real win conditions and make Gojo’s own offensive movement less convenient.
That plan would work better for a while, but Gojo has something the Avengers still haven't seen properly. Hollow Purple would change the fight the first time he uses it.

If Gojo combines Blue and Red and fires Purple through the battlefield, the Avengers would have to move immediately because most of the roster can’t safely stand in front of it. Tony could warn everyone once his sensors pick up the energy building, and Strange could open portals to move people out of the path before the attack reaches them. Captain Marvel, Thor, and Hulk might survive partial contact depending on how much of the attack hits them, but nobody should be volunteering to test that when dodging is possible.

The first Purple would probably miss the most important targets because Strange can move people quickly once he understands something large is coming. It would still destroy a huge section of the battlefield and show the Avengers that letting Gojo prepare another one is a serious risk.

From that point, the team would have to attack while Gojo is setting up stronger techniques instead of waiting to see what happens. Strange could open portals beneath him, Wanda could try restraining him, and the physical Avengers could keep forcing movement whenever they see Blue and Red being brought together.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: The best plan wouldn't involve breaking Infinity at all. Tony would eventually understand that the team needs to attack Gojo through abilities that can affect space around him or create force without traveling toward him in the normal way.

Strange would handle positioning. If his earlier experiment establishes that a Sling Ring portal can actually form in Gojo’s immediate space despite Infinity, his portals could give the team a way to change where Gojo is standing and stop him from choosing every engagement himself. If that interaction fails, he would have to rely on broader battlefield and dimensional manipulation instead. Wanda would become the actual win condition because if her telekinesis can form directly around Gojo, she may be able to hold him long enough for Strange to do something more permanent.

The physical Avengers would support that setup instead of trying to finish Gojo themselves. Thor and Captain Marvel could pressure his positioning from different angles, while Hulk attacks the battlefield around him and places himself between Gojo and the less durable casters whenever Gojo moves offensively. Tony would coordinate timing, and Steve would keep everyone moving so Gojo can’t line several people up for the same attack.

Strange’s best option might be removing Gojo from the normal battlefield entirely, but only if the earlier portal test proves that he can form one in Gojo’s immediate space despite Infinity. In that case, opening a portal beneath him and sending him into the Mirror Dimension could separate Gojo from most of the team and give Strange more control over the environment. Infinity wouldn't disappear there, but Strange could start folding the space around Gojo while Wanda attacks from another angle.

Gojo would understand very quickly that allowing Strange to control the arena is dangerous. Blue could pull Strange out of position before he finishes another large spell, and Gojo’s speed lets him close distance fast enough that Strange would have to defend constantly. The Cloak can help with movement, but it can’t solve the problem by itself once Gojo is focusing on him. Wanda would try to use that opening.

If her telekinesis can grip Gojo directly, she could hold him still while Strange prepares a portal or another spell around him. The Avengers wouldn't need that hold to last very long. A few seconds might be enough to move Gojo into a location where the rest of the team can regroup or to trap him inside the Mirror Dimension temporarily.

The problem is that Gojo still has Blue and Red even while Infinity is protecting him. If Wanda’s restraint doesn’t stop cursed technique use, he can attack her without breaking free physically. A strong Red could knock her out of the fight before she finishes the hold, and Blue could pull Strange away from whatever spell he’s building.

Tony might try stacking every possible source of positional pressure at once. Captain Marvel cuts off an aerial route, Thor fills sections of the battlefield with lightning, Hulk tears up the ground around Gojo, and Strange opens several portals while Wanda focuses on him. The point wouldn’t be to overload automated Infinity with incoming attacks. It would be to restrict where Gojo can comfortably move while protecting Strange and Wanda long enough to attempt their own bypasses.

Gojo’s Six Eyes still gives him a huge advantage in processing everything around him. He’s used to fighting while reading cursed energy, movement, and technique details at an extremely high level, and the Avengers haven't shown anything that simply shuts that perception down. They can make the battlefield chaotic, but chaos alone isn’t enough when Gojo can still understand what matters most.
If Gojo decides the team is getting too close to a real solution, he can use Unlimited Void.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: Physical durability doesn’t provide any demonstrated answer to Unlimited Void. Hulk’s durability, Thor’s endurance, Captain Marvel’s energy absorption, and Tony’s armor have never shown a defense against the kind of information overload the domain produces. Under normal crossover assumptions, anyone caught inside a completed Unlimited Void would therefore be overwhelmingly likely to become incapacitated as their mind is flooded with more information than it can process, although neither universe directly proves every cross-universe neurological interaction.

Strange would recognize that something has changed as soon as the domain forms, but there’s no guarantee he can escape after it is already complete. MCU Strange has dealt with other dimensions and strange spaces before, so he has a better chance than most of the team at understanding what’s happening, although understanding the problem doesn’t mean his mind can ignore the effect.

Wanda is in a similar position. Her powers are mentally driven, which makes Unlimited Void especially dangerous because losing the ability to focus means losing the main thing that gives her a chance against Gojo in the first place.

Gojo also wouldn’t need to keep the domain open for long. Because nobody on this roster has demonstrated a clear resistance to Unlimited Void’s information overload, even a short activation would be overwhelmingly likely to disable most of them long enough for him to end the fight without killing everyone. He could drop Unlimited Void once the Avengers are incapacitated, then remove the few people who recover fastest before they can rebuild their formation.

Strange is probably the only Avenger with a serious argument for avoiding the domain before it closes, using a portal or dimensional movement if he recognizes Gojo’s setup quickly enough. That is a better argument than assuming he can resist Unlimited Void after being caught. The problem is timing: he has to know what Gojo is about to do before the barrier catches him, and the first use gives him almost no reason to understand that.

If Strange somehow gets out, he still has to fight Gojo with most of the team disabled. Wanda may be unconscious or mentally overwhelmed, Tony and the physical roster can’t get through Infinity, and Gojo still has Blue, Red, Purple, and enough cursed energy efficiency to continue. The Avengers have legitimate ways to challenge Infinity, especially through Strange and Wanda. Strange can affect space around Gojo instead of trying to punch through the barrier, and Wanda may be able to apply telekinetic force directly depending on how the crossover mechanics are interpreted. Those two make the fight much more competitive than a simple Gojo versus Hulk or Thor matchup.

Gojo can identify which Avengers matter, target them with Blue or Red, use Hollow Purple if the team gives him enough room, and end the whole exchange with Unlimited Void once he decides the fight has gone far enough.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: The full late stage Avengers could push Gojo harder than almost any individual MCU hero because they have enough different powers to test Infinity from several directions. Thor, Hulk, Captain Marvel, and the rest of the physical roster can keep pressure on him, while Tony helps work out what Infinity is doing and Strange and Wanda look for ways around it.

Strange gives them the strongest tactical option because portals and dimensional effects don’t need to behave like normal attacks. Wanda gives them the best chance of affecting Gojo directly if her telekinesis can form around him without crossing Infinity first. If those 2 get enough time and perfect coordination, the Avengers could create a real opening.

Gojo still has the better overall matchup because the team has to protect a very small number of people while he has several ways to remove them. Once Strange or Wanda goes down, most of the remaining Avengers can’t touch him, and Unlimited Void gives Gojo a way to disable almost everyone at once without testing their physical durability.

So the Avengers could make it competitive and might even create a winning setup under the right conditions, but in a straight fight with everyone using their established Infinity War and Endgame abilities, Gojo would win more often than they would.

scripts.title: What If The Avengers Were In Invincible

sections.name: INTRO
paras: The Avengers arriving in the Invincible universe would change Earth before Mark Grayson ever understands what being a superhero actually costs. We're using the original 6 MCU Avengers shortly before the events of Age of Ultron, so Tony has the Iron Man armor and years of experience after New York, Steve is firmly established as Captain America, Thor has returned to Earth, and Natasha, Clint, and Bruce are still operating alongside them. They arrive in the Invincible universe before Omni-Man kills the Guardians of the Globe, which means Nolan’s original plan is suddenly dealing with 6 more heroes he never expected Earth to have.

At first, nobody has any reason to suspect Nolan. Cecil would see the Avengers as another enormous variable he needs to understand, while the Guardians would probably be more interested in figuring out whether these strangers are allies or the beginning of another invasion. Tony would immediately want access to GDA technology, Steve would be much less comfortable with how much power Cecil operates with in secret, and Thor would be one of the few people on Earth strong enough that Nolan couldn't casually ignore him.

That becomes a serious problem once the Guardians are murdered. The Avengers wouldn't magically solve the mystery overnight, but Tony, Natasha, and Steve give Cecil several new ways to investigate it, while Thor and Hulk make Nolan’s eventual confrontation with Mark far less one-sided. Even if they survive that first crisis, though, beating or driving away 1 Viltrumite only tells the rest of the Empire that Earth now has even more powerful defenders worth dealing with.

So this version of Invincible become part of Cecil’s plans, part of Mark’s development, and eventually part of the reason the Viltrumite Empire has to take Earth more seriously than it ever did before.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: The Avengers’ first contact with this Earth would probably happen through Cecil before anyone else. A dimensional event big enough to drop 6 enhanced people into the middle of the United States would light up GDA systems almost immediately, and Cecil would want eyes on them before the public had time to decide what they were. He would send a controlled response rather than an army because Thor, Hulk, and Iron Man make escalation dangerous before he even knows what they want.

Tony would figure out quickly that the people surrounding them aren't using anything he recognizes from S.H.I.E.L.D. or HYDRA. The weapons, teleportation systems, medical equipment, and surveillance capabilities are all familiar enough to understand but different enough to get his attention. Cecil would notice Tony doing the same thing in reverse, because within minutes Tony is scanning GDA equipment and trying to work out how a government agency he has never heard of developed technology that can move people across the planet almost instantly.

Steve would care more about who Cecil is and what authority he actually has. He has just lived through S.H.I.E.L.D. secretly being compromised by HYDRA, so an intelligence director with black sites, hidden laboratories, disposable operatives, and almost no public oversight is going to make him cautious immediately. Cecil would respect Steve enough to explain the broad version of what the GDA does, but he would leave out the uglier programs because he has no reason to hand strangers every secret on day 1.

The Guardians of the Globe become the easiest way to keep the situation from turning hostile. Cecil introduces them as Earth’s established superhero team, and the meeting makes it clear that the Avengers haven't landed on a world waiting for someone to save it. War Woman, Immortal, Darkwing, Red Rush, Green Ghost, Martian Man, and Aquarus already handle major threats, while Omni-Man has spent years operating beyond the team as the planet's strongest hero.

Nolan would be the person Thor notices first. The way he carries himself, the confidence, and the complete lack of concern around Hulk tell Thor that this man isn’t another costumed human with unusual abilities. Nolan would recognize the same thing in Thor, especially once he learns that Thor comes from another world and has fought armies far beyond Earth.

Their first conversation would stay polite because neither has a reason to start anything. Nolan could present himself as another alien who chose Earth as his home, which is close enough to the truth that he wouldn’t need to invent much. Thor would probably like him at first because Nolan looks exactly like the kind of warrior Thor tends to understand, while Nolan would be much more interested in figuring out how strong Thor actually is.

Hulk creates a different problem for Cecil. Bruce Banner is cooperative, intelligent, and easy enough to speak with, but the GDA would want every scrap of information it could get about the Hulk transformation. Bruce would recognize that interest almost immediately and keep Cecil at a distance, especially once Tony starts pointing out how many of the GDA's questions sound less like medical curiosity and more like weapons research.

Natasha and Clint would spend most of that first period saying far less than everyone else. Natasha would watch Cecil’s people, the Guardians, and Nolan while everyone else talks, and Clint would focus on the physical details of the facility and how heavily guarded the Avengers actually are. Neither of them would assume this Earth is friendly simply because its heroes are. For a short time, the 2 teams could work beside each other without much friction. The Avengers help stop a few emergencies while the GDA works on understanding how they crossed universes, and Tony gets limited access to local technology in return for sharing enough of his own data to make Cecil happy. Mark Grayson is still living mostly as a normal teenager during this period, which means he watches the Avengers show up on the news before he ever expects to become part of their world.
Nolan watches them much more carefully. His mission has always depended on eventually preparing Earth for absorption into the Viltrumite Empire, and the Avengers have

just added several unknown variables to that plan. He doesn’t know whether Thor can seriously injure a Viltrumite, whether Hulk has an upper limit, or how quickly Tony can improve once he studies technology from this universe.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: The Guardians massacre would still be tempting because Nolan understands exactly how dangerous that team becomes if they are allowed to coordinate against him. Red Rush can interfere with his attacks, War Woman and Immortal can hurt him, and the others add enough pressure that even Nolan cannot afford to treat them casually. The Avengers make waiting dangerous because every month Tony learns more about this Earth while Thor becomes another powerful off-world figure Nolan cannot easily predict.

Nolan would avoid bringing the Avengers into the same room when he finally makes his move. The Guardians already trust him enough to answer an emergency summons, while the Avengers are still outsiders who operate separately and spend much of their time dealing with Cecil or trying to find a way home. Nolan can exploit that gap by attacking the Guardians before the 2 teams develop a routine of responding together.

The fight itself would still be brutal, but Nolan’s objective changes slightly. He needs to kill the Guardians quickly enough that no distress signal brings Thor or Tony into the battle halfway through, so he has less room for mistakes than he did originally. Red Rush becomes his first priority because a speedster delaying the fight by even another minute could be enough for outside help to arrive.

The Guardians still manage to injure him badly. Nolan’s strength gives him the advantage, but several of them can hurt him when they coordinate, and he leaves the room bloodied after killing the team. The difference comes immediately afterward because Cecil now has 6 experienced outsiders who were never part of Nolan’s original calculations.

Natasha becomes even more useful than Tony here because she does not need a technological breakthrough to notice behavior. Nolan is supposedly another victim of the attack, yet he is also one of the few beings on Earth physically capable of producing some of the damage around the room. That does not prove he did anything, but it places him in a category of people she would quietly investigate rather than treating him as a wounded witness.

Thor is the hardest Avenger to convince that Nolan may be involved. He has spent enough time around warriors to believe that serious injuries mean something, and Nolan nearly dying alongside the Guardians looks like evidence that he fought with them. Thor would not dismiss Tony or Natasha, but he would want more than suspicion before treating a man he sees as another alien protector like a murderer.

Nolan notices. He has spent years lying convincingly to humans, and Tony Stark is not subtle about distrust once he starts developing it. Natasha is subtler, but Nolan catches enough small changes in how she speaks to him to understand that the Avengers are no longer treating the massacre as a random attack.

Mark's powers appear while all of this is happening. Nolan now has to train his son while managing an investigation that is moving faster than expected, and Mark suddenly has access to heroes his father cannot completely control. The Avengers become part of Mark’s first exposure to superhero life before Nolan has time to shape that experience entirely around Viltrumite ideas.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Mark would be fascinated by the Avengers because they give him several different examples of what being a hero can look like. Steve has no powers anywhere near Nolan’s level and still walks into dangerous situations first, Tony solves problems through preparation and engineering, while Clint and Natasha survive around people far stronger than they are by knowing what they can realistically handle. That matters for Mark because Nolan’s training tends to focus heavily on strength, speed, endurance, and the responsibility that supposedly comes with being Viltrumite.

Steve would get along with Mark almost immediately. Mark is eager, inexperienced, and trying hard to meet standards he barely understands, which Steve has seen before in young soldiers and new Avengers. He would push Mark to think about civilians and judgment before power, especially after seeing Nolan train him through increasingly violent physical lessons.

Tony would take a more practical interest in Mark’s abilities. He would want to know how fast Mark accelerates, how quickly he heals, what kinds of forces hurt him, and whether his flight follows any pattern his systems can measure. Mark would probably enjoy that attention because Tony treats his powers like something interesting rather than something he is supposed to already understand.

Nolan would dislike both relationships for different reasons. Steve gives Mark a moral authority outside his family, while Tony encourages Mark to ask questions about Viltrumite biology that Nolan would rather answer on his own terms. Nolan cannot simply order Mark to stay away from them without making the restriction suspicious, so he tries to present the Avengers as temporary visitors who do not understand the responsibilities Mark will eventually inherit.

Cecil sees the same shift and quietly encourages it. He wants Mark surrounded by people who are not Nolan, especially now that the investigation keeps producing reasons to look more closely at Omni-Man. Cecil still refuses to tell Mark that his father is a suspect because he has no proof and does not know how Mark would react, but he makes sure Avengers missions overlap with Mark whenever possible.

That creates butterfly effects before the truth about Nolan comes out. Mark learns teamwork from people with wildly different power levels instead of spending most of his early career measuring himself against his father. He sees Natasha retreat when a fight is above her weight class, watches Tony change plans after an armor system fails, and learns from Steve that staying in a fight can be reckless when somebody else needs to be rescued.

Eve would probably respond well to the Avengers too. Tony would be fascinated by her ability to rearrange matter, while Bruce would understand immediately how unusual that power is even compared with everything he has seen. Steve would notice that she has better instincts than a lot of older heroes and treat her like someone capable of making her own decisions rather than another teenager to keep out of the room.
The Omni-Man investigation finally starts producing a pattern that Tony cannot ignore. The available evidence keeps pointing toward an attacker strong enough to injure Nolan, fast

enough to overwhelm the Guardians, and present at the exact location where they died. Once Tony compares that with what he has recorded from Nolan’s own movement and strength, the list of plausible suspects gets very short.

Natasha would be the one who stops him from confronting Nolan immediately. She knows they still do not understand Viltrumite limits, and accusing him without a plan could turn a murder investigation into a fight in the middle of a populated area. Steve agrees, while Thor takes longer because accepting the possibility means reconsidering every conversation he has had with Nolan since arriving.

The Avengers begin preparing without telling Mark. Tony starts modifying armor around the forces he has seen Nolan produce, Bruce works with Cecil on ways to survive a confrontation rather than pretending they can contain Nolan permanently, and Thor becomes the person they need nearby if the situation turns violent. Clint and Natasha focus on finding the missing piece that proves motive because knowing Nolan probably killed the Guardians still does not explain why.

Nolan realizes the window is closing. Mark is getting stronger, Cecil is watching him, and the Avengers are beginning to move like a team preparing for an enemy they have not publicly named. He has to decide whether to continue the slow approach he originally intended or tell Mark the truth before somebody else does it for him.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Debbie still becomes crucial because she knows Nolan better than any government agency does. Once Cecil shares enough of the investigation with her, small details that seemed harmless start looking different, and Nolan’s explanations around the Guardians massacre become harder to accept. The Avengers do not replace Debbie's role in uncovering who Nolan is because the emotional evidence comes from years of marriage that none of them can reproduce.

Nolan eventually takes Mark away before Cecil can control the location. He begins telling him about Viltrum, the Empire, and what their family was supposed to accomplish on Earth. Mark has heard enough from Steve and the Avengers by this point that Nolan’s version of duty does not land the same way it might have otherwise.

Mark would still be horrified that his father sees human lives as temporary and insignificant. He also has several living examples of powerful people choosing to protect a world they were not born on, which makes Nolan's argument about Viltrumite superiority even harder to accept. Thor is literally an alien prince who chose to defend Earth repeatedly, so Mark already knows being from a stronger civilization does not force anyone to conquer a weaker one.

Tony reaches them early enough to hear part of Nolan’s explanation. That gives him the motive the investigation was missing, and there is no longer any reason to preserve the pretense that Nolan might be innocent. He tries to keep the first exchange verbal because Mark is standing between them and clearly has no idea what to do.

Nolan makes the choice for everyone when he tries to remove Tony from the conversation. He initially tries to knock Tony out of the exchange and underestimates how much punishment the armor can absorb. Tony survives the hit because he is already armored and expecting violence, but it immediately makes clear that Nolan hits far harder than most enemies he has fought. The armor keeps Tony alive long enough for Thor to arrive before Nolan can follow with something more serious, and the shape of the fight changes the moment Mjolnir comes down.

Thor is one of the first opponents Nolan encounters on Earth who can meet him with enough force to make him adjust immediately. Nolan still has a huge speed advantage over most of the Avengers and far more experience fighting beings on his own physical level, but Thor can take punishment that would kill almost anyone else present and return enough power to hurt him. Their first collision buys Mark time instead of ending the fight.

Bruce transforms once Nolan starts treating the area like a battlefield. Hulk cannot fly after Nolan if he leaves the ground, but close quarters become much more dangerous because Nolan now has to deal with another opponent who can survive impacts that would remove Tony or Steve from the fight entirely. Hulk also gives Cecil something simple to work with because pointing him toward the man hurting Mark requires far less planning than most GDA weapons. Steve, Natasha, and Clint do not pretend they belong in the center of that exchange. Steve organizes evacuation and keeps Mark focused whenever Nolan tries to drag the argument back into Viltrumite ideology, while Natasha and Clint work with Tony's systems to feed information to the heavier hitters. They contribute by keeping the fight from becoming 6 people independently attacking somebody faster than most of them can see.

Nolan can still hurt everyone there. He has enough speed to break away from Hulk, enough strength to damage Thor, and enough experience to recognize that Tony's coordination is making the group more effective than their individual power suggests. What he loses is the ability to spend the entire confrontation brutalizing Mark without anyone capable of stopping him for more than a few seconds.

That changes Mark’s experience completely. He still sees what his father is capable of and hears exactly how little Nolan thinks human life matters, but he does not have to survive that realization alone. Every time Nolan tries to turn the fight into a lesson for his son, somebody else interrupts the lesson by refusing to accept Nolan's version of the world.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: Nolan eventually realizes that staying on Earth means fighting through Thor, Hulk, Mark, and whatever Tony and Cecil can keep throwing at him while the entire planet learns the truth. He might be capable of killing some of them if the battle goes far enough, but the confrontation has already stopped serving the purpose he wanted. Mark is rejecting Viltrum, Earth now knows Nolan is hostile, and every minute he stays gives the GDA more information about how a Viltrumite fights.

His decision to leave would still be emotional. Mark is his son, and that attachment is the part of Nolan's mission he spent years pretending he could control. The Avengers make the physical battle harder, but Mark is still the reason Nolan finally cannot carry the mission through.

Thor would try to follow when Nolan leaves the atmosphere, but Cecil and Tony would have a bigger concern immediately. They have just learned that Nolan is one member of an empire powerful enough to send individuals like him to conquer planets, and there is no reason to assume the next Viltrumite will develop the same attachment to Earth. Nolan escaping tells them they have survived the first encounter with something much larger than one enemy.

Mark takes Nolan’s departure differently with the Avengers around him. He is still shattered by what his father did, but Steve would make sure he understands that rejecting Nolan was a choice Mark made for himself. Thor would have his own perspective because family and duty have already collided repeatedly in his life, while Bruce understands better than most what it feels like to fear the damage somebody with enormous strength can cause.

Tony ends up somewhere between them. After New York and Ultron-era anxieties beginning to take shape, the idea of an invasion force full of Nolan-level enemies would hit exactly the part of Tony that hates being unprepared. He would throw himself into detection systems, orbital monitoring, armor upgrades, and ways to alert Earth before another Viltrumite reaches a city.

Thor gives them information no laboratory can provide. He has fought across different worlds and understands what it means when an empire measures strength through conquest, even if Viltrum is nothing like Asgard politically. He would push Earth to seek allies before the Empire arrives instead of assuming every solution can be built inside one laboratory.

That becomes important when Allen the Alien enters the picture. One of his earlier accidental visits had already led him to encounter Mark after Mark became Invincible, but Nolan’s betrayal gives the Coalition a real reason to take Earth seriously. When Allen returns to gather information about Nolan, he finds an Earth where Mark is working beside Thor, Iron Man, Hulk, and a government agency already preparing for Viltrumite retaliation. Once Allen realizes what has changed, the conversation about the wider war starts much earlier.

Mark suddenly gets access to information Nolan never wanted him to have. He can learn that Viltrum has enemies, that other planets have survived encounters with the Empire, and that Nolan was part of a pattern far larger than the Grayson family. The Avengers hear the same thing and realize Earth does not have to prepare in isolation.

Their arrival has already saved lives because Nolan’s fight with Mark never becomes the same uninterrupted massacre it was before. It has also made Earth more visible, because reports of an Asgardian, Hulk, advanced Stark technology, and a growing alliance around Invincible would eventually reach people beyond the planet. By the time the Viltrumite Empire takes a serious look at Earth again, it will see a world that is harder to conquer and far more interesting than the one Nolan was originally sent to soften up.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Allen changes the entire way the Avengers think about the problem because he’s the first person who can explain Viltrum without speaking from Nolan's point of view. He tells them the Empire has already destroyed civilizations that resisted, that pure blooded Viltrumites are terrifyingly hard to kill, and that the Coalition has spent years looking for anything capable of shifting that balance. Tony goes from preparing for another Nolan to preparing for a military system that can keep sending people like Nolan until Earth stops resisting.

Tony and Bruce spend hours with Allen comparing what the Coalition knows against everything the GDA recorded during Nolan’s fight. They are interested in the same things Cecil is, but their priorities are different. Cecil wants weaknesses he can weaponize as quickly as possible, while Tony is also thinking about warning systems, evacuation, communication with other planets, and how much time Earth could buy before the first serious Viltrumite response arrives.

Steve focuses on the political side because Allen makes it clear that Earth is entering a war whether anyone voted for it or not. He wants the Coalition relationship treated like an actual alliance rather than Cecil privately trading information with aliens under a mountain somewhere. Cecil hates that idea because secrecy has kept the GDA effective for years, but Steve has just watched Nolan hide an invasion inside an ordinary family for 20 years and has very little patience left for plans built around one person controlling all the information.

Mark becomes the bridge between both groups. Allen already sees him as potentially important because he is a Viltrumite who chose Earth, while the Avengers have watched him reject Nolan even when doing so nearly got him killed. Mark still has a lot to learn, but people stop treating him like Nolan’s inexperienced son and start seeing him as someone who may eventually be able to speak to Viltrumites in a way no human can.

Thor takes a particular interest in Mark’s training after learning more about the Empire. He does not try to turn him into an Asgardian warrior or pretend Mjolnir can teach him Viltrumite combat, but he can give Mark something Nolan never did: experience fighting powerful opponents without treating every lesson like domination. Thor makes Mark work on positioning, protecting people weaker than himself, and knowing when drawing an enemy away matters more than winning the exchange in front of him.

Hulk gives Mark a different kind of practice because there is no lecture attached to it. Mark can hit harder without worrying about killing Bruce, and Hulk forces him to deal with somebody who becomes more dangerous once the fight turns messy. Tony records the sessions and points out how often Mark relies on straight-line speed because Nolan trained him to solve problems by hitting through them.

Eve becomes part of those sessions too, and her role grows quickly because the Avengers understand how valuable she is before she does. Tony sees how much flexibility matter manipulation gives her, while Steve keeps pushing her and Mark to plan around each other instead of fighting as 2 separate power sets. Mark starts thinking about what Eve can build, move, isolate, or repair while he handles the opponent, which makes both of them more useful when bigger threats appear.

That improvement comes with a cost. Allen eventually leaves Earth carrying a report for the Coalition that sounds far more impressive than the planet Nolan originally infiltrated. Earth now has a young Viltrumite who openly rejected the Empire, an Asgardian, Hulk, Stark technology, the GDA, Eve, and several experienced heroes coordinating around the same defense plan.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Tony catches the first serious problem because GDA network traffic starts disappearing whenever he asks about anti-Viltrumite research. Cecil has learned enough about Tony by now to know he cannot simply leave sensitive projects sitting on systems Tony can reach, so he begins isolating programs physically. That only convinces Tony there is something worth finding. What they eventually uncover is less important than what it proves about Cecil. He is willing to use dead bodies, dangerous technology, and people who have already crossed ethical lines if

he thinks the result could save Earth later. Steve understands the fear behind that logic, but he refuses to accept a defense system where every terrible decision becomes acceptable as soon as Cecil says the word Viltrumite.

Their argument gets personal because Cecil throws Nolan back at them. He reminds Steve that conventional restraint did almost nothing when one Viltrumite decided to turn on the planet, and the Empire can send more without caring whether Earth thinks the response is morally comfortable. Steve answers that preparing to fight monsters does not require letting the person in charge decide there are no limits left.

Tony is less certain. He has already started designing armor around combat data taken from Nolan, and he knows some of those systems would look horrifying if somebody outside the room saw what they were built to survive. He disagrees with Cecil on control rather than preparation itself, which puts him awkwardly between Steve and the GDA.

Bruce has his own reason to distrust Cecil. The more the GDA learns about Hulk, the more obvious it becomes that Cecil would create a contingency for him too if he could. Bruce does not blame him for thinking about what happens if Hulk loses control, but he knows how quickly “contingency” can turn into somebody deciding Bruce is more useful as a weapon than a person.

Mark watches all of this and learns something Nolan never taught him. Protecting Earth does not automatically put everyone on the same side of every decision. Steve, Cecil, Tony, Bruce, and Mark can all believe Viltrum is dangerous while disagreeing completely about what Earth should become in order to survive it.

That lesson matters when Cecil eventually asks Mark to cooperate with tests designed around Viltrumite weaknesses. Mark agrees to basic medical work because he wants Earth prepared, but he draws a line when Cecil starts asking for more invasive access than he is comfortable giving. Cecil pushes, Mark refuses, and Steve backs him publicly enough that Cecil realizes the Avengers can interfere with his authority in ways the Guardians never did.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: The first Viltrumite who comes after Nolan does not arrive to conquer Earth immediately. Nolan has stopped reporting and failed to complete an assignment that should have been routine, and eventually that silence becomes suspicious enough for the Empire to send someone to Earth and determine what happened. A scout enters the system expecting to investigate Nolan’s failed assignment and instead discovers a coordinated detection network watching for exactly this kind of arrival.

Tony sees the object before it reaches the atmosphere. The warning reaches Cecil, Thor, Mark, Eve, and the GDA at the same time, giving them something they never had when Nolan first came to Earth: preparation. They move civilians away from the likely landing area and make sure Thor and Mark are the first people the visitor sees.

The Viltrumite is more interested in Mark than anyone else. Nolan’s son was supposed to become part of the Empire eventually, yet he is standing beside an alien prince and a human superhero network preparing to resist. Mark is ordered to explain Nolan’s failure and reminded that his blood still makes him Viltrumite whether Earth accepts that or not.

Mark does not need much time to answer. He tells them Nolan left because he could not finish the mission and that Earth knows what Viltrum is now. Thor stays close without speaking over him because this is Mark's family and Mark’s decision, something Nolan almost never allowed him to own.

The scout tests that decision physically once the conversation stops being useful. Mark is stronger and more disciplined than he was during Nolan’s betrayal, but he is still badly outmatched by an experienced Viltrumite. The difference is that Earth already planned around that possibility instead of discovering it during the fight.

Tony's systems feed movement data to Mark and Thor while Eve reshapes the battlefield to keep the fight away from populated areas. Hulk stays near the ground in case the Viltrumite is forced lower, and Cecil keeps heavier options in reserve because using everything at once would tell the Empire exactly what Earth has. The team is trying to learn while surviving, which is a much more useful goal than pretending they can win through one perfect attack.

Thor does most of the work when the fight becomes direct. Mjolnir gives him control over where engagements happen, and his durability lets him keep the Viltrumite occupied long enough for Mark to recover after bad exchanges. He still struggles with the scout’s speed, but every time the Viltrumite commits to Mark, Thor has a clearer opening to punish them.

The visitor eventually pulls away rather than dying on Earth for an intelligence mission. They leave with enough information to know the planet is far more organized than Nolan reported, and Earth gets something just as valuable in return. Tony now has cleaner data from a Viltrumite fighting without Nolan’s emotional hesitation, Mark has experienced the gap between himself and a trained member of the Empire, and everyone understands the next visit may involve more than one.
Cecil calls it a successful defense. Tony looks at the readings and says they have probably just convinced Viltrum to stop underestimating them.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: Allen returns with news that confirms Tony’s concern. The Empire has begun discussing Earth more seriously because Nolan failed there, his son sided with the planet, and another Viltrumite came back reporting resistance strong enough to complicate a normal takeover. The Coalition wants Earth involved more directly because this is the first time in years that a relatively young planet has forced Viltrum to reconsider how casually it approaches conquest.

That invitation causes another argument. Cecil wants access to Coalition intelligence immediately but does not want Earth committing forces to somebody else’s war before its own defenses are ready. Thor believes waiting for Viltrum to choose the battlefield is a mistake, while Steve agrees that allies matter but wants to know what the Coalition actually expects Earth to sacrifice.

Tony sees an opportunity that has nothing to do with throwing Avengers at Viltrumites. Coalition technology has been built by civilizations that have spent far longer fighting the Empire, so even limited access could save years of blind experimentation. He offers technical cooperation first, giving the Coalition selected Stark data in exchange for defensive research, ship detection, and whatever biological information they can legally share.

Allen also brings information about Nolan. He has not returned to Viltrum, which means the Empire is looking for him too. Mark hears that and immediately wants to know where his father went, even after everything Nolan did.

Eventually they learn Nolan is on Thraxa, and Mark decides to go when the situation there becomes impossible to ignore. This time he does not leave Earth with no backup and no idea what he is walking into. Thor goes with him because sending Mark alone to meet the father who nearly killed him would be reckless, while Tony stays behind because Earth cannot empty its strongest defenses every time one crisis happens somewhere else.

Nolan’s reunion with Mark is even more uncomfortable with Thor standing nearby. Nolan has built another life and is beginning to admit how deeply Earth changed him, but Thor has no interest in letting remorse erase what happened. Mark gets to hear his father without being trapped alone inside Nolan’s emotions, which gives him more room to decide what he believes. The Viltrumites who arrive on Thraxa turn the reunion into the first real test of Earth’s new alliances. Mark and Nolan are already capable of fighting them, while Thor adds another opponent they did not expect. Thor cannot carry the entire battle, but his presence changes which Viltrumites can double-team Mark and gives Nolan enough breathing room to protect people he would once have dismissed as weak.

The result still hurts. Viltrumites are fast, experienced, and willing to kill civilians simply because doing so creates openings, and Thor learns quickly that their brutality is closer to warfare than the controlled fights he has been having on Earth. Mark performs better because his training has taught him to stop chasing every opponent who insults or hurts him and keep track of who actually needs protection.

Nolan’s position changes afterward because he has openly fought Viltrum again with witnesses from Earth and the Coalition. He can no longer pretend his relationship with Mark is the only reason he abandoned the Empire. He has made a choice against them, but the Viltrumites still manage to capture him after the battle, leaving Mark and Thor to return without him.

What Nolan revealed before the attack still matters. Mark comes home with information from an experienced Viltrumite who understands the Empire’s culture, tactics, and command structure, even if Nolan himself is now a prisoner. Steve, Cecil, Tony, Natasha, Clint, Bruce, and Thor all know that information could save lives without requiring them to trust Nolan or put him anywhere near Earth’s defenses.

They use what Mark can relay while the Coalition tries to learn what happened to Nolan. If Nolan eventually escapes and rejoins the resistance, his full knowledge could become one of Earth’s most valuable resources, but for now the planet has to prepare without him.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: By the time Viltrum treats Earth as a serious military problem, the planet is almost unrecognizable from the one Nolan first infiltrated. Mark has stronger training and a much larger support system, Eve is involved in planning at a global level, Cecil has more information about the Empire, and the Coalition has an active relationship with Earth. The Avengers have also pushed those groups into working together long before they would have naturally trusted each other.

That still does not make Earth stronger than the Viltrumite Empire. Thor and Hulk are dangerous enough to matter in individual fights, Mark is growing rapidly, and Nolan may eventually become one of Earth’s most valuable defenders, but Viltrum can field multiple experienced warriors and replace losses in a way Earth cannot. Tony cannot manufacture another Thor, and Cecil cannot build enough weapons to make every human soldier survive a Viltrumite attack.

Earth’s advantage comes from becoming difficult to isolate. The Coalition can provide warning and intelligence, Tony can improve how quickly that information reaches defenders, Cecil can move resources around the planet, and Mark can communicate with people who understand Viltrum from the inside. Every piece reduces the chance that the Empire can send 1 person to Earth, kill whoever matters, and control the rest through fear.

The Avengers also change Mark himself. Steve gives him another model for leadership, Thor teaches him how someone born with enormous power can choose service over conquest, Tony teaches him to prepare for opponents instead of relying entirely on instinct, and Natasha and Clint show him how much people without Viltrumite durability can still contribute. Bruce probably understands Mark in the strangest way because both of them live with strength that can become terrifying when emotion takes over.

Cecil changes too, even if he would never admit it. He still keeps secrets and builds contingencies, but the Avengers make it much harder for him to operate without challenge. Steve questions his authority, Tony can uncover things Cecil tries to hide, and Mark is less willing to obey simply because Cecil claims a decision is necessary.

Natasha and Clint would adapt differently. They are the easiest Avengers to overlook once Viltrumites enter the story, but they become extremely useful in the spaces between battles where infiltration, intelligence, and political pressure matter more than punching through somebody's chest. A war this large would eventually involve collaborators, compromised governments, and people willing to trade information for protection, which gives both of them plenty to do without pretending arrows and pistols can solve Viltrumites.

Hulk becomes one of the deterrents Earth keeps in reserve. Bruce would hate being discussed that way, but even he would understand why a planet facing beings like Nolan wants Hulk available. His real contribution could end up being helping Tony study the physics and biology of high-level fights while making sure those experiments never turn into Cecil building a Hulk program behind his back.

The Empire’s response becomes harsher because Earth is clearly developing into a center of resistance. Sending more Viltrumites increases the chance of killing key defenders, but every failed attack also gives Tony, Cecil, Mark, and the Coalition more information. Earth becomes expensive in exactly the way imperial powers hate because conquering it starts requiring resources that could be used somewhere else.

The biggest difference may be that Nolan’s failure stops looking like an isolated family tragedy much earlier. His betrayal exposes Viltrum before the Empire is ready to deal with an organized Earth, and the Avengers help turn that warning into preparation instead of panic. By the time Viltrum finally commits enough force to take the planet seriously, Earth has allies, intelligence, stronger heroes, and a version of Mark who has spent far longer learning from people outside his father’s shadow.

That also makes Earth a much bigger target. The planet now has Stark technology, GDA research, Coalition connections, Eve’s powers, Mark’s Viltrumite blood, Thor, Hulk, and eventually Nolan working against the Empire that sent him there. Viltrum cannot ignore a world collecting that many problems in one place.

So the Avengers give Earth a real chance, but they do it by making the conflict larger. They save people during Nolan's betrayal, accelerate the investigation into him, help Mark grow into a better hero, and force Earth to prepare for Viltrum years earlier than it otherwise would. In
return, Earth goes from a quiet assignment Nolan was supposed to complete from the inside to one of the most obvious centers of resistance the Empire has to deal with.

scripts.title: What If The MCU Never Existed

sections.name: INTRO
paras: In 2005, Marvel made a gamble that could’ve gone very differently. Instead of relying almost entirely on licensing characters to other studios, the company secured financing to start producing its own movies alongside those existing licensing deals, with Iron Man eventually becoming the project that proved the idea could work. If that deal falls apart, or Marvel decides the risk is too high, there’s no Iron Man in 2008 and no MCU waiting behind it.

Spider-Man would still belong to Sony, the X-Men would still be at Fox, and Batman would still be one of the biggest superheroes in the world. What disappears is the company that eventually turned Iron Man, Thor, Captain America, and the Avengers into the center of Hollywood.

And once you remove that, the effects go way beyond Marvel. Robert Downey Jr.’s career changes, Disney’s future changes, DC and Fox get more room to grow, and Hollywood may never become obsessed with turning every successful franchise into its own cinematic universe.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: The point where this timeline changes is 2005. At the time, Marvel was already a huge name in comics, but its movie business worked very differently from what we know today. Spider-Man was being made by Sony, while Fox controlled films built around the X-Men and Fantastic Four. Marvel could make money from licensing and merchandise, but another studio was usually the one financing, producing, and distributing the actual movie. Marvel itself later described its studio operation before 2005 as being focused on licensing characters to outside film and television producers.

Marvel wanted more control, so it arranged a $525 million financing facility that could fund as many as ten movies using characters whose film rights were still available. Paramount would distribute the slate, while Marvel would control production and keep far more of the upside if those movies succeeded. Iron Man and Hulk were added to that financing structure in 2006, setting up the movies that would eventually arrive in 2008.

For this alternate timeline, that financing never closes. The real facility was structured through a special-purpose subsidiary and was non-recourse to Marvel and its other affiliates, with theatrical film rights and related film assets pledged as collateral rather than Marvel simply risking the entire company on the slate. So the divergence would need to happen before closing: maybe the lenders or insurers ultimately refuse the structure, or the final negotiations break down before the money becomes available. Either outcome would leave Marvel in roughly the same position it had been in before, where licensing characters to established studios remains the practical path instead of building this self-financed film slate.

Marvel would still want movies made because Spider-Man and X-Men had already shown how valuable its characters could be on screen. The difference is that it wouldn’t have the money or structure to make those movies under one roof. Characters like Captain America, Thor, and Iron Man could be offered to outside studios individually, and every deal could come with a different producer, director, release plan, and long-term goal.

Marvel would probably remain primarily a licensing and publishing company, with Spider-Man and X-Men still bringing attention to the brand. What it loses is the film strategy that produced the MCU on the timeline we know. There’s no Marvel Studios slate building toward Iron Man in 2008 and The Avengers in 2012, although Marvel could still pursue another financing structure, production partnership, or self-production strategy later. There’s also no guarantee the same studio ends up controlling enough of these characters to build a shared universe if that later attempt happens.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Iron Man is where this change becomes visible to regular audiences. Before 2008, Tony Stark was obviously important in Marvel comics, but he wasn’t anywhere near Spider-Man’s level as a movie character. Marvel itself later said that before the 2008 film, Iron Man was known mostly by comic book fans. The movie changed that very quickly, eventually earning about $582 million worldwide and turning Iron Man into one of Marvel’s biggest brands.

Without Marvel financing its own films, the version of Iron Man we got in 2008 probably never happens. Another studio could eventually license the character and make its own movie, but there’s no reason to assume it uses the same script, director, cast, or tone. Jon Favreau’s movie came out of Marvel’s new production strategy, so removing that strategy removes the exact circumstances that created it.

That changes Robert Downey Jr.’s career too. Casting him as Tony Stark worked so well that the role became tied to him for more than a decade, but in 2008 it still carried some risk. Downey had already been rebuilding his career, and he had other major work around the same period, so losing Iron Man wouldn't mean he disappears from Hollywood. He could still have a successful comeback through other projects, and something like Tropic Thunder would still put him in front of a large audience.

What he probably doesn’t become is the face of the biggest movie franchise of the next decade. There’d be no Tony Stark appearing across Iron Man sequels, Avengers movies, Civil War, and Endgame, which removes the role that eventually made Downey one of the most recognizable actors in the world.

Iron Man himself could end up in a strange position. One studio might develop him as a standalone action franchise, especially after superhero movies continue doing well elsewhere. Another possibility is that he spends years in development while studios keep prioritizing characters with stronger movie records. Spider-Man already had enormous box office success, X-Men had an established series, and Batman was about to hit another level with The Dark Knight. Iron Man wouldn’t have the 2008 success that suddenly proves he belongs beside them.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Captain America and Thor would still have value to Hollywood because superhero movies were already successful before the MCU. Studios had Spider-Man, X-Men, Batman, Fantastic Four, and plenty of other comic properties in development, so there’d be no reason for Marvel’s remaining characters to disappear from theaters forever.

They’d probably take much longer to arrive, though, and the movies would be built as separate franchises. Marvel’s real studio plan eventually had Iron Man 2, Thor, Captain America, and The Avengers lined up as connected releases. By late 2009, Marvel was already publicly listing those films as part of the same production pipeline. Without the studio, each property has to find its own home and convince that company it can work on its own.

Captain America could be an awkward sell during this period because a studio would have to decide whether to make him a World War II movie, bring him directly into the present, or heavily modernize the character. Marvel Studios eventually had the advantage of knowing Steve could begin in the 1940s and then wake up in a world that already contained Iron Man, S.H.I.E.L.D., and the beginning of the Avengers. A standalone studio wouldn't have that larger payoff waiting for him.

Thor has a similar problem. His mythology, Asgard, magic, and cosmic scale make the movie expensive, and without an Avengers plan there’s less reason for a studio to treat him as one piece of something bigger. He could still get made if somebody believes in the character, but that project would be judged entirely on whether Thor can support his own franchise.

The Avengers becomes much harder. The team works in comics because Marvel controls the characters on the page. Movies involve rights, contracts, financing, actors, release schedules, and studios that all want to protect their own franchises. If Marvel keeps licensing characters separately through the late 2000s, it could easily create another version of the problem it already had with Spider-Man and X-Men, where popular Marvel characters exist in movies but can’t simply show up wherever Marvel wants them.

Even if one company eventually tries to make an Avengers movie, it probably wouldn’t have years of setup behind it. The real Avengers reached theaters after audiences had already met Tony Stark, Steve Rogers, Thor, Black Widow, Hawkeye, Nick Fury, and two versions of Hulk through earlier movies. Marvel had taught people that these stories were happening in the same world before asking them to buy a ticket for the crossover.
That 2012 movie then made more than $1.5 billion worldwide and gave Hollywood a very visible example of what interconnected franchises could do. In this timeline, that event never happens.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Disney entered the real timeline at almost the perfect moment. In August 2009, it announced a deal to acquire Marvel for roughly $4 billion. By then, Iron Man had already become a hit, Marvel had successfully launched its own film production business, Iron Man 2 was on the way, and the company was developing Thor, Captain America, and Avengers movies. Disney wasn’t buying a comic publisher that hoped it could someday build its own films. Marvel had already shown that the idea worked.

Without the 2005 financing, Marvel would still own an enormous character library and a valuable licensing business, so Disney could absolutely remain interested. Spider-Man, X-Men, Fantastic Four, and other major names still have value even when their movie rights are tied up elsewhere. Disney’s own announcement focused heavily on Marvel’s characters, global brand, and the ways Disney could use those properties across different businesses.

Disney could wait longer. Marvel could remain independent. Another media company could become interested first. Any of those outcomes are more believable once Marvel loses the proof that it can turn characters it still controls into major movies by itself.

Even if Disney eventually buys Marvel anyway, it wouldn’t inherit the MCU we know. It would inherit a collection of characters spread across licensing agreements, with no Iron Man franchise anchoring a connected slate and no Avengers movie already being prepared for 2012. Disney would have to decide whether it wants to build a studio almost from scratch, keep licensing the characters, or slowly bring more film rights together as old deals expire.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: By the early 2010s, Sony and Fox would be in a much stronger position because they already control Marvel’s most proven movie characters. Sony has Spider-Man, while Fox has the X-Men, Wolverine, Fantastic Four, and the rights needed to develop Deadpool. In the real timeline, both studios had to watch Marvel Studios turn characters like Iron Man and Captain America into brands that could compete with them. Without the MCU, that pressure disappears.

Sony’s position becomes especially important after the Sam Raimi Spider-Man trilogy ends. Spider-Man is far too valuable to leave unused, so Sony would still have strong reason to develop another version of the character. If that process still produces the Andrew Garfield reboot and The Amazing Spider-Man in 2012, the bigger change comes after that. If Sony then reaches roughly the same position by 2014, with The Amazing Spider-Man 2 underperforming compared with expectations and larger Sinister Six and Venom plans losing momentum, the real timeline's next option would no longer exist because there would be no Marvel Studios partnership waiting.
From that point, the branch depends on Sony still being in roughly that same position.

If it is, Sony would either have to keep building around Andrew Garfield or reboot Spider-Man again on its own. In that branch, projects like Sinister Six become much more important because Sony wouldn’t have another successful superhero universe it could send Spider-Man into. The studio would have every reason to keep experimenting until it finds a version that works.

The same could happen with Venom much earlier. Sony eventually proved in 2018 that a Spider-Man-related movie could make a lot of money without Spider-Man even appearing. In a world where there’s no MCU taking up so much of the superhero market, Sony might reach that conclusion sooner and push harder into villains and supporting characters during the mid-2010s.

Fox would have an even better setup because X-Men already works as an ensemble franchise. By 2011, First Class had introduced a younger cast, and Days of Future Past later connected that generation with actors from the original movies. Without Avengers becoming the giant crossover event of 2012, an X-Men movie bringing two timelines and two casts together could feel like one of the biggest superhero events Hollywood had attempted.

The real timeline shows how much potential Fox had in characters like Deadpool and Wolverine. Deadpool became a huge success because of its smaller budget, R rating, comedy, and Ryan Reynolds, while Logan became a critically respected hit in 2017 and showed that superhero movies didn’t all need the same tone. Those exact films and release dates aren’t guaranteed after a 2005 divergence, but their real-world success shows how valuable those parts of Fox’s Marvel library could still be.

That could push Fox to invest more heavily in the X-Men universe instead of treating it as one major franchise among several competing superhero brands. New Mutants, X-Force, Deadpool sequels, and other mutant projects could receive more attention because there’d be no Avengers franchise dominating the conversation every few months.

Fantastic Four would still be the weak point. The 2015 reboot had major production problems and was received badly, so removing the MCU doesn’t suddenly fix that movie. Fox could still try again later, especially if the rest of its Marvel lineup is doing well.

The biggest question comes much later with Disney’s purchase of most of 21st Century Fox. That deal involved far more than Marvel, so the absence of the MCU wouldn’t automatically stop it. Disney wanted major entertainment assets including Avatar, FX, National Geographic, and Fox’s film and television library. The Marvel characters were only one piece of a much larger acquisition.

If that purchase still happens, Disney eventually gets X-Men and Fantastic Four anyway. The difference is that those characters could arrive as Disney’s strongest Marvel film brands instead of being absorbed into a franchise that had already spent a decade making Avengers the center of everything.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: DC would enter this timeline with something Marvel doesn’t have: Christopher Nolan’s Batman movies.

Batman Begins arrived in 2005, The Dark Knight followed in 2008, and The Dark Knight Rises completed the trilogy in 2012. These movies already proved that superhero films could become huge cultural events without any shared universe attached to them. The Dark Knight alone crossed one billion dollars worldwide, and Heath Ledger’s Joker became one of the most famous performances in the genre.
What changes is the pressure to build a connected universe quickly.

In the real timeline, The Avengers made more than $1.5 billion in 2012 and showed every studio what could happen when several superhero films were connected. Warner Bros. already had its own plans for DC characters, but Marvel gave Hollywood a working example of how a shared universe could become bigger than any individual movie.
Without that example, Man of Steel could have a much simpler future.

The movie still makes sense in 2013 because Superman is one of Warner Bros.’ biggest characters and Christopher Nolan was involved as a producer. If it performs similarly, Warner Bros. would probably still want more Superman. What becomes less certain is how quickly Batman, Wonder Woman, and the Justice League get pulled into the same series.

Batman v Superman could still happen because putting Batman and Superman together had been an obvious Hollywood idea for years. Warner Bros. had explored versions of that crossover long before the MCU existed. But the need to use one movie as a launchpad for an entire DC universe would be weaker.

That could give Superman another solo movie first. Wonder Woman could receive her own introduction without needing to appear in Batman v Superman beforehand. A new Batman series could start separately and cross over later if audiences respond well.
Justice League would probably arrive later as a result.

That extra time could help Warner Bros. avoid some of the problems it faced in the real 2010s, where major characters and storylines were introduced quickly while the studio was still deciding what its universe should look like. There’s no guarantee the movies become better because creative problems can still happen regardless of Marvel, but the business pressure around them changes.

DC would also have more room at the box office. There’s no Avengers, Iron Man, Captain America, Thor, or Guardians of the Galaxy constantly taking major release dates. Warner Bros. could place Batman, Superman, and Wonder Woman movies across the calendar without competing against another superhero film every few months.

Wonder Woman could become even more important in this version of Hollywood. Her real-world 2017 movie shows how much audience potential the character had, even though that exact film and release path aren’t guaranteed after the timeline diverges. If DC is the only company with a truly recognizable group of characters that could eventually form a superhero team, Warner Bros. would have even more reason to build around her.

The funny part is that Warner Bros. might do that by moving slower. Without Marvel proving that audiences will follow twenty connected movies, there’s less reason to believe every hero needs to meet immediately. Batman can stay Batman. Superman can have his own series. Wonder Woman can grow separately. Then Justice League can become the event after those characters are already established.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: One of the biggest changes would happen outside Marvel and DC.
