Hollywood has always copied successful ideas. If one studio finds a model that makes billions of dollars, other studios start looking through their own libraries for something similar. The MCU gave them a very specific model to copy and, more importantly, proved that it could work at enormous scale: introduce characters separately, connect their stories, tease future movies, and eventually bring everyone together in a crossover.

That was already normal. Harry Potter had eight movies built around one continuous story. Fast & Furious kept expanding its cast and scope. Transformers became a giant series. Pirates of the Caribbean, Mission: Impossible, and Jurassic Park all showed that audiences would come back for familiar worlds and characters.

The MCU took the idea further because every individual movie could advertise another one. Hollywood was already obsessed with sequels, spin-offs, and expanding successful intellectual property, but the MCU accelerated and validated the more specific idea of building separate films into one deliberately interconnected cinematic universe. Warner Bros. builds DC around interconnected movies. Universal announces the Dark Universe using its classic monsters. Sony repeatedly tries to create a larger world around Spider-Man characters. Even franchises that weren’t originally designed for this kind of structure started looking for spin-offs and shared continuity.

The Dark Universe is probably one of the clearest examples of what could change. Universal had been making monster movies for decades, so Dracula, Frankenstein, the Mummy, and the Invisible Man would still have value. What might disappear is the attempt to package them immediately as one interconnected blockbuster universe.
The Mummy in 2017 could simply be another attempt to revive the monster brand. If it fails, Universal moves on rather than losing the supposed opening chapter of a giant connected franchise.

Post credit scenes would develop differently too. Marvel didn’t invent the idea of putting scenes after the credits. Movies had done that long before Iron Man. What Marvel did was train audiences to expect them as part of the larger story. Nick Fury appearing at the end of Iron Man told audiences that another movie was already being set up, and Marvel kept repeating that idea until people expected to stay in their seats.

Without the MCU, post credit scenes probably remain something directors use occasionally for jokes, sequel teases, or surprises. They wouldn’t carry the same expectation that every blockbuster needs to advertise the next chapter.

The phrase “cinematic universe” itself might never become such a common part of movie marketing. Studios would still create shared worlds when the material naturally supports them. DC characters have crossed over for decades. Godzilla and King Kong can share a universe. Horror franchises can connect characters. There’d still be experiments.

What changes is how quickly studios jump to that plan. A new movie wouldn't need to arrive with five spin-offs already being discussed. A character wouldn’t need a cameo just to set up another project 3 years away. Studios could be more willing to wait and see whether the first movie works before announcing an entire universe around it.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: Removing the MCU also leaves an enormous hole in the release calendar. Between 2008 and the early 2020s, Marvel Studios released dozens of movies, and many of them were positioned as major spring or summer events. Other studios had to plan around Avengers movies, Iron Man sequels, Captain America, Thor, Guardians of the Galaxy, Black Panther, Captain Marvel, and Spider-Man once Sony started working with Marvel.

All of those weekends become available. That doesn’t mean theaters suddenly have fewer blockbusters. Studios would rush to fill the space because audiences still want big movies. The likely winners are franchises that were already successful during the same period.

Fast & Furious could become even more dominant. In the real timeline, Furious 7 made more than $1.5 billion in 2015, showing how large the series could become as it grew from street racing into giant international action movies. The exact film history could change after 2005, but with fewer superhero releases competing for attention, Universal could have even more incentive to push Fast & Furious as its main event series.

Jurassic Park is another franchise with that kind of potential. In the real timeline, Jurassic World made more than $1.6 billion in 2015 despite arriving in a year that also included Avengers: Age of Ultron. That exact movie isn’t guaranteed here, but its performance shows how much theatrical space a revived dinosaur franchise could occupy in a world without Marvel Studios.
Star Wars is another huge one.

Disney bought Lucasfilm in 2012 and released The Force Awakens in 2015. That deal doesn’t depend on the MCU existing. Without Marvel, Disney could lean even harder on Star Wars because it would lose the regular superhero movies that became another major pillar of the company.

That could mean Disney pushes more Star Wars films into production or becomes more cautious because each one carries more weight. Either way, the franchise becomes even more important to Disney’s theatrical business.

Transformers could also hold onto more attention during the early 2010s. Those movies were enormous internationally, especially during the period when Marvel was starting to dominate. Paramount might have even more reason to expand that universe because it wouldn't also be distributing some of Marvel's early films.

Then there are original blockbusters. This is harder to predict because studios were already becoming more dependent on known intellectual property for reasons far bigger than Marvel. Home video revenue was shrinking, international box office mattered more, and familiar brands were easier to market worldwide.

Still, removing two or three MCU releases from some years means studios have more premium dates to fight over. Directors making science fiction, action, animation, and fantasy would have fewer Marvel movies sitting in the biggest windows.

Some films that struggled against superhero competition could perform better. Other studios might take bigger chances simply because the market isn’t as crowded with comic book movies. The superhero genre itself would also feel less constant. Instead of seeing a Marvel movie every few months, audiences might get Batman one season, X-Men later in the year, Spider-Man the next summer, and Superman after that.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: The character who benefits most from all of this could be Spider-Man.

Before the MCU, Spider-Man was already Marvel’s biggest movie superhero. The first Sam Raimi film was one of the defining blockbusters of 2002, Spider-Man 2 became one of the most respected superhero sequels ever made, and Spider-Man 3 was still a huge commercial success despite its mixed reception. The MCU changed Marvel's hierarchy. Iron Man became one of the biggest superheroes in the world. Captain America went from a character who had struggled on film to the lead of billion-dollar movies. Thor became a household name for audiences who had never read the comics. Black Panther, Doctor Strange, Guardians of the Galaxy, and Captain Marvel all became major film properties.

Without that machine, Spider-Man never has to share the top spot with them. Sony would understand how valuable that makes its rights. Any future Marvel owner wanting a dominant movie franchise would still have its most famous hero sitting at another studio. That gives Sony even less reason to compromise unless a partnership offers something it can’t build itself. The 2015 Sony and Marvel agreement that eventually puts Tom Holland into Captain America: Civil War probably doesn’t happen because there’s no MCU Civil War to join. There’s also no Avengers membership waiting as a selling point.

Andrew Garfield could therefore stay Spider-Man longer. That isn’t guaranteed because Sony had its own concerns with The Amazing Spider-Man 2, but the studio’s choices become different when the alternative isn’t sending Spider-Man into the most successful superhero franchise in the world. Sony could make The Amazing Spider-Man 3, recast within the same universe, or reboot again while keeping full control.

Spider-Man also becomes the obvious center of any larger Sony Marvel universe. Venom, Black Cat, Sinister Six, and other characters would be built around how they eventually connect back to him because there’s nowhere else for Sony to send them.

The public image of Marvel would change with him. For a kid growing up in the 2010s, Marvel might still mean Spider-Man first, Wolverine second, and then whoever happens to have a movie at the time. Iron Man wouldn't automatically sit beside Spider-Man on backpacks, toys, theme park merchandise, and advertising. Captain America’s shield wouldn’t become one of the most recognizable symbols in blockbuster cinema.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: By the 2020s, the biggest change would be how Hollywood builds franchises. There’d be no Avengers: Endgame, no decade long Marvel storyline, and far less pressure for every studio to connect all of its biggest characters into one universe.

Disney would feel that loss heavily. Marvel became one of its most reliable brands, so without it, Disney would depend more on Star Wars, Pixar, animation, and its live action remakes. Disney+ would also launch without shows like Loki, WandaVision, or The Falcon and the Winter Soldier because those characters never became major movie stars first.

A lot of careers change too. Robert Downey Jr. could still have a strong comeback, but he wouldn’t spend more than a decade as Tony Stark. Chris Evans and Chris Hemsworth could still become successful actors, but Captain America and Thor wouldn’t define their careers in the same way.

Superhero culture would still be huge. Spider-Man, Batman, Superman, Wolverine, and the X-Men were already popular enough to carry movies without the MCU. What changes is how crowded the genre becomes. Without several Marvel releases every year, superhero movies could feel more like individual events instead of one continuous stream of connected projects. Eventually, another studio might still build a successful cinematic universe. DC, Sony, or Fox would have the characters to try it. It would probably happen later, though, because nobody would have The Avengers proving the model works as early as 2012.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: If the MCU never existed, superhero movies would still survive. Spider-Man, Batman, and the X-Men had already proven there was a huge audience for them.

What changes is everything built around Marvel’s success. Iron Man likely never receives the same MCU-driven rise, The Avengers never become the center of pop culture on the path we know, Sony and Fox have more control over Marvel’s movie identity, and DC gets more room to shape the 2010s.

Hollywood would still chase sequels, spin-offs, and big franchises, but without the MCU validating the specific model of separate films feeding one interconnected universe, constant crossovers and years-ahead shared-universe setup would probably spread much slower.
Marvel changed the way Hollywood thought a franchise could work, and without the MCU, the last 15 years of blockbuster movies would look very different.

scripts.title: What If The Town Hall Was Added To Clash Royale

sections.name: INTRO
paras: The Town Hall sounds like it should be one of the easiest Clash of Clans buildings to bring into Clash Royale, but its weapon is where things get interesting.

You’d place it like a normal defensive building, except the weapon inside would stay off until the Town Hall takes damage. Once it gets hit, the weapon activates and starts helping defend for the rest of the building’s lifetime.

A Hog Rider hitting it too early could give the defender extra value, and using a spell to weaken it before a push could wake the weapon up before your troops even reach it. That gives the card a very different role from something like Cannon or Tesla, because damaging it at the wrong time can make the defense stronger.
The question is what those stats would actually look like, which decks would want it, and whether the Town Hall could fit into Clash Royale without taking over the meta.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: If Supercell added the Town Hall as a real Clash Royale card, I’d start it at 5 Elixir. That puts it above cheap cycle buildings like Cannon, but still low enough that players could reasonably include it in normal decks without turning every defense into a huge commitment. The extra cost would come from the weapon mechanic and the amount of health it needs to survive long enough for that mechanic to matter.

At tournament standard, I’d give the Town Hall around 1,650 hitpoints, a 30 second lifetime, and normal building placement on your side of the Arena. Its weapon would stay inactive when you first place it, so dropping the card by itself wouldn’t give you any defensive damage. The Town Hall only wakes up after an enemy troop or spell deals damage to it.

Once activated, the weapon would work like a simplified version of the weaponized Town Halls from Clash of Clans. Instead of trying to copy every Town Hall level, Clash Royale would need one clean version that players can understand quickly. I’d give it a 6 tile range, around 145 damage per hit, and a 1.2 second attack speed. It would target both ground and air, which already gives it a much wider defensive role than Cannon. Tesla can also cover both, but Tesla’s June rework dropped its lifetime to 25 seconds while increasing its health slightly, so the Town Hall would need a clear reason to cost more without simply becoming a stronger Tesla.

The activation rule handles a lot of that balance. If your opponent never touches the Town Hall, you’ve spent 5 Elixir on a building that only distracts building targeting troops and eventually disappears. Like other temporary buildings, its health would continuously decay over its lifetime, so placing it early doesn’t just waste time before activation; it also means the Town Hall has less health remaining when the push finally reaches it. Once something hits it, the weapon becomes active for whatever lifetime and health it has left. That makes timing the placement important, while placing it late gives the opponent less time to prepare for the weapon once it activates.

I also wouldn’t give the Town Hall death damage. Clash of Clans Town Halls can create dangerous effects after being destroyed depending on the level, but adding another explosion to this version would probably push the card too far. A high health building that starts shooting after taking damage already gives enough value for 1 card.

The weapon should also have a short activation delay, somewhere around 0.8 seconds, before it begins firing. Without that delay, fast win conditions could hit once and immediately take damage before the defender has really earned anything. The small delay lets cards like Hog Rider or Ram Rider get their first hit while still allowing the Town Hall to help if they remain in range.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: The weapon being asleep at the start changes how both players approach the card. Imagine your opponent sends a Hog Rider and you place the Town Hall in the center. The Hog gets pulled toward it like any other building and lands the first hit. That wakes the weapon up, and after the short delay the Town Hall begins shooting the Hog while your Princess Tower helps. From that point, the defender gets more value than they would from a building that only exists to distract.

Players would quickly learn how to take advantage of that timing. Against a larger push, you might intentionally place the Town Hall where the tank reaches it first. A Giant could hit it once, wake the weapon up, and then the Town Hall would begin helping against the troops behind the Giant as they move forward. Since the weapon can target air as well, a support Baby Dragon or Mega Minion wouldn’t automatically ignore it.

The attacker would start thinking about the activation too. If the Town Hall is sitting in the middle of the Arena and hasn’t taken damage yet, throwing a weak spell onto it for no reason could be terrible. You’ve just triggered a 5 Elixir defensive weapon before your actual push arrives.

Earthquake becomes much more interesting. It’s already designed to punish buildings, so a player could use it to chip down the Town Hall before sending a Hog or Royal Hogs. The spell would still activate the weapon, but if enough health is removed first, the building may be destroyed before it gets much value. The June spell nerfs reduced damage to Crown Towers specifically, not normal damage against buildings, so Earthquake would still remain one of the cleanest answers to a card like this.

Lightning would create a similar choice in heavier decks. If the Town Hall is sitting near another valuable troop or tower, the attacker can use Lightning and get 3 targets at once. The Town Hall activates, but it may already be so damaged that the defender only gets a few shots before it disappears.

The defender can’t activate the card by themselves either. Clash Royale doesn’t normally let you damage your own buildings, so there’s no simple trick where you place the Town Hall and immediately turn it on. The opponent has to interact with it first, which stops the card from becoming a guaranteed defensive turret every time it is deployed in the Arena.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Hog Rider would probably be one of the first cards players test against the Town Hall because the interaction is easy to understand. The Town Hall can pull Hog to the center, tank the first hit, then activate and help kill him before he reaches the Princess Tower. At 5 Elixir, though, the defender is spending more than the Hog costs, so the Town Hall needs to survive with enough health to help against whatever comes next.

That’s where Hog cycle decks could punish it. If the defender spends 5 Elixir and the Town Hall is left on low health, the support Musketeer or even the next Hog can cycle back before the defender has another good counter ready. Fast cycle also makes it easier to keep Earthquake in the cycle, and Hog plus Earthquake has always been one of the classic ways to punish any building in the game.

Ram Rider would be a little awkward against the Town Hall. Her health was increased in July, helping her survive longer on offense, and the Town Hall still has to take the charge before its weapon wakes up. If the Ram Rider connects with a charge, that first hit eats up a serious amount of health before the defender gets any defensive damage from the building itself. The Town Hall could still help finish her afterward, but the interaction wouldn’t feel as safe as it does against a regular Hog.

Royal Hogs would put even more pressure on placement. If all 4 are pulled into one Town Hall, they can activate it quickly and start tearing through the health before the weapon can remove them. The defender might need another cheap card on top of the Town Hall to keep the Hogs from getting too much value. Evolved Royal Hogs also had their landing damage reduced earlier in 2026, so they’re less explosive than they were before those nerfs, but they’d still be a strong way to force the building to defend several targets at once.

Giant would be easier to control because he attacks more slowly. He’d walk into the Town Hall, land the first hit, and give the weapon enough time to start working while other defenders deal with the support behind him. A Giant player could still take advantage by placing ranged troops far enough back that the Town Hall keeps shooting the tank instead of switching onto the real damage dealers.

Golem would push that idea much further. A 5 Elixir Town Hall isn’t going to stop a full Golem push alone, and it shouldn’t. The building can distract the Golem and contribute damage once activated, but the defender still needs something for Night Witch, Baby Dragon, Lumberjack, or whatever support is coming behind it. Golem’s Golemites also received a large damage buff back in August 2025, so letting them survive after the main Golem dies is more dangerous than it used to be.

Electro Giant could be one of the rougher matchups depending on how the Town Hall weapon is coded. If the activated weapon counts as a normal attack source for Electro Giant’s counterattack mechanic, he could punish the Town Hall whenever he’s close enough for that interaction to trigger. If Supercell coded the weapon differently, that reflected-damage interaction would have to be defined separately. His health was also buffed again in July this year, so he’d likely survive long enough to make the matchup important either way.

Balloon would probably be one of the reasons the Town Hall needs air targeting. Once Balloon reaches the building and lands its first hit, the weapon activates and begins shooting back, but Balloon’s damage is high enough that the Town Hall might only get a few shots before being destroyed. The defender would still need a proper air card if they want a reliable answer.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Earthquake would probably become its clearest counter. The spell is built to punish buildings, and the Town Hall’s activation mechanic doesn’t remove that weakness. Earthquake wakes the weapon up, but it also burns through enough health that the defender gets much less time to use it. In Hog or Royal Hogs decks, that could make the Town Hall feel risky because the opponent already wants to carry Earthquake for exactly this kind of defense.

Poison would work more slowly. It could activate the Town Hall before the push arrives and keep damaging it while troops move toward the bridge. The defender still gets the weapon, but the Town Hall loses health while part of its limited lifetime expires before the real fight starts.

Fireball would usually be poor value if the Town Hall is the only target. Spending 4 Elixir just to damage a 5 Elixir building while activating its weapon leaves the attacker in a bad trade unless the spell also catches a support troop or tower.

Lightning could become dangerous in heavier matchups because the attacker can hit the Town Hall and two other expensive targets together. If the defender places something like Musketeer or Electro Wizard beside it, the Town Hall starts creating the same spacing problems other expensive buildings already do.

Swarms would depend heavily on the weapon targeting. A single target Town Hall should struggle against Skeleton Army, Goblin Gang, or several cheap units crossing together. The weapon might kill 1 small troop per shot while the rest keep hitting the building, which gives swarm decks a natural way to overwhelm it after something else triggers the activation.

That’s also why I wouldn’t give the weapon splash damage. A Town Hall with high health, air targeting, and area damage would start stepping on Bomb Tower, Tesla, and several defensive troops at the same time. Single target damage makes support cards important and keeps the building from solving every push on its own.

Ranged siege cards would create some of the most interesting interactions. Depending on the specific card and placement, X-Bow or Mortar could potentially pressure or activate the Town Hall from a position where its 6-tile weapon cannot return fire, though their different ranges and Mortar’s minimum-range behavior mean the interaction would not be identical.

That creates a positioning problem rather than simply letting another tank ignore the building. Place the Town Hall where a siege card can reach it safely and you may wake the weapon without getting useful return fire. Place it differently and you still need to make sure incoming building-targeting troops are actually pulled where you want them. The card would reward players who understand building placement instead of giving the same result every time.

Support troops also make activating the weapon early much more valuable for the defender. If a Giant hits the Town Hall first and wakes it up, the weapon could then retarget onto a Musketeer, Baby Dragon, or other support troop if that unit is the next valid target within range. That can put additional pressure on the push while the defender’s remaining troops are still alive.

After these first matchups, the 5 Elixir version still looks playable, but the 1,650 health may already be slightly too generous. If the Town Hall regularly survives one full push and stays active long enough to defend the next one, it would start giving too much defensive value for a single card.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: The Town Hall would fit best in slower control and beatdown decks that already want a building capable of surviving long enough to support a second defense. A 5 Elixir cost makes it awkward in very fast cycle decks, because spending that much on defense can slow down the rotation and make it harder to get back to the main win condition. Decks built around cards like Golem, Giant, Graveyard, or heavier control strategies would be much more comfortable with it.

Graveyard decks could especially benefit from the Town Hall because they already like defending efficiently and turning surviving troops into a counterpush. The building could pull a Hog, Ram Rider, or tank into the middle, activate after taking the first hit, and help clean up whatever remains. If the defender still has something like Knight, Baby Dragon, or another support troop alive afterward, they can move straight into a Graveyard push.

Beatdown decks would use it differently. A Golem player could defend with Town Hall, let the weapon help clear the push, then place Golem once the opponent has already spent Elixir dealing with the building. That could become frustrating if the Town Hall survives for too long, because the defender might get a strong defense and still have enough time to build a huge push behind it.

That’s where the lifetime becomes important. Thirty seconds might be slightly too long for a building that becomes a real defensive tower after activation. If it survives a full push and remains active while the opponent starts the next one, the card starts giving value far beyond the original 5 Elixir.

A shorter lifetime around 25 seconds would probably be healthier. It gives the card enough time to defend the push it was placed for, while making it much less likely that the same Town Hall handles two separate attacks.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: The biggest issue comes from how much value the Town Hall can generate after the weapon activates. A normal building already gives value by pulling win conditions toward the middle. This one starts adding its own damage once the opponent touches it, and because the weapon targets both ground and air, it can keep helping after the first troop dies.

That could make defensive decks too comfortable. Imagine a Giant push reaches the Town Hall, activates it, and then gets cleaned up while the building still has half its health. The attacker now has to either wait for it to disappear, spend another spell on it, or start the next push into an already active defensive weapon. If that happens too often, players would start placing Town Hall early simply to create a long section of the match where attacking feels inefficient.

I’d reduce the health from 1,650 to around 1,500 hitpoints and lower the lifetime to 25 seconds. The weapon damage could stay close to 145 because the activation condition already limits how often it gets full value. The shorter lifetime means the defender has to place it closer to the actual push instead of dropping it early and waiting.

The 5 Elixir cost should stay. Dropping it to 4 would make it much easier to cycle and could let players use it as a cheap distraction even when the weapon never activates. At 6 Elixir, the card might become too expensive compared to Inferno Tower or other strong defensive options.

The activation delay could also increase slightly from 0.8 to 1 second. That gives fast win conditions a little more time to punish the building before it starts firing and keeps the first hit from feeling too safe for the defender.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: The final version I’d release would cost 5 Elixir, have around 1,500 hitpoints at tournament standard, and stay in the Arena for 25 seconds.

The weapon would activate after the Town Hall takes enemy damage and wait 1 second before firing. Once active, it would target ground and air from 6 tiles away, deal around 145 damage, and attack every 1.2 seconds.
There would be no death damage, no splash, and no way for the defender to activate it themselves. Enemy troops and spells would be the only things capable of turning the weapon on.

That gives the card a clear identity without replacing every existing building. Cannon remains cheaper and better for fast cycle. Tesla still gives instant air and ground defense without needing to take damage. Inferno Tower handles huge tanks better, while Bomb Tower remains much stronger against swarms.

The Town Hall would sit between those options as a more flexible building that rewards careful timing. If the defender places it well, the opponent may be forced to activate a strong defensive weapon during the push. If the attacker prepares properly, Earthquake, Lightning, swarms, or a heavy first hit can remove enough health that the weapon never gets much time to work.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: The strongest version wouldn’t need crazy damage or huge health. The interesting part comes from making the attacker think about when the weapon turns on and whether damaging the building early helps or hurts the push.
At 5 Elixir with a shorter lifetime and reasonable health, the Town Hall could become a strong defensive option without replacing Cannon, Tesla, Inferno Tower, or Bomb Tower.
It would probably be annoying during the first few weeks while everyone learns it, but once the counters become clear, it could fit into the game surprisingly well.

scripts.title: What If The X Men Were In The Boys

sections.name: INTRO
paras: When the X-Men first appear, Vought assumes someone else has figured out how to make Supes.

That’s the only explanation that makes sense to them. 8 unknown superhumans have suddenly shown up with abilities that don’t match anyone in their files, and none of them have any connection to Vought.
Then the test results come back.
There’s no Compound V in their blood.

For the first time, Vought is looking at people who were actually born with powers, and that creates a problem they’ve never had to deal with before. If the public finds out superheroes can exist without Vought, the company loses control over the one thing that made it untouchable.
Xavier doesn’t know any of that yet. He’s more concerned with figuring out where they are and whether this world is safe for his team.
Magneto starts asking a different question almost immediately. Why does one corporation seem to own nearly every superhuman on the planet?

sections.name: PART 1
paras: The team has no idea how they got there, and Beast can’t find anything that immediately explains it. Their surroundings look normal enough, but it doesn’t take long before they realize they aren’t simply somewhere else on Earth.

They’re on billboards, tv screens and advertisements. There are movies about them, restaurants using their faces, merchandise built around them and entire news cycles following what they do. To most of the X-Men, it looks strange. They’re used to living in a world where people with powers are feared as often as they’re admired. Here, they’re celebrities.

Xavier sees that as a reason to be careful rather than suspicious. If this world has already accepted superpowered people, then revealing themselves might not create the panic they’d expect back home. His priority is finding somewhere safe for the team while Beast works out whether returning to their own universe is even possible.

Magneto doesn’t share the optimism. What bothers him is how organized everything feels. They belong to the same company. Their public appearances are managed through the same company. Even the language people use around them sounds less like they’re talking about independent heroes and more like they’re discussing employees.

The team still tries to keep a low profile, but 8 people with their abilities can only disappear for so long. Storm stops an accident before anyone is badly hurt. Quicksilver pulls several people clear before most witnesses understand what happened. Someone records part of it.
By the end of the day, the footage is inside Vought. Ashley Barrett’s immediate concern isn’t who these people are. It’s who made them.

Nobody at Vought recognizes the faces. None of them appear in the company’s records, and there’s no sign they belong to any known Supe program. That leaves the possibility Vought hates most: somebody else has started producing enhanced people.

The easiest person to follow turns out to be Beast. He’s the one searching most actively for information, and unlike Xavier or Jean, he can’t hide what he is once somebody gets a clear look at him. Vought security eventually gets access to a piece of biological material left behind during one of the team’s movements.
The sample reaches a lab. What comes back doesn’t fit anything the scientists expect. The cellular abnormalities are real, but there’s no sign of Compound V being responsible for them.
That’s when Vought stops asking who made these people and starts asking how they were born this way.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Vought doesn’t send Homelander after them. Not yet.

A group this unusual is worth more alive and cooperative than dead, so the first contact comes through people who look harmless. Representatives approach Xavier with an offer to talk, presenting Vought as the organization best equipped to help superpowered individuals understand the world they’ve arrived in.
Xavier agrees to the meeting because refusing would tell him very little.
Magneto comes because he doesn’t trust them.
Inside Vought Tower, the difference between the 2 men becomes obvious almost immediately.

Xavier pays attention to what the company is offering. Housing, laboratories, legal protection, access to information and the resources needed to investigate how the X-Men arrived. Those are things the team actually needs.
Magneto pays attention to what Vought wants in return.
Medical examinations. Genetic samples. Interviews about when their abilities first appeared. Questions about whether their parents had powers. Questions about whether children inherit them.
Beast understands why the scientists are interested, but even he notices how quickly the conversation moves away from helping them and toward studying them.

Compound V can create abilities, but it requires Vought to make the intervention. Mutants suggest something else entirely. Their powers are tied to their natural biology, which means the company may be looking at a way for superhuman traits to exist without injections at all.

If this information becomes public before Vought understands it, every part of their business becomes harder to control. Governments could demand access to the research. Competitors could start looking for mutants themselves. More importantly, people might begin asking why Vought spent decades presenting superheroes as something only its system could provide. Xavier doesn’t know the full history of Compound V yet, but he can tell the meeting has stopped being an introduction.

They’re being evaluated. So he gives Vought almost nothing. Beast won’t provide further samples. Jean avoids discussing the extent of her telepathy. Cyclops gives vague answers about training. Storm says even less.

Magneto barely participates. By the time they leave, he’s already made up his mind about the company. What concerns him most is how familiar the process feels. A powerful institution discovers a group of people who are biologically different, then immediately begins deciding how useful they might be and how much control it can gain over them.
Xavier still thinks there’s value in learning more before making an enemy of Vought. Erik thinks Vought has already decided what the X-Men are.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Homelander’s interest begins when he finds out Vought met with the X-Men without him.

He’s used to being the person Vought builds everything around, and now there’s a group of unknown superhumans being discussed in private meetings with scientists and executives. When he asks what makes them important, he gets an answer he doesn’t particularly like.
Nobody gave them powers.

Homelander initially treats that as a technical detail. Compound V or no Compound V, they’re still people with abilities, and in his experience that means there’s a hierarchy. Some are useful, some are impressive, and eventually all of them understand where they stand compared to him. He decides to meet them himself.

There’s no excitement when Homelander enters the room and no nervous effort to impress him. Cyclops watches him closely because he already knows Vought considers this man its most powerful asset. Wolverine barely hides his dislike. Magneto seems more interested in studying Homelander’s reaction to them than anything Homelander says.
Xavier doesn’t need to dig deeply into Homelander’s mind. Even surface impressions are enough to tell him that the public image and the person underneath it are very different.
There’s insecurity beneath the confidence. Anger that rises quickly when he feels dismissed. An obsession with approval that doesn’t fit the image Vought sells to the world.
Xavier pulls back rather than pushing further. Forcing his way into the mind of someone he’s just met would create exactly the kind of conflict he’s trying to avoid.
Homelander notices Xavier watching him anyway. That’s the first moment he becomes uncomfortable around the group. Then there’s everyone else.
Storm doesn’t look physically imposing, but Vought’s own footage has already shown that weather responds to her directly.
Jean’s abilities are harder for them to measure because she’s barely used them publicly.
Wolverine looks like the least complicated member of the team until Homelander hears about his healing.

Magneto is the one that bothers Vought security most. The building around them is filled with metal, which means putting him inside Vought Tower has effectively surrounded him with material he can control.
And Quicksilver is so fast that several cameras have trouble following him properly.
Homelander doesn’t suddenly decide he’s afraid of them. He hasn’t seen enough for that. What changes is that he can’t immediately place them beneath himself.
The meeting ends without violence, but Homelander leaves with a different view of the X-Men than Vought’s scientists have.
Homelander sees people who’ve walked into his world without asking permission, and none of them seem interested in treating him like the center of it.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Butcher hears about the X-Men through the same channels that usually lead him back to Vought.

There’s footage of people with powers who aren’t registered anywhere. Vought has started moving scientists around quietly, and security around one of its research divisions has suddenly increased. To him, that sounds like another experiment the company doesn’t want anyone seeing.

What they find doesn’t make much sense at first. There’s no trail of Compound V, no childhood connection to Vought and no evidence these people were raised inside the same system as every other Supe they’ve investigated. Even their names seem to appear from nowhere.

That changes when Hughie and M.M. manage to trace part of the company’s internal response to the group. Vought’s own scientists are treating the X-Men like something new. They aren’t trying to cover up how they created them. They’re trying to figure out how they exist at all.

Wolverine takes one look at the weapons The Boys are carrying and decides they aren’t there to talk. Butcher sees Logan healing from injuries that would put most Supes down and immediately assumes he’s dealing with another nearly unkillable problem.
Xavier prevents it from going any further.
Once everyone settles down, Butcher explains what Vought actually is.
He tells them about Compound V, the children who were injected with it and the way Vought built an entire superhero industry around something the public was never supposed to understand.

The X-Men had already realized Vought was hiding something, but this puts the company’s interest in their genetics into context. If every known Supe in this world exists because Vought created them, then eight people born with abilities are more than a scientific curiosity.
Butcher still doesn’t trust them.

As far as he’s concerned, powers make people dangerous whether Vought gave them those powers or not. Wolverine doesn’t exactly help his case, and Magneto’s history would only make Butcher more suspicious if he knew all of it.
The difference is that he can’t point to anything the X-Men have actually done to justify treating them like Vought’s Supes.

For once, the people with powers standing in front of him aren’t defending Vought, chasing fame or asking how much money they can make from their abilities. They’re trying to understand why a corporation has spent decades controlling people like them.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: The information Butcher gives them changes how the X-Men approach Vought. They stop treating the company like something they can understand through meetings and start looking at what it doesn’t want them to see. Beast focuses on the science.

With help from information The Boys have collected, he pieces together how Compound V is being used and why Vought was so interested in mutant biology. The company isn’t just comparing two kinds of superhuman. It’s trying to understand whether the mutant trait can be isolated, reproduced or eventually controlled.

Cyclops looks at the problem differently. If Vought learns enough about them, every member of the team becomes a reference point. Wolverine’s healing can be studied. Quicksilver’s speed can be measured. Jean and Xavier become proof that abilities can extend directly into the mind.

That means staying together and waiting for Vought to make the next move only gives the company more time. Magneto wants to destroy the research immediately. For him, the argument is already over. Vought created Supes in laboratories, controlled their careers and built a system where people with powers belonged to the company that made them. There’s no reason to believe mutants would be treated better once Vought understands how valuable they are.

Xavier agrees with the danger but not with Erik’s solution. If Magneto attacks Vought Tower or starts killing researchers, the public won’t know anything about Compound V or what the company was trying to do. They’ll only see an unknown man with extraordinary power attacking one of the most recognizable institutions in the country.

Vought would get the story it needs before mutantkind has even been explained. So Xavier proposes something harder. They need proof. The Boys already have pieces of Vought’s history. The X-Men need evidence tying the company’s current research directly to them.

Jean helps locate where Vought has moved the samples and records from their first contact. Quicksilver can get through areas normal infiltrators would never reach, while Beast knows what information actually matters once they’re inside.

They find enough to confirm Magneto’s suspicion. Vought has already begun mapping their biology against Compound V subjects. There are projections for whether naturally occurring abilities could be detected early in life. There are discussions about inherited traits. There’s even interest in whether mutant characteristics could be combined with V-based enhancement. Xavier now knows peaceful cooperation with Vought is finished. But Magneto notices something else. Charles still thinks exposing the company will make the situation manageable.
Erik has spent too much of his life watching governments decide what to do with people who are different. If Vought falls, someone else will want the research.
That disagreement doesn’t split the team yet, but it creates the first real question about what happens after they expose the truth.
Because stopping Vought is one problem. Stopping the rest of the world from becoming interested in mutants is another.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Vought realizes someone has accessed the research before the X-Men are ready to release it. That forces the company to move first. Publicly, the response is careful.

Reports begin describing the X-Men as unidentified enhanced individuals operating without government oversight. Vought avoids calling them mutants and never mentions that their powers are natural. Instead, the company lets people assume they’re another group of Supes whose origin hasn’t been disclosed.

Privately, the goal is much simpler. They want one of them. Wolverine becomes the safest target. Vought already knows his body can recover from severe injuries, which gives them room to use more force than they could against someone like Beast or Xavier. He’s also easier to isolate than the telepaths and less capable of escaping instantly than Quicksilver.

They track Logan when he leaves the others. The people sent after him aren’t trying to beat him in a fair fight. They use heavy tranquilizers, restraints and enough force to keep him disoriented while they move him before the rest of the team can respond.

For a short time, it works. Vought’s scientists only have limited biological data on Logan, and they underestimate how quickly his healing factor metabolizes the tranquilizers. He wakes up much sooner than their calculations predicted. The restraints don’t last long. By the time Cyclops and Storm reach the site, Wolverine has already turned the attempted capture into a disaster. He’s injured, furious and surrounded by the remains of equipment Vought clearly expected to use on him.
Beast finds the important part. The transport team had medical containment ready before they ever attacked.
This wasn’t an arrest. They planned to take Wolverine somewhere equipped to study him. That ends any remaining argument over whether Vought intends to leave them alone.
Xavier immediately brings the team together and starts preparing to get the evidence out before Vought can destroy it.

Magneto makes a different decision. He goes after the facility connected to the capture operation. Cyclops tries to stop him from turning the situation into exactly the public conflict Xavier has been avoiding, but Erik isn’t interested in waiting anymore. As far as he’s concerned, Vought has moved from observation to abduction. Until now, Magneto could still be accused of assuming the worst.

He tears apart the equipment used to hold powered subjects and destroys the stored samples Vought collected from the X-Men. He avoids killing the ordinary staff who get out of his way, but the message is obvious. Vought isn’t going to study mutants in secret. The problem is that Vought gets exactly what Xavier feared. Cameras catch enough of the attack to control the first version of the story. By the next morning, Magneto is being shown across every major network as an unknown superpowered terrorist attacking a Vought facility.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: The footage has already given him what he wanted. To the public, one of the newcomers has attacked a Vought facility, which means Homelander can step in without looking like the aggressor. More importantly, he finally has a reason to test the group for himself.
He finds them before Xavier can finish organizing the release of Vought’s research.

Cyclops immediately understands what Homelander is doing. This isn’t an arrest. Homelander wants to establish control before the X-Men can change the situation around him, so Scott keeps the team spread out and makes sure nobody gives him a clean target.
Homelander goes for the easiest person to intimidate first and discovers there really isn’t one.

Wolverine takes the opening hit and gets thrown hard enough to tear through part of the building behind him, but he gets back up. Homelander barely has time to process that before Quicksilver starts moving around him, pulling people out of danger and forcing him to keep turning just to follow what’s happening.
That gives Cyclops room to fire.

His optic blast doesn’t put Homelander down, but it moves him, which matters more than the damage itself. Storm follows by filling the area with wind and debris, cutting down Homelander’s visibility while Jean uses her telekinesis to keep him from simply charging through the team.

Most Supes he’s dealt with either depend on raw power or freeze when they realize he’s stronger. The X-Men do neither. Scott keeps changing their positions, Jean keeps interfering with his movement, and Quicksilver keeps removing anyone Homelander tries to isolate.

Magneto doesn’t try to crush Homelander with metal as if that alone will solve the fight. He uses everything around them to block paths, tear apart structures Homelander could use for cover and keep pressure coming from directions Homelander can’t answer all at once.

Homelander is still physically stronger than most of them, and whenever he gets close enough to land a clean hit, the difference is obvious. Storm can’t trade punches with him. Cyclops can’t afford to let him get his hands on him. Even Logan can be thrown around despite healing from the damage.

Jean restrains him long enough for Storm and Cyclops to force him back. Quicksilver gets Wolverine into position, and Logan drives his claws into Homelander before being blasted away almost immediately afterward.
The wound isn’t enough to finish him, but he stops to realize he’s bleeding.

That changes his behavior more than anything else. Until now, Homelander has been angry. Now he’s careful. He stops rushing into the middle of the team and starts using his heat vision from a distance, trying to break their formation before committing again. It’s the first intelligent adjustment he’s made since the fight started, and Xavier notices exactly why it happened.
The X-Men don’t beat him here. Xavier doesn’t want the situation turning into an execution, and Scott knows they still need to expose Vought before the company can bury everything.

Jean restrains Homelander for a few seconds while Magneto tears metal and debris across the space between them and Storm fills the opening with wind and lightning. His hesitation after being wounded gives Scott exactly the opening he needs. He orders the team out before Homelander can break through.

By the time Homelander tears through the obstruction, the X-Men are already gone. He could pursue them, but doing so now means charging blindly into another coordinated fight without knowing what Jean or Magneto can actually do at full strength.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: The fight gives Vought a problem they can’t solve with the usual media cycle. Too many people recorded it.

There’s footage of Homelander attacking the X-Men, footage of Wolverine surviving injuries that should have killed him, and enough clear video of Storm, Cyclops and Jean using their abilities that Vought can’t pretend the group was exaggerated or invented.

They describe the X-Men as unauthorized Supes and suggest they may have been created through an illegal version of Compound V. It’s the safest story because it keeps everything inside the system Vought already understands.

Using the files taken from Vought’s research, Beast puts together evidence showing that the company itself found no Compound V in any of them. The Boys help move the information through channels Vought can’t shut down all at once, while Xavier makes sure the release includes enough medical data to be credible without giving away everything Vought would need to continue experimenting on them.
People have spent years assuming powers come from Vought because, as far as anyone knew, they did. Now there’s proof that eight people exist whose abilities developed naturally.
Vought immediately denies parts of the research, but the problem is that some of the files are its own.

Scientists outside Vought begin asking whether the same mutations could appear in other people. Governments want access to the biological evidence. Parents start wondering whether children could develop powers without ever being exposed to Compound V.

Homelander feels the change before most executives do. For years, the public has treated Supes as something extraordinary partly because Vought controlled where they came from. Homelander sits at the top of that structure. If powers can simply appear in people Vought never touched, then there’s no guarantee the next person born with abilities will work for the company, admire The Seven or care who Homelander is.

Magneto has a different reaction to the same news. He watches the public discussion move from curiosity toward questions about testing, identification and genetic screening, and he recognizes the pattern immediately. The world hasn’t even had time to understand what mutants are, and institutions are already discussing how they might be tracked.

Xavier expected fear. He didn’t expect it to happen this quickly. That forces him to rethink what comes next. Exposing Vought was necessary, but now the X-Men have created a second problem just by existing publicly.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: Vought’s final move isn’t about protecting its reputation anymore. It’s about preventing the research from getting out of its hands permanently.

The company starts destroying internal records, moving biological material and locking down every lab connected to the X-Men. If Vought can’t control the public story, it can at least keep control of the science.
Beast realizes what’s happening when several files they’d been tracking suddenly disappear from Vought’s network.

That gives the X-Men a clear objective. They’re not going to Vought Tower to fight The Seven. They’re going there to destroy the remaining mutant material and take whatever records prove what the company tried to do.

Quicksilver goes in first because speed matters more than force. He clears civilians and reaches the research levels before security can properly respond. Beast follows to identify what needs to be copied and what needs to be destroyed, while Jean stays close enough to protect both of them if Vought sends Supes into the lab.

Storm and Magneto handle the building itself. Storm shuts down exterior access by filling the upper levels with violent wind, making helicopters and aerial support useless. Magneto tears open secured sections without wasting time on the normal entrances, then locks down corridors behind the team so Vought’s security can’t surround them.
That’s when The Seven become involved.
The fight is messy because it isn’t organized into clean matchups. A-Train tries to reach Beast and finds Quicksilver waiting for him. Storm keeps higher floors unstable enough that anyone
trying to attack from above has to deal with her first. Wolverine stays near Cyclops because Scott knows Vought will eventually send its strongest people straight toward the objective.
Homelander arrives last. This time he doesn’t underestimate them. He goes straight for Jean.

She’s the person who disrupted him most in their first fight, and removing her would make it much easier to reach everyone else. Jean catches him with telekinesis before he can close the distance, but holding him takes visible effort. Homelander keeps pushing forward until the floor beneath him starts breaking apart.

Magneto tears apart the metal supports around the room and forces Homelander to deal with several tons of debris at once. Storm adds a lightning strike through the opening, and Cyclops fires before Homelander can fully recover.

None of those attacks alone end the fight. Together, they keep him from reaching Jean. That’s the difference between this team and almost everyone Homelander has fought before. There isn’t one person he can remove and suddenly win. Every time he commits to someone, somebody else changes the battlefield around him.
Beast copies the records that prove Vought knew the X-Men were naturally powered, then destroys the biological samples and the internal work built from them.
The mission is already successful before the fight ends. Cyclops recognizes it and orders the team out instead of staying to chase a victory they don’t need.
Homelander tries to follow. Xavier stops him for the first time. He hits him with enough psychic pressure to interrupt his focus for a few seconds.
By the time Homelander recovers, the X-Men are gone and the research is gone with them. Vought Tower is still standing. Homelander is still alive.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: Getting rid of Vought’s samples doesn’t put things back the way they were. By this point, too many people know mutants exist, and that changes the world far beyond anything the X-Men can control. Vought can deny details of what happened inside its labs, but it can’t convince everyone that naturally born superhumans aren’t real when the evidence is already public.

That creates problems almost immediately. Governments want to know whether mutations can be detected before powers appear. Researchers want access to whatever genetic data is still available. Vought publicly distances itself from the experiments while quietly trying to rebuild what it lost through any information that may have survived outside the main archive.

The public reaction is just as divided. Some people see the X-Men as proof that superhuman abilities aren’t automatically tied to Vought. Others see something much more frightening. Compound V can at least be controlled at the source. Mutations can’t. If people can simply be born with powers, then nobody knows how many mutants might already exist or what abilities they could eventually develop.

Magneto watches that fear spread and finds very little about it surprising. He’s spent most of his life expecting this exact reaction. The names are different and the institutions are different, but the instinct is familiar. People discover something they can’t control, then begin discussing how to identify it before deciding what should be done about it.

That difference between them becomes more important now than anything Vought could’ve offered earlier. They aren’t arguing about whether the company can be trusted anymore. They already know the answer. They’re arguing about what mutantkind should become in a world that has only just learned it exists.

Cyclops sides with Xavier on one point. If the X-Men respond to every government or institution as an enemy before those institutions actually move against them, they’ll help create the war Magneto expects.
Wolverine is less optimistic, but even he knows attacking people because they might eventually turn on mutants isn’t going to make the situation better.

Magneto has no reason to trust this world, but the X-Men are the only people in it who understand exactly what’s beginning to happen. Until they find a way home, abandoning them would mean leaving the future of mutantkind entirely in Xavier’s hands.

The Boys are left dealing with their own change. Butcher hasn’t suddenly become comfortable around people with powers. He still distrusts them, and Wolverine in particular gives him plenty of reasons to keep his distance.
They didn’t ask Vought for contracts. They didn’t chase popularity. When Vought tried to control them, they fought back without turning everyone around them into collateral damage.

For Hughie and M.M., that distinction is easy enough to understand. For Butcher, his anger has always been aimed at Supes as a group, but now there’s a group of superpowered people standing in front of him who have nothing to do with the system that created Homelander.

Homelander handles the new world much worse. He’s still Vought’s biggest weapon and still stronger than almost anyone he meets. Before the X-Men arrived, Homelander understood the hierarchy. Vought created Supes, The Seven sat above them, and he sat above The Seven.

There could be someone else born tomorrow with powers Vought has never seen. There could already be mutants somewhere in the world who don’t know what they are. None of them would owe Homelander anything.
For someone who built his identity around being unique, that possibility is going to stay with him long after the X-Men are gone.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: For decades, the company controlled the source of superhuman power. Compound V gave Vought a way to create Supes, manage them and shape how the public understood them.
Mutants break that system. Their abilities come from biology rather than a Vought lab, which means the next superpowered person could appear anywhere and not belong to a corporation.
That changes the problem Xavier is facing. If more mutants begin appearing, the X-Men will become the first example people look toward when deciding what mutantkind represents.
Magneto already knows fear will be part of that reaction, and for once, even Xavier can see how quickly the world has started asking the wrong questions.
Superhuman power has existed outside its control once and everyone knows it can happen again.

scripts.title: What If Thor Was Reborn With His Memories

sections.name: INTRO
paras: Thor would wake up years before the first Thor movie, back in the body he had when Loki was still beside him, Frigga was still alive, Odin was still ruling Asgard, and none of the worst things in his life had happened yet.

He'd remember all of it. Loki turning against him, Frigga dying during the Dark Elves’ attack, Odin’s death, Hela, Ragnarok, Thanos killing half of Asgard, and the moment Thor hit him with Stormbreaker and realized too late that he should’ve aimed for the head.

The younger Thor wanted the throne and thought strength could solve almost anything. This Thor had already lived through what that attitude cost him. So his first concern wouldn't be proving himself to Odin. It would be his family.

He’d want to keep Loki from reaching the point where everything between them falls apart, save Frigga before the Dark Elves ever reach her, and figure out what Odin is still hiding about Hela before Asgard gets blindsided again.

The problem is that Thor only remembers the future he already lived through. Once Loki makes a different choice, Frigga survives something that killed her before, or Asgard avoids a disaster that was supposed to happen, those memories stop being useful.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: Thor would wake up before his coronation, back when Asgard still looked untouched and almost everyone he eventually lost was still alive. Loki would still be beside him, Frigga would still be in the palace, Odin would still be ruling, and Mjolnir would still be in Thor’s hand. The throne that used to mean everything to him would barely register compared with seeing his family again. He’d remember how badly this day went the first time. Frost Giants entered Odin’s vault, Thor took it as an attack on Asgard, and Loki pushed him toward Jotunheim knowing Odin would see the trip as reckless. That entire chain led to Thor’s banishment, Loki discovering what he was, Odin collapsing into the Odinsleep, and eventually Loki falling from the Bifrost.

So when the vault is attacked again, Thor wouldn't demand retaliation. He’d tell Odin they should find out how the Frost Giants got inside before anyone crosses into Jotunheim. That alone would throw Loki off because he had been counting on Thor reacting exactly the way he always did.

Thor would notice, but he wouldn't accuse him. Loki has already arranged the intrusion, so Thor knows he’s involved, but most of the crimes Thor remembers haven't happened yet. Treating Loki like the man who invaded New York or worked with Thanos would only punish him for a future Thor is actively trying to prevent.

The coronation would probably stop anyway once Odin realizes something is wrong with Thor. His son is suddenly patient, doesn’t care about proving himself through war, and shows almost no frustration when the ceremony is disrupted. Thor could make it even stranger by telling Odin he doesn’t want the throne yet.

Thor could explain that he remembers what happens when pride controls his decisions and that ruling Asgard means more than winning battles. He wouldn't need to tell everyone where those memories came from yet. Odin would still see enough to realize Thor is carrying knowledge and experience he didn’t have the day before.
Thor would eventually ask to speak with Odin and Frigga alone. He could tell them there’s one secret Odin needs to stop keeping before anything else happens. Then he’d say Hela’s name.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Odin would have no easy way to explain how Thor knows about Hela. Her history was deliberately buried, the old murals were covered, and neither Thor nor Loki had been raised knowing they had an older sister. Thor could prove he isn’t guessing by describing the hidden mural beneath the palace artwork and explaining that Hela once fought beside Odin during Asgard’s conquest of the 9 Realms.

Frigga would understand quickly that whatever happened to Thor has given him knowledge from far beyond this point in his life. Odin would be more guarded, especially once Thor tells him that Hela returns after his death and grows stronger when she reaches Asgard.

Thor could also tell him how the original fight ended. Hela destroyed Mjolnir, slaughtered most of Asgard’s forces, and eventually became too powerful for Thor and Loki to stop directly. They survived because Loki released Surtur with the Eternal Flame, destroying Asgard along with Hela.

Odin would have to hear his son explain that the kingdom he spent centuries building eventually burned because his oldest child became impossible to contain. Thor could tell him that hiding Hela until the end made everything worse because nobody had time to prepare for what she was capable of.

Frigga would also want to know what happened to the family. Thor wouldn't turn it into a full history lesson, but he could tell her that she died during an attack by the Dark Elves and that Loki eventually died trying to protect Thor from Thanos. Odin would learn that he dies on Earth before Hela returns, while Thor is left trying to hold together what remains of Asgard afterward.

Thor would be angry about the secrets, but he already had years to live with that anger the first time. He’d use the chance to get answers instead. He could ask Odin where Hela is being held, what exactly keeps her from returning, and whether there is anything Asgard can do before Odin’s death releases her.

Odin may still refuse to explain everything immediately, especially with Loki unaware of his own parentage and the family already carrying several dangerous secrets. Thor would push back on that. He knows exactly what happens when Loki learns the truth in the middle of a crisis and has nobody around him willing to explain it properly.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Thor would insist that Odin and Frigga tell Loki the truth while all of them are still together and nobody is fighting for the throne. Loki would still take it badly. Finding out that he was born a Frost Giant and taken from Jotunheim as a baby would hit the same insecurities he already carries about being treated differently from Thor.

Odin isn’t collapsing in front of him during the confrontation, Thor hasn’t been banished, and Loki hasn't suddenly been left holding the throne while trying to prove he belongs in Asgard. Frigga would be there from the beginning, and Thor could stay with him without trying to argue him out of being angry.

Thor would also admit that he already knew. Loki would immediately want to know how, and this is where Thor would finally tell him enough about the life he remembers to explain why he has been acting differently. He could tell Loki that their relationship eventually falls apart, that Loki ends up leaving Asgard, and that Thor spends years trying to bring him back.

He wouldn't use future crimes as leverage against him. Thor could talk instead about where their relationship eventually ends, with Loki choosing to stand beside him and dying while trying to stop Thanos. That would probably be harder for Loki to process than hearing that he becomes an enemy, because Thor is describing a version of him who eventually chooses his family.

Loki would still distrust parts of the story. He’s spent most of his life competing with Thor, and now Thor is claiming to remember decades of arguments and reconciliations that Loki hasn’t experienced. Thor wouldn't try to prove it with events from the future because Loki has no way to verify them. He could only point to the fact that his behavior has changed before any of those events have happened.

Without the trip to Jotunheim, Thor never gets banished to Earth. Loki never takes control of Asgard through the same crisis, never sends the Destroyer after Thor, and never reaches the confrontation on the Bifrost that ends with him falling into space.
That means Loki may never encounter Thanos the way he did in the original timeline.

The 2012 invasion of New York would almost certainly change with him. Thanos used Loki as the leader of the Chitauri attack and gave him the scepter containing the Mind Stone. If Loki remains in Asgard, Thanos loses the person he originally used to recover the Tesseract from Earth.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Years later, Jane Foster encounters the Aether during the Convergence, and Malekith wakes because the Reality Stone has become active again. Thor remembers Jane becoming its host, Malekith attacking Asgard to retrieve it, and Kurse killing Frigga while she protects Jane.

The Aether could still resurface even though Jane never met Thor during his banishment. The Convergence would still begin opening paths between realms, but Thor couldn't assume Jane's life would place her inside the same anomaly without him ever entering it. Instead, he could have Heimdall and Asgard begin watching the disturbances as the Convergence approaches, looking for the place where the Aether becomes accessible before anyone accidentally reaches it.

So he would prepare for that event long before it arrives. Odin’s records would become much more useful now that Thor knows what he is looking for. Bor fought Malekith thousands of years earlier and believed the Aether had been destroyed, so Thor could push Odin to reopen everything Asgard still has from that war. Frigga and Loki could help with the magical side of the research while Heimdall watches Earth when the Convergence gets close.

If Jane still happens to encounter one of those anomalies and comes back carrying the Aether, Thor could reach her much sooner. Their relationship would be completely different because Jane has never met him before, while Thor remembers loving her, losing her, and eventually seeing her wield Mjolnir years later. He’d have to ignore all of that and focus on keeping her alive. Bringing Jane to Asgard would still make sense because Odin’s healers are among the few people capable of studying what is inside her. This time, everyone would already know Malekith may come for it.

Thor could warn Asgard about Algrim as well. In the original timeline, Algrim deliberately allows himself to be captured, receives a Kursed Stone from Malekith, transforms into Kurse inside Asgard’s prison, and starts freeing prisoners before joining the attack. Thor remembers enough of that to prevent the same infiltration from happening cleanly.

If Asgard intercepts Algrim before he reaches the cells or keeps him isolated under heavy guard, Malekith loses one of his strongest weapons inside the palace. Kurse is still incredibly dangerous if he transforms, but Thor knows who he is and doesn’t have to discover the threat after the prison is already falling apart.

Frigga would be moved away from Jane once the attack begins. Thor could stay near the Aether while Odin handles the larger defense and Loki uses his magic to confuse the Dark Elves moving through the palace. Frigga wouldn't be caught alone against Malekith and Kurse this time.
Malekith could still retreat if the attack fails because Thor wouldn’t have an easy way to stop every Dark Elf ship at once. But Frigga survives, Jane remains alive, and the Aether is still in play.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: Thor already knows Malekith’s end goal. During the Convergence, he wants to release the Aether at the point where the 9 Realms overlap and use it to return the universe to darkness. Thor could use that knowledge to make sure Asgard is waiting for him rather than discovering the plan halfway through the battle.

Loki would probably join Thor in going after him, but under very different circumstances from the original timeline. He isn’t escaping prison, Frigga hasn't died, and he doesn’t need revenge to convince him to help. Malekith is threatening Asgard and carrying one of the Infinity Stones, which is enough reason for both brothers to treat him as their problem.

Thor could still use the Convergence itself against Malekith because he remembers how unstable the boundaries between worlds become. Jane’s equipment and knowledge could help locate the overlapping portals, while Asgard could bring far more soldiers and preparation than Thor had during the original fight in Greenwich.

In the original timeline, Asgard decides it’s too dangerous to keep 2 Infinity Stones together because the Tesseract is already in Odin’s vault, so the Aether is delivered to the Collector. Thor now knows the Collector eventually loses it to Thanos. Sending the Reality Stone there again would make no sense.

The Tesseract creates a problem too. Thor knows Thanos needs both Stones eventually, and he also knows Asgard itself becomes a target once the larger Infinity Stone hunt begins. Keeping both in the same kingdom makes Asgard more valuable to him.

Thor could push Odin to separate them in a way that doesn’t repeat the original choice. The Tesseract could remain under Asgardian protection for now while the Reality Stone is hidden somewhere Thor knows Thanos didn’t reach easily in his original life. Whatever location they choose would have to be one Odin, Frigga, and Loki agree can actually be defended, because Thor wouldn't pretend he remembers a perfect hiding place that was never shown to him.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Once the Dark Elves are dealt with, Thor would start looking for Brunnhilde. He remembers finding her on Sakaar years later and learning she was the only Valkyrie who survived Odin’s attack on Hela, which makes her one of the few people alive who has already seen what Hela can do. Thor doesn’t know when she reached Sakaar, so he couldn’t just travel there and expect her to be waiting for him.

He could start with whatever records Odin still has from the Valkyries’ final mission. Thor would know roughly what happened, but Odin could tell him where they were sent, where survivors might have fled afterward, and whether anyone ever tried to track Brunnhilde once she disappeared. If that trail eventually leads toward Sakaar, Thor could go himself rather than sending Asgardian soldiers after someone who already has every reason to hate Odin. Brunnhilde would probably want nothing to do with him at first. Thor is Odin’s son, Asgard is the place she left behind, and the last time Odin sent her into a battle against Hela almost every Valkyrie died. Thor would have to explain that Hela is still alive and that he already knows she returns after Odin dies.

Brunnhilde could tell Thor what fighting Hela actually felt like before Ragnarok. She saw how quickly Hela created weapons, how difficult it was to close the distance, and how fast the Valkyries were overwhelmed once their formation broke. That gives Thor something more useful than another story from Odin because Brunnhilde remembers the fight from the side that lost it. He already remembers learning to use his lightning without depending on Mjolnir, so he could work on that earlier while Brunnhilde teaches him how Hela reacts when several attackers come at her from different directions. Loki’s illusions could be worked into the same training because Hela has to deal with threats she cannot simply overpower.

Brunnhilde still might refuse to return to Asgard right away. Thor could meet her elsewhere and let her decide when she is ready to go back, which would keep the relationship from turning into Thor dragging another person into a problem because he thinks he knows what is best.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Odin’s final years would look very different because Loki never replaces him and sends him to Earth. He could stay in Asgard with Frigga, Thor, and Loki while the family works through the things he kept hidden for centuries. They would spend years trying to determine whether whatever keeps Hela imprisoned can be reinforced, transferred, or maintained independently of Odin, but nothing they know gives them a reliable replacement for the power holding her back. Thor would use that time to make sure everyone understands what happens when Odin finally dies.

The Eternal Flame would be moved before Hela gets anywhere near Odin’s vault. Thor remembers Hela using it to resurrect Fenris and the dead soldiers buried beneath Asgard, so leaving it where she can reach it would throw away one of the easiest advantages they have. Surtur’s crown could be kept somewhere separate and guarded because Thor knows they may still need it later.

Thor would also have ships prepared before the day comes. Civilians could be moved away from the palace and the Bifrost in stages as Odin gets weaker, which avoids the panic Thor remembers from Hela taking control of the city while everyone is trapped inside it. Heimdall would know the plan and would keep the bridge closed unless Thor specifically tells him otherwise.

When Odin finally dies, Thor, Loki, and Brunnhilde would already be ready for Hela. Thor wouldn't try to hand her Mjolnir or walk straight into the same exchange that ended with the hammer being destroyed. He could open with lightning while Loki fills the area with illusions and Brunnhilde keeps moving around Hela instead of charging directly at her.

Hela would still be extremely hard to hurt. She was able to survive Thor’s strongest attacks in Ragnarok, and Thor already knows that being prepared does not suddenly make her weaker. The difference would show in how much damage she can do around them because she no longer has an undead army and Fenris joining the fight.

If Hela reaches Asgard, the evacuation would already be underway. The army could focus on slowing her instead of trying to protect thousands of civilians at the same time, and Thor could keep pulling the fight away from the ships while Loki helps move people through routes Hela is not watching.

They would try to finish her without destroying Asgard. Thor could hit her with repeated lightning attacks while Brunnhilde attacks whenever Hela turns toward him, and Loki could keep forcing Hela to waste strikes on illusions. The fight could last far longer than the one Thor remembers because they are working together from the start and Hela is fighting without the army she raised from the vault.
