As far as you know, neither side still has the complete GDA procedure needed to reproduce what happened to you, but there is no way to guarantee the Empire retained nothing from the time it spent studying you. It can still come after you, and you know better than to believe one escape means Thragg has forgotten what you represent.
The strength belongs to you now, and so does the choice of what you do with it.

scripts.title: What If YOU Found The Death Note

sections.name: INTRO
paras: You'd probably pick up the Death Note because it’s just sitting there with no explanation. The first rule says that anyone whose name you write will die, and at first you’d assume someone made it as a joke.

Eventually, curiosity would get the better of you. You choose someone whose death you can verify, write the name down, and wait without really expecting anything to happen. When the news confirms that person died exactly the way the notebook said they would, the Death Note stops being something you can dismiss.

Soon after that, Ryuk appears and explains where the notebook came from, what it can do, and that whatever happens next is up to you. From that point on, every name you write becomes something you’d need to live with.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: After Ryuk explains that the notebook is real, you wouldn’t suddenly know what to do with it. Knowing that you can kill someone and actually deciding to do it again are two different things, especially after the first death stops feeling like an experiment and becomes something you caused. You’d probably spend the next few days checking the rules over and over, partly because you want to understand them and partly because reading them feels easier than deciding whether you'll ever write another name.

Ryuk wouldn’t pressure you much because he doesn’t need to. He’s here because he’s bored, and watching you figure out what kind of person you become is more interesting than telling you what to do. That leaves you alone with the choice, which would probably make the notebook feel even heavier. You could lock it away somewhere, go back to normal life, and try to pretend none of this happened, but the knowledge that you can stop someone with a few strokes of a pen would stay in your head every time you see a crime on the news.

The second name would probably come from someone you already feel certain deserves punishment. Maybe it’s a murderer whose face and name are everywhere, someone with enough evidence against them that you don’t have to wonder whether you got the wrong person. You'd tell yourself this is different from the first test because now you know exactly what you're doing, and the person you choose has already hurt people.

Once it happens, you'd start thinking about the notebook in a more practical way. If you can stop one violent criminal, then you can stop another. You don’t have to wait for a trial, worry about someone escaping prison, or depend on a system that sometimes fails. The more cases you read about, the easier it becomes to find people who fit whatever line you’ve decided makes someone worth writing down.

You'd still be careful at the beginning. Writing ten names in one night would feel reckless, and you wouldn’t know whether some pattern could lead back to you. You'd spread the deaths out, choose people from different places, and avoid anyone you know personally because that connection would feel too obvious. Ryuk would probably notice that you're already thinking about getting caught before anyone has even started investigating, and that alone shows how quickly the notebook has changed the way you think.

The rules would become part of that caution. You know the victim dies of a heart attack if you only write the name, and you can specify details if they're physically possible. At first, heart attacks seem safer because they’re simple, but several criminals suddenly dying the same way would eventually look strange. You’d start wondering whether changing the cause of death makes you harder to detect or whether unusual deaths create even more attention.

You'd probably tell yourself you can stop whenever you want. You haven't killed anyone innocent, nobody knows the notebook exists, and Ryuk has already made it clear that he isn’t going to force you to keep writing. The problem is that every time another violent crime appears, stopping starts to feel like choosing to let that person live when you know you could end it. Before long, the Death Note would be hidden somewhere only you can reach, but it wouldn’t stay untouched for very long.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Once enough criminals die, somebody is going to notice. At first, the deaths could be explained individually because heart attacks happen and violent offenders can die for unrelated reasons, but the number eventually becomes difficult to ignore. News outlets would start connecting cases, online communities would build lists, and people would argue over whether there’s actually someone behind it or whether everyone is forcing a pattern onto unrelated deaths. You'd see those conversations before you see any official investigation, and that would probably be the first time the situation becomes exciting and frightening at the same time. People are talking about something you did without knowing you exist, and some of them would support it. Others would call whoever is responsible a murderer, which would be harder to dismiss because that’s exactly what you’ve become, even if you believe the people you chose deserved it.

The attention would affect how you use the notebook. If criminals keep dying at similar times every day, investigators could eventually learn something about your routine, so you'd stop writing names immediately after you find them. You might save several names and use them at different hours, making the deaths happen while you’re asleep, at work, or somewhere that doesn’t match when you actually wrote anything.

That sounds smart until you realize changing the pattern can also become a pattern. L would enter once the case becomes too unusual for ordinary explanations. He wouldn’t know about the Death Note, Ryuk, or anything supernatural, so his investigation would have to begin with what the deaths actually show. The victims are criminals, their identities are being made public, and the killer can apparently reach people without being anywhere near them. That immediately puts information at the center of the case because whoever is doing this needs to know exactly who they’re targeting.

You wouldn’t know much about L at first. The police might announce that an outside investigator is helping, or you could hear his name mentioned without seeing his face. The lack of information would bother you because you've spent the last several weeks knowing far more than everyone looking for you, and now somebody is deliberately keeping information away from you.

L's first useful move would be testing what information the killer needs. He could arrange for certain suspects or criminals to be shown differently across different broadcasts, watching to see which version produces a death. If one area receives a name and face that another area doesn't, then the next victim can tell him something about where the killer is getting information. You wouldn't know that’s what he’s doing until after you react.

Suppose you write down the name of a criminal shown only in one region. When that person dies, L can narrow the killer's information source to that broadcast region. He still has an enormous population to work through, but for the first time he knows where to concentrate the investigation because of one ordinary choice you made while sitting at home.

Once you realize what happened, the investigation starts feeling very different. You’d replay the news coverage, compare what was shown where, and try to understand which death gave him something useful. Ryuk might find the whole thing entertaining, but you’d be thinking about how many other decisions have already told L more than you intended. The regional result still would not identify you, so L would need a narrower bridge. Later, he could keep another criminal’s identity out of broad public coverage while releasing different otherwise-unpublished identities through several legitimate-looking local information feeds with finite subscriber or access logs. He would not need to know which one you personally use. If one of those criminals dies, the channel carrying that identity identifies the relevant access cohort. L can then compare the people who actually received or opened that feed against the timing and behavior he already knows, eventually putting your account or routine among a finite group worth investigating.

Every name becomes something you have to question before writing. Where did you get it? Who else had access to it? Was the information released everywhere or only in one place? Is L putting it in front of you because he wants you to react?

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Once L knows the killer reacts to information, he’d start building tests around that behavior instead of waiting for more deaths. He doesn’t need to understand how you kill people yet because narrowing down who receives the right information is already enough to make progress.

You'd start seeing criminals appear in unusual ways. Some reports might delay names, others could show faces without giving full identities, and certain cases might disappear from national coverage while remaining available locally. At first, those changes could look like normal media decisions, but once you’re watching for them, you’d realize someone is deliberately controlling what reaches the public.

That would force you to change how you choose targets. You could stop relying on live television and start using older cases where the names and faces have been public for months. You might also spread your attention across different countries so the deaths don’t look tied to one source. The problem is that every attempt to hide your habits also changes the type of criminal dying, which gives L new information about how you respond when pressure increases. If recent criminals suddenly stop dying right after the media changes how names are released, L can reasonably assume the killer noticed the test. That tells him the person is following the investigation closely and is intelligent enough to adapt, which makes him more cautious about what he reveals next.

That would probably make you more disciplined. You'd start waiting longer before reacting to anything related to the investigation, even when you think you understand the trap. If L announces something designed to provoke you, you'd let several days pass before changing anything. You might even keep your normal pattern temporarily when every instinct is telling you to stop, just so L can’t be sure you noticed.

The notebook would become part of a routine that has almost nothing to do with justice anymore. Names would be collected, checked, stored, and scheduled based on what creates the least information for the person hunting you. You’d still tell yourself the victims deserve what happens, but the amount of thought going into avoiding L would start taking up more time than deciding who should die.

Ryuk would probably enjoy that change because you’re becoming more interesting to watch. You'd be spending hours studying news reports, police statements, and anything connected to L, while he already knows you're only doing all of this because you chose to keep using the notebook after the first test.

L would eventually take a bigger risk to see whether he can make you react emotionally. He could have someone publicly challenge the killer, calling the murders childish or claiming that whoever is responsible is too afraid to face anyone directly. You wouldn’t know whether the person speaking is L, a decoy, or simply someone working with him.

That uncertainty would matter more than the insult. Killing the person would be incredibly tempting if they appear to be directing the investigation, but doing it immediately would prove that you're watching and that criticism can provoke you. Leaving them alive protects you,
although it also means sitting there while someone publicly attacks everything you’ve been telling yourself about why you use the Death Note.

You'd probably leave them alone. That would be the smarter move, but L would still learn from it because restraint after earlier deaths suggests the killer is thinking about the investigation much more carefully now.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: The more attention the case gets, the harder it becomes to act normal. You still have work, school, family, friends, or whatever your normal routine looked like before the notebook, and none of those people know that you’re spending part of every day deciding who lives and dies. That separation would create mistakes long before the Death Note itself does. You might stay up too late following reports, become distracted during conversations, or react too strongly when someone brings up the killings. None of those things proves anything on its own, but L doesn’t need one perfect piece of evidence if he can build enough smaller observations around the same person.

You'd start controlling your behavior more carefully. Searches about criminals or L would be done away from personal accounts, notes wouldn't stay on devices that can be checked, and the Death Note would need a hiding place that doesn’t look suspicious if someone enters your room. You could even remove several pages and keep them separately, giving yourself a way to use the notebook without carrying the whole thing.

You’d have to decide how much access is worth having. Keeping a piece of the notebook on you means you're never completely separated from it, but getting searched or losing your belongings could expose something you can’t explain. Leaving everything hidden at home feels safer until you start wondering whether someone is watching the house.

L would eventually consider surveillance once the suspect pool becomes small enough. You probably wouldn’t know exactly when that happens, so normal details in your environment would start feeling suspicious. A car parked too long outside could be nothing, a person sitting in the same café twice could be coincidence, and a camera you think you notice might not exist at all.

The danger is letting that suspicion change your behavior. You might close curtains you normally leave open, stop going places you usually visit, or check the notebook every few hours. If you suddenly become far more private the moment L narrows his search, that change itself could matter.

Ryuk would make all of this harder simply by being there. Nobody else can see him unless they touch the notebook, but you can, which means every conversation with him has to happen when you're sure nobody is watching. Even reacting to something he says at the wrong time could make you look strange.

That leaves you spending more time alone with your own decisions, and the notebook would begin feeling less like power and more like something you have to protect every hour of the day. The worst part is that throwing it away no longer feels simple. Even if you stop using it, L is still investigating the deaths that already happened, and getting rid of the notebook doesn’t erase the choices that brought him toward you.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: L’s next step would be narrowing the investigation around people whose access and behavior fit what he has learned. By this point, he strongly suspects the killer needs identifying information - likely both a name and a face - because deaths consistently follow cases where both are publicly available, while withholding identifying details disrupts the pattern. He also knows the killer follows the investigation closely, changes behavior when tests become obvious, and has enough control over the timing of deaths to make simple routine analysis unreliable.

You wouldn’t know exactly how close that puts him, but you’d start seeing signs that the investigation has moved away from broad theories. Police activity around certain people could increase, interviews might become more specific, and some information would stop being released publicly altogether.

That would reduce the number of easy targets you can use. You could keep writing names from older public cases, but doing that forever creates another pattern because the deaths would suddenly shift toward people whose information was already available before L tightened access. You’d have to mix old cases with new ones carefully enough that the change doesn’t look like a response.

That would make the investigation feel real in a way news reports never did. Until then, L exists mostly as a person on the other side of a screen. Once friends, coworkers, classmates, or family members are being asked about routines and behavior, the case is close enough to touch people who have no idea what you've done.
You'd immediately want to know what they were asked. That curiosity would have to be controlled because pushing too hard for details could make you look nervous. You'd listen when
people bring it up naturally, ask only what anyone else would ask, and try to keep your reaction somewhere between concern and disbelief.

If the questions focus on your schedule, then he may have narrowed the timing of the deaths. If they're asking about access to certain broadcasts or police information, then one of his earlier tests probably worked better than you realized. Every question becomes another clue about the investigation, and you’d start using the people around you to understand how close L is without letting them know why you care.

You still have one way to make people disappear, and anyone helping L investigate you could become a possible target. The notebook gives you the power to remove a detective, witness, or investigator if you can learn their name and face, which means the line you set at the beginning is going to get tested sooner or later.

Killing criminals felt easy to justify because you could tell yourself you were preventing future victims. Killing someone because they might expose you would be different, and you’d know it before you ever pick up the pen.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Once L gets close enough that people around you are being questioned, the Death Note stops feeling separate from your normal life. You'd still be choosing criminals most of the time, but now every person involved in the investigation carries a different kind of threat because they could be the one who notices something you missed. That doesn’t mean you’d immediately start killing investigators, especially if you’ve spent this long telling yourself there are limits you won’t cross, but the fact that the option exists would be impossible to ignore.

You'd start thinking more about what happens if your identity is exposed. Getting arrested would mean losing control of the notebook, losing any chance to decide what happens to it, and possibly letting someone else discover what it can do. That gives you a reason to justify more extreme choices without having to admit that fear is driving them. If an investigator gets too close, you could tell yourself removing them protects the notebook from falling into worse hands, even though the real benefit is protecting yourself.

L would keep pushing until that excuse is tested. Instead of repeating the same compartmentalized-name trick you already know to expect, he could build a correlation test around information that is already public. A small group of suspects would naturally encounter different public criminal cases at different times - through ordinary browsing, broadcasts, work or school routines - while surveillance records when each person could realistically have learned each name and face.

He would then compare those exposure windows against later deaths and the schedules you seem to favor. No single match would prove anything, but repeated correlations between the targets you could have encountered and the deaths that follow would give L a genuinely new kind of evidence. Because the names themselves are not secret bait, you cannot defeat the test simply by recognizing that one uniquely assigned criminal was placed in front of you.

Your best response would be making your behavior look boring. You’d keep the same routine, use the same devices, and avoid suddenly changing anything just because surveillance feels more likely. The Death Note would stay hidden for longer periods, and when you do use it, you’d rely on names collected earlier instead of reacting to whatever appears that day. Ryuk would probably find this stage less exciting than the beginning because you’re spending more time waiting than killing, but that waiting is what keeps L from getting a clean pattern.

The pressure would still keep building because you can’t maintain perfect control forever. One mistake in timing, one search made from the wrong place, or one person noticing that you always seem interested in details about the case could put L close enough to start focusing directly on you.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: L wouldn't need absolute proof before treating you like a serious suspect. Once enough information points in the same direction, he’d start watching you more closely and looking for a mistake that only the real killer would make. You might notice people following you, cameras appearing in places that never had them before, or questions that seem casual until you realize they're all built around your schedule and access to information.

You'd know that reacting too strongly only helps him. That means your safest move is continuing life as normally as possible while using the notebook less often. The deaths could slow down, which protects you in one way but creates another problem because L may connect the change to the start of direct surveillance. If Kira’s activity drops right when you become a suspect, that timing could be useful on its own.

You might try to solve that by setting deaths in advance. The notebook allows you to specify a time of death within its rules, so you could prepare names before surveillance becomes intense and let those deaths happen while you’re being watched. That would not clear you, especially because L already suspects the killer can manipulate timing. It would only prevent surveillance from proving that each death requires you to perform some visible action at the moment the victim dies.

At some point, L could arrange a situation where you believe one of the investigators knows your identity. Maybe someone openly approaches you with a question only the killer should understand or makes it clear that the task force is about to search somewhere connected to you. The goal would be seeing whether that person dies soon afterward.

You’d understand what he’s trying to do, which leaves you with a brutal choice. Killing the investigator could protect you if the threat is real, but it also gives L exactly the reaction he expects. Leaving them alive might mean they find the notebook.

The safest response would depend on whether you can identify a genuine gap in surveillance. If you can move the notebook without L detecting the change, you could use that opening to hide it somewhere unrelated to your daily life and keep a removable page separately if you still need access. If you cannot confirm that kind of gap, touching the notebook now may be more dangerous than leaving it where it is, because investigators could follow the movement straight to the evidence.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: Once L is close enough that you can’t assume the investigation will go away, you'd have to prepare for what happens if someone actually finds the notebook. Hiding it in one place wouldn't feel safe anymore, so you'd start separating your access from the main notebook, keeping a small page somewhere else and moving the rest somewhere that has no obvious connection to you. The goal would be making sure one search doesn’t expose everything at once, although every extra hiding place also creates another thing you have to remember, protect, and explain if somebody notices it.

You'd also start thinking about what L would do if he ever learned that the murders require a name and face. By now, he’d already be close to that conclusion through his tests, so protecting your own identity would become more important than finding new targets. You’d avoid situations where your name is unnecessarily connected to the case, keep your face out of anything involving the investigation, and become much more careful around anyone who seems interested in your routine. None of that would look unusual on its own, but maintaining it every day while trying to seem normal would get harder the longer surveillance continues.

Ryuk would probably point out that you could make the problem much easier by using the notebook against L if you ever learn his real name. You’d know that’s true, but finding it would be almost impossible from the outside because L protects his identity far better than the people he investigates. Trying too hard to discover it could also expose how interested you are in one specific detective, so the safer move would be learning as much as possible without making L the center of every decision.

That restraint would matter because L would expect you to become more aggressive as he gets closer. If nobody around the task force suddenly dies and the investigation keeps moving, he has fewer ways to prove that you're willing to kill anyone who threatens you. You'd still be under pressure, but keeping that line intact would stop the case from becoming a simple cycle where every person who gets near the truth ends up dead.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: The final stage of the story would come when L gets close enough that you know one more mistake could end everything. Maybe he arranges another search, narrows the suspect pool to almost nobody, or brings you into direct questioning because he wants to see how you react when the case is placed in front of you. You'd have to sit there knowing that the person across from you may already believe you’re responsible, while giving him nothing he can use to turn suspicion into proof.

That would be where all the choices from earlier start catching up with you. If you kept the notebook hidden carefully, avoided killing investigators, and stopped reacting to obvious traps, L might still struggle to prove anything. He could believe you're Kira and still be unable to explain how the murders happen, especially when deaths continue on schedules you prepared in advance. Suspicion would stay on you, but suspicion alone wouldn't be enough to end the case. The harder choice would come after you leave that room and realize you still have the notebook. You could keep using it and accept that the investigation never really ends, or you could stop writing names and let the pattern disappear over time. Stopping would deny L future murders to test, but if Kira activity suddenly disappears at the exact moment pressure on you peaks, that timing could initially strengthen his suspicion. If you never use the notebook again, though, the correlation becomes increasingly difficult to turn into proof of how the earlier murders actually happened.

Ryuk wouldn’t care which choice you make as long as it stays interesting. He never promised to protect you, and he’d remind you that this was always your decision from the moment you picked the notebook up. That would make the ending much less about beating L and much more about whether you can walk away from the power before protecting it becomes the only thing your life is about.

If you keep using it, the paranoia probably gets worse. Every stranger could be surveillance, every news report could be another test, and every name you write would need to be checked against what L might learn from it. You could survive for a long time if you stay disciplined, but your entire life would start revolving around avoiding one mistake.

If you stop, the notebook would still sit somewhere only you know about, and that might be even harder. You’d know you can use it whenever something terrible happens, and every time you choose not to, you'd have to live with the fact that you could have acted.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: If you found the Death Note, the hardest part probably wouldn’t be learning how it works. The rules are clear enough, and the power is simple once you've seen it happen. The real problem would be how quickly every choice creates another reason to keep using it.

You could still avoid becoming exactly like Light if you keep refusing to kill innocent people just to protect yourself, but that would make surviving L’s investigation much harder. Every limit you keep gives him another way to pressure you, while every limit you break makes it easier to justify the next one.

The Death Note would give you more power than almost anyone could realistically handle, and the longer you keep it, the more your life would revolve around protecting the secret instead of whatever reason made you write the second name in the first place.

scripts.title: What If YOU Had The Infinity Gauntlet

sections.name: INTRO
paras: If you got the infinity gauntlet, the first few seconds would probably decide whether you ever got to use it at all.

You're still a normal person when all 6 Stones lock into place. The energy hits your body immediately, burning through your arm while every Stone starts responding to you at once. Hulk barely survived using them, and Tony died from the same power, so even keeping the Gauntlet on would be dangerous.

You'd start small because you’d have no idea how much your body can handle. Move an object across the room with the Space Stone. Turn a broken glass back a few seconds with Time. Change its shape with Reality and watch it happen right in front of you.

After a few tries, you’d probably start wondering what else you could get away with. Maybe you fix something you broke. Maybe you change something about your life that’s bothered you for years. And once that works, you've got 6 Infinity Stones sitting on your hand and a much bigger question in front of you.
How much are you willing to change?

sections.name: PART 1
paras: You get the Gauntlet because somebody else was already trying to move it through your world. A group of alien scavengers has been using stolen multiversal tech to pull Infinity Stones out of alternate timelines, then carrying them inside a purpose-built copy of the same kind of Gauntlet Thanos once used, designed to channel the combined energy of all 6 Stones instead of dumping all of it directly into the wearer. It still isn't safe for a human body, but that containment is the only reason putting it on doesn't kill you immediately. Their ship makes it to Earth before the device keeping those timelines connected starts failing over New York, and the whole thing comes down hard enough to tear through several buildings before crashing near the river.

You're close enough to see part of the wreckage slide into an empty service area, and while most people are running away, you go over because it looks like somebody might still be trapped inside. That's where you find one of the aliens pinned under a section of the hull with a gold metal glove locked around its arm, and all 6 Stones are already sitting inside it. You've seen enough footage from the Battle of Earth to know exactly what you're looking at, which also means you know touching it is probably a terrible idea.

The ship is still coming apart around you, though, and another section of the hull starts dropping toward the service area. You pull the Gauntlet free, shove your hand inside, and feel the metal close around your arm before you've even worked out what you're trying to do. The energy hits immediately, running from your fingers into your shoulder so hard that your knees buckle and your whole arm locks in place.
Your skin starts burning around the edges of the Gauntlet while the Stones seem to hit you in different ways at the same time. Space suddenly feels less fixed, the last few seconds feel close

enough to reach with Time, and the Mind Stone floods your head with more information than you can properly separate. The Power Stone is the worst part because it feels like raw energy is being forced through a body that was never meant to carry it.

The falling wreckage finally gives you something simple to focus on. You think about getting somewhere safe, raise the Gauntlet almost by instinct, and the Space Stone responds before you understand how you activated it. The service area disappears around you, and you hit the floor of an empty apartment several blocks away with enough force to knock the air out of yourself.

Once you get the Gauntlet off, the damage is obvious. The skin from your hand to your elbow is badly burned, your fingers are shaking, and the muscles in your arm keep tightening whenever you get too close to the Stones again. You sit there for a while staring at the thing because you just moved yourself across New York with one thought, and the only reason you're still alive seems to be that you stopped using it quickly enough.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: You leave the Gauntlet on the floor for the next hour while the news starts filling with footage from the crash. Nobody seems to know what the ship was carrying yet, which gives you a little time, and that’s enough for curiosity to start beating out common sense. Your arm still hurts, so you decide you're only going to test one thing at a time and take the Gauntlet off the second the pain gets worse.

You don't actually know how to isolate one Stone from the other 5, so the first few attempts are mostly trial and error. You focus on the sensation you associated with Space during the crash and try to hold onto that without reaching for anything else. Once the Gauntlet responds, you focus on a glass sitting across the room and picture it moving into your hand. The glass disappears from the table and shows up between your fingers so cleanly that you almost drop it, then you take the Gauntlet off and check your arm again. The fresh damage is there, but it's much smaller than what happened when all 6 Stones reacted together.

That gives you enough confidence to repeat the same process with the Time Stone next, feeling around for the part of the Gauntlet that makes the last few seconds seem close enough to reach. You knock the same glass onto the floor and let it shatter, then focus on what it looked like a few seconds earlier. The pieces slide backward across the room, jump up from the floor, and reconnect until the glass is sitting where it started. Watching it happen is the first time the Gauntlet stops feeling like a weapon and starts feeling like a way to undo mistakes.

The Reality Stone is stranger because there isn’t an obvious direction or distance involved. You look at an old chair, picture it as something completely different, and watch the wood and fabric change under your hand. The chair stays changed after you stop concentrating, but later attempts aren't that consistent. Some alterations hold while others begin reverting once your focus breaks. That tells you the Stone can genuinely rewrite matter, but not that every change you make will automatically stay permanent.

You try the Mind Stone more carefully because the sensation is immediately more invasive. For a few seconds, you become aware of people in nearby apartments without seeing them, and you can feel attention, fear, boredom, and other thoughts sitting just beneath the surface. You pull away before pushing any deeper because the idea of being able to reach into another person's mind feels different from moving a chair or fixing a glass.

The Power Stone gets the shortest test. Even focusing on it makes the Gauntlet heat up around your hand and sends a stronger pulse through your arm, so you leave it alone before finding out what happens if you accidentally release that energy inside an apartment building. The Soul Stone is even harder to understand because it gives you a sense of living people nearby without offering a simple action you can test safely.

By the end of the night, you know enough to stop pretending this is just some alien weapon you found. You can move matter through space, reverse small events, rewrite physical objects, touch minds, and feel living souls around you. Your arm still can’t handle much of it, but the thing sitting beside you can already do more than anything you've ever seen in your life.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: You start using the Gauntlet on your own life because that feels easier than trying to fix the world. Money is the first thing you test, and you keep it small enough that you don’t suddenly create a billion dollars and attract attention. You change a little ordinary material into something valuable, sell enough of it through normal channels, and end up with enough money that rent and bills stop being a problem almost immediately.

That works so easily that you start thinking about older problems. There’s something you lost years ago that still bothers you, so you use the Time Stone to trace it backward and pull it into the present. When that works too, old photos start feeling different because the people inside them no longer seem permanently out of reach.

You eventually choose one person you lost and decide to see whether bringing them back is even possible. You don't know whether the Stones can actually do this, but you attempt to use the Time Stone to isolate that person's own timeline and reach the living state they had immediately before death while the Soul Stone searches for and anchors the identity that belonged to them. To your surprise, the Stones respond by pulling that earlier living state forward into the present instead of rewinding everything around you. The Gauntlet begins burning through your arm almost immediately. The pain spreads past your shoulder, your vision starts going dark, and several Stones are reacting together in a way you haven't felt since the crash.

When the energy finally drops, the person is standing in front of you and remembers dying. That part catches you completely off guard because you were focused on getting them back, not on what coming back would feel like for them. Years have passed for everyone else, relationships continued, families changed, and people built lives around a loss that suddenly isn’t permanent anymore.

You still can’t convince yourself that bringing them back was the wrong choice, especially when you see the people who get to have them again. At the same time, you can see that the Gauntlet didn’t restore the old world around them. It put one person back into a life that kept moving without them, which means even a change that feels obviously good can arrive with problems you never thought to ask about.

You start carrying the Gauntlet more often after that because leaving it somewhere starts to feel irresponsible. Small emergencies become hard to ignore when you know you can fix them in seconds. You rewind a car accident before anybody gets badly hurt, use Reality to remove a
tumor from someone's body, and move food or medical supplies to places that need them without waiting for normal transportation.

The physical damage keeps building, so you eventually try using the Stones on yourself. You rewind some of the burns in your arm with Time, then use Reality to restore damaged tissue while the Gauntlet is still attached. It works well enough that the pain fades and most of the visible damage disappears, but the repair itself still means channeling the Stones through your body and creating more strain. You can extend how long you use the Gauntlet, not cancel its physical cost completely.

That changes how often you reach for the Gauntlet because the biggest consequence you could actually feel every time is becoming manageable. You still know your body can’t naturally survive prolonged use, and even this Gauntlet only contains part of what the Stones are doing to you, but repairing the damage makes repeated short bursts possible in a way sustained use still isn't.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Doctor Strange finds you after you use the Stones on something too large to stay private. A commuter train derails outside the city while you're nearby, and you react before thinking about who might notice. You move several cars away from the wreck with Space, rewind part of the track with Time, and keep the rest of the train from following them off the rails.

Strange shows up later that night and looks at the Gauntlet before he even looks at you. He asks how long you've had it, where the Stones came from, and what you've already changed. You tell him about the crash first, then the smaller experiments, and eventually the person you brought back.

That's the part he spends the most time on. He asks what happened to everyone whose life changed after that person died, whether marriages formed, property changed hands, children were born, or decisions were made because of that loss. You don’t have answers because you only checked whether the person you brought back was alive and okay.

Strange doesn’t tell you that saving them was wrong. He wants you to understand that the Stones react to what you ask for, and you’ve been making changes without always knowing how far the effects spread afterward. Time worries him most because a small local reversal is one thing, while reaching farther back or rewriting a larger event could disturb causality in ways neither of you can predict. You tell him about repairing your arm too, and that makes him even more concerned because the physical damage was one of the few things naturally limiting how often you could use the Gauntlet.

He asks you to hand it over so the Stones can be separated and secured. You refuse because you've already seen what you can do with them, and giving them to somebody else still means trusting one person or one group with the same power. Strange tells you that thinking your judgment is safer than everyone else’s is exactly how this becomes dangerous, but he doesn’t try to take the Gauntlet by force while you're wearing all 6 Stones.

The conversation ends without either of you changing your mind. Strange leaves to warn the others, and you stay behind with the Gauntlet because you still believe what you've done so far has helped more people than it hurt.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: You start thinking bigger once you’ve seen how much you can change without waiting for anyone else. Hunger feels like an obvious place to start because food already exists in huge amounts, and people are still starving because it isn’t getting where it needs to go. You use Space to move excess supplies into distribution centers in areas facing shortages, then use Reality to keep the food from spoiling while it’s transported and handed out.

For the first few days, the result looks exactly like what you hoped for. Shelves fill up, aid groups suddenly have enough supplies, and people who were rationing meals are eating normally again. Then the systems around that food start reacting in ways you didn’t plan for.

Farmers in some of the same regions can’t sell what they grow because huge amounts of free food have appeared overnight. Transport companies start cutting routes because nobody knows whether your deliveries are temporary or whether you’re about to replace part of the supply chain permanently. Governments start arguing over where the food came from, who controls it, and whether depending on an unknown person with the Infinity Stones is safe.

You can see ways to solve every one of those problems too. You could pay the farmers, rebuild the transport system, guarantee prices, or create food whenever a shortage appears. Once you start thinking that way, the Gauntlet begins turning into a way to redesign entire systems instead of helping people through one crisis at a time.

Thor comes to see you while that’s happening, and he’s much less interested in debating every individual use. He’s watched the Stones wipe out half the universe and seen what happened when everyone tried to reverse it. He knows you haven't done anything close to that, but he also knows how quickly one huge decision can affect people who never got a say in it.

You show him the reports from the places where people are eating because of what you did, and he doesn’t argue with the lives that were helped. He asks what you plan to do when a government, community, or individual tells you they don’t want you changing things for them. That question bothers you more than Strange’s did because you still see yourself as someone fixing problems people were already desperate to solve.

You tell Thor you haven't forced anyone to do anything, and he points out that moving resources across borders and reshaping markets already affects people who never agreed to your plan. He asks you to come with him and leave the Gauntlet somewhere it can’t keep changing the world every time you see another problem.

You refuse because you're looking at millions of people who've already benefited from what you did, and walking away now feels harder than it did when all you had was a burned arm and a strange weapon on your floor. Later that night, another war fills the news with footage of civilians running from destroyed buildings, and you're sitting there with 6 Stones that could change the situation before morning.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: You decide to interfere with the war, but you keep the first move narrow enough that you can see exactly what you're changing. You use the Space Stone to open evacuation routes out of the worst areas, move civilians away from active fighting, and get trapped people somewhere safer. Once the immediate danger drops, you use Reality to disable weapons and Time to undo damage in places where buildings have only just collapsed.

For a few hours, it works better than anything you expected. Fighting slows because tanks stop working, ammunition disappears from storage sites, and people who were trapped suddenly have a way out. Then both sides start changing how they operate because they know you're watching. Military leaders move equipment away from places you’re likely to notice, some groups start hiding weapons near civilians, and governments begin accusing each other of secretly working with you.

You respond by making your position public. You tell everyone involved that attacks on civilian areas are going to be stopped, and the Gauntlet on your arm makes it obvious you can actually enforce that. The announcement gets people out of danger, but it also tells every government on Earth who has the Stones and what you’re willing to do with them.

Support builds almost as fast as the fear. Some people see you as the first person powerful enough to stop violence governments have failed to control for years. Others see one ordinary human making decisions that used to belong to entire countries. Militaries start planning around you, markets react to the instability, and political leaders begin asking the Avengers whether you can be stopped if you decide to go further.

The Avengers come to you together after that, and nobody rushes you because they know exactly what could happen if you panic while wearing all 6 Stones. You explain how many people are alive because of what you did and point out that you haven't used the Gauntlet to kill anyone or seize control of a country. From your perspective, you’ve spent the last few days preventing deaths while everyone else keeps warning you about what you might become. Strange asks what happens when the next situation is worse and the people involved refuse to cooperate. You don’t have a good answer because you've already learned how quickly one emergency can turn into several new problems. You agree to stop making large changes for a few days and think about where the line should be, but the agreement starts feeling harder to keep the moment another disaster happens and you know you could fix it before anyone else gets there.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Trying to do less becomes difficult once you’ve learned how much the Stones can show you. The Mind Stone lets you sense fear, panic, anger, and pain across groups you're deliberately focusing on once you're close enough to connect with them, but it doesn't simply tell you where everyone on Earth is suffering. News feeds, emergency reports, and the Space Stone still have to point you toward distant crises. Once you look in on one, though, the people inside it stop feeling distant at all.

You start responding to disasters without changing anything around them permanently. Space gets people out of flooded areas before the water reaches them. Reality helps stop a wildfire from spreading toward a town. Time restores the newly damaged section of a dam to the condition it was in moments before the failure started, keeping the reversal as local and recent as you can before engineers take over. Those interventions seem much cleaner because you're solving a direct emergency and leaving afterward. The harder part comes from choosing which emergency gets your attention first. The Stones make it possible to help almost anywhere, while the constant stream of reports keeps reminding you that people are suffering in places you aren't currently looking at.

That's what makes you start using the Mind Stone differently once you arrive. Instead of only watching a crisis from the outside, you focus on the people directly in front of you and try to understand what they're experiencing. The first time you reach into a crowd, the amount of emotion coming back at you is overwhelming. Fear, grief, anger, relief, and thousands of smaller thoughts blend together until you can barely separate one person from another.

You keep practicing anyway because the information feels useful. If you can understand what people are scared of before a situation gets violent, you can respond earlier. Over time, you also start noticing how easy it would be to push past observation and change what people are feeling instead.

The thought comes up during a riot where both sides are already panicking and nobody is listening to anyone else. You can feel how close the crowd is to breaking into violence, and the Mind Stone makes every angry thought seem almost close enough to reach. You leave without touching anyone’s mind, but afterward you keep thinking about how quickly the whole situation could’ve ended if everyone had calmed down at once.

Strange checks on you again and asks what you've been doing with the Mind Stone. You tell him you've mostly been listening to people and trying to understand what's happening before stepping in. When he asks whether you've changed anybody while connected to them, the question annoys you because the answer is still no and you already know exactly what the Stone could do if you decided otherwise.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: The first time you actually use the Mind Stone on a crowd happens during another violent crisis. Civilians are trapped between armed groups, shots are already being fired, and there isn’t enough time to move everyone before somebody else gets hit. You reach into the people holding the weapons and force the panic down long enough for them to stop shooting and lower what they’re carrying.

The effect only lasts for a short time, but it gives the civilians enough space to get out. Nobody dies while you're connected to them, and when you release the Mind Stone, the people you influenced can think normally again. From where you're standing, the choice feels hard to argue with because you used less than a minute of control to keep a much larger number of people alive.

Thor comes to see you after he hears what happened. He doesn’t focus on the number of lives saved because he already accepts that the intervention worked. He wants to know what you would've done if the fighting started again the second you let go.

You tell him you would’ve stopped it again if people were still in danger. Thor asks how long that keeps going once controlling the crowd becomes easier than waiting for people to make a different choice on their own. You get defensive because you aren’t trying to rule anyone, and the people you affected were already about to kill each other.

The conversation stays with you because the Mind Stone makes the easier version obvious. Keeping everyone calm for an hour would’ve worked better than doing it for a minute. Keeping them calm for a day would’ve made the whole area safer. You can follow that thought as far as you want, and there's no technical limit forcing you to stop at the point you did.

The Avengers start preparing more seriously after that. Strange works on ways to separate you from the Gauntlet if they ever have to, Thor keeps more distance when you're wearing it, and the others stop assuming every disagreement can stay a conversation forever. You can sense some of that planning with the Mind Stone, which makes you start wearing the Gauntlet more often even when you aren't actively using it.

Your control gets better while you're doing this. Time and Reality repair the damage in your arm quickly enough that the Gauntlet can stay on much longer, Space lets you leave almost any situation before it turns physical, and the Mind Stone lets you notice the moment someone nearby starts thinking about taking the Gauntlet away. By then, you're spending more time with all 6 Stones on your hand than off it.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: The next escalation comes from disease because it’s one of the few problems that still feels completely unnecessary to you. You've already used Reality on individual injuries and tumors, so you start wondering why you're waiting for people to suffer one at a time when the same Stone can change living tissue directly.

You spend days testing the limits on smaller groups before trying anything larger, including whether biological changes remain stable after you stop focusing on them. The smaller tests eventually give you a repeatable way to make a specific biological correction persist without continued concentration, and only then do you try scaling that same stabilized change up. You use Reality to remove specific diseases across millions of people while Time helps you reverse some of the damage those illnesses already caused. Hospitals start reporting recoveries that shouldn't be possible, and families that were preparing for years of treatment suddenly get people back who feel healthy again.

The reaction is immediate because entire systems were built around those illnesses. Hospitals start changing treatment plans overnight, drug manufacturers lose demand for products they expected to sell for years, and researchers who spent their careers working on one disease have to figure out what their work means now. None of that compares to the people who are alive because of what you did, but the size of the change is impossible to ignore.

You start thinking about the next step before those systems have even caught up. If the Gauntlet can remove disease, it can also repair failing organs, reverse genetic conditions, and prevent some illnesses from ever developing. You could keep doing this until huge parts of medicine work completely differently, and every new improvement would affect millions of lives you've never met.

Strange returns before you make the next change, this time with Thor and the Avengers behind him. They aren’t showing up because the disease cures failed. They're there because your decisions have moved from helping people in emergencies to changing what life on Earth looks like for everyone at once.

They ask you to take the Gauntlet off and give them time to understand what's already changed. You tell them people are alive right now because you acted, and waiting would've meant letting more of them die while everyone debated the consequences. From your point of view, stopping now feels harder to justify than continuing.

The argument keeps circling back to the same place until you realize how differently you're hearing them. Earlier, Strange sounded cautious. Thor sounded scared of repeating what Thanos did. Now both of them sound like people standing between you and problems you know how to solve, and that thought sits in your head long enough for you to notice it.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: The confrontation stays quiet because everyone knows how dangerous the first physical move would be. Strange asks you to think about how you were using the Gauntlet when you first found it compared with how you're using it now, and Thor tells you he understands why the changes keep getting bigger. He’s seen enough suffering to know how tempting it would be to keep fixing one more thing when you actually have the power to do it.

While they're talking, you can feel how easily the Gauntlet could end the disagreement. Space could move everyone away from you. Reality could strip away their powers. Mind could make them agree. Time could rewind the conversation until you find a version where nobody challenges you in the first place.

You don’t use any of those options, but the fact that they all feel available changes the way you see the moment. Nobody in front of you is attacking. Nobody is trying to hurt civilians. They're disagreeing with you, and you've reached a point where the tools on your hand can erase that disagreement just as easily as they can stop a war or cure a disease.

You look at the people around you through the Mind Stone and feel fear coming from several of them. Some of it is fear of what you could do to them, and some of it is fear of what happens to you if the Gauntlet stays on much longer. That makes the decision feel different from every other time somebody asked you to hand it over.

You take the Gauntlet off yourself and immediately lose the help you were getting from Time and Reality. The tissue you actually repaired stays healed, but the exhaustion, pain, and residual damage you never fully repaired hit you all at once, and Strange catches you before you hit
the floor while the others start separating the Stones. You stay conscious long enough to see them removed one by one, which means the choice stays yours all the way to the end.

They don’t try to undo every change you made because there isn’t a clean way to do that without hurting people who are alive because of those decisions. The cures stay. The people you rescued stay. The person you brought back stays too, even though their return changed lives around them in ways nobody can fully untangle.

The Stones are split up again so no single person can reach all 6 easily. You recover without using cosmic power to speed it up, and for the first time since you found the Gauntlet, you have to accept that some problems are going to stay unsolved for a while.

You did save people with it, and plenty of the changes you made were genuinely good. You also got close enough to unlimited control that disagreement itself started looking like another problem you could solve. Giving the Gauntlet up before acting on that thought is the reason the Avengers never have to find out how far you would’ve gone.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: So if you had the Infinity Gauntlet, the hardest part would be knowing when to stop using them. You could save people, reverse disasters, cure diseases, and change lives in ways nobody else could. The danger starts when every new problem feels like one more thing you’re personally supposed to fix.

If you can eventually take the Gauntlet off while you still have the choice, you probably leave the universe better than you found it. If you can’t, sooner or later everyone else has to start asking how they’re supposed to stop you.

scripts.title: What If YOU Were In Brand New Day

sections.name: INTRO
paras: You wake up in New York expecting another normal day.

By that evening, Damage Control is locking down part of the city, a telekinetic mutant is tearing through one of their facilities looking for something called Vmax, and you’re standing close enough to Spider-Man that he has to pull you out of the way.

You don’t know who Jean Grey is. You don’t know why she’s attacking DODC. It seems like she’s dangerous, Spider-Man is trying to stop her, and Damage Control is supposed to be the side keeping everyone safe.
So when Spider-Man tells you to get out of there, you listen.
At least for a few minutes.

Because once you’re away from the fight, something about it keeps bothering you. Jean wasn’t trying to destroy the building for the sake of it. She was looking for something specific, and whatever Vmax is, she’s desperate enough to keep going after it even with Spider-Man in her way.
You got away from the building, Spider-Man went back after Jean, and for a while you tried to convince yourself it had nothing to do with you.
Then you saw Spider-Man again. This time, you knew Jean wasn’t just attacking damage control for no reason.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: You don’t see Jean again that night. What you do see is Spider-Man.

He finds you a few blocks away from the Damage Control building, after most of the immediate chaos has cleared. You assume he’s checking on everyone who got caught nearby, but he spends more time with you than you expect. He wants to know what you saw, whether Jean came near you, and if she said anything that might explain what she was doing there. You don’t have much to give him. Vmax is the only detail that means anything, and even that means nothing to you yet.

Spider-Man already has an explanation for what happened. Jean is dangerous, she has powers that let her get inside people’s heads, and she’s willing to attack a government facility to get what she wants. Damage Control has dealt with enhanced threats before, so Peter sees no reason to question why they’re involved. From his perspective, Jean crossed the line first. You believe him.

There isn’t much reason not to. Spider-Man just helped keep you alive, while Jean was the person forcing her way through DODC. You’ve also lived in New York long enough to know what Damage Control is supposed to do. When something involving enhanced people gets out of control, they’re the agency that steps in. Whatever Jean is looking for, breaking into one of their buildings doesn’t make her look innocent.

You try to forget about it after that. You go home, check the news, and find almost nothing useful. The reports focus on the attack itself. There’s no explanation for Vmax, no mention of why Jean was searching for it, and nothing about a missing sister. The more you look, the less information there seems to be.
That’s what keeps bothering you.
The next day, you start searching for Jean Grey.

Most of what you find is useless, but eventually her sister’s name appears. Sara Grey. There isn’t enough public information to explain what happened to her, only enough to confirm that she existed and that Jean has been looking for her. Suddenly Vmax could be a person, a location, or simply the last thing she knows connects back to Sara.
You send what you found to Spider-Man through the only contact method he gave you.
You don’t expect him to respond but he does.

When you meet again, Peter still isn’t convinced. He accepts that Jean may be searching for her sister, but that doesn’t erase what she’s capable of doing. He has already seen enough of her powers to understand how dangerous she can be, and finding Sara doesn’t automatically make everyone standing between Jean and that answer disposable.
You can understand that.
What you can’t understand is why Damage Control seems to know so little about a woman Jean is willing to tear through their organization to find.

Peter thinks there could be a simple explanation. Records involving enhanced people aren’t always public. Some cases are classified. Some people disappear into systems ordinary civilians never see. None of that proves DODC hurt Sara.
He isn’t defending them because he knows they’re innocent. He just doesn’t have a reason yet to believe they aren’t.

Over the next couple of days, your involvement stops feeling accidental. You start passing Peter anything you find connected to Sara, Jean or Vmax. Most of it leads nowhere. Peter disappears for long stretches without explaining what he’s doing, then turns up again with another piece of information or another warning to stay away from Jean if you see her.
The more time you spend around him, the stranger Spider-Man becomes.

He’s good with people when someone needs help, but terrible at letting anyone help him. He’ll make sure you get home safely, then vanish before you can ask where he’s going. He remembers small things you mention but avoids almost every question about himself. Even when he’s clearly exhausted, he treats stopping as something he hasn’t earned yet.
Then you start noticing the physical changes.

Something is happening to him beneath the suit. He tries to hide it, but there are moments where his discomfort is obvious. His body is changing in ways he can’t predict or fully control, and Peter doesn’t know why. The changes themselves scare him more than he admits. Instead of asking anyone else to solve it, he treats it like another science problem.

Peter starts working on an inhibitor. It isn’t a cure, and he doesn’t even know what the changes will become. The point is simply to keep them from surfacing while he tries to understand what is happening to him.

You still don’t know his name. You don’t know where he lives or why he seems so uncomfortable whenever his personal life comes up. All you know is that Spider-Man is helping you investigate a missing woman while quietly trying to stop something inside his own body from changing.
Neither problem feels connected yet. Jean is the one who changes that. You see her again before Peter does. This time, there’s no Damage Control building between you.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: You spot Jean before she notices you.

She’s alone this time, moving through the city without the chaos that surrounded her at Damage Control. There are no agents nearby, no Spider-Man, and no obvious reason for you to stay. You know what she can do. Peter has warned you more than once not to get close to her but you stay anyway. Jean recognizes you from the DODC incident. For a moment, nothing happens. Then you feel the pressure in your head.
It isn’t pain exactly. Your memories come at her without your permission. The Damage Control building. Spider-Man pulling you out. The searches you’ve done since then. Sara’s name on your screen.

Jean sees enough to understand that you’ve been looking for her. What surprises you is what you get back. You don’t see everything in her head, but you understand enough to realize Peter has been wrong about one part of this. Jean isn’t chasing Vmax because she wants power.
She’s chasing it because it’s tied to Sara. It was the last clue her sister left behind, and Jean has been following it because she has nothing else.

That doesn’t make Jean safe. When she leaves your mind, you’re still standing there. You expect her to threaten you or try to force information out of you, but she doesn’t need to. She already knows what you know.

You ask about Sara. Jean’s reaction tells you more than an answer would. She doesn’t know where her sister is. She doesn’t know if Sara is alive. She only knows that Damage Control is connected to whatever happened, and that Vmax is the one thing she has left to follow.

When Spider-Man arrives, Jean is already gone. He can tell something happened. You don’t need to explain the pressure in your head before he starts asking if she touched your mind. The concern in his voice is immediate. He checks that you are still yourself, that you can remember where you are, and that Jean didn’t leave anything behind.

You tell him what you learned. Peter listens, but it doesn’t change his position as much as you expect. Jean searching for Sara explains her motive. It doesn’t erase what she’s doing to get there. If she can enter your mind that easily, then she can do the same thing to other people. Peter has no way of knowing how far she’ll go if she thinks someone is keeping Sara from her.
He still sees Jean as the immediate danger. You start seeing Damage Control as the bigger question.

That creates the first real disagreement between you. Peter thinks you’re getting too close to someone who can manipulate people without touching them. You think he’s giving DODC too much trust just because they’re a government agency he’s worked with before. Neither of you has enough proof to settle it.
So you keep investigating.
Peter does too, even if he pretends he’s only checking Jean’s story. That’s when Yelena Belova enters the situation.

She’s already been looking into Damage Control from another angle, and unlike Peter, she doesn’t need much convincing that something inside the agency could be rotten. She doesn’t trust Jean either, but she cares more about whether the facts line up than who looks like the villain from the outside.

Sara Grey existed. Damage Control had records connected to her. Those records aren’t where they should be. Every time you find something useful, another part is missing. Peter stops calling it coincidence. He still won’t say DODC is responsible, but the certainty he had before is gone.

Bruce Banner becomes involved because of that problem. Bruce understands better than almost anyone what it means to live with something inside your body that you’re afraid to let out. He also understands why Peter wants control.

What Peter doesn’t want to hear is that control and suppression aren’t the same thing. Later, Peter crosses paths with MJ, someone from his life before you met him, and she gives him a similar warning.

You still don’t understand who she is to Peter, only that she knows enough about him to speak in a way most people can’t. Peter listens to her, but he doesn’t stop. He keeps working on the inhibitor. Jean keeps looking for Vmax. And Damage Control keeps giving all of you reasons to think there’s something they don’t want found.
The next time Jean makes her move, she goes straight for the main DODC building.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Jean’s next move is different because she’s no longer searching around the edges of Damage Control. She goes straight to the main building, convinced that whatever Vmax is, the answer is there.

By the time you and Peter reach the area, things are already going wrong. Peter realizes Jean has gotten to Bruce Banner and taken control of his mind. Bruce’s inhibitor is removed, and the Hulk is unleashed inside the same situation Peter is already struggling to understand.

That changes the scale of the problem immediately. Peter can’t focus on Jean while Hulk is tearing through the building, and he can’t simply leave Bruce alone either. Frank Castle arrives during the chaos, turning what should have been a contained confrontation into something even harder to control.

You stay close enough to help where you can, mostly by keeping track of what Peter can’t. He’s moving between Bruce, Jean, DODC agents and civilians while trying to stop anyone from getting killed. The more pressure he’s under, the clearer it becomes that he’s still treating Jean as the person who started all of this.
Then Jean gets control of Frank too.

That’s when Peter starts to understand how dangerous the situation can become if she keeps escalating. Frank is already willing to use lethal force in situations where Peter won’t. With Jean inside his head, that becomes another problem Peter has to manage without hurting either of them.

Jean uses the opening to get closer to the vault where she believes Vmax is being kept. Everything she has done up to this point has been building toward that room. Sara gave her one clue, and Jean has convinced herself that opening that vault will finally give her an answer.
When the vault is opened, there is no Vmax inside.
Bill Metzger and the remaining DODC personnel are hiding there instead.
For a few seconds, nobody understands what that means. Jean expected to find something connected to Sara. Instead, she finds the people who have been trying to stop her from reaching the truth.
Peter catches up before Jean can push things any further. He manages to sedate her and gets an inhibitor onto her, shutting down her powers before the situation becomes even worse.

Metzger’s reaction doesn’t look like relief. The vault doesn’t look like a place where someone was simply waiting out an emergency. It feels like a hiding place, and the fact that Jean found Metzger there instead of the answer she was looking for only makes the whole thing stranger. Jean is taken into DODC custody before Peter can stop it. Agents move her while he is still dealing with Bruce, Frank and the civilians caught in the building, insisting she’ll be contained and examined at a secure research facility. A few days earlier, he probably would have accepted that without much hesitation.

Now he doesn’t. You and Yelena start digging into the facility while Peter deals with the damage left behind. Bruce is still unstable after what Jean did to him, Frank is furious about being controlled, and Peter’s own physical changes are getting harder to hide.

For the first time, Peter admits that something about DODC isn’t adding up. You trace the Vmax clue through records connected to Sara. The name never appears as a person, a weapon or a classified project. There is no evidence that DODC ever had anything officially called Vmax.

Then you find the piece everyone else missed. Buried in an old facility inspection file is a damaged photograph from the research wing where Sara was held. Most of the label on one of the vents has been torn away, but enough remains to reconstruct the word. VENTMAX. Only part of the name had been visible, leaving Vmax as the last thing Sara could identify. That vent was inside the same research facility where DODC had taken her. Sara wasn’t being protected there. She was being experimented on. She died inside that facility.

Everything Jean had been doing suddenly fits together. She wasn’t trying to steal a DODC weapon. She had been chasing the last clue her sister left behind because it was the only thing that could lead her back to the place where Sara disappeared. And without you finding that photograph, Peter would still be looking for something called Vmax while Jean remained in DODC custody.

Peter understands what that means for him too. He trusted Damage Control. He helped stop Jean. He put the inhibitor on her himself, and while he was occupied with the chaos that followed, the same organization responsible for Sara’s death took Jean into another research facility.
The mistake is personal now. Peter doesn’t waste time defending himself. He starts working with you and Yelena to get Jean out before DODC can do to her what they did to Sara.
The problem is that Jean learns the truth before you can reach her. By the time you get close to the facility, her grief has already turned into something none of you are prepared for.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: By the time you reach the research facility, Jean already knows what happened to Sara. DODC took her sister, experimented on her, and let her die inside the same system Jean had spent the entire movie trying to get answers from.
Jean then stops looking for information because there’s nothing left to find. Sara is gone, and the people responsible are still standing in front of her.

The grief hits harder than anything Peter has seen from her before. Jean’s power spreads out across New York. People begin freezing where they stand as she reaches into their minds on a scale that makes everything she did earlier look small. Huge parts of the city become trapped inside the same psychic event, unable to move while Jean’s anger and grief keep pushing outward.

Peter knows he has to reach her, but there is a problem he already understands better than anyone else. Jean can get into almost anyone’s head. She did it to Bruce. She did it to Frank. She did it to you.
She still can’t get into his. Whatever is happening with Peter’s Spider-Sense makes his mind harder for Jean to reach. Under normal circumstances, that would be an advantage.

Now it’s getting in the way. You try to get closer to Jean because she already knows your mind. That connection matters, but it is not enough to pull her back. She is too far gone in what happened to Sara, and every attempt to reason with her only brings the same truth back to the surface.

DODC killed her sister. The photograph you found is the reason Peter finally understands what Sara’s last clue actually meant and why Jean refused to let it go. You tell him Vmax was never something Jean wanted. It was Sara trying to leave behind the only piece of the place where she died. Peter realizes this is not a fight he can win by hitting harder. He also realizes that if Jean cannot get through the wall around his mind, then he has to be the one who opens it.
Peter lets her in. Instead of fighting against his mind, she is suddenly inside the memories he has spent years keeping away from everyone else.

She sees May. She sees the way Peter used to talk to her before everything fell apart. She sees the person who raised him, the loss that followed, and what Peter became after she died. She sees how much of his life has been shaped by the belief that getting close to people only gives the world another way to hurt them.
For the first time, Jean is looking at someone who understands what it feels like to lose the person who made the rest of your life make sense.

That is what finally reaches her. Peter doesn’t try to tell Jean that losing Sara was something she should move past. He understands too much to do that. What he shows her is that grief does not have to mean isolation, and that losing someone does not mean every connection after that has to be pushed away.

Jean sees that Peter has been doing exactly that to himself. The same thing she has been doing in a different way. Peter has spent years shutting people out because he thinks that is how he protects them. He has been trying to suppress the physical changes happening inside his own body for the same reason. If something feels dangerous or uncontrollable, his first instinct is to bury it before it can hurt anyone.

Jean pulls out of the minds around her, and people begin moving again as the psychic hold breaks. The immediate danger passes, but the situation is not over. Metzger is still there, and now Jean knows exactly what he was involved in.
She goes after him. This time, it’s not about finding Sara. It’s about revenge.

Peter gets between them before Jean can kill him. Even after everything DODC did, he refuses to let Jean become someone who takes a life because of what they took from her. Stopping Metzger almost costs Peter his own life.

When Peter goes down, Jean is the one who keeps him alive. She uses her telekinesis to stabilize him long enough for help to reach him, holding pressure around the worst of his injuries and keeping him from being moved until everyone around them can get him out. With Peter down and Jean focused on saving him, Metzger uses the confusion to escape the facility before anyone can stop him.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: Peter survives, but the ending does not reset his life back to where it was before Jean appeared.

Frank stays with him at the hospital and helps make sure Peter can leave without exposing who he really is. By this point, Frank knowing Peter’s identity is no longer the biggest change between them.
