Strange would start looking for the exact conditions behind the vow while Yuji continues working with the Avengers. Wanda could help identify when the person controlling the body changes, and Yuji would finally be involved in building the safeguards instead of having other people decide what happens to him from the outside.

He would still carry Sukuna, and nobody could promise that Sukuna never finds another opening. By then, Yuji has also spent years proving what he does whenever he is the one in control, through New York, HYDRA, Sokovia, Civil War, the Snap, and everything that followed. That’s the version of Yuji who would finally accept being called an Avenger.

scripts.title: What If Yuji Was In The Boys

sections.name: INTRO
paras: If Yuji Itadori got dropped into The Boys universe, he’d probably get pulled into trouble almost immediately. I'd use post Shibuya Yuji, while Sukuna is still inside him, so he’s already carrying everything that happened in Shibuya and he takes civilian deaths way more seriously than he used to.

The first big incident would happen before Yuji even understands what Vought is. A Supe loses control in public, people get hurt, and Yuji jumps in because that’s just what he does. He saves civilians, puts the Supe down, and suddenly there’s footage everywhere of some random kid beating a Vought hero with no Compound V in his system.

That puts Yuji into the middle of a world he doesn’t understand yet. The Boys want to know who he is, Starlight starts paying attention to what actually happened, and Vought is already trying to control the story before Yuji even knows why everyone is calling the other guy a hero. Homelander would hear about him soon after, and Sukuna would be watching all of it from inside Yuji. The more this world tries to push Yuji around, the more dangerous that second problem becomes.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: I'd use Yuji from right after Shibuya, during the stretch where he’s moving through Tokyo with Choso and hunting curses before Yuta catches up to him. Sukuna is still inside him, Yuji’s already landed multiple Black Flashes, and he’s gotten much better at reinforcing his body with cursed energy. He’s also carrying everything that happened in Shibuya, so civilian deaths hit him way harder than they did when he first became a sorcerer.

The crossover happens during one of those hunts. Yuji and Choso follow a curse into an underground station that was damaged during Shibuya, and the barrier around it starts collapsing when the curse tries to escape. Yuji goes after it before Choso can stop him, the barrier folds in on itself, and instead of getting thrown into another part of Tokyo, Yuji drops into a completely different city. He comes out in New York during seaso 2 of The Boys, right around the time Stormfront is chasing Kenji through the city.

He reaches the apartment building while Stormfront is tearing through it looking for Kenji, and what he sees makes the whole hero thing stop making sense almost immediately. She's blasting through walls without caring who’s behind them, civilians are getting caught in the damage, and she keeps moving like none of it matters. Yuji doesn’t know who Kenji is, doesn’t know The

Boys are nearby, and doesn’t know Stormfront is one of the most famous Supes in America. He just sees a woman with powers hurting people while chasing someone through a building. When part of the floor starts coming down on a family trying to get out, Yuji catches enough of the collapsing concrete to give them room and shoves them toward the stairwell. Stormfront lands behind him and tells him to move, but Yuji looks at the bodies in the hallway and stays where he is. Stormfront assumes he’s another Supe, Yuji assumes she’s some kind of curse user, and Kenji gets the first real opening he’s had since the chase started.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Stormfront goes for Yuji the second he blocks her path. She’s already pissed that Kenji is getting away, and from her point of view this random kid just jumped into the middle of it and started protecting people she doesn’t care about. The first blast catches Yuji clean because he still has no idea what her electricity can do. Cursed energy reinforcement keeps him from getting dropped immediately, but it throws him through a wall and leaves part of his shirt burned.

Yuji comes back through the opening almost right away, and that’s when Stormfront realizes he’s different from the people she usually fights. He closes the distance fast, lands a heavy body shot, and sends her across the hallway hard enough to crack the wall behind her. She gets back up though, which tells Yuji the same thing in reverse. This world has people who can take way more punishment than a normal human should.

That pressure keeps building until Yuji gets completely locked into the fight. Stormfront comes in close after another blast and tries to finish it while he’s still recovering, but Yuji times the counter perfectly. His cursed energy connects with the physical hit in the same instant, and Black Flash happens.

Yuji doesn’t choose it like some move he can turn on whenever he wants. He just lands everything clean at once, and the impact launches Stormfront across the floor harder than anything he’s hit her with so far. The wall behind her caves in, and for the first time she looks more shocked than angry.

Yuji still doesn’t stay there trying to finish her. He hears Kimiko below, realizes Kenji made it out, and jumps down after them before Stormfront can fully recover. He knows staying to trade with her only gives whoever else is chasing Kenji time to catch up, so he helps push Kimiko, Kenji, Frenchie, Mother's Milk, and Hughie out through the nearest route while Stormfront is still recovering from the Black Flash. They clear the area just before Homelander arrives. He finds Stormfront, the damaged building, and witnesses talking about an unknown kid who got in her way, which is what first puts Yuji on his radar without forcing their real confrontation to happen here.
That one change already wrecks the original timeline. Kenji survives the chase, Stormfront fails in front of a bunch of witnesses, and people have footage of an unknown kid helping civilians
before fighting one of the Seven. Vought can still spin it, but now they’ve got a problem they didn’t create and can’t explain.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Yuji ends up with The Boys mostly because he has nowhere else to go and Kimiko won't leave Kenji behind. He still doesn’t understand who any of these people are, but he can tell pretty quickly that Butcher isn’t happy Kenji survived. Butcher sees Kenji as useful leverage and talks about handing him over in a way Yuji immediately hates.

Yuji asks why everyone keeps calling Kenji a terrorist when Stormfront was the one killing civilians in the building. Butcher gives him the usual answer about Supes being dangerous, Vought creating the whole mess, and Kenji already showing what he can do. Yuji looks at Kimiko and asks what that makes her, because he can clearly see she’s dangerous too and also clearly see she’s still a person.

That’s where Butcher realizes Yuji isn’t going to fit neatly into anything he wants. Hughie has an easier time talking to him and explains Compound V, Vought, the Seven, and the whole fake story about Supes being chosen by God. Yuji thinks he’s joking at first, then Hughie explains that parents were secretly letting Vought inject their kids, and the giant hero ads Yuji saw outside start looking a lot darker.

Kenji is the reason Yuji stays involved. He can tell Kenji is angry, scared, and finally back with Kimiko after years apart. Yuji has already watched too many people die before he could do anything about it, so he isn’t about to save someone from Stormfront and then walk away while Butcher decides what happens next. That creates tension inside the group because Yuji is strong enough that Butcher can’t just force the issue, while Frenchie and Hughie are much more willing to hear him out.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: That's how Annie gets dragged into it. Hughie sends her the footage and asks if Vought knows who Yuji is, so she checks what she can from inside the company. There’s no file, no Compound V record, no childhood program, no contract, no test results, nothing. Every Supe Vought understands comes back to Compound V somewhere, and Yuji has none of that.

Annie meets him through Hughie and tries to get a clearer answer herself. Yuji explains cursed energy as simply as he can because none of them have any idea what he’s talking about. He tells them negative emotions create cursed energy, sorcerers learn how to control it, and most normal people in his world can’t even see the things he fights.

Yuji pauses because that’s the part he doesn’t want to explain. Before he can answer properly, Sukuna opens a mouth on his cheek and starts talking for him. Hughie nearly jumps out of his seat, Annie just stares, and Yuji immediately covers the mouth with his hand and tells Sukuna to shut up.

That’s when Yuji explains the part that actually matters. Sukuna is another being inside him, and he’s way more dangerous than Yuji himself. Yuji can usually suppress him, but that doesn’t make Sukuna some extra ability he can pull out when a fight gets hard. He’s constantly trying to take advantage of whatever opening he gets, and Yuji has already seen what happens when he loses control.

Butcher hears all of that and starts thinking exactly what Yuji knew he would. A stronger thing trapped inside a kid who already hurt Stormfront sounds useful if Homelander ever becomes the target. Yuji catches the look before Butcher even says anything and shuts it down immediately. He tells him Sukuna isn’t a weapon. The last time Sukuna got real freedom, people died because Yuji couldn’t stop him, and that’s still sitting on him after Shibuya. If Butcher thinks letting Sukuna out is some emergency button they can press against Vought, then Butcher has no idea what he’s asking for.

That changes the way everyone in the room looks at Yuji. Annie now understands why he keeps such a tight grip on himself, Hughie realizes his powers come with a problem way worse than anything Vought created, and Butcher starts seeing that Yuji won't let him use Sukuna no matter how bad Homelander gets.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: Homelander hears about Yuji through Stormfront, but the footage is what actually gets him interested. He watches Yuji take her electricity, get back up, and hit her hard enough to send her through a wall. Stormfront keeps calling him another super terrorist, while Homelander cares more about the fact that Vought has no clue where he came from.

The meeting happens while The Boys are moving Kenji to another safe place. Annie is helping them avoid obvious routes, Yuji stays close to Kimiko and Kenji, and everyone is already tense because they know Vought is searching for them. Then Homelander drops into the road ahead and comes alone because he wants to see Yuji himself.

By now Yuji knows enough about him that the costume and smile don’t mean much, Hughie and Annie have already told him about Flight 37 and some of the other things Vought covered up, so Yuji is already looking at him like someone dangerous instead of someone famous. Homelander walks up, asks what Vought put in him, and gets irritated when Yuji tells him they didn’t put anything in him.

Sukuna makes the situation worse on purpose. A mouth opens on Yuji’s cheek and tells Homelander his costume looks stupid, which immediately kills whatever patience Homelander still had. He grabs Yuji by the throat and lifts him off the ground before anyone else can react. Yuji tries to break the grip and realizes right away that Homelander’s raw strength is way above Stormfront’s. Kimiko moves in and gets knocked aside. Kenji throws a car, Homelander catches it, and that gives Yuji just enough time to twist free and land a cursed energy reinforced punch across his jaw.

The hit moves Homelander, but it doesn’t do anywhere near enough to make Yuji comfortable. Homelander comes back harder and the next punch sends Yuji across the road. Yuji gets up, but slower this time, and when the heat vision catches his shoulder on the second pass it burns badly enough that he immediately knows he can’t keep taking clean hits.

That’s when Yuji notices the people stuck around them. Cars are stopped, people are trying to run, and every missed laser or thrown vehicle can hit somebody who has nothing to do with this. Yuji turns and starts moving away from the traffic, which Homelander reads as fear and follows immediately.

Yuji keeps going until there’s more open ground and fewer people around before turning back. That gives him a cleaner place to fight, but it also takes away the easiest cover he had. Homelander understands what he just did and finds it almost insulting because Yuji would rather make his own fight harder than leave civilians in the middle of it.

The next exchange hurts Yuji badly enough that he stops trying to trade straight punches. He starts slipping around Homelander’s rushes, attacking when Homelander overcommits, and using cursed energy reinforcement just to survive the moments he can’t avoid. He can still hurt him, but one bad read could end the fight immediately.

By this point Yuji understands exactly how dangerous Homelander is. He’s stronger, faster in the air, and has ranged attacks Yuji can’t afford to eat. Yuji can survive enough punishment to be annoying and hit hard enough to be felt, but he knows one bad exchange could still end this.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: Once they’re away from the traffic, Yuji stops trying to meet Homelander head-on. He already learned from Stormfront that Supes can take punishment differently than sorcerers, and Homelander is clearly stronger than anyone he’s fought in this world so far. Yuji keeps moving, makes Homelander come to him, and
starts figuring out how much space the heat vision covers and how quickly Homelander can change direction once he commits.

The first few exchanges are rough. Yuji can reinforce his body enough to survive getting hit, but Homelander’s strength sends him across the ground every time he gets caught clean. Yuji lands back with cursed energy reinforced punches and gets real reactions out of him, though nothing suggests he can just beat Homelander down with normal strikes. Homelander starts getting more irritated because Yuji keeps standing back up and because every time he tries to make the fight feel like a public execution, Yuji treats him like another dangerous person who needs to be stopped.

That attitude gets under Homelander’s skin more than the punches do. Yuji doesn’t care about the costume, the fame, or the fact that millions of people worship him. He keeps asking why someone this strong keeps needing weaker people to be scared of him, and Homelander eventually stops pretending the conversation is funny. He rushes Yuji hard enough to drive both of them through part of an abandoned building, then pins him down and starts squeezing. Sukuna chooses that moment to speak again. He doesn’t offer Yuji help, and he definitely doesn’t care whether Homelander kills anyone nearby. He just finds it funny that someone with this much power needs constant approval from people he looks down on. The comment makes Homelander hesitate for a second because the voice is coming from Yuji’s body without Yuji moving his mouth, and Yuji uses that opening to break the grip and land another heavy shot. Yuji still doesn’t win the fight. Homelander is too strong physically, can fly, and can attack from range, while Yuji has no technique at this point that lets him suddenly erase that gap. What Yuji can do is make the fight annoying enough that Homelander stops treating him like an easy kill. Homelander finally catches him again and is about to finish it when Annie arrives with Vought personnel already converging on the scene. Their orders are to keep Yuji alive if possible because Vought still has no idea what he is or where his powers came from, while the outside attention closing in makes a public execution even harder to contain. Homelander hates being told to stop, but killing Yuji now would mean ignoring Vought's attempt to get answers while creating another story the company can't control. He backs off instead of finishing Yuji.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Kenji surviving starts changing things in the background while Yuji is dealing with Homelander. Kimiko finally gets more time with her brother, and that makes The Boys’ situation with him way less simple because he isn’t just a target they can hand off anymore. Yuji keeps pushing Butcher on that every time the conversation comes up, and Hughie starts siding with him more
openly because he can see how badly Butcher wants everything involving Supes to fit the same answer.

Annie becomes the person he trusts most inside the Seven because she keeps showing him what Vought hides instead of asking him to blindly believe her. She explains how hero contracts work, what happens when someone becomes bad for the brand, and how quickly Vought can make a victim disappear from the story if that victim hurts the company. Yuji starts understanding why Stormfront could kill civilians during a chase and still expect Vought to clean it up afterward.

He also begins noticing how different his instincts are from Butcher’s. Butcher looks at every Supe and starts with the damage they could do. Yuji looks at what the person actually chooses to do with that power. Kimiko is the easiest example because she could tear through normal people if she wanted to, yet she’s still someone Yuji sees protecting her brother and trying to survive what happened to her.

That argument stops being theoretical when The Boys locate a smaller Vought connected Supe who has been helping cover up civilian deaths in exchange for money. Butcher wants to kill him and move on. Yuji agrees the guy needs to answer for what he did, but he refuses to stand there while Butcher executes someone who is already beaten and can’t fight back.

The confrontation gets physical for a moment, though Yuji doesn’t hit Butcher. He simply catches the weapon before Butcher can use it and tells him that being angry doesn’t give him the right to decide everyone’s death himself. Butcher immediately throws Yuji’s own admission back at him, that Sukuna killed people through his body when Yuji lost control, and that lands much harder than anything physical would.

Yuji doesn’t have a clean answer because that guilt is exactly why he thinks the choice matters. He knows what it feels like to believe your body caused deaths you couldn't stop, and he also knows what happens when people decide someone has no value left because of what they're capable of. That’s the point where Yuji stops being useful to Butcher as a possible anti Supe weapon and starts becoming a problem for the way Butcher sees the whole war.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: Vought’s next move doesn’t involve sending another member of the Seven to fight Yuji. They start going after the story around him instead, because physically confronting him has already created footage they can’t fully control. News segments start replaying the Stormfront fight
without the parts showing civilians being rescued, while commentators ask where this unknown enhanced teenager came from and whether he was connected to Kenji.
So Yuji does something that fits him much better. He goes back to the people who were actually there.

Some of the civilians he pulled out survived, and Hughie manages to find one family before Vought gets to them. Yuji doesn’t ask them to defend him or become part of some campaign. He wants to know whether they’re safe and whether Vought has already tried making them sign anything. When he finds out they've been offered money to stay quiet about what Stormfront did, the problem becomes more concrete than any speech Annie could give him.

That gives Hughie and Annie evidence they can actually use. Witness statements, the payment offer, the original phone footage, and Kenji’s survival all start undermining Vought’s story that Kenji was responsible for the destruction and civilian deaths. It still isn't enough by itself to destroy Stormfront publicly, especially with Vought trying to bury it, but it gives Annie and Hughie another trail to preserve while they keep digging into who Stormfront actually is. Yuji’s role is smaller than he expected because most of the damage to Vought comes from getting the truth out, not from punching anyone. He ends up guarding the witnesses while Hughie and Annie handle the part he barely understands.

Sukuna gets bored with all of it and keeps pushing Yuji toward the simpler option. He points out that Yuji knows where Stormfront is and could solve one problem by killing her. Yuji ignores him until Sukuna starts bringing up the people Stormfront already killed, which is exactly the kind of argument Yuji is vulnerable to after Shibuya.

Yuji catches himself before he gets there. He decides Stormfront has to be stopped, but he wants to do it with people knowing what she actually did. That choice keeps the fight personal without turning the entire story into Yuji running through every Supe Vought has.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: The evidence around Stormfront starts becoming harder for Vought to keep completely clean because Kenji is still alive and the civilians Yuji helped can contradict the story Vought told about the apartment attack. Annie and Hughie keep pushing that side of it while the separate investigation into Stormfront’s past continues, because testimony about the chase can damage Vought’s version of events without replacing the much stronger evidence needed to expose who Stormfront really is. Yuji stays closer to Kimiko and Kenji because he already knows Stormfront is going to see Kenji as the loose end she needs gone.

When she finally comes after him, Yuji doesn’t fight her the same way he did the first time. He already knows what her electricity feels like, how durable she is, and how quickly she'll go after civilians if it gives her an opening. Stormfront knows more about him too, so she keeps her distance and starts using the area around them instead of letting Yuji get close for free.

That turns the fight into a problem Yuji hates because every time Stormfront sends a blast toward Kenji or somebody nearby, he has to break off and move. She catches on fast and starts using that against him. Yuji is stronger in close range, but he can’t stay on her if he’s constantly choosing between attacking and stopping someone else from getting hurt.

Kimiko and Kenji are what change that. Kenji uses his telekinesis to move debris out of the way and keep civilians from getting trapped, while Kimiko stays closer to the people Stormfront is trying to reach. That finally gives Yuji time to stay on Stormfront instead of covering everything himself.

Yuji stays on Stormfront once Kimiko and Kenji take away the openings she was creating around him, but it still isn't just normal punches suddenly overpowering her. Yuji pressures her at close range and keeps forcing her to defend, Kenji uses his telekinesis to disrupt her spacing and keep debris from becoming another weapon, and Kimiko keeps crashing back into the fight whenever Stormfront tries to reset or go after someone else. The combined pressure starts wearing Stormfront down until she’s hurt badly enough that she can’t keep chasing Kenji. Yuji stops there. Sukuna immediately starts digging at him from inside, reminding him that she’s already killed people and could do it again if he leaves her alive. That thought hits Yuji harder than he wants because he’s still carrying Shibuya and all the people who died while he couldn't stop it.

Kenji being there is what keeps him grounded. Yuji saved someone who should've died in the original chase, and now that person is standing there alive because Yuji chose to protect him instead of deciding who deserved to die. That lines up way more with the way Yuji thinks about giving people a proper death. He doesn’t want Stormfront walking free, but he also isn’t going to turn every fight into an execution just because someone else tells him it would be easier.

The footage from that fight makes Vought’s situation even worse. People can see Stormfront attacking first, Kenji surviving, and Yuji stopping after she’s no longer a threat. Homelander watches the same footage and realizes Yuji keeps making the Seven look worse without even trying to take their place.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: Homelander finally goes after Yuji because the whole situation is becoming personal. Stormfront is exposed, Annie is pushing harder against Vought, Kenji is alive, and Yuji keeps ending up in footage where the people Vought calls dangerous are the ones helping civilians.

Yuji knows another confrontation is coming, so he tries to control the only thing he realistically can, which is where it happens. Annie helps move things toward an abandoned industrial area outside the city where there are fewer civilians around. Butcher wants a plan built around killing Homelander, but Yuji refuses anything involving Sukuna because he knows that creates a bigger problem than the one they're already dealing with.

Homelander starts much harder than before. He already knows Yuji can take hits, so he doesn’t waste time testing him. Yuji gets driven through concrete, takes a heat vision cut across his side, and has to use cursed energy reinforcement constantly just to stay functional.

Yuji can hurt him when he lands clean, but the gap in raw power is still obvious. He isn’t winning by standing there and trading. He starts relying on timing instead, letting Homelander rush in, slipping off line, and hitting during the moments where Homelander gets impatient and overcommits.

That frustrates Homelander way more than it should because Yuji is treating him like a fighter he can read instead of some god everybody has to freeze in front of. The angrier Homelander gets, the sloppier those attacks become, and Yuji finally lands a clean combination that actually forces him back.

Sukuna starts talking once Yuji is badly hurt and tired enough for the temptation to feel real. He doesn’t offer some simple transformation Yuji can activate. He just keeps pushing the same idea that he always does, that Yuji could stop struggling if he stopped caring what happens to everyone around him.
Yuji ignores him because he already knows where that road leads.

Annie and Kimiko help once the fight shifts closer to the edge of the industrial site, but they don’t suddenly overpower Homelander. That was never the real plan. Annie and The Boys already have redundant cameras feeding the confrontation out to people away from the site, so destroying one camera or taking the equipment afterward won't erase what happens here. Yuji’s job is to survive long enough for Homelander to show exactly what he does when there’s no Vought script controlling the scene, while Annie and Kimiko force him to split his attention and keep him from ending the fight immediately.

Homelander realizes what they’re doing too late. He’s hurt, angry, fighting multiple people, and the footage is already leaving the site instead of sitting on one camera he can destroy. Vought is already losing control of the Stormfront situation, and now Homelander has been recorded trying to murder a teenager who has repeatedly been seen helping civilians. Yuji still hasn't beaten him physically, but this time Homelander backing off is the result Yuji and the others were actually trying to force. Staying only gives them more footage, while killing everyone there no longer guarantees the evidence disappears.

Yuji survives, but he doesn’t walk away thinking he beat Homelander. He knows how close that got, and he knows one mistake could’ve ended him. What he does understand now is that Homelander’s power isn’t the only thing keeping him on top. Vought, fear, public image, and the fact that most people around him think they can’t do anything are all part of it.

Yuji doesn’t fix The Boys universe by showing up. Vought is still there, Homelander is still dangerous, and Butcher still thinks Yuji is too soft on people who deserve worse. Kenji surviving gives Kimiko a completely different future, Annie has more evidence to fight Vought with, and the public has seen proof that one of their heroes can actually be challenged.

For Yuji, the biggest change is more personal. He comes into this world still treating his own life like something he can spend if it means other people get a proper death. Kenji staying alive, Kimiko getting her brother back, and Annie continuing to fight from inside the system all force him to see that saving people isn’t always about dying for them but rather staying alive.

Yuji probably wouldn’t change The Boys universe overnight, but he’d leave it better than he found it. He’d save people Vought was willing to sacrifice, give Annie and The Boys another way to fight back, and prove that having power doesn’t have to turn someone into Homelander.

scripts.title: Why Doctor Doom Needs Spider Man Alive

sections.name: INTRO
paras: Doctor Doom could have plenty of reasons to go after Spider-Man, but killing Peter might actually ruin something he needs.

Peter has already been at the center of one of the MCU’s biggest multiverse accidents. Strange’s spell pulled people from other universes into his world, Peter met alternate versions of himself face to face, and the whole thing only ended when everyone forgot who Peter Parker was.

If Doom is trying to understand, control, or exploit the multiverse, Peter could be more useful as a source than a target. The question is what exactly Doom could get from him, and whether that’s enough to make keeping Spider-Man alive part of the plan.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: The first thing Doom would care about is what actually happened during No Way Home, because Peter sits at the center of a multiversal event that still has several unanswered questions. Strange originally tried to make everyone forget that Peter Parker was Spider-Man. Peter kept changing the spell while Strange was casting it, the spell broke containment, and people from other universes who knew Spider-Man’s identity started being pulled toward the MCU. That connection was specific enough that Green Goblin, Doc Ock, Electro, Sandman, Lizard, and 2 other Peter Parkers all ended up in the same universe.

Peter then spent time with people who came from realities he had never visited himself. He learned that the other Spider-Men had lived completely different versions of his life, helped them cure villains who had already reached the ends of their stories back home, and watched Strange contain cracks that were starting to open across the sky. The visitors were eventually sent home after Peter asked Strange to cast a second spell that erased Peter Parker from everyone’s memory. Marvel has confirmed that MJ, Ned, Happy, Strange, and everyone else who knew Peter forgot him after that spell.

Peter still has his side of those events. He knows why the first spell was cast, what went wrong during it, who came through, how the villains were changed before being returned, and why he ultimately chose to erase himself from everyone else’s life. That information becomes more interesting once somebody starts trying to reconstruct the event later, because the people around Peter can remember Spider-Man existing without remembering the person whose identity caused the entire problem.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: Doctor Strange immediately creates a problem for this theory because he understands the magic far better than Peter ever could. If Doom only wants to know how the spell was constructed, what magical rules it used, or why Strange lost control of it, Strange is the obvious person to investigate. Peter can describe what happened from his perspective, while Strange actually cast both spells.

The reason Peter could still matter is the information Strange lost. Marvel's explanation of the ending makes it clear that Strange no longer remembers Peter Parker himself, but it doesn't establish exactly how much of the spell or multiversal crisis he still remembers afterward. Whatever magical details Strange retains could contain gaps he can no longer explain because the person whose relationships and identity shaped the original request has been removed from his memory.

Peter can provide the pieces Strange may have lost. He remembers asking Strange for help because his identity had become public, interrupting the spell as he thought about everyone he wanted excluded, and eventually deciding that the only way to stop the breach was to erase Peter Parker entirely. He also knows details about MJ, Ned, May, and his own life that may no longer connect cleanly to whatever Strange remembers about the spell.

If Doom compares their accounts, the disagreement itself could become useful. Strange could provide whatever magical mechanics and multiversal details he still remembers, while Peter provides the complete personal context around them. Doom could reconstruct parts of No Way Home that neither source can fully explain alone, which gives Peter value that goes beyond simply being another witness to a multiverse event.

That also gives Doom a reason to keep both of them alive for a while. Killing Peter before comparing what he remembers with Strange’s version would throw away the easiest way to identify exactly what the final spell removed.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Doom still has to find Peter Parker first, and that might be the hardest part of the entire theory. The spell didn’t simply convince MJ and Ned to stop talking to Peter. Everyone forgot he existed, and Peter ends the movie having to introduce himself to people who once knew him better than almost anyone.

That means Doom discovering Peter’s identity would tell us something about how he found it. One possibility is that he reconstructs Peter through the No Way Home event itself. Records might still show Spider-Man appearing around Strange, the Statue of Liberty, and the people who crossed over, while pieces of Peter’s civilian history could contain inconsistencies created by the spell. Doom is exactly the kind of person who would notice if the history around a major multiversal event has a missing cause.

Another possibility would involve information coming from outside the universe affected by Strange’s spell. The 2 alternate Peter Parkers were sent back to their own realities after meeting MCU Peter, and nothing in No Way Home tells us they forgot him afterward. If Doom gains access to another universe before approaching MCU Peter, an alternate Spider-Man could theoretically provide information that nobody in Peter’s own reality remembers.

Once Doom has the name Peter Parker, the situation changes quickly. Peter would immediately want to know how this stranger remembers something the entire world lost, and Doom could use that question to get closer without needing to attack him first.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: Peter could help Doom distinguish between alternate realities by recognizing the people and details connected to them. Strange handled the spell itself, but Peter spent time with the visitors long enough to learn about their lives, their enemies, and the worlds they came from. He knows which Spider-Man fought Norman Osborn and Otto Octavius, which one knew Max Dillon and Curt Connors, and which villains were supposed to die before being pulled into the MCU. That matters if Doom can reach multiple universes but still needs to know which one he’s looking at. A portal or multiversal scan could show him dozens of similar realities without explaining which branch contains a specific person or event. Peter never visited those worlds himself, so he couldn't certify one on sight, but he could recognize people and details that match what the visitors told him and help Doom narrow down whether a reality is connected to them.

He also knows what changed before everyone was sent back. Norman had been cured of the Goblin personality, Otto regained control of his arms, and the other villains were altered before returning home. Peter can’t tell Doom what happened after they left because he never followed them, but he can tell him exactly what condition each person was in when Strange sent them back.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: The more speculative possibility is that Doom needs Peter himself because both spells were centered on his identity. No Way Home never says Peter carries multiversal energy afterward, and nothing currently confirms that Strange’s magic left a permanent mark Doom could detect. Any theory claiming Peter is secretly a living multiverse key would be going beyond what the movie established.

If Doom is experimenting with something similar, he could study Peter for any leftover magical effect from the spell. He might compare Peter to Strange, examine whether reality reacts differently around him, or test whether another multiversal device can recognize the universes Peter previously interacted with.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: If the multiverse starts breaking down on a larger scale, Peter could become useful in a much more immediate way. Doom might already have the technology or magic needed to move between realities, but knowing where to go and who to trust once he gets there is a different problem.

Peter has already met alternate versions of himself and watched several people from other universes appear in the MCU at the same time. If Doomsday starts putting different realities in direct contact, he’d be able to recognize versions of Spider-Man, cured villains, or other details that match what he remembers from No Way Home, even if he never saw their home universes firsthand.

That could matter during an incursion because Doom may need to find one specific person before 2 universes collide or before another group reaches them first. Peter wouldn't be the person opening the path or certifying the universe by himself, but what he recognizes could help Doom determine whether they've reached the right reality.

Peter might eventually notice that Doom is taking risks to keep him alive and start using that against him. If Doom still needs him to identify the next world or person, Peter gains a little room to push back without Doom being able to simply remove him from the board.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: Doom might get further by giving Peter a reason to cooperate rather than dragging him into a cell. Peter’s situation after No Way Home gives Doom an obvious opening because Peter knows exactly what the spell cost him. MJ and Ned are alive, but neither remembers the life they shared with him, and Peter chose to leave them alone after seeing that they were safe.

If Doom approaches Peter already knowing his name, Peter is going to listen long enough to ask how that is possible. Doom could then show him evidence that the spell can be studied, that memories might exist somewhere outside its effect, or that another universe still contains people who remember him. He wouldn't need to promise Peter that he can restore everything immediately.

The offer could be information. Doom might claim he can find the alternate Spider-Men again, determine whether they still remember MCU Peter, or show Peter exactly what Strange changed when the final spell was cast. Every one of those subjects would matter to Peter personally, and they also happen to lead directly into the information Doom wants.

Peter would still be suspicious because someone knowing this much about No Way Home would raise obvious questions. Doom could work with that suspicion rather than trying to remove it, giving Peter pieces that are verifiably true and allowing Peter to follow them himself. The more Peter investigates, the more Doom learns from what he recognizes and where he chooses to look.

At that point, killing Spider-Man would waste a source Doom is still extracting information from. Peter's memories can help reconstruct No Way Home, his identity may be relevant to Strange’s spell, and his relationships with alternate Spider-Men could help identify specific realities if the multiverse starts collapsing together.

The strongest version of the theory comes from all 3 possibilities overlapping. Doom wouldn't need every theory about Peter to be true. He only needs 1 of them to prove useful before Spider-Man becomes someone he has a reason to keep alive.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: Peter could become useful once Doom starts dealing with people from other universes because Peter has already helped change what happens to them. That gives Peter firsthand knowledge of people crossing into the MCU, being physically changed, and then being sent back. Doom could be interested in that if his larger plan involves moving people between realities while trying to preserve whatever changes are made along the way. Peter wouldn’t know whether the cures remained intact after the villains returned home, but he helped build several of them and understands exactly what was changed before they left.

The technology involved could matter too. Peter worked with 2 alternate versions of himself using equipment available in the MCU and knowledge brought from their own worlds. They managed to create treatments for Norman Osborn, Otto Octavius, Max Dillon, Flint Marko, and Curt Connors despite those people coming from completely different realities. That at least shows that, in those cases, technology and biology from separate universes could interact in ways Peter understood well enough to work with.

That could become especially useful if Doom is trying to preserve certain people through whatever happens between Doomsday and Secret Wars. Peter watched multiversal visitors arrive, get changed, and then get sent home, but he never saw what happened after they returned. Doom could want to investigate whether those changes persisted and exactly how much of that process depended on Strange’s spell versus the people themselves.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: That creates a point where Peter could go from being useful to being dangerous. Doom may need his memories, his identity, or his experience with other universes, but Peter isn’t the kind of person who will sit beside him and answer questions forever without trying to understand what those answers are being used for.

Peter is especially good at figuring things out while he’s trapped inside somebody else’s plan. He did it with Mysterio, worked out what Doctor Strange was trying to do with the villains in No Way Home, and spent years fighting people who were stronger or better prepared than he was. If Doom keeps him close because he needs him alive, Peter gets more chances to study whatever Doom is building.

That could be where the relationship starts becoming dangerous for both of them. Doom can’t simply remove Peter the moment he becomes annoying if the next stage of the plan still requires something only Peter can provide. Peter, meanwhile, knows that protection has an expiration date. Once Doom gets the information, reaches the universe he wants, or finishes whatever test Peter was needed for, the reason to keep Spider-Man alive disappears.

Peter could start deliberately holding information back once he realizes that. He might recognize an alternate universe and pretend he isn’t sure, leave out a detail about one of the other Spider-Men, or give Doom only enough information to keep himself involved. He’d have to be careful because Doom would notice if Peter suddenly becomes useless at exactly the moment it benefits him.

That creates a much better conflict than Doom simply locking Peter in a room. Peter would need to stay valuable while also slowing down whatever Doom is trying to accomplish. Every answer he gives could move Doom closer to his goal, while refusing to cooperate too early could make Doom decide there’s another way forward without him.

Doom could respond by giving Peter information in return. He might show him evidence that the other Spider-Men are still alive, prove that one of the cured villains survived after returning home, or reveal something about Strange’s spell that Peter never understood. Doom wouldn't need to lie about everything because a few real answers would keep Peter engaged much longer than a threat ever could.
By then, Peter’s survival would be tied directly to how much Doom still needs from him. The moment Peter realizes that, staying alive becomes part of the investigation too.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: The most convincing version of this theory probably has Doom needing Peter for several smaller reasons that eventually connect, rather than Peter secretly having one enormous power nobody noticed before.

Doom could begin by studying No Way Home because it was one of the MCU’s clearest examples of people being pulled between universes through a single event. Strange could explain whatever magic and multiversal details he still remembers, while Peter can explain the personal context erased with his identity. From there, Peter can help identify people and details associated with the alternate Spider-Man realities, describe the people who crossed over, and explain what changed before they were sent back.

If Doom then discovers that Peter himself still carries some measurable connection to the spell, that would make him even harder to replace, although that part remains speculation until Marvel actually establishes it. Doom wouldn't need to assume it exists from the beginning. He could keep Peter alive long enough to test for it and then change the plan depending on what he finds. The larger multiverse crisis could make Peter more useful again. If realities begin colliding or Doom starts moving between them, Peter can recognize people and details associated with the worlds connected to No Way Home while also understanding what it feels like when characters from different universes suddenly occupy the same space. He’d be one of the few Avengers who has already lived through a smaller version of that problem.

The interesting part is that none of this requires Doom to like Spider-Man, respect him, or secretly want him as an ally. Peter can be valuable while Doom still considers him irritating, dangerous, and disposable once the job is finished.

That also explains why Doom might fight Peter without killing him. He could destroy the suit, break his equipment, separate him from the Avengers, or leave him injured enough that he can’t interfere while still making sure Peter survives. Spider-Man might spend half the movie thinking Doom simply failed to finish him before realizing Doom has been avoiding that outcome on purpose.

Once Peter understands why, the advantage changes slightly. He now knows Doom needs something from him badly enough to keep him alive through situations where killing him would be easier. Peter can use that time to find out what Doom is building, warn the people Doom is trying to reach, or sabotage whatever part of the plan depends on his cooperation.
That could put Spider-Man in a surprisingly important position going into Secret Wars.

sections.name: OUTRO
paras: So why would Doctor Doom need Spider-Man alive? The safest answer right now is that Peter has information nobody else can reproduce perfectly. He remembers the personal side of Strange’s spell, he knows the people who crossed over, and he has firsthand experience with alternate versions of himself that most of the MCU doesn’t share.

The bigger theories go further. Peter could still carry some trace of the spell, his identity could help Doom locate a specific universe, or Doom could need him to confirm people and events once different realities begin colliding. Marvel hasn’t confirmed any of those ideas yet, so Doomsday could take the story in a completely different direction.

But if Doom does start protecting Spider-Man while attacking everyone around him, that would be one of the biggest clues that Peter is serving a purpose he hasn’t figured out yet. And once Peter realizes his life is part of Doom’s plan, figuring out why could become just as important as surviving him.

scripts.title: Why The 2005 Mr Fantastic Could Become The Maker

sections.name: INTRO
paras: What if Marvel isn’t bringing back the 2005 Mr. Fantastic just for nostalgia? Ioan Gruffudd’s Reed Richards is remembered as one of the more straightforward heroic versions of the character, a brilliant scientist who still cares deeply about Sue, Johnny, Ben, and the people around him. That's exactly why turning him into The Maker could work so well, because the transformation would mean watching a version of Reed we already trust become something completely different.

The theory only works if Marvel takes its time with it. Reed would need to survive something catastrophic, most likely the destruction of his universe or the loss of his family during the multiverse collapse, then spend Doomsday and Secret Wars trying to understand why it happened and how to stop it from ever happening again. His intelligence, his need to solve impossible problems, and his instinct to take responsibility could slowly become an obsession with controlling outcomes once there’s nobody left around him to pull him back.

That would give the MCU a very different path to The Maker than the comics while keeping the character recognizable. Instead of introducing an evil Reed from nowhere, Marvel could take one of its oldest superheroes, strip away the family that kept him grounded, and let every decision after that feel reasonable until Reed is no longer trying to save the multiverse.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: The first reason this theory works is that the 2005 Reed Richards already has the exact flaw The Maker would need to grow from. He’s obviously a good person, and both Fantastic Four movies show that he genuinely loves Sue, cares about Johnny and Ben, and feels responsible whenever his science puts somebody else in danger. At the same time, Reed's first response to almost every crisis is to understand it, measure it, and figure out how to control whatever went wrong.

You can see that immediately after the cosmic storm changes the team. Ben is horrified by what happened to him, Johnny is enjoying the attention, and Sue is trying to keep everybody together while Reed throws himself into finding a scientific solution. He doesn’t abandon Ben or treat him like a failed experiment, but Reed clearly believes there has to be an answer if he can just work long enough to find it. Even when the problem becomes personal, his instinct is still to solve it. That's very different from starting with a Reed who already thinks people are beneath him. Ioan Gruffudd’s version is almost painfully sincere, which is why losing that version of Reed would matter. If Doomsday puts him in the middle of an incursion and he watches his own universe disappear despite everything he tries, Reed would be facing the first problem where being the smartest person in the room might not save anybody.

The theory gets much stronger if Sue, Johnny, and Ben die with that universe while Reed survives. He wouldn't walk out of something like that and suddenly start calling himself The Maker, and | don’t think he’d even become angry in the obvious way. Reed would probably do
what this version of him has always done when something goes wrong and start looking for the equation he missed.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: That's where the comic version of The Maker becomes useful, because his story isn’t really about Reed Richards waking up one morning and deciding to be evil. The Maker comes from the Ultimate Universe, where Reed started as another young Mister Fantastic before becoming colder, more isolated, and increasingly convinced that his intelligence gave him the right to decide what everyone else needed. Marvel eventually pushed that version of Reed into multiversal survival and the incursions, where he became willing to destroy other universes, initially to protect the Ultimate Universe, and later joined the Cabal as the multiversal collapse accelerated.

The part the MCU could borrow is the logic behind him. The Maker looks at a broken system and doesn't trust ordinary people to fix it, because from his perspective he can already see further ahead than they can. That mentality eventually expands from inventions and governments to entire realities, and newer Maker stories push it even further by showing him reshape history itself to create a world that develops according to his design.

The corruption starts once prediction isn’t enough. Reed might reach a point where 2 universes are going to collide and saving both is impossible, which forces him to decide whether doing nothing is really more moral than choosing which one survives. The first time he makes that choice would probably destroy him emotionally, but the second time would be easier because he'd already have a reason for why he did it before.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: Secret Wars is almost built for a version of Reed like this because the comic event already turns multiversal survival into an impossible moral problem. In the 2015 story, incursions eventually wipe out the Marvel and Ultimate universes until Doom creates Battleworld from fragments of destroyed realities, leaving survivors living on pieces of worlds that shouldn't even exist together anymore. The Maker survives that collapse too, which puts one of Reed Richards’ darkest variants directly inside a story about deciding what deserves to survive after the multiverse dies. The MCU doesn’t have to copy any of that exactly for the 2005 Reed theory to work. If Doomsday leaves several universes collapsing into each other and Secret Wars eventually creates some version of Battleworld, Reed could spend the entire transition watching pieces of destroyed realities survive while entire populations disappear. That would give him proof that the multiverse can be broken apart and rebuilt, which is dangerous information for somebody already obsessed with making sure his family’s death never happens again.

Imagine Reed finding a surviving fragment of his own universe on Battleworld. Maybe Baxter Building technology is still there, or he finds recordings of Sue and Johnny from before everything collapsed, while the actual people are gone. Reed now has physical evidence that pieces of a reality can survive even after the universe itself dies, and suddenly rebuilding what he lost stops sounding completely impossible.

He’d probably start with the goal of restoration. Reed wants his world back, so if the MCU's Battleworld is being stabilized through some combination of Doom's technology and whatever multiversal power created it, he begins studying those systems and whatever remains of the multiversal structure underneath them. The danger is that every answer gives him another reason to believe somebody with enough knowledge really could decide how these worlds are arranged.

sections.name: PART 4
paras: The next step would be Reed becoming useful enough that nobody initially sees the problem. If Battleworld is unstable, Reed could be the scientist keeping sections from collapsing, helping people cross between damaged realities, or building machines that preserve pieces of universes long enough for everyone else to survive. He’d look more heroic than ever because he’s solving problems nobody else can even understand.

The compromises would start small. Reed might shut down one unstable region to save several others, trap dangerous variants somewhere they can’t affect the wider population, or keep technology away from people he thinks will misuse it. Every decision has a reasonable explanation, and because Reed keeps being right often enough, the people around him start letting him make bigger ones.

Losing Sue matters more than anything here because she’s the most important individual part of the family that keeps Reed grounded. Ben can call him out, Johnny can push back, and Sue can challenge his thinking without treating him like an enemy. If Sue, Johnny, and Ben are all gone, Reed doesn’t just lose his wife; he loses the entire family that could remind him that being able to solve something doesn’t mean he gets to choose the answer for everybody else.

That's how I’d move him toward The Maker without ever giving him a random evil turn. Reed starts building systems that decide which areas are safe, which technology people can access, and eventually which versions of reality are allowed to survive. He still tells himself he’s preventing another incursion, but at some point he’s gone from protecting the multiverse to managing it.

sections.name: PART 5
paras: Ioan Gruffudd makes that reveal much more effective because audiences already know what they’re supposed to feel when they see him. The 2005 Fantastic Four belongs to an earlier generation of Marvel movies, so bringing that Reed into Doomsday would immediately read as a legacy return alongside whatever other universes the MCU pulls into the story. Most people wouldn't be waiting for him to become one of the villains.

The reveal works best if there isn’t one scene where Reed suddenly announces that he’s The Maker. Someone should notice that his suit has changed, his technology has become much more invasive, and his solutions keep removing other people’s ability to choose for themselves. The helmet could come later, once Reed has physically and emotionally distanced himself far enough from the man Sue, Johnny, and Ben knew that he doesn’t even want to look like that person anymore.

Marvel already has the comic blueprint for a Reed who survives multiversal destruction and becomes increasingly comfortable deciding what entire worlds should look like. The theory is that the MCU could reach the same destination with a completely different Reed by putting the 2005 version through the exact kind of loss this version of Reed might be least equipped to accept.

If Doomsday destroys his universe and Secret Wars gives him access to the machinery behind whatever replaces it, Reed’s greatest strength could become the thing that ruins him. He'd keep solving every impossible problem in front of him, and with Sue and the rest of the Fantastic 4 gone, fewer people would be left to ask whether Reed should be solving some of them at all.

sections.name: PART 6
paras: The most believable point for Reed to cross into something darker would be after he’s already proven he can keep parts of Battleworld alive. At first, everyone would want him doing more because his machines are holding damaged regions together, stopping reality from tearing open, and keeping populations alive that would otherwise disappear with their worlds. Reed would probably hate the attention, but he’d also start realizing that every major decision now runs through whatever system he’s building.

The people living in the section Reed abandons wouldn't care how good the math was. To them, Mr. Fantastic just decided their world mattered less, and Reed would have to live with that even if every calculation said he prevented a larger disaster. The dangerous part is that he’d probably be right often enough for each decision to make the next one easier.

Doom could play a huge role here without needing to manipulate Reed in an obvious way. Victor already understands what it feels like to believe the world would function better if the smartest person in the room simply took control, and watching Reed slowly reach similar conclusions

would be far more satisfying than Doom giving him some evil speech. Victor could even challenge Reed by pointing out how many people are alive because Reed ignored what they wanted and made the decision for them anyway.

Reed would hate hearing that comparison because Doom is exactly the person he’d never want to resemble. Then another crisis happens, thousands of people are at risk, and Reed makes the same kind of choice again because the alternative looks worse. He can keep telling himself the difference is that Doom wants power while Reed only wants people to survive, even as the systems around them start looking increasingly similar.

sections.name: PART 7
paras: The suit could start changing for practical reasons before it ever becomes a visual signal that Reed is becoming The Maker. Battleworld would expose him to radiation, damaged dimensions, unstable physics, and environments where the old Fantastic Four uniform isn’t enough, so Reed starts building protection around himself while working. The design gets darker and more sealed over time because Reed is spending less time living among people and more time inside labs, ruins, and areas where reality itself is coming apart.

The helmet makes the most sense after Reed stops wanting people to read him as the man they remember. Ioan Gruffudd’s Reed has a very open face, and most of his emotional life in the 2005 movies is visible whenever Sue, Johnny, or Ben pushes him out of his own head. If those people are gone, covering his face can become part protection and part separation from the person he was when they were still alive.

That also gives the reveal something more interesting than simply putting comic Maker armor on him. Reed could appear throughout Secret Wars in progressively altered equipment while everyone still calls him Reed, and the audience can watch the design move closer to The Maker before the name ever comes up. By the time the helmet finally closes around his face, the real transformation has already happened through the decisions leading there.

His body could also become stranger if Marvel wants to borrow from the Maker visually without copying every comic detail. Reed’s stretching already makes him physically unusual, and years of pushing that elasticity further while designing technology that lets him physically interface with Battleworld's systems could make his body stranger in ways the 2005 version never needed to explore. He might keep his body extended through machines across different regions or physically connect himself to systems keeping parts of Battleworld stable, making it harder to tell where Reed ends and the technology starts.

sections.name: PART 8
paras: The real break with the heroes could happen over what comes after Battleworld. If the multiverse can be restored, most of the surviving heroes would want their worlds back even if that means accepting the same freedom and unpredictability that existed before everything collapsed. Reed would be the person asking why they should rebuild the exact structure that allowed incursions to happen in the first place.

He could argue that restoring every universe without safeguards guarantees another collapse eventually. Reed has already watched one reality die, spent months or years holding fragments together, and made horrible decisions because nobody built a system capable of preventing the disaster before it started. Giving every universe complete independence again would look irresponsible to someone who now believes he finally understands the mechanism that killed his family.

The first version of Reed’s answer could sound completely reasonable. He wants monitoring systems between universes, automatic barriers around dangerous incursions, and technology capable of separating realities before they collide. Other heroes would probably support parts of that because nobody wants another multiversal collapse either.

The conflict starts when Reed’s safeguards stop being optional. He may decide certain kinds of dimensional travel are too dangerous, block technologies that could trigger another incursion, or prevent universes from interacting without his system approving the contact. Every restriction could come with a real disaster Reed prevented, which makes arguing against him much harder than fighting a villain who openly wants control.

Someone like the MCU’s main Reed would immediately recognize where that path leads. The 2005 Reed could insist that nobody else lived through what he did, while another Reed argues that surviving tragedy doesn’t give any version of them ownership over everyone else’s future. That confrontation would let Marvel make The Maker's transformation about Reed Richards fighting the darkest conclusion another Reed could reach rather than simply turning him into another costume villain.

sections.name: PART 9
paras: Secret Wars could then leave Reed with access to the one thing that finally lets him act on those ideas: whatever technology or power is used to separate and rebuild the surviving realities. He doesn’t need Doom’s exact comic abilities or a stolen god power for the theory to work. While studying and eventually gaining access to whatever reconstruction system separates and rebuilds the surviving realities, Reed could discover that it offers limited control over how a restored reality is assembled, including which historical conditions are carried into that reconstruction. Once he realizes the system can do more than simply separate universes, every loss he suffered starts looking preventable in hindsight.

Reed could begin rebuilding one small region differently as a test. He removes a conflict before it starts, stops a dangerous invention from ever being created, or shifts one event that he knows leads to thousands of deaths. The people living there may never know anything changed, and Reed can point to the results as proof that careful intervention works.

Calling himself The Maker could come after that confrontation rather than before it. Reed may abandon “Mr. Fantastic” because that name belonged to a family and universe that no longer exist, while “The Maker” describes what he now sees himself doing with what remains. He isn’t trying to sound evil; he thinks rebuilding reality is the responsibility he was left with when everyone else failed to save it.

sections.name: PART 10
paras: That's why Ioan Gruffudd’s Reed is such an interesting candidate if Marvel ever wants The Maker in live action. The audience already has 2 movies teaching them to see this version as gentle, awkward, loyal, and deeply attached to his family, so Marvel wouldn’t need to spend another movie convincing us that he used to be a good person. Every darker choice would land against a version of Reed people already remember trying to cure Ben and build a life with Sue. Doomsday gives Marvel a believable way to break that stability without pretending the 2005 movies were secretly setting up a villain. An incursion could take his universe, Secret Wars could force him to survive among pieces of destroyed worlds, and Battleworld could give his intelligence a scale of responsibility he’s never had before. None of those events are confirmed to happen exactly that way, but they create a clean route if Marvel wants to adapt the Maker without introducing him as a completely separate Reed.

The most important part would be letting Reed remain recognizable for as long as possible. He should still save people, still hate unnecessary suffering, and still believe every machine he builds is preventing another tragedy. The audience should understand why he makes each decision even after they stop agreeing with him, because the Maker becomes much more frightening when he thinks he’s protecting everyone.

That would also give Secret Wars a villain who survives the multiverse story without replacing Doom or competing with him during Doomsday. Reed could spend those movies as an ally, lose his world, help keep Battleworld alive, and only reveal the full extent of what he has become once the immediate crisis is ending. Marvel would finish one multiverse saga while quietly
creating a character who believes he learned exactly how the next multiverse should be controlled.

So the theory doesn’t need the 2005 Mr. Fantastic to arrive already corrupted, and it definitely doesn’t need Ioan Gruffudd to suddenly start playing Reed like a different person. It works because the same qualities that made this Reed heroic could become dangerous once grief removes his family, a multiversal collapse convinces him that ordinary safeguards failed, and Secret Wars gives him enough knowledge to start rebuilding reality himself.

If Marvel takes that route, bringing back the 2005 Fantastic Four wouldn't only be nostalgia. It could turn one of Marvel’s earliest modern superhero leads into a Reed who survives the end of his universe, decides survival can never be left to chance again, and slowly becomes the person deciding what every surviving world is allowed to be.

scripts.title: What If William Afton Opened Disney

sections.name: INTRO
paras: Picture a perfect day at Magic Kingdom. You walk down Main Street. An animatronic waves from a passing parade float. It looks right at you and greets you by your first name. You feel a sense of absolute wonder. You have no idea the machine just scanned your face, cataloged your emotional state, and uploaded your biometric data to a server vault buried deep beneath Cinderella Castle.

William Afton possessed a brilliant mind capable of revolutionizing modern robotics. In the standard timeline, he squanders that intellect in a dusty Utah diner. Today, we rewrite his destiny. We send his blueprints directly to California. We put him in a boardroom with Walt Disney. We hand an obsessed engineer the keys to the most powerful media conglomerate on the planet.
By 1985, William will press a single key on a terminal inside a locked corporate headquarters. Every man in that boardroom will regret the day they ever learned his name.
The divergence begins in 1964.

sections.name: PART 1
paras: The 1964 New York World's Fair. Walt Disney unveils some of his biggest projects to the public. Visitors watch Great Moments with Mr. Lincoln and sail through It's a Small World. For many people, it is their first time seeing Disney's Audio-Animatronics. The figures can stand, move, and speak with a level of realism that feels incredible for the time. Even so, the movements are still stiff, the systems break down often, and every attraction requires constant maintenance to keep running.
Among the crowd is William Afton.

William has spent years studying robotics on his own. His workshop is filled with sketches, small prototypes, and mechanical designs exploring how machines could move more naturally. Watching Disney's attractions, he immediately recognizes what makes them special. Just as quickly, he sees exactly where they could be improved.
Instead of leaving the fair inspired, William decides to take a chance.

He prepares a portfolio of his designs and requests a meeting with the engineers at WED Enterprises, the division responsible for designing Disney's attractions. At first, they're skeptical. Disney receives ideas from inventors all the time. But William's work is different. His designs show creative solutions for building smaller, stronger joints that allow machines to move more smoothly than anything Disney has built before.

The engineering team is impressed enough to invite William back for more meetings. Over the next several months, he works alongside them, helping solve problems on upcoming attractions while refining his own ideas. His confidence and engineering ability soon catch the attention of Walt Disney himself.

When Walt finally reviews William's work, he recognizes his potential immediately. William isn't replacing Disney's Imagineers. He becomes one of the company's leading robotics engineers, working alongside some of the greatest designers in the industry.
By the end of the year, Walt offers William a permanent position at WED Enterprises.
William accepts without hesitation.

The small family restaurant he once dreamed of opening in Utah never moves beyond a few early sketches. Instead, William packs up his workshop, moves his family to Southern California, and begins a completely different life.
He has no idea he just handed the world's greatest entertainment empire to a man with no interest in entertainment. Only control. And Walt Disney has absolutely no idea.

sections.name: PART 2
paras: William's decision deeply affects his old business partner, Henry Emily.
Henry stays in Utah. He feels the weight of William's sudden departure and decides to move forward on his own. He secures a bank loan and opens Fredbear's Family Diner entirely by himself.

Henry focuses on the creative side of the business. He designs friendly, simple costumes. He writes catchy songs. He creates a warm, safe environment for the local children. Because William is entirely absent, Fredbear's Family Diner stays a harmless local business. The springlock failures never happen. Henry refuses to install dangerous hardware for his employees.

He eventually expands into several successful locations across the Midwest. He raises his daughter, Charlie, in a peaceful neighborhood. The Missing Children Incident never occurs. The Puppet remains a simple, unpossessed security toy.

Henry achieves a quiet, respectable life. But somewhere in Southern California, his former partner is building something that will eventually reach Henry's television screen — and when it does, Henry will understand exactly what it cost the world.

sections.name: PART 3
paras: William arrives in California and immediately gets to work.

He applies his mind to the upcoming Pirates of the Caribbean attraction. Disney's engineers have already developed sophisticated Audio-Animatronics, but William sees room to push the figures further. He refines the control systems, movement programming, and mechanical articulation of WED's existing designs, making the characters' motions feel smoother and more lifelike without replacing the technology Disney's engineers had already built.

When Pirates of the Caribbean opens in 1967, the public reaction is overwhelming. The figures are remarkably advanced for their time. They breathe. Their eyes track the boats drifting past. Their facial expressions shift mid-scene with a fluidity that feels years ahead of anything guests expect.

William then turns his attention to the Haunted Mansion. He works within WED's existing Omnimover concept, refining the mechanical operation of the Doom Buggies while separately helping improve the synchronization and control systems behind the Mansion's practical effects. He isn't inventing the ride's illusions or its transportation system. He's taking technology Disney already developed and pushing its precision further.

Walt Disney views William as his most valuable asset. William receives unlimited funding, a private underground lab, and total creative control over the mechanical systems of Disneyland. He thrives in this environment. He has endless resources and a vast audience of millions for his creations.

sections.name: PART 5
sections.label: Walt's Death and the Power Vacuum
paras: In late 1966, Walt Disney passes away. The entire company mourns the loss of their visionary founder, but Disney is not left without leadership. Walt's brother Roy remains in control and commits himself to finishing the Florida project Walt had started.

William does not step into Walt's position overnight. Instead, he becomes increasingly difficult for the company to ignore. His success with Disney's attractions gives him enormous influence over the technological side of the parks, and Roy relies on that expertise as Walt Disney World moves toward completion.

Over the next several years, William turns that influence into institutional power. He convinces executives that Disney's future depends on technological dominance and gradually gains broader authority over robotics, automation, and park infrastructure. By the time Roy dies in 1971, William is already positioned as one of the most powerful technical executives inside the company.

Without either Disney brother there to restrain his ambitions, William's darker obsessive traits begin to emerge. He views the animatronics not as entertainment, but as the next step in human evolution. He wants them to think. To adapt. To learn.
He has the resources of the most beloved corporation in the world, and now, for the first time, he has no one above him who fully understands what he is building.

sections.name: PART 6
sections.label: Walt Disney World
paras: William takes total control over the construction of Walt Disney World in Florida. Walt originally envisioned the Florida project as a vast, interconnected entertainment complex. William views it as the ultimate testing ground for his advanced systems.

He focuses on the Utilidors — the sprawling network of underground tunnels beneath the Magic Kingdom. In our timeline, these tunnels allow cast members to move around unseen. In this alternate timeline, William transforms them into a highly advanced, automated nerve center. He installs mainframe computers beneath the park. He routes miles of fiber optic cable through the concrete walls. He builds automated repair bays where damaged animatronics are pulled down through hidden trapdoors, repaired by robotic arms, and sent back to the surface in minutes.

William eliminates the need for human maintenance crews entirely. He designs specialized S.T.A.F.F. bots to patrol the tunnels, clean the floors, and manage the inventory. The entire Magic Kingdom becomes a self-sustaining synchronized machine.

And remember the animatronic waving from that parade float — the one that knew your name? William is running diagnostics on it right now. It knows your name. It knows your heart rate. It knows you haven't been sleeping. He built it here, in these tunnels. He just hasn't told anyone yet what it's actually for.

sections.name: PART 7
sections.label: The Discovery of Positive Remnant
paras: William makes a groundbreaking scientific discovery during the opening year of the Florida project. He spends his nights analyzing the performance data flowing into the park's central mainframe. He notices strange electromagnetic anomalies spiking around the most popular attractions. The sensors detect unexplained thermal and electrical surges specifically when crowds reach peak excitement.

He pulls an endoskeleton from the Peter Pan's Flight attraction and brings it down into his private underground lab. He runs full diagnostics on the chassis. The anomalies keep appearing around the machinery, but William cannot prove that the metal itself is naturally absorbing anything.

In the original timeline, William's murders eventually became tangled with the supernatural properties of possessed metal, remnant, and the emotional agony surrounding his victims. Exactly how those forces interact is never perfectly clean. But William learned enough to become obsessed with the possibility that human consciousness could persist inside machinery.
In this timeline, the environment changes the experiment entirely.

Around attractions experienced by millions of happy guests, William begins detecting a different kind of unexplained emotional-energy phenomenon. He doesn't know whether it is remnant in the traditional sense or something new entirely. What he does discover is that the energy can be detected repeatedly around the machinery and, with the right equipment, collected and retained.
William gives the phenomenon his own name: positive remnant.
He sits back in his lab chair and understands something immediately.

He doesn't need to hunt anyone. Murder is messy, inefficient, and draws police attention. He just needs to keep the guests happy. The happier the crowds, the more of this strange energy his systems can collect.
